<header>BOOK XV. The Discovery of Solomon's Conjurations.</header>

...that their arts (especially those which consist of charms, impossibilities, conjurations, and witchcrafts, which they used to boast about) are mere foolishness, foolish lies, and dreams. For my part, I could do as much myself, but I do not delight in citing my own proofs and authorities, because my adversaries will say they are partial and not impartial.

### CHAP. XLII.

->Of Solomon's Conjurations, and of the opinion conceived of his skill and practice in them.<-

<margin>It was proven <note>original: "Probatum est"</note> upon a patient before witnesses; therefore, it is no lie.</margin>It is affirmed by various authors that Solomon was the first inventor of those conjurations. Josephus is the first to report this, who in the first book of his *Antiquities of the Jews* <note>original: "De Judæorum antiquitatibus"</note>, chapter 22, soberly recounts the following story. Polydore Virgil and many others repeat this word for word <note>original: "verbatim"</note> in this manner, and seem to believe the fable, of which there is scarcely a true word.

Solomon was the greatest philosopher and philosophized about all things, having full and perfect knowledge of all their properties. But he had a gift given to him from above for the benefit and health of mankind, which is effective against devils. He also made enchantments by which diseases are driven away, and left behind various types of conjurations in writing; when devils yield to these, they are so thoroughly driven away that they never return. 

"This kind of healing is very common among my countrymen," Josephus says, "for I saw a neighbor of mine, one Eleazer, who in the presence of Vespasian, his sons, and the rest of the soldiers, cured many who were possessed by spirits." 

The manner and order of his cure was this: he placed a ring to the nose of the possessed person; under the seal of this ring was enclosed a kind of root whose power Solomon had declared. The scent of it drew the devil out through the man's nose, so that the man fell down. Then Eleazer conjured the devil to depart and never return to him. In the meantime, he mentioned Solomon, reciting incantations of Solomon’s own making. Then Eleazer, being willing to show the bystanders his skill and the wonderful efficacy of his art, set a pot or basin full of water nearby. He commanded the devil that went out of the man to overturn it, thereby giving a sign to the beholders that he had utterly forsaken and left the man. When this was done, no one there doubted how great Solomon’s knowledge and wisdom was. In this, a juggling trick was produced to confirm a deceptive instance of trickery or fraud <note>original: "cogging cast of knavery or cosenage"</note>.

<margin>Book 4, distinction 14. Decree... distinction 21. Section on exorcists <note>original: "Lib. 4. dist. 14. Decret. au. eum. dist. 21. Rub. de exorcist."</note></margin>
<margin>Lessons 5 and 6.</margin>I find another story of Solomon's conjuration cited in the sixth lesson read in the Church of Rome on Saint Margaret's Day, which is far more ridiculous than this one. Also Peter Lombard (the Master of the Sentences), his brother Gratian (the compiler of the *Golden Decrees*), and Durandus in his *Rationale of Divine Offices* <note>original: "Rationale Divinorum"</note> all soberly affirm Solomon's skill in this matter. They specifically affirm this tale: namely, that Solomon enclosed several thousand devils in a brass bowl and left it in a deep hole or lake. Later, the Babylonians found it and, supposing there was gold or silver inside, broke it open; then all the devils flew out, etc. 

You can see that this fable is considered credible because it is thought worthy to be read in the Romish Church as part of their Divine Service. Look in the lessons for the day of Saint Margaret the Virgin, and you shall find these words exactly <note>original: "Verbatim"</note>. I recite this primarily because it serves my purpose in several ways: regarding Solomon's conjurations, the tale of the brass vessel, and the Pope’s own conjurations—which extended to both faith and doctrine—and to show what kind of credit their religion deserves, being so shamefully stained with lies and fables.

<summary>The author dismisses the historical and religious claims that King Solomon invented magical conjurations, labeling stories from Josephus and the Catholic Church as fraudulent fables.</summary>
<keywords>Solomon, conjuration, Josephus, Eleazer, Vespasian, exorcism, Peter Lombard, Gratian, Saint Margaret, brass vessel, Catholic Church, skepticism</keywords>

### CHAPTER 43.
*Lessons read in all Churches where the Pope has authority on Saint Margaret’s day, translated into English, word for word.*

<margin>Lesson on the day of the most holy Margaret, verse 5. <note>original: "Lect. in die sanctissime Marg. ver. 5."</note></margin>
<margin>Lesson 6. <note>original: "Lect. 6."</note></margin>
<margin>Look in the word *Idoni*, page 232.</margin>
<margin>For the priest’s profit, I warrant you.</margin>
<margin>This is common (they say) when a witch or conjurer dies.</margin>

H<gloss>oly</gloss> Margaret requested of God that she might have a conflict face to face with her secret enemy, the Devil. Rising from prayer, she saw a terrible dragon that intended to devour her; but she made the sign of the Cross, and the dragon burst apart in the middle.

Afterwards, she saw another man sitting like a black man <note>original: "Niger." In early modern demonology, devils were frequently depicted as dark-skinned figures or "Moors."</note>, having his hands bound fast to his knees. She took him by the hair of his head, threw him to the ground, and set her foot on his head. After her prayers were made, a light shined from heaven into the prison where she was, and the Cross of Christ was seen in Heaven with a dove sitting on it, who said, *"Blessed are you, O Margaret; the gates of Paradise await your coming."* 

Then she, giving thanks to God, said to the Devil, *"Declare to me your name."* The Devil said, *"Take away your foot from my head, so that I may be able to speak and tell you."* When this was done, the Devil said, *"I am Veltis, one of those whom Solomon shut up in a brass vessel. The Babylonians, thinking that gold had been hidden there, broke the vessel, and then we flew out, ever since lying in wait to annoy the just."* 

But since I have recited a part of her story, you shall also have the end of it; for at the time of her execution, this was her following prayer:

> Grant therefore, O Father, that whoever writes, reads, or hears the story of my passion, or makes a memorial of me, may deserve pardon for all his sins. Whoever calls on me when they are at the point of death, deliver him out of the hands of his adversaries. And I also require, O Lord, that whoever shall build a Church in my honor, [grant] what he asks for his health. Deliver all women in labor who call upon me from the danger thereof.

When her prayer ended, there were many great claps of thunder, and a dove came down from heaven, saying, *"Blessed are you, O Margaret, the spouse of Christ. Such things as you have asked are granted to you; therefore, come into everlasting rest,"* etc. Then the hangman (though she commanded him) refused to cut off her head. She said to him, *"Unless you do it, you can have no part with me"*; and then, behold, he did it, etc. But since I have been—and must continue to be—tedious, I thought it good to refresh my reader with a sorrowful story related to the preceding matter, reported by many grave authors, word for word, in the following manner and form.

### CHAPTER 44.
*A delightful story of a Lombard who, by Saint Margaret's example, insisted on fighting with a real Devil.*

<margin>Misguided zeal. <note>original: "Kacozelia," from the Greek "kakozelia," meaning a poorly handled or perverse imitation.</note></margin>

T<gloss>here</gloss> was (after a sermon was made in which this story of Saint Margaret was recited—for in such stuff consisted not only their church service, but also their sermons in the blind time of Popery) a certain young man, a Lombard. His simplicity was such that he had no respect for the convenience of worldly things, but was entirely concerned with the salvation of his soul. Hearing how great Saint Margaret's triumph was, he began to consider with himself how full of tricks the Devil was. Among other things, he said: *"O, that God would allow the Devil to fight hand to hand in visible form! I would then surely overthrow him in the same way, and would fight with him until I had the victory."* And therefore, about the twelfth hour he...

### THE
# Discovery of Witchcraft:

->PROVING,<-
->That the Compacts and Contracts of WITCHES<-
->with *Devils* and all *Infernal Spirits* or *Familiars*, are but<-
->Erroneous Novelties and Imaginary Conceptions.<-

->*Also revealing*, how far their power extends in killing, tormenting,<-
->consuming <note>original: "consuming"; here meaning wasting away or causing to decline</note>, or curing the bodies of men, women, children, or animals,<-
->by charms, potions <term>original: "philtres"; magic potions, especially love potions</term>, amulets <term>original: "periapts"; charms worn on the body for protection or healing</term>, talismans <term>original: "pentacles"; magical diagrams or stars</term>, curses, and conjurations.<-

->*WHEREIN ALSO*<-
->The unchristian practices and inhumane dealings of<-
->searchers and *witch-finders* <note>original: "witch-tryers"</note> upon *aged, melancholy*, and *superstitious*<-
->people—in extorting confessions by terror and torture,<-
->and in inventing false marks and symptoms—are notably exposed <note>original: "detected"</note>.<-

# THE
# Discovery of Witchcraft:

## PROVING,

->That the compacts and contracts of **WITCHES**<-
->with *devils* and all *infernal spirits* or *familiars* are but<-
->**erroneous novelties** and **imaginary conceptions.**<-
->**Also revealing** how far their **power** extends in *killing, tormenting,*<-
->*wasting away* <note>original: "consuming"</note>, or *curing* the bodies of *men, women, children,* or *animals,*<-
->by **charms, potions** <term>original: "philtres"; magic potions, often intended to incite love</term>, **amulets** <term>original: "periapts"; charms worn on the person to ward off evil or disease</term>, **talismans** <term>original: "pentacles"; symbols or diagrams used in magic</term>, **curses**, and **conjurations.**<-

## WHEREIN ALSO

->The **dishonest swindles** <term>original: "knavish cozenages"</term> of **conjurers** and **enchanting deceivers**, along with<-
->the **impious blasphemy** of **delusional**, doting **wizards**, are<-
->exposed and **revealed.**<-
->**As also**, the **unchristian practices** and **inhumane dealings** of<-
->**searchers** and **witch-finders** <note>original: "witch-tryers"</note> upon *aged, melancholic,* and *superstitious*<-
->people—in **extorting confessions** by **terror** and **torture**,<-
->and in inventing **false marks** and **symptoms**—are notably **exposed.**<-

->*interpreters of dreams, alchemists,* and *potion-makers*; with many other things<-

Because *I know* that your Lordship is by nature wholly inclined, and in purpose earnestly intent, to relieve the *poor*; and that not only with *hospitality* and *charity* <note>original: "alms"</note>, but by various other methods and ways tending to their comfort: having (as it were) dedicated and committed yourself to the help and maintenance of their *condition* <term>original: "estate"; the social or financial status of a person</term>, as is shown by your expense and labor <term>original: "travel"; derived from "travail," meaning hard work or effort</term> on their behalf. Since you also have a special care for supporting their rights and redressing their wrongs, neither despising their *misery* <note>original: "calamity"</note> nor yet forgetting their *complaints*; seeking all means for their *improvement*, and for the reformation of their disorders, even as a true *father* to the *poor*. Finally, because *I* am a humble member of that *commonwealth* where your Lordship is a leading figure, *I* thought this work <note>original: "travel"</note> of mine, on behalf of the poor, the *elderly*, and the *simple-minded* <note>original: "simple"; meaning the uneducated or easily deceived</note>, might be very appropriately dedicated to you; for a weak house requires a strong support. In this respect, *I* thank God for raising up such a mighty *friend* for them as your Lordship, who possesses such knowledge in our *laws*, such discretion in *government*, such experience in these cases, and such authority in the *commonwealth*; and yet you still deign to stoop to the consideration of these lowly and inferior matters, which bring more care and trouble than worldly prestige <note>original: "estimation"</note>.

And since your Lordship knows, or rather practices, the office of a *judge*, whose duty it is to hear with courtesy and to decide with equity; it must be obvious to you that when punishment exceeds the crime <note>original: "fault"</note>, it is to be considered vengeance rather than correction. For in truth, that commonwealth remains in a woeful state where chains and nooses* <note>original: "fetters and haltars"</note> *hold more power than mercy and due compassion.*

However, it is natural for unnatural people, and characteristic of witch-hunters <term>original: "Witchmongers"; Scot's derogatory term for those who promote the belief in and prosecution of witches</term>, to pursue the poor, to accuse the simple, and to kill the innocent. They substitute rigor and malice toward others for what they themselves lack in evidence and discretion, or for what the accused lacks in actual offense or opportunity. But just as a cruel heart and an honest mind seldom meet and eat together from the same dish, so a wise and merciful magistrate and a happy commonwealth cannot be separated. How much then are we indebted to God, who has given us a Queen who is not only the perfect image and pattern of justice, but also (under God) the very fountain and embodiment of mercy and clemency? Because of this, those who hunt most for blood in these days have the least authority to shed it. # The Epistle Dedicatory.

<sig>( a 2 )</sig>

men’s lives and actions were handed over into his hands, and as if he sat at the helm to guide and direct the course of the whole world; they attribute to him enough power and ability to do as great things and as strange miracles as Christ ever did.

But the "experts" <note>original: "Doctors"</note> of this supernatural doctrine say sometimes that the witch does all these things by the power of her charms; sometimes that a spirit devil, or sometimes a physical <note>original: "Corporal"</note> devil, accomplishes it. Sometimes they say that the Devil merely makes the witch believe she has done what he himself has actually worked. Sometimes they say the Devil seems to act by compulsion <note>i.e., being forced by a spell</note>, when in fact he acts most willingly. Finally, the writers on this subject are so eloquent and full of variety that they sometimes write that the Devil does all this by God’s permission only, sometimes by His license, and sometimes by His direct appointment. The result is that (in effect and truth) not the Devil, but the high and mighty King of Kings and Lord of Hosts—God himself—is made obedient and servile, forced to obey and perform the will and commandment of a malicious old witch. God is made to miraculously satisfy her appetite for every trifling vanity as well as for the most horrible executions—acting as the revenger of a doting old woman’s imagined wrongs to the destruction of many innocent children, and as a supporter of her passions to the undoing of many a poor soul. I do not see why a witch might not enchant whenever she wants, just as a liar may lie when he pleases; if so, we would possess nothing except by a witch's license and permission.

And now, indeed, matters have been brought to this point: that all devils, who used to be spiritual, may at their pleasure become physical <note>original: "corporal"</note> and show themselves familiarly to witches and conjurors <term>original: "Conjurors"; those who supposedly summon spirits or demons through rituals</term>, and to no others. They claim that by these people alone, devils may be made tame and kept in a box, and so on. Thus, a malicious old woman may command her devil to plague her neighbor, and the neighbor is afflicted in the exact manner she desires. But then another witch comes along, and she orders her devil to help, and he heals the same person. In this way, they make it a kingdom divided against itself; and therefore I trust it will not endure for long but will shortly be overthrown, according to the words of our Savior: *Every kingdom divided against itself shall be made desolate* <note>original: "Omne regnum in se divisum desolabitur"</note>.

And although some say that the Devil is the witch’s instrument...

# The Epistle Dedicatory.

to bring her purposes and practices to pass; yet others say that she is his instrument to execute his pleasure in anything, and therefore she should be executed. But then (it seems to me) she would be unfairly dealt with and put to death for another's offense; for actions are not judged by their instrumental causes, nor does the end and purpose of what is done depend upon the humble <note>original: "mean"</note> instrument. Finally, if the witch does not do it, why should the witch die for it? But they say that witches are persuaded and think that they actually perform those mischiefs, and have a will to perform what the Devil commits, and that therefore they are worthy to die. By that logic, everyone should be executed who wishes evil to his neighbor, and so forth.

<margin>Proverbs 15.</margin>
But if the human will were punished by man according to its offense against God, we would be driven by the thousands at once to the slaughterhouse or butchery. For "whoever loathes correction shall die." And who could escape execution if this loathing (I say) were punishable by death under civil laws? Also, "the wages <note>original: "reward"</note> of sin is death"; however, not everyone who sins is to be put to death by the magistrate. But, my Lord, it shall be proved in my book, and your Lordship shall find <note>original: "try"</note> it to be true—both here at home in your native country and abroad in your various legal circuits—that (besides those who are *veneficae* <note>Latin: poisoners or sorceresses</note>, who are simply poisoners), there will be found among our witches only two sorts: the first sort are those who are witches by imputation—that is, thought of as such by others (and these are the victims <note>original: "abused"</note>, not the victimizers)—and the other sort by acceptance—being willing to be considered such—and these are mere con artists <note>original: "coseners"</note>.

</margin>
*Erastus* himself—being a principal writer in support of the omnipotence of witches—is forced to confess that these Greek words *mageia* (magic), *manganeia* (sorcery/trickery), and *pharmakeia* (poisoning/spells) <note>original: "μαγεία, μαγγανεία, φαρμακεία"</note> are most commonly used to mean illusion, deceptive packing, conning, fraud, knavery, and deceit. He is further driven to say, "*That in ancient times, the learned were not so foolish as not to see that the promises of magicians and enchanters were false, and nothing else but knavery, conning, and old wives' fables*"; and yet he still defends their flying in the air, their transferring of corn or grass from one field to another, etc.

But as *Erastus* disagrees here with himself and his friends, so there is no agreement among any of those writers, except...

<summary>Scot argues that if witches are merely tools of the Devil, they shouldn't be executed for his deeds; he classifies alleged witches as either poisoners, victims of false accusations, or con artists. He cites Calvin and Erastus to support the idea that magic is largely a matter of trickery and fraud rather than supernatural power.</summary>

# The Epistle Dedicatory.

<margin>
Isa. 59:7.

Ecclus. 27:5.
Prov. 1:16.
Jer. 2:34.
Psalm 39:15.

...in cruelties, absurdities, and impossibilities. These authors, my Lord, who fall into such obvious contradictions and such absurd assertions, are not low-ranking *writers*. Nor are they all *Catholics* <note>original: "Papists"</note>, but are men of such high reputation that their names give more credibility to their cause than their own writings do. For their sake I am sorry, and out of respect for them I have partially suppressed their most foolish <note>original: "fondest"</note> errors and foulest absurdities. I deal specifically with those who most insist on cruelty—those "whose feet are swift to shed blood"—striving (as *Jesus, the son of Sirach*, says) and rushing (as *Solomon, the son of David*, says) to spill the blood of the innocent. Their anger against these poor wretches cannot be satisfied with any liquid other than blood. Therefore, I fear that on that day when the Lord shall say, "*Depart from me, you blood-thirsty men,*" the blood of the souls of the poor will be found on their hands <note>original: "under their wings"</note>.

<margin>
In the Letter to Johann Wier. <note>Johann Wier (1515–1588) was a Dutch physician and early critic of the witch trials.</note>
</margin>
Because I know your Lordship will not conspire against innocent blood, but will instead restrain those who seek to stain <note>original: "imbrew"</note> their hands with it, I have chosen to present their case to you and lay their miserable suffering before your feet. In this, I follow the advice of the learned man *Johannes Brentius*, who said: "If anyone warns the magistrate not to be too harsh toward those miserable women who are called witches, I believe he is a good instrument raised up for this purpose by God himself" <note>original Latin: "Si quis admonuerit Magistratum, ne in miseras illas mulierculas sæviat, eum ego arbitror divinitus excitatum"</note>.

But perhaps those who promote the belief in witches <note>original: "Witchmongers"</note>—that is, those who attribute to *witches* the power that belongs only to God—will say: "*I have chosen your Lordship to be the patron of this book because I think you favor my opinions, and that I might therefore more freely publish my own errors or whims, relying on your Lordship's authority rather than the Word of God or solid reasoning.*" But I swear the opposite is true. By this document, I renounce all protection and reject all friendship that might serve to help suppress or replace the *truth*. I also know that your Lordship is far from allowing any harm to come to people, and is even more an enemy to those who attempt to dishonor God or steal <note>original: "embeazel"</note> the credit due to His immortal glory. Rather, I chose you because I know you are clear-sighted <note>original: "perspicuous"</note> and able to see into the very depths and bottom of these matters, and are not to be carried

<meta>catchword: away</meta>

<summary>Scot argues that many prominent authors are dangerously obsessed with shedding the blood of supposed witches, contradicting both reason and scripture. He explains that he has dedicated the book to Sir Roger Manwood not for political cover, but because of Manwood's perceived legal insight and sense of justice.</summary>

<meta>This page concludes Reginald Scot's dedication to Sir Roger Manwood. Scot appeals to the judge's sense of reason and legal duty to protect the vulnerable from superstitious persecution, arguing that the "epidemic" of witchcraft is fueled primarily by the zeal of those who hunt them.</meta>

# The Epistle Dedicatory.

...throwing away the vain persuasion or superstition of men, custom, time, or the masses, and being moved only by the authority of Truth: I ask for your support in this matter, but only so far as the law of God, the law of Nature, the law of this Land, and the rule of Reason shall require. Nor do I plead for these poor people in any other way than this: that with one hand you may support the good, and with the other suppress the evil. In doing so, you shall be regarded as *a Father to Orphans, an Advocate to Widows, a Guide to the Blind, a Support to the Lame, a Comfort and Encouragement to the honest, and a Scourge and Terror to the Wicked.*

Up to this point, I have been bold enough to test your Lordship’s patience. I am disappointed in myself that I could not express more briefly the matters I have explained at such length. I confess this might cause boredom <note>original: "tediousness"</note>, were it not for your great seriousness and your remarkable persistence in reading and judging, which prevent that from happening. And I wish with all my heart that I could help people understand the core of my writing and not misinterpret <note>original: "misconster"</note> any part of my meaning. Then I would surely be convinced that once the company of Witchmongers <note>Scot's term for those who zealously promote the belief in and prosecution of witches</note> has decreased, the number of "Witches" would also soon be diminished. But the words of the Poet are true:

> *You can by no means do all things bravely alone;* <note>original Latin: *Haudquaquam poteris fortiter omnia solus*</note>
> *For the gods have granted some to excel in war,*
> *To this one the art of dancing, and to that one singing with the voice and lute;*
> *While in the heart of another, great wise*
> *Jupiter has implanted intelligence, etc.* <note>This is a Latin translation of Homer’s *Iliad*, Book 13, lines 729–733.</note>

Therefore, as I am doubtful of succeeding through persuasion—even though I have reason and common sense on my side—I rely instead on earnest wishing. Specifically, I wish for *all people to have an absolute trust in God the Creator, and not in created beings, which is like making human strength <note>original: "flesh"</note> our support.* I wish this so that God may receive his due honor (which many people’s lack of duty has turned into dishonor) and so that there will be less cause for offense and error caused by widely accepted bad examples. And to your Lordship, I wish both an increase of honor and the continuation of good health and happy days.

->Your Lordship's to be commanded,<-

*Reginald Scot.*

<summary>Scot concludes his dedication by urging a rejection of superstition in favor of divine and natural law, arguing that the number of accused witches would drop if the "witchmongers" stopped their agitation. He appeals to Sir Roger Manwood to act as a protector of the marginalized and prays for a return to total trust in God rather than fear of supernatural creatures.</summary>

# To the Right Worshipful,
## Sir **THOMAS SCOT** Knight, etc.

->SIR,<-

I see among other criminals <note>original: "Malefactors"</note>, many poor old women summoned before you for the working of miracles, otherwise called witchcraft; and therefore I thought you also a suitable person to whom I might recommend my book. And here I have occasion to speak of your sincere administration of justice, and of your skill, discretion, and the expense and labor <note>original: "travel," here meaning travail or hard work</note> employed on that behalf, of which I am an eyewitness <note>original Latin: *oculatus testis*</note>. However, I would rather refer the reader to public reputation, and their own eyes and ears, to be satisfied, than to send them to a bookseller’s shop, where many times lies are for sale <note>original: "vendible"</note> and truth is despised. For since I am of your household, of your name, and of your blood—my foot being under your table, my hand in your dish, or rather in your purse—I might be thought to flatter you in that which (I know) would rather offend you than please you. And why should I try to seek favor with my most reliable friend? And if I should only publish those virtues (though they are many) which give me special reason to present this my labor to you, I would be like a painter who describes only the foot of a notable person and leaves all the best features of his body untouched.

I therefore (at this time) only desire you to consider my report concerning the evidence that is commonly brought before you against them. See first whether the evidence is not frivolous, and whether the proofs brought against them are not incredible, consisting of guesses, presumptions, and impossibilities contrary to reason, scripture, and nature. See also what kind of people complain about them—whether they are not of the lowliest, the most foolish, and the most faithless kind of people. Also, may it please you to weigh what accusations and crimes they lay to their charge: namely, "She was at my house recently; she wanted a pot of milk, and she left in a rage because she didn’t get it; she ranted, she cursed, she mumbled and whispered; and finally, she said, 'I’ll get even with you.' And soon after, my child, my cow, my sow, or my chicken died, or was strangely afflicted. No (if it please your Worship), I have further proof; I went to a 'wise woman' <note>term: a folk healer or fortune teller often consulted to identify "witches"</note>, and she told me I had an evil neighbor, and that she would come to my house before long—and so she did. And she told me the woman had a mark on her waist—and so she had. And God forgive me, I have had a bad feeling about her <note>original: "my stomach hath gone against her"</note> for a long time. Her mother before her was considered a witch; she has been beaten and scratched on the face until blood was drawn <note>A common folk belief held that "scratching" a witch so that she bled would break her spell over the victim</note> because she was suspected, and afterwards some of those people were said to recover." These are the "certainties" that I hear in their evidence.

Note also how easily they may be brought to confess that which they never did, nor lies in the power of man to do; and then see whether I have cause to write as I do. Further, if you shall see that a lack of faith, Catholicism <note>original: "Popery"</note>, and many other manifest heresies are supported and encouraged—and those who believe them emboldened—by granting to created beings such infinite power as is snatched out of God’s hand and attributed to witches. Finally, if you shall perceive that I have faithfully and truly described the condition and state of the witch, and also of the witchmonger <note>term: Scot’s word for those who zealously hunt witches or promote the fear of them</note>, and have disproved them by reason, by law, and by the Word of God itself...

<summary>Reginald Scot addresses his relative, Sir Thomas Scot, criticizing the weak and superstitious nature of evidence used in witchcraft trials. He argues that such accusations are usually based on petty social grudges and "impossible" claims that contradict reason and religion.</summary>

...[that you would weigh] all my adversaries' objections and arguments; then let me have your support against those who maliciously oppose me.

<margin>John 5. Proverbs 15:1.</margin>
My greatest adversaries are *young ignorance* and *old custom*. For whatever folly the passage of time has fostered is so superstitiously followed by some, as if no error could ever be associated with long-standing custom. But if the law of nations were to join with such custom to maintain *ignorance* and suppress *knowledge*, the most civilized country in the world would soon become barbaric. For just as knowledge and time reveal errors, so do superstition and *ignorance* breed them over time. Regarding the opinions of those who wish that *ignorance* should be maintained rather than *knowledge* diligently searched for (because knowledge might cause offense), I answer that we are commanded by Christ himself to search for *knowledge*: for, *it is the king's honor (as Solomon says) to search out a matter.*

<margin>Acts 3. Proverbs 9.</margin>
*Aristotle* said to *Alexander* that a well-educated mind was more beautiful than a body dressed in rich clothing. What can be more hateful to man, or offensive to God, than *ignorance*? For through ignorance, the *Jews* put Christ to death. Whoever abandons this ignorance is promised life everlasting; therefore, among *Christians*, it should be hated above all other things. For just as when we wrestle in the dark, we fall into the mud, so when we do not see the truth, we wallow in errors. A blind man may search for a long time in the <term>rushes</term> <note>rushes: stems of plants used as floor coverings in the 16th century, which often hid small objects like needles</note> before he finds a *needle*; and a *doubt* is just as easily resolved by *ignorance*. Finally, truth is no more likely to be found in ignorance than a sweet scent <note>original: "favor"</note> is found in a dunghill. And if they allow men to have knowledge but give them no permission to use it, *men would be much better off without it than having it*: for that is like having a talent <note>A reference to the Biblical Parable of the Talents (Matthew 25), where a servant is punished for burying his money rather than investing it</note> and hiding it in the earth, or putting <margin>Matthew 25. Matthew 5. Luke 8.</margin> a candle under a basket <note>original: "bushel," a unit of dry measure or the container holding it</note>; or like having a ship and letting it sit always in the dock. I can say from experience how "profitable" that is.

But I need say no more about this, for every man sees that no one can be happy who does not know what true happiness means. For what good does it do to have riches and not have the *use* of them? Truly, the Pagans <note>original: "Heathen"</note> deserved more praise in this regard than many *Christians*, for they spared no pain, cost, nor travel to attain *knowledge*. *Pythagoras* traveled from Samos <note>original: "Thamus," likely referring to the philosopher's birthplace, Samos</note> to *Egypt*, and afterwards into *Crete* and *Sparta* <note>original: "Lacedæmonia"</note>; and *Plato* went from *Athens* into *Italy* and *Egypt*, all to find out hidden secrets and knowledge. When a man possesses such knowledge, he seems to transcend mortality. For precious stones and all other creatures, of whatever value, are but counterfeits compared to this jewel; *they are mortal, corruptible, and inconstant, while this is immortal, pure, and certain.* Therefore, if I have searched and found any good thing that ignorance and time have smothered, I commend that same discovery to you. Although I owe you everything I have, I am bold enough to let others share in this poor gift alongside you.

->Your loving Cousin,<-

### Reginald Scot.

# To the Right Worshipful his loving Friends,
## Master Doctor *Coldwell* Dean of *Rochester*;
### AND
## Master Doctor *Redman* Archdeacon of *Canterbury*, etc.

Having identified two such civil magistrates who—for their sound judgment and their handling of justice in this commonwealth—are (in my humble opinion) exceptional individuals, and who I hope will accept my good intentions and test my book against their experience, as the subject matter concerns them deeply; I have now further considered two other fields: namely, Theology <note>original: "Divinity"</note> and Philosophy, which form the foundation of my book. Although I know those magistrates are well-informed in these areas, the judgment and critique of such matters belong more properly to you, whose reputation in these fields has surpassed all others I know in your positions. In that respect, I am bold enough to join you with them, as you are all good neighbors together in this commonwealth and dear friends to me. I do not present this book to you because it is a gift worthy of you, but because you are the right people <note>original: "meet"</note> for it—meaning, to judge it, defend it, and if necessary, correct it. I know you have learned from that serious advisor *Cato* not to shame or discourage anyone. For if I thought you were as eager as you are able to dismiss me for my lack of skill, I would not have been so quick to write to you, knowing your learning; but if I were too shy to write to you, I would show myself ignorant of your courtesy.

I know my own weakness; if such weakness has been able to support this argument, then the cause itself must be very strong. Eloquent words may please the ears, but solid evidence <note>original: "sufficient matter"</note> persuades the heart. Therefore, if I offer a wholesome drink (even if it is weak) in an earthenware <term>terrene</term> <note>terrene: made of earth or clay; humble or rustic</note> dish with a faithful hand, I hope it will be as well received as strong wine offered in a silver bowl by a flatterer. Certainly, it is as much a sign of generosity to receive a small thing thankfully as it is to give and distribute great and costly gifts bountifully; for courtesy provides more than rich rewards can. The tyrant *Dionysius* was not hated as much for his tyranny as for his rude and eccentric behavior. Among the sacrifices of the poor *Israelites*, God was satisfied with a tenth of an <term>ephah</term> <note>ephah: an ancient Hebrew dry measure, roughly equivalent to 22 liters</note> of flour, provided it was fine and good. Christ appreciated the poor widow’s <term>mite</term> <note>mite: a tiny, low-value coin</note>. King *Louis* of *France* accepted a turnip <note>original: "Rape-root"</note> from the simple <note>original: "clownish"</note> *Conan*. *Cyrus* deigned to drink a cup of cold water from the hand of poor *Sinaetes*. Likewise, may it please you to accept this simple book from me, which I faithfully present to you. I do not know if your opinions match mine, but I know your learning and judgment are capable of correcting me where I speak unskillfully, and correcting others when they speak of this subject maliciously.

Some people are like dogs that will bark at my writing, whether I support or refute this argument; just as *Diogenes* snarled at both the *Rhodians* and the *Lacedaemonians*—at the first because they were elegantly dressed <note>original: "brave"</note>, and at the others because they were not. Even *Homer* himself could not avoid insults. I am certain that those who never bothered to learn anything good will go out of their way to find faults here. For my part, I do not fear these conflicts or any of the adversaries I have, if not for certain cowards who I know will bite me behind my back.

But now to the main point. My question is not (as many foolishly <note>original: "fondly"</note> suppose) whether there are witches or not, but whether they can perform the miraculous feats attributed to them. Good Master Dean, is it possible for a man to eat breakfast with you in *Rochester* and have dinner that same day in *Durham* with Master Doctor *Matthew*? Or can your enemy maim you when the ocean lies between you? What physical connection <note>original: "real community"</note> is there between a spirit and a body? Can a spiritual body become physical <note>original: "temporal"</note> at its pleasure? Or can a fleshly <note>original: "carnal"</note> body become invisible? Is it likely that the lives of all princes, magistrates, and subjects should depend on the will—or rather the wish—of a poor, mali-

## To the R E A D E R S.

<margin>Isaiah 11. Proverbs 1.</margin>
To those of you who are wise and discreet, a few words may be enough. Such a person does not judge at first sight, nor condemn based on hearsay, but listens patiently and thereby grows in understanding. This patience produces experience, by which true judgment is guided. Therefore, I do not need to make any further appeal to you, except to ask that you please read my book without the prejudices of the past or prior misconceptions. Having requested this of you, I submit myself to your judgment. 

But to make a solemn appeal to those of you who are biased readers—asking you to set aside partiality, to receive my writing well, and to look upon my book with impartial eyes—would be wasted effort and time poorly spent. For I would no more succeed in this than if, a hundred years ago, I had tried to persuade your ancestors that <term>Robin Good-fellow</term><note>A mischievous sprite or hobgoblin from English folklore, also known as Puck.</note>, that famous and ancient <term>bogeyman</term><note>original: Bull-begger; a form of scarecrow or terrifying object used to frighten children.</note>, was merely a <term>deceiving merchant</term><note>original: cosening Merchant</note> and not actually a devil at all.

If I were to go to a <term>Catholic</term><note>original: Papist</note> and say, "I pray you, believe my writings," in which I will prove all Catholic charms, conjurations, exorcisms, blessings, and curses to be not only ridiculous and ineffective but also ungodly and contrary to **God’s Word**, I would have as much difficulty winning their favor as I will have gaining credit from you here. Nevertheless, I do not doubt that I will handle the subject in such a way that both the <term>Mass-monger</term><note>original: Massemonger; a derogatory term for someone who supports or performs the Roman Catholic Mass.</note> and the <term>Witch-monger</term><note>original: Witchmonger; Scot's term for those who credulously believe in and prosecute witches.</note> will be ashamed of their professions.

But Robin Good-fellow is no longer feared much, and the errors of <term>Catholicism</term><note>original: Popery</note> have been sufficiently exposed. Nevertheless, **witches' charms** and **conjurers' deceptions** are still thought to be effective. Indeed, even the <term>Pagans</term><note>original: Gentiles</note> saw through the fraud of their deceiving oracles, yet our own uninspired prophets and enchanters still make fools of us, to the shame of us all—but especially of the Catholics, who conjure everything and yet achieve nothing. They say to their candles, "I conjure you to last forever," yet they do not burn even a <term>Lord’s Prayer</term><note>original: Pater Noster</note> longer than usual. They conjure water to be healthy for both body and soul, but we see the body is never the better for it, nor the soul in any way reformed by it. Therefore, I wonder why—when they see their own rituals proven false and brought to nothing, or at least lacking any effect—they, above all others, still give such credit, support, and authority to the empty deceptions of **witches** and **conjurers**, as if their **charms** and **rituals** could produce more obvious, certain, and better results than their own.

But my request to all of you who read my book is only this: that you would please compare my words with your own reason and experience, and also with the **Word of God**. If you find yourself convinced and satisfied—or rather, corrected and better informed—on any single point or opinion that you previously held contrary to the truth in a matter that was undecided or never before examined, I ask you to take that as a benefit. Please suspend your judgment, hold back any sentence of condemnation against me, and consider the rest of the book at your further leisure. If this is not enough to persuade you, it cannot do much to annoy you; and then, that which was written without intending offense may be passed over without any resentment.

And although my claim differs somewhat from the old, deep-seated opinion—which I admit is "gray-haired" with age, giving my opponents more authority than reason in maintaining their assumptions and "old wives' tales"—it will fully agree with **God’s** glory and his holy **Word**. And although my **opponents** cling to a few specific words or sentences in **Scripture** that seem to support them, the entire context of the Bible works against them and refutes them. Even their own chosen passages, when rightly understood, do not support them at all. I trust their boastful claim of **antiquity** will appear as stale and decayed as an **apothecary’s drugs** or a **grocer’s spices**, which, the longer they are kept,

And until you have read my book, consider this in your mind: that **Wise-women, Thessalians, Screech-owls, and Hags** <note>original: *Sagæ, Thessalæ, Striges, Lamiæ*; these are Latin terms used in classical literature and law to describe various types of witches, sorceresses, and night-spirits.</note>—which are the only words used that properly signify our "witches"—are not found once in the Old or New Testament. Neither he nor Moses ever spoke a single word about the "witches' bargain" with the Devil, their <term>hagging</term><note>The act of being "hag-ridden" or tormented by a witch in the night.</note>, their riding through the air, their transferring of grain or grass from one field to another, their hurting of children or cattle with words or charms, their bewitching of butter, cheese, or ale, nor even their <term>transubstantiation</term><note>The author uses this theological term (usually referring to the bread and wine becoming the body and blood of Christ) to mock the idea of witches physically transforming themselves or others.</note>.

Because of this, the writers on this subject are not ashamed to say that it is reasonable to claim there were no witches in Job's time. Their reason is that if there had been such witches then in existence, Job would have said he had been bewitched. But indeed, people took no notice in those days of this "doctrine of devils"—that is, these fables of witchcraft—which Peter says shall be much regarded and listened to in the latter days.

However, no matter how ancient this barbaric notion of witches' all-powerfulness is, **Truth** must not be measured by time; for not every old opinion is sound. Truth is not diminished no matter how long it has been suppressed, but it is to be searched for in whatever dark corner it lies hidden. *For it is not like a cup of ale that can be <term>tapped too early</term>.* <note>original: *broached too rathe*; "rathe" means early or premature.</note> Finally, time reveals old errors and discovers new matters of truth. <term>Daneau</term><note>Lambert Daneau (c. 1530–1595), a French Calvinist theologian who wrote about witchcraft.</note> himself says that this question has never been handled until now, nor have the Scriptures concerning this matter ever been fully explained. 

To prove the ancientness of the cause, to confirm the opinions of the ignorant, to strengthen my opponents' arguments, to increase the punishment, and to complete the ruin of these old women, several things are added: 
* The vanity and wickedness of those called witches; 
* The arrogance of those who claim to work wonders; 
* The desire people have to listen to such miraculous matters (since for most people, an impossibility is more believable than a truth); 
* The ignorance of natural causes; 
* The ancient and universal hatred felt toward the name of a "witch"; 
* Their ugly faces, their spiteful words, their curses, and their charms made in rhyme; 
* Their poverty and the fear of many foolish folk; 
* The opinion of some who are wise; 
* The absence of <term>Robin Good-fellow</term> and the **Fairies**, who used to be blamed for such things; 
* The talk of the common people; 
* The authority of the Inquisitors; 
* The learning, skill, agreement, and reputation of the writers on this subject; 
* And the false translations and foolish interpretations used, especially by <term>Catholics</term><note>original: Papists.</note>. 

All these <term>trifles</term><note>original: toyes.</note> take such a hold on men's imaginations that they are led away from considering the facts and instead condemn what they do not understand.

However, by God's grace, I will so clearly expose and disprove these excuses and all their other objections in this book that every <term>witch-monger</term><note>A person who promotes or believes in the reality of witchcraft.</note> shall be embarrassed and all good men satisfied. 

In the meantime, I would wish them to know that if respect for God’s all-powerfulness, the meaning of His Word, the doubtfulness (or rather impossibility) of the case, the weak proofs brought against these women, the harshness used against them, the pity that should be in a Christian heart, or even their innocence, weakness, or age are not enough to stop the rage or harshness with which they are oppressed—then the consideration of their gender should at least encourage some lessening of their punishment. 

For if nature (as **Pliny** reports) has taught a lion not to deal as roughly with a woman as with a man, because she is physically the weaker vessel and in heart more inclined to pity (which **Jeremiah** in his Lamentations seems to confirm), what should a man do in this case, for whom a woman was created as a help and comfort? Even in the law of nature, it is a greater offense to kill a woman than a man—not because the man is not the superior creature, but because a woman is the weaker vessel. Therefore, among all modest and honest persons, it is thought a shame to offer violence or injury to a woman. In this respect, **Virgil** says:

<header>To the Readers.</header>

...vulgar old woman; by which the work of the Creator would be attributed to the power of a created being. Secondly, I write so that the religion of the Gospel may be seen to stand on its own without such foolish nonsense <note>original: "peevish trumpery"</note>. Thirdly, I hope that legal mercy and Christian compassion may be shown toward these poor souls, rather than harshness and extreme punishment. 

This is because those who are commonly accused of **witchcraft** are the least capable of all people to speak for themselves. They often have the most basic and simple education; the advanced stage of their age causes them to become senile <note>original: "dote"</note>; their poverty drives them to beg; and their mistreatment leads them to scold and threaten others (since they have no other way to get revenge). Their <term>melancholic humor</term><note>In the medical theory of the "four humors," an excess of black bile was thought to cause "melancholy," leading to depression, anxiety, and vivid, often dark hallucinations.</note> makes them full of imaginations. It is primarily from this mental state that their vain confessions proceed—such as the claims *that they can transform themselves and others into apes, owls, donkeys, dogs, cats, etc.; that they can fly in the air, kill children with charms, prevent butter from churning, and so on.*

<margin>Ecclesiasticus 35:15.</margin>
And since the powerful support one another, while the cry of poor widows—though it reaches to heaven—is barely heard on earth, I thought it right (to the best of my poor ability) to intercede. I ask that people reconsider some of this common harshness and certain points of hasty judgment. For the world is now in such a state—as **Brenz** <note>original: "Brentius"; Johannes Brenz (1499–1570) was a German Lutheran reformer who expressed skepticism about the reality of witchcraft.</note> affirms in a most godly sermon—that just as when the Heathens persecuted the Christians, if anyone was accused of believing in Christ, the common people cried, "**To the lion!**" <note>original: *Ad Leonem*</note>; so now, if any woman is accused of **witchcraft**, no matter how honest she may be, they cry, "**To the fire!**" <note>original: *Ad Ignem*</note>. 

The difference between the reckless dealings of unskilful people and the grave counsel of more discreet and learned persons can be seen in a story told by **Daneau** <note>original: "Danæus"; Lambert Daneau (c. 1530–1595) was a French Calvinist theologian who, unlike Scot, wrote in support of the reality of witchcraft.</note> himself. In it, he contrasts the recklessness of a few townsmen with the counsel of an entire Senate, essentially preferring the folly of the former over the wisdom of the latter.

At **Orléans on the Loire**, he says, there was a "man-witch" who was not only caught and accused but also convicted and condemned for witchcraft. He appealed his case from there to the High Court of **Paris**. The Senate there saw that the accusation was insufficient and would not allow it, but laughed at it as a trivial matter. In the end, they sent him home, saying he had been accused of a frivolous thing. And yet, despite that, the magistrates of Orléans were so bold that they hanged him a short time later for the same or a very similar offense. In this example, one can see the nature—and, as it were, the disease—of this issue: the simpler and less discreet sort of people are always more hasty and furious in their judgments than men of better reputation and knowledge. 

Nevertheless, **Ewich** <note>original: "Eunichius"; likely referring to Johannes Ewich (1525–1588), a physician who argued that many "witches" were actually suffering from mental illness.</note> says that three things must be carefully considered: what should be thought of witches, what their incantations can actually do, and whether their punishment should extend to death. He says, "I wish these things were as well understood as they are recklessly believed, by both the learned and the unlearned." Furthermore, he says that almost all theologians, physicians, and lawyers—who should know these matters best—have satisfied themselves with old customs and given too much credit to these fables, passing too many hasty and unjust death sentences upon witches. But when a man considers that in times past everyone who strayed from the Church of Rome was judged a heretic, it is less of a marvel that people remain blind and ignorant in this matter as well.

Surely, if the Scriptures had been suppressed for any longer, even more absurd fables would have sprung up and been believed. While such gullibility deserves to be laughed at, the cruelty resulting from it should be lamented with tears. For God knows that many of these poor wretches have more need of help than punishment. A preacher would be more suitable to admonish them than a jailer to keep them; and a physician is more necessary to help them than an executioner or torturer to hang or burn them. To provide proof and a proper trial of this, I will counter Daneau’s story of a "man-witch" (as he calls him) with another "witch" of the same gender.

<margin>Book 15, chapter 18 of *On the Variety of Things* <note>original: *Lib. 15. cap. 18. de varietatib. rerum.*</note></margin>
**Cardan** <note>original: "Cardanus"; Girolamo Cardano (1501–1576) was an influential Italian polymath.</note>, reporting from the mouth of his own father, tells of one **Bernard**, a poor servant. Bernard was very simple and unrefined in his intellect, but very helpful and diligent in his service (and for that reason dearly beloved by his master). Bernard claimed to practice the art of witchcraft and could not be talked out of it. He convinced himself that he knew all things and could make anything happen, largely because certain country people came to him for help and advice, assuming from his own talk that he had some power. Eventually, he was condemned to be burned. He seemed more willing to suffer that torment than to lose his reputation in...

He highlights the "mob mentality" of witch-hunts, noting that local magistrates often ignore the more skeptical and cautious rulings of higher legal bodies.</summary>

<header>To the Readers.</header>

in that regard. But his master, having compassion for him and being in the Prince’s favor himself, perceived his delusional thoughts <note>original: "conceit"</note> to stem from **melancholy** <note>A medical condition believed to be caused by an excess of "black bile," often resulting in depression, anxiety, or vivid hallucinations.</note>. He obtained a twenty-day stay of execution for the man. During that time (he says), his master generously fed him with good, fatty meat and four eggs at every meal, as well as sweet wine—a diet best suited for such a sluggish <note>original: "gross"</note> and weakened body. Once his strength was restored and the excess humor <note>The physical imbalance of fluids once thought to cause illness.</note> was suppressed, he was easily talked out of his absurd and dangerous opinions and his foolish imaginations. Confessing his error and folly—from which no man could previously persuade him to turn—and having received a pardon, he lived for a long time as a good member of the Church. Otherwise, the cruelty of judgment would have discarded and destroyed him.

<margin>
Amos 3:6. <note>“Shall there be evil in a city, and the Lord hath not done it?”</note>
Lamentations 3:38. <note>“Out of the mouth of the most High proceedeth not evil and good?”</note>
Isaiah 45:9. <note>“Woe unto him that striveth with his Maker!”</note>
Romans 9:20. <note>“Nay but, O man, who art thou that repliest against God?”</note>
</margin>

*This history is more believable than the fables of **Sprenger** <note>Jakob Sprenger, co-author of the "Malleus Maleficarum," a famous manual for hunting witches.</note> or the babbling of **Bodin** <note>Jean Bodin, a French jurist who wrote in favor of harsh prosecution for witchcraft.</note>. Their stories do not so much praise the "omnipotence" of **witches** as they do insult God’s glory. For if it is true, as they claim, that our life and death lie in the hand of a witch, then it is false that God makes us live or die, or that through him we have our being, our appointed lifespan, and our numbered days. Surely their **charms** can no more reach to the hurting or killing of men or women than their imaginations can extend to the stealing and carrying away of horses and mares. Neither has God given remedies for sickness or griefs through **words** or **charms**, but through **herbs** and **medicines** which he himself created on earth and gave men knowledge of. He did this so that he might be glorified, because through those means he allows the maladies of men and cattle to be cured, etc. And if there is no affliction or calamity that is not brought to pass by him, then let us defy the **Devil**, renounce all his works, and not so much as once think or dream about this supernatural power of witches. Let us not prosecute those whom our imagination condemns but our reason acquits with such spite. Our evidence against them consists of impossibilities, our proofs of unwritten "truths," and our entire proceedings are based on doubt and difficulty.*

Now, because I dislike the extreme cruelty used against some of these poor <note>original: "silly"</note> souls (whom a simple advocate, given a fair hearing and justice, could rescue from the hands of the Inquisitors themselves), people will say that I deny any punishment at all is due to any witch whatsoever. Indeed, because I expose the folly and godlessness of those who attribute God's power to witches, these **witch-mongers** <note>Those who promote the fear and prosecution of witches.</note> will report that I deny there are any witches at all. "And yet," they say, "look how often the word **witch** is mentioned in the **Scriptures**!" It is as if an idolater, defending images and idols against those who deny their power and godhead and criticize the worship given to them, should say: "How dare you deny the power of images, since their names are so often repeated in the Scriptures?" But truly, I do not deny that there are witches or images; rather, I detest the idolaters' opinions about them. I attribute to God’s work and ordinance what they blame on the power and malice of witches, and I give the honor to God which they ascribe to idols. As for those who truly are either witches or **conjurers** <term>conjurer</term> <note>Someone who claims to summon spirits or use magic, often for fraudulent or deceptive purposes.</note>, let them certainly suffer whatever punishment fits their crime, as provided by the serious judgment of the law.

<summary>Scot argues that many supposed acts of witchcraft are actually delusions caused by the medical condition of melancholy, and he asserts that attributing supernatural power to witches is a form of idolatry that denies God's sovereignty over life and death.</summary>

### CHAPTER I.

*An indictment of the power of witches over weather and natural elements, intended to rebuke those who attribute too much power to them.*

<image-desc>An ornamental woodcut drop cap 'T' with scrolling foliage and floral motifs.</image-desc>

<margin>
Job 1:21.
Job 2:10; 5:17; 13:15.
1 Samuel 3:18.
Job 1:21.
Mark 12.
</margin>
The fables of witchcraft have taken such a fast hold and deep root in the hearts of men that few or none can (nowadays) with patience endure the hand and correction of God. For if any adversity, grief, sickness, loss of children, grain <note>original: "corn"; in this period, "corn" referred to any cereal grain like wheat or barley, not specifically maize.</note>, cattle, or liberty happens to them, they immediately cry out against witches. It is as though there were no God in Israel who orders all things according to His will, punishing both the just and the unjust with griefs, plagues, and afflictions in the manner and form that He sees fit; instead, they believe that certain old women here on earth, called witches, must necessarily be the inventors of all men's calamities, as if they themselves were innocent and had deserved no such punishments. They go so far as to not hesitate to ride and go to those who are either wrongfully termed witches, or else are willing to be thought of as such, seeking comfort and a remedy from them in times of tribulation. This is contrary to God's will and commandment, which bids us resort to Him in all our necessities.

<margin>
In a sermon. <note>original: "In concione"</note>
</margin>
Such faithless people (I say) are also persuaded that neither hail nor snow, thunder nor lightning, rain nor stormy winds come from the heavens at the commandment of God, but are raised by the skill and power of witches and conjurers. Consequently, no sooner is a clap of thunder or a gale of wind heard than they either run to ring bells or cry out to burn witches; or else they burn consecrated objects, hoping by the smoke to drive the Devil out of the air—as though spirits could be frightened away with such outward trifles <note>original: "toies"</note>. However, these actions are themselves true enchantments, as Brentius <note>Johannes Brenz (1499–1570), a German theologian and Protestant Reformer who argued against the reality of weather-making by witches.</note> affirms.

<summary>The author argues that people wrongly blame witches for natural disasters and personal misfortunes that are actually sent by God, often resorting to superstitious remedies instead of faith.</summary>
<keywords>witchcraft, providence, weather magic, superstition, Johannes Brenz, spiritual trial, religious critique</keywords>

<page-num>2</page-num>
<header>Book I. The Discovery of Witchcraft.</header>

<margin>
Psalms 25.
Psalms 83.
Ecclesiasticus 43.

Mark 4:41.
Luke 8:14.
Psalms 107.
Job 38:22.
Ecclesiasticus 43.
Leviticus 26:3, 4.
</margin>
But certainly, it is neither a witch nor a devil, but a glorious God who makes the thunder. I have read in the *Scriptures* that God makes the blustering tempests and whirlwinds, and I find that it is the Lord who deals with them entirely, and that they blow according to His will. But let me see any of them at all rebuke and still the sea in a time of tempest, as *Christ* did; or raise the stormy wind, as God did with His word—then I will believe in them. Has any witch or conjurer, or any creature, entered into the treasures of the snow, or seen the secret places of the hail, which God has prepared for the day of trouble, battle, and war? For my part, I also think with *Jesus Sirach* <note>original: "Jesus Syrach"; refers to the author of the Book of Ecclesiasticus in the Apocrypha.</note> that at God’s command alone the snow falls, and that the wind blows according to His will—He who alone makes all storms cease and who (if we keep His ordinances) will send us rain in due season, and make the land bring forth its increase and the trees of the field give their fruit.

<margin>
Psalms 78:23.
Nahum 1.
</margin>
But our witch-mongers <note>original: "Witch-mongers"; a term used by the author for those who promote or profit from the belief in witches.</note> little think that the Lord commands the clouds above, or opens the doors of heaven, as *David* affirms; or that the Lord goes forth in the tempests and storms, as the Prophet *Nahum* reports. Instead, they believe that *witches* and *conjurers* are then about their business.

The *Marcionists* <note>An early Christian sect that followed the teachings of Marcion of Sinope, believing in two gods: one a harsh creator of the world and another a higher god of mercy.</note> acknowledged one God as the author of good things and another as the ordainer of evil. But these people make the devil a complete God, capable of creating things from nothing, knowing men’s thoughts, and doing that which God never did—such as transubstantiating <note>original: "transubstantiate"; here meaning to miraculously change the physical substance of a person into an animal.</note> men into beasts, and so on. Even if devils could do such things, it does not follow that witches have such power. But if all the devils in Hell were dead, and all the witches in *England* were burned or hanged, I guarantee you we would still have rain, hail, and tempests just as we do now: according to the appointment and will of God, and according to the constitution of the *elements* and the course of the *planets*, in which God has set a perfect and perpetual order.

<margin>
Job 26:8.
Job 37.
Psalms 135.
Jeremiah 10 & 15.
Hosea 13.
Psalms 39, etc.
</margin>
I am also well assured that if all the old women in the world were witches and all the priests were conjurers, we would not have a drop of rain nor a blast of wind more or less because of them. For the Lord has bound the waters in the clouds and has set bounds around the waters until the day and night come to an end. Indeed, it is God who raises the winds and stills them; and He says to the rain and snow, "Be upon the earth," and it falls. The wind of the Lord, and not the wind of witches, shall destroy the treasures of their pleasant vessels and dry up the fountains, says *Hosea*. Let us also learn and confess with the Prophet *David* that we ourselves are the causes of our afflictions, and not cry out against witches when we should be calling upon God for mercy.

<margin>
In the letters to Johann Weyer. <note>original: "In epist. ad Io. Wierum"; Johann Weyer was a physician and early critic of witch trials.</note>
Exodus 13.
Isaiah 66.
Psalms 18:11, 19.
Augustine, Book 3, On the Holy Trinity.
Mark 4:41.
</margin>
The Imperial law, says *Brenz* <note>original: "Brentius"; Johannes Brenz was a German Reformer.</note>, condemns those to death who trouble and infect the air. "But I affirm," he says, "that it is in the power of neither witch nor devil to do so, but in God only." This is despite the fact that *Danaeus*, *Hyperius*, *Hemingius*, *Erastus*, and others—besides *Bodin* and all the Popish writers in general—choose to conclude otherwise. The clouds are called the pillars of God’s tents, God’s chariots, and His pavilions. If that is so, what witch or devil can perform masteries <note>original: "masteries"; meaning feats of supernatural skill or control.</note> over them? *St. Augustine* says: "We must not think that this material world of visible things serves those fallen angels, but only God." <note>original: "Non est putandum istis transgressoribus angelis servire hanc rerum visibilium materiem, sed soli Deo"</note>

Finally, if witches could accomplish these things, why would it have seemed so strange to the people when *Christ* by a miracle commanded both the seas and the winds? For it is written: "Who is this? For both wind and sea obey him."

# Credulity. Of Witchcraft. CHAPTER II. 3

->*The trouble arising from men's credulity in this matter, with a reproof of certain clergymen who are inclined to the commonly held opinion of witches' omnipotence, and a familiar example of it.*<-

<margin>John 10:21.</margin>
<margin>* Psalms 72 & 136.</margin>
<margin>Jeremiah 5.</margin>
<margin>* Haggai 2:18.</margin>
<margin>* Idem. chapter 1.</margin>
<margin>* Joel 1.</margin>
<margin>Leviticus 26.</margin>
But the world is now so bewitched and overrun with this foolish error that even where a man should seek comfort and counsel, he shall be sent (in case of necessity) from God to the Devil, and from the physician to the cheating <note>original: "cosening"; meaning fraudulent or deceptive</note> witch. She will not hesitate to claim she can heal the lame with words (a power which belonged only to Christ and to those whom he assisted with his divine power); indeed, with her familiar spirit and charms, she will claim to cure the blind—even though it is written in the tenth chapter of St. John's Gospel that the Devil cannot open the eyes of the blind. And these witches gain such credibility that I have heard (to my grief) some of the clergy affirm that they have had seventeen or eighteen witches in their parish at one time, meaning those who could work miracles supernaturally.

In saying this, they manifested both their lack of faith and their ignorance in understanding God's Word, as well as their negligence and error in instructing their congregations. For they themselves might understand, and also teach their parishioners, that *God alone works great wonders; and that it is he who sends such punishments to the wicked and such trials to the chosen <note>original: "Elect"</note>, according to the saying of the Prophet Haggai: *“I struck you with blight, mildew, and hail in all the labor of your hands, yet you did not turn to me,” says the Lord.* And therefore the same prophet says in another place: *“You have sown much and bring in little.”* And in both Joel and Leviticus, similar phrases and proofs are used. But more shall be said of this later.

<margin>2 Timothy 4:3, 4.</margin>
<margin>1 Timothy 4:1.</margin>
St. Paul foresaw the blindness and obstinacy of both these blind shepherds and their diseased <note>original: "scabbed"; often used metaphorically for a flock in poor spiritual health</note> sheep when he said, *"They will not endure sound doctrine, but having itching ears, they will accumulate for themselves teachers to suit their own passions, and will turn away from listening to the truth and wander off into myths."* And in later times, *"some will depart from the faith by devoting themselves to deceitful spirits and teachings of demons, who speak lies"* (as witches and conjurers do), *"but reject profane and old wives' fables."* In this sense, Basil <note>Saint Basil the Great, a 4th-century Church Father</note> says: *"Whoever pays attention to enchanters listens to a mythical and frivolous thing."*

But I will recount an example of which I myself was not only an eyewitness <note>original: "oculatus testis"</note>, but have also examined the case and am ready to justify the truth of my report. I do this not because I wish to disgrace godly ministers, but to confirm my previous assertion: that this absurd error has taken root in the very place that should be able to expel all such ridiculous folly and impiety.

<margin>A story of Margaret Simons, a supposed witch.</margin>
At the court sessions <note>original: "Assizes"</note> held at Rochester in the year 1581, one Margaret Simons, the wife of John Simons of Brenchley in Kent, was put on trial for witchcraft. This was at the instigation and complaint of various foolish and malicious people, especially through the efforts of one John Ferral, the vicar of that parish. I spoke with him about the matter and found him both foolishly infatuated <note>original: "assotted"</note> with the case and enviously biased against her—and (what is worse) as unable to give a good account of his own faith as the woman he accused. This is what he specifically charged the poor woman with:

His son (an ill-behaved boy and an apprentice to Robert Scotchford, a cloth-maker living in the parish of Brenchley) passed by her house one day, and her little dog happened to bark at him. Taking this poorly, the boy drew his knife and chased the dog right to her door. She rebuked him with words that the boy resented, yet he could not be persuaded to leave for a long while. At last he returned to his master's house, and within five or six days he fell sick. Then the scuffle between the dog and the boy was remembered, so much so that the vicar (who thought himself so...

# Book I. The Discovery of Credulity. 4

(He felt so privileged, since he little doubted that God would visit his children with sickness) that he calculated—partly through his own judgment and partly (as he himself told me) by the accounts of other witches—that his son was bewitched by her. Indeed, he also told me that this son of his (who was, as it were, beyond any cure) received perfect health at the hands of another witch.

He proceeded even further against her, affirming that always in his parish church, when he desired to read most clearly, his voice failed him so much that he could scarcely be heard at all. This, he said, he could attribute to nothing else but her enchantment. When I informed the poor woman of this, being desirous to hear what she could say for herself, she told me that indeed his voice did fail him often, especially when he strained himself to speak loudest. However, she said that his voice was always hoarse and low, which I perceived to be true. "But Sir," she said, "you shall understand that our Vicar is afflicted with a kind of hoarseness that caused many of our neighbors in this parish, not long ago, to suspect that he had the French-Pox <note>original: "French-Pox"; a common historical term for syphilis</note>. Because of that, they utterly refused to take communion with him until such time as (being ordered to do so by Dr. Lewen, the ordinary <note>original: "the ordinary"; an official, such as a bishop or his deputy, who had immediate jurisdiction in ecclesiastical cases</note>) he had brought a certificate from London, signed by two physicians, stating that his hoarseness proceeded from a disease in the lungs." He published this certificate in the church in the presence of the whole congregation, and by this means he was "cured"—or rather, excused from the shame of his disease. I know this to be true from the accounts of many honest men of that parish. And truly, if one of the jury members had not been wiser than the rest, she would have been condemned based on this and other matters as ridiculous as this. For the name of a "witch" is so hateful, and her power so feared among the common people, that if the most honest person alive happened to be accused of it, she would hardly escape condemnation.

### CHAPTER III.

->*Who those called witches are, with a clear explanation of why people commonly think—and why witches themselves believe—that they can harm children, cattle, etc., with words and imagination; and concerning fraudulent <note>original: "cosening"</note> witches.*<-

<margin>Cardan, *On the Variety of Things* <note>original: "Cardan de var. rerum"; Girolamo Cardano was a 16th-century Italian polymath.</note></margin>One sort of people who are said to be witches are women who are commonly old, lame, bleary-eyed, pale, foul, and full of wrinkles; they are poor, sullen, superstitious, and Catholics <note>original: "Papists"</note>, or those who know no religion at all. In their drowsy minds, the Devil has found a fine seat; so, whatever mischief, accident, calamity, or slaughter occurs, they are easily persuaded that they caused it themselves, imprinting in their minds an earnest and constant imagination of the deed. They are lean and deformed, showing melancholy <term>melancholy</term> <note>In the 16th century, melancholy was considered a physical ailment caused by an excess of "black bile," often leading to depression, hallucinations, or irrational behavior.</note> in their faces to the horror of all who see them. They are senile, scolding, mad, and devilish, not much different from those thought to be possessed by spirits. They are so firm and steadfast in their opinions that anyone who only considers the consistency of their words would easily believe they were telling the truth.

These miserable wretches are so hateful to all their neighbors and so feared that few dare offend them or deny them anything they ask. Because of this, they take it upon themselves—and sometimes even believe—that they can do things beyond the ability of human nature. These women go from house to house and from door to door begging for a pot full of milk, yeast, drink, soup <note>original: "pottage"</note>, or some other relief, without which they could hardly live. Yet they obtain neither beauty, money, promotion, wealth, status <note>original: "worship"</note>, pleasure, honor, knowledge, learning, nor any other benefit whatsoever—neither for their service and pains, nor by their "art," nor even from the Devil's hands (with whom they are said to make a perfect and visible bargain).

<summary>This page recounts a case where a Vicar’s physical illness (likely syphilis) was falsely blamed on witchcraft to protect his reputation, and begins a skeptical description of accused witches as mentally ill, impoverished elderly women.</summary>
<keywords>witchcraft accusations, syphilis, clergy, religious superstition, melancholy, social outcasts, poverty, legal injustice</keywords>
