<meta>This page continues the author's analysis of how social tensions and medical ignorance lead to witchcraft accusations, transitioning from a specific anecdote about a Vicar to a general theory of how "witches" are identified and categorized by society and legal authorities.</meta>

# Miracles. Of Witchcraft. CHAP. IV.

It happens many times that neither their needs nor their expectations are met in the places where they beg or borrow; instead, their bad behavior <note>original: "lewdness"; in this period, it referred to ignorance or general wickedness rather than sexual misconduct</note> is criticized by their neighbors. Furthermore, over time the "witch" becomes hateful and tiresome to her neighbors, and they in turn are despised and treated with spite by her. Thus, sometimes she curses one person, and sometimes another—from the master of the house, his wife, children, and livestock, down to the little pig lying in the sty. In this way, as time passes, they have all displeased her, and she has wished bad luck upon them all, perhaps with formal curses and spells. 

Undoubtedly, eventually some of her neighbors die or fall sick, or some of their children are afflicted with diseases that trouble them strangely, such as strokes <note>original: "Apoplexies"</note>, epilepsy, convulsions, high fevers, worms, etc. These are assumed by ignorant parents to be the vengeance of witches. Indeed, their opinions and fantasies are confirmed and supported by unskilled physicians, according to the common saying: *Witchcraft and enchantment are the cloak of ignorance* <note>original: "Inscitiæ pallium maleficium & incantatio"</note>. In reality, it is physical ailments <note>original: "evil humors"; referring to the ancient medical theory of the four humors</note>, and not strange words, witches, or spirits, that are the causes of such diseases. Also, some of their livestock perish, either by disease or accident. Then, those upon whom such misfortunes fall—considering the reputation of this woman, her words, her displeasure, and her curses, which seem to match their misfortune so perfectly—do not only suspect, but are convinced that all their mishaps are caused solely by her.

<margin>Jean Bodin, book 2, *On the Demon-mania of Witches*, chapter 8 <note>original: "J. Bodin. lib. 2. de dæmon. cap. 8."</note></margin>
The witch, on the other hand, expecting her neighbors' misfortunes and seeing things sometimes happen according to her wishes, curses, and spells (for Bodin himself admits that not more than two in a hundred of their bewitchings or wishes actually take effect), is brought before a judge. Through careful examination of the circumstances, she is led to see how her curses and desires coincided with her neighbors' harms and losses. She then confesses that she (as if she were a goddess) has brought such things to pass. In this, not only she, but the accuser and also the judge are deeply deceived and misled. Through her confession and other circumstances, they are persuaded—to the injury of God’s glory—that she has done, or can do, that which belongs only to God himself.

There is another sort of witches who are absolute frauds <note>original: "coseners"</note>. For the sake of glory, fame, or profit, these people take it upon themselves to do anything that God or the Devil can do: whether it is foretelling the future, revealing secrets, curing illnesses, or working miracles. But I will talk more extensively about these later.

---

### CHAP. IV.

### What miraculous actions are attributed to witches by those who promote witch-hunts <note>original: "Witchmongers"</note>, Papists, and poets.

<margin>*The Hammer of Witches*, part 2, question 1, chapter 2 <note>original: "Mal. Malef. part. 2. quæst. 1. cap. 2."</note></margin>
Although it goes entirely against the grain <note>original: "against the hair"</note> and is contrary to the Devil's will, the witch’s oath, her promise, her loyalty to her master, and contrary to all reason that witches should help anything that is bewitched (instead of advancing their master's business), we nevertheless read in *The Hammer of Witches* <note>original: "Malleo Maleficarum"</note> of three types of witches. This same claim is made by all writers on this subject, both old and new. One type (they say) can hurt but not help; the second can help but not hurt; and the third can both help and hurt. Among the harmful witches, the author says there is one type more animalistic than any kind of beast except wolves, for these usually devour and eat young children and infants of their own kind. These are the ones (he says) who raise hail, tempests, and damaging weather, such as lightning and thunder. These are the ones who cause infertility in men, women, and livestock. These can throw children into bodies of water as they walk with their mothers without being seen. These can make horses kick until they throw their riders.

<summary>The author argues that witchcraft accusations arise from social friction and coincidental misfortunes, which ignorant people and unskilled doctors mistakenly blame on elderly women. He also outlines the classifications of witches found in contemporary demonological texts like the Malleus Maleficarum.</summary>
<keywords>witchcraft, social conflict, Jean Bodin, Malleus Maleficarum, medical ignorance, humors, superstition, judicial error, fraud</keywords>

--- Page 34 ---
<meta>This page continues Scot's catalog of the supernatural abilities commonly attributed to witches by contemporary demonologists, shifting from the social causes of accusations to a specific list of the "miracles" these women were supposedly capable of performing.</meta>

# BOOK I. The Discovery of Miracles

They can travel from place to place through the air while invisible. They can so alter the minds of judges that the judges have no power to punish them. They can grant themselves and others silence and numbness <note>original: "taciturnity and insensibility"</note> during their tortures. They can cause the hands of those who arrest them to tremble and strike terror into their minds. They can reveal hidden and lost things to others, foresee the future, and see distant events as if they were present. They can change people's minds to feel excessive love or hate. They can kill whomever they please with lightning and thunder. They can take away a man's courage and his ability to father children. They can make a woman miscarry and destroy a child in the mother's womb without any noticeable means, whether applied internally or externally. They can kill either man or beast with their mere looks.

<margin>
Ovid, *Metamorphoses*, Book 7.
Lambert Daneau, in his dialogue.
Michael Psellus, *On the Operation of Demons*.
Virgil, in *Damon*.
Horace, *Epodes*, 5.
Tibullus on enchantment, Book 1, Elegy 2.
Ovid, *Heroides* (Letters), 4.
The Law of the Twelve Tables.
*Malleus Maleficarum*.
</margin>
All these things are claimed to be true by Jakob Sprenger and Heinrich Institor in the *Malleus Maleficarum* <note>original: "Malleo Maleficarum"; Latin for "The Hammer of Witches," a famous 14th-century witch-hunting manual</note>, and are confirmed by Nider and the inquisitor Cumanus. They are also supported by Danaeus, Hyperius, and Hemingius, and the claims are multiplied by Jean Bodin and the friar Bartolommeo Spina <note>original: "Bartholomaeus Spineus"</note>. But because I do not wish to diminish the authority of their power in any way, you shall also have the testimony of many other serious authors on this matter, as follows:

<margin>
Lucan, *On the Civil War*, Book 6.
Virgil, *Eclogues*, 8.
Ovid, *The Remedy of Love*, Book 1.
Hyperius, Erastus.
Richard Gallis in his horrible treatise.
Hemingius.
Brian Darcy.
The Windsor Confession.
</margin>
First, Ovid claims that they can raise and suppress lightning and thunder, rain and hail, clouds and winds, storms and earthquakes. Others write that they can pull down the moon and stars. Some write that by merely wishing it, they can send needles into the livers of their enemies. Some say they can move corn while it is still in the field from one place to another. Some say they can cure diseases supernaturally, fly in the air, and dance with devils. Some write that they can take the role of a *Succubus* <note>a demon in female form believed to have sex with men</note> and couple with an *Incubus* <note>a demon in male form believed to have sex with women</note>, and that young prophets are fathered by them. Some say they can transform themselves and others, taking the forms and shapes of donkeys, wolves, ferrets, cows, apes, horses, dogs, and so on. Some say they can keep devils and spirits in the form of toads and cats.

<margin>
Virgil, *Aeneid*, 4.
Marcus Manilius, *Astronomica*, Book 1.
*Malleus Maleficarum*, Part 2, Question 1, Chapter 14.
</margin>
They can raise spirits (as others claim), dry up springs, change the course of running water, block the sun, and stop both day and night, changing one into the other. They can go in and out through auger holes <note>original: "awger-holes"; small holes made by a boring tool</note> and sail in an eggshell, a cockle shell, or a mussel shell through and under stormy seas. They can become invisible and deprive men of their genitals <note>original: "Privities"</note> or otherwise prevent the act of sexual intercourse <note>original: "Venery"</note>. They can bring souls out of their graves. They can tear snakes to pieces with words and kill lambs with their looks. But in this case, one might say that *Poets sing of wonders, but they are not to be believed* <note>original: "Miranda canunt, sed non credenda Poetae"</note>. They can also cause your butter not to form, no matter how long you churn; this is especially likely if either the maids have eaten the cream or the housewife has already sold the butter at the market. I have had some experience with this, although there may be real and natural causes that hinder the process: for example, if you put a little soap or sugar into your churn of cream, the butter will never form, no matter how long you churn. But the *Malleus Maleficarum* says there is no village so small that it does not contain many women who bewitch, infect, and kill cattle and dry up their milk. To support this claim, it cites the words of the Apostle Paul: *Does God take any care for oxen?* <note>original: "Nunquid Deo cura est de Bobus?"; 1 Corinthians 9:9. Scot is mocking how inquisitors used this verse to suggest God does not protect animals from witchcraft.</note>

### CHAP. V.

->A Refutation of the commonly held opinion of Witches and Witchcraft, and how detestable a sin it is to go to them for advice or other help in times of trouble.<-

But whatever is reported or imagined regarding these kinds of witchcraft, I dare to declare it false and legendary—except for cases of fraud <note>original: "cousenage"</note>, senility <note>original: "dotage"</note>, and poisoning. Furthermore, there is no mention of these kinds of witches in the Bible. If Christ had known of them, he would not have neglected to speak out against their arrogance in trying to take over his divine office—such as healing and curing diseases.

# Credulity. Concerning Witchcraft. CHAPTER 6.

...to cure diseases and to perform such miraculous and supernatural acts that he was specifically known, believed, and proclaimed to be God. His actions and cures were consistent (in both order and effect) with the power that our <term>witchmongers</term><note>original: "Witchmongers"; a term used by the author to describe those who believe in, promote, or hunt witches.</note> attribute to witches. However, if there are any people in these days afflicted in the strange way that Christ’s patients are described in the New Testament, we abandon our trust in God to trust in witches. These witches not only use their cheating art to take on the office of Christ in this matter, but they even use his very phrases when speaking to the idolaters who come to seek divine help from them, saying, "Go your way; your son (or your daughter, etc.) shall be well and whole." 

<margin>John 5:6. Mark 5:34.</margin>
<margin>To go to witches, etc., is idolatry.</margin>

It is not enough to discourage a witchmonger from his foolish belief by showing him that the results often turn out contrary to what the witch asserted. In such cases (to his greater condemnation), he simply seeks out witches of even greater fame. If all else fails, he would rather think he arrived an hour too late than that he traveled a mile too far. Truly, for my part, I cannot see what it means to "go a-whoring after strange gods" if this is not it. He who looks at his neighbor's wife and lusts after her has committed adultery. And truly, he who in his heart and by argument maintains that the sacrifice of the Mass is a way to gain favor for the living and the dead is an idolater <note>The author, Reginald Scot, reflects the Protestant views of his time, categorizing Catholic rituals as "idolatrous."</note>; as is he who allows and praises "creeping to the cross" and similar idolatrous actions, even if he does not physically bow his knees.

In the same way, I say that he who attributes such divine power to a witch—power which rightly and only belongs to GOD (as all witchmongers do)—is in his heart a blasphemer, an idolater, and full of gross wickedness, even if he never actually goes or sends to her for help.

### CHAPTER VI.

->*A further refutation of the miraculous and all-powerful strength of witches, using unbeatable arguments and authorities, along with warnings against such foolish belief.*<-

If witches could perform any of the miraculous things attributed to them and others, they would be able to do them repeatedly, at any time or place, or at anyone’s request. For the devil is just as strong at one time as another, just as busy by day as by night, and ready enough to do all kinds of mischief; he does not care whom he abuses. Furthermore, since most witchmongers themselves admit that the devil does not know the thoughts <note>original: "cogitation"</note> of a man's heart, it seems to me that he should sometimes appear to honest and credible people in the solid, physical form he supposedly takes when appearing to witches. Yet, you will never hear this confirmed by a single reliable witness. In reality, the devil enters into the mind and seeks a person's ruin through that path.

<margin>Aristotle, *On the Soul*, Book 2. Acts 8.</margin>
The practice of an art always assumes the power to perform it. Therefore, if they say they can do this or that, they must show how and by what means they do it—which neither the witches nor the witchmongers are able to do. For every action requires the ability of the person doing it <note>original: "the faculty and ability of the agent"</note>, a suitable subject to act upon, and a practical, possible way to apply that power. Now, witches are mortal, and their power depends on the natural connection between their minds and bodies. With their minds, they can only wish and understand; with their bodies, they can do no more than the limits of their earthly senses allow. Therefore, their power does not extend to performing miracles that exceed their own senses or the understanding of others who are wiser than they are. Thus, the necessary strength and power of the "cause" are missing here.

In logic, there can be no more power in the result <note>original: "the thing caused"</note> than there is in the cause itself, or in what proceeds from the cause. And we see that these ignorant and powerless women, or witches, are the "causes" of incantations and charms. In these charms, we will see there is no effect at all, if we will trust our own expe-

Law: *Much*. Law: *If anyone for another, or for himself* <note>original: "L. multum. l. si quis alteri, vel sibi." These are references to Roman legal codes (the Digest) used to argue that the law does not recognize or punish impossible acts.</note>.

It is strange that we should suppose such persons can perform such feats. It is even more strange that we imagine something to be possible for a witch which is physically and sensibly impossible—especially when our neighbor's life depends on our willingness to believe it. We can see the lack of ability, which is always an obstacle both to the act itself and to the legal assumption that it occurred. Because nothing is legally possible that is physically impossible, the judge does not pay attention to what the accused man says, or even what he intended to do; rather, the judge considers what is proved to have been committed, and what naturally falls within a person’s power and will to perform. 

For the law states that to intend to do something impossible is a sign of a madman or a fool, over whom no sentence or judgment can hold. Furthermore, what jury will condemn, or what judge will pass sentence against someone for killing a man at Berwick, when they themselves and many others saw that man at London on the very day the murder was committed? <note>Berwick-upon-Tweed is over 300 miles from London; in the 16th century, traveling this distance in a single day was a physical impossibility.</note> This remains true even if the person confesses to the crime and twenty witnesses testify to it. In this case, I say the judge should not weigh their testimony, as it is legally invalidated; the judge’s authority is meant to correct the flaws of the case and maintain justice and equity.

<margin>An objection answered.</margin>

Since other natural factors might cause the disasters blamed on witches, let us who profess the Gospel and the knowledge of Christ not be bewitched into believing they do things that are physically impossible and logically incredible. If people claim it is done through the Devil's help, and that he can work miracles, why do thieves not conduct their business through miracles? The Devil is just as involved with them as with witches. Such misfortunes as are blamed on witches happen even where no witches exist; indeed, they continue even after witches are hanged and burned. Why, then, should we attribute an effect to a cause that, when removed, allows the effect to happen anyway?

<margin>Miracles have ceased.</margin>

People’s opinions concerning witchcraft are varied and inconsistent.

Surely the natural power of a man or woman cannot be so expanded as to do anything beyond the power and virtue granted and implanted by God. It is the will and mind of man that is corrupted and depraved by the devil. God does not allow anything more than what the natural order he appointed requires. This natural order is nothing other than the ordinary power of God, poured into every creature according to its state and condition.

Instead, some are deceived in one point, and others are tricked in another, until finally, all these impossibilities—and many more—are affirmed as true by various people.

And I have also noted this: when someone is deceived by a deceptive trick <note>original: "cosening toye"</note> of witchcraft and reports it as such—verifying a matter that is completely impossible and false as if they knew it firsthand, having been overtaken by some kind of illusion (which are true enchantments)—that very same man will mock a similar story when told by someone else, calling it a fable unworthy of belief. <margin>Cardano, *On the Variety of Things*, Book 15, Chapter 80. <note>original: "Car. de var. rerum lib. 15. cap. 80."</note></margin> Cardanus writes that the cause of such credulity consists in three points: namely, in the imagination of the melancholic <note>A person suffering from "melancholy," which at the time was thought to be a physical imbalance causing depression or delusions.</note>, in the stubbornness of those who are corrupted by it, and in the deceit of the judges. These judges, being Inquisitors themselves against heretics and witches, both accused and condemned them, receiving for their labor the seizure of the victims' goods. Thus, these Inquisitors added many fables to this subject, lest they should seem to have done an injustice to the poor wretches by condemning and executing them for no offense. But since the rise of Luther's sect <note>Protestantism</note>, these priests have focused even more diligently upon their execution because more wealth is to be gained from them. As a result, they now deal so loosely with witches (due to a lack of profit) that all the practices against them are seen to be nothing but malice, folly, or greed. Whoever searches into this cause, or reads the chief writers on this subject, shall find his words to be true.

It will be objected that we here in England are not now directed by the Pope's laws, and consequently our witches are not troubled or summoned by the Inquisitors of heretical depravity <note>original: "Hereticæ pravitatis"</note>. Nevertheless, the belief in the omnipotence of their words or charms seems to be somewhat maintained in those statutes as a matter generally accepted until now, and not yet examined closely enough to be refuted and decided.

### CHAPTER 9.

*A conclusion to the first book, which previews the tyrannical cruelty of witch-mongers and inquisitors, along with a request for the reader to examine these matters carefully.*

And so that the world may see what treacherous and faithless dealings, what extreme and intolerable tyranny, what gross and foolish <note>original: "fond"</note> absurdities, what unnatural and uncivil discourtesy, what festering <note>original: "canker’d"</note> and spiteful malice, what outrageous and barbarous cruelty, what wicked and false scheming <note>original: "packing"</note>, what cunning and crafty interceptions, what weak <note>original: "bald"</note> and irritable <note>original: "peevish"</note> interpretations, what abominable and devilish inventions, and what outright and plain knavery is practiced against these old women, I will describe the entire process of the Inquisition. This will serve to the everlasting, inexcusable, and obvious shame of all witch-mongers. 

I will not include any of their private or doubtful dealings, nor anything they could either deny as unusual or justly argue against. Instead, I will present things that have been published and renewed in every age since the beginning of the Roman Catholic system <note>original: "Popery"</note>. These are practices established by laws, performed by inquisitors, privileged by princes, commended by scholars <note>original: "Doctors"</note>, and confirmed by Popes, Councils, decrees, and canon law. Finally, these things are believed by all witch-mongers—that is, by those who attribute the power of the Creator to old women and similar creatures. 

I ask you, therefore—even though it may be tedious and unbearable—to listen with compassion to their stories, just as you would want to be heard in your own times of misery. Listen to the accusations, examinations, evidence, confessions, assumptions, interrogations, spells <note>original: "conjurations"</note>, warnings, crimes, tortures, and condemnations that are typically devised and practiced against them.

# BOOK II.

### CHAPTER I.

*What testimonies and witnesses are allowed to give evidence against reputed witches, by the report and permission of the Inquisitors themselves, and those who are specialized writers on this subject.*

<margin>
*Hammer of Witches* <note>original: "Mal. Malef." (*Malleus Maleficarum*)</note>, Question 5, Part 3. Jean Bodin, Book 4, Chapter 2, *On the Demon-mania of Sorcerers*.
Archdeacon on the chapter "alleging the accused" <note>original: "Arch. in C. alle. accusatus"</note> in Selva's commentary on the words.
Jean Bodin, Book 4, Chapter 1, *On the Demon-mania of Sorcerers*.
*Hammer of Witches*, Question 56, Part 3, and Question 5, Part 3. In the same place.
Question 7, Article 2.
</margin>

Excommunicated people, accomplices in the crime, infants, wicked servants, and runaways are to be admitted to bear witness against their mistresses in this matter of witchcraft. This is because (says Bodin, the champion of those who hunt witches) no honest person is able to catch them. Heretics also and other witches shall be permitted to accuse a witch, but not to speak in her defense. And finally, the testimony of all infamous persons <note>People with bad reputations or criminal records.</note> in this case is valid and allowed. Indeed, one wicked person (says Bodin) may be permitted to accuse and condemn a thousand suspected witches.

And although by law, a deadly enemy <note>original: "capital enemy"</note> may be challenged and disqualified as a witness, James Sprenger and Henry Institor <note>The authors of the *Malleus Maleficarum* (1486).</note> (from whom Bodin and all the writers I have ever read receive their information, authority, and arguments) say regarding this point of law: the poor friendless old woman must prove that her deadly enemy would have killed her, and that he has both assaulted and wounded her; otherwise, she pleads her objection in vain. If the judge asks her whether she has any deadly enemies, and she lists others but forgets her accuser, or answers that he *was* her deadly enemy but she hopes he is no longer so, such a person is nevertheless admitted as a witness. And though by law, individual witnesses for separate incidents are not admissible, yet if one testifies she has bewitched her cow, another her sow, and the third her butter—these (say the *Hammer of Witches* and Bodin) are not "single" witnesses, because they all agree that she is a witch.

### CHAPTER II.

*The order of examination of witches by the Inquisitors.*

<margin>
The Scottish custom of accusing a witch.
</margin>
Women suspected of being witches, after their arrest, may not be allowed to go home or to other places to seek people to vouch for them <note>original: "sureties"</note>. For then (says Bodin) the people would be less willing to accuse them, for fear that upon their return home, they would take revenge. In this respect, Bodin greatly praises the Scottish custom and order: where (he says) a hollow piece of wood or a chest is placed in the church, into which anyone may freely cast a small slip of paper containing the name of the witch, the time, place, and deed, and so on. This same chest, being locked with three different locks, is opened every fifteen days by three Inquisitors or officers appointed for that purpose, who keep three different keys. And thus the accuser does not need to be identified, nor be disgraced by the charge of slander or malice toward his poor neighbor.

Furthermore, great persuasion must be used toward all men, women, and children to accuse old women of witchcraft.

Additionally, immunity and favor may always be promised to witches who confess...

# BOOK II.
## The Discovery of Examinations.

...confess and expose others; and on the contrary, threats and violence may be practiced and used.

*Item*, The little children of witches, who will not confess, must be arrested. If they are cleverly manipulated (says Bodin <note>Jean Bodin (1530–1596), a French jurist and prominent writer on demonology.</note>), they will confess against their own mothers.

*Item*, Witches must be examined as suddenly and as unexpectedly as possible. This will so shock them that they will confess anything, assuming the devil has forsaken them. Whereas, if they were first committed to prison, the devil would tamper with them and instruct them on what to do.

*Item*, The Inquisitor, judge, or examiner must begin with small matters first.

<margin>1. Bodin, *On the Demon-mania of Sorcerers*, Book 4, Chapter 4. Law regarding parents as witnesses.</margin>
*Item*, They must be examined on whether their parents were witches or not; for witches (as these Doctors of Law suppose) come by hereditary descent. And Bodin sets down this principle in witchcraft: "If the mother is a witch, so also is the daughter" <note>original: *Si saga fit mater, sic etiam est filia*</note>. This is despite the fact that the law normally forbids such testimony "out of reverence for the blood" <note>original: *Ob sanguinis reverentiam*; a legal principle that relatives should not be forced to testify against one another.</note>.

*Item*, The examiner must look steadfastly into their eyes, for they cannot look directly into a man's face (as Bodin affirms in one place, although in another he says that they kill and destroy both men and beasts with their looks).

*Item*, She must be examined regarding all accusations, presumptions, and faults at one single moment, lest Satan should afterwards dissuade her from confessing.

*Item*, A witch may not be put in prison alone, lest the Devil dissuade her from confession through promises of her safety. For (says Bodin) some who have been in jail have tried to fly away, as they were accustomed to do when they met with Diana and Minerva <note>Roman goddesses often associated in folklore with the "Wild Hunt" or nocturnal assemblies of witches.</note>, etc., and so they broke their own necks against the stone walls.

*Item*, If any woman denies her own confession made without torture, she is nevertheless to be condemned by that confession, just as in any other crime.

*Item*, The Judges must appear to have a pitiful expression and to bemoan them, saying that it was not they, but the Devil, who committed the murder, and that he compelled them to do it. They must make the accused believe that they think they are innocent.

*Item*, If they will confess nothing except upon the rack or through torture, their clothing must be changed, and every hair on their body must be shaven off with a sharp razor.

<margin>King Childebert's cruel method.</margin>
*Item*, If they have charms for silence <term>charms for taciturnity: magical spells believed to prevent a prisoner from feeling pain or speaking during torture.</term> so that they do not feel common tortures and therefore confess nothing, then some sharp instrument must be thrust between every nail of their fingers and toes. This (as Bodin says) was King Childebert’s <note>Likely referring to Childebert I, a 6th-century Frankish King.</note> invention and is to this day the most effective of all others. For by means of that extreme pain, they will (he says) confess anything.

<margin>Paulus Grillandus.</margin>
*Item*, Paulus Grillandus <note>An Italian judge and writer on witchcraft and heresy in the early 1500s.</note>, being an experienced practitioner in these matters, wishes that when witches sleep and feel no pain during torture, the prayer "Lord, you shall open my lips" <note>original: *Domine labia mea aperies*; a reference to Psalm 51:15.</note> should be said. And so (says he), both the torments will be felt and the truth will be uttered: "And thus craft is deceived by craft" <note>original: *Et sic ars deluditur arte*.</note>.

<margin>A subtle and devilish device.</margin>
*Item*, Bodin says that at the time of examination, there should be a pretense of great commotion to terrify the witch. A number of instruments, traps, manacles, ropes, halters, fetters, etc., should be prepared, brought forth, and laid before the person being examined. Also, some people should be recruited to make a most horrible and lamentable cry in the place of torture, as though he or she were upon the rack or in the hands of the torturers. This is so the person being examined may hear it while she is questioned, before she herself is brought into the prison; and perhaps (says he) she will confess the matter because of this.

*Item*, Some crafty spy must be secretly employed to pretend to be a prisoner with her in the same situation. This person may, through conversation, undermine her and so betray and expose her.

*Item*, If she still will not confess, she must be told that she has been detected and accused by others of her companions, even though in truth there is no such matter. In this way, perhaps she will confess, primarily to be revenged upon her adversaries and accusers.

# Evidence of Witchcraft. CHAPTER 3.

---

->*Matters of Evidence against Witches*<-

---

If an old woman threatens or touches someone who is in good health, and that person dies shortly after—or is infected with leprosy, apoplexy <note>A sudden loss of consciousness or a stroke.</note>, or any other strange disease—it is (says Bodin <note>Jean Bodin (1530–1596), a French jurist and influential writer who argued for the reality of witchcraft and the necessity of harsh trials.</note>) an established fact. This is such strong evidence that condemnation or death must follow without further proof, provided that anyone previously mistrusted her or had said before that she was a witch.

*Also*, if anyone enters or leaves a room or house while the doors are shut, it is obvious and sufficient evidence to condemn a witch without further trial. This is something Bodin never actually saw. If he can show me that trick, I will agree with his foolishness. For Christ used the same power after his resurrection—not as a ridiculous toy that every witch could perform, but as a special miracle to strengthen the faith of the Elect <note>In Christian theology, the "Elect" are those chosen by God for salvation.</note>.

*Also*, if a woman bewitches anyone’s eyes, she is to be executed without further proof.

*Also*, if anyone enchants or bewitches men's livestock or crops, or flies through the air, or makes a dog speak, or cuts off any man’s limbs <note>original: "members"</note> and reattaches them to the bodies of men or children, it is sufficient proof for condemnation.

*Also*, presumptions and guesses are sufficient proofs against witches.

<margin>
Bartolomeo de Spina and Jean Bodin, *On the Demon-mania of Sorcerers*, Book 2, Chapter 2.
Alexander.
Law: *Where a number...* regarding witnesses.
Jean Bodin, *On the Demon-mania of Sorcerers*, Book 2, Chapter 1.
</margin>
*Also*, if three witnesses merely say, "Such a woman is a witch," then it is a clear case that she is to be put to death. Bodin says this matter is certain not only by Canon and Civil laws, but also by the opinion of Pope Innocent—the wisest Pope, according to him, who ever lived <note>Bodin likely refers to Pope Innocent VIII, who issued the famous 1484 papal bull against witchcraft.</note>.

*Also*, the complaint of a single reputable man is enough to bring a poor woman to the rack or the pulley <note>Instruments of torture used to extract confessions.</note>.

*Also*, the testimony of a condemned or "infamous" <note>In legal terms, "infamous" referred to those who had lost their legal standing due to prior crimes.</note> person is acceptable and allowed in matters of witchcraft.

*Also*, a witch is not to be set free even if she endures every torture and confesses nothing—unlike suspects in all other criminal cases.

*Also*, although in other cases the testimony of many women at once is disqualified as being insufficient in law—due to the "weakness and frailty of their nature or sex"—yet in this matter, a single woman may serve to accuse and condemn a witch. This applies even if she is a party to the case (either accuser or accused), and even if she is "infamous and shameless" (to use Bodin's words), or even already condemned.

*Also*, a witness who has not been summoned but offers himself to testify is to be heard in this case, though in no other type of case.

*Also*, a mortal enemy (if the hatred is claimed to stem from witchcraft) may testify against a witch, and no objection can be raised against him.

<margin>
Parin. Law: *After the legacy...* regarding those who are unworthy.
Alexander, Chapter 72, Law 2, etc.
In his foolish pamphlet on the execution of the Windsor Witches.
Jean Bodin, Book 4, Chapter 3.
</margin>
*Also*, although proof of perjury <note>Lying under oath.</note> would disqualify a witness in all other causes, in this case, a perjurer is considered a good and lawful witness.

*Also*, the legal representatives and lawyers <note>original: "Proctors and Advocates"</note> in this case are forced to be witnesses against their own clients, which they are never required to do in any other case.

*Also*, none can give evidence against witches concerning their secret meetings <note>original: "assemblies"</note> except for other witches; as Bodin says, no one else is able to do it. However, Richard Gallis <note>Richard Gallis, who wrote a pamphlet about the Windsor witches in 1579.</note> writes that he happened upon a gathering <note>original: "God-speed"</note> and, with his sword and shield <note>original: "buckler"</note>, killed the Devil—or at least wounded him so badly that he made him stink of sulfur <note>original: "brimstone"</note>.

*Also*, Bodin says that because this is an "extraordinary matter," there must be extraordinary procedures used here; and every possible method should be employed, both direct and indirect.

### CHAPTER 4.

->Confessions of witches, by which they are condemned.<-

<margin>
Is there any probability that such people would continue to be witches?
Same author, same place.
Giovanni d’Andrea on the *Speculum*, title on the contesting of lawsuits, part 2; nothing foreign to the same. <note>Giovanni d’Andrea (c. 1270–1348) was an expert in canon law.</note>
Law regarding age 5; nothing on the same, etc.
Jean Bodin, *On the Demon-mania of Sorcerers*, Book 4, Chapter 3.

Some witches confess (says Bodin) because they are eager to die; not for the sake of glory, but out of despair, because they are tormented throughout their lives. But these people must not be spared (he says), even though the law normally excuses such confessions.

The best and most reliable confession is a formal confession <note>original: "shrift"</note> to her priest <note>original: "ghostly father"</note>.

*Also*, if she confesses many things that are false and only one thing that might be true, she is to be taken and executed based on that single confession.

*Also*, a woman is not considered as guilty if she confesses to a falsehood or a lie and denies the truth as one who answers by describing specific circumstances.

*Also*, an ambiguous or doubtful answer is taken as a confession against a witch.

*Also*, Bodin reports that one man confessed he went out—or rather, up into the air—and was transported many miles to a fairies' dance, only because he wanted to spy on where his wife went "hagging" <note>original: "hagging" — acting as a witch or attending a witches' Sabbath.</note> and how she behaved herself. This caused much debate among the Inquisitors and lawyers to decide whether he should be executed along with his wife or not. But it was concluded that he must die because he did not report <note>original: "bewrayed"</note> his wife, which he avoided doing out of respect for the honor of his family <note>original: *Propter reverentiam honoris & familiæ*</note>.

*Also*, if a woman confesses freely to this before she is even questioned, yet later denies it, she is nevertheless to be burned.

*Also*, they claim that this extreme severity is used because not even one in a thousand witches is ever detected. And yet it is claimed by Sprenger in the *Hammer of Witches* <note>original: *M. Mal.* or *Malleus Maleficarum*, the infamous 15th-century witch-hunting manual.</note> that there is no parish so small that it does not have many known witches living there.

### CHAPTER 5.

->Presumptions, by which witches are condemned.<-

<margin>Jean Bodin, *On the Demon-mania of Sorcerers*, Book 4, Chapter 4.</margin>
If any woman’s child happens to die while in her care, such that nobody knows how, it must not be thought or presumed that the mother killed it—unless she is suspected of being a witch. In that case, it is different; for she must be executed based on that suspicion, unless she can prove the negative or the contrary.

*Also*, if the child of a woman suspected of being a witch goes missing, it is to be presumed that she has sacrificed it to the Devil, unless she can prove otherwise.

*Also*, although in other people certain points of their confessions might be thought mistaken and blamed on error, in the cases of witches, all oversights, imperfections, and slips must be judged as unholy and malicious, leading to her ruin and condemnation.

<margin>
Jean Bodin, *On the Demon-mania of Sorcerers*, Book 4, Chapter 4.
The law of the Decurion regarding punishments.
Panormitanus and Felinus on the chapter "Coming," regarding witnesses in the same case, Book 4, numbers 12 through 18. <note>References to medieval legal commentators on church law.</note>
</margin>
*Also*, although a thief is not considered legally infamous <note>Legally "infamous" persons lost certain rights, such as the ability to testify in court.</note> in any matter other than theft, a witch accused <note>original: "defamed"</note> of witchcraft is said to be stained with every kind of fault and infamy universally, even if she has not been convicted. As I said, simply being labeled a "witch" is enough, for rumors and reports are sufficient (says Bodin) to condemn a witch.

*Also*, if any man, woman, or child says that a person is a witch, it is a very strong suspicion (says Bodin) and sufficient to put her on the rack <note>A torture device used to stretch the body to force a confession.</note>, even though in all other cases this is directly against the law.

*Also*, regarding suspicions and guesses against a witch, the common rumor or voice of the people cannot be wrong.

*Also*, if a woman, when she is arrested, cries out or says, "I am ruined; save my life; I will tell you how the matter stands," etc., she is then to be most strongly suspected and condemned to die.

# Chapter VIII.
## *Certain Cautions against Witches, and of their Tortures to procure Confession.*

But to demonstrate their further follies, I will recite some of their "cautions," which were published by the ancient Inquisitors as permanent lessons for their successors, as follows:

The first caution is that which was last rehearsed concerning weeping; which, they say, is an infallible sign.

<margin>
James Sprenger.
Henry Institor. <note>The authors of the *Malleus Maleficarum*.</note>
</margin>
Secondly, the judge must beware that she touches no part of him, especially his bare skin; and he must always wear around his neck blessed salt, palm, herbs, and hallowed wax. These, they say, are not only proven to be effective by the confessions of witches, but also by the practice of the Roman Church, which hallows them specifically for that purpose.

<margin>
*Malleus Maleficarum* Part 3, Question 15.
</margin>
Also, she must come to her arraignment backward—that is, with her backside <note>original: "tail"</note> toward the judge’s face—and the judge must make many signs of the cross as she approaches the bar. And lest we should condemn that as superstition, they anticipate our objection <note>original: "prevent us with a figure"</note> and tell us that this same superstition should not seem superstitious to us. But this resembles the persuasion of a thief who advises his son against stealing, yet tells him he may pick a pocket, cut a purse, or rob someone on the highway.
<margin>
Prolepsis, or Anticipation. <note>A rhetorical term where one speaks as if a future event has already happened or anticipates an objection.</note>
</margin>

One other caution is that she must be shaved, so that not one hair remains on her body. For they say that sometimes witches keep secrets for remaining silent—and for other purposes as well—in their hair, in their private parts <note>original: "privities"</note>, and between their skin and their

### Cautions Concerning Witchcraft: Chapter 8

<margin>Malleus Maleficarum</margin>
...their flesh: For which reason I marvel they do not skin them alive <note>original: "flea them not"</note>. For one of their witches would not burn, even in the middle of the flame, as the *Malleus Maleficarum* <note>original: "M. Mal." – The most famous medieval treatise on the prosecution of witches, written by Heinrich Kramer and Jacob Sprenger.</note> reports, until a charm written on a small scroll was found hidden between her skin and her flesh and taken away. This was recorded so seriously and faithfully by the Inquisitors themselves that one may believe it if they wish, though indeed it is a complete lie.
<margin>Jean Bodin. In the year 1485, a rogue Inquisitor.</margin>
Jean Bodin <note>A prominent French jurist and demonologist.</note> cites a similar story of a witch who could not be strangled by the executioner, despite his best efforts. But it is most true that the Inquisitor Cumanus in a single year shaved forty-one poor women and burned them all when he had finished.

<margin>Question 16: concerning the time and manner of causing terror.</margin>
Another caution is that at the time and place of torture, the holy objects mentioned before, along with the "seven words spoken on the Cross" <note>the traditional Seven Last Words of Christ</note>, should be hung around the witch's neck. Additionally, the length of Christ in wax <note>a wax candle or cord measuring the alleged height of Jesus</note> should be tied around her naked body, along with the relics of saints, and so on.
<margin>The blasphemous Pope Julius, the third of that name.</margin>
All this material, they say, will work so powerfully within and upon the victims that when they are racked and tortured, they can hardly stop themselves from confessing. In such a case, I have no doubt that the Pope who blasphemed Christ—cursing his Mother over a peacock and cursing God with great insults over a piece of pork—would, with even less compulsion, have renounced the Trinity and worshipped the Devil on his knees.

Another caution is that after she has been racked and has undergone all the tortures devised for that purpose, and after she has been forced to drink holy water, she should be brought again to the place of torture. In the midst of her torments, the accusations against her are to be read to her, and the witnesses (if they are willing) should be brought face to face with her. Finally, she is to be asked whether, as a trial of her innocence, she will undergo the judgment of "glowing iron" <note>original: *Candentis ferri*</note>,
<margin>Malleus Maleficarum, Part 3, Question 16.</margin>
which involves carrying a certain weight of burning iron in her bare hand. However, they say that this trial must not be granted under any circumstances. For both the *Malleus Maleficarum* and Bodin also affirm that many things may be promised, but nothing needs to be performed; for they have the authority to make promises, but no commission to actually fulfill them.

Another caution is that the judge must take care that once she begins to confess, he does not cut off her examination but continues it night and day. For many times, while the inquisitors break for dinner, she "returns to her vomit" <note>a biblical idiom meaning to return to one's previous state or lies</note>.

Another caution is that after the witch has confessed to harming men and animals, she should be asked how long she has had an *Incubus* <term>Incubus: a demon traditionally believed to have sexual relations with women</term>, when she renounced the faith, when she made the "real league" <note>a formal pact with the Devil</note>, and what that league consists of, etc. This is indeed the chief cause of all their incredible and impossible confessions; for on the rack, once they have begun to lie, they will say whatever the tormentor wants to hear.

The last caution is that if she will not confess, she should be taken to some strong castle or jail. After a few days, the jailer must make her believe he is going to a far-off country. Then, some of her "friends" must come to her and promise that if she will confess to them, they will help her escape from prison—which they could easily do, the keeper being away. This method, says the *Malleus Maleficarum*, has worked when all other means have failed.

<margin>Malleus Maleficarum, Part 3, Question 16, Action 11.</margin>
And it must not be omitted here that they confess on Fridays more than at any other time. Now, say James Sprenger and Henry Institor <note>The authors of the *Malleus Maleficarum*</note>, we must tell the whole truth: namely, that if she confesses nothing, she should be dismissed by law. And yet, by their order, she may under no circumstances be released on bail, but must be put into a private cell and there be "talked with" by some "crafty person" (those are their exact words). In the meantime, there must be eavesdroppers with pen and ink behind the wall to listen to and note down what she confesses. Or perhaps some of her old companions and acquaintances may come in and talk with her about old matters, and so she is betrayed <note>original: "bewrayed"</note> by eavesdroppers. Thus, there shall be no end to torture until she has confessed whatever they desire.

<meta>This page continues Reginald Scot’s skeptical examination of the legal and theological arguments used to persecute supposed witches. Having previously mocked the superstitions of the "Malleus Maleficarum," he now addresses the specific legal charges leveled by the French jurist Jean Bodin.</meta>

# Book II. The Discovery of Witchcraft <note>original: "The Discovery Crimes" — Likely a reference to the book's full title, *The Discovery of Witchcraft*.</note>

### CHAPTER 9.

#### The fifteen crimes charged against *witches* by *witch-believers* <note>original: "Witchmongers" — A term Scot used for those who promoted the fear and persecution of witches.</note>; specifically by *Jean Bodin* in *On the Demon-Mania of Sorcerers* <note>original: "Dæmonomania" — A highly influential 1580 work by the French jurist Jean Bodin that argued for the extreme prosecution of witches.</note>.

<margin>1.</margin> They deny God and all religion.
*Answer:* Then let them die for it, or at the least be treated like non-believers <note>original: "Infidels"</note> or apostates.

<margin>2.</margin> They curse, blaspheme, and provoke God with all spite.
*Answer:* Then let them face the law expressed in Leviticus 24 and Deuteronomy 13 and 17.

<margin>3.</margin> They pledge their faith to the Devil, and they worship and offer sacrifice to him.
*Answer:* Let such people also be judged by the same law.

<margin>4.</margin> They solemnly vow and promise all their offspring to the Devil.
*Answer:* This promise comes from an unsound mind and is not to be taken seriously, because they cannot actually perform it, nor will it ever be proved true. However, if it is done by anyone of sound mind, let the curse of Jeremiah 32:36 light upon them—namely, the sword, famine, and pestilence.

<margin>5.</margin> They sacrifice their own children to the Devil before baptism, holding them up in the air to him, and then thrust a needle into their brains.
*Answer:* If this is true, I do not defend them in it; there is a law to judge them by. However, it is so contrary to common sense and nature that it would be foolish to believe it, whether based on Bodin’s bare word or his assumptions—especially when so little benefit and such great danger and trouble follow for the witches because of it.

<margin>6.</margin> They burn their children after they have sacrificed them.
*Answer:* Then let them receive the punishment given to those who offered their children to Moloch in Leviticus 20. But these are mere inventions of witch-believers and Inquisitors who have wrung such confessions from them through extreme torture; otherwise, they have believed false reports or eventually won these confessions through flattery, fair words, and promises.

<margin>7.</margin> They swear to the Devil to bring as many people into that society as they can.
*Answer:* This is false, and it is proven so elsewhere in this book.

<margin>8.</margin> They swear by the name of the Devil.
*Answer:* I never heard any such oath, nor do we have any legal authority to kill those who swear in that way, though indeed it is very wicked and impious.

<margin>9.</margin> They commit incestuous adultery with spirits.
*Answer:* This is a stale, ridiculous lie, as is clearly proven later in this work.

<margin>10.</margin> They boil infants after they have murdered them unbaptized, until their flesh is made into a liquid <note>original: "potable" — drinkable.</note>.
*Answer:* This is untrue, incredible, and impossible.

<margin>11.</margin> They eat the flesh and drink the blood of men and children openly.
*Answer:* Then they are kin to the *Anthropophagi* <note>original: "Anthropophagi" — A Greek term for man-eaters or cannibals.</note> and cannibals. But I believe not one honest man in England or in France will claim that he has seen any of these persons called witches do so; if they did, I believe it would poison them.

<margin>12.</margin> They kill men with poison.
*Answer:* Let them be hanged for their actions.

<margin>13.</margin> They kill men’s cattle.
*Answer:* Then let a lawsuit for damages <note>original: "action of trespass"</note> be brought against them for doing so.

<margin>14.</margin> They bewitch men's crops <note>original: "corn"</note> and bring hunger and barrenness to the country; they ride and fly in the air, bring storms, create tempests, etc.
*Answer:* If they can do that, then I will worship them as Gods; for those are not the works of man, nor yet of a witch, as I have argued extensively elsewhere.

<margin>15.</margin> They have sexual intercourse <note>original: "venery"</note> with a demon called an *Incubus* <note>In folklore, a male demon believed to lie upon sleeping women to have sexual intercourse with them.</note>, even when they lie in bed with their husbands, and they have children by them who become the best witches.
**Answer:** This is the final lie, which is very ridiculous and has been disproved by me elsewhere.

# CHAPTER 10.

## *A refutation of the previously alleged crimes cobbled together by Bodin, and the only way to escape the Inquisitors.*

If more ridiculous or abominable crimes could have been invented, these poor women (whose chief fault is that they are scolds <note>original: "scolds" — women labeled as troublesome, loud, or argumentative.</note>) would have been charged with them.

In this formal list of charges <note>original: "libel"</note>, you see everything that "witches" are accused of, and also everything that any witch-believer <note>original: "Witchmonger" — Scot's term for those who promoted the persecution of witches.</note> provides or maliciously attributes to the power and practice of witches.

<margin>The question or matter in controversy: that is to say, the proposition or theme.</margin>
Some of these crimes might not only be within the power and will of a witch, but could be accomplished by natural means. Therefore, the matter in question—namely, whether a witch can work wonders supernaturally—is not decided by them. For many a rogue and prostitute <note>original: "knave and whore"</note> more commonly carries out those lewd actions than those who are called witches and are hanged for their efforts.

Some of these crimes laid to the charge of witches are also denied by me, and the accusers cannot prove them to be true or committed by any single witch. Other crimes are so absurd, supernatural, and impossible that they are mocked by almost all men and condemned as false, foolish <note>original: "fond"</note>, and fabulous reports—so much so that the very witch-believers themselves are ashamed to hear of them.

If one part is untrue, why should the rest not be thought false? For all these things are charged against them at once, even by the greatest doctors and patrons of the sect of witch-believers, who produce just as many "proofs" for the witches' supernatural and impossible actions as they do for the others. Thus, if one part of their accusation is false, the other part deserves no credit. If everything alleged of their doings were true, why should we believe in Christ because of his miracles, when a witch supposedly does as great wonders as he ever did?

<margin>A common error.</margin>
But some will say: "As for those absurd and Catholic <note>original: "Popish" — a derogatory term for Roman Catholic.</note> writers, they are not to be credited in all their allegations touching these matters." But I assure you that almost all sorts of writers on this subject—from the Doctors of the Church to the academic theologians <note>original: "School-men"</note>, Protestants and Catholics, the learned and unlearned, poets and historians, Jews, Christians, and Pagans—agree on these impossible and ridiculous matters. Indeed, these writers from whom I gather the most absurdities are considered the ones with the best credit and authority on this subject. The reason is that the matter was never thoroughly examined; instead, every fable was believed because the word "*witch*" is mentioned so often in Scripture.

<margin>The only way for witches to avoid the Inquisitors' hands.</margin>
Those who have looked deeper into the orders and customs of the Inquisitors also say that there is no way in the world for these poor women to escape the Inquisitors' hands (and consequently, burning) except to grease their palms with money <note>original: "gild their hands with money"</note>. Through this, the Inquisitors often take pity on them and release them as "sufficiently cleared." For the Inquisitors have the authority to exchange physical punishment for a fine, applying the money to the office of their Inquisition. By this, they reap such profit that many of these helpless <note>original: "silly" — in this period, the word meant "deserving of pity" or "vulnerable."</note> women pay them yearly pensions just so they won't be punished again.

<summary>Scot refutes the supernatural accusations against witches, arguing that if the impossible claims are false, the entire case fails; he further alleges that the Inquisition uses these charges primarily as a tool for financial extortion.</summary>

# BOOK II. The Discovery of the Inquisitor’s Failure.

### CHAPTER 11.

->*The opinion of Cornelius Agrippa concerning witches, his legal defense of a poor woman accused of witchcraft, and how he convinced the Inquisitors.*<-

Cornelius Agrippa says that while he was in Italy, many Inquisitors in the Duchy of Milan <note>original: "Millen"</note> troubled various honest and noble matrons, secretly extorting much money from them until their trickery was discovered. Furthermore, he says that while serving as an advocate or legal counselor in the commonwealth of Maastricht <note>original: "Maestright"</note> in Brabant, he had a fierce argument with an Inquisitor. This Inquisitor, through unjust accusations, had dragged a poor country woman into his slaughterhouse <note>original: "butchery" — here referring to a place of torture or execution</note> and to an improper place, not so much to examine her as to torment her. 

When Agrippa undertook to defend her, he declared that in the acts alleged, there was no proof, sign, or evidence that could justify her being tortured. The Inquisitor stubbornly denied this, saying, "There is one thing which is sufficient proof and evidence: her mother was burned as a witch in the past." 

When Agrippa replied, affirming that this point was irrelevant <note>original: "impertinent"</note> and ought to be rejected by the judge as it was the deed of another person, he provided the Inquisitor with legal reasons and laws to support his case. The Inquisitor replied again that his point was valid because witches used to sacrifice their children to the Devil as soon as they were born. He also claimed they usually conceived by spirits transformed into a man’s shape, and that witchcraft was therefore naturally ingrained in the child as an inherited disease.

<margin>A harsh verbal attack against a cruel Inquisitor.</margin>
Replying against the Inquisitor's folly and superstitious blindness, Agrippa said: "O you wicked priest! Is this your theology? Do you habitually draw poor, guiltless women to the rack using these forged devices? Do you use such sentences to judge others as heretics, when you are more of a heretic than either Faustus or Donatus? <note>Faustus of Mileve and Donatus Magnus were famous early Christian heretics.</note> Even if it were as you say, do you not nullify the grace of God’s ordinance—namely, Baptism? Are the words spoken in Baptism said in vain? Shall the Devil remain in the child, or the child remain in the power of the Devil, after being consecrated there and then to Christ Jesus in the Name of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Ghost? Even if you defend the false opinions of those who claim that spirits mating with women can father children, you are more foolish than any of them; for they never believed that any of those Devils, along with their 'stolen seed,' could pass part of their nature into the child. Though we are indeed born as children of the Devil and damnation, yet through grace in Christ during baptism, Satan is cast out. We are made new creatures in the Lord, from whom no one can be separated by another person's deeds."

The Inquisitor, being offended by this, threatened to prosecute the advocate as a supporter of heretics or witches. Nevertheless, Agrippa did not stop defending the helpless <note>original: "silly"</note> woman. Through the power of the law, he delivered her from the claws of the bloody monk. The monk and the woman's accusers were condemned to pay a large sum of money to the Charter of the Church of Mainz <note>original: "Mentz"</note> and remained infamous in the eyes of almost all men after that time.

By the way, you must understand that this was only a minor Inquisitor. He did not have as large a commission as Cumanus, Sprenger <note>Heinrich Kramer and Jacob Sprenger, authors of the *Malleus Maleficarum*, a famous witch-hunting manual.</note>, and others had; nor did he have the power that the Spanish Inquisitors have today. These modern Inquisitors will allow no advocates for the poor souls, unless the torturer or executioner can be called an advocate. You may read a summary of this Inquisition in a few words set out by Master <margin>John Foxe in the *Acts and Monuments*.</margin> John Foxe in the *Acts and Monuments* <note>Commonly known as *Foxe’s Book of Martyrs*.</note>. Among the Inquisitors, witches and heretics hold the same reputation, except that the severity is greater against witches. Because of their simplicity, the Inquisitors can more boldly tyrannize and triumph over them.

<summary>Reginald Scot recounts an anecdote by Cornelius Agrippa, who legally defended a woman against an Inquisitor arguing that witchcraft is a biological, inherited trait. Agrippa successfully argued that the sacrament of Baptism cleanses any such "inherited" evil, exposing the Inquisitor’s theological errors and corruption.</summary>

# Torments of Witchcraft. CHAPTER 12.

### CHAPTER 12.

->*How the fear of death and the pain of torture can force people to act, and why it is no surprise that "witches" condemn themselves through confessions that were tyrannically extorted.*<-

Anyone who reads church histories, or remembers the persecutions during the reign of Queen Mary <note>original: "Queen Maries time." Mary I of England (reigned 1553–1558), who famously executed many Protestants for heresy.</note>, will find that many good men fell away for fear of persecution and later returned to the Lord. It is no wonder, then, if a poor woman—the kind of woman described elsewhere in this book—is forced to confess to such absurd and false impossibilities when she is tormented as described in these last few pages. Human flesh and blood are simply unable to endure such a trial. How can she, in the midst of such horrible torture and pain, promise herself to remain constant or avoid confessing anything? What does it profit her to persist in denying the unjust charges laid against her? On one hand, there is no end to her torments; on the other hand, if she continues to maintain her innocence, her accusers simply say she is using <term>charms for silence</term> <note>original: "charms for taciturnity." Inquisitors often believed that if a prisoner could withstand torture without confessing, it was proof they were using magic to block the pain or the ability to speak.</note>.

<margin>Peter’s betrayal and denial of Christ.</margin>
The Apostle Peter denied, cursed, and swore he did not know his master and our Savior Jesus Christ, all because of the threats of a servant girl—or rather, because of a question she asked. In that moment, Peter was not nearly as trapped as these poor "witches" are. They are not examined by girls, but by shrewd Inquisitors who seek to confiscate their property. These men come to the place of judgment with minds set on their bloody purpose, sparing no kind of lure, threat, or torture until they have forced out of the women whatever serves their own desires or ensures the victims' destruction.

<margin>Daneau in his Dialogue.</margin> <note>original: "Danaeus." Lambert Daneau (c. 1530–1595), a French Calvinist theologian who wrote a famous dialogue on witches.</note>
<margin>1 Corinthians 10.</margin>
Peter, I say, was in the presence of his Lord and Master, Christ, who had instructed him in true knowledge for many years. Peter had been warned of his weakness only four or five hours earlier and had made a solemn, faithful promise to the contrary. Yet, without any compulsion other than a question from a girl, he acted against his conscience, abandoned his Master, and denied him three times. Peter was an enlightened man, placed in high dignity and much closer to Christ than any "witch" could be. Her fall cannot be as great as Peter’s because she never climbed half as many steps as he did. A pastor’s fall is much more shameful than the straying of one of his sheep, just as an ambassador’s conspiracy is more hateful than the dishonesty of a common person, or a captain’s treason is more damaging than a private soldier's mutiny. 

If you say that Peter repented, I answer that the "witch" often does the same; in that case, I do not see why mercy should not be shown to her. It would be a massive temptation for a simple old woman if a visible Devil (who is as ugly in shape as Daneau and others claim he is) were to assault her in the manner they describe—especially when the Bible promises that no one will be tempted beyond their strength. These poor old women are usually unlearned, unwarned, and lacking in legal counsel or friends. They lack the judgment and discretion to manage their lives and speech. Their nature is more weak and fragile than that of men, and they are much more subject to <term>melancholy</term> <note>In the 16th century, melancholy was considered a physical illness caused by an imbalance of "black bile," often blamed for causing depression, hallucinations, and irrational behavior.</note>. Their upbringing and social circle are so lowly that nothing extraordinary should be expected of them. Furthermore, their age is usually so advanced that they are decrepit, a condition that makes them prone to these delusions.

Finally, Christ clearly forgave Peter, even though his offense was committed against both Christ's divine and human nature. Afterward, Christ even trusted him to lead his followers <note>original: "feed his sheep"</note> and showed him great favor, friendship, and love. Therefore, I do not see why we cannot show compassion to these poor souls if they show themselves to be sorrowful for their false beliefs and wicked thoughts.

<summary>Reginald Scot argues that confessions of witchcraft are unreliable because they are extracted through extreme torture. He compares the weakness of accused women to the Apostle Peter’s denial of Christ, suggesting that if a great Apostle could fail under pressure, a vulnerable old woman surely would as well.</summary>

# BOOK III.

### CHAPTER 1.

*The witches' bargain with the Devil, according to the Hammer of Witches <note>original: "M. Mal." referring to the **Malleus Maleficarum**, the famous 1486 treatise on the prosecution of witches.</note>, Jean Bodin, Johannes Nider, Lambert Daneau, Michael Psellus, Thomas Erastus, Niels Hemmingsen, Bernardo Rategno da Como, Thomas Aquinas, Bartolommeo de Spina, etc.*

---

That which has deceived so many in this matter of witchcraft, and seems both so horrible and intolerable, is a clear bargain that (they say) is made between the Devil and the witch. Many men of great learning believe it to be true and publish it as such in their writings; which (by God's grace) shall be proved as pointless and false as the rest.

<margin>The double bargain of witches with the Devil.</margin>
The nature of their bargain or profession is twofold: one is solemn and public, the other secret and private. The one called solemn or public is when witches gather at specific assemblies at scheduled times, where they not only see the Devil in a visible form but also converse and talk familiarly with him. In this meeting, the Devil urges them to remain faithful to him, promising them a long life and prosperity. Then the gathered witches present a new disciple (whom they call a novice) to him. If the Devil finds that the young witch is ready and eager to renounce the Christian faith, despise any of the seven sacraments, trample on crosses, spit during the elevation <note>original: "elevation." The part of the Catholic Mass where the priest raises the bread and wine for the congregation to adore.</note>, break their fast on fasting days, and fast on Sundays, the Devil offers his hand. The novice, joining hand in hand with him, promises to observe and keep all the Devil’s commandments.

<margin>The Hammer of Witches, concerning the manner of profession <note>original: "Mal. Malef. de modo professionis."</note>.</margin>
Once this is done, the Devil begins to be bolder with her, telling her plainly that all this is not enough for his purposes. Therefore, he requires homage from her; indeed, he also tells her that she must grant him both her body and soul to be tormented in everlasting fire, which she agrees to. Then he commands her to recruit as many men, women, and children as she can to enter this society. Then he teaches them to make ointments from the internal organs and limbs of children, which allow them to fly through the air and fulfill all their desires. Thus, if there are any children who are unbaptized, or not protected by the sign of the cross or prayers <note>original: "orizons." From the Old French *oraison*, meaning prayers.</note>, the witches can and do snatch them from their mothers' sides in the night, or out of their cradles, or otherwise kill them during their ceremonies. After burial, they steal them from their graves and boil them in a cauldron until their flesh becomes liquid <note>original: "potable."</note>. From the thickest part of this mixture, they make ointments for flying through the air, but the thinner potion they put into flasks <note>original: "flaggons."</note>. Whoever drinks from these flasks while observing certain ceremonies immediately becomes a master—or rather, a mistress—of that practice and skill.

<summary>Scot outlines the elaborate and gruesome "bargain" that demonologists claimed witches made with the Devil, involving the renunciation of Christ and the ritual murder of infants. This description serves as a foundation for Scot's upcoming arguments that such claims are physically impossible and based on superstition.</summary>

# BOOK III.

Witches' songs. Of Witchcraft. CHAPTER II.

### CHAPTER II.

->*The order of the witches' homage done (as it is written by foolish Inquisitors and spiteful witch-hunters) to the Devil in person; of their songs and dances, specifically La Volta, and of other ceremonies, as well as their journeys.*<-

<margin>Homage of witches to the Devil.</margin>
Sometimes their homage, along with their oath and bargain, is accepted for a set term of years; sometimes forever. Sometimes it consists of denying the entire Christian faith, and sometimes only in part. The first is when the soul is absolutely surrendered to the Devil and the fires of hell. The other is when they have only bargained to follow certain ceremonies and rules of the Church, such as hiding their sins during confession <note>original: "Shrift." The ritual of confession to a priest.</note>, fasting on Sundays, and so on. This is done either by oath, verbal protest, or by a written contract—sometimes sealed with wax, sometimes signed with blood, and sometimes by kissing the Devil’s bare buttocks, as did a doctor named Edlin, who (as Bodin says) was burned for witchcraft.

<margin>Bartolommeo de Spina, chapter 1, in the year of the *Hammer of Witches*.</margin>
You must also understand that after they have feasted elegantly with the Devil and the Queen of the Fairies—having eaten a whole fat ox and emptied a barrel of Malmsey wine <term>Malmsey: A sweet, potent wine originally from Greece, popular in medieval and early modern Europe.</term> and a bin of bread at some nobleman’s house in the middle of the night—nothing is found missing in the morning. For the Lady Sibylla, Minerva, or Diana strikes the barrel and the bin with a golden rod, and they are fully refilled again. Yes, she even causes the ox's bones to be brought and laid together upon its hide, folds the four corners together, places her golden rod on top, and the ox rises again in its former state. And yet, when they return home, they are nearly starving from hunger, as Spina says <note>original: "Spineus." Bartolommeo de Spina (c. 1475–1546), an Italian Dominican and influential writer on witchcraft.</note>. <margin>The same author, in the same place.</margin> And this must be an absolute rule: that every two weeks, or at the very least every month, each witch must kill at least one child as her share.

<margin>Jean Bodin, *On the Demon-mania of Witches*, book 2, chapter 4.</margin>
And here some of Monsieur Bodin’s lies may be included. He says that at these magical gatherings, the witches never fail to dance, and in their dance, they sing these words: "*Har har, Devil, Devil, dance here, dance here, play here, play here, Sabbath, Sabbath.*" And while they sing and dance, everyone has a broom in her hand and holds it up high. <margin>*Hammer of Witches*.</margin> Furthermore, he says that these night-walkings—or rather, night-dancings—brought that dance called *La Volta* <term>La Volta: A lively, turning dance for couples that was considered scandalous by some because of the high leaps and physical contact involved.</term> out of Italy and into France.

A part of their pact is to scrape off the oil received during "extreme folly" (I should have said "extreme unction" <note>extreme unction: The Catholic sacrament of anointing the sick or dying with oil.</note>). But if that is so dangerous, those who prepare the corpses for burial had better be very careful not to rub off the oil, which could also be pushed off the forehead in many other ways. If that happens, I perceive all its power is gone, and so much for that. But I wonder how they manage to preserve the water poured on them during baptism, which I believe is at least as powerful as the oil; yet I think it is usually wiped and washed off within twenty-four hours after the baptism. But this matches the rest of their nonsense.

And it should be noted that the Inquisitors claim that during the entire time of the witch's journey <note>original: "excourse." A journey or expedition; here referring to a witch flying to a Sabbath.</note>, the Devil takes the place and room of the witch, looking so much like her that her husband in his bed cannot tell her apart from his wife by touch, speech, or appearance. Yes, the wife leaves her husband's arms without him noticing, and leaves the Devil in her place visibly. In this, their gullibility is unbelievable: they claim to have a physical body in <margin>Paolo Grillandi, *On Fortune*, volume 10, tract.</margin> the imaginary play, but a phantom body in the actual bed. And yet (of course) they say that at the name of Jesus, or at the sign of the cross, all these physical witches vanish away.
