### CHAPTER III.

->*How witches are summoned to appear before the Devil; of their riding in the air; of their accounts; of their conference with the Devil; of his supplies and their discussion; and of their farewells and sacrifices, according to Daneau, Psellus, etc.*<-

<margin>Daneau in *Dialogues*, chapter 4.</margin>Up to this point, the text consists mostly of the exact words found in the *Malleus Maleficarum* <note>original: "M. Mal." Latin for "The Hammer of Witches," the famous 15th-century inquisitor's manual.</note> or Bodin, or rather in both; or else in the new *Malleus Maleficarum*, or at the very least from some writer or another who maintains the almighty power of witches. But Daneau <note>original: "Danæus." Lambert Daneau, a French Calvinist theologian.</note> says that the Devil often meets them at markets and fairs in the form of a court summoner and warns them to appear at their assemblies at a certain hour of the night. This is so he may learn whom they have killed and how much progress they have made. If they are lame, he says the Devil gives them a staff to transport them there invisibly through the air. Then they begin dancing and singing obscene <note>original: "bawdy"</note> songs, where he leads the dance himself. After the dance and other discussions are over, he provides for their needs by giving them powders and roots to intoxicate others with. He gives every novice a mark, made either with his teeth or his claws; then they kiss the Devil’s bare buttocks and depart, making sure to offer him dogs, cats, hens, or their own blood every day afterward. Daneau reports all of this as a <margin>Ibid. Also in *Dialogues*, chapter 3.</margin>truth, almost as if from his own firsthand knowledge. And yet elsewhere he says that in these matters, they are only dreaming and do not actually do the things they confess because of their physical sickness <term>distemperature: A physical or mental illness caused by an imbalance of the four humors.</term> caused by their melancholic humor <term>melancholick humor: In early medicine, black bile was thought to cause depression, hallucinations, and delusions.</term>. Therefore, he says, these things which they report about themselves are nothing but mere illusions.

Psellus adds to this that certain magical heretics—namely the Eutychians—gather together every Good Friday at night. After putting out the candles, they commit incestuous adultery: the father with the daughter, the sister with the brother, and the son with the mother. Nine months later, they return and give birth. Then, cutting their children into pieces, they fill their pots <margin>Cardano, *On the Variety of Things*, book 15, chapter 80.</margin> with the blood, burn the bodies, and mix the ashes into the blood to preserve it for magical purposes. Cardano writes (though in my opinion, it is not very likely) that these excursions and dances, etc., originated with certain heretics called the Dulcinists <note>original: "Dulcini." Followers of Fra Dolcino, a 14th-century radical preacher accused of similar ritual crimes.</note>. They devised those feasts of Bacchus called "Orgia" <note>original: "Orgia." Ecstatic rites associated with the god Bacchus/Dionysus.</note>, where these kinds of people gathered openly. These gatherings began with rioting and ended with this folly. When these feasts were prohibited, they nevertheless attended them secretly; and when they could not do that, they performed them only in their imagination. Even to this day, he says, a certain image or resemblance of this remains among our melancholic women.

### CHAPTER IV.

->*That no real league can be made with the Devil; of the first author of this league, and the weak proofs offered by opponents for the same.*<-

If this league is false—as are the rest of their confessions—then the arguments of the "witch-mongers" <note>Scot’s derogatory term for those who believe in and hunt witches.</note> fall to the ground. All the writers on this subject take this bargain as a certainty, a proven fact, and their primary rule. But surely the contracts <note>original: "indentures." Legal agreements.</note> containing those agreements are "sealed with butter," and the document tags are but baubles <note>original: "bables." Meaningless toys or nonsense.</note>. What firm bargain can be made between a physical body and a spiritual one? Let any wise or honest man tell me if he has been either a participant or a witness, and I will believe him. But as for the authority, proof, or testimony upon which all this nonsense <note>original: "geer." Gear, stuff, or business.</note> stands, if you

<header>Witches' private league. Of Witchcraft. Chapter 5.</header>

<margin>*The Hammer of Witches* <note>original: "Mal. Malef." for *Malleus Maleficarum*.</note>, part 2, question 7, chapter 2.</margin>
If you read *The Hammer of Witches*, you shall find things to the shame of the reporters (who contradict each other so much in their stories) and to the reproach of those who believe such absurd lies.

<margin>On what basis this "real league" began to gain credibility.</margin>
The initial credibility of this claim rests upon the confession of a worthless <note>original: "baggage"</note> young man condemned to be burned for witchcraft. To prolong his life (if the story is even true, which is taken from Nider <note>Johannes Nider, a 15th-century theologian and author of the *Formicarius*.</note>), he told the inquisitors: "If I knew that I might obtain a pardon, I would discover all that I know of witchcraft." Once this condition was accepted and a pardon promised, he spoke as follows—partly in hope of freedom and partly to be rid of his wife.

The novice or young disciple goes to a church with the mistress of that profession on a Sunday morning, before the blessing <note>original: "conjuration"</note> of holy water. There, the novice renounces the faith and promises to observe (or rather, omit) ceremonies during meetings and perform other such follies. Finally, they do homage to their "young master," the Devil, as they agreed in their covenant.

But what is notable in that story is that this young witch, fearing that his wife's testimony would reveal his own trickery <note>original: "knavery"</note>, told the inquisitor: "In truth, my wife is as guilty as I am, but I am sure she will never confess any of these details, even if she were burned a thousand times."

And we must not forget that despite his remorse, his confession, and his accusation of his own wife—and contrary to the inquisitors' promise and oath—both he and his wife were burned at the stake. These were the first people to "discover" this notable league upon which the fable of witchcraft is built, and through which similar confessions have been extorted and exaggerated from others since that time.

---

### CHAPTER 5.

->*Concerning the private league: a notable tale by Bodin regarding a French lady, with a rebuttal.*<-

<margin>The nature of the witches' private league with the Devil.</margin>
The nature of their private league is said to be when the Devil—sometimes invisible and sometimes visible—talks with them privately in the midst of other people. He promises that if they follow his advice, he will supply all their needs and make all their efforts successful. He begins with small matters to which they secretly consent, and they do not join the fairies' assemblies.

In this situation, it seems to me that the Devil, in such a physical or bodily shape, would surely encounter people who would refuse to consent to his suggestions (unless you claim he can read their thoughts), and thus he would be exposed. Also, unless these people were idiots, they would notice him and abandon him for breaking his agreements. Yet, all the writers on this subject maintain that these bargains and assemblies exist, and Bodin <note>Jean Bodin, a prominent French jurist and demonologist.</note> confirms them with over a hundred lies; among them, I will recount one for several reasons.

<margin>Jean Bodin, *On the Demon-Mania of Witches* <note>original: "de dæmonomania"</note>, book 2, chapter 4.</margin>
<margin>This does not agree with the interpretation of those who say this is only done by the power of the league, nor with those who attribute it to magic words; note this well <note>original: "quoth nota."</note>.</margin>
He claims there was a noblewoman in Lyon <note>original: "Lions"</note> who, while in bed with her lover, suddenly got up in the night and lit a candle. When she had done so, she took a jar of ointment and rubbed it over her body. After speaking a few words, she was carried away. Her bed-fellow, seeing this, leaped out of bed, took the candle, and searched for the lady all around the chamber and in every corner. Although he could not find her, he found her jar of ointment. Desiring to know its power, he smeared himself with it just as he had seen her do. And although he was not superstitious enough to use any magic words to help him, Bodin claims that by the power of that ointment alone, he was immediately transported to Lorraine into an assembly of witches.

->CHAP. XXIII.<-
->*Of Various Gods in Various Countries.*<-

<margin>Beasts, birds, vermin, fish, herbs and other worthless items <note>original: "trumpery"</note> worshipped as gods.</margin>
<insert>T</insert>he *Egyptians* were even more foolish in this regard than the *Romans* (I mean the *Heathen Romans* of that time, and not the *Catholic* <note>original: "Popish"</note> *Romans* of today—for no nation comes close to these in any kind of idolatry). The *Egyptians* worshipped *Anubis* in the form of a dog because he loved dogs and hunting. Indeed, they worshipped all living creatures: specifically, among the beasts, a bullock, a dog, and a cat; among flying birds, the *Ibis* (which is a bird with a long beak that naturally devours venomous things and harmful serpents) and a sparrow-hawk. Of fish, they had two gods: namely, the *Lepidotus* fish <note>original: "Lepidotus piscis"</note> and the *Oxyrhynchus*. The *Saites* and *Thebans* took a sheep as their god. In the city of *Lycopolis*, they worshipped a wolf; in *Hermopolis*, the *Cynocephalus* <note>A dog-headed creature or baboon</note>; the *Leontopolitans*, a lion; in *Latopolis*, a fish in the Nile called the *Latus*. In the city of *Cynopolis*, they worshipped *Anubis*. At *Babylon*, near *Memphis*, they made an onion their god; the *Thebans* an eagle; the *Mendesians* a goat; the *Persians* a fire called *Ormazd*; the *Arabians* worshipped *Bacchus*, *Venus*, and *Dusares*; the *Boeotians*, *Amphiaraus*; the *Africans*, *Mopsus*; the *Scythians*, *Minerva*; the people of *Naucratis*, *Serapis*, which is a serpent. *Astarte* (being, as *Cicero* writes, the fourth *Venus*, and the one, as others affirm, whom *Solomon* worshipped at the request of his concubines) was the goddess of the *Assyrians*. At *Noricum*, which is part of *Bavaria*, they worshipped *Tibilenus*; the *Moors* worshipped *Juba*; the *Macedonians*, *Cabirus*; the *Paeonians*, *Uranus*. At *Samos*, *Juno* was their goddess; at *Paphos*, *Venus*; at *Lemnos*, *Vulcan*; at *Naxos*, *Liber*; at *Lampsacus*, *Priapus* (represented with oversized genitals), who was set up at the *Hellespont* to be adored. On the island of *Diomedea*, they worshipped *Diomedes*; at *Delphi*, *Apollo*; and at *Ephesus*, *Diana* was worshipped. And because they would rather "play a small game than be left out" <note>An idiom meaning they would settle for minor gods rather than have none at all.</note>, they had *Acharnus of Cyrene* to protect them from flies and maggots <note>original: "flie-blows"</note>; *Hercules Canopius* to protect them from fleas; and *Apollo* from *Delphi* to keep their cheese from being eaten by mice.
<margin>The high gods and their assistants.</margin>The *Greeks* were the first, as far as I can learn, to have assigned the gods their principal kingdoms and offices: such as *Jupiter* to rule in Heaven, *Pluto* in Hell, *Neptune* in the Sea, and so on. To these they joined various commissioners as assistants; to *Jupiter*, they added *Saturn*, *Mars*, *Venus*, *Mercury*, and *Minerva*; to *Neptune*, they added *Nereus*, and others. *Tutilina* was merely a mediator to *Jupiter*, pleading with him not to destroy the corn with thunder or storms; people usually lit candles before her in the temple to appease those storms, following the same *Catholic* <note>original: "Popish"</note> custom seen in these days.
<margin>The number of gods among the heathens.</margin>But I cannot repeat them all by name, for the gods of the *Gentiles* <term>Gentiles: A term for non-Jewish people, often used here to refer to pagans or heathens.</term> were recorded by *Varro* and others to number thirty thousand and upward. By this, the reasonable reader may judge their superstitious blindness.

<header>Refutation of Witchcraft Confessions. CHAPTER 7.</header>

# CHAPTER 7.

->A Refutation of the Objection regarding the Confessions of Witches.<-

It is admitted (some say by way of objection) even by these women themselves, that they do these and other such horrible things that deserve death with all severity, etc. To this I answer: whoever carefully examines <note>original: "considerately beholdeth"</note> their confessions will perceive them all to be worthless, trivial, false, inconsistent, and of no weight—except for their disregard for and ignorance of religion, which is more the fault of the neglectful minister <note>original: "Pastor"</note> than of the simple woman.

<margin>
Compulsory confession, such as by the Spanish <note>original: "Hispanical"</note> Inquisition. See the *Hammer of Witches* <note>original: "Mal. Malef." (*Malleus Maleficarum*)</note> and Jean Bodin.
Persuasive confession, such as by flattery. See Brian Darcy against Ursula Kempe; Jean Bodin; *Hammer of Witches*; and the Law concerning punishments for absentees, Book 2, with the commentary on those who committed suicide before being sentenced <note>original: "L. absent. de penis. L. 2. cum glof. de iis; qui ante senient. mortui sunt, sibi necem consciente."</note>.
</margin>
First, if their confession is made under duress, by force or authority, or by persuasion and under the guise of friendship, it is not to be regarded. This is because the extreme nature of threats and tortures provokes it, or the use of smooth talk and allurements compels it. If the confession is freely given, many circumstances must be considered: for instance, whether she appears to be trying to destroy her neighbor, which often happens because of a resentful and malicious "melancholic humor" <note>In early medicine, an excess of "black bile" was thought to cause depression, paranoia, or erratic behavior.</note>. Furthermore, one must consider whether, in that same melancholic mood and frantic state, she desires to end her own life <note>original: "abridgement of her own daies"</note>. Aristotle says this often happens to persons subject to melancholic passions. Jean Bodin and James Sprenger <note>Authors of famous demonological texts like *The Malleus Maleficarum*.</note> also say this of these old women called witches, who many times (as they affirm) refuse to live, even threatening the judges that if they are not burned, they will kill themselves and thus make the judges responsible for their spiritual ruin <note>original: "damnation"</note>.

I myself have known a case where a man could not succeed in being accepted as a sufficient witness against himself; he immediately went and threw himself into a pond of water and drowned. But the law says: *No credit should be given to one who wishes to die* <note>original: "Volenti mori non est habenda fides"</note>. Also, as I have proved elsewhere, they sometimes confess to things of which they were never guilty, believing they did what they did not do because of certain circumstances. And just as they sometimes confess to impossibilities—such as flying in the air, transforming <note>original: "transubstantiate"</note> themselves, raising storms, or moving grain—they also (I say) confess voluntarily to things no man could prove, and no man would guess or believe, unless he were as mad as they are. Thus, they willfully bring death upon themselves, which proves they have an unsound mind.

<margin>
Absurdities in the confessions of witches.
</margin>
If they confess to something that has indeed been committed by them, such as poisoning or any other kind of murder that is within the physical power of such persons to accomplish, I do not stand to defend their cause. However, I would wish that even in those cases, credit is not given too rashly, nor proceedings used too hastily against them. Instead, the causes, properties, and circumstances of everything should be duly considered and diligently examined. For you must understand that just as they sometimes confess they have murdered their neighbors with a wish, a word, or a look, they also confess that by giving an apple or some such thing to a pregnant woman, they have killed the child in the mother's womb, even when nothing was added to the object that could naturally be harmful or injurious.

In the same way, they confess that with a touch of their bare hand, they sometimes kill a man who is in perfect health and physical strength, even when all his clothes are between their hand and his skin.

But if this confession of theirs is examined by Theology, Philosophy, Medicine, Law, or Conscience, it will be found false and insufficient. First, because the age of working miracles has ended. Second, no reason can be given for a thing so far beyond all reason. Third, no substance <note>original: "receipt"</note> can be so powerful that when it is touched with a bare hand (from which the veins pass through the body to the heart), it would not harm the person holding it, and yet retain the power

### ->CHAPTER XXV.<-

->A Comparison between the Heathens and the Catholics, regarding their excuses for Idolatry.<-

<margin>Grammarians call those "divi" who were made gods from men. <note>original Latin: "Divos vocant Grammatici qui ex hominibus dii facti sunt."</note></margin>
And because I know that the <term>Papists</term> <note>Papists: a derogatory term for Roman Catholics used by Protestant writers to imply they followed the Pope rather than God</note> will say that their Idols are Saints and no such Devils as the gods of the <term>Gentiles</term> <note>Gentiles: here referring to ancient Pagans or non-Christians</note> were, you may tell them that not only their Saints, but the very Images of them, were called *Divi*. While that word signifies "gods"—and so by consequence Idols or Fiends—simply add an "l" to it, and it is "Divill" (Devil) in English. But they will also say that I do them wrong to mock them, because these were holy men and holy women. I grant some of them were so, and were further from allowing the Popish idolatry performed in their names than they are grieved by the derision used against them now. Indeed, just as Silver and Gold are made into Idols by those who love them too well and seek them too much, so are these holy men and women made into Idols by those who worship them and attribute to them such honor as belongs to God alone.

<margin>Cicero, *On the Nature of the Gods*. <note>original: "Cic. de natur. deorum."</note></margin>
The Heathen gods were, for the most part, good men and profitable members of the commonwealth in which they lived, and they deserved fame, etc.; in which respect people made gods of them after they were dead, just as they made Devils of such Emperors and Philosophers as they hated or who had deserved poorly among them. And is it not even so, or worse, in the commonwealth and Church of Popery? Does not the Pope excommunicate, curse, and condemn as Heretics—driving to the bottomless pit of Hell and proclaiming to the very Devils—all those who either write, speak, or think contrary to his idolatrous doctrine?

When Cicero derided the Heathen gods and attacked those who yielded such servile honor to them, he knew the persons to whom such abuse was committed had been well-deserving as civil citizens, and that good fame was due to them, but not divine status. Indeed, the infidels who honored those gods (hoping to receive benefits for their devotion) knew and understood that the statues and images before whom they poured forth their prayers with such reverence were merely stocks and stones, and only pictures of the persons whom they resembled. Yes, they also knew that the parties themselves were creatures, and could not do as much as the Catholics and <term>witchmongers</term> <note>witchmongers: those who believe in or trade in the superstitions of witchcraft</note> think the <term>Rood of Grace</term> <note>Rood of Grace: a famous mechanical crucifix at Boxley Abbey that could move its eyes and lips, later exposed as a fraud during the Reformation</note> or Mother Bungie could do.

<margin>The Catholics see a speck in another’s eye, but no beam in their own. <note>A reference to the biblical parable in Matthew 7:3-5.</note></margin>
And yet the Catholics can see the abuse of the Heathens, but they are not allowed to hear of their own idolatry, which is more gross and damnable than the others.

# Melancholy of Witchcraft. CHAP. IX.

### CHAPTER IX.

#### *How melancholy deceives <note>original: "abuseth"</note> old women, and the effects of it shown through various examples.*

If anyone carefully observes their words, actions, thoughts, and gestures, he will perceive that melancholy filling their heads and occupying their brains has deprived, or rather corrupted <note>original: "depraved"</note>, their judgment and all their senses. I am not talking about fraudulent <note>original: "cousening"</note> witches, but about poor melancholic women who are themselves deceived. For you must understand that the power melancholy has, and the effects it produces in the body of a man, or rather a woman, are almost incredible. For just as some of these melancholic people imagine they are witches and can perform wonders and do whatever they want by witchcraft, others troubled by this disease imagine many strange, incredible, and impossible things. Some believe they are monarchs and princes and that all other men are their subjects; some believe they are wild animals; some that they are <term>urinals</term> <note>urinals: in this context, glass medical vessels used for inspecting urine, which were very fragile and easily broken</note> or earthen pots, greatly fearing they will be broken. Some think that everyone they meet wants to take them to the gallows, and yet in the end, they hang themselves. One thought that Atlas—whom the poets falsely claim holds up the heavens on his shoulders—would grow weary and let the sky fall on him. Another would spend a whole day upon a stage, imagining that he both heard and saw <term>interludes</term> <note>interludes: short dramatic performances or plays</note>, and entertained himself greatly with them. One Theophilus, a physician who was otherwise considered sane (as it is said), imagined he heard and saw musicians continually playing instruments in a certain part of his house. One Bessus, who had killed his father, was famously caught because he imagined a swallow mocked <note>original: "upbraided"</note> him for it; so he revealed the murder himself.

<margin>Of one who, through melancholy, was led to think he had a nose as big as a house, etc.</margin>
But the most notable example of this is a man who was in great distress, imagining his nose was as big as a house. No friend or physician could free him from this idea, nor ease his grief, nor satisfy his imagination in that regard, until finally, a physician more expert in this <term>humor</term> <note>humor: in ancient medicine, the "four humors" (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile/melancholy) were believed to control health and personality. An excess of black bile was thought to cause "melancholy," or mental illness.</note> than the others used the following trick. First, when he was supposed to enter the bedroom door—which was wide open—he suddenly stopped and pulled back, so that he would not come any closer than the doorway. The melancholic man, wondering at this, asked why he behaved that way. The physician answered him in this manner: "Sir, your nose is so large that I can hardly enter your room without touching it, and consequently hurting it." "Look!" said the patient, "This is the man who must help me; the rest of my friends flatter me and try to hide my illness from me." "Well," said the physician, "I will cure you, but you must be willing to endure a little pain during the treatment." The man promised to endure it patiently and felt a certain hope of recovery. Then the physician entered the room, creeping close to the walls, appearing to fear touching and hurting the nose. Then he blindfolded the patient. Once that was done, he grabbed him by the nose with a pair of pincers and threw into a tub—which he had placed before his patient—a great amount of blood along with many pieces of bullock's livers, which he had secretly brought into the room while the man’s eyes were covered. Then he allowed him to see it. After doing this two or three times, the melancholic humor was so moderated <note>original: "qualified"</note> that the man’s mind was satisfied, his grief was eased, and his disease was cured.

Thrasibulus, also called Thrasillus, being severely oppressed by this melancholic humor, imagined that all the ships arriving at the port of <term>Piraeus</term> <note>Piraeus: the main port of ancient Athens</note> belonged to him. He would count them and command the sailors to set sail, etc., celebrating their safe returns and mourning for their misfortunes. The Italian whom we called here in England "the Monarch" was possessed by a similar spirit or idea. <margin>Danaeus in *Dialogues*, chapter 3.</margin> Danaeus himself reports that he saw one who

Now, if the imagination of a melancholic person can be preoccupied with causes that are both false and impossible, why should an old "witch" be thought free from such fantasies? As learned philosophers and physicians say, when the "melancholic flux" <note>This refers to the cessation of menstruation (menopause), which early modern medicine believed caused a buildup of "melancholy" or black bile in the body.</note> or issue of blood stops in their old age, this melancholy must necessarily increase within them. Due to the weakness of both their bodies and brains, they are the people most likely to encounter such melancholic imaginations—and these imaginations stay with them even after they lose their common sense. Jean Bodin <note>A famous French jurist and demonologist who argued for the reality of witchcraft.</note> labors to disprove this, but in doing so, he shows himself to be as poor a physician as he is a theologian elsewhere.

But if these women can imagine that they can transform their own bodies (which nevertheless remain in their original shape), how much more credible is it that they may falsely suppose they can hurt and weaken other men's bodies? Or even less, that they can prevent butter from forming in a churn? But what is it that they will not imagine—and consequently confess—that they can do? This is especially true when they are so earnestly persuaded to confess, so severely tormented, and so craftily examined with promises of favor. Such promises make them imagine that they shall live in great credit and wealth ever after.

If you read about the executions of witches, whether in the past in other countries or recently in this land, you will see such impossibilities confessed that no one in their right mind would believe them. Among other such false confessions, we read that there was a witch who confessed at the time of her execution that she had raised all the storms and caused all the frosts and harsh weather that happened in the winter of 1565—and many grave and wise men actually believed her.

### CHAPTER X.

#### That voluntary confessions may be falsely made to the ruin of those confessors, and regarding the strange effects of melancholy, proven by a familiar and recent example.

But to show that even voluntary confessions in these cases can be falsely made (even though they lead to the destruction of the person confessing) and that melancholy can drive the imagination to that effect, I will cite a notable instance. The parties involved are still alive and living in the parish of Sellindge <note>original: "Sellenge"</note> in Kent, and the matter happened not long ago in this way.

<margin>
A story from Kent of a recent incident.
</margin>
A woman named Ade Davie, the wife of Simon Davie, a farmer <note>original: "husband-man"</note>, was considered a very honest person from a good family. As her husband told me, and as is well known in these parts, she suddenly became more pensive and sad than in the past. Although this grieved him, he was reluctant to let it show, fearing his wife might be troubled or his neighbors might find out and accuse him of "ill husbandry" <note>In this context, "husbandry" refers to the management of his household and domestic affairs; being unable to manage a wife's behavior was a source of social shame.</note>—which is much hated in these parts. 

But when her sadness turned to a severe mental disturbance <note>original: "perturbation of mind"</note>, she lost her usual rest at night. She began sighing and crying secretly with many tears. He had to ask the cause of her extraordinary mourning. Although she hid the truth at first, claiming nothing was wrong, she soon after fell on her knees before him. She begged him to forgive her, saying she had grievously offended both God and him. Her poor husband was shocked by her behavior and comforted her as best he could, asking what was causing her grief. She told him that, contrary to God's Law and to the offense of all good Christians, and to the injury of him and especially...

<meta>This page continues the account of a woman (likely Ade Davie of Kent) who, suffering from "melancholy" (depression or mental illness), became convinced she had made a pact with the Devil. The author uses this case to argue that confessions of witchcraft are often the result of a disturbed mind rather than actual supernatural events.</meta>

<page-num>31</page-num>

# The Confutations of Witchcraft Confessions. Melancholy. Chapter 10.

<margin>Note the Christian comfort of the husband to his wife.</margin>
...to the loss of her own soul, she had bargained and given her soul to the Devil, to be surrendered to him within a short time. To this, her husband answered, saying, "Wife, be of good cheer; this bargain of yours is void and of no effect. For you have sold that which is not yours to sell, since it belongs to Christ, who has bought it and dearly paid for it—even with his blood which he shed upon the Cross. Therefore, the Devil has no claim on you." After this, with similar submission, tears, and penitence, she said to him, "Oh husband, I have committed yet another fault and done you more injury: for I have bewitched you and your children." "Be content," said he, "by the grace of God, Jesus Christ shall 'unwitch' <note>To break or reverse a spell.</note> us; for no evil can happen to those who fear God."

And (as truly as the Lord lives) this was the nature of his words to me, which I know is true, as it comes from sincere lips and from one who fears God. Now, when the time approached that the Devil was supposed to come and take possession of the woman according to his bargain, the husband watched and prayed earnestly. He had his wife read Psalms and prayers for mercy at God's hands. Suddenly, about midnight, there was a great rumbling below under his chamber window, which terrified them exceedingly. For they believed that the Devil was below, though he had no power to come up because of their fervent prayer.

<margin>Refutation.</margin>
Anyone noting this woman's first and second confession—freely and voluntarily made—and how everything aligned to add credit to her story and provide evidence for her condemnation, would surely think that if Jean Bodin <note>A famous French jurist and demonologist who advocated for the execution of witches.</note> were the foreman of her jury, he would cry, "Guilty!" He would hasten the execution of a woman who would have said as much before any judge in the world if she had been examined, and would have confessed no less if she had been put on trial. 

But God knows, she was innocent of any of these crimes. However, she was brought low and pressed down by the weight of this "humor" <note>Early modern medicine believed the body was governed by four "humors" or fluids. An excess of "black bile" caused "melancholy," a condition associated with depression and hallucinations.</note>, so much so that both her rest and sleep were taken away from her. Her imagination was troubled and disquieted with despair and other such thoughts that grew from her condition. And yet I believe if any mishap had happened to her husband or his children, few "witchmongers" <note>Those who zealously hunt or believe in the power of witches.</note> would have judged it as anything other than her having bewitched them. She (for her part) was so constantly persuaded that she was a witch that she judged herself worthy of death. To the extent that while she was kept in her room, she could not see anyone carrying a bundle of sticks <note>original: "faggot"</note> to the fire without saying it was to make a fire to burn her for witchcraft. But God knows she had bewitched no one, nor did she inflict any hurt upon anyone by her imagination, except unto herself.

<margin>A comical conclusion.</margin>
And as for the rumbling, it was caused by a sheep which had been skinned and hung by the walls, and a dog had come and was eating it; this created the noise I mentioned before. Now that she has recovered, she remains a very honest woman, far from such wickedness, and ashamed of her old fantasies, which she perceives grew out of her melancholy.

### CHAPTER XI.

*The strange and diverse effects of Melancholy, and how that same humor, overflowing in "witches" (or rather, old women), fills them with marvelous imaginations; and why their confessions are not to be believed.*

<margin>Girolamo Cardano, *On the Variety of Things*, Book 8. Johann Weyer, *On the Deceptions of Demons*, Book 6.</margin>
But in truth, this melancholic humor (as the best physicians affirm) is the cause of all their strange, impossible, and incredible confessions. These are so foolish <note>original: "fond"</note> that I wonder how any men can be deceived by them. However, although these feelings appear in the mind of man, they are bred in the body and proceed from this humor, which is the very dregs of blood. It nourishes and feeds those places from which proceed fears, troubling thoughts, superstitions, fastings, labors, and such things.

<meta>This page continues the argument that confessions of witchcraft are symptoms of mental illness ("melancholy") rather than evidence of supernatural crimes. The author, Reginald Scot, is debating contemporary demonologists like Jean Bodin by citing medical authorities like Johann Weyer and Thomas Erastus.</meta>

<page-num>32</page-num>

# BOOK III. The Discovery of Witches' Pacts Refuted.

<margin>
Aristotle, *On Dreams*.
Girolamo Cardano, Book 8, *On the Variety of Things*.
</margin>
This [melancholy] causes people to endure torments and (as some say) to foresee things to come. It preserves health by being cold and dry, yet it makes men prone to leanness and to the quartan ague <note>A fever that returns every fourth day, historically associated with an excess of "black bile" or melancholy.</note>. Those who are afflicted by it are self-destructive, brave in suffering injuries, but fearful of offering violence—unless the humor <note>The "humors" were bodily fluids (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile) believed to control a person's health and temperament.</note> is hot. They learn foreign languages with little effort (as Aristotle and others claim).

<margin>
Jean Bodin against Johann Weyer.
</margin>
If the imaginations <note>original: "phantasies"</note> of our witches were not corrupted, nor their wills confused by this humor, they would not so willingly and readily confess to things that put their lives in danger, and of which they could never otherwise be convicted. Jean Bodin, using a lawyer’s logic rather than medical knowledge, argues the opposite; he acts as though melancholy were furthest of all from these old women whom we call witches, mocking the most famous and noble physician Johann Weyer for his opinion on the matter. But because I am no physician, I will set a physician against him: namely Thomas Erastus, who says that these witches—due to their corrupt imaginations overflowing with melancholic humors because of their old age—dream and imagine they hurt things that they neither could nor did hurt. Thus, they think they know an art which they have neither learned nor understood.

But why should more credit be given to witches when they say they have made a real bargain with the Devil, killed a cow, bewitched butter, weakened a child, or cursed <term>fore-spoken</term> a neighbor, than when they confess to transforming themselves, making it rain or hail, flying through the air, becoming invisible, or moving grain in the fields from one place to another? If you think their confessions are sound in one case, why should you say they are corrupt in the other, when the confession of all these things is made at the same moment and affirmed with the same consistency—or rather, audacity? But you see that some of these things are impossible, and therefore you realize those confessions are empty and false. Yet you think the other things *might* be possible, and seeing them confess to them, you conclude "from possibility to reality" <note>original: *A posse ad esse*</note>, being persuaded it is true simply because you think it *could* be true. But I say, along with theologians and philosophers, that what is imagined about witchcraft has no truth in action or existence outside of their imagination. The witch (for the most part) is preoccupied with false causes. For whoever desires to bring about an impossible thing has a vain, idle, and childish belief born from an unsound mind. As the saying goes: "The will of a sound mind is the desire for a possible thing" <note>original: *Sanae mentis voluntas, voluntas rei possibilis est*</note>.

***

### CHAPTER XII.
#### A Refutation of Witches' Confessions, Especially Concerning Their Pact.

<margin>An objection.</margin>
But it is objected that witches confess to renouncing the faith. The argument is that their confession must be true, or else they would not make it, and their crime must be worthy of death, or else they should not be executed.

<margin>The resolution.</margin>
To this I answer as before: that their confessions are either forced out of them or proceed from an unsound mind. Indeed, I say further: that we ourselves—who are of sound mind and yet seek any way to salvation other than Jesus Christ, or break his commandments, or do not follow in his footsteps with a lively faith—not only renounce the faith, but God himself. Therefore, when they confess to forsaking God and embracing Satan, they are doing what we all effectively do [through sin]. Regarding the horrible part of their confession about the "league" <term>pact or alliance</term> that involves killing their own and others' children, boiling them to make potions or stews, and the effects of those mixtures; their Good Friday meetings (the day of their supposed delivery), their acts of incest, and their return after nine months—when usually women are neither able to make such a journey nor return—it is all so horrible, unnatural, unlikely, and impossible that if I...

# BOOK III. Witches' Tempests. CHAP. XIII.

...if I should behold such things with my own eyes, I would rather think myself dreaming, drunk, or somehow deprived of my senses, than give credit to such horrible and filthy matters.

<margin>A forged miracle.</margin>
How does the oil or the soup of a boiled <note>original: "fodden"</note> child have such power that a staff anointed with it can carry people through the air? Their drinkable liquor, which they say creates "Masters" of that craft—is it not ridiculous? And is it not, in the opinion of all philosophers, physicians, and theologians, completely devoid of the power attributed to it?

Their refusal to fast on Fridays, their fasting on Sundays, their spitting during the time of the Elevation <note>A part of the Catholic Mass where the priest raises the bread and wine; Scot, a Protestant, is noting that these "witch-like" behaviors are often just anti-Catholic gestures.</note>, their refusal of holy water, and their despising of superstitious crosses, etc.—which are all good steps toward true Christianity—help me to disprove the rest of their confessions.

### CHAP. XIII.

*A Refutation of Witches' Confessions regarding the making of Tempests and Rain; of the natural cause of Rain, and that Witches or Devils have no power to do such things.*

<margin>The methods that witches use to make rain, etc. Nider, *The Hammer of Witches* <note>original: "Malleus Maleficarum"</note>, Jean Bodin, Friar Bartholomeus, Hemmingius, Lambert Daneau, etc. *The Hammer of Witches*, part 2, question 1, chapter 11.</margin>
To speak more generally of all the impossible actions attributed to them, as well as their false confessions: I say that there is no one who acknowledges God to be the only Almighty and the only worker of all miracles—nor anyone endowed with common sense—but will deny that the elements obey witches and are at their command. Nor will they believe that witches can, at their pleasure, send rain, hail, tempests, thunder, or lightning. Would an old, doting woman be able to do this by casting a flint stone over her left shoulder toward the West? Or by hurling a little sea-sand up into the sky <note>original: "the Element"</note>? Or by wetting a broom-twig in water and sprinkling it in the air? Or by digging a pit in the earth, filling it with water, and stirring it with her finger? Or by boiling hogs' bristles? Or by laying sticks across a bank where there isn't a drop of water? Or by burying sage until it rots? All these things are confessed by "witches" and affirmed by authors to be the means that witches use to stir up extraordinary tempests and rain.

We read in *The Hammer of Witches* <note>original: "M. Maleficarum"</note> that a little girl, walking abroad with her father on his land, heard him complain of a drought and wish for rain. "Why Father," said the child, "I can make it rain or hail whenever and wherever I want." He asked where she had learned this. She said from her mother, who forbade her to tell anyone. He asked how her mother taught her. She answered that her mother committed her to a "Master" who would do anything for her at any time. "Why then," said he, "make it rain, but only in my field." So she went to the stream and threw up water in her Master’s name, and it rained immediately. Proceeding further with her father, she made it hail in another field at his request. Based on this, he accused his wife and had her burned; he then had his child "re-baptized"—a circumstance common among Catholics <note>original: "Papists"</note> and witch-hunters <note>original: "Witch-mongers"</note>. Regardless of how the first part was proven, there is no doubt that the latter part—the execution—was thoroughly carried out.

If they could indeed bring these things to pass at their pleasure, then they could also hinder the course of all other natural things and ordinances
<margin>He who can lie can steal, just as he who can work can play.</margin>
appointed by God. For example, they could make it stay dry when it should rain, or turn high noon into midnight. By those means, I say, the Divine power would become a slave to the will of a witch, so that we could neither eat nor drink without their permission.

I think Seneca <note>Lucius Annaeus Seneca, a Roman Stoic philosopher.</note> might satisfy these gullible or rather idolatrous people who go chasing after these witches—believing everything attributed to them to the dishonor of God’s glory. He says that the unrefined people and our ignorant predecessors believed that rain and...

<meta>This page continues Reginald Scot's argument that witches have no power over the weather. He moves from discussing the absurdity of "witch-salve" to a theological and scientific explanation of why only God controls the elements, citing the Bible and natural philosophy.</meta>

<page-num>34</page-num>
<header>Book III. The Discovery of Witches Impeached <note>original: "impeached" here means challenged or called into question</note>.</header>

...and showers might be procured and stopped by witches' charms and enchantments. It is so manifest that nothing can be achieved by such things that we do not need to go to any school of philosophy to learn how to refute that idea.

<margin>Jeremiah 16:22. *The gods of the nations are demons* <note>original: "Dii gentium demonia"</note>. The natural generation of hail and rain.</margin>
But Jeremiah, through the Word of God, completely confutes everything devised to support that foolish opinion, saying: *Are there any among the idols of the nations that send rain, or give showers from heaven? Are you not the same Lord our God?* We will trust in you, for you create and do all these things. I may therefore boldly say, along with Johannes Brentius <note>original: "Brentius"; a 16th-century German Lutheran reformer</note>, that it is neither in the power of witches nor devils to accomplish that matter, but in God alone. For when vapors are drawn and lifted up from the earth by the power of the sun into the middle region of the air, the coldness there compresses and thickens those vapors. These become clouds and are dissolved again by the heat of the sun, which creates rain or hail—rain, if the drops do not freeze into hail along the way. When these circumstances are considered alongside the course of the whole of Scripture, it is clear that it cannot be in the power of a witch or a devil to produce rain or fair weather.

<margin>Job 1; Job 1:16; Job 2:5. *The Hammer of Witches* <note>original: "Mal. Malef." or Malleus Maleficarum</note>, part 1, question 2.</margin>
And as for the story of Job being used against me in this case (where a witch is not even mentioned), I have answered that specifically elsewhere. Therefore, I will only say this here: that even in that story—where it pleased God (as Jean Calvin says) to use language suited to our limited understanding <note>original: "gross capacities"</note>, as we cannot grasp spiritual communication or heavenly affairs—the Devil asked God to stretch out *his* hand and touch everything Job had. Although he seems to grant Satan's request, God himself sent fire from heaven, etc. From this, it can be gathered that although God said, "He is in your hand," it was the Lord’s hand that punished Job, and not the hand of the Devil. The Devil did not say, "Give me leave to plague him," but rather, "Lay *your* hand upon him." And when Job remained faithful despite all his afflictions in his children, body, and goods, the Devil is said to come again to God and say, as before: "Now stretch out *your* hand and touch his bones and his flesh." This argues both that the Devil could not do it himself and that he did not do it the first time. It should also be remembered here that *The Hammer of Witches* and the rest of the witch-mongers <note>Scot's term for those who promote the belief in and persecution of witches</note> deny that there were any witches in Job’s time. But see more about this elsewhere.

### CHAP. XIV.

#### *What would happen if the confessions of witches or the opinions of witch-mongers were true regarding the effects of witchcraft, enchantments, etc.*

<margin>But these suppositions are false; therefore, the consequences are not true.</margin>
If it were true that witches confess what they do, or what all writers write, or what witch-mongers report, or what fools believe, we would never have butter in the churn, nor a cow in the pasture <note>original: "close"</note>, nor corn in the field, nor fair weather outdoors, nor health inside our homes. Or, if what is contained in *The Hammer of Witches*, the works of Jean Bodin, etc., or in the English pamphlets recently published about the executions of witches were true—specifically the things witches are said to confess—what creature could live in safety? Why would there be a need for such military preparations, or such trouble and expense in that regard? No prince would be able to reign or live in the land. For just as Lambert Daneau <note>original: "Danaeus"</note> says that a witch named Martin killed the Emperor of Germany with witchcraft, so would our witches (if they could) destroy all our government officials <note>original: "Magistrates"</note>. One old witch could overthrow a Royal Army. If that were so, why would we need any guns, or incendiary weapons <note>original: "wild-fire"</note>, or any other instruments of war? A witch could supply all needs and fulfill a prince's will in this matter without any cost or the bloodshed of his people.

If it is objected that witches work through the Devil, and Christian princes...

...the <note>The text continues from the previous page's catchword "the."</note> authorities argue that princes are not to deal with witches in that way. I answer that princes inclined toward battle would have no moral qualms about it, especially those who undertake unjust wars. Such rulers use other aids, devices, and engines of war that are just as unlawful and devilish as witchcraft. In their camps, neither the rules of religion nor Christian order are observed; indeed, rapes, murders, blasphemies, and thefts are most commonly and freely committed there. ### C H A P T E R 15.

*Examples of foreign nations who used the assistance of witches in their wars; of "eye-biting" witches in Ireland; and of two archers who were said to shoot with the help of familiar spirits.*

<margin>Witches in wars.</margin>
In the wars between the Kings of Denmark and Sweden in 1563, the Danes wrote that the King of Sweden carried four old witches with him in his camp. They claimed these witches used charms to so "disable" <note>original: "qualified"; here meaning to alter the state of or weaken</note> the Danes that they were unable to harm their enemies. Whenever the Danes attempted any military enterprise, they were so weakened by those witches that they could achieve nothing. Although this story was not believed at first, eventually one of these witches was taken prisoner and confessed to the whole matter. It was said that the magical threads, lines, and characters <note>Magical symbols or inscriptions.</note> were found in the highways and puddles.

<margin>Witches who use the "Evil Eye."</margin>
The Irish people are wonderfully devoted to the belief and practice of this. They claim that not only their children but even their cattle are "eye-bitten" (as they call it) when they suddenly fall sick. They even call one category of their witches "eye-biters" for that very reason. Yes, they will even insist that they can rhyme a man or a beast to death <note>A reference to the ancient Irish belief that poets or bards could kill through satirical or magical verses.</note>. Furthermore, the West-Indians and the Russians <note>original: "Muscovites"</note> do the same, and the Huns (as Gregory of Tours writes) used the help of witches in times of war.

<margin>Pumber the Archer.</margin>
I find another story written in *The Hammer of Witches* and repeated by Jean Bodin: that a soldier named Pumber killed three of the enemy every day with his bow and arrows through witchcraft. He shot them as they were peering over the walls of a besieged castle until, in the end, he had killed them all except one. The "proof" of the archer’s dishonest dealings was offered as follows: because he rarely missed when he shot; because he killed exactly three a day; and because he had shot three arrows into a single rod <note>A feat of extreme accuracy, similar to splitting an arrow.</note>. This was the same man who shot a penny off his son’s head and had another arrow ready to kill the Duke of Rheingraf <note>original: "Remgrave"</note> who had commanded him to do it. Undoubtedly, because of his extraordinary skill in shooting, he was reputed to be a witch, performing feats that others could not do—nor even imagine to be within human power. Yet, in truth, there was no miracle, no witchcraft, no impossibility, nor even any great difficulty involved.

<margin>A skillful archer punished by an unskilled Justice.</margin>
But I can match this last story with a local example. At Town Malling in Kent, one of Queen Mary’s Justices—acting on the complaints of many "wise" men and a few foolish boys—imprisoned <note>original: "laid by the heels"</note> an archer because he shot so near the center of the target <note>original: "the white at Buts"</note>. The Justice was informed and persuaded that the poor man played with a "Fly"—otherwise known as a devil or a familiar spirit <note>A "fly" was a common term for a minor demon or spirit that served a witch.</note>. Because the Justice was told that the archer shot better than any common shooting he had ever heard of or seen, he conceived that it could not be done in God’s name, but only by enchantment. He supposed that the archer, by abusing the...

### CHAPTER 16.

->*Authorities condemning the fantastical confessions of witches, and how a Popish doctor takes it upon himself to disprove them.*<-

<margin>
Council of Ancyra <note>original: "Concil. Anquirens." usually referring to the Council of Ancyra (314 AD), which produced the *Canon Episcopi*</note> in the decree 26, question 5, Canon *Episcopi*. Augustine, *On the Spirit and the Soul*, chapter 8. Gianfrancesco Ponzinibio, *Treatise on Sorcerers* <note>original: "Fran. Ponzinib. tract. de lam." (de lamiis)</note>, number 49. Paolo Grillandi, *On Witchcraft and Fortune-telling* <note>original: "Grillandus de ac sort." (de sortilegiis)</note>, number 6. In the history or life of Saint Germain.
</margin>

Certain general Councils, by their decrees, have condemned the confessions and erroneous beliefs of witches as being vain, fantastical, and legendary. This includes even those beliefs that are part of their "covenant," upon which our witch-hunters so heavily rely: namely, their night-walks and meetings with *Herodias* <note>A biblical figure often associated in medieval folklore with the "Wild Hunt" or nocturnal processions led by pagan goddesses.</note> and the pagan gods. They claim that during these times, they travel great distances in a very short space of time on hobby-horses; they also speak of transubstantiation <note>Here referring to magical shapeshifting or the transformation of substances.</note>, their eating of children and snatching them from their mothers' sides, and their entering into men’s houses through cracks and little holes where even a fly could hardly squeeze through, thereby disquieting the inhabitants. All of these things are not only said by a general Council to be merely fantastical and imaginations within dreams, but are also affirmed as such by ancient writers.

The words of the Council are these: "It must not be overlooked that certain wicked women, following Satan’s provocations and seduced by the illusions of demons, believe and profess that during the night they ride abroad with *Diana*, the goddess of the pagans, or else with *Herodias*, with an innumerable multitude upon certain beasts. They claim to pass over many countries and nations in the silence of the night, doing whatever those fairies or ladies command," etc. And it continues: "Let all ministers, therefore, in their various parishes, preach to God’s people so that they may know all these things are false," etc. The same Council further states: "Therefore, whoever believes that any creature can be either created by them, changed for better or worse, or transformed into any other kind or likeness by anyone but the Creator himself, is certainly an infidel and worse than a pagan."

And if this is to be believed, then all their bargains and assemblies are unbelievable, as they are only confirmed by certain foolish and forced confessions and by a legend of Saint Germain. He supposedly watched the fairies or witches at a late-night banquet <term>reer banquet: a "rear-supper," an additional meal or feast eaten late at night</term> and, through his holiness, made them stay there until he sent messengers to the houses of the neighbors who seemed to be present. He found them all in bed and so cried out that these were demons appearing in the likeness of those men. Even if this story were true (though it is false), it would serve well to disprove these meetings and night-walks. For if the demons are only present in the likeness of witches, then the claims attributed to the witches themselves in this matter are false.

<margin>
*The Hammer of Witches* <note>original: "Malleus Mal." (Malleus Maleficarum)</note>, questions regarding witches, chapters 21, 22, 23, etc.
</margin>

But because the old "Hammer" of Sprenger and Institor <note>Jakob Sprenger and Heinrich Kramer (Latinized as Institoris), authors of the infamous 1487 witch-hunting manual *Malleus Maleficarum*.</note> in their book, *The Hammer of Witches*, was insufficient to knock down the authority of this Council, a young blockhead <term>beetle-head: a dull-witted person; a "beetle" was also a heavy wooden mallet</term> called Friar Bartolommeo della Spina <note>original: "Bartholomaeus Spinaus"</note> has made a new leaden mallet to beat down the Council and kill these old women. In this work, imitating Aesop's donkey <note>A reference to Aesop's fables where a donkey tries to imitate a pet dog and ends up kicking its master.</note>, he kicks at the Pope with his heels, asserting on his own credit that the Council is false and erroneous. He claims its doctrine deviates from the Popish Church and is not authentic but apocryphal. He says (though untruthfully) that the Council was not called by the commandment of the Pope nor ratified by his authority—which, he claims, is enough to annul all Councils. "For surely," says this Friar (who at this moment is a chief Inquisitor), "if the words of this Council were to be accepted, both I and all my predecessors have published notorious lies and committed many injurious executions—" <note>The sentence ends abruptly at the page break.</note>

He also critiques the Inquisitor Bartolommeo della Spina for attempting to bypass these established church decrees in order to justify the prosecution of witches.</summary>

<meta>This page continues a legal and theological argument regarding the validity of confessions made by those accused of witchcraft, asserting that such confessions are often the result of delusion rather than factual reality.</meta>

<margin>Augustine, *The City of God*. Isidore of Seville, *Etymologies*, Book 8, Chapter 9. *Canon Mirum*. Ponzinibio, *On Witches*, Volume 10. Laws concerning "Error" and "When after," regarding ignorance of law and fact, and laws regarding interrogations.</margin>behalf is insufficient to take away the life of anyone, or to gain such credit as to be believed without further proof. For, as Augustine and Isidore, along with other sounder theologians say, these illusory <note>original: "peritigious"; from the Latin *praestigium*, referring to deceptive tricks or illusions</note> things which are performed by witches are fantastical <note>meaning: imaginary or based on delusions</note>. So too do the sounder decrees of Councils and Church Canons agree that in such cases, there is no ground for a criminal lawsuit. And the law says that the confession of such people who are deceived must necessarily be mistaken, and therefore is not to be accepted; for, *A confession must hold to what is true and possible* <note>original: "Confessio debet tenere verum & possibile"</note>. But these things [witchcraft] are contrary to both law and nature, and therefore it does not follow that because these witches confess to them, it is actually so. For the confession differs from the actual act, or from the possibility of the act. And whatever is contrary to nature fails in its basic principles, and therefore is naturally impossible.

<margin>Per the commentaries of Baldus and others on the law of confession; also per the law of Nerva and others. *Malleus Maleficarum*, Part 3, Question 5, Chapter 11.</margin>The Law also says, *In criminal cases, we must not normally rely on the confession of the accused alone* <note>original: "In criminalibus regulariter non statur soli confessioni rei"</note>. In criminal cases, or those concerning a person's life, we must not absolutely rely on the confession of the accused party; instead, in these matters, proofs must be brought that are clearer than light itself. In this crime, nobody should be condemned based on mere suspicions. And where it is objected and urged that since God alone knows the thoughts of the heart, there is no other way of proof except by confession, it is answered in the law as follows: Their confession in this case describes an outward act that is impossible in both law and nature, and is also unlikely to be true; and therefore, *What is not likely should not be considered* <note>original: "Quod verisimile non est, attendi non debet"</note>. So, though their confessions may be worthy of punishment because they show a will to commit such mischief, they are not worthy of belief as proof that they actually have such power. For, *If the deed is absent, and they suffer only from their own opinion, they are to be counted among the fools* <note>original: "Si factum absit, solaque opinione laborent, è stultorum genere sunt"</note>. Neither may any man be condemned for criminal causes by law based on suspicions, nor yet by the testimony of a single witness; nor even by the accusation of a mortal enemy, who indeed should not be allowed to give evidence in this case—though it pleases the *Malleus Maleficarum* <note>original: "M. Mal."; the infamous 15th-century treatise on the prosecution of witches</note> and Bodin <note>Jean Bodin (1530–1596), a French jurist and demonologist</note> to claim the opposite. But beyond all fairness, these Inquisitors have enough tricks and devices to plague and kill these poor souls; for they say their fault is the greatest of all because of their sexual union with the Devil, and therefore they are to be punished as heretics in four ways: namely, with excommunication, loss of status, loss of goods, and also with death.

<margin>*Malleus Maleficarum*, Question 14, Part 1. Laws concerning wrongdoers. Affirmed by *Malleus Maleficarum*, Question 17.</margin>And indeed they find laws and provide the means to maintain this bloody disposition of theirs. For it is written in their Popish Canons that as for these kinds of heretics, no matter how much they repent and return to the faith, they may not be kept alive or held in perpetual prison, but must be put to an extreme death. Yes, the *Malleus Maleficarum* writes that a witch's sin is the sin against the Holy Ghost—that is, unpardonable. It even claims that it is greater than the sin of the fallen angels. In this respect, I wonder why Moses did not deliver three tables of law to the children of Israel, or at the very least, why he did not present specific commandments against it. It is not believable that the greatest sin would be included within a lesser one, and so on.

But when these "witchmongers" <note>a derogatory term for those who promote or profit from the hunt for witches</note> are defeated in the argument concerning these confessions—so that their tyrannical arguments cannot prevail to soak the magistrates' hands in as much blood as they desire—they turn to accusing the women of other crimes, so that the world might think they had some justification for maintaining their malicious fury against them.

# CHAPTER 19.

## Concerning Four Capital Crimes Alleged against Witches, all fully answered and refuted as frivolous.

<margin>1. Idolatry refuted.</margin>
First, they charge them with idolatry; but alas, this is without any reason. Such people are properly known to us to be idolaters who perform external worship to idols or foreign gods. The absolute furthest idolatry can be stretched is to say that those who are guilty of it are people who hope for and seek salvation from idols—or from anyone other than God. Or, it includes those who fix their entire mind and love upon any creature so much that the power of God is neglected and despised because of it. 

But witches neither seek nor believe they have salvation from the hands of devils; they are only deceived by them. The instruments of their imagination are corrupted and so deluded that they suppose, confess, and say they can do things that are as far beyond their power and nature to do as it would be to kill a man at York before noon when they had been seen at London that same morning, and so on. But if these latter "idolaters," whose idolatry is only spiritual and committed in the mind, should be punished by death, then every covetous man or anyone else who sets his affection too much on any earthly creature would be executed—and yet, perhaps, the witch might escape scot-free.

<margin>2. Apostasy refuted.</margin>
Secondly, apostasy <note>The total desertion or departure from one's religion or faith.</note> is charged against them, from which it is inferred that they are worthy to die. But apostasy occurs when someone of sound judgment abandons the Gospel—having learned it and known it well—and does not only embrace impiety and infidelity, but opposes and resists the truth they previously professed. But alas, these poor women do not try to defend any impiety, but repent after receiving good advice.

<margin>3. Seducing of the people refuted.</margin>
Thirdly, they would have them executed for seducing the people. But God knows they have very little skill in rhetoric or art to seduce anyone—unless telling a tale of *Robin Good-fellow* <note>A mischievous nature spirit or "puck" in English folklore.</note> counts as deceiving and seducing. Neither their age nor their sex allows the opinion or accusation to be just, for they themselves are poor, seduced souls. I, for my part (as I have said elsewhere), have proved this point to be clearly false.

<margin>4. Sexual intercourse with an *Incubus* <note>A male demon believed to have sexual intercourse with sleeping women.</note> refuted.</margin>
Fourthly, regarding the accusation used by all writers against them for their sexual intercourse with an *Incubus*: the foolishness of men's belief is as much to be wondered at and mocked as the witches' own vain and impossible confessions. For the Devil is a spirit and has neither flesh nor bones, which are required to perform this action. Since he also lacks all physical organs, substance, and semen produced from blood, it would be foolish to spend too much time refuting something that does not exist in nature. 

And yet, I must say something about this because the belief in it is so strong and universally accepted, and the fables about it are so numerous. Because of this, writers like the authors of the *Malleus Maleficarum* <note>original: "M. Mal."; a famous 15th-century treatise on the prosecution of witches.</note>, Bodin, Hemingius, Hyperius, Daneau, Erastus, and others who take it upon themselves to write on this subject, are so deceived—or rather, they seek to deceive others. I wonder at their foolish credulity in this matter. For they claim, without doubt, that the Devil plays the part of a *Succubus* <note>A demon in female form.</note> to a man and carries away his "seed of generation," which he then delivers as an *Incubus* to a woman. <margin>How the Devil plays the Succubus and Incubus.</margin> They say that the woman is often made pregnant that way. They even claim that such a child will naturally become a witch, and they assert that Merlin was born in this manner.

<summary>The author systematically refutes four common legal charges against witches—idolatry, apostasy, seduction, and intercourse with demons—arguing that these claims are based on physical impossibilities and the delusions of the accused.</summary>

# BOOK III. The Discovery of the Lewd Incubus.

### CHAPTER 20.

<margin>An introductory warning to the readers.</margin>
Because I am forced—in order to more clearly expose and reveal this most filthy and horrible error—to stain my paper by writing certain of their beastly and lewd assertions and examples used to confirm their doctrine, I feel both ashamed and reluctant to even think about such filthiness, even though it is for the purpose of condemning it. I must urge you, the readers of this book, whose chaste ears cannot well endure to hear of such abominable lusts <note>original: "Lecheries"</note> as are gathered from the books of those witch-mongers <note>original: "Witch-mongers"; the author's term for those who credulously believe in and promote the reality of witchcraft and the persecution of "witches."</note> (though they are Doctors of Divinity and otherwise people of great authority and reputation), to skip over the next few pages. In these chapters, I have, like a stable-hand <note>original: "Groom"</note>, tossed their lewd material—which I myself loathe—as if into a stinking corner. I hope, however, that the other parts of my writing shall remain pleasant, and that this section is covered as discreetly as possible.

## CHAPTER I.

### Concerning the opinions of "witch-mongers" regarding evil spirits, and how they claim these spirits create themselves in a more excellent form than God made us.

<margin>*Hammer of Witches* <note>original: "Mal. malef." or *Malleus Maleficarum*</note>, part 2, chapter 4, question 1.</margin>
James Sprenger and Heinrich Institoris, in the *Hammer of Witches*, agreeing with Jean Bodin, Bartolommeo de Spina, Lambert Daneau, Thomas Erastus, Niels Hemmingsen, and the rest, engage in a lewd discourse. They labor to prove, through a foolish kind of philosophy, that evil spirits can not only take earthly forms and the shapes of men, but also counterfeit hearing, seeing, and so on. They likewise claim that these spirits can eat and devour food, and also retain, digest, and expel <note>original: "avoid"</note> it. Finally, they claim these spirits perform various activities, but especially excel in the use and art of sexual intercourse <note>original: "Venery"</note>. For the *Hammer of Witches* says that the eyes and ears of the mind are far more subtle than physical eyes or carnal ears. Indeed, it is affirmed there that just as they take on bodies and the appearance of limbs, so they take on minds and the likenesses of their operations. But, by the way, I would have them answer this question: our minds and souls are spiritual things. If our physical ears are blocked, what can they hear or understand of any external wisdom? And truly, a person with such a body as they imagine for these spirits—which create themselves, etc.—would be made of a far more excellent substance than the bodies God made in Paradise. Thus, the devil's craftsmanship would exceed the handiwork of God the Father, the Creator of all things.
<margin>If his physical eyes were out, he would see very poorly indeed.</margin>

### Of lewd *Incubi* and *Succubi*, and whether the action of sexual intercourse may be performed between witches and devils, and when witches first yielded to the *Incubus*.

<margin>Nider in *The Formicarius* <note>original: "fornicario"; likely a typo for Nider's *Formicarius* (The Anthill)</note>. Thomas of Cantimpré in *The Book of Bees*. In the sentences, distinction 4, article 4. Genesis 6:4.</margin>
Previously (they say), the *Incubus* <note>A male demon believed to have sexual relations with women.</note> was forced to ravish women against their will until the year 1400. But now, since that time, witches consent willingly to their desires—so much so that some witches have practiced that trade of lechery with an *Incubus* for twenty or thirty days together, as was confessed by forty-eight witches burned at Ravensburg <note>original: "Ravenspurge"</note>. But what "fine fellows" the *Incubus* fathers upon these witches is allegedly proven by Thomas Aquinas, Jean Bodin, the *Hammer of Witches*, Andreas Hyperius, and others.

This is supposedly proven, first, by the Devil's cunning in distinguishing the differences in the human seed. Secondly, by his understanding of the physical readiness of women to receive such seed. Thirdly, by his knowledge of the constellations, which are favorable to such physical effects. And lastly, by the excellent physical constitution <note>original: "complexion"</note> of those the Devil chooses to father such notable people upon, who are supposedly the cause of the greatness and excellence of children born this way.

There can be no certain <note>original: "infallible"</note> rule given, though a probable distinction may be set down, as to whether an *Incubus*, in the act of sexual intercourse <note>original: "Venery"</note>, always pours seed out of his assumed body. And if it is said that the seed will grow cold on the way and so lose its natural heat, and consequently its power, the *Hammer of Witches*, Lambert Daneau, and the rest answer that the Devil can carry it in such a way that no heat shall leave it, and so on.

### CHAPTER IV.

*That the power of reproduction is hindered both outwardly and inwardly by witches; and of various men who had their genitals taken from them by witches, and restored again by the same means.*

They also claim that the power of reproduction <note>original: "Generation"</note> is hindered by witches, both inwardly and outwardly. For internally, they suppress a man's courage and stop the passage of his seed so that it cannot descend to the reproductive organs. They also cause outward harm using images, herbs, and so on. To prove this is true, you shall hear certain stories from the *Hammer of Witches* <note>original: "M. Mal." or *Malleus Maleficarum*, a 15th-century treatise on the prosecution of witches</note> that are worth noting.

<margin>*Hammer of Witches*, part 2, question 1, chapter 6.</margin> A young priest at Meersburg <note>original: "Mespurge"</note>, in the Diocese of Constance, was bewitched so that he had no power to sleep with <note>original: "occupy"</note> any women other than one. To be delivered from that bondage, he sought to flee to another country where he might practice that "priestly occupation" more freely. But it was all in vain, for he was always brought back as far by night as he went forward during the day—sometimes by land, and sometimes through the air as if he flew. And if this is not true, I am sure that James Sprenger <note>one of the primary authors of the *Malleus Maleficarum*</note> is lying.

For further confirmation of our belief in the *Incubus*, the *Hammer of Witches* cites a story of a notable matter that happened at Ravensburg <note>original: "Ravenspurge"</note>, which is just as true and as "clean" as the rest. A young man lying with a girl in that town (he says) was forced to leave his "instruments of lovemaking" <note>original: "instruments of Venery"</note> behind him by means of that deceptive art of witchcraft, so that in that place nothing could be seen or felt but his plain body. This young man was told by another witch to go to the woman he suspected and ask for her help, by fair means or foul. Meeting her soon after, he treated her kindly, but that was useless. Therefore, he caught her by the throat and began to strangle her with a towel, saying, "Restore my tool to me, or you shall die for it!" She became swollen and black in the face, and because of his violent handling she was ready to die. She said, "Let me go, and I will help you." While he was loosening the towel, she put her hand into his codpiece <note>a pouch at the crotch of tight-fitting breeches</note> and touched the place, saying, "Now you have your desire." And at that very instant, he felt himself restored.

<margin>James Sprenger in *Hammer of Witches*, part 2, question 1.</margin> Also, a reverend father—notorious for his life, holiness, and knowledge, and a friar of the order and company in Speyer <note>original: "Spire"</note>—reported that a young man in Speyer made a pitiful complaint to him about a similar loss. But the father’s gravity did not allow him to believe such reports easily, and therefore he made the young man untie his codpiece strings <note>original: "untruss his cod-piece-point"</note> and saw that the complaint was true and justified. He then advised, or rather commanded, the youth to go to the witch he suspected and entreat her with flattering words to be so kind as to restore his "instrument." He obtained it by those means and soon returned to show his gratitude, telling the holy father of his success. But the father only believed him because he insisted on being an eyewitness <note>original: "Oculatus testis"</note>; he made the youth pull down his breeches and so was satisfied of the truth and certainty of it.

### C H A P. V.

->How Bishop *Sylvanus’s* lechery was exposed and then covered up. How maids with yellow hair are most troubled by *Incubus* demons. How married men are bewitched to sleep with other men's wives while rejecting their own.<-

You shall read in the *Golden Legend* how, in the nighttime, an *Incubus* <note>a demon believed to have sex with sleeping women</note> came to a lady's bedside and made passionate love to her. Being offended by this, she cried out so loudly that company arrived and found him under her bed in the likeness of the holy Bishop *Sylvanus*. This holy man was much defamed by the incident, until at length this infamy was cleared by the confession of a devil at *St. Jerome’s* tomb. Oh, what an excellent piece of witchcraft was worked by *Sylvanus*! 

Similarly, *St. Christine* insisted on taking another maid's *Incubus* and lying in her place; the story says she was severely oppressed <note>original: "accloyed"; weighed down or physically overwhelmed</note>. She was a "shrew" <note>a malicious or ill-tempered woman; here likely a pun on her boldness</note> indeed, to insist on changing beds with her companion who was troubled every night by an *Incubus*, just to deal with him herself.
