Also, it is written in the *Legend* regarding *St. Bernard*, that a pretty girl who had used the body of an *Incubus* for six or seven years in *Aquitaine* (being perhaps weary of him because he had grown old) decided she wanted to go to *St. Bernard* for a while. But the *Incubus* told her that if she forsook him after he had been her true lover for so long, he would be revenged upon her. However, regardless of what might happen, she went to *St. Bernard*, who gave her his staff and told her to lay it in the bed beside her. And indeed, the Devil—fearing the bed-staff, or perhaps fearing that *St. Bernard* himself lay there—did not dare to approach her chamber that night. What he did afterward, I am uncertain. You may find other details of this, and many other such "bawdy lies," in the *Golden Legend*. 

But here again, we must not forget the Inquisitors’ note: that many men are so bewitched that they cannot sleep with their own wives, yet they are perfectly capable of doing so with anyone else's wife. This "witchcraft" is practiced among many bad husbands, for whom it would be a very good excuse to say they were simply bewitched.

### CHAPTER IX.

#### A strange cure performed for one who was bothered by an Incubus.

<margin>Jason Pratensis, *On the Disease of the Brain*, chapter 16 <note>original: "Jason Pratensis de cerebri morbo, cap. 16."</note>.</margin>
Now, being tired of repeating so many most horrible lecheries, and the very filthy and fictional actions and passions of witches, along with the spirit known as the *Incubus*: I will end with a true story taken from *Jason Pratensis*, which, although it is crude, is not quite as unclean as the rest.

<margin>The priest is stubborn in the error of his imagination <note>original: "fantasie"</note>.</margin>
Recently, a Catholic priest <note>original: "Mass-Priest"</note> came to me (he says), making a pitiful moan and saying that if I did not help him, he would be ruined and utterly destroyed, so great was his illness. For, he said, "I used to be fair and fat, and of an excellent complexion; and look how I appear now, being a mere ghost consisting of skin and bone," etc. "What is the matter?" asked *Jason*. "I will show you, sir," said the priest. "Almost every night, a certain woman, unknown to me, comes and lies so heavily upon my chest that I cannot catch my breath. I have no power to cry out, nor do my hands work to shove her away, nor my feet to move away from her." I smiled (said *Jason*) and told him that he was afflicted with a disease called *Incubus*, or the "mare" <note>The "nightmare," then thought to be a physical weight or a spirit sitting on the chest</note>, and the rest was fantasy and vain imagination. I see her when she comes upon me and I struggle to push her back, but I am so weakened that I cannot. For a remedy, I have run from place to place, but I could get no help. At length, I went to an old friar who was considered an eccentric fellow, and I thought I would get help from him. But I got nothing at all from him except that, for a remedy, he told me to pray to God—whom, I am sure, I had already tired out with my long prayers. Then I went to an old woman," said the priest, "who was said to be a clever witch. And although," he said, "respect for my religious orders somewhat terrified me from following her advice, my many needs and especially my pains moved me to test her words. # Of Spirits in General: Devils and Spirits. Chapter 1. 41

These spirits invisibly accompany many righteous men and protect cities and countries from plagues, war, and the infestations of wicked spirits. It is the role of these principalities to contend and wage war against the powers of darkness, leading to the confusion of the Kingdom of Darkness.

<margin>What spirits may be summoned.</margin>
12. But those spirits that belong to this outward world and are of the elemental quality—subject to a beginning and an end, and to varying lifespans—may be solicited by incantations. They can also inform magicians of all the secrets of nature, yet they do so vaguely (because they lack physical organs), so that it is hardly possible for anyone who has fellowship with them to learn any manual skill perfectly and clearly from them.

<margin>The nature of the Astral Spirits.</margin>
13. Many have debated the natures of these astral spirits. Some allege that they are part of the fallen angels and, consequently, subject to the torments of hell at the last judgment. Others claim they are the departed souls of men and women, confined to these outward elements until the end of the world <note>original: "Consummation"</note>. Finally, others—such as *Del Rio* <note>Martin Del Rio (1551–1608) was a famous Jesuit theologian and author of a major work on magic and demonology.</note>, *Nagar* the Indian magician, and the Platonists—affirm *that their nature is halfway between heaven and hell, and that they reign in a third kingdom separate from both, having no other judgment or doom to expect forever.*

<margin>Their ranks.</margin>
14. But to speak more closely of their nature, they come from the astral source <note>original: "source of the Stars"</note> and have their own lifespans, where some live hundreds and some thousands of years. Their food is the *Gas* <term>original: Gas; a term coined by Jan Baptist van Helmont to describe the "life-spirit" or volatile essence of a substance</term> of the water and the *Blas* <term>original: Blas; another Helmontian term referring to the motive power or vital influence of the stars and atmosphere</term> of the air. In their appearance or countenances, they differ in vigor and cheerfulness. They occupy various places in this world, such as woods, mountains, waters, air, fiery flames, clouds, stars, mines, and hidden treasures, as well as ancient buildings and sites where people were killed. Some, again, are familiar in houses and frequently converse with and appear to mortals.

<margin>Their actions and emotions.</margin>
15. They are capable of hunger, grief, passion, and frustration. They do not have anything within them that would lead them to God, being merely composed of the most spiritual part of the elements. When they are worn out, they return into their proper essence or primary quality again, just as ice returns to water when it is melted. They meet in mighty troops and wage war against one another. They also reproduce with each other and have power sometimes to cause great disturbances in the air and clouds. They can also clothe themselves with visible bodies made from the four elements, appearing in companies upon hills and mountains. They often deceive and delude those who observe apparitions, who mistake such sights for omens of great change; in reality, these are nothing but the sports and pastimes of these frolicsome spirits, such as armies in the air, troops marching on the land, noises and slaughter, tempests and lightning, and so on.

<margin>The distinct orders of starry spirits.</margin>
16. These astral spirits should be considered in various ways. Some are separate and independent beings that are not assigned to any specific work or service. Others are subservient to the angels who have dominion over the influences of the stars. Others are the astral spirits of deceased people which (if the person was disturbed and troubled at their death) continue for many years in the atmosphere of this world among these airy spirits. This causes great restlessness for the soul of the person to whom they belong. There are various reasons why such spirits do not rest: 
1. When they are enchanted by witchcraft and bound to wander for a set number of years—such as twenty-one or twenty-eight years <note>original: "thrice or fourtimes seven"</note>—before they can be dissolved into nothingness. 
2. When the person has been murdered, so that the spirit can never be at rest until the crime is discovered. 
3. When desires and lusts for a wife, children, house, lands, or money are very strong at their departure. It is a certain truth that this same spirit belonging to the stars will hanker after these things; it is drawn back by the strong desires and obsession of the imagination <note>original: "fixation of the Imagination"</note> which is left behind. It can never be at rest until the thing for which it is disturbed is accomplished. 
4. When treasure has been hidden, or any secret thing has been committed...

### CHAPTER XI.

### *That the Nightmare is a natural disease: with remedies for it: besides the magical cures expressed here.*

<margin>What the Nightmare <term>original: "Incubus"</term> is, and who is most troubled by it.</margin>
But in truth, this "Incubus" is a bodily disease (as has been said), although it extends to a disturbance of the mind. Some call it "the Mare," and it oppresses many in their sleep so severely that they are unable to call for help or move themselves under the burden of that heavy fluid <note>original: "humor" — in early medicine, the body was thought to be governed by four fluids or humors</note>. It is produced by a thick vapor proceeding from indigestion and rawness in the stomach. When this vapor ascends into the head, it oppresses the brain, so much so that many are weakened by it, being haunted by it nightly. Those most troubled with this disease are people who, being subject to it, lie flat on their backs; thus, to turn and lie on one's side is an immediate remedy. Likewise, if anyone hears the groaning of the sufferer and speaks to them so as to wake them, they are immediately relieved. However, there are magical cures for it; for example:

> *St. George, St. George, our Lady’s knight,*
> *He walked by day, so did he by night:*
> *Until such time as he her found,*
> *He beat her, and he bound her,*
> *Until she pledged her truth to him,*
> *That she would not come to him that night.*

In this charm, St. George, our Lady's knight, was named three times as "St. George."
*Also*, hang a stone over the bed of the afflicted person. This stone must naturally have a hole in it through which a string may be placed, and so be hung over the diseased or bewitched party, whether it be a man, woman, or horse <note>These are often called "hag stones" or "holey stones" in folklore, used to protect against witchcraft</note>.

<margin>*Malleus Maleficarum*, part 2, question 2, chapter 1, column 2. Leonhart Fuchs, *On the Method of Curing*.</margin>
*Also*, you shall read in the *Malleus Maleficarum* <note>original: "M. Malefic." — The Hammer of Witches, a famous 15th-century manual for hunting witches</note> that excommunication is very notable, and better than any charm for this purpose. There are also other verses and charms devised for this disease, which is the common cloak used to hide the ignorance of bad physicians. But Leonhart Fuchs <note>A famous German physician (1501–1566)</note>, in his first book and 13th chapter, does not only describe this disease and its causes, but also sets down very learnedly the cure for it, to the utter confusion of the "witch-mongers'" folly in this matter. Hyperius <note>Andreas Hyperius (1511–1564), a Flemish theologian</note>, being much bewitched and blinded in this matter of witchcraft, hovers around the interpretation of Genesis 6—from which the opinion of the Incubus and Succubus <note>Male and female demons thought to have sex with sleeping humans</note> is twisted. He cites the verse: "The sons of God saw the daughters of men, that they were beautiful, and they took for themselves wives from all whom they chose, etc." <note>original: "Viderunt filii Dei filias hominum, quod elegantes essent, acceperunt sibi in uxores ex omnibus, quas elegerant, &c."</note>. He seems to maintain that absurd opinion based on hearsay; and yet in the end, he is driven to conclude this: namely, that regarding the evil spirits Incubus and Succubus, no firm reason or proof can be brought out of Scripture. He uses these very words: "Let these be spoken as probabilities, since we are destitute of the support of the Scriptures in this cause" <note>original: "Hæ ut probabilia dicta sunto, quandoquidem Scripturarum præsidio hac in causa destituimur."</note>. This is as if he should say, "Take this as spoken as a likelihood based on human reason, because we lack the Bible to maintain the truth of the cause."

<margin>Tertullian in the book *On the Apparel of Women*. Sulpicius Severus in his *Summary of Sacred History*.</margin>
Tertullian and Sulpicius Severus interpret the "Sons of God" in that passage to be angels or evil spirits who became enamored with the beauty of those girls, and finally fathered giants by them. This is thoroughly disproved by John Chrysostom in his 22nd sermon on Genesis, but especially by the context of the text itself.

### CHAPTER XII.

#### Geoffrey Chaucer’s judgment on the trickery of the Incubus.

Now, after all this long discourse on abominable, hidden wickedness, I will conclude here with certain verses by Geoffrey Chaucer. Just as he sniffed out the absurdities of the Catholic Church <note>original: "Popery" — a derogatory term for Roman Catholicism used by Protestant writers of this era</note>, he also discovered the priests' trickery regarding this matter of the Incubus. As much as the times would allow him, he mocked their foolishness and falsehood in this way:

<margin>Geoffrey Chaucer in the beginning of *The Wife of Bath’s Tale*.</margin>
> *For now the great charity and prayers*
> *Of licensed beggars <note>original: "Limitors" — friars licensed to beg within a specific limit or area</note> and other holy friars,*
> *That search every land and every stream,*
> *As thick as motes in a sunbeam,*
> *Blessing halls, kitchens, chambers, and private rooms <note>original: "Bowers"</note>,*
> *Cities, towns <note>original: "Boroughs"</note>, castles, and high towers,*
> *Villages <note>original: "Thropes" — from "thorp," an Old English word for a village or hamlet</note>, barns, sheep-pens, and dairies,*
> *This is why there are now no fairies;*
> *For where an elf used to walk,*
> *There walks now the friar himself,*
> *In the mid-mornings <note>original: "under meals"</note> and in the early hours,*
> *And says his morning prayers <note>original: "matins"</note> and his holy things*
> *As he goes about his assigned district;*
> *Women may walk safely up and down,*
> *In every bush and under every tree,*
> *There is no other Incubus but him, etc.*

## CHAPTER I.

First, regarding the Devil, Bodin says that he most properly and commonly transforms himself into a goat, supporting that opinion with the 33rd and 34th chapters of **Isaiah** <note>original: "Esay"</note>, where there is not one tiny bit of evidence pointing to any such purpose. He even accuses one of the highest princes in Christendom, in recent times, of being one of these kinds of witches, so that he could turn himself into a wolf whenever he wished. He asserts that the prince was spotted and often seen performing that villainy because he wanted to be considered the King of all Witches. He says that this transformation is most common in Greece and throughout all of Asia, as traveling merchants have reported to him. For in the year 1542, when **Sultan Suleiman** <note>original: "Solimon"</note> reigned, there was such a force and multitude of these kinds of wolves in **Constantinople** <note>Modern-day Istanbul</note> that the Emperor gathered 150 of them into one flock, and they departed out of the city in the presence of all the people.

Of Astral Spirits. **Devils and Spirits. Chapter 3.** 45

Chapter 3.

*Regarding the astral spirits of deceased men: what they are, why they reappear, and what witchcraft may be performed through them.*

<margin>The spirits of men return again.</margin>
1. Just as the independent astral spirits—those which do not belong to any specific deceased person—survive or continue for many years, so too do the spirits of people who died in a state of discontent or melancholy. It is often known that they return again, causing terror to families and households as they wait for an opportunity to unburden themselves so that they may finally enter their desired rest.

<margin>All people have starry spirits.</margin>
2. Many people believe *that what appears is only the Devil taking their likeness.* However, more learned scholars have sufficiently demonstrated through example and experience *that the apparition truly belongs to the deceased person.* Nor can it easily be denied that every man and woman, while they live their natural life, possesses a sidereal <note>original: "Syderial," meaning relating to the stars or constellations</note> or starry spirit. This spirit originates entirely from elemental properties. Depending on whether the person’s capacity was weak or strong, this spirit continues for a longer or shorter time after the body’s death.

<margin>What types of people most frequently reappear.</margin>
3. People who are secretly murdered, and those who secretly kill themselves, most frequently appear again. They wander near the place where their corpse <note>original: "Carcaſe"</note> is located until their radical moisture <term>radical moisture: In Renaissance medicine, a vital fluid believed to sustain life; once it dried up, the body and its immediate spirit would fully dissolve.</term> is completely consumed. According to the opinion of Paracelsus, after that moisture is gone, they can no longer reappear; instead, they are resolved back into their original state, or *Astrum* <note>original: "Astrum" (Latin for star or celestial body)</note>, after a certain number of months or years, depending on the strength of that first attraction which was the only cause of their returning.

<margin>The manner and time of their appearance.</margin>
4. The ways and times they appear vary. Sometimes, before the person to whom they belong departs this life, they forewarn him through external visions that the day of his death is approaching. This is reported of Codrus Laenus, to whom an empty, meager ghost appeared at midnight, signifying to him *how sad and mournful <note>original: "lachrymable"</note> a tragedy was soon to attend him, and also adding that the ghost would visit him during its execution.* This proved to be true; at the very instant his treacherous wife stabbed him in the heart, he suddenly beheld the same ghost making preparations for his burial while he was still alive after the fatal wound was given.

<margin>The reason for it.</margin>
5. Sometimes the starry spirit of a person appears to a beloved companion many hundreds of miles away, even when that companion was unaware of the person's death. It has often been heard that while none of the deceased person’s family or kindred were disturbed by the spirit or even aware of its presence, it would reveal itself to some of its most intimate acquaintances. It begs them to perform some ceremony or another so that it may return to rest, or else it reveals some treasure hidden by the person while alive, or some murder they had committed. However, the most frequent cause of their returning is when the person has been privately murdered.

<margin>The power of magicians over them.</margin>
6. Such is the poisonous malice and bloody spirit of murderers that it is not enough for them to have privately robbed their victims of their lives; they also use certain earnest wishes, curses, and conjurations to command <note>original: "adjure"</note> them to never have the power to appear again for a certain term of years. These wishes, being earnestly cast out from the hellish root within the murderer, exceedingly torment the murdered person's spirit, making a deep impression upon it. Thus, the spirit is always in continual sorrow and anguish until the term of years expires and the murder is made known to the world. After this discovery, it returns to perfect rest. This is well known to those experienced in witchcraft and cruel murders, though it is not common for those who murder only once.

# BOOK V. The Discovery of Witches' Transformations.

<margin>Irony.</margin>
The reason why witches are most commonly turned into wolves, he says, is because they usually eat children, just as wolves eat cattle. Likewise <note>original: "Item"</note>, the reason why others are truly turned into donkeys <note>original: "Asses"</note> is because those people have been too eager to understand the secrets of witches. As for why witches are turned into cats, he provides no reason; therefore (to help him finish that explanation), I say that witches are bad-tempered women <term>queans: a derogatory term for a woman, often implying she is ill-tempered or of low character</term>, and they often scratch one another or their neighbors' faces, and therefore perhaps they are turned into cats. But I have silenced twenty of these witch-believers <note>original: "Witchmongers"</note> with this one question: namely, whether a witch who can turn a woman into a cat can also turn a cat into a woman?

->Absurd reasons brought by Bodin, and others like him, for the confirmation of transformations.<-

<margin>Genesis 19:24, 26, 27.</margin>
These examples and reasons might make us doubt whether every donkey, wolf, or cat we see was actually a man, a woman, or a child. I wonder that no one uses this distinction when defining what a human being is. But why should one argue against these supposed creations and re-creations when Bodin dismisses all our arguments with a single word? He admits that none can create anything but God, acknowledges the weight of the Church laws <note>original: "Canons"</note>, and even embraces the opinions of the theologians who write against him on this matter. Indeed, he now affirms (contrary to what he has said elsewhere) that the Devil cannot alter his own form. And look, this is his distinction: "The essential form (that is, reason) is not changed, but only the shape or figure" <note>original: "Non essentialis forma (id est ratio) sed figura solum permutatur"</note>. By this, he claims it is easy enough to create men or beasts with life, so long as they remain without reason. However, I think it is an easier matter to turn Bodin’s reason into the reason of a donkey than to turn his body into the shape of a sheep. He claims the latter is easy because Lot’s wife was turned into a stone by the Devil, which only shows his gross ignorance. It is as if God—who commanded Lot under pain of death not to look back and who destroyed the city of Sodom at that very instant—had not also turned her into a pillar of salt. <header>A Man Turned into a Donkey. On Witchcraft. CHAPTER 3.</header>

### CHAPTER III.

### About a Man Turned into a Donkey, and Returned Again into a Man, by One of Bodin's Witches: Saint Augustine's Opinion Thereof.

<margin>Why the devil would the witch choose to target the Englishman?</margin>
<margin>A strange metamorphosis of the body, but not of the mind.</margin>
It happened in the city of Salamis <note>original: "Salamin"</note>, in the Kingdom of Cyprus (which has a good harbor), that a ship laden with merchandise stayed there for a short time. In the meantime, many of the soldiers and mariners went ashore to gather fresh provisions. Among them, a certain Englishman—a sturdy young man—went to a woman's house a little way out of the city and not far from the seaside to see if she had any eggs to sell. The woman, seeing that he was a healthy <term>lusty: in this context, healthy and strong</term> young man, a stranger far from his country—meaning that if he went missing, there would be less investigation—considered how to destroy him. She asked him to stay there a while while she went to fetch some eggs for him. However, she stayed away so long that the young man called out to her, asking her to hurry. He told her the tide would soon turn, and the ship would leave him behind. Nevertheless, after wasting some time, she finally brought him a few eggs and told him to return to her if the ship had already departed. The young man headed back toward the ship, but before boarding, he felt he had to eat an egg or two to satisfy his hunger. Within a short time, he became mute and lost his mind, as he later claimed. When he tried to board the ship, the sailors beat him back with a club <term>cudgel: a short, thick stick used as a weapon</term>, saying, "What plague <term>murren: an infectious disease of cattle, used here as a curse or exclamation</term> ails this donkey? Where the devil is this donkey going?" The donkey, or the young man—I am not sure which name to call him—being repeatedly driven away and hearing them call him a donkey, realized he could not speak a word. Yet, he could understand everyone. He realized he had been bewitched by the woman at whose house he had been. Therefore, since he could not get onto the boat and was forced to stay and watch it depart, being beaten from place to place like a donkey, he remembered the witch's words and the words of his own companions who called him a donkey. He returned to the witch's house and remained in her service for three years, doing no work with his hands, but carrying whatever burdens she laid on his back. His only comfort was that although he was considered a donkey by strangers and beasts, the witch and all her kind knew he was actually a man.

<margin>Note the devotion of the donkey.</margin>
After three years had passed, early one morning, he went into town ahead of his mistress. She stayed behind for a moment, perhaps to relieve herself. In the meantime, being near a church, he heard a small sanctus bell <term>Saccaring bell: a small bell rung during the Mass, specifically at the elevation of the Host</term> ringing for the elevation of the Host during a morning Mass. Not daring to enter the church for fear of being beaten and driven out with clubs, he knelt down in the churchyard with great devotion on his hind legs and lifted his forefeet over his head, just as the priest holds up the Sacrament during the elevation. Certain merchants from Genoa <note>original: "Genua"</note> saw this miraculous sight and watched in wonder. Soon, the witch arrived with a club in her hand and began beating the donkey away. Because such types of witchcraft were reportedly very common in those parts, the merchants arranged to have both the donkey and the witch arrested <term>attached: legally seized or arrested</term> by a judge. Under interrogation and torture on the rack, she confessed to everything and promised that if she were allowed to go home, she would restore him to his human form. Being released for that purpose, she did so. Nevertheless, they arrested her again and burned her, and the young man returned to his own country with a joyful and happy heart.

### *A summary of the former fable, with a refutation of it, after a proper examination.*

Concerning the truth or probability of this play-act <note>original: "enterlude"</note> between Bodin, the *Malleus Maleficarum*, the witch, the donkey, the Mass, the merchants, the inquisitors, the torturers, and so on: First, I wonder at the miracle of this transformation <note>original: "Transubstantiation" – Scot is likely mocking the Catholic doctrine of the Eucharist by applying the term to the donkey story</note>. In my discussion of spirits and devils, which is the 17th book of this volume.

But where was the young man's own human shape during those three years when he was turned into a donkey? It is a certain and general rule that two physical forms <term>substantial forms: the essential nature or shape of a thing</term> cannot exist in one subject *at the same time* <note>original: "simul & semel"</note>, which these authors themselves admit. The form of the beast occupied some space in the air, and so I think the form of the man should have done so as well. To turn a man's body—without him feeling it—into such a thin, airy nature that it can neither be seen nor felt may seem unlikely, but it is actually impossible. The air is unstable and does not stay in one place; therefore, this airy creature would soon be carried off into another region, as I have proved elsewhere at length. But in reality, our bodies are visible, sensitive, and physical, and are endowed with many other excellent properties that all the devils in hell are unable to alter. Not one hair of our head can perish, fall away, or be transformed without the special providence of Almighty God.

<margin>
Lambert Daneau in *Dialogue on Witches*, chapter 3. Augustine, *The City of God*, chapters 17 and 18. <note>original: "Dan. in dialog. cap 3. Aug. lib. de Civ. Dei. cap. 17. 18."</note>
</margin>

To continue regarding the likelihood of this story: what a coincidence it was that this young man from England, having just landed in those parts, and that old woman of Cyprus—both being of such low social status—could understand each other's speech! England and Cyprus are many hundreds of miles apart, and their languages are very different. I am certain that in these days, when trade is more common and learning is more valued, few young or old sailors in this kingdom can speak or understand the language spoken in Salamis <note>original: "Salamin"</note>, Cyprus, which is a kind of Greek; and just as few old women there can speak our language. But Jean Bodin will say, "You hear that at the Inquisitor’s command, and through the torturer's punishment, she promised to restore him to his own shape—and so she did, being forced to do so." I answer that just as the whole story is a godless <note>original: "impious"</note> fable, so this claim is false and contradicts their own doctrine, which maintains that the witch does nothing except by the permission and leave of God. For if she could do or undo such a thing at her own pleasure, or at the command of the Inquisitors, or for fear of the torturers, or for love of the person, or out of remorse, then it is not done by the extraordinary permission or direction of God—unless you want to make God a partner to old witches. For my part, I wonder most how they can toss and turn a man's body so much—making it smaller and larger, such as like a mouse or a donkey—and yet the man feels no pain all the while. I am not the only one confused by this; for Lambert Daneau <note>original: "Danaus"</note>, a major supporter of their follies, says that although Augustine and Apuleius write very credibly about these matters, he will never believe that witches can change men into other forms like donkeys, apes, wolves, bears, or mice.

# BOOK V. THE DISCOVERY. THE FORMER LIES CONFUTED.

<margin>Philippians 1:23</margin>
...is dead. And surely, when the soul has departed from the body, the life of man is dissolved; and therefore **Paul** wished to be dissolved so that he might be with Christ. The body of man is subject to various kinds of fevers, sicknesses, and infirmities to which a donkey's body is not inclined; and man's body must be fed with bread, etc., and not with hay. Bodin’s donkey-headed man must either eat hay or nothing, as appears in the story. Man’s body is also subject to death and has its days numbered. If this fellow had died in the meantime—as his hour might have come, for all the devils, the witch, or **Bodin** knew—I wonder then what would have become of this donkey? Or how the witch could have restored him to his shape? Or whether he should have risen at the Day of Judgment in a donkey’s body and shape?

<margin>1 Corinthians 15:44</margin>
*For Paul says that the very body which is sown and buried as a natural body is raised as a spiritual body.* The life of Jesus is made manifest in our mortal flesh, and not in the flesh of a donkey.

God has endowed every man and every thing with its own proper nature, substance, form, qualities, and gifts, and directs their ways. As for the ways of a donkey, He takes no such care; however, they also have their own distinct properties and

<margin>1 Corinthians 15:39</margin>
substance specific to themselves. *For there is one flesh (says Paul) of men, another flesh of beasts, another of fishes, and another of birds:* And therefore it is absolutely against the ordinance of God (who has made me a man) that I should fly like a bird, or swim like a fish, or creep like a worm, or become a donkey in shape. Insofar as even if God would give me leave, I could not do it; for it would be contrary to His own order and decree, and to the constitution of any

<margin>Psalm 119</margin>
body which He has made. Yes, the spirits themselves have their laws and limits prescribed, beyond which they cannot pass even a hair’s breadth; otherwise, God would be contrary to Himself, which is far from His nature. Neither is God's omnipotence limited by this, but rather the devil's impotence is manifested; he has no power other than that which God from the beginning has appointed to him, consistent with his nature and substance. He may well be restrained from his power and will, but beyond that he cannot pass, being God's minister only in that which He has enabled him to do from the beginning: which is that he, being a spirit, may (with God’s permission and ordinance) vitiate <term>vitiate: to spoil, impair, or corrupt the quality or spirit of something</term> and corrupt the spirit and will of man, in which he is very diligent.

What a beastly assertion it is that a man, whom God has made according to His own similitude and likeness, should be turned into a beast by a witch! What an impiety it is to affirm that a donkey’s body is the temple of the Holy Ghost? Or that a donkey is the child of God, and God is his Father, as is said of man? Which **Paul** so divinely refutes in his letter to the Corinthians, saying,

<margin>1 Corinthians 6:19, 15, 2, 13</margin>
*That our bodies are the members of Christ: in which we are to glorify God, for the body is for the Lord, and the Lord is for the body.* Surely he does not mean for a donkey’s body, as by this time I hope is clear; so much so that **Bodin** might go hide himself for shame. This is especially true when he understands that even into these bodies of ours, which God has framed after His own likeness, He has also breathed that spirit which **Bodin** says is now remaining within a donkey’s body—a creature which

<margin>Psalm 8:5, 6, 7, 8</margin>
God has subjected in such servitude under the foot of man. God is so mindful of man that He has made him a little lower than the angels—even than Himself—and crowned him with glory and honor <note>original: "worship"</note>, and gave him dominion over the works of His hands, putting all things under his feet: all sheep and oxen, yes, wolves, donkeys, and all other beasts of the field, the birds <note>original: "souls" (likely an OCR error for "fowls")</note> of the air, the fish of the sea, etc. Bodin’s favorite poet, **Ovid**, whose ***Metamorphoses*** counts for so much in his eyes, says this to the overthrow of this fantastical imagination:

->He gave man a face turned upward, and commanded him to behold the sky,<-

...mountains, caves, marshlands <note>original: "fens"</note>, mines, ruins, desolate places, and ancient buildings. The ancient pagans called these by various names, such as nymphs, satyrs, lamias <note>original: "Lamii," a type of female demon or witch</note>, dryads <note>original: "Dryades," tree spirits</note>, sylvans <note>original: "Sylvanes," forest spirits</note>, and kobolds <note>original: "Cobali," mischievous spirits or goblins</note>. More specifically, they spoke of the fairies, who primarily inhabit mountains and the caverns of the earth. Their nature is to create strange apparitions on the earth in meadows or on mountains. These look like men, women, soldiers, kings, ladies, children, and horsemen clothed in green. According to legend, they steal hemp stalks from the fields at night to transform them into horses.

Besides this, it is credibly stated and believed by many that "changelings" <note>children believed to have been secretly substituted by fairies</note> or those suffering from lunacy have been brought by such spirits and hobgoblins. They supposedly take away the true child and leave these others in their place. Such people are commonly "half out of their wits" and prone to many strange <note>original: "Antick"</note> behaviors and extravagant fantasies. However, these conditions actually result from the powerful influence of the planets at the time of their birth <note>the author is arguing for an astrological explanation rather than a folkloric one</note>, rather than from such foolish superstitions.

8. These cheerful <note>original: "jocund"</note> and playful spirits are said to amuse themselves at night <margin>Fairies.</margin> by tumbling and playing pranks on servants and shepherds in country houses. They pinch them until they are black and blue and sometimes leave bread, butter, and cheese for them. If the people refuse to eat this food, some misfortune will undoubtedly happen to them because of these fairies. Many people have been taken away by these spirits for a fortnight or a month at a time, carried in chariots through the air over hills, valleys, rocks, and precipices. Eventually, they are found lying in some meadow or mountain, having lost their senses and usually missing one of their limbs as well.

9. Certainly, the *Lares* and *Penates* <note>original: Roman household gods</note> or domestic spirits of the ancient pagans <margin>Household spirits.</margin> were nothing other than spirits of this kind. For several years, they would reside in one house until they were offended or some wrong was committed by the family. They would then depart and never be heard of again. Plenty of such examples can be found in the works of Olaus Magnus <note>a 16th-century Swedish historian</note> and in Hector Boethius's <note>a 16th-century Scottish historian</note> history of Scotland. These authors relate wonderful stories about "Robin Goodfellows" <note>a mischievous nature sprite or "puck"</note> and other such spirits that have been familiar among mankind.

10. Luridan, a familiar spirit of this kind, lived for many years on the island of <margin>Luridan, a familiar spirit.</margin> Pomona <note>the largest island of the Orkneys in Scotland</note>. He performed the work of both a man-servant and a maid-servant with wonderful diligence for the families he haunted. He swept their rooms, washed their dishes, and made their fires before anyone was awake in the morning. This Luridan claimed that he was the astral genius <note>a protective spirit or guiding entity associated with the stars</note> of that island.

To support the idea of witches' transportations <note>the belief that witches were physically moved through the air by demons</note>, they point to the words of the Gospel, where it is said that the Devil *takes up Christ and sets him on a pinnacle of the Temple, and on a mountain, etc.* Even if this had happened in the way and form they imagine, it does not follow that witches could do the same, nor that the Devil would do it for them at their whim; for spirits do not know a person's thoughts, nor can they communicate with them in that way. But I answer that even if the passage were to be understood as literally <note>original: "grossly"</note> as they imagine, it would still contribute nothing to their argument. For I hope they will not say that Christ had prepared any ointments <note>original: "ointments," referring to "flying ointments" witches were said to use</note> or entered into any pact <note>original: "league"</note> with the Devil, and by virtue of that was transported out of the wilderness to the top of the Temple in Jerusalem. Nor would they say that the Devil could have mastery over his body—he whose soul the Devil could never seize—especially when Christ could have (with a flick of his finger) called upon and received the assistance of many legions of angels. Neither, I think, will they presume to make Christ a participant in the Devil’s purpose and sin in that matter.

If they say this was an act brought about by the special providence of God and by His appointment so that the Scripture might be fulfilled, then what do our <term>witchmongers</term> <note>a derogatory term for those who believe in and promote the reality of witchcraft</note> gain from this passage? First, they may not use a unique, specific example to prove such a broad, general argument. Furthermore, if it were by God's special providence and appointment, then why should it not be done by the hand of God, as it was in the story of Job? Or, if it were God’s special purpose and pleasure that such an extraordinary matter be accomplished by the hand of the Devil, could not God have given the wicked angel extraordinary power and clothed him in an extraordinary shape? By this, he might be made an instrument able to accomplish the task, just as God did with His angel who carried Habakkuk to Daniel, and with those He sent to destroy Sodom? But you must understand that this was done in a vision and was not a physical reality <note>original: "verity of action"</note>. Thus, they have a very weak argument <note>original: "cold pull"</note from this passage, which is the primary piece of Scripture they cite for their transportations.

<margin>
John Calvin in the *Harmony of the Gospels* <note>original: "Harmon. Evang."</note> on Matthew 4 and Luke 4.
</margin>
Hear, therefore, what Calvin says in his commentary on that passage: *“The question is whether Christ was actually carried up high, or whether it was only in a vision? Many stubbornly insist that his body was truly and physically—as they say—taken up, because they think it is too great an insult for Christ to be made subject to the Devil’s illusions. But this objection is easily refuted. For it is not absurd to grant that all this was done through God's permission or Christ's voluntary subjection, as long as we do not believe that he suffered these temptations inwardly—that is to say, in his mind or soul. And that which is afterwards set down by the Evangelist, where the Devil showed him all the kingdoms of the world and their glory, and that this was done (as it is said in Luke) in the blink of an eye, is more consistent with a vision than with a physical action.”* These are the very words of Calvin, which do not differ by one syllable or five words from what I had written on the matter before I even looked for his opinion. This, I hope, will be sufficient to overthrow the claims of those who base their theories of transportation and flying in the air on this text.

<margin>
Ezekiel 3:12, 14.
</margin>

There, he will see the exact same words used regarding a vision; except that where Christ is said to be taken up by the Devil, Ezekiel is taken up, lifted up, and carried by the Spirit of God—and yet it was in a vision. But those who build the supernatural framework of <term>transubstantiation</term> <note>the Catholic doctrine that the bread and wine of the Eucharist physically become the body and blood of Christ</note> upon this sandy foundation have even less reason for their beliefs, as almost all...

### CHAPTER VIII.

->The argument of those who believe in witchcraft <note>original: "Witchmongers"</note> concerning the history of Job answered.<-

These believers in witchcraft, for lack of better arguments, often bring up the story of Job against me, even though there is not a single word in that story that supports them or goes against my position—so much so that the name of a witch is not even mentioned in the entire book. But (I ask you) what believer in witchcraft today, seeing someone as afflicted as Job, would not claim he were bewitched—even though Job never says so? <margin>Job 1:14-15.</margin> For first, a messenger came to him and said:

> "Your oxen were plowing, and your asses were feeding in their places; and the Sabeans attacked and took them. Yes, they have slain your servants with the edge of the sword, and I alone have escaped to tell you." <margin>16.</margin> And while he was still speaking, another came and said, "The fire of God has fallen from heaven and has burnt up your sheep and your servants and consumed them, and I alone have escaped to tell you." <margin>17.</margin> And while he was still speaking, another came and said, "The Chaldeans formed three raiding parties <note>original: "bands"</note> and fell upon your camels and have taken them, and have slain your servants with the edge of the sword, and I alone have escaped to tell you." <margin>18.</margin> And while he was still speaking, another came and said, "Your sons and your daughters were eating and drinking wine in their eldest brother's house, and <margin>19.</margin> behold, there came a great wind from across the wilderness and struck the four corners of the house, and it fell upon your children, and they are dead, and I alone have escaped to tell you."

<margin>Job 2:7.</margin> Besides all this, he was struck with boils from the sole of his foot to the crown of his head. If any man in these days named Job were handled this way by the appointment or hand of God, I guarantee you that all the old women in the county would be summoned before the court <note>original: "Coram nobis," a legal term meaning "before us," referring to a summons to the King's Bench</note>. Warrants would be sent out on every side, and public and private inquiries would be made as to which old women had lately visited Job’s house, or any of the places where these misfortunes occurred. 

If any poor old woman had happened within two or three months to have borrowed a small favor <note>original: "courtesie of sealing"</note>, or had come to fetch a pot of milk, or if she had asked for charity and was refused by Job, there would be argument enough to bring her to ruin. To be even more certain of catching the "right" witch, astrological charts would be drawn <note>original: "figures must have been cast"</note>, and the divination of the sieve and shears <note>original: "sive and shears," a common folk magic method used to identify criminals or witches</note> would be put to work. Indeed, rather than let the witch escape, a conjurer would be paid to draw a magic circle and raise a devil to tell the truth. Mother Bungy <note>a legendary or well-known "witch" or fortune-teller used here as a stereotypical example</note> would be consulted, and after she learned the name of the woman Job suspected most, she would confirm the suspicion with clever <note>original: "artificial"</note> accusations. In the end, some woman or other would be hanged for it. <margin>John Calvin on Job 1:21.</margin> 

But as Job said, "The Lord gave"; he did not say, "The Devil or the Witch <note>original: "Lamia"</note> took them," but "The Lord has taken them away" <note>original: "Dominus dedit; Diabolus vel Lamia, sed Dominus abstulit"</note>. This agrees with the meaning of the text, where it is written that at every one of Job's afflictions, the Devil asked God...

God laid his hand upon him. In this way, Job attributed no part of his calamity to Devils, Witches, or even to Conjurers and their enchantments, as we have learned to do today. Neither did he sin, nor did he do God any wrong, when he acknowledged God as the one responsible. But we dishonor God greatly when we attribute either the power or the unique nature of God the Creator to a creature.

<margin>John Calvin, *Sermons on Job*, Sermon 8 on Chapter 2. Wolfgang Musculus, *Common Places of the Christian Religion* <note>original: "Muscul. in loc. comm."</note>.</margin>
Calvin says we take much away from God's glory and omnipotence when we say He merely gives Satan permission to do it. This, he says, is to mock God's justice. It is such a foolish <note>original: "fond"</note> assertion that if donkeys could speak, they would speak more wisely than that. For a temporal judge does not say to the executioner <note>original: "hangman"</note>, "I give you permission to hang this offender," but instead commands him to do it. But the supporters of the witches' supposed total power say: "Do you not see how the Devil actually and physically tempted and plagued Job?" I answer, first, that there is no physical or visible Devil named or seen in any part of those circumstances. Second, it was the hand of God that did it. Third, as there is no shared relationship <note>original: "community"</note> between the person of a witch and the person of a devil, there was no conversation or conspiracy <note>original: "practise"</note> between them in this case.

<margin>John Calvin in his *Sermons upon Job*.</margin>
And regarding the communication between God and the Devil, look at what Calvin says while writing—or rather preaching—specifically on that passage where they think they have such a great advantage. When Satan is said to appear before God, it does not happen in a specific physical place, but the Scripture speaks this way to adapt itself to our limited human understanding <note>original: "rudeness"</note>. Certainly, the Devil in this and similar cases is an instrument to carry out God’s will, and not his own. Therefore, it is an ignorant and ungodly saying (as Calvin judges it) to claim that God only permits and tolerates the Devil. For if Satan were left to his own liberty, Calvin says, we would be overwhelmed in an instant. And undoubtedly, if he had the power to hurt the body at will, there would be no way to resist; for he would come upon us invisibly and strike us on the head. Indeed, he would watch for the best people and kill them while they were in the middle of some wicked act. If they say God commands him, nobody disagrees; but as for God giving him *permission*, I say with Calvin that the Devil is not in such favor with God as to obtain such a request from His hands.

<margin>John Calvin, *Sermons on Job*, Sermon 5 on Chapter 1.</margin>
And while according to the opinions and arguments of our witch-believers <note>original: "Witchmongers"</note>, the witch hires the Devil and the Devil asks God's permission to plague whoever the witch wants, there is not (as I have said) any such physical communication between the Devil and a witch as the witch-believers imagine. Neither is God moved at all by Satan’s request, for he has no such favor or grace with Him as to obtain anything from His hands.

<margin>*The Hammer of Witches* <note>original: "Mal. Malef." refers to the *Malleus Maleficarum*</note>, part 1, question 1; also part 1, question 4. Note what is said concerning the book of Job.</margin>
But the author of *The Hammer of Witches* and his friends deny that there were any witches in Job's time. Indeed, the witch-believers are content to say that none were found to practice this art in Christ's time, from his birth to his death—a period of thirty-three years. They say if there had been any, they would have been mentioned then. As for the authority of the book of Job, there is no question that it is fully canonical and authentic. However, many writers, both Jewish and others, believe that Moses was the author of this book and that he set it as a mirror <note>original: "looking-glasse"</note> before the people. His intent was so that the children of Abraham (from whose race Moses himself came) might know that God showed favor to others who were not of the same lineage, and be ashamed of their own wickedness, seeing how an uncircumcised Pagan <note>original: "Painime"</note> had conducted himself so well. Regarding this argument, Calvin (though he had written on the same topic) says that because it is uncertain whether it was a factual event <note>original: "Res gesta"</note> or an illustrative example <note>original: "Exempli gratia"</note>, we must leave it in suspense. Nevertheless, he says, let us accept what is beyond doubt: namely, that the Holy Spirit authored the book so that the Jews would know God has always had a people to serve him throughout the world, even among those who were not Jews or separated from other nations.

I, for my part, do not deny the truth of the story. However, I must confess that I think there was no such physical performance <note>original: "corporal interlude"</note> between God, the

Of Astral Spirits. Devils and Spirits. CHAP. IV. 55

<margin>Astral spirits serve the devil.</margin>
29. At the urging of infernal spirits, these astral spirits are often sent to terrify people with nighttime visions. They take on the appearance of monstrous beasts or the ghosts of deceased friends. Furthermore, they are often encouraged to tempt and provoke people suffering from melancholy to kill themselves <note>original: "execute themselves"</note>. They have countless other ways of carrying out the desires of wicked spirits through malicious prompting and secret strategies designed to destroy mortal men. This happens especially when a task is too difficult for the Devil’s subtle and purely spiritual nature to accomplish on its own, because the work belongs to the "astral source" or the physical world. Since these uncertain spirits belong to that realm, they are frequently asked to act as go-betweens in the treacherous plots that hellish spirits hatch against the lives of mortals.

<margin>Why the devil requires their help.</margin>
30. More specifically, the spirits belonging to the element of fire are the most active in this kind of service, being naturally inclined toward it as the previous section has shown. However, according to their various ranks and categories, some are more spiteful and malicious in their actions than others. Every kind of astral spirit is obedient to the kingdom of darkness. Indeed, the devilish spirits can achieve little or nothing in this external realm of the stars and elements—affecting the bodies or possessions of mankind—without their help. This is because the bodies of demons are too coarse <note>original: "crude"</note> to directly transmit their influence through dreams, trances <note>original: "raptures"</note>, potions <note>original: "philtres"</note>, charms, or astrological alignments <note>original: "constellations"</note>. This will be made clear in the following chapter on the nature of infernal beings, where the character and capacity of every damned spirit is explained according to the truths of ancient philosophy.

<margin>Underground spirits.</margin>
31. Let us now leave the spirits of fire to explain the nature of subterranean <term>subterranean: underground</term> beings, whose orders, species, and degrees are diverse. They are divided into these categories: the spirits of deceased men, the souls of deceased men, separate astral spirits, separate semi-infernal spirits, and spirits associated with the astrological alignments where any of the seven metals—namely Lead (*Saturn*), Tin (*Jupiter*), Iron (*Mars*), Gold (*Sol*), Silver (*Luna*), Copper (*Venus*), and Quicksilver (*Mercury*)—are found in the depths of the earth. Just as the natures of minerals are distinct from one another, these underground spirits differ in their nature and abilities regarding their locations, shapes, names, and qualities.

<margin>Spirits of the mountains, caves, and tombs.</margin>
32. However, they are not all confined to the kingdom of metals. There are also spirits of the mountains, valleys, caves, depths, and gaps <note>original: *hiata's*</note> or chasms of the earth, as well as those of hidden treasures, tombs, vaults, and burial places. To this last group belong the astral spirits of deceased mortals, who delight in hovering over the old corpses to which they once belonged. They seek to be released and diligently wonder why they are being held there. These spirits live in silent caves and solitary vaults where the deceased lie until their radical moisture <note>original: *Humidum Radicale*; in early medicine, this was the essential fluid believed to sustain life and hold the body together</note> is completely dried up <note>original: *exsiccate*</note>. After the body is totally dry, their activities cease, and they are utterly extinguished and gone.

<margin>Spirits of hidden treasures.</margin>
33. To the next category belong those spirits who guard hidden treasures. Because of their nature, they deeply resent humans benefiting from or finding such wealth. They constantly haunt places where money is concealed, carrying malevolent and poisonous influences to wither the lives and limbs of anyone who dares to try and find it. For example, Peters of Devonshire and his associates, who used magic rituals <note>original: "conjuration"</note> to dig for such protected treasures, were supposedly crumbled into atoms—reduced to ashes with his companions in the blink of an eye.

<margin>The nature of such spirits.</margin>
34. On this point, we have plenty of examples of people being destroyed after using magical experiments to discover hidden treasures. These instances seem to prove that the spirits haunting these places belong more to the "infernal hierarchy" (hell) than the "astral" one, considering they are so hostile and determined to harm mortal men so that the great purpose of the Prince of Darkness may be fulfilled.

...of conjuration. Sometimes jugglers <note>original: "Juglers" — in this context, street performers or tricksters who use sleight of hand to deceive.</note> are called witches. Sometimes they are also called sorcerers—those who oppose the Gospel of Christ and lead others astray through forceful persuasion. Sometimes a murderer who uses poison is called a witch. <note>original: "a Murtherer with poyson" — highlighting that the biblical word for witch, *pharmakeia*, is related to the word for pharmacist or poisoner.</note> Sometimes they are termed so by the very meaning of their names, such as *Elymas*, which signifies a "sorcerer." <note>Elymas is a magician mentioned in Acts 13:8 who opposed the apostle Paul.</note> Sometimes it is because they study strange and pointless arts. <note>original: "curious and vain arts" — a common term for occult or forbidden practices.</note> Sometimes the word is used to describe the wounding or grieving of the heart. <note>The author references the Song of Solomon (Canticles) 4:9, where the Hebrew word is sometimes associated with being "bewitched" or "ravished" by love.</note> Indeed, the very word *Magus* (which is Latin for "magician") is translated as "witch," even though in the past it was always used in a positive sense. <note>original: "Magus" — referring to the Magi or wise men, whose title became associated with sorcery over time.</note> And today, in the English language, it is used interchangeably to say "She is a witch" or "She is a wise woman."

Sometimes interpreters of dreams, sometimes soothsayers, and sometimes those who observe the flight of birds, the crossing of toads, or the spilling of salt, etc., are called witches. Sometimes a man or woman is called a witch if they claim to perform miracles for money or fame, yet in reality they can do nothing. Sometimes the word "witch" is used in everyday speech as a nickname for those who are old, lame, bad-tempered, <note>original: "curst"</note> or suffering from melancholy. <note>original: "melancholike" — a clinical term at the time for what we now call depression, often believed to cause delusions.</note> But as for the old women who are said to harm children with their "evil eye," <note>original: "hurt children with their eyes"</note> kill lambs with a look, pull the moon down from the sky, <note>This refers to a classical myth about "Thessalian witches" who could supposedly draw down the moon.</note> make such a foolish bargain, or swear allegiance to the Devil—you will not find any such witches or such actions described in the Bible.

<summary>The author argues that the term "witch" has been applied loosely to many different groups—from poisoners and tricksters to the depressed—and asserts that the supernatural "hag" of popular folklore is not found in the Bible.</summary>

# BOOK VI.

## CHAP. I.

->*The explanation of this Hebrew word* Chasaph; *in which the objection contained in* Exodus 22 *is answered—namely*, You shall not suffer a witch to live; *and also concerning* Simon Magus, *Acts* 8.<-

<margin>Josephus in *Antiquities of the Jews*.</margin>
**C**hasaph, being a Hebrew word, is translated into Latin as *Veneficium* <note>original: *Veneficium* — meaning the act of poisoning or preparing sorcerous potions.</note>, and is in English "poisoning," or "witchcraft," if you prefer. The Hebrew sentence written in Exodus 22 is translated by the seventy interpreters <note>Referring to the Septuagint, the ancient Greek translation of the Old Testament.</note> into Greek as *pharmakous ouk epizosete* <note>original: φαρμακοὺς οὐκ ἐπιζώσετε — "you shall not allow poisoners to live."</note>, which in Latin is, *Veneficos (sive) Veneficas non retinebitis in vita* <note>original: "You shall not keep alive male or female poisoners."</note>; in English, *You shall not suffer any poisoners, or* (as it is usually translated) *witches to live*. This sentence is interpreted by Josephus—a man born Hebrew and of great reputation, learning, and fame—in this way: *Let none of the children of Israel have any poison that is deadly, or prepared for any hurtful use. If anyone is apprehended with such stuff, let him be put to death, and suffer that which he meant to do to those for whom he prepared it.* The Rabbis' explanation agrees with this. The *Lex Cornelia* <note>The Cornelian Law, an ancient Roman law regarding assassins and poisoners (*de sicariis et veneficis*).</note> does not differ from this sense—namely, that he must suffer death who either makes, sells, or possesses any poison with the intent to kill any man. This word is found in the following places: Exodus 22:18, Deuteronomy 18:10, 2 Samuel 9:22, Daniel 2:2, 2 Chronicles 33:6, Isaiah 47:9, 12, Malachi 3:5, Jeremiah 27:9, Micah 5:2, and Nahum 3:4 (twice). However, in all our English translations, *Chasaph* is translated as "witchcraft."

<margin>Galatians 3:1.</margin>
And because I wish to avoid both wordiness and argument at the same time, I will admit that *Veneficae* <note>The Latin feminine plural for "poisoners" or "sorceresses."</note> were such witches as did much harm with their poisons among the children of Israel. I will not deny that such people remain to this day, bewitching men and making them believe that by the virtue of words and certain ceremonies, they bring about the mischiefs and poisonings <note>original: "intoxications" — in this era, it specifically referred to the administration of poison.</note> which they actually accomplish through poisons. And this abuse in the deceiving <note>original: "cosenage" — trickery or fraud.</note> of people, together with taking God’s name in vain, is reproved in many places of the Scripture especially by the name of witchcraft, even where no poisons are involved. This matches the sense which St. Paul used to the Galatians in these words, where he shows plainly that the true meaning of witchcraft is deception: *O you foolish Galatians* (he says) *who has bewitched you?*—that is to say, who has deceived or abused you, making you believe a thing which is not true? By this, he does not mean to ask them who has deprived them of their health, life, cattle, or children with charms or poisons, but rather who has abused or deceived them to make them believe lies. <margin>Job 15:12.</margin> This phrase is also used in Job 15. But so that we may be thoroughly convinced of the true meaning of this phrase used by Paul in Galatians 3, let us examine the description of a notable witch called Simon Magus, provided by St. Luke. <margin>Acts 8:9.</margin> *There was* (he says) *in the city of Samaria, a certain man called Simon, who used witchcraft and bewitched the people of Samaria, saying that he himself was some great man.* I ask: in what other thing here do we see any witchcraft, other than that he deceived the people, making them believe he could work miracles, when in truth he could do no such thing? This clearly appears in the 13th and 19th verses of the same chapter, where he wondered at the miracles performed by the...

Although Plato, with his master Socrates—the chief pillars of these vanities—say that one Pamphilus <note>Scot refers to the "Myth of Er" from Plato's *Republic*, where Er (sometimes called Pamphilus in early modern texts) returns from the afterlife.</note> was called up out of hell, who when he came among the people, told many incredible tales concerning infernal actions. But here I adopt the proverb: *Plato is a friend, Socrates is a friend, but truth is a greater friend.* <note>original Latin: "Amicus Plato, amicus Socrates, sed major amica veritas."</note>

So that this last precept, or the last part of it, extending to that which can be done by neither witch nor devil, may well explain the other parts and points of it. For it is not meant by this that they can actually do such things; but that they make men believe they do them, and thereby cheat the people, and take upon themselves the office of God, and with it also blaspheme his holy name and take it in vain; as appears by the words of charms and conjurations, which you shall see if you look into these words *Habar* and *Idoni* <note>Hebrew terms used in the Bible; *Habar* refers to "charmer" or "spell-caster," and *Idoni* refers to a "wizard" or "knowing one."</note>.

In the same way, I say you may see that by the prohibition of divination by augury and of soothsayings, etc.—who are witches and can indeed do nothing but lie and cheat the people—the law of God condemns them not because they can work miracles, but because they say they can do that which belongs to God, and for their cheating, etc. Concerning other points of witchcraft contained therein, and because some cannot otherwise be satisfied, I will cite under one sentence the decrees, the mind of Saint Augustine, the Council of Orléans <note>original: "Aurelian Councel" — one of several church councils held in Orléans, France, which often addressed pagan superstitions.</note>, and the determination of Paris, namely: "Whoever observes or gives heed to soothsayings, divinations, witchcraft, etc., or gives credit to any such, he renounces Christianity and shall be counted a pagan and an enemy to God; yes, and he errs both in Faith and Philosophy." And the reason is expressed within the Canon law, namely: "Because by this there is attributed to a creature that which belongs to God only and alone." So that under this one sentence—"You shall not suffer a poisoner or a witch to live"—both murder and witchcraft are forbidden; the murder consisting in poison, the witchcraft in cheating or blasphemy.

# Book VI. The Discovery Of Poisoning.

### CHAPTER III.

*That women have used poisoning in all ages more than men, and the danger of poisoning.*

<margin>Pliny, Book 25, Chapter 2.</margin>
Just as women in all ages have been considered most likely to conceive of witchcraft and to be the Devil’s special instruments and primary practitioners of it, so it also appears that they have been the first inventors and the greatest practitioners of poisoning. They are more naturally inclined toward it than men, according to the saying of Quintilian: "I would more easily believe a man capable of robbery, and a woman capable of poisoning" <note>original: "*Latrocinium facilius in viro, veneficium in fæmina credam*"</note>. Pliny is of the same opinion when he says, "The skill of women in poisonings is superior" <note>original: "*Scientiam fœminarum in veneficiis prævalere*"</note>. To be brief: Augustine, Livy, Valerius, Diodorus, and many others agree that women were the first inventors and practitioners of the art of poisoning. As for the rest of their "cunning," and the low regard in which it was held, it may be seen in these verses by Horace, wherein he not only declares the vanity of witchcraft but also explains the other terms we are currently discussing.

> ->*You laugh at dreams, magical terrors, miracles, witches,*<-
> ->*Night-walking spirits, and Thessalian omens.*<-
> <note>original Latin: *Somnia, terrores Magicos, miracula, sagas, / Nocturnos lemures, portentáq; Thessala rides.*</note>
>
> ->*These dreams and magical terrors,*<-
> ->*These miracles and witches,*<-
> ->*Night-walking spirits, or Thessalian bogeymen,*<-
> ->*Value them not two rushes.*<-
> <note>original: "Thessala bugs" — "Bugs" here refers to bugbears or terrifying spirits associated with Thessaly, a region in Greece famous for sorcery.</note>

Here Horace, as you see, treats all our witches' cunning as ridiculous. However, he does not include their art of poisoning in this, which he seems to think is the only part that is actually harmful. Pythagoras and Democritus provide the names of a great many magical herbs and stones, though today both their virtues and the things themselves are unknown. For example, there was *Marmaritin*, by which spirits might be raised; *Archimedon*, which would make one reveal in their sleep all the secrets of their heart; and others like *Adincantida*, *Calicia*, *Mevais*, *Chirocineta*, etc., which all had their several virtues, or rather, poisons. But all of these are now forgotten; indeed, in their place, we have only hog's dung and chervil <note>A common herb in the parsley family.</note> as the only things with which our witches work "miracles."

Truly, this art of poisoning called *Veneficium* <term>Veneficium: A Latin term that can mean both "witchcraft" and "the act of poisoning," highlighting how the two concepts were historically linked.</term> is the most abominable of all others. By it, murders may be committed where no suspicion can be gathered and no resistance can be made. The strong cannot avoid the weak; the wise cannot prevent the foolish; the godly cannot be protected from the hands of the wicked. Children may kill their parents, the servant the master, and the wife her husband—so secretly, so inevitably, and so incurably that it has been thought the most hateful kind of murder. As Ovid says:

# Poisoning and Witchcraft. CHAPTER IV.

The monk who poisoned King John was a true *Veneficus* <note>original: *Veneficus*, meaning both a poisoner and a sorcerer</note>—that is, both a witch and a murderer. For he killed the King with poison and persuaded the people with lies that he had performed a good and worthy deed; and undoubtedly, many were so bewitched that they thought he did very well in doing so. <margin>Ennead 4, Book 4 <note>original: *Ennead. 4. lib. 4.*, referring to the historical works of Marcus Antonius Sabellicus</note></margin> Antonius Sabellicus writes of a horrible poisoning murder committed by women in Rome, where 170 women were executed after being duly convicted; additionally, 20 women of that group were poisoned by the very poison they had prepared for others.

### CHAPTER IV.

->*Of various poisoning practices, otherwise called Veneficia <note>original: *Veneficia*, the Latin term for both poisoning and witchcraft</note>, committed in Italy, Genoa, Milan, and Wittenberg; also how they were discovered and executed.*<-

<margin>Poisoning in Italy.</margin> Another practice, not unlike the one mentioned in the previous chapter, occurred in Casale Monferrato at Saluzzo in Italy in the year 1536. There, 40 *Veneficæ* <note>original: *Venificæ*, female poisoners or witches</note>, being part of a single conspiracy, renewed a plague that had almost ended. They smeared an ointment and a powder on the posts and doors of people's houses, so that entire families were poisoned; they had prepared over 40 pots of that substance for this purpose. Along with this, they redirected inheritances as they pleased, until at last they killed the brother and only son of a man named Necus. It was noted that hardly anyone died in those houses except the masters and their children, which drew much attention. Furthermore, it was observed that a woman named Androgina frequented the houses, especially of those who died. Once she was suspected, arrested, and questioned, she confessed to the crime, the conspiracy, and the circumstances, as has been shown. 

The same villainy was later practiced at Genoa, and <margin>Poisoning in Genoa and Milan.</margin> the offenders were executed. At Milan, there was another similar attempt that failed to take effect. This art <note>meaning the "art" of poisoning, often confused with witchcraft</note> consists as much in the poisoning of cattle as of men; and that which is done with poisons to cattle to destroy them is as commonly attributed to witches' charms as the other. I do not doubt that some who wish to be thought skilled in incantations and the performing of miracles have experience in this area. For it is written by various authors that if wolf dung is hidden in the mangers, racks, or in the hedges around the pastures where cattle graze, all the beasts that smell it (because of the natural antipathy between the nature of the wolf and other cattle) not only refuse to eat but run about as if they were mad or, as they say, bewitched. <margin><unclear>sh.e. di lix O</unclear></margin>

But Wierus <note>Johann Weyer (1515–1588), a Dutch physician whose work "De Praestigiis Daemonum" argued that those accused of witchcraft were often mentally ill or victims of natural causes</note> tells a notable story of a *Veneficus* <note>original: *Veneficus*, a poisoner</note>, or destroyer of cattle, which I thought appropriate to repeat here. He says that in the Dukedom of <margin>Of a Butcher who was a true Poisoning Witch.</margin> Württemberg, not far from Tübingen, there was a butcher in the year 1564 who made a deal with a town for all the hides of their dead cattle, called in those parts "morts" <note>archaic term for cattle that died of disease or natural causes rather than being slaughtered</note>. He secretly killed great numbers of their bullocks, sheep, pigs, and so on with poison. Through his deal for the hides and tallow, he became incredibly rich. At last, falling under suspicion, he was questioned and confessed to the crime and how he did it. He was put to death with hot tongs, which were used to pull his flesh from his bones. For our part, we would have executed five poor women before we would ever suspect one rich butcher.

<summary>This page discusses historical cases of mass poisoning in Italy and Germany, explaining how physical crimes like spreading toxins or poisoning livestock were frequently misidentified as supernatural witchcraft. Scot highlights the social prejudice that leads people to suspect poor women while ignoring the crimes of wealthy men.</summary>

### CHAPTER V.

->*A great objection answered regarding this kind of witchcraft called Veneficium <note>original: *Veneficium*, a Latin term meaning both poisoning and sorcery</note>.*<-

It is argued that if poisoning were included under the category of manslaughter, it would have been a useless repetition and a disorganized approach by Moses to establish a separate law against poisoners <note>original: *Veneficas*</note> specifically. However, it should satisfy any reasonable Christian to know that it was the pleasure of the Holy Spirit to establish a specific article for this, as it is a more hateful, wicked, and dangerous thing than any other type of murder. 

Furthermore, anyone who reads the law of Moses or the New Testament of Christ himself will find this kind of repetition and restatement of the law to be very common. For instance, as it is written in Exodus 22:21, *“You shall not wrong or oppress a stranger, for you were strangers in the land of Egypt”*; these same words are found repeated in Leviticus 19:33. The clipping and shaving of heads and beards is forbidden in Deuteronomy 27, which was previously prohibited in chapter 22. It is written in Exodus 20, *“You shall not steal,”* and it is repeated in Leviticus 19 and in Deuteronomy 5. Murder is generally forbidden in Exodus 20, as well as in chapter 22, and repeated in Numbers 35. But the best example is that magic is forbidden in three separate places: once in Leviticus 19 and twice in Leviticus 20. A person might as well complain to the Holy Spirit about those repetitions as they do about this one.

### CHAPTER VI.

->*Regarding the types of mixtures that make up the witchcraft called Veneficium: concerning love-potions, and the refutation of them by poets.*<-

As for this kind of witchcraft, the main part of it consists of certain mixtures <note>original: "confections"</note> prepared by wicked people to induce love. These are actually nothing but poisons that deprive some people of the use of their brains, and thus of the senses and understanding of the mind. In other cases, they take away life, which is more common than the former. These are called *Philtra* <note>love potions</note>, or *Pocula amatoria* <note>love-cups</note>, or *Venenosa pocula* <note>poisonous cups</note>, or *Hippomanes* <note>a substance traditionally believed to be an aphrodisiac, sometimes associated with a newborn foal’s forehead or a specific plant</note>. These are used by bad and ignorant physicians more often than by witches or conjurers. 

How worthless these trifles <note>original: "bables"</note> are for their intended purpose can be seen in the opinions of the poets themselves, from whom the reputation of this stuff was originally derived. First, you shall hear what Ovid says—he wrote about the very art of love, and did so so skillfully and with such feeling that he is considered the leading expert in that science.

<margin>Ovid, *The Art of Love*, Book 2 <note>original: *Ovid lib. 2. de arte amandi*</note></margin>

# CHAPTER VII.

->*It is proved by more credible writers that love-cups cause death through venom rather than through any art of love; and with what trifles <note>original: toyes</note> they destroy cattle and procure love.*<-

But because there is no certainty or trust in these poets, who say and unsay things, playing with these subjects so that the wise may perceive they hold them in derision, let us see what other graver authors say of this. Eusebius of Caesarea writes that the poet Lucretius was killed by one of those poisoned cups given by lovers. <margin>Jerome, *Against Rufinus*; Pliny, Book 25, Chapter 3; Josephus, Book 11, *Antiquities of the Jews*; Aristotle, Book 8, *History of Animals*, Chapter 24; Johann Weyer, *De Veneficiis* <note>On Poisonings</note>, Chapter 40.</margin> Jerome reports that a woman named Livia killed her husband with one because she hated him too much, and Lucilla killed hers because she loved him too much. Callisthenes killed the Roman general Lucius Lucullus with a love-potion, as Plutarch and Cornelius Nepos say. Pliny and Josephus report that Caesonia killed her husband, the Emperor Caligula, with a love-potion <note>original: *amatorio poculo*</note>, which was actually pure poison. Aristotle says that everything believed regarding the effectiveness of these matters is nothing but lies and old wives' tales. He who wishes to read more arguments and histories concerning these poisons should look in Johann Weyer's *On Poisonings* <note>original: *J. Wier. de Veneficiis*</note>.
