# Book VI. The Discovery of Poisoning <note>original: *Veneficium*</note>.

<margin>Trifles to mock fools <note>original: "Toyes to mock Apes"</note>.</margin>
The trifles <note>original: "toyes"</note> which are said to bring about love, and are presented in their poison-filled <note>original: "poyson loving"</note> cups, are these: the hair growing on the tip of a wolf's tail; a wolf's penis <note>original: "yard"</note>; a little fish called a *Remora* <note>A suckerfish, believed in antiquity to have the power to stop ships</note>; the brain of a cat, a newt, or a lizard; the bone of a green frog whose flesh was eaten away by ants <note>original: "pismires"</note>—the left bone of which (they say) creates love, while the bone on the right side creates hate. It is also said that if a frog's bones are stripped of flesh by ants, some will float and some will sink: those that sink, if hung up in a white linen cloth, create love; but if a person is touched by them, hate is produced. Another experiment involves young swallows: a single brood or nest is taken and buried in an earthenware jar <note>original: "crock"</note> underground until they starve. Those found with their mouths open serve to create love; those with their mouths shut serve to produce hate. 

Besides these, many other follies are suggested to the simple-minded for this purpose, such as the clothes of the dead, candles burning before a corpse, and needles used to sew dead bodies into their shrouds <note>original: "sockt into their sheets"</note>. I will omit various other items out of respect for the reader and because of the foul language required to describe them; <margin>Dioscorides, *On Medical Matters* <note>original: *de materia medicin.*</note>.</margin> however, you may see them in detail if you read Dioscorides or various other learned physicians. In the meantime, anyone who wishes to see more experiments regarding this matter should <margin>Leonardo Vairus, *On Enchantment*, Book 2, Chapter 11, near the end <note>original: *L. Vairus de fascin. lib. 2. cap. 11. prope finem.*</note>.</margin> read Leonardo Vairus’s *On Enchantment*, newly published in this present year of 1583. In that book, Vairus (with a blasphemous <note>original: "incestuous"</note> mouth) directly claims that Christ and his Apostles were sorcerers <note>original: *Venefici*</note>. He pursues that argument very foolishly <note>original: "fondly"</note>, with as much Catholic <note>original: "Popish"</note> folly as possible, striving to prove it lawful to charm and enchant vermin, and so on.

### C H A P. VIII.

->*Jean Bodin, triumphing against Johann Wier, is caught out by incorrect Greek and a false interpretation of it.*<-

<margin>Jean Bodin <note>A famous French jurist and demonologist who wrote "De la démonomanie des sorciers" (1580).</note>.</margin>
Monsieur Bodin triumphs over Doctor Wier <note>Johann Wier, a physician and student of Agrippa who argued that "witches" were actually suffering from mental illness.</note> here, pronouncing a heavy sentence upon him because Wier links this word to poison. But Bodin reigns—or rather, rides—over him even more for speaking "false Greek." Bodin claims Wier calls poisoners <note>original: *Veneficos*</note> *pharmakōdous* <note>original: φαρμακώδous</note>, which is about as true as the rest of the reports and fables of witches' miracles contained in Bodin's book of devilish devices. For in truth, Wier uses no such word; he says they are called *pharmakeus* <note>original: φαρμακὲυς</note>, though he should have written it *pharmakeus* <note>original: φαρμακεὺς</note>. The true accent was omitted and a "d" was inserted that should have been left out, which has nothing to do with the substance of the matter and must certainly be the printer's fault.

But Bodin reasons in this way: the word *pharmakeus* is sometimes used for "magicians" or "conjurers" <note>original: *Magos* or *Præstigiatores*</note>; *therefore* <note>original: *Ergo*</note>, it should be understood that way in the translation of the Septuagint <note>The earliest Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible.</note>. In this, Bodin demonstrates his bad logic more than Wier's bad Greek. For it is well known to those learned in this tongue that the usual and proper meaning of this word, with all its derivatives and compounds, signifies "poisoners by medicine" <note>original: *Veneficos*</note>. Since that is the most common and proper meaning, why would the translators use a meaning that is less common and not at all proper? Thus, Bodin reasons and concludes with his new-found logic and old-found Greek: "Sometimes it means this, though improperly or rather metaphorically; *therefore* <note>original: *Ergo*</note>, in that specific passage it must be taken that way," even when another more fitting word could have been used. This argument, being vain, agrees well with his other vain actions. The Septuagint translators would have been very short on words if that were the case. But if no proper word could be found when they had occasion to speak of witchcraft in their translations, they used *magian*, *maggagian*, etc. Therefore, they likely saw some difference between those terms and the other, and knew of some reason that moved them to use the word for poisoning <note>original: φαρμακὲια, *Veneficium*</note>.

# BOOK VII.

## CHAP. I.

### *Of the Hebrew word Ob, what it signifies, and where it is found; of those called "Pythonisses" or ventriloquists <note>original: "Ventriloquæ"</note>, who they are, and what their practices are; with experiences and examples shown.*

<margin>The Holy Maid of Kent was a ventriloquist <note>original: "Ventiloqua"</note>.</margin>
This word *Ob* is translated as *Pytho* <note>a spirit of divination</note> or *divining spirit* <note>original: "Pythonicus spiritus"</note> in Deuteronomy 18, Isaiah 19, 1 Samuel 28, 2 Kings 23, etc. Sometimes, though improperly, it is translated as *Magician* <note>original: "Magus"</note>, as in 2 Samuel 23. But *Ob* most properly means a "bottle" <note>referring to a leather wine-skin</note>, and is used in this context because these "Pythonists" <note>practitioners of divination</note> spoke with a hollow sound, as if from the bottom of their bellies. For this reason, they are appropriately called *ventriloquists* <note>original: "Ventriloqui", literally "belly-speakers"</note> in Latin. One of this sort was Elizabeth Barton, the "Holy Maid of Kent" <note>a 16th-century woman who gained fame for her religious trances before being executed for treason against Henry VIII</note>, and others. These are people who claim to give oracles, to tell where lost things have gone, and finally, to accuse <note>original: "appeach"</note> others of mischief which they themselves have most commonly brought to pass. By doing so, they often destroy the good reputation of honest women and other neighbors with whom they are displeased. To prove this, and setting aside a hundred other frauds <note>original: "cosenages"</note> that I could recite at this time, I will begin with a true story of a girl practicing her diabolical witchcraft and ventriloquism <note>original: "Ventriloquie"</note> in the year 1574 at Westwell in Kent (within six miles of where I live). This was recorded and noted by two ministers and preachers of God's Word, four substantial farmers <note>original: "Yeomen"</note>, and three women of good reputation, whose names are written below.

<margin>October 13, 1574. Compare this story with the Woman of Endor in 1 Samuel 18, and see whether the same might not be accomplished by this device.</margin>
Mildred, the illegitimate <note>original: "base"</note> daughter of Alice Norrington, and now a servant to William Spooner of Westwell in the County of Kent, being seventeen years of age, was on October 13—both in the night and day—possessed by Satan. About two o'clock in the afternoon of that day, there came to Spooner's house Roger Newman, Minister of Westwell, and John Brainford, Minister of Kennington, with others whose names are listed below. They offered their prayers to God to assist them in that needy case, and then commanded Satan—in the name of the Eternal God and of His Son Jesus Christ—to speak with a voice they might understand and to declare where he came from. But he would not speak; instead, he roared and cried out mightily. Although we commanded him many times, in the name of God and His Son Jesus Christ and by His mighty power, to speak, he still would not, until he had gone through all his delays, such as roaring, crying, struggling, and gnashing of teeth, as well as grimacing <note>original: "mowing"</note> and other terrifying expressions. He was so strong in the girl that four men could scarcely hold her down. This continued for nearly two hours. Sometimes we charged him earnestly to speak, and again prayed to God to assist us. At last, he spoke, but very strangely, saying: "He comes, he comes," which he repeated many times, and "He goes, he goes." Then we charged him to tell us who sent him. He said, "I lay in her way like a log, and I made her run like fire, but I could not hurt her." "And why so?" we asked. "Because God kept her," he said. "When did you come to her?" we asked. "Tonight in her bed," he said. Then we charged him, as before, to tell what he was, who sent him, and what his name was. At first he said, "The Devil,"

### CHAP. VI.

->Treating of the Nature, Force, and Forms of Charms, <term>Periapts</term><note>original: "Periaptis"; charms or amulets worn on the body for protection</note>, Amulets, Pentacles, Conjurations, Ceremonies, etc.<-

<margin>Signs before Spirits appear.</margin>
1. Before appearances are made, after the forms of conjuration are repeated, the infernal spirits make various and wonderful shows, noises, and attempts as forerunners to their appearance. At the first attempts of beginners in conjuration, they are accompanied with noises, tremblings, flashes, howlings, and most dreadful shrieks, until, after further progress and experience, they approach nearer to this elemental nature, so that by degrees they can become clearly visible to their <term>exorcist</term><note>original: "Exorcist"; here meaning one who summons or controls spirits</note>.

<margin>An account of a Magician.</margin>
2. When *Chiancungi* and his sister *Napala* did first attempt to call up spirits, they began with the spirit *Bokim*, in the twentieth degree. They hung a vault underground with black cloth on both the top and bottom, lining it throughout. Having drawn the Circle of the Order of Thrones, with the seven planets and their magical characters in the center, they proceeded to the ceremonies of conjuration. After they had frequently repeated the forms of calling and nothing as yet appeared, they grew so desperate that, forsaking the circle and every defensive character or ceremony, they at last betook themselves to the most accursed and detestable branch of magic, which consists of confederacy <note>original: "Confederacy"; a formal pact or league with a spirit</note>. Having summoned the aforementioned spirit *Bokim* by a solemn league, they obtained 155 years from the spirit, entering into a covenant with it for their bodies, souls, and works.

<margin>His actions.</margin>
3. In this damned life they continued, performing strange wonders in every country. By the help of this magician, the *Tartars* destroyed above 100 sail of ships belonging to *China*. He brought many losses upon that kingdom in their children, fruits, corn, silk, and navigation. He could frequently transport himself through the air and carry a thousand-pound weight in one hand, to the astonishment of all who knew him. He had many public contests with magicians of other countries—trials of skill in the magical art—wherein he was said to excel all who had ever come before him.

<margin>Another Magician.</margin>
4. Another such person was *Louis Gaufredi*, a French priest who had made a pact with the Devil and served him for 14 years in these detestable works. He sacrificed infants to him, worshipped him in a filthy shape, and tempted others to join their magical society or nocturnal conventions <note>original: "nocturnal Conventions"; likely referring to the Witches' Sabbath</note>. In these meetings, as it is reported, they always feasted and snacked on various dainties which, though they seemed delightful, were nonetheless tasteless and unsavory.

<margin>What Charms are.</margin>
5. Leaving these stories, something shall be said of charms and spells, as they are divided in the following manner: First, such amulets as are engraved and molded in the fashion of money or coin, which serve to provoke love and familiarity in a desired person when hung about the neck during certain planetary hours. Secondly, spells or charms on parchment with magical characters, used as periapts to cure diseases or to make one valiant, mindful, and constant. Thirdly, "corselets," which are an ancient Danish charm of necklaces composed of <term>thunder-stones</term><note>original: "Thunder-stones"; prehistoric stone tools once believed to have fallen from the sky during storms</note> engraved with magical letters to resist all harmful influences and the danger of lightning.

<margin>Pentacles.</margin>
6. Pentacles are a fourth sort of accessory which conjurers, charmers, and magicians use. They are made with five corners, corresponding to the five senses, with the operation thereof inscribed upon the corners. The material they are composed of is fine linen, doubled, and joined with <term>cerecloth</term><note>original: "Cere-cloth"; fabric treated with wax or tallow, often used in magic or for wrapping the dead</note> in between. The magician holds this figure in his hand, lifting it up from the skirt of his garment to which it is attached when spirits that are raised are stubborn and rebellious, refusing to conform to the ceremonies and rites of magic.

<margin>Their force.</margin>
7. Also, by holding forth pentacles while saying these words, *Glauron, Amoz, Amozula*...

## CHAPTER II.

->*How the wicked practice of the <term>Pythonist</term><note>original: "Pythonist"; a person supposedly possessed by a spirit of divination, named after the Delphic Python of Greek mythology</note> of Westwell came to light, and by whom she was examined; and that all her diabolical speech was but <term>ventriloquism</term><note>original: "Ventriloquie"; the act of throwing one's voice, used here to describe fraudulent spirit possession</note> and plain <term>deception</term><note>original: "cousenage"; fraud or trickery</note>, which is proved by her own confession.*<-

<margin>Matthew 24:24.</margin>
It is written, that in the latter days there shall be shown strange illusions, etc., so much so that (if it were possible) the very elect shall be deceived. However, St. Paul says, *There shall be lying and false wonders.* Nevertheless, this sentence, and others like it, have often been thrown in my face and are urged by various writers to prove the miraculous working of witches, which I will treat more largely in another place. However, by the way, I must confess that I take that sentence to be spoken of the Antichrist—namely, the Pope. He has miraculously, contrary to nature, philosophy, and all divinity—while being of low birth and calling, crude in learning, and most commonly a very <term>clumsy person</term><note>original: "lubber"; a big, clumsy, or stupid person</note> in terms of valor, beauty, or activity—placed himself in the most lofty and delicate seat. He has put almost all Christian Princes' heads not only under his <term>control</term><note>original: "girdle"</note>, but under his foot, etc.

Surely, the tragedy of this Pythonist is not inferior to a thousand stories which will hardly be blotted out of the memory and belief of either the common people or the learned. How could this story possibly be discredited, having testimony of such authority? How could Mother *Alice* escape condemnation and hanging, being put on trial upon this evidence? Many a poor woman has been thrown away based on a <term>deceptive</term><note>original: "cosening"</note> oracle, or rather a false lie, devised by *Feats* the <term>Juggler</term><note>original: "Jugler"; in this period, a term for a magician or street performer</note> through the malicious instigation of some of her adversaries.

<margin>The Ventriloquist of Westwell discovered.</margin>
But however cunningly this last cited certificate is written, or whatever show of truth and plain dealing it carries, there may be found contained within it enough matter to detect its deceptive knavery. Yet many have been deeply deceived by it and can hardly be moved from believing it; they cannot even endure to hear it criticized without great disdain. And know this by the way: that in the past, <term>Robin Goodfellow</term><note>A mischievous nature spirit or "Puck" from English folklore</note> and <term>Hobgoblin</term> were just as terrifying and just as believable to the people as hags and witches are now. In time to come, a "witch" will be just as much derided and condemned, and as plainly understood to be a fraud, as the illusion and knavery of Robin Goodfellow. In truth, those who maintain belief in walking spirits and their transformations have no reason to deny the existence of Robin Goodfellow, about whom there have been just as many and as credible tales as there are about witches. The only difference is that it did not please the translators of the Bible to call spirits by the name of "Robin Goodfellow," even though they have termed diviners, soothsayers, poisoners, and deceivers by the name of "witches."

<meta>This page continues the investigation into the case of the "Pythonist of Westwell," Mildred Norrington, showing how her alleged spirit possession was debunked by local authorities and comparing it to other famous frauds of the era.</meta>

<page-num>74</page-num>
<header>Book VII. The Discovery of <term>Ventriloquism</term><note>original: "Ventriloquæ"</note>.</header>

<margin>The <term>Pythonist</term> of Westwell convicted by her own confession.</margin>
But to make short work of refuting this dishonest woman's scheme and <term>deception</term><note>original: "cosenage"; fraud or trickery</note>; you should understand that upon the rumor of her divinity and miraculous trances, she was summoned before *Mr. Thomas Wotton* of *Boughton Malherbe*. He was a man of great honor and wisdom, and possessed rare and singular skill in deciding and ordering matters in this Commonwealth. Through his discreet handling of the matter, with the assistance and aid of *Mr. George Darrell, Esq.*—who was also a very good and discreet Justice of that same district—the fraud was found out and the <term>deception</term> confessed, and she received deserved punishment. Her confession was not won according to the methods of the *Spanish* Inquisition—that is, through extreme torture—nor yet by guile or flattery, nor by mere assumptions. Instead, through a wise and perfect trial of every circumstance, the illusion was clearly disclosed. It was not (I say) done the way witches are commonly convicted and condemned—namely, through malicious accusations, guesses, assumptions, and extorted confessions that are contrary to sense and possibility, and for actions for which they can show no proof or example to the wise, either by direct or indirect means. Rather, after her proper trial, she demonstrated her feats, illusions, and trances, along with the rest of all her "miraculous" works, in the presence of various gentlemen and gentlewomen of great honor and credit at *Boughton Malherbe*, in the house of the said *Mr. Wotton*. Now, compare this girl with the *Witch of Endor*, and you shall see that both deceptions may be performed by the same art.

### CHAPTER III.

#### Bodin's claims concerning the <term>Pythonist</term> of Endor, with a true story of a counterfeit Dutchman.

<margin>Jean Bodin, *Of the Demon-mania of Sorcerers*, Book 3, Chapter 2. <note>original: "J. Bodin lib. de dæmon. 3 cap. 2."</note></margin>
Upon similar tales, *Jean Bodin* built his doctrine, calling those "Atheists" who will not believe him. He adds to this kind of witchcraft the miraculous works of various young women who would vomit pins, rags, etc., as one *Agnes Briggs* and *Rachel Pinder* of *London* did, until their miracles were detected and they were sentenced to public penance. He cites others of that sort who were supposedly bound to posts by devils with garters or similar materials, using knots that could not be undone—which is actually an <term>Egyptian's</term><note>original: "Ægyptians"; at the time, this often referred to Romani people or traveling performers known for sleight-of-hand</note> juggling or deceptive trick. His whole book consists of such foolish lies joined with lewd tales; I guarantee you there are no fewer than two hundred fables and just as many impossibilities in it. And just as these two girls, along with the girl of *Westwell*, were detected in their <term>deception</term>, so likewise a *Dutchman* at *Maidstone*—long after he had accomplished such knaveries to the astonishment of a great number of good men—was revealed to be a deceiving knave. This was despite his miracles being printed and published in *London* in the year 1572, with the following title on the front of the book:

> A very wonderful and strange Miracle of God shown upon a *Dutchman* of the age of 23 years, who was possessed by ten devils, and was by God's mighty providence dispossessed of them again on the 27th of January last past, 1572.

The Mayor of *Maidstone*, along with several of his colleagues, subscribed to this, chiefly through the persuasion of *Nicasius Vander-Sceure*, the Minister of the *Dutch Church* there; *John Stickelbow*, whom (as it is said there) God made the instrument to cast out the devils; and four other credible persons of the *Dutch Church*. The story is so strange and so cunningly performed that had his knavery not later brought him into suspicion, he would have gotten away without this fraud being suspected. A great many other such miracles have been lately printed, of which several have been exposed; and all the rest, doubtlessly, if [they were put to]...

### CHAP. IV.

->Concerning the great Oracle of Apollo the <term>Priestess</term><note>original: "Pythonist"; referring to the Pythia, the priestess of the Oracle of Delphi</note>, and how men of all sorts have been deceived, and that even the Apostles have mistaken the nature of Spirits; with an unanswerable argument that Spirits cannot take physical shapes.<-

<margin>The <term>ambiguities</term><note>original: "Amphibologies"</note> of Oracles.</margin>
With this kind of Witchcraft, *Apollo* and his Oracles abused and deceived the whole world—an idol so famous that I need not spend much time describing it. The Princes and Monarchs of the earth placed no small confidence in it. The Priests who lived off it were so cunning that they also overtook almost all the godly and learned men of that age. They did this partly with their doubtful answers, such as the one made to *Pyrrhus* in these words: "I say that you, son of Aeacus, the Romans are able to conquer" <note>original Latin: "Aio te Aeacida Romanos vincere posse." This is a famous grammatical ambiguity: it can mean "I say you can conquer the Romans" or "I say the Romans can conquer you."</note>. And to the Ambassadors of *Croesus*, in these words: "If Croesus leads an army against the Persians, he shall destroy a great empire" <note>original Latin: "Si Cresus arma Persis inferat, magnum Imperium evertet." Croesus destroyed his own empire by attacking.</note>. And otherwise like this: "Croesus, by crossing the Halys, shall overthrow a great power of wealth" <note>original Latin: "Cresus Halin penetrans, magnam subvertet opum vim." The Halys was the river marking the border of his kingdom.</note>; or this: "Croesus shall lose the Halys, having crossed many kingdoms, etc." <note>original Latin: "Cresus perdet Halin, transgressus plurima regna, &c."</note>.

<margin>The subtlety of Oracles.</margin>
They also succeeded partly through conspiracy, by which they knew men’s errands before they even arrived; and partly by cunning, such as promising victory upon the sacrifice of some person of such high status that the victory would sooner be neglected than the murder accomplished. And even if it were done, there would be such conditions attached that there always remained a <term>loophole</term><note>original: "starting hole"</note> and enough matter to argue over—such as requiring the sacrificed party to be a Virgin, or not a bastard, etc. Furthermore, when only two outcomes are proposed, and where a simple "yes" or "no" answers the question, it is an even bet that an idiot will guess correctly. Thus, if things turned out poorly, the fault was always blamed on the Interpreter, and not on the Oracle or the Prophet.

But why should I marvel that the multitude and common people have been abused in this, since Lawyers, Philosophers, Physicians, Astronomers, Divines, General Councils, and Princes have been deceived and seduced with great negligence and ignorance? They have swallowed and devoured a deeply rooted opinion received from their elders without a proper examination of the circumstances.

Nevertheless, the godly and learned Fathers (as it appears) have always taken special care that they did not attribute such devilish devices to God. Instead, they referred them to the one who is indeed the inventor and author—the Devil—though not the personal executor in the manner and form they supposed. Thus, their matters of faith were not damaged by these beliefs. But who can be certain of not being deceived in matters concerning Spirits, when the Apostles themselves were so far from knowing them? Even after the Resurrection of Christ, having heard 

<margin>John 20. 9.</margin>
him preach and explain the Scriptures throughout his lifetime, they showed themselves not only ignorant of the subject but also to have misunderstood it. Did not the Apostle *Thomas* think that Christ himself had been a Spirit, until Christ told him plainly that a Spirit was not the kind of creature that had flesh and bones, which (he said) *Thomas* could see were in him? And to further certify and satisfy his mind, he invited him to see his hands and feel his sides. If the answer some people give to this is true—namely, that Spirits can take the forms and shapes of bodies at their pleasure—then *Thomas* could have answered Christ and remained unsatisfied. He might have said, "Oh Sir, what are you telling

...[does it matter to] me that Spirits have no flesh and bones? For if they can take shapes and forms, then perhaps you have done so as well. This is an argument that all the <term>witch-hunters</term><note>original: "Witchmongers"</note> in the world will never be able to answer.

Some of those who maintain the creation, transformation, transportation, and <term>physical manifestation</term><note>original: "Transubstantiation"; here referring to the belief that a spirit can take on a substantial, fleshy body.</note> of witches argue that spirits cannot be felt, even if they can be seen. They answer the biblical passage I cited earlier by suggesting that it was the sense of touch, and not sight, that was meant to satisfy *Thomas*. But anyone who carefully considers the text and its context will see that the fault of *Thomas’s* disbelief was revealed and condemned for a second reason: he would not trust his own eyes, nor the report of his fellow Apostles. <margin>John 20:29.</margin> They might have been considered too gullible in this instance if spirits really could take on different shapes whenever they pleased. *Jesus* says to him, *"Because you have seen (and not, because you have felt), you believe."* Likewise, he says, *"Blessed are they who believe and do not see (and not, they who believe and do not feel)."* By this, he notes that our physical eyes can distinguish between a spirit and a natural body. He reproves Thomas because he relied so much on his external senses in a case where faith should have prevailed; even here, in a matter of faith revealed in the Word, Thomas would not believe the miracle that was shown to him in a most natural and perceptible way.

<margin>Erasmus, folio 62.</margin>
However, <term>Thomas Erastus</term><note>A Swiss physician and theologian (1524–1583).</note> says, as do <term>Andreas Hyperius</term><note>A Flemish Protestant theologian (1511–1564).</note>, <term>Niels Hemmingsen</term><note>original: "Hemingius"; a Danish theologian (1513–1600).</note>, <term>Lambert Daneau</term><note>original: "Danaeus"; a French Reformed theologian (c. 1530–1595).</note>, the authors of the *<term>Malleus Maleficarum</term>*<note>original: "M. Mal."; the "Hammer of Witches," the most famous medieval treatise on the prosecution of witches.</note>, <term>Jean Bodin</term><note>A French jurist and demonologist (1530–1596).</note>, and others, that evil spirits eat, drink, and keep company with men. They claim spirits can take tangible forms, providing examples such as the <term>German or Augsburg Ghost</term><note>original: "Spectrum Germanicum seu Augustanum"</note> and the Angel whose feet *Lot* washed. They act as though because God can grant his messengers bodies whenever he chooses, the Devil and every other spirit can do the same. <margin>Luke 24:37; Mark 16:14; Matthew 14:26; Chapters 20 & 16:11.</margin> The way the eleven Apostles were deceived in this matter appears in *Luke* 24 and *Mark* 16, as well as in *Matthew* 14, where the Apostles and disciples were all mistaken, thinking Christ was a spirit when he walked on the sea. And why shouldn't they be mistaken in this, just as they thought Christ spoke of an earthly kingdom when he preached about the Kingdom of Heaven? They misunderstood that greatly, just as when he told them to beware of the "leaven" of the Pharisees, and they thought he was talking about literal bread.

### CHAPTER V.

### Why Apollo was called Pytho, why those Witches were called Pythonists: Gregory’s Letter to the Devil.

<margin>Eusebius, book 7, chapter 25.</margin>
But to return to our Oracle of *Apollo* at *Delphi* <note>original: "Delphos"</note>, who was called *Pytho* because *Apollo* slew a serpent by that name (which is where the *Pythonists* get their name): I ask you to carefully consider this story. I will faithfully recount it from the ecclesiastical history written by <term>Eusebius</term><note>An early Christian historian (c. 260–339 AD).</note>. The spirit, feeling compassion for the priest's situation and his distress, appeared to him and told him plainly that his recent guest, *Gregory*, was the cause of all his misery. He then argued with *Gregory* about the rudeness he had shown in return for...

### C H A P. VI.
#### *Apollo*, who was called *Pytho*, compared to the *Rood of Grace*: *Gregory's* Letter to the Devil disproved.

What need is there for many words to disprove this fable? For if Gregory had been an honest man, he would never have willingly allowed the people to be further deceived by such a lying spirit. Or, if he had been half as holy as *Eusebius* claims he was, he would not have consented or yielded to such a wicked request from the priest, nor have written such an impious letter—not even if good might have come from it. Therefore, by the impossibility and folly contained within the story, as well as the impiety (of which I am willing to excuse Gregory), you may perceive it to be a lie. I think those who still maintain that the Devil gave answers through the idol of *Apollo*, etc., may find enough evidence to change their mistaken opinions in the fact that it is recorded that men skilled in <term>divination</term><note>original: "Augury"; specifically the practice of interpreting omens from the flight of birds, but used here for fortune-telling in general.</note> took it upon themselves to give oracles at *Delphi* in the place of *Apollo*; one of these was *Tifanius*, the son of *Antiochus*. But the answer given by idols is worthless. 

<margin>Zechariah 10.</margin>

Our own **Rood of Grace**, along with the help of "little **Saint Rumbold**," was not inferior to the idol of *Apollo*. <note>The "Rood of Grace" was a famous mechanical crucifix at Boxley Abbey in Kent that could move its eyes and lips; it was exposed as a fraud during the Reformation.</note> For these could not work truly external miracles, but they could manifest the internal thoughts of the heart, I believe, with a more lifelike show of both humanity and divinity than the other. If you read *Mr. Lambarde's* book, *A Perambulation of Kent*, this shall partly appear. 

<margin>*William Lambarde, under the heading "Boxley."*</margin>

But if you talk with those who have actually seen it, you will be satisfied on this point. And yet, in the blind time of <term>Popery</term><note>A derogatory term for Roman Catholicism, common in the 16th and 17th centuries.</note>, no one could—under pain of damnation or danger of death—even suspect the fraud. Indeed, what Papists will even now confess they were idols? This is despite the fact that the wires that made their eyes goggle and the pins that fastened them to the posts to make them seem heavy were seen and burned together with the images themselves—the knavery of the priests was betrayed, and every circumstance of it was detected and made clear.

### C H A P. VII.
#### *How various great scholars and good authors have been deceived in this matter of spirits through false reports, and by being too gullible have published lies, which are disproved by* Aristotle *and the Scriptures.*

*Plutarch*, *Livy*, and *Valerius Maximus*, along with many other serious authors, having been deceived by false reports, wrote that in times past beasts spoke, and that images could speak and weep, and shed drops of blood, and even walk from place to place. They claim this was done by the activity of spirits. But I agree rather with *Aristotle*, that it was brought to pass "by the deceptions of men and priests." <note>original: "Hominum & sacerdotum deceptionibus"</note> And therefore, let us follow *Isaiah's* advice, who says, "When they shall say to you..."

<margin>Isaiah 8:19.</margin>

### CHAPTER VIII.

### Concerning the Witch of Endor, and whether she truly accomplished the raising of Samuel, or did so by deceit; the opinions of several theologians on this matter.

<margin>1 Samuel 28</margin>
The Woman of Endor is categorized under this word *Ob* <note>A Hebrew term often translated as "medium" or "familiar spirit."</note>; for she is called a *Pythoness* <note>original: *Pythonissa*; a term for a female seer or medium, derived from the Oracle of Pytho (Delphi).</note>. It is written in 1 Samuel 28 that she raised Samuel from the dead; and the other words of the text are strongly phrased to suggest his actual resurrection. The mind and opinion of Jesus Sirach <note>The author of the Book of Ecclesiasticus in the Apocrypha.</note> clearly appears to be that Samuel was raised in person from his grave, as you will plainly perceive if you read Ecclesiasticus 46:19–20. However, he does not debate there whether the story is true or false, but only cites certain verses of 1 Samuel 28 literally, encouraging good manners and the imitation of our virtuous predecessors. He repeats the examples of various excellent men—namely, Samuel—just as the text itself presents the matter according to the deceived mind and imagination of Saul and his servants. Therefore, in truth, Sirach spoke there according to the opinion of Saul, who believed it to be so; otherwise, it is neither heresy nor treason to say that Saul was deceived.

<margin>
Wisdom 3.
Psalms 92 & 97.
Chrysostom, Homily 31 on Matthew.
Luke 16.
</margin>
He who weighs that passage well and looks at it advisedly shall see that Samuel was not raised from the dead, but that it was an illusion or deception practiced by the witch. For the souls of the righteous are in the hands of God, according to what Chrysostom says: "Souls stay in a certain place awaiting judgment, and cannot move from there." <note>original: "Animae in certo loco expectantes iudicium, & inde non possunt removere."</note> Neither is it God's will that the *living* should be taught by the dead. These things are confirmed and approved by the example of Lazarus and the rich man <note>Dives</note>; where it appears, according to Deuteronomy 18, that He will not have the living taught by the dead, but will have us stick to His Word, in which His will and testament are declared. Indeed, Nicholas of Lyra and Dionysius the Carthusian lean greatly toward this latter view. Lyra says, "That just as when Balaam would have raised a devil, God intervened; so did He in this case bring up Samuel when the witch would have raised her devil." This is a probable interpretation. But yet they dare not stand by that opinion, lest they should damage Saint Augustine's reputation. They admit that Augustine remained of the opinion—without contradiction from the Church—that Samuel was not raised; for he says directly, "That Samuel himself was not called up." <note>original: "Ipsum Samuelem non fuisse evocatum."</note> And indeed, if he were raised, it was either voluntarily or by force; if it were voluntarily, his sin would have been equal to the witch's.

<margin>
Augustine, Book on Questions of the Old and New Testament, question 27. Also part 2, chapter 26. Also question 5, "no wonder." To Simplician, book 2, question 3. To Dulcitius, question 6. Also book 2 of Christian Doctrine.
Deuteronomy 18.
Exodus 20.
</margin>
And Peter Martyr, I think, says more to the purpose in these words: "This must have been done by God's good will, or by the force of magic art; it could not be done by His good will, because He forbade it; nor by art, because witches have no power over the godly." <note>original: "Hoc oportuit fieri aut Dei beneplacito, aut vi artis magicae: beneplacito fieri non potuit, quia prohibuerat: nec arte, quia magi in pios nihil possunt."</note> Where it is answered by some that the commandment was only to prohibit the Jews from asking counsel of the dead, and so there was no fault in Samuel for giving counsel, we might as well excuse our neighbor's wife for consenting to our filthy desires because it is only written in the Decalogue, "You shall not desire your neighbor's wife." But, indeed, Samuel was directly forbidden to answer Saul before he died; and therefore it was unlikely that God would appoint him to do it when he was dead.

# CHAP. IX.

## *That Samuel was not actually raised, how Bodin and all Papists are foolish in this matter, and that souls cannot be raised by witchcraft.*

Furthermore, it is unlikely that God would answer Saul through the deceased *Samuel* when He refused to answer him through the living *Samuel*. It is most unlikely of all that God would answer him by way of a *Devil* after refusing to do so by way of a Prophet. The entire course of Scripture witnesses and proves that he was not brought up *by force* <note>original: "per force"</note>, as our own reason also helps us understand. For what peaceful rest could the souls of the elect enjoy or possess in *Abraham's* bosom if they could be plucked from there at a witch's call and command? If that were so, the Devil would have power in heaven—a place where he is unworthy to be himself, and therefore unfit to command others.

<margin><unclear>Tertullian, Book on the Soul, chapter 57. Justin, question 52.</unclear> *Jean Bodin, On the Demon-mania of Witches, book 2, chapter 3.* *1 Samuel 28.* *1 Corinthians 5.* *Justin Martyr in the dialogue with Trypho the Jew.* *Lactantius, book 7, chapter 13.* *1 Corinthians 15:51.* *Jude, verse 9.*</margin>
Many other Church Fathers are flatly against the idea of *Samuel* being raised; namely, *Tertullian* in his book *On the Soul* <note>original: "De anima"</note>; *Justin Martyr* in his *Explanations, question 25*; *Rabanus* in his *Letters to Abbot Bonosus* <note>original: "epistolis ad Bonos. Abat."</note>; and *Origen* in his *History of Balaam* <note>original: "historia de Bileamo"</note>, among others. Others <term>dote</term><note>original: "dote"; to act foolishly or show excessive, misguided fondness for an idea.</note> exceedingly in this matter—namely, *Jean Bodin* and all Papists in general, as well as Rabbi *Saadia Gaon* <note>original: "Sedias Hajas"</note> and all the *Hebrew* scholars, except for Rabbi *David Kimchi*, who is the best writer of all the Rabbis (though none of them are truly any good). 

In maintaining this position, *Bodin* falls into many absurdities. He tries to prove that *Saul* was one of the elect by focusing on the "small" faults he had committed; he claims the greatest matter charged against Saul was merely saving the *Amalekites'* cattle. He insists Saul was an elect person, confirming his opinion with many ridiculous fables and the following argument: Saul’s fault was too minor to deserve damnation, just as *Paul* would not have the incestuous man punished too severely so that his soul might be saved. *Justin Martyr*, in another passage, was not only deceived regarding the actual raising of *Samuel’s* soul, but even affirmed that all the souls of the prophets and righteous men are subject to the power of witches. 

Yet the Heathens were even more <term>fond</term><note>original: "fond"; in this period, it meant foolish or trivial.</note> in this regard. As *Lactantius* affirms, they boasted that they could call up the souls of the dead, even though they believed that souls died along with their bodies. From this, it can be seen how the world has always been deceived in matters of witchcraft and conjuration. Necromancers affirm that any person's spirit may be called up—or "recalled," as they term it—before one year has passed since their departure from the body. *Cornelius Agrippa*, in his book *On Occult Philosophy* <note>original: "De occulta Philosophia"</note>, says this may be done through certain natural forces and bonds. 

Therefore, in times past, corpses were accompanied and watched with lights, sprinkled with holy water, perfumed with incense, and purified with prayer as long as they remained above ground. Otherwise, as the Hebrew teachers say, the Serpent would devour them as the food appointed to him by God in Genesis 3. They also cite the passage, "*We shall not all sleep, but we shall be changed*" (1 Corinthians 15:51), arguing that many shall remain as perpetual meat for the Serpent. From this arises the contention between the Serpent and Michael concerning the body of *Moses*, as mentioned in Scripture (Jude 1:9). I admit that *Augustine* and the rest of the Doctors of the Church who deny the raising of *Samuel* conclude that the Devil was brought up in his likeness instead; with all due respect, I hope I may dissent from their opinions. <note>The author, Reginald Scot, typically argues that such events were not demonic appearances but rather human trickery and illusions.</note>

He cites numerous Church Fathers to support his skeptical view while dismissing the arguments of those who believe in literal necromancy.</summary>

# Book VII. The Discovery of Saul and Samuel.

### C H A P. X.

->*That neither the Devil nor Samuel was raised, but that it was a mere deception, according to the methods of our spirit-mediums <term>Pythonists</term>.*<-

<margin>Pietro Pomponazzi, *Book on Incantations*, chapter 2.</margin>
Again, if the Devil appeared and not Samuel, why does the book of Ecclesiasticus say that he "slept"? For the Devil neither sleeps nor dies. In truth, we may conclude that it was neither the Devil in person, nor Samuel. Instead, a situation is described here according to the deceived opinion and imagination of Saul. However, *Augustine* says that both of these views may easily be defended. But we do not need to seek an explanation from so far away—for indeed, it seems to me, it is far-fetched <note>original: "Longe petita"</note>—nor do we need to descend as low as hell to bring up a Devil to explain this passage. For it is ridiculous, as *Pomponazzi* <note>original: "Pompanacius"</note> says, to abandon obvious things that can be proven by natural reason in order to seek unknown things which cannot possibly be conceived or tested by any rule of reason.

But since we have the freedom, according to Saint *Augustine's* rule, to deviate from the literal text in passages of Scripture that seem to contain either contradiction or absurdity, and to create a godly interpretation agreeable to the Word; let us admit that Samuel was not raised, for that would be contrary to the Word of God. Instead, let us see whether this illusion might not be devised by the art and cunning of the woman, without any of these supernatural inventions. I could cite a hundred Roman Catholic <note>original: "Papistical"</note> and fraudulent <note>original: "cosening"</note> practices just as difficult as this and just as skillfully handled. It is surely to be expected that if it had been a Devil, the text would 
<margin>Jean Bodin, *On the Demon-mania of Witches*, book 2, chapter 3.</margin>
have noted it somewhere in the story, which it does not. But Bodin helps me exceedingly on this point, where he says he abandons the opinions of Augustine, Tertullian, and Rabbi David Kimchi, who claim it was the Devil that was raised up. This, says Bodin, could not be; because in that same conversation between Saul and Samuel, the name of *Jehovah* is repeated five times, and the Devil cannot endure the hearing of that name.

### C H A P. XI.

->*The objection of the witch-believers <term>Witchmongers</term> concerning this passage fully answered, and what circumstances are to be considered for understanding this story, which is plainly explained from the beginning of 1 Samuel 28 to verse 12.*<-

<margin>Peter Martyr Vermigli, *Commentary on 1 Samuel 28:9*.</margin>
Where such a supernatural miracle is performed, it is undoubtedly a testimony of truth, as *Peter Martyr* affirms. In this case, it would have been a witness of lies; for, says he, a matter of such weight cannot be attributed to the Devil, but it is the mighty power of God that accomplishes it. And even if it lay in a witch's power to call up a Devil, it certainly 
<margin>Isaiah 42:8.</margin>
does not lie in a witch's power to work such miracles; for God will not give His power and glory to any creature. To understand this passage, we must diligently examine its circumstances. It was well known that Saul, before he went to the Witch, was in despair over the mercy and goodness of God—partly because Samuel told him long before that he would be overthrown and David would take his place, and partly because God had previously refused to answer him, either through Samuel while he lived, or through any other Prophet, or by Urim or Thummim, etc. 
<margin>1 Samuel 28.</margin>
And if you desire to see this matter discussed, turn to 1 Samuel 28 and compare my words with it.

### CHAPTER XII.

-> 1 Samuel 28:12, 13, 14 explained: wherein it is shown that **Saul** was swindled and deceived by the **witch**; and that **Samuel** was not raised is proven by the **witch's** own words. <-

<margin>The method of the Witch of Endor's swindling of Saul.</margin>
The method and circumstances of their communication, or of her conjuring ritual, are not set down word-for-word in the text, but the effect of it is briefly touched upon. Yet I will show you the common routine of their conjuring, and especially the one she used at this time. When **Saul** had told her that he wanted **Samuel** brought up to him, she left his presence and went into her private chamber <note>original: "Closet"</note>. There, she undoubtedly had her "familiar"—specifically, some dishonest, crafty priest—and made **Saul** stand at the door like a fool (as if standing there helplessly) to hear the deceptive answers, but not to see the deceptive handling of it or the faking of the matter. And so she goes to work, using standard words of conjuring, of which there are many varieties and forms (some of which I will have occasion to repeat in another place). You can see how **tricksters** <note>original: "Juglers"</note> (who are inferior **conjurers**) speak certain routine nonsense words to lead the eye away from noticing their sleight of hand, while they lead the mind to imagine and suppose that they are dealing with **spirits**, saying: **"Hey, fortune's fury, I never believe <note>original: "nunq; credo"</note>, pass, pass, when will you come, sirrah!"** So, likely after many such words were spoken, she said to herself, "Look, now the matter is accomplished, for I see wonderful things!" Thus, when **Saul** heard these words, he longed to
<margin>1 Samuel 28:13</margin>
know everything and asked her what she saw. By this, you may know that **Saul** saw
<margin>Verse 21</margin>
nothing, but stood outside like a <term>blockhead</term> <note>original: "mome"</note> while she played her part in her private room. This appears most evidently in the 21st verse of this chapter, where it is said, **"Then the woman came out to Saul."** However, a little before that, she skillfully faked that she saw **Samuel**, and thereby claimed to know it was **Saul** who had come to her. By this, the whole world may see her swindling and her deceit; for based on what was said before, she must have already known it was him. And (I ask you) why should she not have suspected him to be **Saul** earlier, when he specifically asked her to bring **Samuel** to him, just as easily as she did when **Samuel** allegedly appeared to her?

Well, to the question previously asked by **Saul**, she answers and lies, saying that
<margin>Verse 13</margin>
she saw **angels** or **gods** ascending out of the earth. Then she proceeds with her enchanting phrases and routine spells, so that **Saul** gathers and supposes that she has raised a man; otherwise, his question does not follow anything previously spoken. For when she has said, "I saw angels ascending, etc.," the next thing he says is, **"What does he look like?"** <note>original: "What fashion is he of?"</note> This question, I say, does not follow from her last spoken words. And to this she did not answer directly that it was **Samuel**, but that it was **"an old man wrapped in a cloak"**—as though she did not recognize the most famous man in **Israel**, who had been her neighbor for many years, upon whom (while he lived) every 
<margin>Verse 12</margin>
eye was fixed, and whom she also knew less than a quarter of an hour before, as he was the means by which she became acquainted with **Saul**. Read the text and see.

->*To make one or many balls disappear (or rather, to move them away).*<-

If you take one ball, or more, and seem to put it into your other hand, and while you use charming words, you move them out of your right hand into your lap, it will seem strange. For when you immediately open your left hand, the sharpest observers will say it is in your other hand, which you may also then open; and when they see nothing there, they are greatly deceived <note>original: "overtaken"</note>.

->*How to hit a joker <note>original: "wag"</note> on the knuckles.*<-

<margin>This feat tends chiefly toward laughter and mirth.</margin>
But I will stop speaking any more about the ball, for I could keep you here all day on this topic, and yet I would not be able to teach you how to use it, nor would you scarcely understand what I mean or write concerning it. But certainly, many are persuaded that it is a spirit or a "fly" <note>A "fly" was a common term for a familiar spirit or a demonic helper, often thought to take the shape of an insect</note>, etc. Remember <note>original: "Memorandum"</note>, the right hand must always be kept open and straight—only keep the palm from view—and therefore you may end with this miracle. Lay one ball upon your shoulder, another on your arm, and the third on the table. Because the ball is round and will not easily stay on the point of your knife, you must ask a bystander to place it there, saying that you intend to throw all three balls into your mouth at once. While holding a knife like a pen in your hand, as he is placing the ball on the tip of your knife, you can easily and quickly hit him on the fingers, for the actual trick will be hard to perform.

### CHAPTER 24.
->*On the Moving <note>original: "Conveyance"</note> of Money.*<-

<margin>The money must not be of too small or too large a circumference, or it will hinder the trick <note>original: "conveyance"</note>.</margin>
The moving of money is not much inferior to the ball trick, but it is much easier to do. The main place to hide a piece of money is in the palm of your hand. The best coin to use is a tester <note>A "Testor" or "teston" was a silver coin worth sixpence</note>; but with practice, all coins will be similar, unless the money is very small—in which case it should be kept between the fingers, almost at the fingertips, whereas the ball is kept lower, near the palm.

->*To move money out of one of your hands into the other by sleight of hand <note>original: "Legierdemain"</note>.*<-

<margin>This is quite good if it is handled skillfully; for both the ear and the eye are deceived by this device.</margin>
First, you must hold your right hand open and place a tester, or some large coin, in it. Then, place the tip of your left middle finger on top of it. Say some words, and suddenly pull your right hand away from your finger (with which you held down the tester). By bending your hand just a little, you will still retain the tester inside it. As you quickly draw your right hand through your left, you will seem to have left the tester there, especially if you close your left hand at the right time. To make it appear even more convincing, you may take a knife and seem to knock it against the coin so that it makes a loud sound; but instead of hitting the coin in the left hand (where there is none), you shall hold the point of the knife firmly with the left hand and knock it against the tester held in the other hand. It will sound as if it is hitting the money in the left hand. Then say your words and open your hand; when nothing is seen, the audience will wonder how the tester was removed.

### CHAPTER XIV.

->*Opinions of some learned men that Samuel was indeed raised, not by the witch's art or power, but by a special miracle of God: that there are no such visions in these our days, and that our witches cannot do the like.*<-

<margin>Jean Bodin and Leonardo Vairus differ on this point.</margin>
<margin>A bold, discreet, and faithful challenge.</margin>
Ajas and Sadajas <note>likely referring to medieval Jewish commentators such as Rashi or Abarbanel</note> write that when the woman saw the miracle indeed—something greater than she expected or was accustomed to—she began to cry out that this was a vision indeed, and a true one, not performed by her art but by the power of God. This explanation is far more probable than the judgments of our recent writers on the subject and agrees with the explanations of various good theologians. *Gelasius* <note>likely Pope Gelasius I</note> says it was the actual spirit of *Samuel*; and where he allowed himself to be worshipped, it was only as a civil salutation and courtesy. He argues that God intervened with *Samuel*, just as He did with *Elijah* <note>original: "Elias"</note> when he met the messenger of *Ahaziah* <note>original: "Ochozias"</note> when he sent to consult *Beelzebub* the god of *Ekron* <note>original: "Acharon"</note>. And here it should be noted that the proponents of witchcraft <note>original: "Witchmongers"</note> are stuck on this point: for the Papists say it cannot be a Devil because the name *Jehovah* is mentioned three or five times in the story. Upon this piece of Scripture, arguments are daily devised to prove and maintain the miraculous actions of witchcraft and the raising of the dead through conjurations. And yet, even if it were true that *Samuel* himself was raised, or the Devil in his likeness, and that the Witch of *Endor* did it by her art and cunning, etc., it serves more to disprove than to prove the claims of our modern witches, who can perform neither that kind of miracle nor any other in any place or company where their juggling and deception might be seen and exposed. And I challenge them all (even at the risk of my life) to show one single miracle, such as Christ truly performed, or such as they suppose this witch did by diabolical means—provided it is not done with trickery or hidden helpers <note>original: "confederacy"</note> to give it a false appearance. Neither are there any such visions shown in these days.

<meta>This page continues the author's skeptical examination of supernatural phenomena. Having previously discussed the "Witch of Endor," the author now shifts to a broader critique of "walking spirits" and modern-day "miracles," arguing that many reported sightings are either frauds, psychological delusions, or relics of old folklore that are fading with the spread of the Protestant Reformation.</meta>

# Walking Spirits of Witchcraft. CHAPTER 15.

<margin>* At Canterbury by R. Lee Esq. and others, in the year 1573. At Rye by Mr. Maymor and others, in the year 1577.</margin>
In the past, God did send his visible angels to men, but now we do not hear of such apparitions, nor are they necessary. Indeed, it pleased God in former times, by the hand of Moses and his prophets, and especially by his son Christ and his apostles, to work great miracles for the establishment of the faith. But now, whatever is necessary for our salvation is contained in the Word of God. Our faith is already confirmed and our Church established by miracles; therefore, to seek for them now is a sign of lack of faith. The Catholics <note>original: "Papists"</note> (if you notice) are greatly afflicted with this, as appears in their "lying legends" <note>likely referring to *The Golden Legend*, a collection of hagiographies</note>. But in truth, their miracles are most commonly knaveries, especially those of priests, of which I could cite a thousand. If you read the story of *Bel and the Dragon* <note>a story from the Apocrypha where Daniel exposes a priestly fraud</note>, you shall find a deceptive miracle of some antiquity. If you wish to see newer devices, read Weyer, Cardan, Bale, and especially Lavater, etc. There have been some walking spirits in these parts, so "conjured" <note>here meaning exposed or driven out by legal or rational means</note> not long ago, that afterwards they took little delight in making any more appearances.

***

### CHAPTER 15.

->**Concerning empty apparitions: how people have been brought to fear "bugs" <term>specters or bogeymen</term>; which is partly corrected by the preaching of the Gospel: the true effect of Christ's miracles.**<-

<margin>Johann Weyer, book 3, chapter 8. Theodore of Byzantium. Lavater, *On Ghosts*. Cardan, *On the Variety of Things*. Peucer, etc. Lavater, *On Ghosts*.</margin>
But certainly, some scoundrel in a white sheet has deceived and abused many thousands in that way, especially when *Robin Good-fellow* <note>a mischievous nature spirit or "puck" in English folklore</note> caused such a disturbance in the countryside. But you should understand that these "bugs" <term>imaginary terrors</term> are especially seen and feared by sick folk, children, women, and cowards, who through weakness of mind and body are shaken by empty dreams and continual fear. The Scythians, being a stout and warlike nation (as various writers report), never see any empty sights or spirits. It is a common saying: "A lion fears no bogeyman." 

But in our childhood, our mothers' maids terrified us with an ugly Devil having horns on his head, fire in his mouth, and a tail on his backside, eyes like basins, fangs like a dog, claws like a bear, skin like a Black person <note>original: "Niger"; referring to the historical artistic tradition of depicting demons with dark skin</note>, and a voice roaring like a lion. Because of this, we startle and are afraid when we hear someone cry "Boo!" They have so frightened us with "bull-beggars" <term>bugbears</term>, spirits, witches, urchins <note>mischievous spirits, often in the form of hedgehogs</note>, elves, hags, fairies, satyrs, pans, fauns, silens, Kit-with-the-candlestick <note>a Will-o'-the-wisp</note>, tritons, centaurs, dwarves, giants, imps, "calcars" <term>astrologers or schemers</term>, conjurers, nymphs, changelings, the incubus, Robin Good-fellow, the "spoorn" <note>an old name for a phantom or ghost</note>, the "mare" <note>the nightmare spirit</note>, the man in the oak, the "hell-wain" <term>death coach</term>, the "fire-drake" <term>fire-dragon or meteor</term>, the "puckle" <term>goblin</term>, Tom-thumb, hob-goblin, Tom-tumbler, Boneless, and such other "bugs" <term>specters</term>, that we are afraid of our own shadows. 

It reaches the point where some never fear the Devil except on a dark night; and then even a shorn sheep is a "perilous beast" and is often mistaken for our father's soul—especially in a churchyard, where a very brave man in the past scarcely dared to pass by night without his hair standing on end. For very serious writers report that spirits most often take the shape of women appearing to monks, etc., and of beasts: dogs, swine, horses, goats, cats, and hares; or of birds, such as crows, night-owls, and screech-owls. But they delight most in the likeness of snakes and dragons. Well, thanks be to God, this wretched and cowardly lack of faith has been partly forgotten since the preaching of the Gospel; and doubtless, the rest of those illusions will in a short time (by God’s grace) be detected and vanish away.

<margin>Cardan, *On the Variety of Things*. Johann Weyer, *On the Deceptions of Demons*, etc. Athanasius, *On the Incarnation of the Word* <note>original: "De humanitate verbi"</note>.</margin>
Various writers report that in Germany, since Martin Luther’s time, spirits and devils have not appeared in person as they used to do in the past. This argument is taken up by the ancient Fathers to prove the end and ceasing of oracles. For in times past (says Athanasius), devils in empty shapes did ensnare men with their illusions, hiding themselves in waters, stones, woods, etc. But now that the word of God has appeared, those sights, spirits, and the mockeries of idols have ceased. Truly, if all such oracles, as that of Apollo, etc., (before the coming of Christ) had been true and occurred according to the reports which have been brought to us through various ages and from far-off countries,

<header>BOOK VII. The Discovery of Miracles.</header>

<margin>The true end of Miracles.</margin>
<margin>John 2:23. Acts 2:22. John 5.</margin>
...without priestly fraud or guile, or even if the spirits of prophecy and the working of miracles had been inserted into an idol, as has been supposed; yet we Christians may believe that Christ's coming was not so fruitless and harmful to us as to take away his spirit of prophecy and divination from the mouths of his chosen people and good prophets—giving no answers of anything to come through them, nor by *Urim* or *Thummim* <note>Urim and Thummim: ancient Hebrew tools used by the High Priest to determine God's will</note>, as he used to do—and yet still leave the Devil in the mouth of a witch or an idol to prophesy or work miracles, etc. Such a thing would only hinder his glorious Gospel, discredit his Church, and further infidelity and false religion. In fact, the working of miracles was the primary, or at least the most special means that moved men to believe in Christ, as appears in various places in the Gospel, and especially in *John*, where it is written, *That a great multitude followed him, because they saw his miracles which he did, etc.* [John 6:2]. Nay, is it not written, *That Jesus was approved by God among the Jews, with miracles, wonders and signs?* [Acts 2:22]. And yet, if we compare the miracles performed by Christ and those attributed to witches, the witches' miracles would seem more common and in no way inferior to his.

### CHAPTER XVI.

#### *Witches' miracles compared to Christ's; that God is the creator of all things; of Apollo, and of his names and portraiture.*

<margin>An ironic comparison.</margin>
<margin>Malleus Maleficarum part 2, question 1, chapter 14. Acts 17. 1 Timothy 6:13. Colossians 1:16. Athanasian Creed.</margin>
If the Witch of Endor had performed that which many believe she did, it might have been compared with the raising up of *Lazarus*. Tell me, is not turning water into milk as difficult a matter as turning water into wine? And yet, as you may read in the Gospel, Christ did the one as his first miracle; so may you read in the *Malleus Maleficarum* <note>original: "M. Mal.", the standard 15th-century handbook for witch-hunters</note> and in *Bodin* <note>Jean Bodin (1530–1596), a French jurist and writer on demonology</note> that witches can easily do the other—yes, and what is even more, they can make butter out of water. But to avoid all petty objections, and lest there should appear to be more substance in Christ’s miracle than the others, you shall find in the *Malleus Maleficarum* that they can even change water into wine. *What is it to attribute to a creature the power and work of the Creator, if this is not it?* Christ says, *The works that I do, no one else can do.* <note>original Latin: "Opera quæ ego facio nemo potest facere." cf. John 15:24</note> The creation of substance was never granted to man or angel; *therefore*, it was granted neither to witch nor devil. For God is the only giver of life and being, and by him all things are made, visible and invisible.

<margin>Apollo and Python exposed.</margin>
Finally, this woman of *Endor* is called in the Scripture a *Pythonissa* <note>Pythonissa: a term for a woman possessed by a foretelling spirit, derived from the Pythian oracle at Delphi</note>; by which it may appear that she was nothing but a deceiver. For *Pytho* himself, from whom the word *Pythonissa* is derived, was a counterfeit. The original story of *Apollo*, who was called *Pytho* because he killed a serpent of that name, is merely a poetic fable. The poets say he was the god of music, medicine <note>original: "physick"</note>, poetry, and archery. In heaven he is called *Sol* [the Sun], on earth *Liber Pater* [Bacchus], and in hell *Apollo*. He is said to flourish always with perpetual youth, and therefore he is depicted without a beard. His statue was kept as an oracle-giver, and the priests who attended it at *Delphos* [Delphi] were deceivers, called *Pythonists* after *Pytho* (just as *Papists* are named after the *Papa* or Pope). Afterward, all women who practiced that trade were named *Pythonissae*, as was this woman of *Endor*. But because it concerns this matter, I will briefly note the opinions of various learned men and certain other proofs which I find in the Scripture regarding the ceasing of miracles, prophecies, and oracles.

# BOOK VIII.

## CHAPTER I.

### *That Miracles Have Ceased.*

<margin>
Psalm 136:4, 72:18, & 88:11.
Isaiah 42:8.
John 3:2 & 7:16.
In annotations on John 3.
Isaiah 45.
</margin>
Although in the past it pleased God to extraordinarily show miracles among his people to strengthen their faith in the Messiah—and again, at his coming, to confirm their faith by his wonderful deeds and the special graces and gifts he bestowed upon the Apostles—yet we read throughout the Scriptures that it is the Lord alone who works great wonders. Indeed, David says that among the dead, God will show no wonders (as in the case of Samuel). I also find that God will not give his glory and power to any creature. Nicodemus, being a Pharisee, could say that no man could perform such miracles as Christ did unless God were with him—according to the words of the Prophet to those gods and idols who claimed the power of God: "Do either good or ill if you can, etc." Thus, the Prophet knew and taught that none but God could work miracles. Infinite examples for this purpose could be brought from the Scripture, which I will omit and pass over for the sake of brevity.

<margin>
Augustine, *On the Words of the Lord according to Matthew*, Sermon 18. <note>original: "August. de verbis Dom. secundum. Mat. ser. 18."</note>
James 5:15.
John Calvin, *Institutes*, Book 4, Chapter 19, Section 18.
The same, in the same place, Section 19.
Isaiah 9:7.
Acts 20:10.
The same, in the same place; namely, John Calvin. <note>original: "nempe J. Cal."</note>
</margin>
St. Augustine, among other reasons by which he proves the cessation of miracles, says: "Now, blind flesh does not open the eyes of the blind by a miracle of God, but the eyes of our hearts are opened by the word of God. Now, our dead bodies are no longer raised by a miracle, but our dead bodies remain in the grave while our souls are raised to life by Christ. Now, the ears of the deaf are not opened by a miracle, but those who previously had their ears shut now have them opened for their salvation." The miraculous healing of the sick through anointing, mentioned by St. James, is used as an objection by many—especially by the Catholics <note>original: "Papists"</note>—to maintain their Sacrament of Extreme Unction <note>term: Extreme Unction: The ritual of anointing the dying, now called the Anointing of the Sick</note>. This is clumsily <note>original: "apishly"</note> and uselessly practiced in the Roman Church as if the miraculous gift continued to this day. 

In this matter, you shall see what Calvin says in his *Institutes*: "The grace of healing," he says, "spoken of by St. James, has vanished away, as have the other miracles which the Lord intended to show only for a time, so that he might make the new preaching of the Gospel marvelous forever." "Why," he asks, "do these people (meaning the miracle-mongers) not appoint some Pool of Siloam <note>original: "Siloah"</note> to swim in, where at certain regular times sick people may plunge themselves? Why do they not lie on top of the dead, just as Paul raised a dead child by that means?" "Truly," he says, "James spoke of the miracle of anointing for that time while the Church still enjoyed such blessings from God." Likewise, he says that the Lord is present with his people in all ages, and as often as there is need, he helps their illnesses no less than in ancient times. However, he does not express his manifest power or distribute miracles through the hands of the Apostles as he once did, because that gift was only for a limited time. Calvin concludes there by saying: "They say such virtues or miracles remain, but experience says no." 

And see how they agree among themselves. Lambert Daneau <note>original: "Danaeus"</note> says that neither a witch nor the Devil can work miracles. Giles Alley says directly that witches do work miracles. Calvin says they have all ceased. All "witchmongers" <note>term: Witchmongers: A derogatory term for those who promote the belief in and the hunting of witches</note> say they continue. But some argue that Catholic miracles have vanished and gone, yet the miracles of witches remain in full force.

## CHAPTER II.
### *The gift of Prophecy has ceased.*

<margin>
Isaiah 41:23.
Ecclesiastes 6:12.
1 Samuel 28.
Romans 12.
1 Corinthians 12.
1 Peter 1.
</margin>
That witches, the Woman of Endor <note>the biblical medium consulted by King Saul</note>, and even her "familiar" or the Devil cannot tell what is to come may plainly appear by the words of the Prophet, who says, "Show what things are to come, and we will say you are indeed gods" <note>Isaiah 41:23</note>. This agrees with what Solomon says: "Who can tell a man what shall happen to him under the sun?" <note>Ecclesiastes 6:12</note>. "Indeed, I can!" says the Witch of Endor to Saul. But I will rather believe Paul and Peter, who say that prophecy is the gift of God and not a worldly thing, rather than a cheating woman <note>original: "cosening quean"</note> who takes it upon herself to do everything but can do nothing but beguile men. 

Up steps another "Bungie" <note>likely a generic name for a fortune-teller, referring back to Mother Bungie</note>, and she can tell you where your lost horse or donkey is, or what has become of anything you have lost, just as Samuel could; she claims to know what you have done throughout your life, as Christ told the woman of Sychar <note>original: "Sichar"</note> at Jacob's well; <margin>John 4.</margin> and even what your business is before you speak, as Elisha <note>original: "Elizeus"</note> did.

<margin>Peter Martyr, *Common Places*, 9, section 17. <note>original: "P. Martyr. loc. com. 9. sect. 17."</note></margin>
Peter Martyr says that only God and man know the heart of man, and therefore the Devil must be excluded, citing these passages: "Only God is the searcher of hearts" <note>original Latin: "Solus Deus est scrutator cordium"</note>; and, "No one knows the things of a man, except the spirit of the man which is within him" <note>original Latin: "Nemo scit quae sunt hominis, nisi spiritus hominis qui est in eo"</note>. Solomon says, "You alone know the thoughts of men" <note>original Latin: "Tu solus nosti cogitationes hominum"</note>. And Jeremiah says, speaking for God, "I am God, searching hearts and minds" <note>original Latin: "Ego Deus scrutans corda & renes"</note>. Also, Matthew says of Christ, "But Jesus, seeing their thoughts" <note>original Latin: "Jesus autem videns cogitationes eorum"</note>; in Scripture, He is called the searcher and knower of the thoughts in the heart, as appears in Acts 1 and 15, Romans 8, Matthew 9, 12, and 22, Mark 2, Luke 6, 7, and 11, John 1, 2, 6, and 13, Revelation <note>original: "Apoc."</note> 2 and 3, and in countless other places.

<margin>Peter Martyr, *Common Places*.</margin>
The same Peter Martyr also says that the Devil may suspect but not know our thoughts; for if he knew our thoughts, he would understand our faith, and if he did, he would never assault us with a single temptation. Indeed, we read that Samuel could tell where lost things had strayed, etc.; but we see <margin>Hebrews 1:1-2.</margin> that gift also ceased with the coming of Christ, according to the saying of Paul: "At various times and in different ways, God spoke in the past through our fathers the Prophets; in these last days, He has spoken to us by His Son, etc." And therefore I say that the gift of prophecy, with which God once endowed His people, has also ceased, and counterfeits and cheaters have come in their place, according to this <margin>2 Peter 2:1.</margin> saying of Peter: "There were false Prophets among the people, even as there shall be false..."

...false teachers among you, and so on. And do not think that such a notable gift would be taken away from the beloved and the chosen people of God and committed instead to Mother Bungie <note>original: "Mother Bungie"; a famous 16th-century English woman often cited in skeptics' texts as a representative of fraudulent fortune-tellers.</note> and others of her profession.

The words of the Prophet Zechariah <note>original: "Zechary"</note> are clear regarding the end of both the good and the bad prophet: *I will cause the prophets and unclean spirits to depart out of the land, and when any shall still prophesy, his parents shall say to him, "You shall not live, for you speak lies in the name of the Lord"; and his parents shall pierce him through when he prophesies*, and so on. No, no; the foretelling of things to come <margin>John Chrysostom in the Gospel of John, Homily 18. Peter of Blois, Epistle 49.</margin> is the work of God alone, who manages all things gently, and whose counsel no man has ever shared. To know our labors, the times, and the moments—these are things God has placed within His own power. Also, Phavorinus <note>original: "Phavorinus"; a 2nd-century Roman philosopher and orator.</note> says that if these "cold" <note>uninspired or fraudulent</note> prophets or oracle-givers tell you of prosperity and then deceive you, you are made miserable through vain expectation; if they tell you of adversity and lie, you are made miserable through vain fear. Therefore, I say we might as well expect to hear prophecies at the Tabernacle, from the burning bush, from the Cherubim among the clouds, from the angels within the Ark, or out of the flame, as to expect an oracle from a prophet in these days.

But suppose someone in our nation <note>original: "Common-wealth"</note> should step forward and claim to be a prophet (as many frantic <note>original: "frantick"; meaning insane or delusional</note> people do); who would believe him? Would they not think instead that he was a wicked person? <margin>Statutes of Elizabeth I, Year 5; Canon laws regarding evildoers and mathematicians <note>At this time, "mathematician" often implied someone who practiced astrology or divination.</note></margin> See the Statutes of Elizabeth I, Year 5 <note>referring to the 1562 Act against "fond and fantastical prophecies"</note>, to see if there are not laws made against them, condemning their arrogance and trickery <note>original: "cosenage"</note>; see also the canon laws to the same effect.
