### CHAPTER III.
#### That Oracles have ceased.

<margin>Thucydides, Book 2. Cicero, On Divination, Book 2.</margin>
Regarding oracles, which for the most part were idols of silver, gold, wood, stone, and so on—within whose bodies some say unclean spirits hid themselves and gave answers, while others say that vapors <note>original: "exhalations"</note> rising out of the ground inspired their minds, through which their priests delivered oracles. They claimed spirits and winds rose from that soil and granted those men the gift of prophesying things to come, though in truth they were all devices to cheat the people for the profit of the priests. These priests received the "idol's answers" overnight and delivered them back to the idol-worshipers the next morning. You shall understand that, even if it had been as they supposed, for the reasons and proofs already mentioned, they should now cease. Whatever has an affinity with such miraculous actions—such as witchcraft, conjuration, and so on—has been struck down and nailed to the cross with Christ. He has broken the power of devils and satisfied God’s justice; He has also trodden them under His feet and subdued them. At His coming, the prophet Zechariah says, <margin>Zechariah 13:2.</margin> *The Lord will cut the names of idols out of the land, and they shall be remembered no more; and He will then cause the prophets and unclean spirits to depart out of the land.* It is also <margin>Micah 5:12.</margin> written, *I will cut off your enchanters <note>original: "Inchanters"</note> out of your hand, and you shall have no more soothsayers.* Indeed, the Gospel of Christ has so thoroughly exposed their dishonesty <note>original: "knavery"</note> that since it has been preached, their pride has been humbled <note>original: "their combs are cut"; a metaphor from cockfighting meaning to be subdued or lose status</note>, and few who are wise pay them any mind. And if ever these prophecies were to take effect, it must have been at the coming of Christ, at which point you see the devils were troubled and grew weak when they met Him, saying—or rather crying out to Him in this way: *Son of God, why have you come to torture us before the time?* <note>original Latin: "Fili Dei, cur venisti nos cruciare ante tempus?"</note> O Son of God, why do you come to trouble us (or ruin us) before our appointed time? He indeed prevented them, and He now remains our defender and protector from the devil's claws. So, you see now that there is no room left for such "guests" as these.

However, you shall hear the opinions of others who have been as deceived as yourselves in this matter; yet even they are forced to admit that God has appointed His Son to strike down the power of devils, satisfy God’s justice, and heal our wound received by the fall of Adam, according to God’s promise...

...in Genesis 3: "The seed of the woman shall tread down the serpent," or the Devil. Eusebius—in his first book *Concerning the Preaching of the Gospel* <note>original: "De praedicatione Evangelii"</note>, the title of which is *That the power of Devils is taken away by the coming of Christ*—says: "All answers made by Devils, and all soothsayings and divinations of men, have gone and vanished away." Likewise, he cites Porphyry <note>Porphyry (c. 234–305 AD) was a Neoplatonic philosopher and an opponent of early Christianity.</note> in his book against the Christian religion, wherein these words are repeated: "It is no wonder that the plague is so rampant in this city; for ever since Jesus has been worshipped, we can obtain nothing good from the hands of our gods." 

Cicero wrote of this decline and ceasing of oracles long before, noting that it had even happened before his own time. However, Chrysostom, living long after Cicero, says that the god Apollo was forced to admit that as long as any relic of a martyr was held to his nose, he could not provide any answer or oracle. Thus, one may perceive that the heathens were wiser in this regard than many Christians, who in times past were called *Opponents of Enchantments* <note>original: "Oppugnatores incantamentorum"</note>, just as the English Princes are called *Defenders of the Faith* <note>original: "Defensores fidei"</note>. Plutarch calls Boeotia (as we call babblers) by the name of "Many Words" because of the multitude of oracles there; which now, he says, are like a spring or fountain that has dried up. If even one remained, I would ride five hundred miles to see it; but in the whole world there is not one to be seen at this hour, Popish deceptions <note>original: "cozenages"</note> excepted.

<margin>
Porphyry wrote verses in Apollo's name concerning the death of Apollo, cited by Jean Bodin, folio 6.
</margin>
But Plutarch says that the cause of this decline of oracles was the Devil's death, whose life he held to be limited and mortal, saying they died of old age; and that the divining priests were blown up by a whirlwind and sunk by an earthquake. Others attributed it to the position of the planets, suggesting that when they passed over those locations, they carried that art away with them, and it might return by their future revolution, and so on. Eusebius also cites from him the story of Pan; because it serves this purpose, I will include it here. Since it mentions the Devil's death, you may believe it if you wish <note>original: "if you list"</note>, but I will not, being assured that he is kept alive to punish the wicked and those who attribute the power of Almighty God to such idols.

### CHAP. IV.

->A tale written by many grave authors, and believed by many wise men, concerning the Devil's death. Another story written by Papists and believed by all Catholics, approving of the Devil's honesty, conscience, and courtesy.<-

<margin>
Thamus, having little to do, thought to play with his company, whom he might easily trick with such a jest.
</margin>
Plutarch says that his countryman Epitherses told him that as he passed by sea into Italy, with many passengers in his boat, the wind completely ceased one evening while they were near the Echinades islands. The ship, drifting with the tide, was eventually brought to Paxi. While some slept, others drank <note>original: "quaft"</note>, and others were awake (perhaps in as bad a state as the rest), a voice was suddenly heard after supper calling "Thamus!" in such a way that everyone marveled. This Thamus was a pilot born in Egypt, unknown to many of those on the ship. Therefore, being called twice, he answered nothing; but the third time he answered. The other voice, even louder, commanded him that when he came to Palodes, he should tell them that "the great god Pan is departed." 

At this, everyone was astonished (as Epitherses affirmed). Consulting on what was best to do, Thamus concluded that if the wind were high, they must pass by in silence; but if the weather were calm, he must speak what he had heard. When they came to Palodes and the weather was calm, Thamus looked out toward the land and cried aloud that "the great god Pan is deceased." Immediately, there followed a lamentable noise from a multitude of people, full of great wonder and admiration. Because there were many in the ship, the report of this event was quickly brought to Rome, and Thamus was sent for by the Emperor Tiberius. Tiberius gave such credit to the story that he diligently inquired and asked who that Pan was. The learned men around him supposed that Pan was the son of Mercury and Penelope, and so on. Eusebius says...

...faith, that this happened in the time of Tiberius the Emperor, when Christ expelled all Devils, etc. *Paulus Martius*, in his notes upon *Ovid’s Fasti*, says that this voice was heard from the island of Paxi <note>original: "Paxe"</note> that very night that Christ suffered, in the nineteenth year of Tiberius.
<margin>A detection of Thamus's knavery.</margin>
Surely, this was a humorous prank <note>original: "merry jest"</note> devised by Thamus, who with some confederates thought to make sport with the passengers—some of whom were asleep, some drunk, and others at play, etc.—while the first voice was used. And at the second voice—namely, when he was to deliver his message—he, being an old pilot, knew where some noise was common due to an echo in the sea, and thought he would (to the astonishment of the passengers) accomplish his trick if the weather remained calm. By this it may appear that in cases of tempests or other emergencies, he would rather attend to more serious business than to that ridiculous matter. For why else should he not do his errand in rough weather as well as in calm? Or, why would he need to tell the Devil about it, when the Devil told it to him before, and could have delivered the message himself with much more speed?

<margin>The Golden Legend <note>original: "Legend aur." or *Legenda Aurea*</note> in the Life of Saint Andrew, folio 39.</margin>
But you shall read in the *Golden Legend* a fable—an "Oracle," I should say—that is more authentic; for many will say that the previous story was a profane tale, and not as canonical as those verified by the Pope’s authority. Thus it is written: A woman in labor <note>original: "travel"</note> sent her sister to Diana, who was the Devil in an idol (as all those oracles are said to be), and desired her to make her prayers, or rather a request, to know if she would have a safe delivery. This the sister did, but the 
<margin>A gentle and a godly Devil.</margin>
Devil answered, "Why do you pray to me? I cannot help you. Go and pray to Andrew the Apostle, and he may help your sister," etc. Look at that! This was not only a gentle, but a godly Devil, pitying the woman’s case; by revealing his own inability, he gave more power to St. Andrew. I know some Protestants will say that the Devil, to maintain idolatry, etc., referred the maid to St. Andrew. But what answer will the Catholics <note>original: "Papists"</note> make, who think it great piety to pray to Saints, and so, by consequence, must see it as a documented courtesy in the Devil to send her to St. Andrew, who would not fail to help her?

### CHAP. V.

->*The judgments of the ancient Fathers regarding Oracles and their abolition, and how they have now been transferred from Delphi to Rome.*<-

<margin>Athanasius, *On the Incarnation of the Word* <note>original: "De human. verb."</note>, folios 51 and 64.</margin>
You shall find the opinions of the Fathers—that Oracles ceased with the coming of Christ—in the following places: namely, *Justin Martyr, In Dialogues Against the Jews; Athanasius, On the Incarnation of the Word; Augustine, The City of God; Eusebius, Book 7, Chapter 6*; also *Book 5, Chapters 1 and 8; Rupert, On John, Books 10 and 12; Plutarch, On the Obsolescence of Oracles; and Pliny, Book 30 of Natural History.* Finally, *Athanasius* concludes that in times past, there were oracles in Delphi <note>original: "Delphos"</note>, Boeotia, Lycia, and other places; but now, since Christ is preached to all men, this madness has ceased. So you see that whatever high regard the ancient Fathers once held (by hearsay) for those miraculous matters of idols and oracles, they themselves now refuse to bear witness to them, and even affirm that ever since Christ’s coming, their "miracles" have been stopped.

As for the cessation of the knaveries and deceptive <note>original: "cosening"</note> devices of priests, I see no authority in Scripture or from the ancient Fathers to suggest they have ended. Rather, the contrary is true: that strange illusions shall be shown by them even until the end. And truly, whoever knows and observes the order and devices used in Catholic <note>original: "Popish"</note> pilgrimages shall see both the oracles and their conclusions remaining, having been, as it were, transferred from Delphi to Rome. There, that "adulterous generation" <note>A biblical reference to Matthew 12:39, where Jesus rebukes those who demand a sign.</note> continually seeks a sign, even though they have Moses and the Prophets, and even Christ and his Apostles as well.

### CHAPTER VI.

->Where and how tricksters <note>original: "coseners"</note>, witches, and priests were accustomed to give oracles and to perform their feats.<-

<margin>Strabo, *Geography*, Book 16. Johann Weyer, *On the Illusions of Demons*, Book 1, Chapter 12 <note>original: *de præst. dam. cap. 12.*</note></margin>
These deceptive oracles—or rather the people giving them—used, I say, to perform their feats and work their miracles most commonly through young women, animals, statues <note>original: "Images"</note>, dens, cloisters, dark holes, trees, and in churches or churchyards. In these places, priests, monks, and friars had laid their plots and formed their conspiracies beforehand to beguile the world, to gain money, and to add credit to their profession. This practice began in the Oaks of Dodona, where there was a wood in which the trees (they say) could speak. This was actually done by a rogue hiding in a hollow tree that appeared solid to the simple-minded people. This wood was in Molossia, a part of Greece called Epirus, and it was named the Oracle of Dodona. There were many oracles in Egypt: namely, those of Hercules, Apollo, Minerva, Diana, Mars, Jupiter, and of the ox Apis, who was the son of Jupiter, but his statue was worshipped in the likeness of an ox. Latona, who was the mother of Apollo, was an oracle in the city of Buto <note>original: "Bute"</note>. The priests of Apollo, who always faked fury and madness, gave oracles in the temple called Clarius, within the city of Colophon in Greece. At Thebes in Boeotia, and also in Lebadea, Trophonius was the chief oracle. At Memphis, a cow; at Corinth, an ox called Mnevis; in Arsinoe, a crocodile; in Athens, a prophet called Amphiaraus, who indeed died at Thebes, where they say the earth opened and swallowed him up alive <note>original: "quick"</note>. At Delphi <note>original: "Delphos"</note> was the great temple of Apollo, where demons gave oracles through maidens (as some say), though in reality it was done by priests. It was built upon Mount Parnassus in Greece. The defenders of oracles say that just as rivers are often diverted to another course, so likewise the spirit which inspired the chief prophets may be silent for a time and revive again by the turning of the ages <note>original: "revolution"</note>.

<margin>Henry Howard in his *Defensative against the Poison of Supposed Prophecies*.</margin>
<margin>In whose days oracles ceased in England.</margin>
<margin>Zechariah 10:2. Psalm 115:5, 6. Isaiah 41:23.</margin>
Demetrius says that the spirits who attended the oracles grew weary of the people's curiosity and persistence <note>original: "importunity"</note>, and forsook the temple out of shame. But as one who has lately written against prophecies says, it is no wonder that when the spirit-messengers <note>original: "familiars"</note> who speak through hollow trunks <note>original: "trunks"</note> were driven from their hiding places for fear of discovery, the "almighty" wooden blocks lost their senses. For these are all gone now, and their trickery has been exposed, so they can no longer abuse the world with such trifles <note>original: "bables"</note>. But whereas these great doctors suppose that the cause of their departure was the coming of Christ, they are mistaken if they mean that the Devil died as soon as He was born, or that he then gave up his occupation. For the Roman Catholic Church <note>original: "Popish Church"</note> has made a constant practice of this, partly for their own private profit, lucre, and gain, and partly to be held in high esteem by the world and in admiration among the simple. But indeed, people who have learned of Christ and have been familiar with His Word have discovered and rejected the vanity and abomination of this. If those doctors had lived until today, they would have said and written that oracles had ceased—or rather been driven out of England—in the time of King Henry VIII and of Queen Elizabeth, his daughter. They have done so much in that regard that at this hour, oracles are not only all gone but forgotten here in this English nation, where they once swarmed as thick as they did in Boeotia or in any other place in the world. But the credit they had depended not upon their merit, but upon the gullibility of others. Now, therefore, I will conclude and make an end of this matter with the opinion and saying of the Prophet: *Vain is the answer of idols. For they have eyes and see not, ears and hear not, mouths and speak not, etc.* And, *Let them show what is to come, and I will say they are gods indeed.*

# BOOK IX.

## CHAPTER I.

*The Hebrew word Kasam <note>Kasam: Hebrew for "divination" or "soothsaying."</note> explained, and how far a Christian may predict future things.*

<margin>
*Johann Weyer, Book 1, On the Illusions of Demons.* <note>original: *J. Wier. lib. 1. de præst. dæmon.*</note>
</margin>
Kasam (as Johann Weyer <note>original: *John Wierius*</note> affirms based on his own knowledge, and as he reports from the words of Andreas Maes <note>original: *Andreas Masius*</note>) differs little in meaning from the previous word *Ob* <note>In previous chapters, the author defined "Ob" as a spirit or a medium.</note>. It means to prophesy <note>original: *Viticinari*</note>, and is most commonly used in a negative sense, as in Deuteronomy 18 and Jeremiah 27, etc. However, it is sometimes used in a positive sense, as in Isaiah 3:2. To foretell things to come based on probable conjectures—so long as we do not reach further than human capacity allows—is not (in my opinion) unlawful. Rather, it is a commendable demonstration of wisdom and judgment. These are the good gifts and noble blessings of God, for which we ought to be thankful. We should also give him due honor and praise for the noble order he has established in nature, praying that he lightens our hearts with the beams of his wisdom so we may more and more profit from the true knowledge of his handiwork.

<margin>
Not all divinations are to be condemned.
</margin>
But some people are so overly scrupulous <note>original: "nice"</note> that they generally condemn all sorts of divinations. They deny those things in nature that have manifest causes and are so framed that they foreshadow things to come. In that showing, they warn us of events to follow, exhibiting signs of unknown and future matters to be judged by the order, law, and course of nature set before us by God.

On the other hand, some are so bewitched by folly that they give creatures the respect that belongs only to God, the Creator of all things. They claim that the public and private destinies of all human affairs—and anything a man might want to know about things past or future—are revealed to us in the heavens. They believe that all things can be known through the stars and planets. These people also insist that nothing should be undertaken or attempted without a favorable alignment <note>original: "aspect"</note> of the planets. By these and other similar devices, they corrupt and profane the ancient and commendable observations of our ancestors. One such person was Colebrasus, who taught that all of human life was governed by the seven planets; though he was a Christian, he was condemned for heresy.

<margin>
*Colebrasus's* erroneous and impious opinion.
</margin>
But let us embrace and allow this philosophy and prophesying only as far as the Word of God permits and recommends it to us.

<meta>catchword: CHAP.</meta>

<summary>This page explores the Hebrew term "Kasam," defining it as divination or prophesying. The author argues that while superstitious astrology is heretical, it is both natural and lawful for humans to use wisdom to predict the future based on the observable laws of nature created by God.</summary>

### C H A P. II.

->*Proofs from the Old and New Testaments that certain observations of the weather are lawful.*<-

<margin>Genesis 1:14 & 9:13; Ecclesiasticus 43; Psalm 19:1–2 & 50:6; Ecclesiasticus 43; Baruch 3; Luke 12:54–55; Matthew 16:2–3.</margin>
When God by his Word and Wisdom had made the heavens and placed the stars in the firmament, he said, *"Let them be for signs, and for seasons, and for days, and years."* When he created the rainbow in the clouds, he said it should be for a sign and token unto us. This we find true, not only of the Great Flood <note>original: "flood past"</note> but also of the showers to come. And therefore, according to the advice of Jesus Ben Sirach <note>original: "Jesus Sirachs"; the author of the Book of Ecclesiasticus</note>, "Let us behold it, and praise him that made it." The Prophet David says, *"The heavens declare the glory of God, and the earth shows his handiwork: day unto day utters the same, and night unto night teaches knowledge."* It is also written, "That by the commandment of the Holy One, the stars are placed and continue in their order, and fail not in their watch." It appears that Christ himself did not altogether neglect the course and order of the heavens, in that he said, *"When you see a cloud rise out of the west, straightway you say a shower comes; and so it is. And when you see the south wind blow, you say it will be hot, and so it comes to pass."* Again, *"When it is evening, you say fair weather, for the sky is red; and in the morning you say, today shall be a tempest, for the sky is red and lowering."* In this, he notes that these things truly come to pass according to ancient observation and to the rules of astronomy <note>original: "rule Astronomical"</note>; yet he also, by the words that follow, admonishes us that in attending too much to those observations, we must not neglect to follow our Christian calling <note>term: "Vocation"</note>.

<margin>Lactantius against Astrologers <note>original: "Lactant. contra Astrologos."</note>; Peucer on Astrology, page 383 <note>original: "Peucer. de Astrol. pag. 383."</note>.</margin>
The physician is commended to us and allowed in the Scriptures; but to put such trust in him as to neglect and distrust God is severely forbidden and reproved. Surely, it is most necessary for us to know and observe various astrological rules; otherwise, we could not efficiently <note>original: "with opportunity"</note> dispatch our ordinary affairs. And yet Lactantius <note>A 4th-century Christian author</note> condemns and counts it among the number of witchcrafts; a judgment from which John Calvin <note>The Protestant Reformer</note> does not much vary. The poor husbandman <note>term: farmer</note> perceives that the waxing of the Moon <note>original: "increase of the Moon"</note> makes plants and living creatures fruitful, so that during the Full Moon they are at their best strength, decaying in the wane, and in the conjunction <note>term: the New Moon phase, when the Moon is between the Earth and the Sun</note> they utterly wither and fade. When they have once learned this by observation, use, and practice, they organize their business accordingly—such as their times and seasons to sow, to plant, to prune, to bleed their cattle <note>original: "let their Cattel blood"</note>, to cut, etc.

### C H A P. III.

->*That certain observations are neutral <note>original: "indifferent"</note>, certain ridiculous, and certain impious; and from where that cunning is derived regarding Apollo and the fortune-tellers <note>term: Aruspices; ancient Roman diviners who interpreted omens from the entrails of animals</note>.*<-

<margin>The ridiculous art of casting horoscopes <note>original: "Nativity-casting"</note>.</margin>
I do not know whether to disallow or condemn the curious observations used by our elders, who made conjectures based on the time of birth <note>original: "Nativities"</note>. For example, they claimed that if Saturn and Mercury were opposite in any animal sign <note>term: "brute sign"; signs of the Zodiac represented by animals, like Aries or Leo</note>, a man born then would be dumb or stammer much—whereas it is daily seen that children naturally imitate their parents' conditions in that regard. Also, they have noted that one born during the waxing of the Moon <note>original: "Spring of the Moon"</note> shall be healthy; but if born during the wane, when the Moon is utterly diminished, the child cannot live; and if born during the conjunction, the child cannot last long.

<margin>The most impious opinion of Julius Maternus.</margin>
But I am sure the opinion of Julius Firmicus Maternus <note>A 4th-century Roman lawyer and astrologer</note> is most impious. He writes that he who is born when Saturn is in Leo shall live long and, after his death, shall go to heaven immediately. So too is the opinion of Albumazar <note>A 9th-century Persian astrologer</note>, who says that whoever prays to God when the Moon is in the "Head of the Dragon" <note>term: "Capite Draconis"; the ascending node of the Moon, considered highly significant in medieval astrology</note> shall be heard, and

<summary>This page argues that observing the weather and the stars for practical purposes—such as farming and medicine—is biblically supported and necessary, while warning against superstitious and impious forms of astrology like extreme horoscope-casting.</summary>

...and obtain his prayer. Furthermore, to act as a trivial prophet <note>original: "play the cold Prophet"</note>, such as counting it good or bad luck when salt or wine falls on the table or is spilled, etc., or to predict that guests are coming to your house because of the chattering of magpies <term>original: "Pies or Haggisters"; haggister is a dialect term for a magpie</term>, for which no logical reason can be given, is completely vanity and superstition, as shall be shown more fully hereafter. But to lead simple people to believe that a man or woman can foretell good or evil fortune is mere witchcraft or fraud <term>original: "cosenage"</term>; for God alone searches the heart and does not deliver his counsel to such wicked outcasts <note>original: "lewd reprobates"</note>. <margin>Jean Bodin. Lambert Daneau. Thomas Erastus. Niels Hemmingsen. *The Hammer of Witches* <note>original: "Mal. Malef." (Malleus Maleficarum)</note>. Thomas Aquinas, etc.</margin> I know various writers claim that witches foretell things as if prompted by a real Devil, and that he, in turn, learns it from the prophecies written in the Scriptures and by other clever tricks <note>original: "nimble sleights"</note> in which he surpasses any other earthly creature. They claim that this same Devil, or one of his companions, runs or flies as far as Rochester to Mother Bungie <note>Mother Bungie was a famous "cunning woman" or reputed witch in 16th-century Rochester</note>, or to Canterbury to M. T., or to Delphi to Apollo, or to Aesculapius in Pergamum, or to some other idol or witch. There, acting as an oracle, he answers all questions through his understanding of the prophecies contained in the Old Testament—especially in Daniel and Isaiah—by which the Devil knew of the transfer of the empire <note>original: "translation of the Monarchy"</note> from Babylon to Greece, etc. But either these writers have learned this from some oracle or witch themselves, or else I do not know where the Devil they find it. Indeed, it is certain that in this they show themselves to be witches and foolish diviners, for they find no such thing written in God's Word.

<margin>The passions of Apollo.</margin> Of the idol called Apollo, I have already spoken somewhat in the previous section regarding the spirit of divination <note>original: "Ob or Pytho"</note>, and I shall have occasion to speak of it again later. Therefore, at this time it shall suffice to tell you that the reputation it gained was through the craft and cunning of the priests who served there. With their counterfeit miracles, they so bewitched the people that they thought such power was contained in the bodies of those idols—power which God has not promised even to his angels or chosen people. For it is said that if Apollo were in a rage <note>original: "in a chafe"</note>, he would sweat; if he felt remorse for the afflicted and could not help them, he would shed tears—which I believe might have been wiped away with the same handkerchief that wiped and dried the face of the Rood of Grace when it was in similar distress <note>The Rood of Grace was a famous mechanical crucifix at Boxley Abbey that appeared to move and weep; it was exposed as a fraudulent machine during the Reformation</note>. This is just like another sort of bewitching priests called Haruspices <term>Ancient Roman priests who practiced divination by inspecting the entrails of animals</term>, who prophesied victory to Alexander the Great because an eagle landed on his head. That eagle might, I believe, be kept in the same cage as Muhammad's dove, which supposedly picked peas <note>original: "peason"</note> out of his ear <note>A common medieval and early modern legend claimed Muhammad trained a dove to eat from his ear to trick people into thinking the Holy Spirit was whispering to him</note>.

## C H A P. IV.

*The predictions of soothsayers and wicked priests; the prognostications of astronomers and physicians are allowable; divine prophecy is holy and good.*

<margin>What prophecies are allowable.</margin> <margin>Jean Bodin, *On the Demon-mania of Witches*, Book 1, Chapter 4.</margin> The fraudulent tricks of oracular priests and monks are, and have been, especially most abominable. The superstitious observations of senseless augurs <term>Ancient Roman officials who interpreted the will of the gods by observing the flight of birds</term> and soothsayers—which are contrary to philosophy and without the authority of Scripture—are very ungodly and ridiculous. However, I do not reject the prognostications of astronomers, nor the conjectures or warnings of physicians, nor yet the interpretations of philosophers; although, compared to the divine prophecies contained in Holy Scripture, they are not to be valued or regarded. For the purpose of the former and the latter is very different; and while the Scriptures contain only the words and will of God, the others are mingled with most horrible lies and deceptions. For though there are many among them who are learned and godly, there also lurk in corners a great number of counterfeits and fraudsters of the same profession. Jean Bodin makes this distinction between divine prophets and enchanters: namely, that the one always tells the truth, while the words of the other (proceeding from the Devil) are always false—or for every one truth, they tell a hundred lies. And if that is so, why may not every witch be thought as clever as Apollo? And why is not every counterfeit fraudster as good a witch as Mother Bungie?

For the odds are that they will hit upon the truth once in a hundred divinations, just as well as the best of them.

### CHAPTER V.

*The diversity of true prophets; of Urim and the prophetic use of the twelve precious stones contained within it; and of the divine voice called Echo.*

<margin>Different degrees of prophecy.</margin>
It appears that even among holy prophets, there were different kinds. For although David and Solomon included most excellent mysteries and notable allegories in their *Psalms* and *Parables*, they were not endowed with the same degree of prophecy that Elijah <note>original: "Ely"</note> and Elisha were, and so on.
<margin>2 Kings 2 <note>original: "2 Reg. 2."</note></margin>
For whenever it is said that God spoke to David or Solomon, it is understood to have been done through the prophets; for Nathan or Gad were the messengers and prophets who revealed God's will to David. And Ahijah <note>original: "Ahiam"</note> the Shilonite was sent from God to Solomon. Likewise, the spirit of prophecy that Elijah <note>original: "Elias"</note> possessed was doubled upon Elisha. Also, some prophets prophesied throughout their lives, while others had only one vision, and some had more according to God's pleasure. Indeed, some prophesied things to the people that did not come to pass, which happened when God's wrath was calmed by repentance. But these prophets were always considered by the people to be wise and godly, whereas the pagan <note>original: "Heathen"</note> prophets were always known and said to be mad and foolish, as is written both of the prophets of the Sibyl and of Apollo—and as is seen today in the Indies, and so on.

<margin>Jean Bodin.</margin>
But neither Bodin <note>Jean Bodin was a famous French jurist and writer who argued strongly for the reality of witchcraft</note> nor any witch-hunter <note>original: "Witchmonger"</note> in the world will ever be able to prove that any of these extraordinary gifts remain today, though in his book on "demonic madness" <note>original: *De la démonomanie des sorciers* (1580)</note> he tries to make people believe it. For these gifts were miraculously maintained by God among the Jews, who were instructed by them about all things that were to happen, or were otherwise informed by the Urim <term>The Urim and Thummim were sacred objects used by ancient Hebrew priests to determine the will of God through divine light or lots</term>. Through the brightness of the twelve precious stones contained in it, the priest could predict <note>original: "Prognosticate"</note> or explain anything. As Josephus <note>Flavius Josephus, a 1st-century Jewish historian</note> reports, <margin>Josephus, *Antiquities of the Jews*.</margin> <margin>Joshua son of Levi, in the book *Pirkei Avot* <note>original: "Josue filius Levi lib. Pirkeaboth"</note>.</margin> this brightness and power <note>original: "vertue"</note> ceased two hundred years before he was born. Consequently, since that time, no answers regarding God's will and pleasure have been yielded by it. Nevertheless, the Hebrews write that there has been a divine voice heard among them ever since that time, which in Latin is called "The Daughter of the Voice" <note>original: *Filia vocis*, known in Hebrew as *Bath Kol*</note>, in Greek "Echo" <note>original: ἠχὼ</note>, and in English "The Daughter of Speech."

### CHAPTER VI.

*Concerning conditional prophecies; what the prophecies in the Old Testament deal with and who published them; and the answers of witch-hunters to objections against the supernatural actions of witches.*

<margin>Conditional prophecies.</margin>
Christ and his apostles prophesied about the calamities and afflictions that would grieve and disturb the Church of God in this life. They also spoke of the Last Judgment and of the signs and omens <note>original: "tokens"</note> that would be shown before that day, and finally, of everything necessary for us to know in advance. However, such is the mercy of God that all prophecies, threats, plagues, and punishments are tied to the condition of repentance. On the other hand, physical <note>original: "corporal"</note> blessings are linked to the conditions of the cross and discipline <note>original: "castigation"</note>. Thus, because the mysteries of our salvation have been revealed to us through them, we should not seek new signs and miracles. Instead, we should pay attention to the teachings <note>original: "doctrine"</note> of the apostles, who preached that Christ was revealed and crucified for our sins, his Resurrection, his Ascension, and thereby the redemption of all who believe, and so on.

The prophecies in the Old Testament deal with the duration, the government, and the different types of states; the distinction between the four great empires <note>original: "Monarchies"</note>; and...

<summary>This page distinguishes between the genuine, divine prophecy of the biblical era and the perceived madness of pagan oracles. It argues that extraordinary spiritual gifts like the Urim have ceased, and that modern claims of supernatural prophecy (such as those by Jean Bodin) are unfounded.</summary>

<header>Miracles of Witchcraft. CHAPTER VII.</header>

<margin>The subject of the Prophecies of the Old Testament.</margin>
<margin>Deuteronomy 18:15.</margin>
of their order, decay, and restoration <note>original: "instauration"</note>; of the changes and ruins of the Kingdoms of Judah, Israel, Egypt, Persia, Greece, etc.; and especially of the coming of our Savior Jesus Christ, and how he should be born of a Virgin, and where, of his Tribe, Passion, Resurrection, etc. These Prophecies were published by God’s special and peculiar Prophets, endowed with his particular and excellent gifts, according to his promise: *I will raise them up a Prophet out of the midst of their Brethren, I will put my words in his mouth*, etc. Although this was specifically spoken of Christ, yet it was also spoken of those particular Prophets who were placed among them by God to declare his will, and who were also figures of Christ, the Prophet himself. Now, if prophecy is an extraordinary gift of God and a thing peculiar to himself—as no creature can be a prophet or show what is to come without his special assistance—why should we believe that those wicked <note>original: "lewd"</note> persons can perform, through divinations and miracles, that which is not in human, but in Divine power to accomplish?

<margin>Ecclesiastes 9:5.</margin>
<margin>1 Samuel 28.</margin>
However, when I deny that witches can ride in the air and the miraculous circumstances thereof, they immediately object to me that *Enoch and Elijah were taken up bodily into heaven; and Habakkuk was carried in the air to feed Daniel*; and so they falsely oppose the Devil's or a witch’s power against the virtue of the Holy Ghost. If I mock the poets' opinions, saying that witches cannot *draw the moon down from heaven* <note>original: "Cælo deducere Lunam"</note>, etc., they tell me that at Joshua’s battle, *the sun stayed*; and at the passion of Christ, *there was palpable darkness*. If I deny their skill in the interpretation of dreams, advising them to remember Jeremiah’s counsel *not to follow or trust the interpreters of dreams*, they reproach me with Daniel and Joseph—because one of them interpreted the dreams of Pharaoh, the Egyptian King, and the other those of Nebuchadnezzar, the Persian King. If I say with Solomon, *that the dead know nothing, and that the dead know us not, nor can they be moved out of Abraham’s bosom*, etc., they produce the story of Samuel. In doing this, I say they set the power of a creature as high as the Creator. If I say that these witches cannot transform <note>original: "transubstantiate"</note> themselves or others into beasts, etc., they cite the story of Nebuchadnezzar, as though he were indeed made a physical beast, and that also by witchcraft; and they strengthen that assertion with the fables of Circe and Ulysses’ companions, etc.

### CHAPTER VII.

->What were the miracles expressed in the Old Testament; and what are they in the New Testament; and that we are not now to look for any more miracles.<-

<margin>Genesis 11:6.</margin>
<margin>Genesis 21.</margin>
<margin>Daniel 11.</margin>
The miracles expressed in the Old Testament were many, but the purpose of them all was one, though they were diverse and different in appearance. For instance, the sacrifices of Moses, Elijah, and Solomon, being abundantly wet, were burned with fire from heaven, etc. There was the variety of tongues at the building of Babylon; Isaac’s birth to Sarah when she was naturally past childbearing; the passage through the Red Sea; and Daniel’s foretelling of the four Monarchies, in the fourth of which he clearly foretells the coming of the Lord. All these, and many others expressed in the Old Testament, were merciful instructions and notable miracles to strengthen the faith of God’s people in their Messiah. If you had gone to Delphi <note>original: "Delphos"</note>, Apollo would have made you believe with his ambiguous <note>original: "Amphibological"</note> answers that he could have foretold you all these things.

<margin>A summary of Christ's Miracles.</margin>
<margin>Matthew 12:25, 26.</margin>
The miracles performed by Christ were the *raising up of the dead* (which many would attribute to the woman of Endor, and also to our witches and conjurers); *the restoring of limbs to the lame; sight to the blind; speech to the dumb*; and finally, *the healing of all diseases*. Many believe our witches can do these things—indeed, they even take it upon themselves to claim they can. As for *casting out of Devils* (which was another kind of miracle common with Christ), witches and conjurers are said to be as good at it as he ever was. And yet, if you believe Christ’s words, it cannot be so; for he says, *Every Kingdom divided against itself shall be brought to ruin.*

He addresses common biblical counter-arguments used by believers in witchcraft, asserting that supernatural feats like flight or transformation are the domain of God alone.</summary>

And this is enough regarding the word *Kasam* <note>original: "Kafam" — likely a reference to the Hebrew root *qasam*, meaning to practice divination or sorcery</note>.

# BOOK 10. The Discovery of Dreams.

Just as a glass shows the image or figure placed opposite to it, so in dreams, the fantasy and imagination inform the understanding of such things as haunt the outward senses. Regarding this, the Poet says:

> Do not worry about dreams; for what the human mind desires while hoping during its waking hours, it sees that very same thing during sleep. <note>original: "Somnia ne cures; nam mens humana quod optat, Dum vigilat sperans, per somnum cernit id ipsum."</note>

->Translated into English by *Abraham Fleming*:<-

> Pay no attention to dreams—and why? Because the mind
> Catches a glimpse in sleep of those things
> Which it wishes and hopes to find
> During the time it is awake.

***

### CHAPTER 3.

->*The opinions of various ancient writers concerning dreams, and how they differ in no small way; the causes of dreams.*<-

<margin>A disagreement in opinions about dreams.</margin>
Synesius, Themiftius, Democritus, and others, basing their views on examples that chance has sometimes proven true, persuade men that no dream is in vain. They affirm that heavenly influences produce various forms in physical matter. From these same influences, visions and dreams are impressed upon the <term>fantastical power</term> <note>the faculty of imagination</note>, which acts as an instrument aligned with a celestial disposition to produce certain effects—especially during sleep. At that time, the mind (being free from bodily cares) can more freely receive heavenly influences. Through this, many things are revealed to those sleeping in dreams which those who are awake cannot see. *Plato* attributes them to the forms and innate knowledge of the soul; *Avicenna* <note>original: "Avicen"</note> to the "last intelligence" that moves the Moon, through the light that illuminates the imagination in sleep; *Aristotle* to the imaginative sense; *Averroes* to the faculty of imagination; and *Albertus Magnus* <note>original: "Albert"</note> to the influence of superior <note>celestial</note> bodies.

***

### CHAPTER 4.

->*Arguments against interpreters of dreams; the ordinary cause of dreams; Hemingius’s opinion on diabolical dreams; the era of dream interpretation has ended.*<-

There are books circulating on this matter under the name of *Abraham*, who (as *Philo* says in his book *On Giants* <note>original: "lib. gigantum"</note>) was the inventor of the interpretation of dreams; there are similar books attributed to *Solomon* and *Daniel*. But *Cicero*, in his book *On Divination* <note>original: "lib. de divinatione"</note>, refutes the vanity and folly of those who put their trust in dreams. Furthermore, the interpreters of dreams have no certainty before the dream occurs, nor even afterward; yet, when something happens later, they then twist the dream to fit the event that has occurred.

<margin>The Pleasant Art of the Interpretation of Dreams, 1568.</margin>
Certainly, men rarely fail to dream at night of those things they meditate upon by day. During the day, they see many different things and conceive of them separately in their minds; then, those mixed concepts, being stored away in the chamber of the memory, struggle together. Because the imagination cannot distinguish or process them properly, a specific vision gathered from many different thoughts is formed and combined into one. Therefore, in my opinion, it is a waste of time to study the interpretation of dreams. Anyone who wishes to see the folly and vanity of this may read a pointless treatise published by *Thomas Hill*, a Londoner, in 1568.

<summary>Scot examines the classical and medieval theories of dreaming, citing various philosophers' views on celestial influence versus psychological causes, ultimately arguing that dream interpretation is a vain and baseless practice.</summary>
<keywords>Dreams, Synesius, Aristotle, Avicenna, Averroes, Cicero, Thomas Hill, divination, imagination, celestial influence, memory</keywords>

<meta>This page continues Book 10 of Reginald Scot’s work, concluding the discussion on the three types of diabolical dreams proposed by Niels Hemmingsen and beginning Chapter 5, which argues against the power of witches to control human thoughts through dreams.</meta>

Dreams of Witchcraft. CHAPTER 5. 101

<margin>
Niels Hemmingsen <note>original: "N. Hemin."</note> in his *Admonitions on Avoiding Magical Superstitions* <note>original: "in admonitionib. de superstitionib. Magicis vitandis"</note>.
</margin>
Lastly, there are diabolical dreams, which Niels Hemmingsen <note>original: "Nicholaus Hemingius," a 16th-century Danish theologian</note> divides into three sorts. The first is when the Devil himself immediately (meaning physically) offers the subject matter of a dream. Secondly, when the Devil shows revelations to those who have requested them from him. Thirdly, when magicians use their art to ensure that other men dream whatever the magicians wish. Assuredly these—and all the rest, depending on how they are used—are very "magical" and devilish dreams. For although we may receive comfort of mind through those called *divine dreams*, and health of body through *physical dreams* <note>medical dreams reflecting the body's internal state</note>, yet we are deluded if we <margin>The purpose and use of prophecy, interpretation of dreams, the working of miracles, etc.</margin> take it upon ourselves to perform the office of God by revealing or interpreting them. 

The same is true if we attribute miraculous effects to them now, when we see that the gifts of prophecy, the interpretation of dreams, and the performing of miracles have ceased. These were special and unique gifts from God intended to confirm the truth of His Word and to establish His people in the faith of the Messiah. That Messiah has now been revealed to us both in the Testament and in the blood of our Savior, Jesus Christ. To do otherwise is to be bewitched; we both abuse and offend the majesty of God and also seduce, delude, and trick everyone who gives us credit because of our persuasion and their own easy belief.

***

### CHAPTER 5.

->*That neither witches nor anyone else can use words or herbs to force whatever thoughts or dreams they want into the mind of a sleeping person; and the true source of "magical" dreams.*<-

<margin>
Look for such material in my book by Hartmann.
</margin>
I admit there may be herbs and stones found and known to physicians which can induce dreams. There are other herbs and stones that may cause someone to reveal all the secrets of their mind while the body sleeps, or at least cause them to talk in their sleep. But I deny that witches or magicians have the power—by words, herbs, and curses—to thrust into the mind or conscience of a man whatever they please by the virtue of their charms, herbs, stones, or <term>familiars</term> <note>supernatural entities believed to assist witches</note>, as Hemmingsen believes. At the same time, I confess that the Devil works hard both by day and by night to seduce man and lead him away from God. Indeed, he does this in no way more than by placing himself as a "god" in the minds of those who are so gullible that they attribute to him, or to witches, things that only God has the power to accomplish.

<margin>
Daniel 2.
Genesis 11:8.
Genesis 37 & 11.
Isaiah 11.
Daniel 2.
</margin>
Does not Daniel the Prophet say, regarding this very case, *It is the Lord only who knows such secrets as are required for the exposition of dreams?* And does not Joseph repeat those very words to Pharaoh’s officers who consulted him? You may find a great number of examples of divine dreams in the Scripture—those, I mean, through which it pleased God to reveal His will. As for physical dreams, we may read about them in books and see them in our own experience daily, or rather nightly. Dreams that are <term>casual</term> <note>original: "casual"; meaning accidental or occurring by chance rather than by divine intent</note> are also common, arising (as has been said) from a person’s many affairs and business. 

Those which are called "magical" or "diabolical" dreams in these days might better be called <term>melancholical</term> <note>caused by an excess of "black bile," one of the four humors thought to cause depression or dark visions</note>. For out of that black vapor in sleep, as <margin>Aristotle, *On Dreams* <note>original: "Aristot. de somnio"</note>.</margin> Aristotle says, some horrible thing appears, like the image of an ugly devil. Sometimes other terrible visions, imaginations, plans, and practices also appear. For instance, we read of a certain man who dreamed that someone appeared to him and told him to throw himself into a deep pit, promising he would reap great benefit from God by doing so. The miserable wretch believed it, did it, and killed himself. Now, I confess that the *interpretation* or the execution of that dream was indeed diabolical; but the dream itself was accidental, derived from the heavy and black humor of melancholy.

### CHAPTER VI.

#### *How men have been bewitched, cozened <note>original: "cofened"; meaning cheated or tricked</note>, or abused by dreams to dig and search for money.*

<margin>Such people would be embarked in the Ship of Fools <note>A reference to Sebastian Brant’s famous 1494 satire *Das Narrenschiff*, which cataloged various types of human ignorance and vice.</note>.</margin>
I myself could show how many people have been bewitched by dreams and thereby driven to exhaust themselves by digging and searching for money, etc., because they or someone else dreamed of it. I have known many wise men who were abused in that way by very simple persons, even when no actual dream occurred, but only "waking dreams" <note>fantasies or delusions while awake</note>. This has been used in the past as one of the cleverest cheating tricks; indeed, a very formal art has been devised for it, including many excellent superstitions and ceremonies, which I will set down as briefly as possible. <margin>An English Proverb.</margin> Nonetheless, here in England, this proverb has been common: *Dreams prove contrary*. This is according to the answer given by a priest’s boy to his master, who told the boy he had dreamed he kissed the boy's tail <note>buttocks</note>. "Yes, Master," says the boy, "but dreams prove contrary: you must kiss mine."

---

### CHAPTER VII.

#### *The Art and Order to be used in digging for money revealed by dreams: how to procure pleasant dreams: concerning morning and midnight dreams.*

<margin>Note this superstitious foolishness <note>original: "dotage"</note>.</margin>
Three crosses must be made upon a hazel wand, and certain blasphemous and impious words must be said over it; to this must be added certain symbols <note>original: "characters"</note> and strange <note>original: "barbarous"</note> names. While the treasure is being dug up, one must read the Psalms: *Out of the depths* <note>original: "De profundis"</note>, *The Mass* <note>original: "Missa"</note>, *May he have mercy on us* <note>original: "Misereatur nostri"</note>, *Requiem*, *The Lord's Prayer* <note>original: "Pater Noster"</note>, *Hail Mary* <note>original: "Ave Maria"</note>, and *And lead us not into temptation, but deliver us from evil, Amen* <note>original: "Et ne nos inducas in tentationem, sed libera nos à malo, Amen"</note>. Also: *From the gate of hell, I believe I shall see good things, etc.* <note>original: "A porta inferni credo videre bona, &c."</note>, *Wait for the Lord* <note>original: "Expectate Dominum"</note>, and *Eternal rest* <note>original: "Requiem aeternam"</note>. Then a certain prayer is said. And if the time for digging is neglected, the Devil will carry all the treasure away. See other more absolute conjurations for this purpose under the word *Idoni* <note>A Hebrew-derived term for a "familiar spirit" or "soothsayer"</note> later in this book.

<margin>Giambattista della Porta <note>original: "J. Bap. Neap."</note> in *Natural Magic*, Book 2, chapters 26, pages 83 & 84.</margin>
You shall find in the works of Giambattista della Porta <note>original: "Johannes Baptista Neapolitanus," a famous Italian polymath and occultist</note> various recipes using herbs and potions to produce pleasant or fearful dreams, and also perfumes for that purpose. He affirms that dreams in the dead of night are commonly absurd <note>original: "preposterous"</note> and monstrous; but in the morning, when the gross humors <note>In ancient medicine, "humors" were bodily fluids (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, black bile) that governed health and personality.</note> are spent, more pleasant and certain dreams occur because the blood is purer than at other times. The reason for this is explained there.

### CHAPTER VIII.

#### *Sundry recipes <note>original: "receipts"</note> and ointments made and used for the transportation of witches and other miraculous effects: an instance of this reported and credited by some who are learned.*

It shall not be out of place here to repeat a description of an ointment intended for this purpose, recounted by the aforementioned Giambattista della Porta. I will set down his words on this matter.

<meta>This page continues Reginald Scot's "The Discovery of Witchcraft," Book 10. <page-num>103</page-num>
<header>Witch Transportations. Concerning Witchcraft. CHAPTER 8. <note>The original header labels this as Chapter 9, but it follows Chapter 7 and precedes a second Chapter 9 heading; it functions as the conclusion of the previous discussion on ointments.</note></header>

<margin>Recipes <note>original: "Receipts"</note> or formulas for the miraculous transportation of Witches.</margin>
The recipe is as follows:
Take the fat of young children and boil <note>original: "seeth"</note> it with water in a brass <note>original: "brazen"</note> vessel, saving the thickest of what remains boiled at the bottom. This they store and keep until there is an occasion to use it. They add to this *Eleoselinum* <note>original: "Eleoselinum"; Wild Celery or Mountain Parsley</note>, *Aconitum* <note>original: "Aconitum"; Aconite or Wolfsbane</note>, *Frondes populeas* <note>original: "Frondes populeas"; Poplar leaves</note>, mountain parsley, wolfsbane, leaves of the poplar, and soot.

Another recipe for the same purpose:
*Sium* <note>original: "Sium"; Water-parsnip</note>, *Acarum vulgare* <note>original: "Acarum vulgare"; Common Sweet Flag</note>, *Pentaphyllon* <note>original: "Pentaphyllon"; Cinquefoil</note>, yellow watercress, common acorus, cinquefoil, the blood of a bat <note>original: "Flitter-mouse"</note>, *Solanum Somniferum* and oil <note>original: "Solanum Somniferum & oleum"; Sleeping Nightshade and oil</note>. They crush all these together and then rub all parts of their bodies thoroughly until they look red and become very hot, so that the pores may be opened and their flesh becomes permeable and loose. They add to this either fat or oil instead, so that the force of the ointment may pierce inward more easily and thus be more effective.

<margin>Old women, whom they call "striges" <note>original: "striges"; screech-owls or hags</note> because of their resemblance to those birds, and who suck the blood of little children lying in their cradles at night.</margin>
By this means (he says), on a moonlight night, they seem to be carried through the air to feasting, singing, dancing, kissing, embracing <note>original: "culling"</note>, and other acts of lust <note>original: "Venery"</note> with such youths as they love and desire most. For (he says) the force of their imagination is so powerful that almost all that part of the brain where the memory is located is full of such fantasies. And because they are naturally prone to believe anything, they receive such impressions and steadfast fantasies into their minds that even their spirits are altered by them—thinking of nothing else, either by day or by night. This is further encouraged in their imaginations by the fact that their usual food is commonly nothing but beets, roots, nuts, beans, peas, and so on.

Now (he says), when I considered this thoroughly, remaining doubtful of the matter, I encountered a witch who of her own accord promised to run an errand for me immediately from far-off countries. She asked everyone I had brought to witness the matter to leave the chamber. When she had undressed herself and rubbed <note>original: "froted"</note> her body with certain ointments (an action we watched through a crack or little hole in the door), she fell down into an extremely sound and heavy sleep due to the force of those sleep-inducing <note>original: "soporiferous"</note> ointments. We then broke open the door and beat her severely, but the depth of her sleep was such that it took away her sense of feeling, and we left for a time. Now, when her strength and powers were exhausted and faded, she awoke on her own and began to speak many vain and delirious <note>original: "doting"</note> words, claiming that she had traveled over both seas and mountains and giving us many untrue and false reports. We earnestly denied them, yet she shamelessly insisted they were true. This (he says) will not happen to everyone, but only to old women who are "melancholic" <note>In the "four humors" theory of medicine, a melancholic person was thought to be cold and dry, making them prone to depression and vivid hallucinations.</note>, whose nature is extremely cold and whose internal vapors are small; they both perceive and remember what they see in that trance-like state of theirs.

On one hand, it would be a marvel if those things happened in dreams (which the witches nevertheless claim to be otherwise) and yet, when those witches awake, they neither...

It is held and maintained by many, and gathered from the 12th chapter of *Numbers*, that everything written or spoken by the prophets among the children of *Israel* (except for *Moses*) was presented to them through dreams. And indeed, it is clear that many things which the unlearned think were physically completed were actually only performed in dreams and visions. For example, when *Solomon* asked God for the gift of wisdom, that was (I say) in a dream; as was the occasion when he received the promise that the kingdom of *Israel* would continue in his lineage. So was *Isaiah's* vision in the 6th chapter of his prophecy, as well as that of *Ezekiel* in chapter 12. Finally, where *Jeremiah* was commanded *to hide his belt in a crack of a rock at the river Euphrates in Babylon*, and that after certain days it rotted there, it must have been in a dream; for *Jeremiah* was never (or at least not then) at Babylon. # Dreams and Witchcraft. Chapter 10.

If you read *Artemidorus* <note>original: "Artemidorus," a 2nd-century Greek author famous for his work on dream interpretation, the "Oneirocritica"</note>, you will read many stories of people who dreamed of things that later came to pass. # BOOK XI.

->CHAPTER I.<-

*The Hebrew word* Nahas *explained; concerning the* Art of Augury; *who invented it; how* messy a Science it is; *the* multitude of Sacrifices *and* Sacrificers of the Heathen, *and the reasons for them.*

<margin>The messy Art of Augury.</margin>
*NAHAS* <note>original: "Nahas," a Hebrew word (נָחַשׁ) generally meaning to practice divination or observe omens</note> refers to the practice of observing the flight of birds and encompasses all other such observations where men make guesses based on uncertain trifles <term>toyes</term>. It is found in Deuteronomy 18 and in 2 Chronicles 33, as well as elsewhere. Regarding this Art of Augury <note>original: "Augury," the practice of interpreting omens from the behavior of birds</note>, Tiresias <note>original: "Tyresias," a famous blind prophet of Thebes in Greek mythology</note>, the King of the Thebans, is said to be the first inventor. However, Tages first published the rules <term>discipline</term> of it while he was only a little boy, as Cicero reports from the books of the Etruscans <note>original: "Hetruscans"</note> themselves. Some points of this Art are considered more advanced and profound than others, and yet they are more crude and messy than the rest—specifically, divination based on the internal organs <term>entrails</term> of beasts, which the Gentiles especially observed in their sacrifices. Indeed, Marcus Varro <note>original: "Marcus Varro," an ancient Roman scholar and writer</note>, seeing the absurdity of it, said that these gods were not only idle but very slovenly <note>original: "slovens," meaning messy or dirty people</note> for choosing to hide their secrets and counsel in the guts and bowels of animals.

The vain, absurd, and superstitious way the Heathen used this kind of divination in their sacrifices is proven by their actions and ceremonies practiced in that regard, both in the past and at this very hour. The Egyptians had 666 different sorts and kinds of sacrifices; the Romans had almost as many; the Greeks <note>original: "Grecians"</note> had nearly as many as they; the Persians and Medians <note>original: "Medes"</note> were not far behind them. The Indians and other nations currently have sacrifices full of variety, and even more full of barbarous impiety. In various places, these people offer sacrifices to the Devil, hoping thereby to move him to mercy <term>lenity</term>. Indeed, they commonly sacrifice those enemies they have captured in war, just as we read that the Gentiles in ancient times offered sacrifice to appease the wrath and anger of their false <term>feigned</term> gods.

---

->CHAPTER II.<-

*Regarding the Jews' sacrifice to* Moloch; *a discussion on that topic, and on* Purgatory.

<margin>2 Kings 23:10. 2 Chronicles 33:6.</margin>

<margin>An unanswerable argument against Purgatory.</margin>
The Jews used one kind of diabolical sacrifice that was never taught to them by Moses—namely, offering their children to Moloch <note>original: "Moloch," an ancient Canaanite deity associated with child sacrifice</note>, making their sons and their daughters run through the fire. They supposed that there was such grace and power <term>efficacy</term> in that action as other witches claim to be in charms and words. Therefore, among other points of witchcraft, this is specifically and by name forbidden by Moses. We read of no more miracles performed by this than by any other kind of witchcraft mentioned in the Old or New Testament. It was not a ceremony appointed by God, nor a symbolic foreshadowing <term>figure</term> of Christ. Perhaps it might be a sacrament, or rather a symbol of Purgatory <note>Scot is likely using "Purgatory" sarcastically here to link Catholic doctrine with ancient pagan superstitions</note>—a place that was not mentioned <note>original: "remembred"</note> by Moses. Neither was there any sacrifice appointed by the Law for the relief of the souls of Israelites who were supposedly tormented there. Without any doubt, this would not

This sacrificing to *Moloch* (as some claim) was common among the *Gentiles*, from whom the *Jews* brought it into *Israel*; and there (most likely) the Eutichists <note>The Eutychians were a 5th-century heretical sect, though Scot may be using the term more broadly to describe those he considers heretics.</note> learned this abomination.

### CHAPTER III.

->*The Cannibals' cruelty: how Popish sacrifices exceed the tyranny of the Jews or Gentiles.*<-

<margin>Against the Papists' abominable and blasphemous Sacrifice of the Mass.</margin>
**T**he barbarism <note>original: "incivility"</note> and cruel sacrifices of Popish priests even exceed those of both the *Jew* and the *Gentile*; for these priests take it upon themselves to sacrifice Christ himself. To make their tyranny even more obvious, they are not content to have killed him once, but daily and hourly torment him with new deaths. Indeed, they are not ashamed to swear that with their physical hands they tear his human substance, breaking it into small pieces <note>original: "gobbets"</note>, and with their actual teeth chew his flesh and bones, contrary to both Divine and human nature—and contrary to the prophecy which says, *There shall not a bone of him be broken.*
<margin>Psalm 34:20.</margin>
Finally, at the end of their sacrifices (as they say), they eat him up raw and swallow every limb and part of him down into their guts. Last of all, they convey him into the place where they deposit the remains of everything else they have devoured that day. This same barbarous impiety exceeds the cruelty of all others, for all the *Gentiles* consumed their sacrifices with fire, which they considered to be holy.

### CHAPTER IV.

->*The superstition of the Heathen concerning the element of fire, and how it came to be so revered among them; of their corruptions, and how they had some hint of the holy Fathers' actions in that regard.*<-

**A**s for the element of fire and the superstition surrounding it in these matters, you should understand that many superstitious people of all nations have received and revered it as the most holy thing among their sacrifices. In fact, they have worshipped it among their gods, calling it *Orimasda* <note>original: "Orimasda," likely referring to Ahura Mazda, the Zoroastrian deity associated with light and fire.</note> (that is, holy fire and Divine light). The Greeks called it *Hestia* <note>original: "ἑστίαν"</note>, and the Romans, *Vesta*, which means *The fire of the Lord.* They had surely heard of the fire that came down from heaven and consumed the offerings <note>original: "oblations"</note> of the Fathers, and they understood it to be God himself. For only the bare names of things reached the Heathen from the teachings of the godly Fathers and Patriarchs—and these were so obscured with fables, corrupted with lies, overwhelmed with superstitions, and disguised with ceremonies that it is hard to judge where they originated. I suppose some cause of this was partly the transfer of governments, by which one nation learned folly from another, and partly blind devotion without knowledge of God’s Word—but especially the lack of Grace, which they did not seek according to God's commandment and will. That the *Gentiles* had some hint <note>original: "inkling"</note> of the godly Fathers' actions may appear in various ways.
<margin>The Gymnosophists of India and their apish imitation of Isaiah.</margin>
Do not the *Muscovites* <note>people of the Grand Duchy of Moscow, or Russia</note> and *Indian* prophets <term>Gymnosophists</term> today, like apes, imitate *Isaiah* <note>original: "Esay"</note>? Because he went naked for certain years, they, for their part, fake madness and drink potions for that purpose, thinking that whatever they say in their madness will certainly come to pass. But this is discussed more extensively before under the word *Kasam* <note>original: "Kasam," a Hebrew word for divination previously defined in the text.</note>.

->### CHAPTER V.<-

->*Regarding Roman Sacrifices: the high regard they had for Augury; and the Twelve Tables.*<-

**T**he Romans, even after they had grown into a great civilization <note>original: "civility"</note> and enjoyed a most flourishing state and commonwealth, would sometimes sacrifice themselves, sometimes their children, and sometimes their friends, etc., consuming them with fire, which they considered holy. Such was the high regard <note>original: "estimation"</note> attributed to the practice of divination through the entrails of beasts. At *Rome*, the chief princes themselves practiced this; namely, *Romulus*, *Fabius Maximus*, and others, to the extent that a decree was made by the entire Senate that six of the chief magistrates' sons should be sent out from time to time to learn the mystery of these arts of augury and divination in *Etruria* <note>original: "Hetruria," an ancient civilization in central Italy famous for its soothsayers.</note>, where the skill and knowledge of it most abounded. When they returned home well-informed and instructed in this art, their reputation and dignity were such that they were accounted, reputed, and taken to be the interpreters of the gods—or rather, the intermediaries between the gods and men. No high priest, nor any other great officer, was elected unless these men either nominated them absolutely or presented two names from which the Senate had to choose one.

<margin>The Law of the Twelve Tables.</margin>In their ancient laws <note>The Twelve Tables were the foundation of Roman law, established c. 450 BCE.</note> were written these words: *Prodigia & portenta ad Hetruscos aruspices (si Senatus jusserit) deferunto, Hetruriæq; principes disciplinam discunto. Quibus divis decreverunt, procuranto, iidem fulgura & ostenta pianto, auspicia servanto, auguri parento:* <note>original Latin: "Let prodigies and portents be referred to the Etruscan soothsayers (if the Senate so orders), and let the princes of Etruria learn the discipline. Let them manage the matters decreed to whichever gods they choose; let them also atone for lightning strikes and omens, observe the auspices, and obey the augur."</note> the effect of which words is this: Let all prodigious and ominous matters be carried to the soothsayers of *Etruria*, at the will and commandment of the Senate; and let the young princes be sent to *Etruria*, there to learn that discipline, or to be instructed in that art and knowledge. Let there be always some official <note>original: "Solicitor"</note> to learn which gods have decreed or determined their matters; and let sacrifices be made to them in times of lightning, or at any strange or supernatural appearance. Let all such tokens used for conjecture be observed; and whatever the soothsayer commands, let it be religiously obeyed.

---

->### CHAPTER VI.<-

->*Colleges of Augurs: their office, their number, and the meaning of Augury; that those who practiced that art were swindlers; their profession, their places of exercise, their apparel, and their superstition.*<-

**R**omulus established three colleges or groups <note>original: "Centuries"</note> of these kinds of soothsayers, who alone (and no others) had the authority to interpret the minds and warnings of the gods. Afterward, that number was increased to five, and after that to nine, for the number had to be odd. In the end, they increased so quickly that the authorities were forced to make a decree to halt further establishments, similar to our Statute of *Mortmain*. <margin>Magna Charta 3 Henry III. c. 36; 7 Edward I. c. 15; 2 Richard II. c. 5. <note>These are English statutes designed to prevent land from passing into the "dead hand" of the Church, used here as a historical comparison.</note></margin> Nevertheless, *Sulla* <note>original: "Sylla"</note> (contrary to all orders and constitutions made before) increased that number to twenty-four.

And though *Augury* <note>original: "Augurium"</note> is most properly that divination which is gathered by observing birds, yet because this word *Nahas* <note>A Hebrew term for divination or omens, discussed by Scot in previous chapters.</note> encompasses all other kinds of divination, such as *extispicium* <term>the inspection of entrails</term>, *haruspicy* <term>divination by animal sacrifice</term>, etc.—which involves guessing based on the entrails of beasts as well as various other ways—I will speak a little of such arts as were regarded beyond measure by our ancestors. I omit physiognomy and palmistry and such like because of their tediousness and folly. I do not intend to uncover every detail, but rather to refute the vanity of these arts, and especially of the professors of them, which are and always have been swindling <note>original: "cousening"</note> arts, and in them...

<header>Augury. of Witchcraft. CHAP. VIII.</header>

...contained both special and distinct kinds of witchcraft. For the masters of these arts <note>original: "faculties"</note> have always presumed to take the place and name of God; blasphemously claiming for themselves His omnipotent power to foretell the future, etc. In truth, they could do nothing but put on a show of things that are not.

<margin>A clear revelation of the deception <note>original: "cosenage"</note> of augurs.</margin>
One thing that exposes their deception is that they could never work for or predict anything for the poor or lower class of people. For portentous signs (they claim) always concerned great estates and noble people. Matters affecting the lower sort were considered inferior causes, though the superstitious commoners would still try to learn about them. However, the professors of this art did not descend so low as to communicate with them. These practitioners were priests—who in all ages and nations have been powerful figures <note>original: "jolly fellows"</note>—whose office was to predict what would happen, regarding either good luck or misfortune. They would interpret the minds, warnings, and threats of the gods, and foretell calamities which might be removed or lessened through their sacrifices and public acts of penance <note>original: "contrition"</note>. 

Before beginning their work, they followed many observations very superstitiously, pretending that every bird and beast was sent by the gods as an omen of some kind. Therefore, they first chose a clear day and fair weather for their business. Specific locations were assigned for this in both *Rome* and *Etruria* <note>original: "Hetruria"</note>, where they observed every quarter of the sky <note>original: "element"</note>—which way to look and where to stand. Their clothing was very priest-like, in a fashion distinct from all others, especially during their prayers, where they could not omit a single word or syllable. Because of this, one person would read the service while the rest repeated it after him, in the manner of a procession.

---

## CHAPTER VII.

->*The Times and Seasons for practicing Augury, including the Method, Order, and Ceremonies involved.*<-

<margin>Note the superstitious ceremonies of the augurs <note>OCR original: "Angurers"</note>.</margin>
They paid just as much attention to the timing of their ministry. They had to begin at midnight and end at noon, not working during the decline of the day but while it was increasing. They did not work during the sixth or seventh hour of the day, nor after the month of August. This was because young birds are flying about then and are sickly or imperfect while molting their feathers and migrating; thus, no certain guess could be made of the gods' purposes through them during those seasons. But in the proper times, they would stand with a curved wand in their hand, facing East, at the top of a high tower. When the weather was clear, they watched for birds, noting where they came from, where they flew, and how they flapped <note>original: "wag"</note> their wings, etc.

---

## CHAPTER VIII.

->*Regarding the Signs and Tokens by which Augurs prophesied; observations of the Internal and External parts of Beasts, and their behavior in the Slaughterhouse.*<-

These types of practitioners <note>original: "Witches"</note> whom we are now discussing also predicted good or bad luck based on the health or imperfection of the entrails of beasts. They looked for natural excess or infirmities, or an abundance of unnecessary fluids <note>original: "humours"</note> appearing in the internal parts and bowels of the sacrificed animals. As for the external parts, they always ensured beforehand that the animal was without blemish.

<margin>Observations in the art of augury.</margin>

And yet there were many signs and notes to be taken of the external actions of those animals at the time of sacrifice: such as if they would not quietly be brought to the place of execution, but had to be forcibly hauled; or if they broke loose; or if by chance, cunning, or strength they withstood the first blow; or if after the butcher's blow they leaped up, roared, or stood still; or being fallen, kicked, or would not quietly die, or did not bleed well; or if any bad news had been heard, or any bad sight seen at the time of slaughter or sacrifice. These were all signs of ill luck and unhappy success. On the other side, if the slaughterman performed his office well—provided the beast had been well chosen, not infected, but whole and sound, and in the end cleanly killed—all was considered safe; for then the gods smiled.
