### C H A P. IX.

->*A refutation of augury; Plato’s respected opinion of it, and of contrary events and false predictions.*<-

<margin>Plato in *Phaedrus*, in *Timaeus*, and in his books on the *Republic* <note>original: "Plato in Phedro, in Timeo, in lib. de Republ."</note>.</margin>
But what credit is to be given to such trifles <note>original: "toyes"</note> and coincidences, which do not arise from nature but are gathered by the superstition of the interpreters? As for birds, who is so ignorant that they do not realize that one flies one way and another another way simply to attend to their personal needs? And yet other forms of divination are even more vain and foolish. Nevertheless, Plato thinks a commonwealth cannot stand without this art and numbers it among the liberal sciences. These fellows promised Pompey, Cassius, and Caesar that none of them should die before they were old, and that they would die in their own houses in great honor; and yet they all died quite the opposite way. However, the heathens in this point <margin>In which the Papists are more blameworthy than the heathens.</margin> were not so much to be blamed as the "sacrificing Papists" <note>The author uses "sacrificing Papists" as a derogatory term for Roman Catholics, comparing the Catholic Mass to pagan animal sacrifices.</note>. For the heathens were directed to this without the knowledge of God's promises, nor did they know the purpose for which such ceremonies and sacrifices were originally instituted. They only understood by an uncertain and vague rumor <note>original: "slender report"</note> that God used to send good or ill success to the children of Israel and to the old Patriarchs and Fathers, based on his acceptance or rejection of their sacrifices and offerings. But men in all ages have been so desirous to know the outcome of their purposes and the sequence of things to come—to see the end of their fear and hope—that a simple witch who has learned anything in the art of deception <note>original: "cosenage"</note> may make a great many complete fools.

***

### C H A P. X.

->*The deceptive art of Sortilege or Lottery, practiced especially by Egyptian vagabonds; of permitted lots, of Pythagoras’s lot, etc.*<-

<margin>Sortilege or divination by lots.</margin>
The counterfeit Egyptians <note>During this period, "Egyptians" was the common term for the Romani people (from which "Gypsy" is derived), who were often accused of being vagabonds and frauds.</note>, who were indeed deceptive vagabonds practicing the art called *Sortilegium* <note>Latin: divination by drawing lots</note>, had no small credit among the multitude. However, their divinations were no better than their game of "fast and loose" <note>A cheating game involving a leather strap or rope, designed to trick onlookers</note>, or the witches' cures and harms, or the soothsayers' answers, or the conjurers' raising up of spirits, or the oracles of Apollo or the "Rood of Grace" <note>The Rood of Grace was a famous mechanical crucifix at Boxley Abbey that could move its eyes and lips, exposed during the Reformation as a fraud used to trick pilgrims</note>, or the jugglers' tricks of sleight of hand <note>original: "Legierdemain"</note>, or the Papists' exorcisms, or the witches' charms, or counterfeit visions, and other deceivers' knaveries. Regarding this, it was said: *"Let there not be found among you a Menahas"*—that is, a fortune-teller <note>original: "Non inveniatur inter vos Menahas, that is, Sortilegus." This is a reference to the Latin Vulgate's translation of Deuteronomy 18:10, forbidding various types of divination</note>—who were like these Egyptian deceivers. As for other lots, they were used, and that lawfully, as appears by Jonah and others who were holy men, and as may be seen among all commonwealths for the deciding of various controversies, etc., wherein your neighbor is not mistreated nor God in any way offended. But in truth, I think that because of the deception that may so easily be used in this, God forbade it in the commonwealth of the Jews, though in its proper use it...

<margin>Leviticus 16:1, Numbers 33 and 36, Joshua 14, 1 Chronicles 24 and 26, Proverbs 18, Jonah 1, Acts 1.</margin>
The casting of lots was allowed in matters of great weight, as appears in both the Old and New Testaments. It was used in doubtful cases and for the distribution of goods, as well as in elections, the dividing of inheritances, and the settling of disputes. I will skip over the practice of "Lots comprised in Verses"—concerning the luck that follows from suddenly turning to a page in the works of Virgil, Homer, or any other author—because it is a childish and ridiculous trifle <note>original: "toy"</note>, much like children playing "First and Second" or the game called "The Philosopher's Table." For more on that nonsense, I refer you to the bauble itself, or to Jean Bodin, or some other such "sober" writer on the subject, of whom there is no shortage.

<margin>Regarding Pythagoras's lot.</margin>
There is also a method called "Pythagoras’s Lot," which some say Aristotle believed in. In this practice, letters are assigned specific numerical values. Practitioners use these to divine outcomes based on people's names. By adding the numbers of each letter into a total sum, they grant victory to whoever has the higher number, whether the question concerns war, life, marriage, or success. They even claim that an unequal number of vowels in a name portends <note>original: "portendeth"</note> a loss in a fight or physical injury—something godparents could easily prevent at a christening if that were actually the case.

### CHAP. XI.

### *Of the Kabbalistic Art, consisting of traditions and unwritten varieties learned by heart, and how it is divided.*

<margin>The Kabbalistic Art divided.</margin>
This is also the place to discuss the Kabbalistic Art, which consists of unwritten truths. The Jews believe and boast <note>original: "brag"</note> that God himself gave these to Moses on Mount Sinai. They claim these were afterwards taught only through the "living voice" (orally) through successive generations without being written down until the time of Esdras <note>The biblical scribe Ezra</note>. In the same way, the scholars of Archippus <note>Archippus was a famous follower of Pythagoras; his students were known for their prodigious memories</note> used their wits and memory instead of books. They divide this art into two parts. The first part explains the secrets of the Law and the Bible using philosophical reasoning. They say King Solomon was very skilled <note>original: "cunning"</note> in this, because it is written in the Hebrew histories that he spoke about everything from the cedar of Lebanon even to the hyssop, as well as birds and beasts. The other part is a kind of symbolic divinity focused on the highest contemplation—of divine and angelic powers <note>original: "vertues"</note>, and of holy names and signs. In this art, letters, numbers, figures, objects, and even the dots <note>original: "pricks"</note> over letters, lines, points, and accents are all said to signify profound things and great secrets. Atheists suggest that Moses performed all his miracles using these arts. They believe that by these means, they can hold power over angels and demons and perform miracles themselves. Indeed, they claim that all the miracles performed by the Prophets—and even by Christ himself—were accomplished through these methods.

<margin>Cornelius Agrippa, in his book *On the Vanity of the Sciences* <note>original: "C. Agrippa lib. de vanit. scient."</note>. The blasphemy of the Kabbalists.</margin>
But Cornelius Agrippa, having searched to the bottom of this art, says it is nothing but superstition and folly. Otherwise, you can be sure Christ would not have hidden it from his Church. The Jews claimed to be skillful in the "Names of God" for this reason. But there is no other name in Heaven or Earth by which we might be saved except the name of Jesus; and by that, we do not mean his bare name, but his power and goodness toward us. These Kabbalists further boast that they can find out the unspeakable mysteries of God and secrets that are not even in the Scripture. They use this to take it upon themselves to prophesy and work miracles. Indeed, by this art, they can make whatever they want out of the Scripture, just as Valeria Proba <note>A 4th-century Roman poet who created a "Cento," a poem made of lines from Virgil rearranged to tell the story of the Bible</note> picked certain verses out of Virgil and applied them to Christ. Therefore, these "permutations" <note>original: "Revolutions"</note> are nothing but allegorical games devised by idle men obsessed with letters, points, and numbers (which the Hebrew language easily allows) to delude and deceive the simple and ignorant. They call this "Alphabet-based" or "Arithmetical Divinity," which they claim Christ showed only to his Apostles, and which Paul says he speaks of only among "perfect" <note>spiritually mature</note> men. Because these are supposedly high mysteries, they are not to be committed...

<margin>At the Council of Trent <note>original: "In Concil. Trident."</note></margin>
The Kabbalistic art has been committed to writing and so made popular. Anyone who reads anything of this art must surely think of the Pope’s cunning practices in this regard. He claims to hold "in the casket of his heart" <note>original: "In scrinio pectoris"</note> not only the interpretation of all laws, both divine and human, but also the authority to add to them or withdraw from them at his pleasure. He may lawfully do this even with the Scriptures—either by addition or subtraction—according to his own papal <note>original: "pontifical"</note> liking. As an example, he has added the *Apocrypha* (to which he might just as well have joined *St. Augustine's* works, or the body of Civil Law, etc.). Furthermore, he has subtracted from the Decalogue, or Ten Commandments, not just one or two words, but an entire precept: namely the second commandment <note>referring to the prohibition of graven images, which the author notes was removed in some Catholic catechisms</note>, which it pleased him to strike out with his pen. Truly, he might as well, by the same authority, have erased the Gospel of *St. Mark* from the New Testament.

### CHAP. XII.

->*When, how, and in what way sacrifices were first ordained, how they were profaned, and how the Pope corrupts the sacraments of Christ.*<-

<margin>
Genesis 2:17.
Genesis 3:6.
Genesis 3:15.
Leviticus 12:3, etc.
</margin>
At the beginning, God showed our father *Adam*, by the prohibition of the apple, that He would have man live under a law, in obedience and submission, and not wander like a beast without order or discipline. After man had transgressed and thereby deserved God's heavy displeasure, His mercy nonetheless prevailed. Taking compassion upon man, He promised the *Messiah* <note>original: "Messias"</note>, who would be born of a woman and crush the serpent's head. He declared by clear evidence that His pleasure was for man to be restored to favor and grace through *Christ*. Binding the minds of men to this promise to be fixed upon their *Messiah*, He established symbols <note>original: "Figures"</note> and ceremonies to nourish their faith. He confirmed these with miracles, while prohibiting and excluding all human inventions in that regard. Upon His promise being renewed, He enjoined and established a new form of worship through which He wanted His promises to be constantly observed, faithfully believed, and reverently respected. He ordained six sorts of divine sacrifices: three were propitiatory <note>meaning: intended to atone for sin</note>—not as if they earned the forgiveness of sins themselves, but as symbols of Christ's atonement—and the other three were for thanksgiving. These sacrifices were full of ceremonies; they were seasoned with consecrated salt and lit with fire kept in the Tabernacle of the Lord, which fire (some believe) was sent down from heaven. God Himself commanded these rites and ceremonies to our forefathers—*Noah*, *Abraham*, *Isaac*, *Jacob*, etc.—promising them both the growth of their families and the coming of their *Messiah*. But over time, through the instigation of the Devil, wantonness, negligence, and contempt abolished this institution of God. In the end, God Himself was forgotten among them, and they became pagans and heathens, devising their own ways until every country had invented and established both new sacrifices and new gods particular to themselves. <margin>A sharp critique <note>original: "gird"</note> of the Pope for his audacity <note>original: "sawciness"</note> in God's matters.</margin> The Pope follows their example by profaning Christ's sacraments, disguising them with his own inventions and superstitious ceremonies, and incorporating into them the folly of all nations. Because even little children now perceive and mock this, I will move on and return to the Gentiles (the heathens), whom I cannot excuse of deception <note>original: "cozenage"</note>, superstition, or vanity. For if God allowed false prophets among the children of *Israel* (God's chosen people) and hypocrites within the Church of *Christ*, it is no wonder there were such people among the heathens who neither professed nor knew Him.

<header>Superstitious Auguries of Witchcraft. CHAPTER XIV. 113</header>

### CHAPTER XIII.

#### *Concerning the Objects upon which the Augurs used to Predict the Future, with certain Cautions and Notes.*

The Pagans <note>original: "Gentiles"</note>, who write about this matter, list a countless multitude of objects from which they predict good or bad luck. A great deal is made of sneezing, where the number of sneezes and the time they occur are carefully noted. The tingling in the finger, the elbow, the toe, the knee, etc., are also specific signs to be observed in this art. However, the flight of birds and the meeting of beasts are especially noted, with this general rule: the object or event used for divination must be sudden and unexpected. This same concern is shown by children and some old fools when gathering primroses, herb-paris <note>original: "True-loves"</note>, and four-leaf clovers <note>original: "four-leaved grass"</note>. Also considered are: the person to whom such an object appears unexpectedly; the intention of the diviner, which determines how the encountered object is interpreted as an omen; the hour in which the object is suddenly met without prior knowledge, and so forth.

<margin>Pliny, *Natural History*, Book 10, Chapter 6.
Aristotle, *On Auguries*.</margin>
Pliny reports that Griffins <note>original: "Gryphes"</note> always fly to the place of a slaughter two or three days before a battle is fought; this was supposedly seen and proven at the Battle of Troy. Because of this, the Griffin was considered the primary bird of Augury. But among the countless number of ominous <note>original: "portentous"</note> beasts, birds, serpents, and other creatures, the toad is the most excellent object. Its ugly deformity is said to signify sweet and pleasant fortune; because of this, some superstitious witches keep toads as their familiars <term>spirit companions believed to assist witches</term>. And one person of good reputation (whom I could name), having summoned the witches themselves, starved several of their demons, which they kept in boxes in the shape of toads.

<margin>Plutarch is mistaken here, for all his learning.</margin>
Plutarch of Chaeronea <note>original: "Plutarch Cheronaus"</note> says that the place and position of the signs we receive by Augury are especially important. If we receive them on the left side, good luck follows; if on the right side, bad luck ensues. This is because earthly and mortal things are opposite and contrary to divine and heavenly things; for what the Gods deliver with their right hand falls to our left side, and vice versa.

---

### CHAPTER XIV.

#### *The division of Augury; persons eligible for the Colleges of Augury; and their Superstition.*

<margin>Agostino Nifo <note>original: "Aug. Niphus"</note>, *On Auguries*, Book 1.</margin>
The later diviners in these mysteries have divided their soothsayings into twelve "Superstitions," as Agostino Nifo <note>a 16th-century Italian philosopher</note> calls them. The first is prosperity; the second is ill luck, such as when one leaves his house and sees an unlucky beast lying on the right side of his path; the third is destiny; the fourth is fortune; the fifth is bad luck, as when an unfortunate beast feeds on the right side of your path; the sixth is utility; the seventh is injury; the eighth is called a precaution <term>original: "cautel"</term>, such as when a beast follows someone and stops at their side without passing them, which is a sign of good luck; the ninth is unhappiness, which is the opposite of the eighth, as when the beast passes in front of someone; the tenth is perfection; the eleventh is imperfection; and the twelfth is confusion. So far, Nifo.

<margin>Who were not eligible for the College of Augurs among the Romans.</margin>
Among the Romans, no one could be admitted into the College of Augurs who had a boil <note>original: "bile"</note> or had been bitten by a dog, etc. During their rituals, even at midday, they lit candles. From these practices, the Papists <note>a derogatory term for Roman Catholics</note> bring into their Church those elements of paganism <note>original: "infidelity"</note>. Finally, their observations were so endless and ridiculous that not even a spark could fly out of a fire without them believing it signaled something.

### CHAPTER XV.

->*Concerning the foolish and superstitious beliefs and observations of the common people.*<-

<margin>O vain folly and foolish vanity!</margin>Among us, there are many women and effeminate men (always Catholics <note>original: "Papists"</note>, as may be seen by their superstition) who perform great divinations based on the spilling of salt, wine, etc. In their observation of days and hours, they use as much witchcraft as in anything else. For if someone happens to fall from a horse, whether on a slippery path or because of a stumble, he will note the day and hour and consider that time unlucky for a journey. Alternatively, he who meets with misfortune will wonder whether he encountered a cat or a hare when he first stepped out his door in the morning; or if he stumbled at the threshold on his way out; or if he put his shirt on inside out; or his left shoe on his right foot—which <term>Augustus Caesar</term> considered the worst luck <margin>Martin de Arles, in his *Treatise on Superstition against Witchcraft* <note>original: *Tractatus de superstitionibus contra maleficia*</note>.</margin> that could happen. 

But above all other nations (as <term>Martin de Arles</term> testifies), the <term>Spaniards</term> are the most superstitious in this regard; and within <term>Spain</term>, the people of the province of <term>Lusitania</term> <note>Lusitania: The Roman name for the region comprising most of modern Portugal.</note> are the most foolish. For one will say, "I had a dream tonight," or <margin>Appian, *On the Civil Wars*.</margin> "a crow croaked upon my house," or "an owl flew by me and screeched" (an omen <note>original: "Augury"</note> that <term>Lucius Sylla</term> believed caused his death), or "a cock crowed at the wrong hour." Another says, "The moon is new <note>original: "at the prime"</note>"; another, "the sun rose in a cloud and looked pale," or "a star shot and shone in the sky," or "a strange cat came into the <margin>Augury-related trifles <note>original: "Augurifical toyes"</note>.</margin> house," or "a hen fell from the roof." 

Many people will go back to bed if they sneeze before their shoes are on their feet; some will grip their left thumb in their right hand when they hiccup <note>original: "hickot"</note>; or else they will hold their chin with their right hand while a Gospel is being sung. Some think it very bad luck if a child, or any other living creature, passes between two friends as they walk together, for they say it foretells a division in their friendship. Among the Catholics themselves, if any hunters happened to meet a friar or a priest while hunting, they thought it such bad luck that they would leash their hounds and go home, despairing of any more sport that day. Truly <note>original: "Marry"</note>, if they had engaged in sexual intercourse <note>original: "used venery"</note> with a beggar, they believed they would win all the money they gambled for that day at dice. Similar folly is attributed to those who observe (as true or likely) old verses, in which there can be no logical cause for the effects described, since such things are brought to pass only by God’s power and at his pleasure. Of this sort are the following:

## C H A P. XVI.

*How ancient writers differ about the matter, the manner, and the means by which omens* <note>original: "things augurifical"</note> *are moved.*

<margin>*Averroes. 12th book of Metaphysics.*</margin>
Theophrastus and *Themistius* affirm that whatever happens to man suddenly and by chance comes from the Providence of God. Thus, *Themistius* concludes that men, in that respect, prophesy when they speak whatever comes into their brain suddenly, even though they do not know or understand what they are saying. And since God has a care for us, it agrees with reason (as *Theophrastus* says) that he shows us by some means whatever shall happen. For, along with *Pythagoras*, he concludes that all omens and auguries are the voices and words of God, by which he foretells the good or evil that shall occur.

*Trismegistus* <note>Hermes Trismegistus, a legendary Hellenistic figure associated with hermetic philosophy and magic.</note> affirms that all things related to augury are moved by demons; *Porphyry* says by gods, or rather good angels, according to the opinion of *Plotinus* and *Iamblichus*. Some others affirm they are moved by the Moon wandering through the twelve signs of the Zodiac, because the Moon has dominion over all sudden matters. The *Egyptian* astronomers hold that the Moon does not order those ominous <note>original: "portentous"</note> matters, but a *wandering star* <note>original: "Stella errans"; an early term for a planet.</note>, etc.

<header>BOOK XI. The Discovery of Augury and Augurers.</header>

## CHAPTER XVII.

->*How ridiculous the art of Augury is; how Cato mocked it; Aristotle's reasoning against it; the foolish interpretations of Augurers, and who allowed or disallowed it.*<-

<margin>The foolish <note>original: "fond"</note> art of Augury refuted.</margin>
Truly, all these observations—being grounded neither on God’s Word nor on physical or philosophical reason—are vanities, superstitions, lies, and mere witchcraft. By these means, the world has for a long time been, and still is, abused and cheated. It is written: "It is not for you to know the times and the seasons which the Father has put in His own power" <note>original: "Non est vestrum scire tempora & momenta, &c."; Acts 1:7</note>. The most godly men and the wisest philosophers have given no credit to this practice. St. Augustine says, "Whoever believes in these divinations, let him know that he has betrayed the Christian faith and his baptism, and is a pagan and an enemy of God" <note>original: "Qui his divinationibus credit, sciat se fidem Christianam & baptismum prævaricasse, & Paganum Deiq; inimicum esse."</note>. Someone once told Cato that a rat had carried away and eaten his hose <note>original: "Hose"; here referring to leggings or stockings</note>, which the man said was a wonderful sign. "No," said Cato, "I do not think so; but if the hose had eaten the rat, that would have been a wonderful sign indeed." When Nonius told Cicero that they would have good success in battle because seven eagles were captured in Pompey’s camp, he answered: "No doubt it will be exactly so, if we happen to be fighting against magpies <note>original: "Pies"</note>." He gave a similar answer to Labienus, who prophesied success through such divinations, saying that it was through the hope of such toys that Pompey lost all his tents <note>original: "Pavillions"</note> not long before.

<margin>Aristotle, *On Sleep and Dreams*.</margin>
What wise man would think that God would commit His counsel to a jackdaw, an owl, a pig, or a toad; or that He would hide His secret purposes in the dung and bowels of beasts? Aristotle reasons this way: Augury or divinations are neither the causes nor the effects of things to come; therefore, they do not truly foretell things, except by chance. It is like if I dream that my friend will come to my house, and he actually comes; yet neither the dream nor the imagination is any more the cause of my friend's coming than the chattering of a magpie.

<margin>Augustine, *On Christian Doctrine*, Book 2, chapters 2 and 3; Psalm 4:2; Pliny, *Natural History*, Book 28, chapter 2; Thomas Aquinas.</margin>
When Hannibal overthrew Marcus Marcellus, the sacrificed beast was missing a piece of its heart. Therefore, forsooth <note>original: "forsooth"; an archaic term for "truly," often used sarcastically here to mean "according to them"</note>, when Marius sacrificed at Utica and the beast lacked its liver, he was expected to have the same success. These are their interpretations <note>original: "Collections"</note>, and they are as vain as saying that the building of Tenterden steeple was the cause of the Goodwin Sands, or the decay of Sandwich Haven <note>A famous English proverb about a "false cause" fallacy—attributing the creation of dangerous sandbanks to the building of a church tower simply because they happened around the same time.</note>. St. Augustine says that these observations are most superstitious. But we read in the fourth Psalm a sentence which should dissuade any Christian from this folly and impiety: "O you sons of men, how long will you turn my glory into shame, loving vanity and seeking lies?" The same is found in many other places of Scripture.

<margin>Aquinas, *On Fortune*.</margin>
Of those who allow this folly, I can commend Pliny best. He says that the effect of these auguries depends on how we take them: for if we take them in a positive way, they are signs of good luck; if we take them in a negative way, ill luck follows; but if we neglect them and do not weigh them at all, they do neither good nor harm. Thomas Aquinas reasons in this way: the stars, whose course is certain, have a greater affinity and connection with human actions than auguries do; and yet our actions are neither directed by nor proceed from the stars. This is also witnessed by Ptolemy, who said, "A wise man will rule over the stars" <note>original: "Sapiens dominabitur astris"</note>.

<header>Augury. of Witchcraft. CHAP. XX.</header>

### CHAPTER XVIII.

->Foolish <note>original: "Fond"</note> Distinctions of the Heathen Writers concerning Augury.<-

<margin>C. Epidius. Homer, Iliad, Book 19.</margin>
The Pagans <note>original: "Heathen"</note> made a distinction between divine, natural, and casual auguries. Divine auguries were those which men were led to believe were done miraculously: such as when dogs spoke, as happened during the expulsion of Tarquinius <note>Tarquinius Superbus, the legendary final King of Rome</note> from his kingdom; or when trees spoke, as occurred before the death of Caesar; or when horses spoke, as did a horse named Xanthus <note>In the *Iliad*, Achilles' horse Xanthus is briefly given the power of speech by the goddess Hera to prophesy Achilles' death</note>. Many learned Christians admit that such things, if they indeed have a divine cause, may be called divine auguries—or rather, forewarnings from God and tokens either of His blessings or His displeasure. For instance, the Star was a token of safe passage to the Magi who sought Christ, and the crowing of the cock was an augury to Peter for his conversion. Many other such divinations or auguries (if it be lawful to call them that) are to be found in the Scriptures.

---

### CHAPTER XIX.

->*Of Natural and Casual Augury: the one allowed, and the other disallowed.*<-

Natural augury is a physical or philosophical observation; this is because human and natural reason can be provided for such events. For example, if one hears a cock crow many times in a row, a person may guess that rain will follow shortly. The same applies to the crying of rooks and their extraordinary use of their wings in flight; through a natural instinct provoked by the influence of the heavenly bodies, they are moved to know the seasons according to the weather, as is necessary for their natures. Therefore, Jeremiah says, "The kite in the sky knows her appointed time" <note>original: "Milvus in cœlo cognovit tempus suum"; Jeremiah 8:7</note>. Likewise, a physician may argue that a patient is gaining strength when he hears him sneeze twice, which provides a natural cause to judge and make a conjecture upon. But it is certainly purely accidental <note>original: "casual"</note>, as well as very foolish and incredible, to think that by two sneezes a man should be certain of good luck or success in his business; or that by meeting a toad, a man should escape a danger or achieve an enterprise, and so forth.

---

### CHAPTER XX.

->*A Refutation <note>original: "Confutation"</note> of Casual Augury which is mere Witchcraft, and the uncertainty upon which those Divinations are grounded.*<-

Many pages would not be enough to contain all that the imagination works in men or women; for just as its qualities are strange and almost incredible, a full discourse on it would be long and tedious—a subject I have had occasion to speak of elsewhere. But the power of our imagination does not extend to beasts, nor does it reach birds; therefore, it does not apply here. Neither can a random occurrence on the right or left side be good or bad luck in itself. Why should any event or augury be good simply because it comes from that part of the heavens where the "good" or beneficial stars are placed? By that logic, all living things on that side should be good and happy; but we see the contrary by experience, and just as frequently as the opposite.

<margin>The vanity of casual augury.</margin>
A similar absurdity and error exists in those who believe in these divinations because the stars over the Ninth House <note>In astrology, the Ninth House relates to travel, philosophy, and "divine" messages</note> have dominion at the time of the augury. If it were supposed to betoken good luck, joy, or gladness to hear a noise in the house when the Moon is in Aries; and conversely, if it were a sign of ill luck, sorrow, or grief for a beast to come into the house while the Moon is in that same sign: then there might

...could be found a foul error and contradiction <note>original: "contrariety"</note>. And because both may happen at once, the rule must necessarily be false and ridiculous. And if there were any certain rules or signs <note>original: "notes"</note> to be gathered in these divinations, the abuse within them is such that the Word of God must be proven true there; namely, <margin>Isaiah 44:25.</margin> *I will destroy the signs of soothsayers, and make those who guess <note>original: "conjecture"</note> fools.*

---

### CHAPTER XXI.

->*Figure-casters <note>Astrologers</note> are Witches; the uncertainty of their art and their contradictions; Cornelius Agrippa’s judgment <note>original: "sentence"</note> against Judicial Astrology <note>The branch of astrology used to predict earthly events and human fate</note>.*<-

<margin>The vain and trivial <note>original: "trifling"</note> tricks of figure-casters.</margin>
These casters of figures may be numbered among the cheating <note>original: "cosening"</note> witches whose practice is beyond their understanding <note>original: "reach"</note>. Their purpose is profit <note>original: "gain"</note>, their knowledge is stolen from poets, and their uncertainty and complete vanity are more clearly mocked <note>original: "derided"</note> in the Scriptures than any other folly. Upon this, many other trivial vanities are rooted and grounded, such as physiognomy <note>judging character from facial features</note>, palmistry, interpreting dreams, monsters <note>unnatural omens</note>, auguries, etc. The practitioners of these arts confess that astrology is the necessary key to unlock the knowledge of all their secrets. For these fellows set up a chart <note>original: "figure"</note> of the heavens, by the interpretation of which (together with guesses about similarities and signs), they seek to find out the meaning of the "significators" <note>planets or signs that represent specific areas of life</note>. They attribute the outcomes of all things to them, contrary to truth, reason, and theology <note>original: "divinity"</note>. Their rules are so inconsistent that few writers agree even on the very principles of the art. For the Rabbis, the old and new writers, and the very best philosophers disagree <note>original: "dissent"</note> on the main foundations, differing on the properties of the "houses" <note>the 12 divisions of the zodiac</note> from which they squeeze their predictions of the future. They even argue about the number of celestial spheres, having not yet resolved how to establish the beginnings and ends of the houses; for Ptolemy creates them one way, Campanus another, and so on.

<margin>Johannes Regiomontanus <note>original: "Johan. Montiregius"</note> in a letter to Blanchinus, and Guillaume de Saint-Cloud <note>original: "Gulielmus de sancto Clodoald"</note>, Rabbi Levi, Cornelius Agrippa in his book *On the Vanity of Sciences* <note>original: "de vanit. scient."</note>, Archelaus, Cassander, Eudoxus, etc.</margin>
And as Alpetragius <note>original: "Alpetragus," a 12th-century astronomer</note> thinks that there are various movements in the heavens as yet unknown to men, so others affirm (not without probability) that there may be stars and celestial bodies to which these movements correspond <note>original: "accord"</note> that cannot be seen, either because of their extreme height or because they have not yet been tested by any observation of the art. The true motion of Mars is not yet understood, nor is it possible to find out the true entry of the Sun into the equinoctial points. It is not denied that the astronomers themselves have received their insight <note>original: "light"</note> and their very art from poets; without their fables, the twelve signs and the northern and southern constellations <note>original: "figures"</note> would never have ascended into heaven. And yet (as Cornelius Agrippa says) astrologers live, cheat men, and profit by these fables, while the poets who invented them live in poverty <note>original: "beggery"</note>.

The most skillful mathematicians confess that it is impossible to find out anything certain regarding the knowledge of astrological judgments, both because of the countless causes that work together with the heavens—all of which must be considered together—and also because influences do not force <note>original: "constrain"</note> but merely incline. For many ordinary and extraordinary factors <note>original: "occasions"</note> interrupt them, such as education, custom, location, integrity <note>original: "honesty"</note>, birth, blood, sickness, health, strength, weakness, food, drink, freedom of mind, learning, etc. And those who have written the rules of judgment and agree most closely—being of equal authority and learning—publish such contradictory <note>original: "contrary"</note> opinions on the same thing that it is impossible for an astrologer to announce a certainty based on such variable opinions; otherwise, based on such uncertain reports, no man is able to judge this matter. So (according to Ptolemy) the foreknowledge of future things by the stars depends as well upon the feelings <note>original: "affections"</note> of the mind as upon the observation of the planets, resulting from chance rather than art; by this means they deceive others and are <margin>to <unclear>prove</unclear> <unclear>the</unclear> uncertainty <unclear>Agrippa</unclear></margin> deceived themselves as well.

<header>Astrologers. Of Witchcraft. CHAPTER XXII.</header>

## CHAPTER XXII.

### *The cunning <note>original: "subtilty"</note> of Astrologers to maintain the credit of their art; why they remain in credit, and certain impieties contained in astrologers' assertions.*

<margin>Astrologers' predictions <note>original: "Prognostications"</note> are like the answers of Oracles.</margin>
**I**f you observe the clever ones, you will see them speak obscurely of things to come, devising doubtful predictions with practiced trickery <note>original: "artificial subtilty"</note>. These are easily applied to every thing, time, prince, and nation; and if anything happens according to their divinations, they reinforce their old predictions with new reasons. Nevertheless, in the multitude and variety of stars—even in the very midst of them—they find some places in a good alignment <note>original: "aspect"</note> and some in a bad one. They take this opportunity to say whatever they wish, promising some men honor, long life, wealth, victory, children, marriage, friends, offices, and finally, everlasting happiness. But if they are displeased with anyone, they say the stars are not favorable to them, and they threaten them with hanging, drowning, poverty <note>original: "beggery"</note>, sickness, misfortune, and so on. And if one of these predictions turns out right, then they triumph beyond measure. If the predictors are found to be lying and forging constantly (without having the same luck as the blind man who happened to kill the crow), they will excuse the matter by saying that *the wise man rules the stars* <note>original: "Sapiens dominatur astris"</note>. However, according to the words of Cornelius Agrippa, neither the wise man rules the stars, nor do the stars rule the wise man, but God rules them both. Cornelius Tacitus says that they are a people disloyal to princes, deceiving those who believe them. And Varro says that the vanity of all superstitions flows from the bosom of astrology. And if our lives and fortunes do not depend on the stars, then it must be granted that the astrologers search where nothing is to be found. But we are so foolish, distrustful, and gullible <note>original: "credulous"</note> that we fear the fables of Robin Goodfellow <note>A mischievous sprite or "puck" from English folklore</note>, astrologers, and witches more than reality. We believe more in things that do not exist than in things that do. The more impossible a thing is, the more we stand in fear of it; and the less likely it is to be true, the more we believe it. If we were not like this, I think (along with Cornelius Agrippa) that these diviners, astrologers, conjurers, and cheaters <note>original: "coseners"</note> would die of hunger.

And our foolish, light belief—forgetting things past, neglecting things present, and being very hasty to know things to come—comforts and maintains these cheaters. In other men, telling a single lie makes their word so mistrusted that everything else they say, even if true, is ignored. In contrast, among these cheating diviners, one truth spoken by chance <note>original: "hap"</note> gives such credit to all their lies that ever after we believe whatever they say, no matter how incredible, impossible, or false it may be. <margin>Sir Thomas More’s mockery <note>original: "frump"</note> of judicial astrologers.</margin> Sir Thomas More says they do not even know who is in their own chambers, nor who is making them cuckolds <term>cuckold: a man whose wife is unfaithful</term>, yet they take upon themselves all this cunning, knowledge, and great foresight. But to increase their credit, or rather to reveal their boldness <note>original: "impudency"</note>, they say the gift of prophecy, the force of religion, the secrets of conscience, the power of devils, the virtue of miracles, the efficacy of prayers, and the state of the life to come all depend only upon the stars and are given and known by them alone. <margin>Astrological blasphemies.</margin> For they say that when the sign of Gemini has ascended, and Saturn and Mercury are joined in Aquarius <note>original: "Aquary"</note> in the ninth house of the heavens, a prophet is born; and therefore they claim Christ had so many virtues because he had Saturn and Gemini in that place. Indeed, these astrologers do not hesitate to say that the stars distribute all sorts of religions, with Jupiter being the special patron. They claim that Jupiter joined with Saturn makes the religion of the Jews; with Mercury, that of the Christians; and with the Moon, that of Antichristianity. Yes, they affirm that every man's faith may be known to them as well as to God. They even claim that Christ himself used the selection of auspicious hours <note>original: "election of hours"</note> in his miracles, so that the Jews could not hurt him while he went to Jerusalem. They point to when he said to his disciples who forbade him to go, <margin>John 11:8, 9.</margin> *Are there not twelve hours in the day?*

### CHAPTER XXIII.

> *Those who have the power to drive away devils by their presence alone; those who shall receive from God whatever they ask in prayer; and those who shall obtain everlasting life through constellations, as astrologers <note>original: "Nativity-casters"</note> claim.*

<margin>The folly of our astrologers <note>original: "Genethliaks"</note> or nativity-casters.</margin>
<margin>Seneca, *Natural Questions*, Book 4 <note>original: "Senec. lib. de quæst. natural. 4."</note></margin>
**T**hey also say that he who has *Mars* favorably positioned in the ninth house of the heavens shall have the power to drive away devils from the possessed by his presence alone. And he who prays to God when he finds the *Moon* and *Jupiter* joined with the *Dragon’s Head* <note>term: the "Dragon's Head" refers to the North Node of the Moon, considered a point of great favor in astrology</note> in the middle of the heavens shall obtain whatever he asks. They even claim that *Jupiter* and *Saturn* grant the blessedness of the life to come. Furthermore, they say if anyone has *Saturn* favorably positioned in *Leo* at their birth, his soul shall have everlasting life. To these claims subscribe Peter d'Abano <note>original: "Peter de Appona"</note>, Roger Bacon, Guido Bonatti, Arnaldus de Villa Nova, and the Cardinal of Algeciras <note>original: "Alia"</note>. 

Furthermore, the providence of God is denied, and the miracles of Christ are diminished when these powers of the heavens and their influences are promoted in such a manner. Moses, Isaiah, Job, and Jeremiah seem to dislike and reject this; and in Rome in times past, astrology was banished, and later condemned by Emperor Justinian under pain of death. Finally, Seneca mocked these soothsaying witches in this way: "Among the people of Cleonae," he says, "there was a custom involving hail-watchers <note>original: "chalazophylakes"</note> (who were gazers into the air, watching for when a hailstorm might fall). When they saw by any cloud that a shower was imminent and at hand, the custom was—because of the damage it might do to their vines—to diligently warn the people. The people did not provide cloaks or any such defense against the storm, but instead provided sacrifices. The rich offered roosters and white lambs; the poor would mutilate themselves by cutting their thumbs, as though," Seneca says, "that little bit of blood would ascend up to the clouds and provide any relief in the matter."

<margin>Hilarius Pickmair in *Ars Apodemica* <note>original: "arte Apodemica"</note>.</margin>
<margin>Joannes Garropius in *Venetian and Hyperborean Antiquities*. Zechariah 10:1-2 <note>original: "Joannes Garropius in Venet. & Hyperb. Zac. 10. 1, 2."</note></margin>
And here, by the way, I will share with you a Venetian superstition of great antiquity, which is still in use today (for all I can read to the contrary). It is written that every year, usually on Ascension Day, the Duke of Venice, accompanied by the high officials of the state, goes with great ceremony to the sea. After certain ceremonies are finished, he throws into the water a gold ring of great value and prestige as a peace offering <note>original: "Pacificatory oblation"</note>. Their ancestors supposed that by this act, the wrath of the sea was calmed. But this action, as a recent writer says, is intended to "marry the sea to themselves" <note>original: "Desponsare sibi mare"</note>.

Let us therefore, according to the Prophet’s advice, *Ask rain of the Lord in the time of the latter rain; and the Lord shall make white clouds, and give them showers of rain, etc. For surely, the idols (as the same Prophet says) have spoken vanity, the soothsayers have seen a lie, and the dreamers have told a false thing; they comfort in vain, and therefore the people went away like sheep, etc.* If any "sheep-biter" <note>term: a shifty or malicious person; a common insult of the era</note> or "witch-monger" <note>term: Scot’s term for those who credulously believe in or hunt witches</note> wishes to follow them, they shall go alone for all I care.

# BOOK 12.

## CHAPTER 1.

*The Hebrew word Habar explained, where also the supposed secret force of charms and enchantments is shown, and the effectiveness of words is declared in various ways.*

The Hebrew word *Habar* <note>original: "Habar" (חָבַר), meaning to join, bind, or charm</note>, being in Greek *Epathin* <note>original: "Epathin," likely referring to the Greek "epaoide" (ἐπαοιδή), meaning an incantation or spell</note>, and in Latin *Incantare* <note>original: "Incantare," meaning to enchant or chant a spell</note>, is in English "to enchant," or (if you prefer) "to bewitch." In these enchantments, certain words, verses, or charms, etc., are secretly spoken, in which there is thought to be a miraculous effectiveness. There is a great variety of these; but whether it be by charms, voices, images, symbols <note>original: "Characters"</note>, stones, plants, metals, herbs, etc., there must always be a special form of words used alongside them—either divine, diabolical, nonsensical <note>original: "Insensible"</note>, or Catholic <note>original: "Papistical" - a derogatory term for Roman Catholic rituals</note>—upon which all the power of the work is supposed to depend. This word is specifically used in Psalm 58, which is the place my opponents <margin>Psalm 58:4, 5.</margin> use as their strongest argument against me. Yet, it seems to me it supports my view so clearly that they will never be able to answer it. For there it plainly appears *that the snake <note>original: "Adder"</note> does not hear the voice of the charmer, no matter how cunningly he charms.* This is contrary to the fables of the poets, who say:

<margin>Virgil, in *Damon* (Eclogue 8).</margin>
->The cold snake in the meadows is burst by singing.<-
-><note>original Latin: "Frigidus in pratis cantando rumpitur anguis."</note><-

->Translated into English by *Abraham Fleming* <note>A 16th-century scholar and translator of Virgil</note>:<-
->*The chilly snake in meadows green,*<-
->*With charms is burst in pieces clean.*<-

But more shall be said about this later in the proper place. I admit that words sometimes have singular power and effectiveness, either in persuasion or dissuasion, as well as in various other ways. Through them, some are converted from the path of destruction to the state of salvation; and likewise the opposite, according to the saying of Solomon: *Death and life are in the power <margin>Proverbs 18; 2 Chronicles 30; Psalm 10; Psalm 51; Psalm 139; Jeremiah 32; Isaiah 6; Isaiah 50; Exodus 7, 8, 9; Proverbs 16.</margin> of the tongue.* But even in that, God works all in all, both in framing the heart of the listener and in directing the tongue of the speaker, as appears in many places of the Holy Scriptures.

***

## CHAPTER 2.

*What is forbidden in the Scriptures concerning witchcraft; regarding the operation of words; the superstition of the Cabalists and Catholics; who creates substances; to imitate God in some cases is presumption; words of sanctification.*

That which is forbidden in the Scriptures regarding enchantment or witchcraft is not the "wonderful working with words." For where words have had a miraculous operation, there has always been the special providence, power, and grace of God demonstrated to strengthen the faith...

# BOOK XII. The Discovery of Witches described.

<margin>Acts 5.</margin>
...of God’s people and to the advancement of the Gospel, as when the Apostle killed Ananias and Sapphira with a single word. But the profanation of God's name, the seducing, abusing, and cheating <note>original: "cosening"</note> of the people, and human arrogance <note>original: "presumption"</note> are prohibited by this. Many people take it upon themselves—after reciting names that God in the Scripture seems to reserve for himself—to predict the future, perform miracles, and reveal crimes <note>original: "detect fellonies"</note>, and so on. This is like how the Cabalists <note>Jewish mystics who sought secret meanings in the Hebrew Bible</note> in the past claimed to work wonders through the ten names of God and his Angels mentioned in the Scriptures. Similarly, the Catholics <note>original: "Papists"</note> today promise health of body and soul to themselves and others through similar names, crosses, Gospels hung around their necks, Masses, exorcisms, holy water, and a thousand other consecrated—or rather, cursed <note>original: "execrated"</note>—objects.

<margin>Jonah 1.</margin>
Just as we should not imitate the Catholics in this, we also ought not to try to copy or resemble God in those actions that are uniquely his—he who created all things with his word. For neither we, nor all the conjurers, Cabalists, Catholics, soothsayers, enchanters, witches, or charmers in the world—nor any other human or even diabolical skill—can add any strength to God's workmanship so as to create anything new or transform one thing into another. Human art may add new qualities, but no new substance can be made or created by man. And since art fails here, certainly neither the illusions of devils nor the skill of witches can truly accomplish such things. For nothing comes or goes because of the sound of words, except what God has ordained in nature through ordinary speech or by his special decree. Indeed, words of sanctification are necessary and 
<margin>1 Timothy 4:5. Words of sanctification, and what they consist of.</margin>
commendable, according to Saint Paul's rule: *Let your food be sanctified by the Word of God and by prayer.* But "sanctification" here does not mean a change in the substance of the food, or adding any new strength to it. Rather, it is sanctified because it is received with thanksgiving and prayers, so that our bodies may be refreshed and our souls made more capable of glorifying God.

### CHAPTER III.

->What effects and offenses the charms of witches bring; how incapable witches are, and how unlikely they are to do the things they are thought to do; what would follow if the things they are charged with were true.<-

<margin>An ample description of women commonly called Witches.</margin>
The words and other illusions of witches, charmers, and conjurers may not have the operation and effect they are commonly thought to have, yet they are offensive to the majesty and name of God, obscuring the truth of both theology <note>original: "Divinity"</note> and philosophy. For if God alone gives life and being to all creatures, who else could put such life or feeling into an object of gold, silver, bread, or wax, as people imagine? If priests, devils, or witches could do so, then divine power would be challenged and outdone by magical skill, and God's creatures would be made slaves to a witch's pleasure. If what is attributed to witches were true, what could not be accomplished by these incantations? And yet, these are women who never went to school in their lives, nor had any teachers; they are therefore without art or learning. They are poor, and thus unable to obtain the metals or stones needed to perform strange feats through natural magic. They are old and stiff, and therefore not nimble enough to deceive your eyes with sleight of hand <note>original: "legierdemain"</note>. They are heavy and usually lame, and thus unfit to fly through the air or dance with fairies. They are sad, melancholy, sullen, and miserable; therefore, it would be "against the grain" <note>original: "Invita Minerva" - a Latin idiom meaning against one's natural inclination or without the help of the goddess of wisdom</note> for them to banquet or dance with Minerva <note>the Roman goddess of wisdom and weaving</note>, or with Herodias <note>a figure from the New Testament, but in medieval lore, she was often identified as a leader of the "nocturnal society" or "Wild Hunt" alongside the goddess Diana</note>, as is the common opinion of all writers on this subject. On the other hand, we see they are so malicious and spiteful that if they, or their devils, could control the weather <note>original: "trouble the Element"</note>, we would never have fair weather. If they could kill men, children, or cattle, they would spare no one;

<summary>Scot argues that witches and magicians have no real power to create or transform matter, as such power belongs to God alone. He characterizes accused witches as poor, uneducated, and physically frail women who are logically incapable of the supernatural feats attributed to them.</summary>

but would instead destroy and kill whole countries and households. If they could transfer grain (as is claimed) from their neighbor's field into their own, none of them would be poor, and no one else would be rich. If they could transform themselves and others (as it is most constantly claimed), oh, what a number of apes and owls would be made of us! If an *Incubus* <note>a demon believed to have sex with sleeping women</note> could father *Merlins* <note>the legendary wizard, supposedly born of a demon</note> among us, we would have a great many cold-blooded prophets.

## CHAP. IV.

### *Why God forbade the practice of Witchcraft; the absurdity of the Law of the Twelve Tables, upon which the belief in their miraculous actions is based; of their wondrous works.*

<margin>A common and universal error.</margin>
Though it is clear that the Holy Spirit forbids this art because of the abuse of God's name and the deception <note>original: "cosenage"</note> involved in it, I must admit that the customs and laws of almost all nations declare that all these miraculous works I have mentioned—and many other more wonderful things—were attributed to the power of witches. These laws, along with the executions and legal proceedings <note>original: "judicials"</note> based on them, and the witches' confessions, have deceived almost the whole world. What absurdities concerning witchcraft are written in the *Law of the Twelve Tables*, which was the highest and most ancient law of the Romans? It is from these that the strongest argument for the omnipotent power of witches is framed: that the wisdom of such lawmakers could not be mistaken. On the contrary, I believe a stronger argument can be made on our side: that is, if the chief and principal laws of the world are ridiculous, vain, false, incredible, and even contrary to God's law in this case, then the rest of the laws and arguments to that effect should be suspected. If that logic held, it might prove all the Catholic <note>original: "Popish"</note> laws against Protestants, and the pagan <note>original: "Heathenish"</note> laws against Christians, to be good and valid—for surely they would not have made them unless they were good. Would it not (don't you think) be a strange proclamation that no man, under pain of death, should pull the moon out of heaven? And yet many of the most learned "witch-mongers" <note>those who promote or believe in the power of witches</note> 
<margin>
1. *Jean Bodin.*
*Lambert Daneau.*
*Andreas Hyperius.*
*Niels Hemmingsen.*
*Bartolomæus Spina.*
*The Hammer of Witches.* <note>original: "Mal. Malef." or Malleus Maleficarum</note>
</margin>
base their arguments on even weaker grounds; specifically in this way: "We find in poets that witches performed such and such miracles; therefore, they can accomplish this or that wonder." The words of the law are these: *Let him who has enchanted crops suffer the penalty. Neither lure away another's crops by chanting, nor by enchanting; do not render a field barren* <note>original: "Qui fru-ges incantasset poenas dato. Neve alienam segetem pellexeris excantando, neg. incantando; Ne agrum defruganto"</note>. The meaning in English is this: Let him be executed who bewitches grain; do not transfer other men's grain into your ground by enchantment; take care that you do not enchant at all, nor make your neighbor's field barren. He who does these things shall die, etc.

## CHAP. V.

### *An instance of one summoned under the Law of the Twelve Tables, where the said law is proved ridiculous; of two witches who could do wonders.*

Although among us, we think people are bewitched when they suddenly become poor, and not those who grow rich quickly; yet you should understand that at Rome (as Pliny reports) under these articles, one C. Furius Cressus was summoned <note>original: "convented"</note> before Spurius Albinus. Even though he had been a free man for only a short time after being released from slavery, by practicing only farming <note>original: "occupying only tillage"</note>, he grew rich suddenly because he had good crops. Thus, it was suspected that he transferred his neighbors' grain into his own fields. No plea, no delay, no excuse, no denial 
<margin>A notable defense <note>original: "purgation"</note> of C. Furius Cressus, summoned as a witch.</margin>
would help him—neither in jest nor through serious or honest means. Instead, he was assigned a specific day to answer for his life. And therefore

fearing the sentence of condemnation, which was to be given there by the voice and verdict of three men (just as we here are tried by twelve), made his appearance on the day assigned. He brought with him his ploughs and harrows, spades and shovels, and other instruments of husbandry; his oxen, horses, and working bullocks; his servants; and also his daughter, who was a sturdy girl and a good housewife, and also (as *Piso* <note>Gaius Calpurnius Piso, a Roman historian</note> reports) well-dressed in her apparel. As for the labor, sweat, watching, care, and diligence which I have used in this regard, I cannot show them at this time." And by this means, he was dismissed with the consent of the court, who otherwise (as it was thought) would hardly have escaped the sentence of condemnation and the punishment of death.

<margin>*Malleus Maleficarum*, part 2, question 1, chapter 5.</margin>
It is constantly affirmed in the *Malleus Maleficarum* <note>original: "M. Mal."; the "Hammer of Witches," a famous 14th-century Catholic treatise on the prosecution of witches</note> that *Stafus* used to always hide himself in a mousehole, and had a disciple called *Hoppo*, who made *Stadlin* a master witch. All of them could, whenever they wished, invisibly transfer a third of their neighbors' dung, hay, corn, etc., into their own ground; create hail, tempests, and floods with thunder and lightning; and kill children, cattle, etc.; reveal hidden things; and perform many other tricks whenever and wherever they pleased. But these two did not fare as well with the Inquisitors as the other man did with the Roman and heathen judges. Nevertheless, *Stafus* was too clever for them all: for none of the lawyers or Inquisitors could bring him to appear before them, if what "witch-mongers" <note>the author's term for those who promote the belief in and persecution of witches</note> write in these matters is true.

### Chap. VI.

->Laws provided for the punishment of such witches as work miracles (some of which are mentioned), and of certain Popish laws published against them.<-

---

<margin>Punishment of impossibilities.</margin>
<margin>A wise law of Pope Innocent and Julius, were it not that they lacked wisdom when they made it.</margin>
There are other laws of other nations made to this unbelievable effect: for instance, the *Salic Law* <note>original: "Lex Salicarum"; an ancient Germanic legal code</note> provides punishment for those who fly in the air from place to place and meet at their nightly assemblies and grand banquets, carrying silverware and such items with them, etc. This is as if we should make a law to hang a man for taking a church in his hand at Dover and throwing it to Calais. And because in this case, Popish laws shall be shown to be as foolish and wicked as any others—and especially as tyrannical as those which are most cruel—you shall hear what fine new laws the Church of Rome has lately devised. These, therefore, are the words of Pope *Innocent VIII* to the Inquisitors of Germany <note>original: "Almaine"</note>, and of Pope *Julius II* sent to the Inquisitors of Bergamo <note>original: "Bergomen"</note>: "It has come to our ears that many wicked persons of both sexes, using the company of the demons known as the *Incubus* and *Succubus* <note>demons believed to have sexual intercourse with sleeping humans; an incubus is male and a succubus is female</note>, along with incantations, charms, and conjurations, etc., do destroy the births of women with child, the offspring of all cattle, the corn of the field, the grapes of the vines, and the fruit of the trees. Also, they afflict men, women, and all kinds of cattle and beasts of the field. With their said enchantments, etc., they utterly extinguish, suffocate, and spoil all vineyards, orchards, meadows, pastures, grass, green corn, ripe corn, and all other legumes <note>original: "Podware"; crops that grow in pods, like peas or beans</note>. Indeed, men and women themselves are so afflicted by their curses with external and internal pains and diseases that men cannot father, nor women bring forth any children, nor even accomplish the duty of marriage—denying the faith which they professed in baptism, to the destruction of their own souls, etc. Our pleasure, therefore, is that all impediments that may hinder the Office of the Inquisition be utterly removed from among the people, lest this blot of heresy proceed to poison and defile those who are still innocent. Therefore, we do ordain, by virtue of Apostolic Authority, that our Inquisitors of High Germany may execute the Office of Inquisition..."

# CHAPTER 8.

*Poetry and Popery <note>The author uses "Popery" as a derogatory term for the practices of the Roman Catholic Church.</note> compared in enchantments; Catholic witch-believers <note>original: "Witchmongers"</note> have more advantage in this than Protestants.*

<margin>Ovid, *Metamorphoses* Book 3, Fable 2. Ovid, *Metamorphoses* Book 14, Fables 5, 6.</margin>
You see in these verses that the poets (whether in earnest or in jest, I do not know) ascribe more to witches and their charms than can be found in either human or diabolical power. I do not doubt that most readers will admit these stories are fables <note>original: "fabulous"</note>; although the most learned of my adversaries—for lack of Scripture—are forced to produce these poems as proof. For lack of judgment, I am sure, they actually think that Actaeon's transformation <note>In Greek myth, Actaeon was turned into a stag by the goddess Diana.</note> was real. And why not, just as well as the metamorphosis or transubstantiation of Ulysses' companions into swine, which St. Augustine and so many great scholars <note>original: "Clerks"</note> believe and report?

<margin>The author's transition to his intended goal.</margin>
Nevertheless, Catholic <note>original: "Popish"</note> writers, I confess, have an advantage here over us Protestants: for, besides these poetic proofs, they have the word and authority of the Pope himself and others of that "holy crew." I intend to set down some of their charms, conjurations, blessings, and cursings for you to sample. I want you to understand that poets are not nearly as shameless <note>original: "impudent"</note> as Catholics in this regard, nor do they seem as ignorant, profane, or impious. Therefore, I will show you how loudly they lie and what powers they ascribe to their charms and conjurations; and alongside these, I will include all manner of witches' charms as clearly as I can.

# CHAPTER 9.

*Catholic periapts <term>An amulet or charm worn on the body to ward off disease or bad luck.</term>, amulets and charms: the Agnus Dei, a "waistcoat of proof" <note>A magical garment believed to make the wearer invulnerable to weapons.</note>, a charm for the falling evil <term>A historical term for epilepsy.</term>, a document brought to St. Leo from Heaven by an angel, the virtues of St. Savior's Epistle, a charm against thieves, a document found in Christ's wounds, the power of the Cross, etc.*

The virtues listed in the following verses (written by Pope Urban V to the Emperor of the Greeks) are contained in a periapt or tablet to be worn continually, called an *Agnus Dei* <note>Latin: "Lamb of God." A small devotional object blessed by the Pope.</note>. This is a little cake of wax featuring a picture of a lamb carrying a flag on one side and Christ's head on the other. It is hollow so that the Gospel of St. John, written on fine paper, can be placed inside. It is composed and made exactly as they themselves report:

> Balsam and pure wax, with the water of Chrism <note>Holy oil used in Catholic rituals.</note>,
> Create the lamb, which great gift I give to you,
> As if born from the font, sanctified through mysteries:
> It drives away lightning from above and every evil thing,
> It shatters sin, just as Christ's blood does, and overcomes it.
> The pregnant woman is preserved, and the birth is delivered safely;
> It brings gifts to the worthy; it destroys the power of fire;
> When carried purely, it rescues one from the waves of the sea.
> <note>original Latin: "Balsamus & munda cera, cum Chrismatis unda / Conficiunt agnum, quod munus do tibi magnum, / Fonte velut natum, per mystica sanctificatum: / Fulgura de sursum depellit, & omne malignum, / Peccatum frangit, ut Christi sanguis, & angit, / Pregnans servatur, simul & partus liberatur; / Dona refert dignis, virtutem destruit ignis, / Portatus munde de fluctibus eripit unda."</note>

### A Charm against Shot, or a Waistcoat of Proof <note>A "Waistcoat of Proof" was a garment believed to make the wearer "bulletproof" or invulnerable to weapons through magical or divine protection.</note>.

Before the introduction of these *Agnus Deis* <note>original: "Agnus Dei's"; wax medallions blessed by the Pope, often imprinted with the figure of a lamb.</note>, a holy garment called a "Waistcoat for Necessity" was much used by our forefathers as a holy relic, etc. It was supposedly given by the Pope, or some similar "Arch-Conjurer," who promised all manner of immunity to the wearer; so much so that he could not be hurt by any shot or other violence. Additionally, any woman who wore it would have a quick delivery in childbirth. The composition of it was in the following order:

<margin>The manner of making a Waistcoat of Proof.</margin> On Christmas Day at night, a thread must be spun from flax by a young virgin girl, in the name of the Devil; and it must be woven by her, and also worked with a needle. In the breast or front part of it, two heads must be made with needlework; on the head at the right side must be a hat and a long beard; the left head must have a crown, and it must be so horrible that it resembles Beelzebub <note>A name for the Devil; literally "Lord of the Flies."</note>; and on each side of the waistcoat a cross must be made.

### C H A P T E R X.

-> How to make Holy Water, and its virtues; Saint Rufinus's Charm regarding the wearing and hearing of the Name of *Jesus*; that the Sacrament of Confession and the Eucharist are of as much efficacy as other Charms, and magnified by *L. Varius*. <-

If I did the job thoroughly, I should show you the composition of all their materials and how they prepare them, but it would be too long. And therefore, you shall only have in this place a few notes for the composition of certain recipes <term>receipts: formulas or prescriptions for making something, in this context, religious or magical items.</term>, which—instead of an Apothecary—if you deliver them to any priest who performs the early morning mass <term>morrow-mass Priest</term>, he will make them as well as the Pope himself. By Mary <note>original: "Mary" – a common oath referring to the Virgin Mary.</note>, now they grow more expensive with every Parliament, although at the same time, they sell many stale drugs of their own.

<margin>In the dedication of the church.</margin>
If you look in the Catholic <note>original: "Popish"</note> Pontifical <note>A liturgical book containing the rites performed by bishops.</note>, you shall see how they make their holy Water; namely, in this way: *I command <note>original: "conjure"</note> you, you creature of Water, in the Name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost, that you drive the Devil out of every corner and hole of this Church and Altar, so that he does not remain within our boundaries—we who are just and righteous.* <margin>In the Rationale of Divine Offices.</margin> And water used in this way (as Durandus <note>William Durand (c. 1230–1296), a medieval writer on the liturgy.</note> says) has power by its own nature to drive away Devils. If you wish to learn to make any more of this Catholic <note>original: "Popish"</note> material, you may go to the very Mass-Book and find many good recipes; truly, if you search Durandus, etc., you shall find them in abundance.

I know that all these Charms and all these worthless concoctions (though they were far more impious and foolish) will be maintained and defended by those who promote the Mass <note>original: "Mass-mongers"</note>, just as the rest will be by those who promote belief in witches <note>original: "Witch-mongers"</note>. And therefore I will in this place insert a Charm, the authority of which is equal with the rest, desiring to hear their opinions on it. I find in a book called *The Orchard of Lenten Sermons* <note>original: "Pomarium sermonum quadragesimalium," a collection of sermons by Pelbartus of Themeswar.</note> that Saint Francis, seeing Saint Rufinus provoked by the Devil to think himself damned, <margin>Orchard of Sermons, sermon 32.</margin> commanded Rufinus to say this Charm when he next met with this Devil: *Open your mouth, and I will put dung in there* <note>original: "Aperi os; & ibi imponam stercus"</note>, which is as much as to say in English (as Scot mockingly interprets it): "Open your mouth, and I will put in a plum"—a very ruffianly Charm <note>Scot is making a pun on the name "Rufinus" and "ruffianly."</note>.

</margin>
Leonardo Vair <note>original: "Leonard Varius"</note> writes in his book, *Concerning true, pious, and holy amulets that destroy the evil eye and all witchcraft* <note>original: "De veris, piis, ac sanctis amuletis fascinum atque omnia veneficia destruentibus"</note>; in which he specifically recommends that the name of *Jesus* be worn. However, he praises the Sacrament of Confession above all things. He says that while Christ, with his power, only threw Devils out of people's bodies, the Priest drives the Devil out of a person's soul through confession. <margin>The same author, in the same place.</margin> For he says that these words of the Priest, when he says, "*I absolve you*" <note>original: "Ego te absolvo"</note>, are as effective at driving away the Princes of Darkness—through the mighty power of that saying—as was the voice of God when he drove away the darkness of the world by saying at the beginning, "*Let there be light*" <note>original: "Fiat lux"</note>. He also recommends the Sacrament of the Eucharist, solitude, and silence as wholesome things to drive away Devils. Finally, he says that if an *Agnus Dei* <note>term: A wax disc blessed by the Pope, usually impressed with the figure of a lamb, worn as a holy protective object.</note> is added to this and worn around the neck by someone without sin, nothing is lacking that is good and healthy for this purpose. But he concludes that you must also make signs on your forehead by crossing yourself when you put on your shoes and at every other action; he claims this is an immediate remedy to drive away Devils, for they cannot stand it.

---

## CHAPTER XI.

### *Regarding the Excellent Balm used by Moses, foolishly <note>original: "apishly"</note> counterfeited in the Church of Rome.*

The excellent Balm that *Moses* made truly possessed many wonderful virtues, besides its pleasant and comforting fragrance. In his civil laws <note>original: "Politick Laws"</note>, *Moses* commanded that Kings, Queens, and Princes be anointed with it during their lawful elections and Coronations, until the everlasting King <note>Referring to Jesus Christ.</note> had taken on human form. This is now foolishly imitated in the *Roman Catholic* Church with various terrifying conjurations: three breaths blown in the shape of a cross (enough to make a queasy stomach vomit), nine mumbles, and three curtsies, saying while doing so, "*Hail, holy oil; three times hail, holy Balm*" <note>original: "Ave sanctum oleum, ter Ave sanctum Balsamum"</note>. In this way, the Devil is supposedly thrust out and the Holy Spirit let into his place. But as for *Moses's* Balm, it is not currently to be found in *Rome* or anywhere else that I can discover. Following this Catholic pattern, witches and other superstitious people use formal charms and conjurations; many bad Physicians also practice these when their medical learning fails, as will appear by the examples that follow.

---

## CHAPTER XII.

### *The opinion of Ferrarius regarding Charms, Periapts, Appensions, Amulets, etc. Regarding "Homerical Medicines," and the power of constant Belief.*

<margin>
Argerius Ferrarius, *On the Method of Healing*, Book 2, Chapter 11.
Regarding Homeric medication.
</margin>
Argerius Ferrarius, a Physician of great reputation in these days, says that since no diet or medicine can so completely extinguish a disease that no dregs or remnants remain, Physicians therefore use physical attachments <note>original: "Alligations"</note>, items hung around the neck <note>term: "Appensions" and "Periapts" were amulets or charms worn on the body for medical or magical protection.</note>, amulets, charms, and mystical characters. He believes these might do some good, and he is certain they can do no harm. He argues that it is necessary and useful for a Physician to leave nothing undone that can be devised for a patient's recovery, and that many great cures are performed by such means. He cites a great number of experiments from *Alexander Trallianus, Aetius, Octavianus, Marcellus, Philodotus, Archigines, Philostratus, Pliny, and Dioscorides*. He would even make men believe that *Galen*—who <margin>This should be examined to see if Galen is being slandered.</margin> in truth despised and mocked all those vanities—recanted his former opinion in his later days. Ferrarius claims Galen took back all his attacks against these magical cures and even wrote a book titled *On Homeric Medicine* <note>original: "De Homerica Medicatione"</note>. No man could ever find this book except for one *Alexander Trallianus*, who says he saw it; and he further affirms,

Galen, *On Preserving Health*, Book 1. <note>original: "Galen de tuenda sanit. lib. 1."</note>

...affirms that it is an honest man's part to cure the sick by hook or by crook, or by any means whatsoever. <margin>
Alexander of Tralles <note>original: "Trallian"</note>, Book 9, Chapter 15.
</margin>
As for example (says Trallian), Galen—having now changed his mind on this opinion—holds and writes that the bones which stick in one's throat are expelled and cast out by the force of charms and enchanting words. Yes, he even claims that through these means the stone, the colic, the falling sickness <term>epilepsy</term>, and all fevers, gouts, fluxes <term>excessive discharges or dysentery</term>, fistulas, hemorrhages, and finally whatever condition (even beyond the skill of himself or any other foolish physician) is cured and perfectly healed by words of enchantment. But Augier Ferrier <note>original: "M. Ferrarius." Ferrier was a 16th-century French physician.</note> (although he allowed and practiced this kind of medicine) nevertheless protests that he thinks it is effective in no other way than through the power of "constant opinion" <note>Essentially, the placebo effect or the power of belief.</note>. Thus, he affirms that neither the character <term>a symbolic glyph or sigil</term>, nor the charm, nor the witch, nor the Devil accomplishes the cure. As he says, the experiment of the toothache will clearly demonstrate this, wherein the cure is worked by the confidence or doubt of both the patient and the doctor, according to the poet's saying:

->*Neither the hellish furies nor the stars of heaven live within us;*<-
->*The spirit that thrives within us does those things.*<-
<note>original: "Nos habitat non Tartara, sed nec sidera cæli, / Spiritus in nobis qui viget illa facit."</note>

->Translated into English by *Abraham Fleming*:<-

->*No hellish furies dwell in us,*<-
->*Nor stars with heavenly influence;*<-
->*The spirit that lives and rules in us,*<-
->*Does everything skillfully.*<-

This (he says) happens to the unlearned through the opinion they form of the characters and holy words. But the learned, who know the force of the mind and imagination, work miracles by those means. Thus, the unlearned must have external helps to do that which the learned can do with a word only. He says that this is called *Homerica medicatio* <note>Homeric medicine.</note> because Homer discovered blood suppressed by words and infections healed by or through mysteries.
