### CHAPTER 13.

*Of the effects of amulets; the aim of Augier Ferrier in his praise of charms, etc.; four sorts of Homeric medicines and the choice thereof; and of imagination.*

<margin>
Ferrier, *On Easy Cures*, Book 2, Chapter 1. <note>original: "Ferrar. de cast. curat. lib. 2. cap. 1."</note>
</margin>
Regarding my own opinion of these amulets, characters, and such other baubles <note>original: "bables"</note>, I have sufficiently expressed it elsewhere, and I will reveal the vanity of these superstitious trifles more extensively later. Therefore, at this time, I only say that those amulets which are to be hung or carried about one—if they consist of herbs, roots, stones, or some metal—may have various medicinal operations. By the virtue given to them by God in their creation, they may work strange effects and cures; however, to attribute this virtue to any other matter is witchcraft. And whereas Augier Ferrier commends certain amulets that have no appearance of physical operation—such as a nail taken from a Cross, Holy Water, and the very sign of the Cross, along with such other Popish <note>Scot uses "Popish" as a derogatory term for Roman Catholic practices.</note> stuff—I think he labors more to draw men toward Catholicism than to teach or persuade them in the truth of medicine or philosophy. I suspect this all the more because he himself sees the fraud in it, confessing that where these magical physicians apply three seeds of three-leaved grass...

...grass to a Tertian Ague <term>a fever that recurs every third day, often associated with malaria</term>, and four to a Quartain <term>a fever that recurs every fourth day</term>, suggesting that the specific number is not actually important.

<margin>Four sorts of Homeric medicines, and which is the principal.</margin>
But regarding these Homeric <note>original: "Homerical"; these are charms or medicines believed to work through the power of words or ancient authority</note> medicines, he says there are four types, of which amulets, characters <term>magical symbols or sigils</term>, and charms are three. Of this kind of illusion, he cites as an example how Philodotus <note>A physician mentioned in classical or Renaissance medical anecdotes</note> put a cap of lead upon the head of someone who imagined he was headless, by which the person was delivered from his disease or delusion.

<margin>The force of a fixed fancy, opinion, or conceit.</margin>
**Additionally**, another physician cured a woman who imagined that a serpent or snake was continually gnawing and tearing her entrails; and that was done only by giving her a vomit <term>an emetic medicine</term> and by secretly tossing into the vomited matter a little serpent or snake, similar to the one she imagined was in her belly.

**Additionally**, another man imagined that he was always burning in a fire; a fire was secretly placed under his bed, which—being taken out before his face—satisfied his imagination and his heat was calmed. To this belongs the fact that the hiccup <note>original: "Hickot"</note> is cured with sudden fear or strange news; indeed, by that means agues and many other strange and extreme diseases have been healed. And some who have lain so sick and sore with the gout that they could not move a joint have—through sudden fear of fire or the collapse of houses—forgotten their infirmities and pains and have run away. But in my treatise upon melancholy and the effects of imagination, and in the discourse of Natural Magic, you shall see these matters discussed at length.

### C H A P. XIV.

->*A Selection of Charms against the Falling Evil, the biting of a mad dog, the stinging of a scorpion, the toothache, for a woman in labor, for the King's Evil, to get a thorn out of any limb, or a bone out of one's throat; charms to be said while fasting, or at the gathering of herbs, for sore eyes, to open locks, against spirits, for the bots in a horse, and especially for the Duke of Alba's horse, for sour wines, etc.*<-

There are innumerable charms used by conjurers, bad physicians, wicked surgeons <note>original: "Chirurgians"</note>, melancholic witches, and swindlers <note>original: "Coseners"</note> for all diseases and pains—especially for those conditions that bad physicians and surgeons do not know how to cure, and in truth, they are good material to hide their ignorance; of which I will repeat some.

Take the sick man by the hand and whisper these words softly in his ear: *I conjure you by the sun and moon, and by the gospel of this day delivered by God to Hubert, Giles, Cornelius, and John, that you rise and fall no more.* Alternatively: drink spring water at night out of the skull of one who has been slain. Alternatively: eat a pig killed with a knife that slew a man. Alternatively, as follows:

<note>original Latin: "Ananizapta ferit mortem, dum lædere quærit, / Est mala mors capta, dum dicitur Ananizapta: / Ananizapta Dei nunc miserere mei."</note>

> *And death shall be taken captive.*

### *Against the biting of a Mad-Dog.*

<margin>Jean Bodin, *On the Demon-mania of Sorcerers*, Book 3, Chapter 5.</margin>
**P**ut a silver ring on the finger, inside of which these words are engraved: ✠ *Habay* ✠ *habar* ✠ *hebar* ✠ and say to the person bitten by a mad dog, "I am your Savior, do not lose your life." Then prick him in the nose three times, so that at each time he bleeds. Otherwise, take pills made from the skull of someone who has been hanged. Otherwise: write upon a piece of bread: *Irioni, khiriora, effer, khuder, feres*; and let it be eaten by the party who was bitten. Otherwise: *O King of glory, Jesus Christ, come with peace: In the name of the Father the greatest, in the name of the Son the greatest, in the name of the Holy Spirit the most excellent. Gasper, Melchior, Balthasar præx max Deus max."</note>.

But in truth, this condition is very dangerous; so much so that if it is not quickly and skillfully prevented, either death or a frenzy ensues through the infection of the fluid <note>original: "humor"</note> left in the wound from the bite of a mad dog. Because bad surgeons <note>original: "Chirurgians"</note> cannot cure it, they have used foolish, deceptive charms. But Dodoens <note>original: "Dodoneus"; referring to Rembert Dodoens, a famous Flemish physician and botanist</note> says in his *Herbal* that the herb Alyssum <note>original: "Alysson"; also known as Madwort, historically believed to cure rabies</note> cures it; an experiment which I have no doubt will prove more true than all the charms in the world. But where he says, *that hanging the same herb at a man's gate or entry preserves him and his cattle from enchantment or bewitching*, he is overtaken with folly.

**T**hrow over the top of the house where a woman in labor <note>original: "travel"</note> lies, a stone or any other thing that has killed three living creatures, namely: *a man, a wild boar, and a she-bear.*

### *To heal the King’s or Queen’s Evil, or any other soreness in the Throat.*

**R**emedies to cure the King’s or Queen’s Evil <note>Scrofula, a form of tuberculosis affecting the lymph nodes, traditionally believed to be cured by the monarch's touch</note> are: first, to touch the place with the hand of someone who died an untimely death. Otherwise: *Let a virgin fasting lay her hand on the sore and say, "Apollo denies that the heat of the plague can increase where a naked virgin quenches it"* <note>original Latin: "Apollo denyeth that the heat of the Plague can increase where a naked Virgin quencheth it"</note>; and spit three times upon it.

### *A Charm in the Romish Church, upon Saint Blaise’s day, that will fetch a Thorn out of any place of one's body, a bone out of the Throat, etc. Lesson 3.*

**F**or the fetching of a thorn out of any part of one’s body, or a bone out of the throat, you shall read a charm used in the Roman Church on St. Blaise’s Day <note>February 3rd; St. Blaise is the patron saint of throat ailments</note>; namely, "Call upon God, and remember St. Blaise." This St. Blaise could also heal all wild beasts that were sick or lame by the laying on of his hands.

### *A Charm for a Headache.*

Tie a noose <note>original: "halter"</note> around your head that was previously used to hang someone.

### *A Charm to be recited every morning by a witch while fasting, or at least before she goes out in public.*

The fire bites, the fire bites, the fire bites; hog dung <note>original: "Hogs-turd"</note> over it, hog dung over it, hog dung over it. The Father with you, the Son with me, the Holy Ghost between us both to be: (Repeat three times) <note>original: "ter," Latin for "thrice"</note>. ### *Another Charm that witches use when gathering their medicinal herbs.*

<margin>* Though neither the herb nor the witch ever actually went there.</margin>

> Hail to you, holy herb,
> Growing on the ground;

### *An old woman’s charm, with which she did much good in the countryside and became famous.*

An old woman who healed all diseases of cattle (for which she never took any reward except a penny and a loaf of bread), being seriously questioned about what words she used to achieve this, confessed that after she had touched the sick animal, she always left immediately, saying:

> My loaf in my lap,
> My penny in my purse;
> You are never the better,
> And I am never the worse.

### *Another similar charm.*

<margin>Note the power of a persistent opinion or a fixed imagination.</margin>

A noblewoman with sore eyes complained to someone who promised to help her if she would follow his advice. This advice was simply to wear a sealed scroll around her neck, which she was forbidden to look inside. Having hope that it would cure her, she accepted the condition and stopped her constant weeping—tears she had shed while mourning the miserable darkness she feared she would have to endure. In a short time, her eyes were much improved. But alas! Soon after, she lost that precious "jewel," and consequently returned to her habitual weeping and her sore eyes. However, when her "jewel" or scroll was found again, her dear friends looked inside, and it contained only this short poem <note>original: "Posie"</note>:

<margin>* Spell the word backward, and you will soon see the crude nature of this charm or trick.</margin>

> The Devil pull out both your eyes,
> And * shit <note>original: "etish"; spelled backward</note> in the holes as well.

From this, you can see in part what a persistent opinion can achieve, according to the saying of Plato: If a person's imagination <note>original: "fansie"</note> or mind assures them that a harmful thing will do them good, it may actually do so, etc.

### *A Charm to Open Locks.*

<margin>Thievish charms.</margin>
Just as the herbs called Aethiopides <note>original: "Æthiopides"; an herb described by ancient writers like Pliny as having the power to open locks or dry up rivers.</note> will open all locks (if everything Enchanters say is true) with the help of certain words, there are also charms and amulets <note>original: "Periapts"; charms or talismans worn on the body for protection.</note> which can do just as much without any herbs. For example: take a piece of wax that was used in a baptismal rite, <note>original: "wax crossed in baptism"</note> print certain flowers into it, and tie them into the back tail of your shirt. When you want to undo a lock, blow into it three times, saying: *Arato hoc partiko hoc maratarykin.* <note>These are likely "barbarous words"—nonsense sounds intended to seem powerful because they are unintelligible.</note> "I open this door in the name of the one whom I am forced to break, just as you broke the gates of Hell. In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit, Amen." <note>original: "In Nomine Patris, & Filii, & spiritus sancti, Amen."</note>

### *A Charm to Drive Away Spirits that Haunt any House.*

<margin>This is called and considered the Paracelsian charm. Psalm 150. Luke 16. Psalm 68.</margin>
Hang this sentence, written upon virgin parchment, in each of the four corners of your house: "Let every spirit praise the Lord: <note>original: "Omnis spiritus laudet Dominum"</note> They have Moses and the Prophets: <note>original: "Mosen habent & Prophetas"</note> Let God arise, and let his enemies be scattered." <note>original: "Exurgat Deus, & dissipentur inimici ejus." Scot references Psalm 64, but this verse is actually Psalm 68:1.</note>

### *A Clever Procedure for one who is Possessed.*

The possessed person must go on his or her knees to the Church, no matter how far away it is from their lodging. They must crawl without leaving the path—using the common highway—in that manner, regardless of how foul and dirty it may be. They must not avoid anything that lies in the way until they come to the Church, where they must devoutly hear Mass; and then recovery follows.
<margin>Note: Remember that the hearing of Mass must not be omitted under any circumstances.</margin>

---

### *Another for the Same Purpose.*

A poor beggar must be asked to say five *Pater-nosters* <note>The Lord's Prayer ("Our Father")</note> and five *Aves* <note>The "Hail Mary"</note>. The first is to be said in the name of the possessed or bewitched person because Christ was led into the garden; the second, because Christ sweat both water and blood; the third, because Christ was condemned; the fourth, because he was crucified while innocent; and the fifth, because he suffered to take away our sins. Then the sick person must hear Mass for eight days straight, standing in the place where the Gospel is read, and must mix holy water with his food and drink; holy salt must also be part of the mixture.

### *Another to the Same Effect.*

<margin>Johannes Anglicus <note>John of Gaddesden, a 14th-century English physician.</note> citing Constantine, Walter, Bernard, Gilbert, etc.</margin>
The sick man must fast for three days, and then he and his parents must come to Church on an Ember Friday <note>A day of fasting and prayer at the start of one of the four seasons.</note> and hear the Mass appointed for that day; and likewise on the following Saturday and Sunday. The Priest must read over the sick man’s head that Gospel which is read in September, during the grape harvest, after the Feast of the Holy Cross. During the Ember days <note>original: "In diebus quatuor temporum"</note>, let him write it down and carry it around his neck, and he shall be cured.

Doubtless Jesus Christ could have no loophole <note>original: "starting hole"; a hiding place or means of escape.</note>, but was by this charm completely blocked and pursued; so much so that he was forced to perform the cure. For it appears by this that it would have been insufficient for him to have said, "Depart out of this man, you unclean spirit," and that when he said those words, he did not actually accomplish it. I do not think there can be found among all the heathen superstitious fables, or among the witches, conjurers, poets, knaves, deceivers, fools, etc., that ever wrote, so impudent and impious a lie or charm as is read in *Bernardino de’ Busti*. <note>A 15th-century Franciscan author.</note> There, to cure a sick man, Christ's body—specifically a wafer-cake <note>The Eucharistic bread or Host.</note>—was applied to the outside of his side, and it entered into his heart in the sight of all the bystanders. Now, if respected authors report such lies, what credit should we give to the "old wives' tales" that Sprenger, Institor, <note>Heinrich Kramer, author of the *Malleus Maleficarum*.</note> Bodin, and others write? We should give them as much credit as we give to *Ovid's Metamorphoses*, *Aesop's Fables*, *More’s Utopia*, and various other fantasies, which have as much truth in them as a blind man has sight in his eye.

### A Charm for the Bots in a Horse.

<note>original: "Bots"; parasitic larvae that infect the stomach and intestines of horses.</note>

You must both say and do this for the diseased horse three days together, before sunrise: *In the Name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit; I exorcise you, worm, by God the Father, and the Son, and the Holy Spirit* <note>original Latin: "In Nomine Patris & filii & Spiritus sancti; Exorcizo te vermem per Deum Patrem, & filium & spiritum sanctum"</note>; that is, **In the Name of God the Father, the Son, and the Holy Ghost, I conjure you, O Worm, by God the Father, the Son, and the Holy Ghost; that you neither eat nor drink the flesh, blood, or bones of this horse; and that you may hereby be made as patient as Job, and as good as Saint John the Baptist, when he baptized Christ in the Jordan. In the Name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit.** And then say three *Pater-nosters* <note>Our Fathers</note>, and three *Aves* <note>Hail Marys</note>, into the right ear of the horse, to the glory of the Holy Trinity. **Lord, Son, Spirit, Mary.** <note>original Latin: "Dominus Filius Spiritus Maria."</note>

<margin>The blacksmiths will give them little thanks for this prayer.</margin>
There are also various books printed, apparently with the authority of the Church of Rome, containing many medicinal prayers—not only against all diseases of horses, but also for every hindrance and fault in a horse. It has gone so far that if a shoe falls off in the middle of a journey, there is a prayer to guarantee your horse's hoof so that it will not break, no matter how far he is from the blacksmith's forge.

Also, the Duke of Alba's <note>Fernando Álvarez de Toledo, a Spanish general and governor in the Netherlands.</note> horse was consecrated, or canonized, in the Low Countries during a solemn Mass. At this Mass, the Pope's Bull <note>An official papal edict or decree.</note> and also his charm were published (which I will recite later); meanwhile, the Duke sat as Viceroy with his consecrated standard in his hand until the Mass was finished.

### A Charm against Vinegar.

<margin>O notable blasphemy!</margin>
To prevent wine from turning sour <note>original: "wax not eager"; "eager" is from the French "aigre," meaning sour or sharp.</note>, write on the vessel: **"Taste and see, for the Lord is sweet."** <note>original Latin: "Gustate & videte, quoniam suavis est Dominus"; a quote from Psalm 34:8.</note>

<meta>This page continues Reginald Scot’s argument against the reality of magic, specifically addressing the claim that serpents can be charmed. He contrasts the metaphorical language of the Bible with the literal, though fictional, claims of Roman poets to show that magic is a literary invention rather than a physical reality.</meta>

### Chapter 15

#### The enchanting of serpents and snakes; objections answered concerning the same; foolish <note>original: "fond"</note> reasons why charms take effect on them. Muhammad’s pigeon. A miracle performed by an ass at Memphis in Egypt. Catholic <note>original: "Popish"</note> charms against serpents. Regarding miracle-workers, the taming of snakes, and Bodin’s <note>Jean Bodin (1530–1596), a French jurist and writer on demonology whom Scot frequently critiques.</note> lie about snakes.

<margin>Psalm 58:4, 5</margin> Concerning the charming of serpents and snakes, my opponents (as I have mentioned) believe they have a great advantage based on the words of David in Psalm 58 and Jeremiah chapter 8, where they interpret one Prophet using Virgil and the other using Ovid. For the words of David are these: *Their poison is like the poison of a serpent; they are like a deaf adder that stops its ear and does not hear the voice of the charmer, no matter how cunningly he charms.* <margin>Virgil, Eclogue 8</margin> The words of Virgil are these: "The cold snake in the meadows is burst by singing" <note>original: *Frigidus in pratis cantando rumpitur anguis*</note>. It is as if he were saying, "David, you are lying," for the cold-natured snake is supposedly broken all to pieces in the field where it lies by the charms of the enchanters. <margin>Ovid, Metamorphoses 7</margin> Then comes Ovid, and he takes the side of his fellow countryman, speaking in the persona of a witch: "I break the viper's jaws with words and charms" <note>original: *Vipereas rumpo verbis & carmine fauces*</note>. However, Jeremiah, on the other hand, opposes this poetic witch, and he not only defends but explains the words of his fellow prophet—and he does so not in his own name, but in the name of Almighty God, <margin>Jeremiah 8:17</margin> saying: *I will send serpents and cockatrices <note>A mythical serpent, also called a basilisk, said to kill with its breath or gaze.</note> among you which cannot be charmed.*

Now, let any impartial <note>original: "indifferent"</note> man (whether Christian or Heathen) judge whether the words and intentions of the Prophets do not directly oppose these poets' words (I will not say their intentions, for I am sure they were merely joking and trifling, following the common fables of lying poets). Indeed, I can counter those two poets with two others—namely, Propertius and Horace. One of them playfully mocks, while the other seriously challenges their fantastic poetry regarding the power and omnipotence of witches. For while Virgil, Ovid, and others write that witches can fetch down the moon and stars from heaven with their charms, Propertius mocks them in the following words:

<note>original Latin: "At vos deductæ quibus est fallacia Lunæ, / Et labor in magicis sacra piare focis, / En agedum dominæ mentem convertite nostræ, / Et facite illa meo palleat ore magis, / Tunc ego crediderim vobis & sidera & amnes / Posse Circeis ducere carminibus."</note>

->Translated into English by Abraham Fleming:<-

> But you who use the subtle trick <note>original: "flight," likely meaning "sleight" or skill.</note>
> Of fetching down the Moon from skies,
> And with bright, enchanting fire
> Attempt to purify your sacrifice:
> Look now, go ahead, change (if you can)
> Our lady's mind and stubborn heart,
> And make her face more pale and wan
> Than mine. If you can do this by magic art,
> Then I will readily believe
> That by your witching charms you can
> Remove <note>original: "remeeve"</note> the stars from the sky above,
> And turn rivers back from where they ran.

### The Aspects of the Planets.

*   ☌ <term>Conjunction</term>: This is the best aspect when involving good planets, and the worst when involving evil ones.
*   \* <term>Sextile</term>: This is a moderate aspect in terms of its goodness or badness.
*   △ <term>Trine</term>: This aspect represents a state of enmity that is not fully complete <note>original: "not full perfect." While modern astrology views the Trine as harmonious, historical texts sometimes classified aspects differently based on the elements.</note>.
*   ☍ <term>Opposition</term>: This aspect represents the most complete or "perfect" enmity.

### How the Day is Divided or Distinguished.

A natural day is the span of twenty-four hours, including the night, and begins at one o'clock in the morning <note>original: "after midnight"</note>. An artificial day is the span of time between the rising and the setting <note>original: "falling"</note> of the Sun, etc.; all the rest is night, which begins at sunset.

Below follows a table showing how the day and the night are divided into hours and assigned to the rule <note>original: "regiment"</note> of the planets.

<margin>Feats of his dog and Mahomet’s pigeon.</margin>
...part) are such that they cannot be made tame or trained through human industry or skill to do anything that might provoke wonder. Examples of such training include **Bomelio’s** dog, or **Mahomet’s** pigeon, which would return to him while he was in the middle of his army camp and pick a pea <note>original: "Pease"</note> out of his ear. It was done in such a way that many of the people thought the Holy Ghost came and told him a story in his ear. That same pigeon also brought him a scroll on which was written, "Be you king" <note>original: "Rex esto"</note>, and laid it on his neck. And because I have spoken of the trainability <note>original: "docility"</note> of a dog and a pigeon, although I could cite an infinite number of similar tales, I will be bold enough to trouble you with only one more.

<margin>A story demonstrating the great obedience of an ass.</margin>
At Memphis in Egypt, among other juggling tricks <note>original: "jugling knacks"</note> that were usually shown there, there was one man who took such pains with an ass that he had taught it all the following qualities. For profit, he had a stage built and an assembly of people meet. When this was done, in the manner of a play, he came in with his ass and said, "The Sultan has great need of asses to help carry stones and other materials toward the great building he is currently working on." The ass immediately fell down to the ground and, by every sign, showed himself to be sick, and at length appeared to die <note>original: "give up the ghost"</note>. Because of this, the juggler begged the assembly for money to cover his loss. Having gathered all the money he could, he said, "Now, my masters, you shall see that my ass is still alive and is only faking, because he wanted some money to buy himself feed <note>original: "provender"</note>, knowing that I was poor and in need of relief." 

Upon this, he insisted on making a wager that his ass was alive, even though to everyone else it seemed completely dead. When someone had bet money with him on the matter, he commanded the ass to rise, but it lay still as though it were dead. Then he beat it with a club <note>original: "Cudgel"</note>, but that did no good until he addressed his speech to the ass, saying (as before) in front of the whole audience: "The Sultan has commanded that all the people shall ride out tomorrow to see the celebration <note>original: "triumph"</note>, and that the fair ladies will then ride upon the finest asses and will give them excellent feed, and every ass shall drink from the fresh water of the Nile <note>original: "Nilus"</note>." And then, look! The ass suddenly jumped up and pranced about excitedly. 

"Look," said his master, "now I have won! But in truth, the Mayor <note>original: "Major"</note> has borrowed my ass for the use of his wife, that old, ugly <note>original: "ill-favoured"</note> witch." Immediately upon hearing this, the ass hung down his ears and limped severely <note>original: "halted down right"</note>, as though he were completely lame. Then his master said, "I see you love pretty young girls." At those words, the ass looked up with a joyful expression. Then his master told him to go choose one who should ride upon him, and he ran to a very handsome woman and touched her with his head, and so on. <margin>Jean Bodin, *Of the Demonomania of Witches*, book 2, chapter 6.</margin> A snake will never be brought to such familiarity, and so forth. **Bodin** says that this was a man in the form of an ass, but I might rather think that **Bodin** is an ass in the form of a man. Well, to return to our serpents, I will tell you a story concerning the charming of them and the outcome of it.

In the city of Salisbury <note>original: "Salisborough"</note>, there was an enchanter who, before all the people, took it upon himself to summon all the serpents and snakes within a one-mile radius into a great pit or ditch, and there to kill them. When all the serpents were gathered together, as he stood upon the edge of the pit, there came at last a great and horrible serpent which would not be forced down by all the power of his incantations. Instead (while all the others were dead), it flew upon the enchanter, clasped him around his middle, and drew him down into the ditch, and there killed him. 

You must think that this was a devil in a serpent's likeness which, out of the love he had for those poor snakes, killed the sorcerer—to teach all other witches to beware of such wicked practices. <margin>*Malleus Maleficarum* <note>The Hammer of Witches</note>, part 2, question 2, chapter 9; Jean Bodin.</margin> And surely, if this is not true, there are a great number of lies contained in the *Malleus Maleficarum* and in the writings of **Jean Bodin**. If this is well weighed and understood, it strikes to the ground all the arguments of those "witch-mongers" <note>those who promote the reality of witchcraft</note> who struggle to twist miraculous witchcraft out of this topic. For they disagree significantly, with some denying and some affirming that serpents can be bewitched. Nevertheless, because you shall see how Popery <note>Catholicism</note> agrees with Paganism in every point, I will recite certain charms against witchcraft.

# BOOK XII. The Discovery of Charms, etc.

...against vipers, which are mostly allowed by the Church of Rome, as follows:

<margin>Exorcisms or conjurations against serpents.</margin>
> I conjure you, O serpent, in this hour, by the five holy wounds of our Lord, that you do not move from this place, but stay here as certainly as God was born of a pure Virgin. Otherwise, I conjure you, serpent, in the Name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit <note>original: "In Nomine Patris, & Filii, & Spiritus sancti"</note>: I command you, serpent, by our Lady Saint Mary, that you neither hurt me nor any other Christian, as certainly as God was born of an immaculate Virgin; in which respect I take you up: in the Name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit <note>original: "In Nomine Patris, & Filii, & Spiritus Sancti"</note>: *Ely lash eiter, ely lash eiter, ely lash eiter*. Otherwise, O vermin, you must come just as God came to the Jews.

In another instance, Lucius Varius says that a serpent shrivels up from oak leaves <note>original: "Serpens quernis frondibus contracta"</note>; that is, a serpent touched with oak leaves dies, and stops even at the beginning of its <margin>Lucius Varius, *On Fascination*, book 1, chapter 4.</margin> movement if a feather of the ibis bird is cast or thrown upon it. He also says that a viper struck or hit with a reed is stunned, and when touched with a beech branch, it immediately becomes numb and stiff.

<margin>Those who falsely claim kinship with blessed Paul and Saint Catherine.</margin>
Here it should be remembered that many people boast they are of Saint Paul's race and kinship, showing marks on their bodies like the shapes of serpents. The Papists claim these marks appeared on everyone from Saint Paul’s lineage. Indeed, they also say that all his kinsfolk can handle serpents or any poison without danger. Others likewise brag they have a Catherine wheel <note>A spiked wheel used for the martyrdom of Saint Catherine, often used as a heraldic or symbolic mark.</note> upon their bodies; they say they are kin to Saint Catherine, and that they can carry burning coals in their bare hands, dip their hands in scalding hot liquid, and even enter hot ovens. 
<margin>Jean Bodin, *On the Demon-mania of Witches*, book 1, chapter 3.</margin> 
The last of these is nothing but a joke and can be done by anyone who wishes to try (just as a dishonest fellow in London used to do, by staying in the oven for no time at all). However, there is a show made of the others as if they were certain and undisputed. This is done by anointing the hands with the juice of mallows, mercury, urine, etc., which for a short time act as protections <note>original: "defensatives"</note> against scalding liquids and scorching fires.

But those who take it upon themselves to perform these mysteries and miracles do indeed (after reciting these and similar words and charms) pick up snakes and vipers in their bare hands. Sometimes they even put them around their necks without being hurt, to the terror and astonishment of the onlookers, who naturally both fear and loathe all serpents. But these charmers (take my word for it) do not dare trust their charms. Instead, they use a trick that any man may lawfully use, and the lawful use of it ensures they remain safe and take no harm, no matter how much they handle them. Truly, as some say, they pull out the snakes' teeth beforehand with a woolen rag; but the certainty is that they weary the snakes out. 

Surely this is a kind of witchcraft which I call "private conspiracy." Jean Bodin <note>A famous French jurist and writer on witchcraft.</note> says that all the snakes in one country were driven into another region by charms and verses; perhaps he means Ireland, where <margin>Saint Patrick</margin> Saint Patrick is said to have done so through his holiness, etc.

<margin>Malleus Maleficarum, part 2, question 2, chapter 1.</margin>
<margin>Sprenger and Institor</margin>
James Sprenger and Heinrich Institor <note>The authors of the *Malleus Maleficarum*, the most famous medieval treatise on hunting witches.</note> affirm that serpents, snakes, and their skins surpass all other creatures for use in witchcraft. They claim witches bury them under people's thresholds—either of the house or the cattle stalls—to cause barrenness in both women and animals. They even claim the very earth and ashes of these snakes continue to have the power of enchantments <note>original: "fascinations"</note>. Because of this, they advise all men to occasionally dig away the earth under their thresholds and sprinkle holy water in that spot. They also suggest hanging branches (blessed on Midsummer Day) at the stall doors where the cattle stay. They provide examples of this based on the lies of witches or perhaps their own lies, which I will omit because I see my book is growing larger than I intended it to be.

The author argues these "miracles" are actually the result of natural tricks, such as defanging snakes or using protective ointments on the skin.</summary>

### CHAPTER XVI.

*Charms to carry water in a sieve; to know what is spoken of us behind our backs; for bleary eyes; to make seeds grow well; regarding images made of wax; how to be rid of a witch and how to hang her up; notable authorities against waxen images; and a story revealing the trickery of waxen images.*

<margin>
Leonardus Vairus, *On Fascination*, book 1, chapter 5.
A Tuscan Vestal prayer. <note>original: "Oratio Tusca vestalis"</note>
</margin>
Leonardus Vairus says that there was a prayer in existence by which water or other liquids could be carried in a sieve. I believe it was actually "clam clay" <note>original: "clam clay"; likely meaning sticky or moist clay used to plug the holes</note>, which a crow taught a maid. She was promised a cake of such a great size that it would require as much flour as she could wet with the water she brought in a sieve. By using the clay to seal the holes, she brought in enough water to get a huge cake, and so she tricked her sisters, and so on. I heard this tale among my grandmother’s maids, and by it, I can explain this "witchcraft." Similarly, by the tingling of the ear, men in the past believed they could tell what was being spoken of them. If anyone sees a scorpion and says the word "Bud," he shall not be stung or bitten by it. <margin>Regarding the word "Bud" and the Greek letters Π and Α.</margin> These two Greek letters, Pi (Π) and Alpha (Α), written on paper and hung around one's neck, preserve the person from bleary eyes <note>original: "bleereyedness"; an inflammation or redness of the eyes</note>. Cumin or hempseed sown while using curses and insulting words supposedly grows faster and better. *Berosus Anianus* claims witchcraft is of great antiquity; for he says that Ham <note>original: "Cham"</note>, touching his father's nakedness, uttered a charm by which his father became emasculated or deprived of his generative powers.

---

### *A charm teaching how to hurt whom you wish with images of wax, etc.*

Make an image in the name of the person you would hurt or kill, using new virgin wax <note>wax that has never been used for any other purpose</note>. Under the right armpit place a swallow's heart, and the liver under the left. Then hang around its neck a new thread in a new needle, pricked into the body part which you would have hurt, while reciting certain words. These words are omitted here to avoid encouraging foolish superstition and gullibility; if they were included, I guarantee they would do no harm, except to make people fools and deceive the simple-minded <note>original: "catch Gudgeons"</note>. In other cases, these images are sometimes made of brass, and then the hand is placed where the foot should be, and the foot where the hand, with the face turned downward. Alternatively, for a greater mischief, a similar image is made in the form of a man or woman, upon whose head is written the specific name of the person; and on his or her ribs these words: *Ailif, casyl, zaze, hit, mel meltat*. Then the image must be buried.

Alternatively, under the influence of Mars, two images must be prepared: one of wax, the other of the earth from a dead man's grave. <margin>The practitioner of these charms must have skill in planetary motions, or else he is just wasting his time. <note>original: "go shoo the Goose"; a common idiom for a fruitless or foolish task.</note></margin> Each image must have in its hand a sword with which a man has been killed, and the one who is to be slain must have his head thrust through with a "foin" <note>a thrusting strike with a weapon</note>. In both images, certain peculiar characters must be written, and then they must be hidden in a specific place. In another case, to obtain a woman's love, an image of the beloved must be made in the hour of Venus using virgin wax. A character is written on it, and it is warmed by a fire; while doing this, the name of some angel must be mentioned. 

To be utterly rid of a witch and to hang her up by the hair, you must prepare an image from the earth of a dead man and "baptize" it in another man's name. The name, along with a magical character, must be written on it. Then it must be perfumed with a rotten bone, and then these Psalms must be read backward: *O Lord, our Lord* <note>original: "Domine Dominus noster"</note>, *The Lord is my light* <note>original: "Dominus illuminatio mea"</note>, *O Lord, hear my prayer* <note>original: "Domine exaudi orationem meam"</note>, and *O God, do not be silent regarding my praise* <note>original: "Deus laudem meam ne tacueris"</note>. Finally, bury it, first in one place and afterwards in another. 

However, it is written in the twenty-first article of the *Determination of Paris* <note>A famous theological ruling against magic issued by the University of Paris in 1398</note> that to claim that images of brass, lead, gold, or of white or red wax—or of any other material—when conjured, baptized, consecrated, or rather cursed through these magical arts on certain days, have wonderful virtues or the powers claimed in these books, is an error in faith, natural philosophy, and true astronomy. But concerning these images, it is certain that they are much feared among the people and much used among cheating <note>original: "cousening"</note> witches, as partly appears elsewhere in this discourse of mine, and as you may see by the contents of the following story. Not long since, a young maiden (dwelling at New Romney here in Kent), being the daughter of one Mr. L. Stuppeny (late Jurat <term>Jurat</term> <note>a municipal officer or magistrate in certain English towns, similar to an alderman</note> of the same town, but dead before this event) and afterward the wife of Thomas Eps (who is at this moment the Mayor of Romney), was visited with sickness. Her mother and father-in-law, being misled by a belief in a witch's supernatural power, went to a famous witch called Mother Baker, who lived not far from there at a place called Stone Street. 

According to the cheating custom of witches, she asked whether they did not suspect some bad neighbor. They answered that indeed they doubted a woman near them (and yet this same woman was considered a good person by the more honest and wiser sort of her neighbors). Nevertheless, the witch told them that there was great cause for their suspicion: "For that person," she said, "is the very party that caused the maiden’s destruction by making a heart of wax and pricking it with pins and needles." She also claimed that this neighbor had hidden the heart in some secret corner of the house. 

This being believed, the house was searched by reliable people, but nothing could be found. When the witch or "wise woman" was told of this, she stuck to her claim and insisted on going to the house herself where she (as she claimed) would certainly find it. When she arrived, she used her cunning, as it happened, to her own downfall, or at least to her detection. For she did exactly what some of the wiser people suspected she would: she secretly laid down such an image as she had described before in a corner which had already been most diligently searched and looked into by others. By this means, her cheating was clearly revealed <note>original: "bewrayed"</note>. 

And I wish that all those who promote belief in witches might pay for their wicked resort to enchanters, their consultation with witches, and those who have familiar spirits, as some of these people did—specifically by the order of the High Commissioners <note>The Court of High Commission was the supreme ecclesiastical court in England</note>, which, partly out of respect for the neighborhood and partly for other considerations, I will leave unmentioned.

### Charms to find out a Thief.

<margin>O most wonderful virtue hidden in the letters of Saint Helen's holy Name!</margin>
**T**he method for finding a thief is this: turn your face to the East, and make a cross upon crystal with olive oil. Under the cross, write these two words: (*Saint Helen.*) Then a child who is innocent, and a chaste virgin born in true wedlock (not born out of wedlock), of the age of ten years, must take the crystal in their hand. Behind the child's back, kneeling on your knees, you must devoutly and reverently say this prayer three times: *I beseech you, my Lady Saint Helen, mother of King Constantine, who found the Cross whereon Christ died: by that holy devotion and discovery of the Cross, and by the same Cross, and by the joy which you felt at its finding, and by the love which you bear to your son Constantine, and by the great goodness which you always use, that you show me in this crystal whatever I ask or desire to know, Amen.* And when the child sees the angel in the crystal, ask whatever you wish, and the angel will provide the answer. *Take note* <note>original: *Memorandum*</note> that this must be done exactly at sunrise when the weather is fair and clear.

<margin>Cardanus, Book 16, Concerning the Variety of Things, Chapter 93.</margin>
*Cardanus* <note>Girolamo Cardano (1501–1576), a famous Italian polymath and physician</note> mocks these and similar fables, and sets down his judgment accordingly in the sixteenth book of *Concerning the Variety of Things*. These conjurers and cheats <note>original: "coseners"</note>, forsooth, claim they will show you the thief who has stolen anything from you in a glass, and this is their procedure: they take a glass vial full of holy water and set it upon a linen cloth which has been purified, not only by washing, but by ritual sacrifice, etc. On the mouth of the vial or urinal <note>a glass vessel used for medical examination</note>, two olive leaves must be laid across each other, while a short conjuration is spoken over it by a child, specifically: "Good angel, bright angel, by your holiness and my virginity, show me the thief" <note>original Latin: *Angele bone, Angele candide, per tuam sanctitatem, meamq; virginitatem, ostende mihi furem*</note>. This is accompanied by three *Our Fathers*, three *Hail Marys*, and between each of them, a cross is made with the thumbnail upon the mouth of the vial. Then, they claim, angels shall be seen ascending and descending like motes of dust in the sunbeams.

<margin>* For if the Cross be forgotten, the whole thing is worthless <note>original: "not worth a pudding"</note>.</margin>
The thief, all this while, shall suffer great torments, and his face shall be seen plainly—as plainly, I believe, as the Man in the Moon. For in truth, there are tricks <note>original: "toyes"</note> cleverly hidden in the glass which will make the water bubble, and devices to make images appear in the bubbles. There are also optical glasses <note>early lenses or prisms</note> which will show many images of various forms to anyone who looks into them, and...

->Another way to find a thief who has stolen anything from you.<-

Go to the seaside and gather as many pebbles as there are persons you suspect in the matter; carry them home, throw them into the fire, and bury them under the threshold where the parties are likely to walk over. Let them lie there for three days, and then, before sunrise, take them away. Then, set a bowl <note>original: "Porrenger"</note> full of water inside a circle, in which must be drawn crosses in every direction, as many as can fit in it. Upon these must be written: "Christ overcomes, Christ reigns, Christ commands." The bowl must also be marked with a cross, and a form of conjuration must be pronounced. Then, each stone must be thrown into the water in the name of the suspected person. When you put in the stone belonging to the one who is guilty, the stone will make the water boil as though glowing-hot iron were placed in it. This is a mere sleight of hand trick, and can be accomplished in several ways.

->To put out the thief's eye.<-

Read the seven Penitential Psalms with the Litany, and then a terrible prayer to Christ and God the Father must be said, including a curse against the thief. Then, in the middle of your footprint on the ground where you stand, draw a circle like an eye and write certain strange <note>original: "barbarous"</note> names around it. With a cooper’s hammer or an adze <term>adze: a tool similar to an axe with a curved blade used for shaping wood</term>, drive a consecrated bronze nail into the middle of it, saying, "You are righteous, O Lord, and your judgments are just" <note>original: *Justus es Domine, & justa judicia tua* (Psalm 119:137)</note>. Then the thief shall be revealed by his crying out.

->Another way to find out a thief.<-

<margin>These are mere toys to mock fools <note>original: "Apes"</note>, and contain no worthy invention.</margin>Stick a pair of shears into the rim <note>original: "rind"</note> of a sieve, and let two persons set the tip of each of their forefingers upon the upper part of the shears, holding it with the sieve suspended steadily above the ground. Ask Saint Peter and Saint Paul whether A, B, or C has stolen the lost item; at the naming of the guilty person, the sieve will spin around. This is a common practice in all countries, and is indeed a mere trifle <note>original: "bable"</note>. For some cause of that motion arises from the beating of the pulse, another from the slight movement of the fingers, and another by the wind caught in the sieve, etc., at the pleasure of the holders. Another cause may be the imagination, which, upon the thought at the naming of the person, alters the common rhythm of the pulse. This can be easily understood by the example of a ring held steadily by a thread between the finger and thumb over (or rather inside) a goblet or glass; within a short time, it will strike against the side as many times as the holder thinks the hour of the clock is, and then it will stop. Whoever tries this will find it to be true.

->A charm to find or punish a thief.<-

Regarding this matter of catching thieves through words, I will cite one charm called *Saint Adelbert's curse*. It is long enough to weary the reader, and its "substantial" content includes all the blasphemous speech and cursing permitted in the Church of Rome as an excommunication and enchantment.

# The Discovery of Witchcraft. Chapter XVII.

### Saint Adelbert’s Curse or Charm against Thieves.

**By** the authority of the Almighty Father, the Son, and the Holy Ghost, and by the holy Virgin Mary, Mother of our Lord Jesus Christ, and the holy Angels and Archangels, and Saint *Michael*, and Saint *John* the Baptist, and on behalf of Saint *Peter* the Apostle, and the rest of the Apostles, and of Saint *Stephen*, and of all the Martyrs, of Saint *Sylvester*, and of Saint *Adelbert*, and all the Confessors, and Saint *Alegand*, and all the holy Virgins, and of all the Saints in Heaven and Earth, unto whom there is given power to bind and loose: we do excommunicate, damn, curse, and bind with the knots and bands of Excommunication; and we do separate from the boundaries and limits of our holy Mother the Church, all those thieves, sacrilegious persons, predatory thieves <note>original: "ravenous Catchers"</note>, doers, counselors, assistants, male or female, who have committed this theft or mischief, <margin>This is not doing good to our enemies, nor praying for those who hurt and hate us, as Christ encourages.</margin> or have seized any part of it for their own use. Let their share be with *Dathan* and *Abiram* <note>Biblical figures who were swallowed by the earth after rebelling against Moses.</note>, whom the Earth swallowed up for their sins and pride, and let them have a part with *Judas* who betrayed Christ, *Amen*: and with Pontius *Pilate*, and with those who said to the Lord, *Depart from us, we will not understand your ways*; let their children be made orphans. Cursed be they in the field, in the grove, in the woods, in their houses, barns, chambers, and beds; and cursed be they in the court, on the way, in the town, in the castle, in the water, in the church, in the churchyard, in the place of judgment, in battle, in their home, in the marketplace, in their talk, in silence, in eating, in watching, in sleeping, in drinking, in feeling, in sitting, in kneeling, in standing, in lying, in idleness, in all their work, in their body and soul, in their five wits <note>The "five wits" refers to the five senses: sight, hearing, smell, taste, and touch.</note>, and in every place. Cursed be the fruit of their wombs, and cursed be the fruit of their lands, and cursed be all that they have. Cursed be their navels, their spleens, their bladders. Cursed be their thighs, their legs, their feet, their toes, their necks, their shoulders. Also, in some countries, they nail a wolf’s head to the door. 

Also, they hang *Scilla* (which is either a root or, more likely in this context, garlic) from the roof of the house to keep away witches and spirits; they do the same with *Alicium* <note>likely *Allium*, another variety of garlic or onion</note> as well.

Also, Apuleius <note>A 2nd-century Roman writer and philosopher</note> says that Mercury gave to Ulysses, when he approached the enchantress Circe, an herb called *Verbascum*, which in English is called mullein, *tapsus barbatus*, or lungwort; and that herb preserved him from her enchantments. 

Also, both Pliny and Homer say that the herb called *Moly* is an excellent herb against enchantments, and they all agree that Ulysses escaped Circe’s sorceries and enchantments because of it. Likewise, people went to work in various ways in these cases; some used this defensive measure, and others used that preservative against incantations.

## Book XII. The Discovery of Charms, etc.

<margin>Olaus the Goth, *Description of the Northern Peoples*, Book 3, Chapter 8.</margin>Furthermore, wasn't it the custom or superstition of the Catholics <note>original: "Papists"</note> during storms <note>original: "Tempests"</note> to ring their bells against devils? They trusted more in the clanging of their bells than in their own prayers to God with fasting and prayer—the tools assigned by Him for all troubles and dangers. This followed the tradition of the *Thracian Priests*, who would roar and cry out with all the noise they could make during those storms. *Olaus Gothus* says that his countrymen would shoot into the air to help their gods, whom they believed were then fighting <note>original: "together by the ears"</note> with others; they even had consecrated arrows called *Arrows of Jupiter* <note>original: *Sagittæ Joviales*</note>, just as our Catholics had. Also, instead of bells, they had great hammers called *Hammers of Jupiter* <note>original: *Mallei Joviales*</note> to make a noise during thunder. In some countries, people run out of their houses during a storm, blessing themselves with a cheese marked with a cross made by a rope's end on *Ascension Day*. Also, throwing three hailstones into a fire during a storm, followed by saying three *Our Fathers* <note>original: *Pater Nosters*</note>, three *Hail Marys* <note>original: *Aves*</note>, the *Gospel of Saint John*, and "In the end, let the storm flee" <note>original: *In fine fugiat Tempestas*</note>, is considered an instant remedy. *Furthermore*, hanging an egg laid on *Ascension Day* from the roof of the house preserves it from all harm. <margin>* A witch's conjuration to make hail cease and dissolve.</margin> *Furthermore, I conjure you, hail and wind, by the five wounds of Christ, by the three nails which pierced His hands and His feet, and by the four Evangelists—Matthew, Mark, Luke, and John—that you come down dissolved into water.* *Furthermore*, it has been a common practice during storms to carry out the Sacraments and relics, etc. *Furthermore*, the Catholic Church uses excommunication as a primary charm against storms and many dumb animals. ->Cures started and completed by Witchcraft.<-

<margin>See Johann Weyer <note>original: *J. Wier.*</note>, chapter 11, compare. The surgeon here most shamelessly begins his trickery.</margin>
There was a bold fellow who took it upon himself to be a notable surgeon <term>Chirurgion</term> in the Duchy of Mainz <note>original: *Mentz*</note> in 1567. A gentleman named Elibert, who had been tormented with sickness, went to him wearing a kerchief on his head, according to the custom of sick people. But the surgeon made him pull off his kerchief and commanded him to drink with him freely. The sick man said he dared not, for he was forbidden by physicians to do so. "Nonsense," said this "cunning man," "they do not know your disease; be ruled by me, and take your drink heartily." For he thought that when the man was well-intoxicated, he might more easily deceive <term>beguile</term> him in his bargain and make his reward greater, which he was to receive in part beforehand. When they had drunk well, he called the sick man aside and told him the greatness and danger of his disease, and how it grew by means of witchcraft. He said it would be universally spread in his house and among all his livestock if it were not prevented, and he shamelessly persuaded the sick man to receive a cure from him. 

After the bargain was made, he asked the sick man whether he had anyone at home whom he might certainly trust. The sick man answered that he had a daughter and a servant. The con artist <term>Cousener</term> asked how old his daughter was. The patient said twenty. "Well," said the con artist, "that is fit for our purpose." Then he made the mother and father kneel on their knees to their daughter and desire her to obey the physician in all things, and that she would do everything as he commanded her; otherwise, her father could not be restored to his health. Out of respect for this, her parents humbly begged her on their knees to do so. 

Then he assigned her to bring to his lodging her father’s hair, and her mother’s, and the hair of all those whom he kept in his house—both men and women—as well as that of his cattle. When she came to him with it, according to the deal made and her parents' commandment, he led her down into a low parlor where, after having made a long speech, he opened a book that lay on the table <note>original: *boord*</note> and laid two knives across it with many elaborate words. <margin>A pretended ritual of conjuration.</margin> Then he performed a conjuration and made strange characters, and at length he made a circle on the ground, in which he caused her to stick one of those conjured knives; after many more strange words, he made her stick the other knife beside it. Then the maid fell down in a swoon from fear, so that he was forced to rub <term>frote</term> her and put a piece of bread soaked in wine <term>sop</term> into her mouth; after receiving it, she was deeply troubled and amazed. Then he made her uncover her breasts so that when they were bare, he toyed with them in various ways for a long time. Then he made her lie face upward, all uncovered and bare below her breasts. In this, the maid was loath to obey him; she resisted and, out of shame, forbade that villainy. Then the knave said, "Your father's destruction is at hand; for unless you will be ruled, he and all..."

### Another Witchcraft or Knavery practiced by the same Surgeon <term>Chirurgion</term>.

<margin>Three morsels: the first charmed with Christ's Birth, the second with his Passion, the third with his Resurrection.</margin>
This surgeon treated a nobleman who lay sick with a fever <term>Ague</term>, offering him three pieces of a root to be eaten in three morsels. He said to the first, "I wish Christ had not been born"; to the second, "I wish he had not suffered"; to the third, "I wish he had not risen again." Then, putting them around the sick man's neck, he said, "Be of good cheer; and if he loses them, whoever picks them up shall also take away his fever." Otherwise:

> Jesus Christ who was born, deliver you from this infirmity ✠ Jesus Christ who died ✠ deliver you from this infirmity ✠ Jesus Christ who rose again ✠ deliver you from this infirmity.

Then, five "Our Fathers" <note>original: *Paater nosters*</note> and five "Hail Marys" <note>original: *Aves*</note> must be said daily.

### Another Experiment for one bewitched.

<margin>A swindling physician and a foolish patient.</margin>
Another such swindling physician persuaded a man who had a swollen belly <term>Timpany</term> that there was one old viper and two young ones kept in his belly by witchcraft. But the physician was watched so that he could not secretly place vipers into the man's waste or excrement after his purges. At length, he told the party that he would suffer the pains of childbirth if it were not prevented, and therefore he must put his hand into his buttocks <note>original: "Breech"</note> and pull out those worms there. But the mother of the sick party, having been warned of this, said she could do that herself. So the swindler was stopped, the patient died only of the swelling, and the rogue fled the country.

### Otherwise.

<margin>Jean Bodin <note>original: *Joh. Bodin.*</note>. Misguided imitation <note>original: *Kacozelia* – a term Bodin used for the devil's "evil imitation" of divine miracles.</note></margin>
Monsieur Bodin <note>Jean Bodin, a famous French jurist and demonologist</note> tells of a witch who, undertaking to cure a woman bewitched, had a Mass sung at midnight in our Lady's Chapel. When she had lain upon the sick party and breathed certain words upon her, the woman was healed. In this, Bodin says she followed the example of Elisha the prophet, who raised the Shunammite's son. This story must surely be true; for Goodman Hardivin Blefensis, his host at the Sign of the Lion, told him the story.

</margin>
It is also helpful to learn how to know whether a sick man is bewitched or not; this is the practice used for it. You must hold molten lead over the sick person's body and pour it into a porringer <note>a small bowl</note> full of water. If any image appears upon the lead, you may know the person is bewitched.

### CHAPTER 19.

->*That one act of witchcraft may lawfully counter another.*<-

<margin>
*Duns Scotus in Book 4, distinction 34, concerning authority.*
</margin>
Duns Scotus, Hostiensis, Geoffrey, and all the old canon lawyers agree that it is lawful to remove witchcraft with witchcraft, and to "crush vanities with vanities" <note>original: *Et vana vanis contundere*</note>. And Scotus says it would be folly to refrain from countering witchcraft with witchcraft, for (he says) there can be no inconvenience in it, because the one who overthrows the witchcraft does not agree with the works of the Devil. Therefore, he says further that it is meritorious to extinguish and overthrow the Devil's works in this way. It is as if he were saying it does not matter even though Saint Paul says, "You shall not do evil that good may come of it" <note>original: *Non facies malum ut inde veniat bonum*</note>.

<margin>
*Distinction 4.*
*Geoffrey in his Summary.*
</margin>
Lambert says that witchcraft may be removed by the same means by which it was brought. But Geoffrey argues strongly against those who oppose this. Pope Nicholas V gave permission and leave to Bishop Miraties (who was so bewitched in his private parts that he could not perform the act of <term>Venery: sexual intercourse</term>) to seek a remedy from witches. This was the clause of his dispensation: "that of two evils, the greater should be avoided" <note>original: *Ut ex duobus malis fugiatur majus*</note>. And so a witch, by taking the Bishop's doublet <note>a man's close-fitting jacket</note>, cured him and killed the other witch—or so says the story, which can be seen in the *Malleus Maleficarum* and various other writers.

---

### CHAPTER 20.

->*Who are exempt from witches; what bodies are most susceptible to being bewitched, or becoming witches; why women are witches more often than men, and what they are.*<-

<margin>
*Malleus Maleficarum, part 2, question 1, chapter 1.*
</margin>
Now, if you want to know which persons are exempt from witches, you must understand that they are those who cannot be bewitched. Among their number, first, are the Inquisitors and those who carry out public justice upon witches. <margin>* See more on this in a little printed book.</margin> However, a Justice of the Peace in Essex (whom for various reasons I have left unnamed) not long ago thought he was bewitched at the very moment he examined a witch, so that his leg was broken because of it, etc. This was either false, or else this rule is untrue, or—more likely—both ideas are harmful to God's providence. Secondly, those who duly observe the rites and ceremonies of the holy Church and worship them with reverence—through the sprinkling of holy water, receiving consecrated salt, the lawful use of candles hallowed on Candlemas Day, and green leaves consecrated on Palm Sunday (which things they say the Church uses for limiting the Devil's power)—are preserved from witchcraft. Thirdly, some are preserved by their good angels, who attend and wait upon them.

<margin>
*Leonardo Vairo, book on fascination, Book 1, chapter 12.*
</margin>
But I must not omit here the reasons they bring to prove which bodies are more susceptible and effective at practicing the art of <term>fascination: the "evil eye" or the power to harm by looking</term>. First, they say it is the force of celestial bodies, which impartially communicate their virtues to men, beasts, trees, stones, etc. But this gift and natural influence of fascination may be increased in a man according to his emotions and disturbances, such as anger, fear, love, hate, etc. For through hate (says Vairo), a fiery inflammation enters the eye of man, which being...

And finally he says that all beautiful things whatsoever are quickly subject to being bewitched; namely, handsome young men, fair women, those naturally born to be rich, fine beasts, beautiful horses, lush corn, beautiful trees, etc. Indeed, a friend of his told him that he saw someone break a precious stone into pieces just with their eye. And he tells all of this as seriously as if it were true. If it were true, honest women could be witches despite all the Inquisitors; nor could anyone avoid being a witch unless she locked herself in a room.

### CHAPTER XXI.

->*What miracles "witchmongers" <note>Scot's term for those who believe in and promote the persecution of witches.</note> report to have been done by witches' words, etc. Contradictions among witchmongers themselves; how animals are cured by this; concerning bewitched butter; a charm against witches and a counter-charm; the effects of charms and words proved by Leonardo Vairus to be wonderful.*<-

If I were to try to recite all charms, I would be undertaking an infinite task. For the writers who believe in witchcraft hold the opinion that almost anything can be achieved through them; and they believe it does not matter <note>original: "it skilleth not"</note> whether the words of the charm are understandable or not, as long as the charmer has a steady intention to bring their desire about. And then, what is it that cannot be done by words? <margin>Leonardo Vairus, *On Charms*, Book 1, chapter 5.</margin> For Leonardo Vairus says that old women have weakened and killed children with words, and have made pregnant women miscarry; they have made men waste away to death; they have killed horses and deprived sheep of their milk; <margin>* According to Ovid's saying of Proteus and Medea, which he indeed cites for this reason: "Now water, now a bird, now an ox, now a deer he went away" <note>original: *Nunc aqua, nunc ales, modo bos, modo cervus abibat.*</note></margin> transformed men into beasts, flown in the air, tamed and stopped wild beasts, driven all harmful <note>original: "noisome"</note> cattle and vermin from corn, vines, and herbs, stopped serpents, etc.—and all with words. 

He even claims that with certain words spoken in a bull's ear by a witch, the bull has fallen down to the ground as if dead. Indeed, some by the power of words have walked upon a sharp sword and walked upon hot, glowing coals without being hurt. With words (he says) very heavy weights and burdens have been lifted; and with words wild horses, wild bulls, and also mad dogs have been tamed. With words they have killed worms and other vermine, and stopped all manner of bleeding and discharges <note>original: "fluxes"</note>. With words all the diseases in the human body are healed and wounds cured; arrows are pulled out of men's bones with wonderful strangeness and skill. Yes (he says), there are many who can heal all dog bites, or snake stings, or any other poison—and all with nothing but spoken words. And that

In this regard, by the way, I must not omit this special note given by the *Malleus Maleficarum*: namely, that holy water may not be sprinkled upon bewitched beasts, but must be poured into their mouths. And yet he and also Nider say that it is lawful to bless and sanctify beasts as well as men, both by written charms and also by holy words spoken. For (says Nider) if your cow <note>original: "Kine"</note> is bewitched, three crosses, three *Our Fathers* <note>original: "Pater-nosters"</note>, and three *Hail Marys* <note>original: "Aves"</note> will certainly cure her, as will all other church ceremonies. And this is a certain maxim: that those who are delivered from witchcraft by confession <note>original: "shrift"</note> are ever after much molested in the night (I believe by their spiritual fathers). Also, they lose money out of their purses and caskets, as the *Malleus Maleficarum* says he knows by experience. 

Also, one general rule is given by the *Malleus Maleficarum* to all butter-sellers <note>original: "Butter-wives"</note> and dairy maids: that they neither give nor lend any butter, milk, or cheese to any witches, who always make a habit of begging for them when they mean to work mischief upon your cows or dairy products <note>original: "white-meats"</note>. 

In reality, there are three substances mixed together in milk: namely butter, cheese, and whey. If it is kept too long, or in an unsuitable place, or is handled slovenly so that it becomes stale and sour—which happens sometimes in the winter, but more often in the summer—when it is over the fire, the cheese and butter run together and congeal. It will then become stringy like birdlime <note>A sticky substance traditionally used to catch birds on branches.</note>, so that you may wind it about a stick, and in a short time it will be so dry that you may beat it into powder. This change, being strange, is wondered at and blamed on witches. 

And from this sometimes comes the reason why butter does not form <note>original: "cometh not"</note>. When the country people see that it does not form, they then obtain a little butter from the suspected witch's house, from which three balls must be made in the name of the Holy Trinity. If these are put into the churn <note>original: "Chern"</note>, the butter will immediately form and the witchcraft will cease; *thus trickery is deceived by trickery* <note>original: "Sic ars deluditur arte"</note>. But if you put a little sugar or soap into the churn among the cream, the butter will never form, which is plain witchcraft if it is handled secretly, skillfully, and privately. There are twenty different ways to make your butter form, which I omit for the sake of brevity—such as binding your churn with a rope, or thrusting a red-hot spit <note>A metal rod used for roasting meat.</note> into it, etc. But your best remedy and surest way is to look well to your dairy-maid or wife, to ensure she neither eats up the cream nor sells away your butter.

->*A Charm to find the woman who bewitched your cows.*<-

Put a pair of trousers <note>original: "Breeches"</note> upon the cow's head, and beat her out of the pasture with a good stick <note>original: "Cudgel"</note> upon a Friday; she will run straight to the witch's door and strike at it with her horns.

->*Another charm for those who have bewitched any kind of cattle.*<-

<margin>
A ridiculous charm.
</margin>
When any of your cattle are killed by witchcraft, hurry to the place where the carcass lies and drag <note>original: "trail"</note> the bowels of the beast to your house. Do not pull them in through the door, but under the threshold of the house into the kitchen. There, make a fire and set a gridiron over it, and lay the innards or the bowels upon it. As they grow hot, so shall the witch's entrails be tormented with extreme heat and pain. But you must then lock your doors, lest the witch come and take away a coal from your fire; for if she does, her torments will cease. ->A special charm to preserve all cattle from witchcraft.<-

<margin>In any case, observe the festival time, or else you spoil everything.</margin>
At Easter, you must take certain drops that lie uppermost on the holy Paschal candle and make a little wax candle from them. On some Sunday morning early <note>original: "rathe"</note>, light it and hold it so that it may drop upon and between the horns and ears of the beast, saying, "In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the double Holy Spirit" <note>original: "In Nomine Patris, & Filii, & duplex ss."</note>. Then, burn the beast a little between the horns or on the ears with the same wax. Whatever wax is left, stick it in the shape of a cross around the stable or stall, or upon the threshold, or over the door where the cattle go in and out. For that entire year, your cattle shall never be bewitched. Otherwise, Jacob of Chusa, a Carthusian monk, shows how bread, water, and salt are conjured. He says that if either man or beast receives holy bread and holy water for nine days together—along with three *Our Fathers* <note>original: "Pater-nosters"</note> and three *Hail Marys* <note>original: "Aves"</note> in honor of the Trinity and of Saint Hubert <note>The patron saint of hunters and protection against rabies.</note>—it preserves that man or beast from all diseases and defends them against all assaults of witchcraft, of Satan, or of a mad dog, etc.

Look, this is their stuff, maintained to be at least effective, if not wholesome, by all Catholics <note>original: "Papists"</note> and <term>witchmongers</term> <note>Those who promote or profit from the fear of witches.</note>, and especially by the most recent and arrogant writers. But to prove these things to be effective, God knows their reasons are base and absurd. For they write as if they take the matter in question for granted, and by that means, they think they have proven it. <margin>Leonardus Vairus, *On Fascination*, Book 1, chapter 1.</margin> For Leonardus Vairus says at the beginning of his book that there is no doubt about this supernatural matter because a number of writers agree on it, and a number of stories confirm it, and many poets handle the same argument. Furthermore, he argues it is true because in the Twelve Tables <note>The earliest code of Roman laws.</note> there is a law against it; because the consent of the common people is fully behind it; because immoderate praise is to be considered a kind of witchcraft; because old women have such charms and superstitious means to preserve themselves from it; because those who dismiss the credit of such miracles are mocked; and because <margin>Wisdom 4, Galatians 3, Psalm 119.</margin> Solomon says, "The bewitching of wickedness obscures things that are good" <note>original: "Fascinatio malignitatis obscurat bona" (Wisdom of Solomon 4:12).</note>; and because the Apostle says, "O foolish Galatians, who has bewitched you?" <note>original: "O insensati Galatæ, quis vos fascinavit?" (Galatians 3:1).</note>; and because it is written, "They that fear you will see me" <note>original: "Qui timent te, videbunt me" (Psalm 119:74).</note>. Finally, he says—lest you should seem to distrust or take anything away from the credit of so many grave men, from histories, and the common opinion of all men—he intends in no way to prove that there is miraculous working by witchcraft and <term>fascination</term> <note>The act of bewitching through the gaze or words.</note>; and he proceeds accordingly, as he promised.

## CHAPTER XXIII.

->*A Refutation of the power and virtue falsely attributed to Charms and Amulets, by the Authorities of ancient Writers, both Divines and Physicians.*<-

My meaning is not that these words, in their bare letter, can do anything toward your ease or comfort in this matter, or that it would be wholesome for your body or soul to wear them about your neck. For if that were the case, I would wish you to wear the whole Bible, which must certainly be more effective than any single part of it. But I do not find that the Apostles, or any of them in the Primitive Church, ever carried St. John’s Gospel or any *Agnus Dei* <note>original: "Agnus Dei"—a wax medallion blessed by the Pope, often used as a protective amulet.</note> about them so that they might be preserved from "bugs" <term>In this context, "bugs" refers to bugbears, bogies, or terrifying spirits, rather than insects.</term>; neither did they look into the four corners of the house, or on the roof, or under the threshold to find evidence of witchcraft and then burn it to be freed from the same, according to the Popish <note>A derogatory term for Roman Catholic practices.</note> rules. <margin>Malleus Maleficarum, part 2, question 2, chapter 6.</margin> Neither did they seek to obtain grace through specific verses or prayers made to Saints at particular hours; nor did they speak of any old women who practiced such trades. Neither did Christ at any time use or command holy water or crosses, etc., to be used as terrors against the Devil, who was not afraid to assault Christ himself when He was on Earth. And therefore, it is a very vain thing to think that the Devil fears these trifles or any external matter. Let us then cast away these profane and "old wives' fables." For (as Origen <note>An influential early Christian scholar and theologian (c. 184–253 AD).</note> says) *Incantations are the mockeries of demons and the torch of idolatry;* <note>original: "Incantationes sunt Dæmonum irrisiones, idololatriæ fax"</note>

O notable sentence from a Heathen philosopher!

## CHAPTER 1.

->The meaning of the Hebrew word *Hartumim*, where it is found written in the Scriptures, and how it is translated in various ways: by which the objection regarding Pharaoh's magicians is later answered in this book; also concerning Natural Magic, which is not evil in itself.<-

Jerome <note>original: "Hieronymus"</note> on Genesis 41:8, 24. On Exodus 7:13. On Daniel 1:20.
</margin>
*Hartumim* <term>Hartumim: A Hebrew word likely derived from Egyptian, used in the Bible to describe the magicians or sacred scribes of Pharaoh's court.</term> is not a native Hebrew word, but is borrowed from some other nation. However, it is used by the Hebrews in these places: specifically, Genesis 41:8, 24; Exodus 7:13, 24 and 8:7, 18 and 9:11; Daniel 1:20 and 2:2. Jerome sometimes translates it as *interpreters of dreams* <note>original: "Conjectores"</note>, sometimes *evildoers* <note>original: "Malefici"</note>, and sometimes *soothsayers* <note>original: "Arioli"</note>; which we, for the most part, translate by the word *witches*. But the right meaning of this may be understood by the fact that the enchanters of Pharaoh, being magicians of Egypt, were called *Hartumim*. And yet in Exodus, they are named in some Latin translations as *poisoners* or *sorcerers* <note>original: "Venefici"</note>. Rabbi Levi says it signifies those who do strange and wonderful things through natural means, artifice, and deceit. Rabbi Isaac Natar affirms that such people were so named because they claimed singular wisdom among the Gentiles. Aben Ezra explains it to mean those who know the secrets of Nature and the qualities of stones and herbs, etc., which is attained by skill, and especially by Natural Magic. But we, either for lack of vocabulary or knowledge, call them all by the name and term of *witches*.

<margin>
The author’s intention regarding the subject to be discussed hereafter.
</margin>
Certainly, God endows physical bodies with wonderful graces, the perfect knowledge of which man has not reached. On the one hand, there is among them such mutual attraction, association, and harmony; and on the other hand, such natural conflict and hidden hostility, that many things are performed that astonish human capacity. But when deceit and diabolical words are coupled with these things, then it extends to witchcraft and conjuration, as those natural effects are falsely attributed to them. So, here I shall have some occasion to say something about Natural Magic <term>Natural Magic: A historical term for what we might now call experimental science or chemistry; the study of the hidden properties of natural things (like magnets or medicinal herbs) without involving spirits.</term>, because under it lies hidden the "poison" of this word *Hartumim*. This art is said by some to be the depth and the very absolute perfection of natural philosophy, demonstrating the active part of it. Through the aid of natural virtues and by the appropriate application of them, works are made public that exceed all capacity and admiration—and yet, these are done not so much by art as by nature. This art in itself is not evil, for it consists in searching out the nature, causes, and effects of things. As far as I can see, it has been more corrupted and profaned by us Christians than by either Jews or Gentiles.

<summary>This page analyzes the Hebrew word "Hartumim," used to describe Pharaoh's magicians, arguing that it originally referred to practitioners of natural science or "Natural Magic" rather than demonic witchcraft. The author suggests that many "miracles" are actually natural phenomena that are misunderstood or falsely attributed to the devil.</summary>
