<header>Book 12. The Discovery of Natural Magic.</header>

## CHAPTER 2.

### *How the philosophers in times past traveled for the knowledge of Natural Magic; concerning Solomon's knowledge of it; who is to be called a Natural Magician; a distinction between types of magic, and why it is condemned as witchcraft.*

<margin>Wisdom of Solomon 7:17–21.</margin>
<margin>See Fidoni. <note>likely a reference to a specific commentator or text, possibly Fincelius or a similar author.</note></margin>
<margin>Ecclesiastes 7:25.</margin>
Many philosophers, namely *Plato*, *Pythagoras*, *Empedocles*, *Democritus*, and others, traveled all over the world to find and learn the knowledge of this art; upon their return, they preached, taught, practiced, and published it. Indeed, it appears from the Wise Men <note>original: "Magicians"</note> who came to adore Christ that the knowledge and reputation of this art was greater than we currently realize or value. But of all people, *Solomon* was the greatest traveler in this art, as may be seen throughout the Book of *Ecclesiastes*, and especially in the Book of *Wisdom*, where he says: *God has given me the true science of things, so that I know how the world was made, and the power of the elements; the beginning, the end, and the middle of times; how the times alter and the seasons change; the course of the year and the position of the stars; the nature of living things and the fury of beasts; the power of the wind and the thoughts of men; the diversities of plants and the virtues of roots; and all things both secret and known,* etc. Finally, he was so skilled in this art that he is said to have been a conjurer or a witch, and is still considered so in the Roman Catholic <note>original: "Romish"</note> Church today. By this, you may see how fools and Papists <note>a derogatory term for Roman Catholics</note> are inclined to believe false accusations in matters of witchcraft and conjuration. The less knowledge we have of this art, the more we hold it in contempt. In this respect, *Plato* spoke truly to *Dionysius* when he said, "They make a mockery of philosophy who deliver it to profane and unrefined people." Certainly, the witchcraft, conjuration, and enchantment attributed to *Solomon* is gathered from these following words of his: *I applied my mind to knowledge, and to search and seek out science, wisdom, and understanding; to know the foolishness of the ungodly, and the error of doting fools.* In this art of Natural Magic (unless great care is taken), a student will soon be deceived. For many—writing from reports without actual experience—mistake their authors and record one thing for another. Then, when the conclusion is found to be false, the experiment falls into contempt and eventually seems ridiculous, even if it was actually true. *Pliny* and *Albert* <note>Albertus Magnus, a 13th-century philosopher and scientist</note>, being inquisitive writers on this subject, are often deceived; to the point that *Pliny* is called a "noble liar" and *Albert* a "rustic liar"—the one lying by hearsay, the other by relying on faulty authorities.

<margin>A Magician described and the Art distinguished.</margin>
A "Magician" is indeed what the Romans <note>original: "Latines"</note> call a wise man, just as *Numa Pompilius* <note>the legendary second king of Rome, known for his wisdom and religious laws</note> was among the Romans; the Greeks called such a person a "Philosopher," as *Socrates* was among them; the Egyptians called him a "Priest," as *Hermes* <note>Hermes Trismegistus</note> was; and the *Cabalists* <note>practitioners of Jewish mysticism</note> called them "Prophets." But although these people distinguished between types of this art—viewing one part as infamous because it was too devoted to wicked, vain, and impious curiosity (such as movements, numbers, figures, sounds, voices, tunes, lights, mental states, and words) and the other parts as commendable (as they taught many good and necessary things, like the times and seasons to sow, plant, till, and cut, and various other things which I will explain to you later)—we generally condemn the whole art without distinction as a form of witchcraft. We have learned to hate it before we even know it, claiming that everything is witchcraft if our dull minds <note>original: "gross heads"</note> cannot understand it; yet we are willing to believe that an old, senile woman can master it. In this, we fail to consider how God bestows His gifts and has established an order in His works, embedding various virtues in them for the comfort of His creatures, and especially for the use and benefit of mankind. Neither do we consider that Art is the servant of Nature, waiting upon her as her handmaid.

<summary>The author argues that "Natural Magic" is actually a form of ancient science and philosophy practiced by figures like Solomon and Plato, and laments that it is often unfairly condemned as witchcraft due to ignorance.</summary>

### CHAPTER 3.

#### *What secrets lie hidden, and what is taught in natural magic; how God's glory is magnified by it, and that it is nothing but the work of nature.*

<margin>Read Pliny’s *Natural History*; Cardan’s *On the Variety of Things*; Albertus Magnus’s *On the Secret Properties of Things*; Giambattista della Porta of Naples’s *Natural Magic*; and many others.</margin>
In this art of natural magic, Almighty God has hidden many secret mysteries, through which a man may learn the properties, qualities, and knowledge of all nature. For it teaches how to accomplish things with such timing and opportunity that common people think it is miraculous, and believe it can be achieved no other way than by witchcraft. Yet in truth, natural magic is nothing else but the work of nature. For just as in farming, nature produces corn and herbs, so art—being nature's servant—prepares them. In this, times and seasons must be greatly respected, for "it is the year, not the field, that produces the harvest." <note>original Latin: "Annus, non arvus producit aristas."</note>

<margin>Natural magic has a double purpose, which proves its excellence.</margin>
But while many necessary and serious things are taught here, it also partly consists of experiments and conclusions that are merely toys; nevertheless, these lie hidden in nature, and being unknown, they seem miraculous—especially when they are mixed and corrupted with clever illusions or sleight of hand <term>original: "Legierdemain"</term>, from which the reputation of witchcraft is derived. But once they are learned and known, they are looked down upon and appear ridiculous. For a thing is only wonderful to the viewer when he cannot understand its cause or reason, according to the saying of Ephesius, "A miracle is explained by the very thing that makes it seem like a miracle." <note>original Latin: "Miraculum solvitur unde videtur esse miraculum."</note> Therefore, a man might take great pains and spend much money to learn something of no value—a mere juggling trick. Because of this, it is said that a man should not learn philosophy to become rich, but must gain riches to learn philosophy; for the secrets of nature are never opened to lazy people, misers, or fools <note>original: "sluggards, niggards, and dizzards"</note>. Undoubtedly, a man may gather from this art things that, when published, shall demonstrate the glory of God and be beneficial to the public in many ways. The first is done by revealing His works; the second, by skillfully applying them to our use and service.

---

### CHAPTER 4.

#### *What strange things are brought to pass by natural magic.*

<margin>Pomponazzi’s *Book on Incantations*, chapter 3; Johann Weyer’s *On Demons*; Caspar Peucer; Gerolamo Cardan; etc.</margin>
The daily use and practice of medicine takes away all wonder at its amazing effects. Many other things of less importance, being more secret and rare, seem more miraculous. For example—if it is true what Giambattista della Porta <note>original: "I. Bap. Neap." refers to Giambattista della Porta of Naples, author of "Magia Naturalis."</note> and many other writers constantly affirm—if you tie a wild bull to a fig tree, he will immediately become tame; or if you hang an old rooster on it, its meat will immediately become tender. Likewise, the feathers of an eagle consume all other feathers if they are mixed together. In these cases, it cannot be denied that nature shows herself to be a capable craftswoman. But it seems impossible that a little fish only half a foot long, called a *Remora* or *Remiligo* (or by some an *Echenis* <note>The remora or suckerfish was anciently believed to have the power to stop ships in their tracks by clinging to the hull.</note>), could stop a mighty ship with all its cargo and rigging even while under sail. And yet it is affirmed by so many serious authors that I dare not deny it—especially because I see other equally strange effects of nature: such as the properties of the lodestone <note>A naturally magnetized mineral (magnetite) used in compasses.</note>, which is so beneficial to the sailor; and of rhubarb, which only affects yellow bile <note>original: "choler." In the ancient medical theory of the four humors, rhubarb was believed to specifically purge yellow bile without affecting phlegm or black bile.</note> and purges neither phlegm nor melancholy, and is as beneficial to the physician as the magnet is to the sailor.

<summary>This page argues that natural magic is a legitimate branch of science that studies the hidden properties of nature to glorify God and benefit society, distinguishing it from the illusions of witchcraft. It cites various classical and contemporary authors to provide examples of nature's "miraculous" yet natural powers, such as magnets and the medicinal properties of plants.</summary>

<header>166 BOOK 13. The Discovery of the Operations of Waters.</header>

### CHAP. V.

->*The incredible power of waters, both standing and running; of wells, lakes, rivers, and their wonderful effects.*<-

<margin>From recent experience near Coventry, etc.</margin>
<margin>Aristotle in *History of Animals*.</margin>
<margin>Pliny on the color of wool.</margin>
The power of waters and their various properties are also incredible. I do not mean prepared or distilled waters; for it would be endless to discuss their powers, especially regarding medicines. But even here in England, we have natural springs, wells, and waters—both standing and running—of excellent properties. If we had not seen them and experienced them ourselves, we would not believe they existed in nature <note>original Latin: *rerum natura*</note>. And setting aside their physical nature (for which we cannot be as thankful to God as they are healthy for our bodies), is it not miraculous that wood is transformed into stone <term>petrifaction</term> by the quality of various waters here in England? This same power is also found in a lake near the city of Mazaca <note>modern-day Kayseri</note> in Cappadocia. There is a river called Scamander <note>original: "Scarmandrus"</note> that turns sheep yellow. Indeed, there are many waters—as in Pontus, Thessaly, and the land of Assyria, and in a river of Thrace (as Aristotle says)—where, if a white sheep that is pregnant drinks from it, the lamb will be black. Strabo writes of the river called Crathis <note>original: "Crantes"</note> on the borders of Italy, running toward Taranto <note>original: "Tarentum"</note>, where men's hair is turned white or yellow when washed in it. Pliny writes that whatever color the veins are under a ram's tongue, the lambs will be that same color or colors. There is a lake in a field called Cornetus where, at the bottom, the carcasses of snakes, newts <note>original: "Ewts"</note>, and other serpents clearly appear to the eye; however, if you reach in your hand to pull them out, you will find nothing there. Water drips out of a rock in Arcadia which neither a silver nor a bronze bowl <note>original: "boll"</note> can hold, but instead it leaps out and splashes away; yet it will remain motionless in the hoof of a mule. Such results (I assure you) were not unknown to Jannes and Jambres <note>Jannes and Jambres were the Egyptian magicians who opposed Moses in the Book of Exodus</note>.

---

### CHAP. VI.

->*The powers and qualities of various precious stones; of deceptive jewelers <term>original: "cousening Lapidaries"</term>, etc.*<-

<margin>Ludovicus Coelius Rhodiginus, *Ancient Readings*, book 11, chapter 70.</margin>
<margin>Bartholomaeus Anglicus, book 16.</margin>
<margin>* Avicenna, *Canon*, book 2, section 2, chapter 124. Serapion, chapter 100. Dioscorides, book 5, chapter 93.</margin>
The excellent powers and qualities of stones, discovered, understood, and tested by this art, are wonderful. However, many completely false and legendary things are added to their true effects. I thought it good to partially test the reader's patience and skill with these. An agate <note>original: "Aggat"</note> (they say) has power against the bites of scorpions or serpents. It is written (though I will not swear by it) that it makes a man eloquent and wins the favor of princes; even that its smoke <note>original: "fume"</note> turns away storms. *Alectorius* is a stone about the size of a bean, as clear as crystal, taken from the stomach of a cock that has been castrated <term>original: "gelt"</term> or made a capon for four years. If it is held in the mouth, it relieves thirst; it makes a husband love his wife and makes the wearer invincible—for it was said that Milo <note>Milo of Croton, a famous ancient Greek wrestler</note> used this to overcome his enemies. A *Cram-pock* <note>likely a "cramp-stone," used as a charm against illness or misfortune</note> delivers one from prison. *Chelidonius* is a stone taken out of a swallow which cures melancholy. However, some authors say it is the herb <note>celandine</note> with which swallows restore the sight of their young, even if their eyes have been poked out with a tool. *Geranites* is taken from a crane, and *Draconites* from a dragon. But it should be noted that such stones must be taken out of the bellies of the serpents, beasts, or birds while they are still alive; otherwise, they vanish along with the life, and so they retain the powers of the stars they were born under. Amethyst <note>original: "Amethystus"</note> makes a drunk man sober and refreshes the wit. Coral preserves those who carry it from fascination <term>the "evil eye" or a hypnotic spell</term> or bewitching, and for this reason, they are hung around children's necks. But where that superstition...

# The Discovery of Witchcraft. CHAPTER VI.

Where this tradition originated and who invented the lie, I do not know; but I see how people are inclined to believe it by the sheer number of **corals** that were used. I find in reputable authors that while it remains in the sea, it is a plant-like stone, and when it is brought out into the air, it hardens and turns the color of blood. They say it drives away poisons and preserves health; indeed, some write that it provokes rain and darkens the sun, protecting the wearer from being deceived. **Hyacinth** <note>original: "Hyacinthus"; likely referring to zircon or a blue sapphire</note> does all that the other does and also protects against lightning. **Oinothera** <note>a plant or stone legendary for taming wild beasts</note> hung about the neck, collar, or yoke, [tames beasts] instantly. A **Topaz** heals a person suffering from madness <term>lunatic</term>. An **Eagle-stone** <term>Aetites</term> rattles as if there were a little stone inside its belly; it is good for treating epilepsy <term>Falling-sickness</term> and for preventing premature birth.

**Amethyst**, as mentioned before, resists drunkenness, so that those wearing it shall be able to drink freely and recover quickly even if they are as "drunk as apes"; it is also said to make a man wise. **Chalcedony** makes the wearer lucky in legal disputes, quickens the body's energy, and is also effective against the illusions of the Devil and fanciful thoughts arising from melancholy.

<margin>Pliny, Book 37, Chapter 10.
Albertus, Book 2, Chapter 7.
Solinus, Chapter 32.</margin>

**Carnelian** <note>original: "Corneolus"</note> calms the heat of the mind and softens malice; it stops "bloody fluxes" <term>hemorrhages</term>, especially for women troubled by their menstrual cycles <term>flowers</term>. **Heliotrope** <note>Bloodstone</note>, as mentioned before, darkens the sun, brings on showers, stops bleeding, earns the wearer a good reputation, keeps them in health, and prevents them from being deceived. If this were true, one of these would be worth more than a thousand diamonds. **Hyacinth** delivers one from the danger of lightning, drives away poison and plague-like infections, and has many other virtues. **Iris** <note>likely Iris quartz</note> helps a woman with a speedy childbirth and causes rainbows to appear. A **Sapphire** preserves the limbs and makes them lively; it helps with fevers <term>Agues</term> and Gout, and prevents the wearer from being afraid. It has power against venom and stops nosebleeds if applied frequently.

<margin>* Rabbi Moses' Aphorisms, part 22. Isidore, Book 14, Chapter 3. Savonarola.</margin>

An **Emerald** <note>original: "Smaragd"</note> is good for the eyesight and discourages sexual desire <term>carnal copulation</term>; it makes one rich and eloquent. A **Topaz** increases wealth, heals bouts of madness, and stops bleeding. **Mephis** (as Aaron and Hermes report, cited from Albertus Magnus), when ground into powder and drunk with water, makes a person insensitive to torture.

By this you may understand that just as God has bestowed most excellent and wonderful virtues upon these stones and similar natural objects, human superstition and folly have led many to ascribe even more virtues to them—or different ones than they actually possess. Others boast that they can add new qualities to them. In this lies a part of witchcraft and the common deception <term>couzenage</term> used sometimes by jewelers <term>Lapidaries</term> for profit, and sometimes by others for deceitful purposes. I will describe some of this vanity here because it fits well with the subject. And it should not be forgotten or omitted that Pharaoh's magicians were likely quite skilled in these arts.

Nevertheless, I will first give you the opinion of one who claimed to be a very skillful and experienced jeweler, as appears in a book of his own writing, published under the title *Dactylotheca* <note>meaning "The Cabinet of Rings" or a treatise on gems</note>, which I believe is available from booksellers. His assertion follows:

<margin>Marbod of Rennes [Marbodeus Gallus] in his *Dactylotheca*, page 56.</margin>

# BOOK XIII. The Discovery of Precious Stones.

->Translated into English by Abraham Fleming:<-

<margin>The power of gems and precious little stones is denied because it is hidden and very rarely is perceived by the senses. <note>original: "Vis gemmarum & lapillorum preciosorum negatur, quia occulta est, rarissimeque sub sensum cadit."</note></margin>

Evax, an ancient Arabian King,
is said to have written
A treatise, and to have bestowed it
upon the grace of Nero,
(Who was the second to reign in the world
after the time of Augustus),
Regarding the various types of precious stones,
their names, and in what climate
And country they were to be found,
their colors and their appearance,
Their private power and secret force,
which, with true knowledge,
Reveals their hidden causes
through very clear effects.
And we consider this
a noble and rare thing,
That the skillful care of learned physicians <term>original: "leeches"; an old term for doctors</term>

<column-break/>

is aided in this matter,
And are thereby helped and taught
with the aid of stones to drive
Away from men the illnesses
that afflict them.
No less specific benefits
of all other things are also
Administered and given to men,
if the authors are not lying,
To whom these things are said to be
most clearly known.
It will not appear as a false
or doubtful case to anyone,
But that by heavenly influence,
every precious pearl and stone
Has a fixed power and virtue
deeply embedded in its substance.

From this it can be concluded that stones possess certain specific virtues, which are granted to them by a special influence of the planets and a proper proportion of the elements. Their substance is a very fine and pure compound consisting of well-balanced matter without any coarse mixtures. This is proven in India and Ethiopia, where the sun—being in the east <note>original: "orient"</note> and at its zenith <note>original: "meridional"</note>—shows its power more effectively, causing more precious stones to be created there than in western <note>original: "Occident"</note> or northern <note>original: "Septentrional"</note> countries.

<margin>Many more authors of no less antiquity and learning may be named.</margin>

Several ancients agree with this opinion; specifically, Alexander the Peripatetic <note>original: "Alexander Peripateticus"</note>, Hermes, Evax, Bocchos, Zoroaster, Isaac the Jew <note>original: "Isaac Judaeus"</note>, Zacharias of Babylon <note>original: "Zacharias Babylonicus"</note>, and many others besides.

---

### CHAP. VII.

->How precious stones receive their powers; how inquisitive <term>original: "curious"</term> magicians use them, and concerning their seals.<-

<margin>Pliny, book 37, chapter 10. Albertus Magnus, book 2, chapter 1. Solinus, chapter 11. Dionysius in the cabinet, the chapter on temperaments and tempered things. <note>original: "Plin. lib. 37. cap. 10. Albert. minor. lib. 2. cap. 1. Solin. cap. 11. Diurius in scrin. cap. de complexionibus & complexatis."</note></margin>

Inquisitive magicians claim that these stones receive their powers entirely from the planets and heavenly bodies. They possess not only the specific actions of the planets but sometimes the very images and impressions of the stars naturally engraved within them. Otherwise, they should always have engraved upon them the likenesses of such monsters, beasts, and other designs as the magicians imagine to be both internal in operation and external in appearance, as expressed in the planets.

For example, on an **Agate** <note>original: "Achate"</note> are engraved serpents or venomous beasts—and sometimes a man riding a serpent. They know this figure to be **Aesculapius**, which is the celestial serpent constellation; by this, they say, poisons and the stings of serpents and scorpions are cured. These stones grow in the River Achates, where the largest scorpions are bred, and their harmfulness is neutralized there; through the power of the scorpions, the stone's virtue is awakened and increased.

Furthermore, if they wish to induce love for the fulfillment of sexual desire <term>original: "Venery"</term>, they engrave and depict on the stones loving embraces, charming faces, gestures, words, and kisses in suitable figures. For the desires of the mind are in harmony with the nature of the stones, which must also be set in rings and upon foils made of metals that have an affinity with those stones through the influence of the planets they are associated with. In this way, they may gather greater power for their work.

# Hartumim <note>original: "Hartumim"; a Hebrew term for the Egyptian "sacred scribes" or magicians</note> of Witchcraft. CHAPTER VII.

Georgius Pictorius of Villingen, Doctor of Medicine, in his commentaries on Marbod’s *Dactylotheca* <note>original: "dactyl."; Marbod of Rennes wrote a famous work on the properties of gems and rings called the *Dactylotheca*</note>.

As for example, they make the images of **Saturn** in lead, of the **Sun** <note>original: "Sol"</note> in gold, and of the **Moon** <note>original: "Luna"</note> in silver. Indeed, there is no small regard to be had for the certain and due times to be observed in the engraving of them; for in this way they are made with more life, and the influences and configurations of the planets are thereby made to abound in them more fully. As if you wish to procure love, you must work during suitable, proper, and friendly astrological aspects, such as in the hour of **Venus**, etc. To cause a debate, the direct contrary order is to be taken. If you determine to make the image of **Venus**, you must wait to be under **Aquarius** or **Capricorn**; for **Saturn**, **Taurus**, and **Libra** must be avoided. There are many other observations, such as avoiding the unlucky position <note>original: "feat"; likely meaning "seat" or astrological house</note> and place of the planets when you would bring a happy thing to pass, and especially that it be not done in the end, declination, or "heel" (as they term it) of its course; for then the planet mourns and is dull.

Such signs as ascend in the day must be taken in the day; if they increase in the night, then you must go to work by night, etc. For in **Aries**, **Leo**, and **Sagittarius** there is a certain "Triplicity" <term>triplicity: a group of three zodiac signs belonging to the same element</term>, wherein the Sun has dominion by day, **Jupiter** by night, and in the twilight the cold star of **Saturn**. But because there shall be no excuse lacking for the faults noticed in this, they say that the virtues of all stones decay through the passage of time, so that such results are not now to be expected in all respects as they are written. However, **Jannes** and **Jambres** <note>Jannes and Jambres were the traditional names of the Egyptian magicians who opposed Moses in the Book of Exodus</note> were living in that time, and in no inconvenient place; and therefore they were likely to have had that help toward the deceiving of **Pharaoh**.

Girolamo Cardano, *On the Variety of Things*, Book 16, Chapter 90.

### CHAPTER VIII.

->*The Sympathy and Antipathy of Natural and Elementary Bodies Declared by Various Examples of Beasts, Birds, Plants, etc.*<-

If I should write about the strange effects of sympathy <note>original: "Sympathia"</note> and antipathy <note>original: "Antipathia"</note>, I would take great pains to make you wonder, and yet you would hardly believe me. And if I should publish such conclusions as are common and known, you would not regard them. And yet Empedocles thought all things were brought about by this. It is almost incredible that the grunting or the squealing <note>original: "wheeking"</note> of a little pig, or the sight of a simple sheep, should terrify a mighty elephant; and yet by those means, the Romans put to flight Pyrrhus and his entire army <note>original: "Hoast"</note>. One would hardly believe that a rooster's <note>original: "his"</note> comb or his crowing should intimidate <note>original: "abash"</note> a powerful <note>original: "puissant"</note> lion; but the experience of this has satisfied the whole world. Who would think that a serpent would avoid the shadow of an ash tree? etc. But it does not seem strange, because it is common, that some men, otherwise hardy and strong enough, would not dare to stay in the presence of or endure the sight of a cat. Or that a swallow of drink should so overcome a man that no part or member of his body can perform its duty; and should also so corrupt and alter his senses, understanding, memory, and judgment that he becomes a literal beast in everything except his shape. <header>Magicians <note>original: "Hartumim," a Hebrew word for magicians or soothsayers</note>. Of Witchcraft. CHAPTER 9.</header>

<margin>Read a little tract by Erasmus titled *On Friendship* <note>original: "De amicitia"</note>, where enough is said regarding this point.</margin>
The friendly association between a fox and a serpent is almost incredible. How loving the lizard is to a man, we may read about even if we cannot see it. Yet some affirm that our newt is not only like the lizard in shape, but also in temperament. A spaniel does not differ much from this affection toward humans, of which I could cite incredible stories. The friendship <note>original: "Amity"</note> between a kestrel <note>original: "Castrel," a small hawk</note> and a pigeon is much noted among writers, and especially how the kestrel defends the pigeon from her enemy, the sparrow-hawk—an act of which they say the dove is not ignorant. Besides these, there is the wonderful operation and virtue of herbs, which would be infinite to repeat; therefore, I will only refer you to *Mattioli's* <note>original: "Mattheolus"</note> Herbal or to *Dodoens* <note>original: "Dodonaeus"</note>. There is among herbs such natural accord and discord that some prosper much better in another's company, while some wither away when planted near one another. The lily and the rose rejoice in each other's neighborhood. The iris <note>original: "Flag"</note> and the fern bush abhor each other so much that one can hardly live beside the other. The cucumber loves water and hates oil to the death. And so you shall not say that herbs have no virtue—since I cite none in this place—I am content to reveal two or three small qualities and virtues which are affirmed to be in herbs. Truly <note>original: "marry"</note>, simple as they may be, Jannes and Jambres <note>The biblical names for the Egyptian magicians who opposed Moses</note> might have done much with them if they had possessed them.

<margin>Xanthus in his first History, book 25, chapter 2.</margin>
If you prick out a young swallow’s eyes, the old swallow restores their sight again with the application (so they say) of a little celandine <note>A yellow-flowered herb in the poppy family</note>. *Xanthus*, the author of histories, reports that a young dragon that was dead was revived by her mother with an herb called Balim. And *Juba* <note>Juba II, a scholar-king of Numidia and Mauretania</note> says that a man in Arabia who was dead was revived by the virtue of another herb.

### CHAPTER 9.

->The former matter proven by many examples of the living and the dead.<-

<margin>Common experience can justify this.</margin>
As we see strange operations and natural love and dissension in stones, herbs, and so on, we also read that in the body of a man there are equally strange natural properties and virtues. But if the French King uses it no worse than our Princess <note>Queen Elizabeth I</note> does, God will not be offended by it; for her Majesty only uses godly and divine prayer, along with some alms, and refers the cure to God and to the physician.
<margin>Plutarch in the *Life of Cato*.</margin>

<header>BOOK 13. The Discovery of a Harlot's Poison.</header>

And Giambattista della Porta <note>original: "J. Bap. For many strange properties remain in specific parts of a living creature which are not spread universally through the whole body; just as the eye does not smell, the nose does not see, and the ear does not taste.

# CHAPTER 10.

->*The bewitching venom contained in the body of a harlot: how her eyes, her tongue, her beauty, and her behavior bewitch some men; and concerning bones and horns that possess great virtue.*<-

<margin>
The venom or poison of a harlot.
</margin>
The "virtue" <note>term: in this context, "virtue" means a specific power or inherent quality</note> contained within the body of a harlot—or rather the venom proceeding out of it—may be viewed with great wonder. For her eye infects, entices, and (if I may say so) bewitches those who often think themselves well-armed against such people. Her tongue, her gestures, her behavior, her beauty, and other allurements poison and intoxicate the mind. Indeed, her company encourages shamelessness, corrupts virginity, and ruins and consumes the bodies, goods, and very souls of men. Finally, her body destroys and rots the very flesh and bones of a man's body. Because this is common, we do not wonder at it at all; indeed, we do not hold the movement of the sun, the moon, or the stars in as much awe as we do a mechanical globe <note>original: "Globe," referring to an orrery or astronomical model</note> that mimics their order, which is in comparison but a bauble made by a craftsman. I think that if Christ himself had continued performing miracles for a long time, and had left that power permanently and commonly in the Church, those miracles would have fallen into contempt and would not have been valued, according to his own saying: "A prophet is not respected in his own country."
<margin>
Matthew 13.
Mark 6.
Luke 4.
John 4.
</margin>

I could recite infinite properties with which God has endowed the human body that are worthy of admiration and fitting for this discussion. Regarding other living creatures, God has likewise (for His glory and our benefit) bestowed most excellent and miraculous gifts and virtues upon their bodies and members, in various and wonderful ways.

<margin>
Wonderful natural effects in the bones of fish, beasts, etc.
</margin>
We see that a bone taken out of a carp's head stops bleeding, yet no other part of that fish does so. The bone in a hare's foot eases a cramp, though no other bone or part of the hare does. How precious is the bone growing out of the forehead of a unicorn—if the horn we see actually grows there, which is doubted—and of how little account are the rest of its bones! We do not marvel at such excellence, nor at the noble and innumerable virtues of herbs, because it has pleased God to make them common to us. This perhaps might have partly assisted Jannes and Jambres <note>These are the traditional names of the Egyptian magicians who opposed Moses</note> in the hardening of Pharaoh’s heart. Also see Marsilio Ficino, book 4, chapter 1; Girolamo Cardano's *On the Variety of Things*; Giambattista della Porta's *On Natural Magic*; and the works of Peucer, Weyer, Pomponazzi, Fernel, and others.

### CHAPTER II.

How the wicked practice of the spirit-speaker <note>original: "Pythonist"</note> of Westwell came to light, and by whom she was examined; and that all her diabolical speech was nothing but ventriloquism and plain deception <note>original: "cosenage"</note>, which is proved by her own confession.

<margin>Matthew 24:24</margin>
It is written, *“That in the latter days there shall be shown strange illusions, etc., so much so that (if it were possible) the very elect shall be deceived.”* Furthermore, Saint Paul says, *“There shall be lying and false wonders.”* Nevertheless, this sentence and others like it have been often thrown in my face <note>original: "laid in my dish"</note> and are urged by various writers to prove the miraculous workings of witches, which I will treat more largely in another place. However, in passing, I must confess that I take that sentence to be spoken of the Antichrist—namely, the Pope. The Pope—who miraculously, contrary to nature, philosophy, and all divinity, being of low birth and calling, coarse in learning, and in stature, beauty, or activity most commonly a very clumsy oaf <note>original: "lubber"</note>—has placed himself in the most lofty and delicate seat, putting the heads of almost all Christian princes not only under his belt <note>original: "girdle"</note>, but under his foot, etc.

Surely, the tragedy of this spirit-speaker <note>original: "Pythonist"</note> is not inferior to a thousand stories which will hardly be blotted out of the memory and belief of either the common people or the learned. How could this story possibly be discredited, having testimony of such authority? How could Mother Alice escape condemnation and hanging, being arraigned upon this evidence? For a poor woman might be cast away <note>meaning: executed</note> based on a deceptive <note>original: "cosening"</note> oracle, or rather a false lie devised by Feats the Juggler <note>a famous contemporary magician/conman</note> through the malicious instigation of some of her adversaries.

<margin>The ventriloquist <note>original: "Ventriloqua"</note> of Westwell discovered.</margin>

And yet many have been deeply deceived by it and can hardly be moved from believing it; indeed, they cannot endure to hear it reproved without great disdain. And you should know this in passing: that in the past, **Robin Goodfellow** and **Hobgoblin** were as terrible and as credible to the people as hags and witches are now. In time to come, a witch will be as much derided and condemned, and as plainly perceived, as the illusion and knavery of **Robin Goodfellow**. And in truth, those who maintain the existence of walking spirits, with their transformations, etc., have no reason to deny **Robin Goodfellow**, about whom there have been as many and as credible tales as about witches—except that it has not pleased the translators of the Bible to call spirits by the name of **Robin Goodfellow**, whereas they have termed diviners, soothsayers, poisoners <note>The OCR reads "prisoners," but the context of Bible translation refers to *veneficii* or poisoners/sorcerers</note>, and fraudsters <note>original: "coseners"</note> by the name of witches.

# Book VII. The Discovery: Ventriloquism <note>original: "Ventriloqua"</note>.

<margin>The medium <term>original: "Pythonist"</term> of Ivel convicted by her own confession.</margin>

But to make short work of disproving this deceitful <note>original: "bastardly queans"</note> enterprise and fraud, you shall understand that after the rumor of her divinity and miraculous trances, she was summoned before Mr. Thomas Wotton of Bocton Malherbe. He was a man of great status and wisdom, known for his rare and singular skill in deciding and ordering matters in this Commonwealth. Through his discreet handling of the matter, with the assistance and aid of Mr. George Darrel, Esq. (also a very good and discreet Justice of the same district), the fraud was discovered and the trickery confessed, and she received well-deserved <note>original: "condigne"</note> punishment. Her confession was not obtained according to the methods of the Spanish Inquisition—that is, through extreme torture—nor yet by guile, flattery, or mere assumptions. Instead, through a wise and perfect trial of every circumstance, the illusion was clearly revealed. It was not (I say) handled the way "witches" are commonly accused and condemned—which is through malicious accusations, guesses, presumptions, and forced confessions that go against common sense and possibility, for actions they can never prove nor demonstrate to wise men by any direct or indirect means. Rather, after her proper trial, she demonstrated her feats, illusions, and trances, along with the rest of all her "miraculous" works, in the presence of various gentlemen and gentlewomen of great status and credit at Bocton Malherbe, in the house of the said Mr. Wotton. Now, compare this girl with the Witch of Endor <note>The biblical medium of Endor whom King Saul consulted; the author argues her "miracles" were also just ventriloquism and fraud.</note>, and you shall see that both frauds may be performed by the same art.

->### CHAPTER III.<-
->*Bodin's nonsense <note>original: "flusfe" (fluff/nonsense)</note> concerning the medium of Endor, with a true story of a counterfeit Dutchman.*<-

<margin>7. Bodin, *On the Demon-mania of Witches*, book 3, chapter 2 <note>original: "lib. de dæmon. 3 cap. 2."</note>.</margin>

Upon similar tales, Jean Bodin <note>A famous French jurist and demonologist who argued for the reality of witchcraft.</note> built his doctrine, calling them "atheists" who will not believe him. He adds to this kind of witchcraft the miraculous works of various young women who would spit up <note>original: "spue"</note> pins, rags <note>original: "clowts"</note>, and so on—as Agnes Brigs and Rachel Pinder of London did, until their "miracles" were detected and they were sentenced to open penance. He cites others of that sort who were supposedly bound by devils with garters or similar materials to posts, using knots that could not be undone—which is actually an Egyptian <note>The author uses "Egyptian" here to refer to the tricks of Romani people or traveling entertainers, often called "jugglers" or "gypsies."</note> juggling or cheating trick. His whole book consists of such foolish lies joined with lewd tales; I guarantee you there are no fewer than two hundred fables and just as many impossibilities in it. And just as these two girls, along with the Maiden of Westwell, were caught in their fraud, so too a Dutchman at Maidstone was revealed to be a cheating rogue. This happened long after he had performed such knaveries to the astonishment of many good men; his "miracles" were even printed and published in London in the year 1572, with the following title on the book:

*A very wonderful and strange Miracle of God shown upon a Dutchman of the age of 23 years, who was possessed by ten Devils, and was by God’s mighty providence dispossessed of them again, on the 27th of January last past, 1572.*

The Mayor of Maidstone, along with several of his colleagues, signed off on this, chiefly because they were persuaded by Nicasius Vander-Sceure, the Minister of the Dutch Church there, and John Stikelbow, whom (as it is said there) God made the instrument to cast out the devils, along with four other credible members of the Dutch Church. The story is so strange and so skillfully performed that, had his own later villainy not brought him under suspicion, he would have gotten away with this fraud undetected. A great many other such "miracles" have been lately printed, several of which have been exposed; and undoubtedly all the rest would be as well, if they were put to a proper <meta>Catchword: trial</meta> trial.

# CHAPTER XIV.

## *Regarding Public Conspiracy, and What It Consists Of.*

**P**ublic conspiracy occurs when an agreement is made beforehand between various people; where one acts as the lead and the others as assistants to perform "miracles"—or rather, to swindle and deceive the audience. For example, I might tell you in front of a crowd what you have thought, what you have done, or what you will do, when you and I had already agreed upon those details earlier. If this is handled cleverly and secretly, it will cause great amazement among the spectators—especially when they have already been stunned and deceived by experiments in natural magic, mathematical tricks, or sleight of hand. Such were, for the most part, the performances and devices of *Feats* <note>likely referring to a contemporary juggler or performer named Feats</note>; in which, you can be certain, **Jannes** and **Jambres** <note>the traditional names for the Egyptian magicians who opposed Moses</note> were expert, active, and ready.

# CHAPTER XV.

## *How Men Have Been Deceived by Words of Double Meaning, with Various Examples.*

<margin>A joke among boatmen regarding Stone Church in Kent, claiming it is as "light" at midnight as at midday.</margin>
**S**ome have taught, and others have written down, certain experiments in which they used such words of double meaning <note>original: "Equivocation"</note> that many people have been tricked and deceived through their own hasty belief. Thus, as I have said, they have sometimes reported, taught, and written things according to how their own minds understood them, which was contrary to the truth and the actual meaning of the author. It is a common joke among the boatmen of the *Thames* to show the Parish Church of *Stone* to their passengers, calling it the "Lantern of *Kent*." They claim, and not untruly, that the church is as "light" (meaning in weight, not in brightness) at midnight as it is at noon. Because of this, some gullible people are made to believe—and will even insist and swear—that there is such a constant light in that church that a person could see to read there at any time of night without a candle.

A distinguished philosopher, whom (out of respect for his fame and learning) I will decline to name, was tricked by his hostess at *Dover*. She jokingly told him that if he could keep certain pebbles (found on the seashore) in his mouth, he would not vomit <note>original: "perbreak"</note> until he reached *Calais*, no matter how rough and stormy the seas were. When he tried this and was not forced by sickness to vomit—nor to lose his stones, as he certainly would have if he had vomited—he thought his hostess had revealed a great secret to him. He did not suspect her ambiguous <note>original: "amphibological"</note> speech. Therefore, he thought it a worthy observation to be recorded among miraculous and medicinal stones, and he inserted it into his book among other experiments collected with great industry, learning, travel, and judgment. All these trifles help a subtle swindler <note>original: "Cosener"</note> gain credit with the public. Indeed, to further their reputations, many will whisper prophecies of their own invention into the ears of those who are not the sharpest, such as predicting what the weather will be. <margin>A weak excuse to save their reputation for cleverness.</margin> If the prediction turns out to be true, they boast and triumph as if they had won a great victory. If it does not, they deny the matter, "forget" it, excuse it, or brush it off—claiming they told someone else the opposite in earnest and only said that one thing as a joke. *Pharaoh's* magicians could have used all these methods to maintain their deceptions and illusions, leading to the hardening of *Pharaoh's* heart.

To this category belong all kinds of charms, amulets <note>original: "Periapts"</note>, protective symbols, and other such superstitions, both Catholic and non-religious. If the things that Catholics, conjurers, or witches claim to do were actually true, we would daily see the very miracles that *Pharaoh’s* magicians only seemed to

# CHAPTER XVI.

->*How some are deceived by Natural Magic, and various examples of it when illusion is added; regarding Jacob’s spotted sheep, and a Black person.*<-

<margin>The danger of holding the opinion that whatever exceeds our understanding is divine, supernatural, etc.</margin>
But just as these notable and wonderful experiments and conclusions found in nature itself (through wisdom, learning, and hard work) greatly challenge and astonish the human mind, so (I say) when deceit and illusion are added to them, then the intellect, faith, and constancy of man are tested and tried. For if we grant that something is divine, supernatural, and miraculous simply because we cannot understand it, then a witch, a Catholic <note>original: "Papist"</note>, a conjurer, a swindler, and a juggler may make us believe they are gods. Otherwise, with even more impiety, we shall attribute such power and omnipotence to them—or to the Devil—as only and properly belongs to God. For example: by conspiracy or deception (as I have said before), I may seem to reveal the secret thoughts of the heart, which (as we learn in God's Book) no one knows or searches except God himself. Therefore, whoever believes that I can do what I only seem to do makes a god of me and is an idolater. In this respect, whenever we hear a Catholic, witch, conjurer, or swindler claim for themselves more than lies in human power to perform, we may know and boldly say it is a trick of dishonesty <note>original: "knack of Knavery"</note>, and no miracle at all. Furthermore, we may know that when we do understand it, it will not be worth knowing. And at the discovery of these "miraculous" toys, we shall stop wondering at them and begin to wonder at ourselves—that we could be so deceived by such trifles <note>original: "Bables" or baubles</note>. However, those things that God has hidden secretly in nature are to be weighed with great admiration and searched out with such industry as may befit a Christian: I mean, in a way that neither God nor our neighbor is offended, a respect which Jannes and Jambres certainly never had. We find in the Scriptures various natural and secret experiments practiced, such as that of Jacob using spotted sheep <note>Referring to Genesis 30, where Jacob influenced the coloring of his flocks</note>. These are confirmed by secular <note>original: "prophane"</note> authors and verified not only in lambs and sheep, but in horses, peacocks, rabbits <note>original: "Conies"</note>, etc. <margin>Giambattista della Porta of Naples in *Natural Magic* <note>original: "J. Bap Neapol. in natural. mag."</note></margin> We also read of a woman who gave birth to a Black child <note>original: "Black-Moor"</note> because an old Black man <note>original: "Black-Moor"</note> was in her house at the time of her conception, whom she gazed upon in her imagination <note>original: "fantasie"</note>, as is supposed. However, a jealous husband will not be satisfied with such imaginative fantasies; for in truth, a Black person <note>original: "Black-Moor"</note> never fails to beget Black children, regardless of what color the other parent is; and so conversely <note>original: "Et sic contra"</note>.

->C H A P T E R XVIII.<-

*How to produce or create monsters by the magical art, and why Pharaoh’s magicians could not create lice.*

<margin>Natural conclusions.</margin>
Strato, Democritus, Empedocles, and recently Giambattista della Porta of Naples teach the methods by which monsters may be produced from both beasts and birds. Aristotle himself teaches how to make a chicken have four legs and as many wings using only a double-yolked egg; by this same method, a serpent may be made to have many legs. Or anything that produces eggs can likewise be made double, or have members added or removed; the viler <note>meaning "lower" or "less complex" in the biological hierarchy of the time</note> the creature, the more quickly it is brought to monstrous deformity, whereas this is harder to achieve in more noble creatures. There are also <margin>How to produce any bird from an egg without the natural help of the hen.</margin> clever experiments involving an egg to produce any bird without the natural help of the hen. This is achieved if the egg is laid in the powder of dried hen's dung mixed with some of the hen's feathers and stirred every four hours. You may also produce (as they say) the most venomous, troublesome, and dangerous serpent called a cockatrice <term>cockatrice: a mythical serpent-like creature, often said to be born from a yolkless egg laid by a rooster and hatched by a toad</term> by melting a little arsenic and the poison of serpents, or some other strong venom, and drowning an egg in it for several days; the operation will be more successful if the egg is set upright. This may also be done if the egg is laid in dung, which of all things provides the most singular and natural heat; and as Giambattista della Porta says, it is *the mother of marvels* <note>original: "Mirabilium rerum parens"</note>. He also <margin>* The mother of marvels.</margin> writes that the hairs of a menstruating woman <note>original: "Crines fæminæ menstruosæ"</note> are turned into serpents within a short time; and he further says that basil, when beaten and placed in a moist spot between two tiles, engenders scorpions. The ashes of a duck, placed between two dishes and set in a moist spot, engenders a huge toad, which is also achieved by menstruous blood <note>original: "Quod etiam efficit sanguis menstruosus"</note>. Many writers conclude that there are <margin>Two kinds of toads: natural and temporary.</margin> two kinds of toads: one bred by the natural course and order of generation, and the other growing of themselves—called "temporary"—being engendered only by rain showers and dust. As Giambattista della Porta says, these are easy to make. Plutarch and Heraclides say they have seen these descend in the rain, crawling on the rooftops, etc. Also, Aelian says he saw frogs and toads whose heads and shoulders were alive and had become flesh, while the hind parts were still only earth; they crawled on two feet, the others not yet being fashioned or fully formed. And Macrobius reports that in Egypt, mice grow from earth and showers, as do frogs, toads, and serpents in other places. They say that Damnatus Hispanus could make them whenever and as many as he desired. He is <margin>Maggots generated from the internal organs of a beast are good for fishing.</margin> no good angler who does not know how quickly the entrails of a beast, when buried, will engender maggots (which in more polite terms are called "gentles" <term>gentles: a traditional term for maggots used as fishing bait</term>), which are a good bait for small fish. Whoever knows the method of preserving silkworms may see a similar conclusion, because in winter that is a dead seed which in summer is a living creature. Such and even greater experiments might have been known to Jannes and Jambres <note>The traditional names for the Pharaoh's magicians mentioned in 2 Timothy 3:8</note> and served their purpose well, especially with the excuses, delays, and cunning they could join with them. But to proceed and come a little closer to their feats, and to show you a trick <note>original: "knack"</note> beyond their cunning: I can assure you that from the fat of a man or a woman, lice are generated in a very short time; and yet I say Pharaoh's magicians could not make them with all the cunning they had. By this, you may perceive,

### CHAPTER XIX.

#### That great matters may be achieved by this art when princes value and support it; concerning various wonderful experiments, and strange conclusions using perspective glasses <note>early lenses and mirrors used for optical effects</note>, etc.

<margin>Wonderful experiments.</margin>
However, these are but trifles compared to other experiments of this kind, especially when great princes support and give encouragement to students of those magical arts. In these countries and in this age, such study is prohibited rather than allowed because of the frequent abuses coupled with it; yet it is truly these arts that arouse wonder and the high opinion of miraculous workings. For example, if I claim that with certain charms and Popish <note>a derogatory term for Roman Catholic</note> prayers I can set a horse's or an ass's head upon a man's shoulders, I will not be believed; or if I do it, I shall be thought a witch. And yet if the experiments of Giambattista della Porta <note>original: "J. Bap. Neap.," a famous Italian polymath and author of "Natural Magic"</note> are true, it is no difficult matter to make it seem so. A charm from a witch or a Papist joined with the experiment will also make the wonder seem to proceed from the charm. The words used in such cases are irrelevant and may be recited at the pleasure of the witch or cozener <note>a fraud or trickster</note>.

<margin>To set a horse’s or an ass’s head on a man’s neck and shoulders.</margin>
But the method for this is: cut off the head of a horse or an ass (before it dies, otherwise its power or strength will be less effective) and make an earthen vessel large enough to contain it. Fill the vessel with the animal's oil and fat, cover it closely, and coat it over with loam <note>a mixture of clay and straw</note>. Let it boil over a soft fire continually for three days, so that the boiled flesh turns into oil until the bare bones may be seen. Beat the hair into powder and mix it with the oil; then, anoint the heads of the bystanders, and they shall seem to have horses' or asses' heads. If the heads of beasts are anointed with similar oil made from a human head, they shall seem to have human faces, as various authors soberly affirm. If a lamp is anointed with this, everything shall seem most monstrous. It is also written that if that which is called *sperma* <note>original: "sperma," referring here to the reproductive seed or essential biological fluid</note> in any beast is burned, and any person's face is anointed with it, they shall seem to have the same face as that beast. But if you grind arsenic very fine and boil it with a little sulfur in a covered pot, and kindle it with a new candle, the bystanders will seem to be headless. *Aqua composita* <note>original: "Aqua composita," a strong alcoholic spirit or medicinal brandy</note> and salt being set on fire in the night, with all other lights extinguished, make the bystanders look like dead men. All these things might have been very well understood, known, and practiced by Jannes and Jambres <note>the traditional names of the Egyptian magicians who opposed Moses</note>.

<margin>Strange things to be done by perspective glasses.</margin>
But the wondrous devices, miraculous sights, and illusions created and contained in glass far exceed all others; for this, the art of perspective <note>the science of optics and lenses</note> is very necessary. It reveals the illusions of those whose experiments are seen in various sorts of glasses, such as: hollow <note>concave</note>, plain <note>flat</note>, embossed <note>convex</note>, columnar <note>cylindrical</note>, pyramidal or pointed <note>original: "pyramidate or piked"</note>, scroll-shaped <note>original: "turbinal"</note>, bulging <note>original: "bounched"</note>, round <note>spherical</note>, cornered <note>polygonal</note>, inverted, everted <note>turned outward</note>, solid <note>original: "massie"</note>, regular, irregular, colored, and clear glasses. For you may have glasses so made that whatever image or appearance you form in your imagination, you will think you see it within the glass. Others are so framed that one may see what others are doing in far-distant places; others through which you shall see men hanging in the air; others where you may perceive men flying in the air; others in which you may see one person coming and another going; others where one image shall seem to be a hundred, and so on. There are also glasses in which one man may see another man's...

### CHAPTER XX.
### A Comparison between Pharaoh's Magicians and our Witches, and how their Skill consisted in juggling tricks.

<margin>A monkey-like <term>apish</term> imitation by Jannes and Jambres in performing wonders.</margin>
<margin>John Calvin, *Institutes*, Book 1, Chapter 8. Clement, *Recognitions*, Book 3.</margin>
<margin>Thomas Erastus in his debate concerning witches.</margin>
<margin>Actions impossible for Devils: Therefore <note>original: "Ergo"</note> impossible for Witches, Conjurers, etc.</margin>
Thus you see that it has pleased God to show to men who seek knowledge such skill in finding out, compounding, and framing strange and secret things, that he seems to have bestowed upon man some part of his own Divinity. However, God (from nothing, by his Word) has created all things, and does at his will, beyond the power and also the reach of man, accomplish whatever he pleases. And such miracles in times past he performed by the hands of his Prophets, as he did here by Moses in the presence of Pharaoh, which Jannes and Jambres <note>traditionally the names of the Egyptian magicians who opposed Moses</note> imitated like monkeys. But to claim that they by themselves, or by all the Devils in Hell, could actually do as Moses did by the power of the Holy Ghost, is worse than having no faith at all. If anyone objects and says that our witches can do such feats with words and charms as Pharaoh's magicians did by their art, I deny it; and all the world will never be able to prove it. That which they did was done openly, whereas our witches and conjurers never do anything in the open; so these people cannot do as those magicians did. And yet (as Calvin says of them) they were nothing but jugglers <note>meaning sleight-of-hand performers or tricksters</note>. Neither could they do as many suppose. For as Clement says, "These magicians seemed to perform these wonders rather than actually working them." And if they only made deceptive <term>prestigious</term> shows of things, I say it was more than our witches can do. For witchcrafts (as Erastus himself confesses in the course of his argument) are but "old wives' tales." If the magicians' serpent had been a real serpent, it must have been transformed out of the rod. And that would have been a double work of God: namely, the ending of one substance and the creation of another. These are actions beyond the Devil's power, for he can neither make a body become no body, nor make no body become a body; just as he cannot make something into nothing, or nothing into something; and as for opposite things, he cannot make them one; indeed, they cannot make a single hair either white or black. If Pharaoh's magicians had made real frogs suddenly, why could they not drive them away again? If they could not harm the frogs, why should we think they could create them? Or that our witches—who cannot even successfully fake them—can kill cattle and other creatures with words or wishes? And there-

Therefore I say with Iamblichus, "The things we imagine when we are bewitched have no truth of action or essence at all, other than the imagination itself" <note>original Latin: *Quæ fascinati imaginamur, præter imaginamenta nullam habent actionis & essentiæ veritatem*</note>; Such things as we, being bewitched, imagine have no truth at all, either in action or essence, besides the bare imagination.

### CHAPTER 21.

->That the serpents and frogs were truly presented, and the water poisoned indeed by Jannes and Jambres <note>In Jewish and Christian tradition, these are the names given to the Egyptian magicians who opposed Moses</note>; of false prophets and of their miracles; of Balaam’s ass.<-

<margin>Pharaoh’s magicians were not masters of their own actions.</margin>
Truly, I think there would be no harm in admitting that the serpents and frogs were truly presented, and the water truly poisoned by Jannes and Jambres—not because they could perform such miracles by themselves, or through their familiar spirits or devils, but because God, using the hands of those counterfeit frauds <note>original: "coseners"—swindlers or tricksters</note>, overtook them against their own expectations. He compelled them, in their ridiculous wickedness, to be instruments of His will and vengeance upon their master, Pharaoh. Thus, by their hands, God showed some miracles which He Himself performed, as appears in the Book of Exodus.
<margin>Exodus 10. God uses the wicked as instruments to execute His counsels and judgments.</margin>
For God put the Spirit of Truth into Balaam's <note>A prophet mentioned in the Book of Numbers who was hired to curse the Israelites but was compelled by God to bless them instead</note> mouth, even though he was hired to curse His people. And although he was a corrupt and false prophet and engaged in a wicked plan, yet God made him an instrument (against his will) to the confusion of the wicked. If it pleased God to do this here as a special work to show His omnipotence and confirm His people's faith in the doctrine of their Messiah delivered to them by the prophet Moses, then it was miraculous and extraordinary, and not to be expected now. And (as some suppose) there was then a group or "crew" of false prophets who could also foretell things to come and work miracles. I answer that it was extraordinary and miraculous, and that it pleased God to test His people in that way; but He does not work in this manner these days, for the performing of miracles has ceased. Likewise, in this case, it might well serve God's glory to use the hands of Pharaoh's magicians to harden their master's heart, and to make their illusions and ridiculous notions become real effects.
<margin>The contrary effects that the miracles of the Egyptian magicians produced in the heart of Pharaoh.</margin>
For God had promised and determined to harden the heart of Pharaoh. As for the miracles that Moses performed, they softened <note>original: "mollified"</note> his heart so much that he always relented upon seeing them. To the greatness of Moses's miracles were added such modesty and patience as might have moved even a heart of steel or flint. But Pharaoh's stubbornness <note>original: "frowardness"</note> always increased because of the magicians' actions; we find no other example or resemblance of this in the Scriptures. And even though such people were permitted and used by God in those days to accomplish His will and secret purpose, it does not follow that now—when God's will is fully revealed to us in His Word, and His Son has been revealed (for whose sake, or rather for the manifestation of whose coming, all those things were permitted or performed)—such things and such people should still continue. Thus, I conclude that once the cause is removed, the result no longer remains. To claim that our modern witches and conjurers hold the same position as those biblical figures is to mock and despise God’s wonderful works, and to set against them mere trickery <note>original: "cosenages"</note>, juggling tricks, and worthless things. Therefore, just as they must confess that no one in these days can do as Moses did, it may also be answered that no one in these days can do as Jannes and Jambres did. If they had been false prophets instead of mere jugglers <note>In this period, "juggler" referred to a sleight-of-hand performer or stage magician</note>, they would have been even more privileged to surpass our old women or conjurers in performing miracles or prophesying, etc. For who can be compared with Balaam? Indeed, I dare say that Balaam’s ass performed a greater and more supernatural miracle than either the Pope or all the conjurers and witches in the world can do today.

To conclude, it can be affirmed (and there are clear enough proofs) that our jugglers come much closer to resembling Pharaoh’s magicians than

<margin>That the art of juggling is more, or at least no less, strange in performing miracles than conjuring, witchcraft, etc.</margin>
...either witches or conjurers, and make a more vivid display of performing miracles than any enchanters can do; for these jugglers practice showing in action what witches only do in words and terms. But so you do not think I have no reason for maintaining my opinion on this matter, I will stop using a multitude of words to elaborate on this topic. Instead, I refer you to the following treatise on the art of juggling, where you shall read of strange practices and skillful maneuvers. Because these cannot be easily described in speech so that they would immediately be understood by those of you who wish to practice them, I have caused them to be set forth in form and figure <note>This refers to the woodcut illustrations included in the original text to demonstrate tricks.</note>, so that your understanding might be helped by visual demonstrations. And when you have perused that whole revelation of juggling, compare the wonders there with the wonders attributed to conjurers and witches (not omitting Pharaoh's sorcerers by any means in this comparison). I believe you will then be convinced that the miracles done in Pharaoh’s sight by them, and the miracles ascribed to witches and conjurers, etc., may well be taken for false miracles, mere delusions, and such actions as are commonly practiced by skillful jugglers—whether by legerdemain <term>legerdemain: sleight of hand; literally "light of hand" from the French *léger de main*</term>, confederacy <note>original: "confederacy"—the use of hidden accomplices or assistants.</note>, or otherwise.

## CHAPTER 22.

### *The art of juggling revealed, and in what points it principally consists.*

<margin>In what ways juggling is acceptable and even commendable.</margin>
Now, because the opportunity is provided, and the matter is so relevant to my purpose—and also because the essence of witchcraft and trickery <note>original: "cozenage"—cheating or swindling</note> is so clearly shown in the art of juggling—I thought it good to reveal it along with the rest of the other deceitful arts. I am sorry that it falls to my lot to lay open the secrets of this mystery to the detriment of those poor men who live by it. Their actions in this regard are not only tolerable but greatly commendable, provided they do not abuse the name of God or make the people attribute His power to them. They should always acknowledge what their art actually consists of, so that other unlawful and impious arts may be more easily detected and exposed by them.

<margin>The three principal points in which legerdemain, or nimbleness of hand, consists.</margin>
The true art of juggling, therefore, consists in legerdemain; namely, the nimble movement of the hand, which is especially performed in three ways. The first and most important consists in hiding and moving balls; the second in the transformation of coins; the third in the shuffling of cards. He who is expert in these may provide much pleasure and many tricks, and possesses more skill than all other witches or magicians. All other parts of this art are taught as soon as they are revealed; but this specific part cannot be taught by any description or instruction without practice and the passage of time. And since I intend to reveal rather than teach these mysteries, it will be enough to inform you that the aim and purpose of jugglers is only to deceive people's eyes and judgments. Now, therefore, my meaning is to dissect, in words as plain as I can, certain specific tricks of that art. Some are pleasant and delightful, others are frightening and seemingly desperate, but all are nothing more than mere delusions or counterfeit actions, as you shall soon see by careful observation of every trick I describe hereafter.

# BOOK XIII. The Discovery of Sleight of Hand <note>original: "Juggling"</note> with Balls.

### CHAPTER XXIII.

### *Regarding the Ball, and the method of sleight of hand <note>original: "Legierdemain"</note> with it, as well as notable feats with one or several balls.*

<margin>Great variety of play with the balls, etc.</margin>
Concerning the ball, the games and tricks involving it are infinite, so much so that if you can handle them well through practice, you may perform a hundred feats with them. But whether you seem to throw the ball into your left hand, or into your mouth, or into a pot, or up into the air, etc., it is to be kept hidden in your right hand. If you practice first with a lead bullet, you shall perform it sooner and better with balls of cork. The first place to learn to position a large ball is in the palm of your hand, held with your ring finger; but a small ball is to be placed with your thumb between your ring finger and middle finger. Then you are to practice doing it between the other fingers, then between the forefinger and the thumb, or with the forefinger and middle finger together; this is where the greatest and most remarkable skill is shown.

<margin>These feats are to be performed nimbly, cleanly, and swiftly, so that the eyes of the onlookers cannot discern or perceive the trick.</margin>
Lastly, you should practice holding the same ball in the palm of your hand, and with use, you shall not only seem to throw any ball away while still retaining it in your hand, but you shall keep four or five as cleanly as one. Once this is mastered, you shall perform wonderful feats; for example:

Lay three or four balls before you, and as many small candlesticks, bowls, or salt-cellar covers (which are the best). Then first, seem to put one ball into your left hand, and at the same time seem to hold it fast. Then take one of the candlesticks, or any other object (having a hollow base and not being too large), and seem to put the ball, which is thought to be in your left hand, underneath it. In the same way, seem to place the other balls under the other candlesticks. All this while, the onlookers will suppose each ball is under each candlestick. Once this is done, some charm or formula of words is commonly used. Then take up one candlestick with one hand and blow on it, saying, "Look, you see that it is gone!" Similarly, look under each candlestick with the same style and words, and the
<margin>Remember that the juggler must maintain a good demeanor <note>original: "grace"</note> regarding the matter, for that is very necessary.</margin>
onlookers will wonder where they have gone. But if, in lifting up the candlesticks with your right hand, you leave all three or four balls under one of them (which you may easily do with practice by turning them all down with your hand and holding them fast with your little and ring fingers), and take the candlestick with your other fingers and cast the balls up into its hollow base (so they will not roll away so quickly), the bystander will be greatly astonished <note>original: "astonied"</note>. But it will seem wonderfully strange if, while showing how nothing remains under another of those candlesticks taken up with your left hand, you leave behind a large ball or any other object; the miracle will be even greater. For first, they think you have pulled away all the balls by magic; then, that you have brought them all together again by similar means; and they neither think nor expect that any other object remains behind under any of them. Therefore, after many other feats are done, return to your candlesticks, remembering where you left the large ball, and do not touch it yet. Instead, having another similar ball about you, seem to place it in the manner and form described above under a candlestick that stands furthest away from the one where the ball actually lies. And when you seem to move that ball from under that candlestick with words or charms, and afterward reveal it under the candlestick you haven't touched, it will (as I say) seem wonderfully strange.

Then use words to make them seem to swell, then open your hand, etc. This play is to be...

### To make one or many balls vanish into nothing.

**I**f you take one ball, or more, and pretend to put it into your other hand, while you use magical incantations <note>original: "charming words"</note>, you can slip them out of your right hand into your lap. This will seem strange, for when you open your left hand, the most observant onlookers will immediately say it is in your other hand. You may then open that hand as well; when they see nothing there, they are greatly deceived.

### How to tap a joker on the knuckles.

<margin>This trick is intended chiefly to cause laughter and amusement.</margin>
**B**ut I will stop speaking further about the ball, for I could keep you here all day with this, and yet I would hardly be able to teach you how to use it, nor would you scarcely understand what I mean or write about it. However, many people are certainly persuaded that the ball is a spirit or a "fly" <note>original: "Fly"; a term for a familiar spirit or a demon in the shape of an insect</note>, etc. *Note*, that the right hand must always be kept open and straight, only keeping the palm from view; therefore, you may end with this "miracle." Place one ball on your shoulder, another on your arm, and the third on the table. Because it is round and will not easily stay on the point of your knife, you must ask a bystander to lay it there. Tell him that you intend to throw all three balls into your mouth at once. While holding the knife like a pen in your hand, as he is laying the ball upon the point of your knife, you can easily and quickly tap him on the fingers—for the actual trick of catching the balls would be very difficult to do.

## CHAPTER XXIV.

### Of the Movement <note>original: "Conveyance"</note> of Money.

<margin>The money must not be too small or too large in circumference, or it will hinder the trick.</margin>
**T**he moving of money is not much inferior to the ball tricks, but it is much easier to do. The principal place to hide a piece of money is the palm of your hand. The best coin to use is a <term>tester</term> <note>original: "Testor"; a silver coin worth about sixpence</note>, but with practice, all coins will feel the same, unless the money is very small. In that case, it is to be kept between the fingers, almost at the fingertips, whereas the ball is to be kept lower, near the palm.

### To move money from one of your hands into the other by sleight of hand.

<margin>This is a clever trick if it is handled skillfully, for both the ear and the eye are deceived by this device.</margin>
**F**irst, you must hold your right hand open and lay a <term>tester</term> or some large piece of money in it. Then, place the tip of your long left finger upon it. Say some words, and suddenly jerk your right hand away from the finger you used to hold down the <term>tester</term>. By curving your hand just a little, you will retain the <term>tester</term> inside it. Suddenly (as I said) drawing your right hand across your left, you will seem to have left the <term>tester</term> there, especially if you close your left hand at the right moment. To make it appear even more authentic, you may take a knife and seem to knock it against the coin so that it makes a loud sound. But instead of knocking the coin in the left hand (where there is none), you shall hold the point of the knife firmly with the left hand and knock it against the <term>tester</term> held in the other hand. It will be thought to hit against the money in the left hand. Then say your words and open your hand; when nothing is seen, people will marvel at how the <term>tester</term> was moved.
