### BOOK VII.
### The Discovery

<margin>2 Kings 4</margin>
...admonition to all future generations, as should be prejudicial to his kingdom, and also be free of all impiety. But such a divine sentence does much to maintain the witch’s credit and to increase her profits. However, concerning the truth of this prophecy, there are many debatable questions: First, whether the battle was fought the next day? Second, whether all his sons were killed with him? *Also*, whether they went to heaven or hell together; for if they were with *Samuel*, they must be in heaven, and if they were with *Satan*, they must be in hell. But even if every part of this prophecy were false—such as the fact that all his sons were not slain (*Ishbosheth* lived and reigned in *Israel* for two years after *Saul’s* death), and that the battle did not take place on the very next day, and that wicked *Saul*, after he killed himself, was not with the good *Samuel*—yet this witch gave a shrewd guess as to the outcome. Whether it was true or false does not matter for my purpose, and therefore I will omit it. But regarding the opinion of those who say it was the Devil because those things came to pass, I would very much like to know from them where they learned that Devils foreknow the future? If they say he only guesses based on probabilities, then the witch may also do the same.

<margin>Canon 26, Question 5: "No wonder" <note>original: "nec mirum"</note></margin>
But here I must not forget the Decrees, which conclude that *Samuel* did not actually appear to *Saul*. Instead, they suggest that the historian set forth *Saul’s* state of mind and *Samuel’s* condition, along with certain things that were said and seen, while omitting whether they were true or false. Furthermore, it suggests it would be a great offense for a person to believe the literal words of the story. And if you do not like this explanation, I can easily align myself with the opinion of some very learned men who explain this passage with great probability in this way: namely, that this <term>Pythonist</term> <note>A person believed to be possessed by a spirit of divination; named after the Pythian Oracle.</note> being a <term>Ventriloquist</term> <note>original: "Ventriloquus" — literally one who speaks from the belly.</note> (that is, speaking as if from the bottom of her stomach) cast herself into a trance. In this way, she deceived *Saul*, answering him in *Samuel’s* name with a counterfeit, hollow voice—just as the young woman of *Westwell* spoke, whose story I have recounted at length earlier on pages 71 and 72. This is true ventriloquism.

<margin>Right Ventriloquism.</margin>

### CHAP. XIV.

> Opinions of some learned men that *Samuel* was indeed raised, not by the witch's art or power, but by a special miracle of *God*; that there are no such visions in these our days; and that our witches cannot do the like.

*Jas* and *Sadajas* <note>Likely referring to Jewish commentators such as Saadia Gaon.</note> write that when the woman saw the miracle happen for real—which was more than she expected or was accustomed to—she began to cry out that this was a true vision indeed, not performed by her art but by the power of *God*. This explanation is far more probable than the judgments of our recent writers on the matter and agrees with the explanations of various good theologians. Gelasius says it was the actual spirit of *Samuel*; and where he allowed himself to be worshipped, it was only a gesture of civil respect and courtesy. He argues that *God* interposed *Samuel* there, just as He sent *Elijah* to the messenger of *Ahaziah* when he sent to consult Beelzebub, the god of *Ekron*. Here it should be noted that the <term>Witchmongers</term> <note>The author's term for those who promote or believe in the reality of witchcraft.</note> are trapped on this point: for the Catholics say it cannot be a Devil because the name *Jehovah* is mentioned three or five times in the story. Arguments are devised daily from this piece of Scripture to prove and maintain the miraculous actions of witchcraft and the raising of the dead by conjuring. And yet, even if it were true that *Samuel* himself was raised, or the Devil in his likeness, and that the Witch of *Endor* did it by her art and cunning, it serves more to disprove than to prove the abilities of our modern witches. They can neither perform that kind of miracle nor any other in any place or company where their juggling and trickery might be seen and exposed. I challenge them all (even at the risk of my life) to show one single miracle like those *Christ* truly performed, or like what they suppose this witch did diabolically—provided it is not done with trickery or secret help to make it look real. No such visions are shown in these days.

<margin>Jean Bodin and Leonardo Vairus differ on this point.</margin>
<margin>A bold, discreet, and faithful challenge.</margin>

# Walking Spirits. Of Witchcraft. CHAPTER 15.

In the past, God did send his visible Angels to men; but now we do not hear of such apparitions, nor are they necessary. Indeed, it pleased God in former times—by the hand of Moses and his Prophets, and especially by his Son Christ and his Apostles—to work great miracles for the establishment of the faith. But now, whatever is necessary for our salvation is contained in the Word of God. Our faith is already confirmed and our Church established by miracles; therefore, to seek for them now is a sign of lack of faith <note>original: "Infidelity"</note>. The Papists <note>Roman Catholics</note>, if you notice, are greatly obsessed with these, as appears in their "lying legends." In truth, their miracles are most commonly frauds <note>original: "knaveries"</note>, especially those performed by priests, of which I could cite a thousand examples. If you read the story of *Bel and the Dragon* <note>An apocryphal book of the Bible involving a detective-like exposure of a priestly fraud</note>, you shall find a deceptive miracle of great antiquity. If you wish to see more recent devices, read Weyer, Cardan, Balcus, and especially Lavater, etc. There have been some "walking miracles" in these parts, so "conjured" <note>meaning exposed or dealt with</note> not long ago, that they afterwards had little desire to make any more appearances.

<margin>At Canterbury by R. Lee Esq. and others, in the year 1573. At Rye by Mr. Maymor and others, in the year 1577.</margin>

### CHAPTER 15.

*Concerning hollow apparitions: how people have been brought to fear "Bugs"; which is partly corrected by the preaching of the Gospel; and the true effect of Christ’s miracles.*

<insert>B</insert>ut certainly, some rascal in a white sheet has deceived and abused many thousands in that way, especially when Robin Goodfellow <note>A mischievous nature spirit or "Puck" from English folklore</note> caused such a commotion <note>original: "kept such a coil"</note> in the countryside. But you should understand that these <term>Bugs</term> <gloss>bogeymen or imaginary terrors</gloss> are especially seen and feared by sick people, children, women, and cowards, who, through weakness of mind and body, are shaken by empty dreams and continual fear. The Scythians, being a stout and warlike nation (as various writers report), never see empty visions or spirits. It is a common saying: "A lion fears no bugs." 

But in our childhood, our mothers' maids so terrified us with an ugly Devil having horns on his head, fire in his mouth, a tail on his backside, eyes like basins, fangs like a dog, claws like a bear, skin like a Black man <note>original: "Niger"</note>, and a voice roaring like a lion, that we start and are afraid when we hear someone cry "Boo!" <note>original: "Bough"</note>. They have so frightened <note>original: "frayed"</note> us with bull-beggars, spirits, witches, urchins <note>spirits often appearing as hedgehogs</note>, elves, hags, fairies, satyrs, pans, fauns, sylvans, tritons, centaurs, dwarfs, giants, imps, <term>calcars</term> <gloss>astrologers or those who calculate nativities</gloss>, conjurers, nymphs, changelings, incubi, Robin Goodfellow, the spoorn <note>original: "Spoon," a phantom</note>, the mare <note>the "nightmare" demon</note>, the man in the oak, the <term>hell-wain</term> <gloss>a phantom death-wagon</gloss>, the <term>firedrake</term> <gloss>a fire-spirit or meteor</gloss>, the puckle <note>a small Puck or goblin</note>, Tom Thumb, hobgoblins, Tom-tumbler, Boneless, and such other "bugs," that we are afraid of our own shadows. 

It has come to the point that some never fear the Devil except on a dark night; and then a shorn <note>original: "polled"</note> sheep is a perilous beast, and is many times mistaken for our father's soul—especially in a churchyard, where a very brave man in the past scarcely dared to pass by night without his hair standing on end. For very serious writers report that spirits appear as beasts, dogs, swine, horses, goats, cats, and hares; or as birds, such as crows, night-owls, and screech-owls; but they delight most in the form of snakes and dragons. 

Well, thanks be to God, this wretched and cowardly lack of faith has been partly forgotten since the preaching of the Gospel. Doubtless, the rest of those illusions will in a short time (by God's grace) be detected and vanish away. Various writers report that in Germany, since Martin Luther’s time, spirits and devils have not appeared in person as they used to do in the past. This argument is taken up by the ancient Church Fathers to prove that oracles have ended and ceased. For in times past (says Athanasius in his book *On the Incarnation of the Word*), devils deceptively entangled men with their illusions, hiding themselves in waters, stones, woods, etc. But now that the word of God has appeared, those lights, spirits, and the mockery of images have ceased. Truly, if all such oracles—like that of Apollo, etc.—before the coming of Christ had been true and performed according to the reports brought to us through various ages and from far countries, then...

<margin>John 5.</margin>
...without priestly fraud or guile, or as if the spirits of miracles had been inserted into an idol, as Christians may conceive. Christ’s coming was not so [ineffective] for us in this point as to take away his spirit of prophecy and divination from the mouths of his chosen people and good prophets—giving no answers of anything to come through them, nor by *Urim* or *Thummim* <note>Urim and Thummim: objects used by ancient Hebrew priests to determine God's will.</note> as he used to do—and yet leave the Devil in the mouth of a witch or an idol to prophesy or work miracles, etc. To do so would be to the hindrance of his glorious Gospel, to the discredit of his Church, and to the promotion of infidelity and false religion. 

In reality, the working of miracles was the only—or at least the most special—means that moved men to believe in Christ, as appears in various places in the Gospel, and especially in *John*, where it is written, *That a great multitude followed him, because they saw his miracles which he did, etc.* Nay, is it not written, *That Jesus was approved by God among the Jews, with miracles, wonders and signs*? And yet, if we compare the miracles performed by Christ with those that are attributed to witches, the witches' miracles shall appear more common and in no way inferior to his.

### CHAP. XVI.
->Witches' miracles compared to Christ's; that God is the creator of all things; of Apollo, and of his names and appearance.<-

<margin>An ironic comparison.</margin>
<margin>Malleus Maleficarum, part 2, question 1, chapter 14.</margin>
<margin>Acts 17.</margin>
<margin>1 Tim. 6:13.</margin>
<margin>Col. 1:16.</margin>
<margin>Athanasian Creed.</margin>
If the Witch of *Endor* had performed what many believe regarding that matter, it might have been compared with the raising of *Lazarus* from the dead. I ask you, is not the converting of water into milk just as difficult a matter as the turning of water into wine? And yet, just as you may read in the Gospel that Christ performed this first miracle, so you may read in the *Malleus Maleficarum* <note>original: "M. Mal."; a famous 15th-century manual for hunting witches.</note> and in Bodin <note>Jean Bodin, an influential 16th-century writer on demonology.</note> that witches can easily do the other; yes, and what is even more, they claim that from water they can make butter. 

But to avoid all arguments, and lest there should appear to be more power in Christ’s miracle than the others, you shall find in the *Malleus Maleficarum* that they claim witches can change water into wine. What is it to attribute the power and work of the Creator to a creature, if this is not? Christ says, "The works that I do, no man can do" <note>original: "Opera quæ ego facio nemo poteft facere."</note>. The creation of substance was never granted to man nor angel; therefore, it was granted neither to witch nor devil. For God is the only giver of life and being, and by him all things are made, visible and invisible.

<margin>Apollo and Pytho revealed.</margin>
Finally, this woman of *Endor* is called a *Pythonissa* <note>A woman possessed by a spirit of divination; a medium.</note> in the Scripture; by which it may appear that she was nothing but a deceiver. For *Pytho* himself, from whom the word *Pythonissa* is derived, was a counterfeit. And the original story of *Apollo*, who was called *Pytho* because he killed a serpent of that name, is but a poetic fable. For the poets say he was the god of music, medicine, poetry, and archery. In heaven he is called *Sol* <note>The Sun</note>, on earth *Liber Pater* <note>Free Father; an epithet for the god Bacchus</note>, and in hell *Apollo*. He always flourishes with perpetual youth, and therefore he is depicted without a beard. 

His image was kept as an oracle-giver, and the priests who attended it at *Delphi* <note>original: "Delphos"</note> were deceivers; they were called *Pythonists* after *Pytho*, just as "Papists" <note>A derogatory term for Roman Catholics.</note> are named after the *Papa* (the Pope). Afterwards, all women who practiced that trade were named *Pythonissas*, as was this woman of Endor. But because it concerns this matter, I will briefly note the opinions of various learned men and certain other proofs which I find in the Scripture regarding the ceasing of miracles, prophecies, and oracles.

<summary>The author argues that if witches could truly perform miracles like turning water to wine or raising the dead, their power would rival Christ's, which is theologically impossible. He further identifies the "Witch of Endor" as a mere deceiver (Pythonissa), linking the term to the fraudulent pagan oracles of Apollo.</summary>

### BOOK VIII.

## CHAPTER I.

# That Miracles Have Ceased.

<margin>Psalm 136:4</margin>
<margin>& 72:18</margin>
<margin>& 88:11</margin>
<margin>John 3:2</margin>
<margin>& 7:16</margin>
<margin>In annotations on John 3</margin>
<margin>Isaiah 45</margin>
<image-desc>Large decorated initial 'A' at the beginning of the paragraph.</image-desc>Although in times past, it pleased God to extraordinarily show miracles among his people to strengthen their faith in the Messiah; and again, at his coming, to confirm their faith by his wonderful deeds and the special graces and gifts bestowed by him upon the Apostles, etc., yet we ordinarily read in the Scriptures that it is the Lord who works great wonders. Indeed, David says that (as in this case of Samuel) God himself shows no wonders. I find also that God will not give his glory and power to a creature. Nicodemus, being a Pharisee, could say that no man could do such miracles as Christ did unless God were with him—according to the saying of the Prophet to those gods and idols who took on the power of God: "Do either good or ill if you can," etc. So as the Prophet knew, this purpose might be brought out of the Scripture, which I will omit and skip over for brevity.

<margin>Augustine, *On the Words of the Lord according to Matthew*, sermon 18.</margin>
<margin>James 5:15</margin>
<margin>J. Calvin, *Institutes*, book 4, chapter 19, section 18.</margin>
<margin>Ibid. section 19.</margin>
<margin>Isaiah 9:7</margin>
<margin>Acts 20:10</margin>
<margin>Ibid.</margin>
<margin>Namely J. Calvin.</margin>
St. **Augustine**, among other reasons by which he proves the ceasing of miracles, says: "Now blind flesh does not open the eyes of the blind by the miracle of God, but the eyes of our heart are opened by the word of God. Now our dead corpse is no longer raised up by a miracle, but our dead bodies will still be raised up on the last day by Christ. Now the ears of the deaf are not opened by miracle, but those who had their ears shut before now have them opened for their salvation." The miraculous healing of the sick by anointing, spoken of by St. **James**, is objected to by many, especially by the Papists <note>original: "Papists"; a common 16th-century derogatory term for Roman Catholics</note>, for the maintenance of their Sacrament of Extreme Unction <term>Extreme Unction</term> <note>Now known as the Anointing of the Sick, this is a Catholic rite for the spiritual and physical relief of the dying.</note>. This is foolishly and vainly used in the Roman Church as though the miraculous gift continued to this day. In this regard, you shall see what **Calvin** says in his *Institutes*. The grace of healing, he says, spoken of by St. James, has vanished away, as have the other miracles which the Lord intended to show only for a time, so that he might make the new preaching of the Gospel marvelous forever. "Why," he asks, "do these miracle-mongers not appoint some Siloam <note>original: "Siloah"; a reference to the Pool of Siloam in Jerusalem where Jesus healed a blind man</note> to swim in, where sick people may plunge themselves at certain regular times? Why do they not lie down upon the dead, since **Paul** raised up a dead child by that means?" Truly, he says, when James spoke of the miracle of anointing, he spoke for that time while the gift of the Holy Spirit still flourished. He adds that the Lord is present with his people in all ages, and as often as there is need, he helps their sicknesses no less than in ancient times. But he does not so clearly reveal his power, nor distribute miracles as if by the hands of the Apostles, because that gift was only for a time. Chrysostom <note>original: "cercus"; a likely printer's error for Chrysostom, an Early Christian Church Father frequently cited in this context</note> even then concluded thus: "They say such virtues or miracles remain, but experience says no." And see how they agree among themselves: **Daneau** <note>original: "Danæus"; Lambert Daneau (c. 1530–1595), a French Reformed theologian</note> says that neither witch nor devil can work miracles. **Calvin** says they have all ceased. All witch-mongers <term>witch-mongers</term> <note>A term used by the author to describe people who promote or believe in the power of witches.</note> say they continue. But some affirm that Popish miracles have vanished and gone away, while witches' miracles remain in full force.

<summary>The author argues that the era of divine miracles ended after the time of the Apostles, citing theologians like Augustine and Calvin to dispute Catholic rituals and contemporary beliefs in the supernatural powers of witches.</summary>

force. Just as Saint *Loy* <note>original: "S. But let all the witch-promoters <note>original: "Witchmongers"</note>, and especially the miracle-promoters in the world, answer me this hypothetical case: suppose a woman accused of witchcraft should say to them that she is a true prophet of the Lord, and that He reveals those secret mysteries to her by which she exposes the wicked acts and imaginations of the ungodly, and that through Him she works miracles and prophecies, and so on. I think they must either give in or confess that the age of miracles has ended. But such things (says Cardan <note>original: "Cardigan," likely a transcription error for the philosopher Girolamo Cardano</note>) as seem miraculous are chiefly done by deceit, sleight of hand <note>original: "Legierdemain"</note>, or conspiracy; otherwise, they may simply seem impossible, or else things are claimed to be done that never were, nor ever can be, done.

### CHAPTER II.
->The gift of Prophecy has ceased.<-

<margin>Isaiah 41:23.</margin>
<margin>Ecclesiastes 6:12.</margin>
<margin>1 Samuel 28:8.</margin>
<margin>Romans 12.</margin>
<margin>1 Corinthians 13.</margin>
<margin>1 Peter 1.</margin>
That neither witches, nor the Medium <note>original: "Woman"</note> of *Endor*, nor even her familiar spirit or the Devil can tell what is to come, may plainly appear by the words of the prophet, who says, *Show us what things are to come, and we will say you are indeed gods*. This is according to what *Solomon* says: *Who can tell a man what shall happen to him under the sun?* "Indeed, I can," says the Witch of *Endor* to *Saul*. But I will rather believe *Paul* and *Peter*, who say that prophecy is the gift of God and no worldly thing, rather than a deceitful woman <note>original: "cosening quean"</note> who takes it upon herself to do all things and yet can do nothing but beguile men. 

Up steps another person like *Bungie*, and he can tell you where your horse or your donkey is located, or what has become of anything you have lost, just as *Samuel* could; and what you have done throughout your past life, just as *Christ* did for the woman of *Sychar* at *Jacob’s* well; yes, and even what your business is before you speak, just as Elisha <note>original: "Elizeus"</note> did.

<margin>John 4.</margin>
<margin>Peter Martyr, Common Places, Part 9, Section 17.</margin>
*Peter Martyr* <note>Pietro Martire Vermigli, a Reformed theologian</note> says that only God and man know the heart of man, and that the Devil must be excluded, citing these passages: *Only God is the searcher of hearts* <note>original: "Solus Deus scrutator cordium"</note>; and *No one knows the things of a man except the spirit of the man which is within him* <note>original: "Nemo scit quæ sunt hominis, nisi spiritus hominis qui est in eo"</note>. *Solomon* says, *You alone know the thoughts of men* <note>original: "Tu solus nosti cogitationes hominum"</note>. And *Jeremiah* says, in the person of God, *I am God, searching hearts and minds* <note>original: "Ego Deus scrutans corda & renes"; "renes" literally means kidneys, then thought to be the seat of emotion</note>. Also, *Matthew* says of *Christ*: *And Jesus, seeing their thoughts* <note>original: "Jesus autem videns cogitationes eorum"</note>; He who in Scripture is called the Searcher of the thoughts in the heart, as appears in Acts 1 and 15, Romans 8, Matthew 9, 12, and 22, Mark 2, Luke 6, 7, and 11, John 1, 2, 6, and 13, Revelation <note>original: "Apoc."</note> 2 and 3, and in countless other places.

<margin>Peter Martyr in Common Places.</margin>
<margin>Hebrews 1:2.</margin>
<margin>2 Peter 1:21.</margin>
The same *Peter Martyr* also says that the Devil may suspect but cannot know our thoughts; for if he knew our thoughts, he would understand our faith, and if he did, he would never assault us with a single temptation. It is true that *Samuel* could tell where lost things had strayed, and so on. But we see that this gift also ceased with the coming of *Christ*, according to the saying of *Paul*: *At various times and in different manners, God spoke in the old times by our fathers the prophets; in these last days, He has spoken to us by His Son, etc.* Therefore, the gift of prophecy, with which God endowed His people in times past, has also ceased, and counterfeits and swindlers <note>original: "coseners"</note> have come in their place, according to this saying of *Peter: There were false prophets among the people, even as there shall be*...

# Oracles of Witchcraft. CHAPTER 3.

...false teachers among you, and so forth. And do not think that such a notable gift would be taken away from the beloved and chosen people of God and given to Mother Bungie <note>A contemporary nickname for a woman accused of being a witch or a local "wise woman."</note> and others of her profession.

<margin>Zechariah 13:2, 3</margin>

The words of the Prophet Zechariah are clear regarding the end of both good and bad prophets: *“I will cause the prophets and unclean spirits to depart from the land; and if any should still prophesy, his parents shall pierce him through when he prophesies,”* and so on. No, indeed; foretelling the future is the work of God alone, who "disposes all things sweetly," and whose counsel no man has ever shared. God has kept the knowledge of our labors, times, and moments in His own power. Also, Favorinus <note>original: "Phavorinus"; a Roman-era Greek philosopher and orator</note> says that if these unconvincing <note>original: "cold"</note> prophets or oracles tell you of prosperity and deceive you, you are made miserable through vain expectation; if they tell you of adversity and lie, you are made miserable through vain fear. Therefore, I say we might as well expect to hear prophecies at the Tabernacle, in the burning bush, from the Cherubim among the clouds, from the Angels within the Ark, or out of the flame, as to expect an oracle from a prophet in these days.

<margin>Canon law regarding evildoers and mathematicians <note>In this context, "mathematicians" refers to astrologers or those using numbers for divination.</note></margin>
But suppose someone in our Commonwealth should stand up and claim to be a prophet (as many frantic people do); who would believe him? Who would not think instead that he was a dishonest person? Look at the Statutes of the fifth year of Elizabeth I <note>Referring to the 1563 "Act against fond and fantastical prophecies."</note> to see if there are not laws made against them, condemning their arrogance and trickery <note>original: "cosenage"</note>. The canon laws <note>Laws of the church</note> also say the same.

### CHAPTER 3.
->That Oracles have ceased.<-

<margin>Thucydides, Book 2</margin>
<margin>Cicero, *On Divination*, Book 2</margin>
Regarding oracles, which were mostly idols of silver, gold, wood, stone, and so on: some say unclean spirits hid inside their bodies and gave answers. Others say that vapors <note>original: "exhalations"</note> rising out of the ground inspired the minds of their priests to give out oracles. They suggest that spirits and winds rose from that soil and endowed those men with the gift of prophesying future events. In truth, however, they were all devices to cheat <note>original: "cosen"</note> the people for the profit of the priests, who received the idols' answers the night before and delivered them back to the idolaters the next morning. You should understand that even if it were as they supposed, for the reasons and proofs already mentioned, these oracles should now cease. Anything related to such miraculous actions—like witchcraft or conjuration—has been struck down <note>original: "knocked on the head"</note> and nailed to the cross with Christ. He has broken the power of devils, satisfied God’s justice, and has trodden them under His feet and subdued them. 

<margin>Zechariah 13:2</margin>
<margin>Micah 5:12</margin>
At His coming, the Prophet Zechariah says that the names of idols will be taken out of the land and they shall no longer be remembered; He will then cause the prophets and unclean spirits to leave the land. It is also written, *“I will cut off your sorcerers from your hand, and you shall have no more soothsayers.”* Indeed, the Gospel of Christ has so exposed their trickery that since its preaching, their pride has been humbled <note>original: "their combes are cut"</note>, and only those who are foolish pay them any attention. If these prophecies were ever to take effect, it had to be at the coming of Christ. You see that the devils were troubled and grew faint when they met Him, crying out—or rather exclaiming—in this way: "Son of God, why have you come to torture us before the appointed time?" <note>original Latin: *Fili Dei, cur venisti nos cruciare ante tempus?* See Matthew 8:29.</note>. He indeed prevented them, and He now remains our defender and protector from the devil's claws. So you see, there is no room left for such "guests" anymore.

However, you shall hear the opinions of others who have been as much deceived as yourselves in this matter. Yet even they are driven to confess that God has appointed His Son to beat down the power of devils, to satisfy God’s justice, and to heal the wound we received from the fall of Adam, according to God’s promise...

Eusebius, in the fifth book of his work *On the Preaching of the Gospel* <note>original: *De prædicatione Evangelii*</note>—the title of which is *That the Power of Devils is Taken Away by the Coming of Christ*—says: "All answers made by Devils, all soothsayings and divinations of men are gone and vanished away." However, John Chrysostom, living long after Cicero, says that the god Apollo was forced to admit that as long as any relic of a Christian martyr was held to his nose, he could not provide any answer or oracle.

So one may perceive that the Heathens were wiser in this regard than many Christians, who in times past were called "Opponents of enchantments" <term>original: *Oppugnatores incantamentorum*</term>, just as the English Princes are called "Defenders of the Faith" <term>original: *Defensores fidei*</term>. Plutarch calls Boeotia (as we call talkative people "babblers") by the name "Many Words" because of the multitude of oracles there; which now, he says, are like a spring or fountain that has dried up. If any oracle remained, I would ride five hundred miles to see it; but in the whole world there is not one to be seen at this hour, Catholic frauds <note>original: "Popish cozenages"</note> excepted.

But Plutarch says that the cause of this failing of oracles was the Devil's death, whose life he held to be limited <note>original: "determinable"</note> and mortal, saying they died of old age; and that the divining priests were blown up by a whirlwind and swallowed by an earthquake. Others imputed it to be the light of the place of Pan, which because it is relevant to this purpose, I will insert here. And since it mentions the Devil's death, you may believe it if you wish; I certainly will not, being assured that he is kept alive to punish the wicked and those who attribute the power of Almighty God to those idols.

### CHAPTER IV
A tale written by many serious authors and believed by many wise men concerning the Devil's death. Another story written by Papists and believed by all Catholics, affirming the Devil's honesty, conscience, and courtesy.

Plutarch says that his countryman Epitherses told him that as he traveled by sea to Italy, with many passengers in his boat, one evening when they were near the Echinades Islands, the wind completely ceased. The ship, drifting with the tide, was brought at last to Paxos. While some slept, others drank <note>original: "quaffed"</note>, and others were awake (perhaps in as bad a state as the rest), after supper suddenly a voice was heard calling "Thamus" in such a way that every man wondered.

<margin>Thamus, having little to do, thought to play a joke on his company, whom he might easily trick with such a jest.</margin>
This Thamus was a pilot born in Egypt, unknown to many who were in the ship. Therefore, being called twice, he answered nothing; but the third time he answered. The other voice, even louder, commanded him that when he came to Palodes, he should tell them that "The great god Pan is departed." At this, everyone was astonished (as Epitherses affirmed). Discussing what was best to do, Thamus concluded that if the wind were high, they must pass by in silence; but if the weather were calm, he must speak what he had heard. But when they came to Palodes and the weather was calm, Thamus looked out toward the land and cried aloud that the great god Pan was deceased; and immediately there followed a mournful noise from a multitude of people, as if in great wonder and amazement. And because there were many in the ship, the news of it was quickly brought to Rome, and Thamus was sent for by the Emperor Tiberius, who gave such credit to the story that he diligently inquired and asked who that Pan was. The learned men about him supposed that Pan was the son of Mercury and Penelope, etc. Eusebius...

# Oracles of Witchcraft.

## CHAPTER V.

<margin>Paulus Martius, in his notes on Ovid's *Fasti* <note>original: "Ovids Fasti"</note>, says that this voice was heard from the island of Paxae on the very night that Christ suffered.</margin>

<margin>A detection of Thamus's trickery.</margin>

<margin>*Golden Legend*, the life of Saint Andrew, folio 39. <note>original: "Legend. au. vita sancti Andreæ"</note></margin>

<margin>A gentle and a godly Devil.</margin>

Indeed, he says that this happened in the time of the Emperor *Tiberius*, when Christ expelled all devils, and so on. *Paulus Martius*, in his notes on Ovid's *Fasti*, says that this voice was heard from the island of *Paxae* on the very night that Christ suffered, in the nineteenth year of *Tiberius*. Surely, this was a merry jest devised by *Thamus*, who intended to make sport with the passengers. Some of these passengers were old acquaintances of *Thamus*, and others were at play when the first voice was used. 

At the second voice—that is, when he was to deliver his message—he, being an experienced pilot, knew where some noise was common due to an echo in the sea. He thought he would accomplish his trick (to the astonishment of the passengers) if the weather proved calm. From this, it appears that in cases of tempests or other emergencies, he would attend to more serious business rather than to that ridiculous matter. For why else should he not perform his errand in rough weather as well as in calm? Or why would he need to tell the Devil about it, when the Devil told him first, and could have done the errand himself with much more speed?

But you shall read a fable in the *Golden Legend*—an "Oracle," I should say—that is considered more authentic. Many will say that the story of Thamus was a secular story and not as "canonical" as those verified by the Pope's authority. And thus it is written: A woman in labor <term>travel: childbirth or labor</term> sent her sister to the goddess *Diana* (who was the Devil in an idol, as all those Oracles are said to be). She asked her sister to make her prayers, or rather a request, to know if the delivery would be safe. This the sister did, but the Devil answered: *“Why do you pray to me? I cannot help you. Go instead and pray to Andrew the Apostle, and he may help your sister.”* Look at that! This was not only a gentle but a "godly" Devil, pitying the woman’s situation. By revealing his own inability, he gave more credit to Saint *Andrew*. I know some Protestants will say that the Devil referred the maid to St. *Andrew* just to maintain the practice of idolatry. But what answer will the Papists <note>original: "Papists"; a derogatory term for Roman Catholics</note> make? They think it great piety to pray to Saints, and therefore must conclude it was a piece of honest courtesy for the Devil to send her to Saint *Andrew*, who would surely help her.

## CHAPTER V.

### The judgments of the ancient Fathers concerning Oracles and their abolishment; and that they have now been transferred from Delphi to Rome.

<margin>Justin Martyr, *Dialogue with Trypho* <note>original: "In dialogis adversus Judæos"</note>; Athanasius, *On the Incarnation of the Word* <note>original: "De humanitate verbi"</note>; Augustine, *The City of God* <note>original: "De Civitate Dei"</note>; Eusebius, book 7, chapter 6; also book 5, chapters 1 and 8; Rupert of Deutz, on John, books 10 and 12; Plutarch, *On the Obsolescence of Oracles* <note>original: "De abolitione oraculorum"</note>; Pliny, *Natural History*, book 30, pages 59 and 64.</margin>

You shall find the opinions of the Church Fathers—that Oracles ceased upon the coming of Christ—in the following places: *Justin Martyr* in his *Dialogue against the Jews*; *Athanasius* in *On the Incarnation of the Word*; *Augustine* in *The City of God*; *Eusebius*, book 7, chapter 6, and book 5, chapters 1 and 8; *Rupert*, in books 10 and 12; *Plutarch* in *On the Obsolescence of Oracles*; and *Pliny* in book 30 of his *Natural History*. 

Finally, *Athanasius* concludes that in times past, there were Oracles in Boeotia, Lycia, and other places; but now, since Christ is preached to all men, this madness has ceased. So you see that whatever estimation the ancient Fathers once held (by hearsay) regarding those miraculous matters of idols and oracles, they themselves now refuse to bear witness to them. Instead, they affirm that ever since Christ’s coming, those miracles have been stopped.

As for the cessation of the knavery and deceptive tricks of priests, I see no authority in Scripture or the ancient Fathers to suggest they have ended. Rather, the contrary is suggested: that strange illusions shall be shown by them even until the end of the world. And truly, anyone who knows and observes the methods and devices used in Roman Catholic pilgrimages shall see that both the Oracles and their conclusions remain. It is as if they were transferred from *Delphi* to *Rome*, where that "adulterous generation" <note>A biblical reference to those seeking signs rather than faith</note> continually seeks a sign, even though they already have Moses and the Prophets, and even Christ and his Apostles.

<summary>Scot argues that the famous "Great Pan is dead" oracle was a human prank by a pilot named Thamus and suggests that while ancient demonic oracles may have ceased with Christ, priestly deception continues in the form of Catholic pilgrimages and "miracles."</summary>

### CHAP. VI.

->Where and in what manner <term>Coseners</term><note>original: "Coseners"; swindlers or con artists</note>, Witches, and Priests were accustomed to give Oracles, and to perform their tricks.<-

<margin>Strabo, *Geography*, book 16.</margin>
<margin>Johann Weyer, *On the Illusions of Demons*, book 1, chapter 12.</margin>
These swindling *oracles*, or rather *oracle-mongers*, were accustomed (I say) to practice their tricks and to perform their miracles most commonly through *maids*, *beasts*, *images*, *dens*, *cloisters*, dark holes, *trees*, *churches*, or *churchyards*, etc. This was where *priests*, *monks*, and *friars* had laid their plots and made their secret agreements beforehand to beguile the world, to gain money, and to add credit to their profession. This practice began in the *oaks* of *Dodona* in the wood; it was said that the *trees* there could speak. But this was done by a rogue in a hollow tree that appeared solid to the simple-minded people. This *wood* was in *Molossia*, a part of *Greece* called *Epirus*, and it was named *Dodona’s Oracle*. There were many *oracles* in *Egypt*, namely: of *Hercules*, of *Apollo*, of *Minerva*, of *Diana*, of *Mars*, of *Jupiter*, and of the *ox Apis* (who was the son of *Jupiter*, though his image was worshipped in the likeness of an *ox*). *Latona*, who was the mother of *Apollo*, was an *oracle* in the city of *Buto*. The *priests* of *Apollo*, who always faked fury and madness, gave *oracles* in the *temple* called *Clarius*, within the city of *Colophon* in *Greece*. At *Thebes* in *Boeotia*, and also in *Lebadea*, *Trophonius* was the chief *oracle*. At *Memphis*, it was a *cow*; at *Corinth*, an *ox* called *Minaeus*; in *Arsinoe*, a *crocodile*; in *Athens*, a *prophet* called *Amphiaraus*—who actually died at *Thebes*, where they say the earth opened and swallowed him up alive. At *Delphi* was the great *temple* of *Apollo*, where demons gave *oracles* through young women (as some say), though in truth it was done by *priests*. It was built upon Mount *Parnassus* in *Greece*. The defenders of *oracles* say that just as rivers are often diverted to another course, so likewise the spirit which inspired the chief *prophets* may for a time be silent and then revive again through a cycle of time.

<margin>Henry Howard in his *Defensative against the Poison of Supposed Prophecies*.</margin>
*Demetrius* says that the spirits which attended on *oracles* grew weary of the people's curiosity and persistent demands, and for shame forsook the *temple*. But as one who has recently written against *prophecies* says, it is no wonder that when the "almighty blocks" <note>An "almighty block" refers to a wooden idol or a person as dull as a block of wood.</note> lost their senses, for these are all gone now; their knavery is discovered, so they can no longer abuse the world with such trifles. But whereas these great *Doctors* suppose that the cause of their departure was the coming of *Christ*; if they mean that the *Devil* died as soon as He was born, or that he then gave up his occupation, they are deceived. For the *Roman Catholic Church* has made a continual practice of this, partly for their own private profit, lucre, and gain, and partly to be held in high esteem by the *world* and in admiration among the simple. But indeed, men who have learned of *Christ* and have been familiar with His Word have discovered and shaken off the vanity and abomination of this. If those *Doctors* had lived until today, they would have said and written that *oracles* had ceased, or rather been driven out of *England*, <margin>In whose days Oracles ceased in England.</margin> in the time of *King Henry VIII* and of *Queen Elizabeth I*, his daughter. They have done so much in that regard that at this hour, oracles are not only all gone, but forgotten here in this *English nation*, where they once swarmed as thick as they did in *Boeotia* or in any other place in the world. But the credit they had depended not upon their own merit, but upon the gullibility of others. Now, therefore, I will conclude and make an end of this matter with the opinion and saying of the *prophet*: *Vain is the answer of idols. For they have eyes and see not, ears and hear not, mouths and speak not, etc. And: Let them show what is to come, and I will say they are gods indeed*.

<margin>Zechariah 10:2.</margin>
<margin>Psalm 115:5, 6.</margin>
<margin>Isaiah 41:23.</margin>

### BOOK IX.

#### CHAPTER I.

The Hebrew word *Kasam* <note>original: Kafam</note> explained, and how far a Christian may speculate regarding things to come.

<image-desc>Large decorative initial capital 'K' with intricate floral and leaf designs.</image-desc>
*Kasam* (as Johann Weyer <note>original: John Wierius; a 16th-century physician and opponent of witch-hunts</note> affirms from his own knowledge, and as reported on the word of Andreas Masius <note>a Flemish scholar of ancient languages</note>) differs little in meaning from the former word *Ob* <note>a Hebrew term for a medium or spirit</note>; signifying *to prophesy* <note>original Latin: Viticinari</note>. It is most commonly used in a negative sense, as in Deuteronomy 18 and Jeremiah 27, etc. However, it is sometimes used in a positive sense, as in Isaiah 3:2. To foretell things to come based upon probable conjectures—so long as we reach no further than what is appropriate for human capacity—is not (in my opinion) unlawful. Rather, it is a commendable display of wisdom and judgment, which are the good gifts and noble blessings of God, for which we ought to be thankful. We should also yield due honor and praise to Him for the noble order He has established in nature, praying Him to enlighten our hearts with the beams of His wisdom, so that we may more and more profit in the true knowledge of the workmanship of His hands. But some people are so overly scrupulous that they generally condemn all sorts of divinations, even denying those things that have obvious causes in nature. These natural events are designed to foreshadow things to come and, in that showing, they warn us of things that will follow, exhibiting signs of unknown and future matters to be judged by the order, law, and course of nature presented to us by God.
<margin>Johann Weyer, Book 1, *On the Deceptions of Demons* <note>original: wier. lib. 1. de praest. dæmon.</note></margin>
<margin>Not all divinations are to be condemned.</margin>

And some, on the other side, are so bewitched with folly that they attribute to created things that respect which rightly and truly belongs to God, the Creator of all things. They claim that the public and private destinies of all human matters—and whatever a man would want to know of things past or present—are manifested to us in the heavens, as if all things might be known through the stars and planets. These people also insist that nothing should be undertaken or attempted without a favorable alignment of the planets. By these and other similar devices, they corrupt and profane the ancient and commendable observations of our ancestors; as did Colebras <note>original: Colebrafus; likely a reference to a historical figure or sect associated with astrological heresy</note>, who taught that all of human life was governed by the seven planets—and yet he was a Christian, though condemned for heresy. But let us embrace and allow this philosophy and prophesying only so far as the Word of God permits and commends it to us.
<margin>The erroneous and impious opinion of Colebras <note>original: Colebrafus</note>.</margin>

### CHAP. II.

->Proofs from the Old and New Testaments that certain observations of the weather are lawful.<-

<margin>Genesis 1:14; 9:13.</margin>
<margin>Ecclesiasticus 43.</margin>
<margin>Psalm 19:1, 2; 50:6.</margin>
<margin>Ecclesiasticus 43.</margin>
<margin>Baruch 3.</margin>
<margin>Luke 12:54, 55.</margin>
<margin>Matthew 16:2, 3.</margin>
When God, by His Word and Wisdom, had made the heavens and placed the stars in the firmament, He said, *“Let them be for signs, and for seasons, and for days and years.”* When He created the rainbow in the clouds, He said it should be for a *sign and token to us.* We find this to be true, not only regarding the past flood, but also of showers to come. And therefore, according to the advice of Jesus Sirach <note>The author of the Book of Ecclesiasticus in the Apocrypha</note>, *“Let us behold it, and praise Him in it.”* The Prophet David says, *“The heavens declare the glory of God, and the earth shows His handiwork; day unto day utters the same, and night unto night teaches knowledge.”* It is also written, *“That by the commandment of the Holy One, the stars are placed and continue in their order, and do not fail in their watch.”* It appears that Christ Himself did not altogether ignore the course and order of the heavens, in that He said, *“When you see a cloud rise out of the west, straightway you say a shower comes; and so it is. And when you see the south wind blow, you say it will be hot, and so it comes to pass.”* Again, *“When it is evening, you say fair weather, for the sky is red; and in the morning you say, today shall be a tempest, for the sky is red and lowering <note>dark and threatening</note>.”* In this, He notes that these things truly come to pass according to ancient observation and the rules of astronomy; however, He also uses the following words to warn us that by attending too much to those observations, we might neglect to follow our Christian calling.

<margin>Lactantius, Against the Astrologers <note>original: "Lactant. contra Astrologos"</note>.</margin>
<margin>Peucer, On Astrology, page 383 <note>original: "Peucer. de Astrol."</note>.</margin>
The physician is recommended to us and allowed in the Scriptures; but to put such trust in him as to neglect and distrust God is severely forbidden and reproved. Surely, it is most necessary for us to know and observe various astronomical rules; otherwise, we could not conveniently dispatch our ordinary affairs. And yet Lactantius <note>An early Christian author (c. 250–325 AD)</note> condemns and lists the various types of witchcraft, an opinion from which Calvin does not much differ. The poor husbandman <note>A farmer or tiller of the soil</note> perceives that the increase of the moon makes plants and living creatures fruitful, so that during the full moon they are in their best strength, decaying during the waning moon, and utterly withering and fading during the conjunction <note>the new moon, when it is aligned with the sun</note>. Once they have learned this by observation, use, and practice, they distribute their business accordingly—such as their times to sow, to plant, to prune, to bleed their cattle, to castrate them, etc.

### CHAP. III.

->That certain observations are neutral, certain ridiculous, and certain impious; and from where that knowledge is derived concerning Apollo and the Haruspicies.<-

<margin>The ridiculous art of casting nativities.</margin>
I do not know whether to reject or criticize the detailed observations used by our ancestors, who made conjectures based on nativities <note>birth charts or horoscopes</note>. For example, they claimed that if Saturn and Mercury were opposite each other in any "brute" <note>original: "brute sign"; zodiac signs representing animals, such as Aries or Leo, which were thought to affect speech</note> sign, a man born then would be mute or stammer much; whereas it is daily seen that children naturally imitate their parents' conditions in that regard. They have also noted that one born during the waxing of the moon shall be healthy; but during the time of the waning moon, when the moon’s light is utterly decayed, the child then born cannot live; and during the conjunction, it cannot long continue.

<margin>Julius Maternus's most impious opinion.</margin>
But I am sure the opinion of Julius Maternus <note>Firmicus Maternus, a 4th-century legal official and astrologer</note> is most impious. He writes that he who is born when Saturn is in Leo shall live long, and after his death shall go to heaven immediately. And so is this opinion of Albumazar <note>Abu Ma'shar, a famous Persian astrologer</note>, who says that whoever prays to God when the moon is in the *Head of the Dragon* <note>original: "Capite Draconis"; the point where the moon's orbit crosses the ecliptic going north</note> shall be heard, and...

### To thrust a bodkin into your head without harm.

<margin>The method and means of performing this trick.</margin>
Take a <term>bodkin</term> <note>a small, sharp, pointed tool for piercing holes in fabric or leather</note> made so that the handle <note>original: "haft"</note> is hollow, allowing the blade to slide into it as soon as you hold the point upward. Set the point to your forehead and pretend to thrust it into your head. With a little sponge hidden in your hand, you can bring out blood or wine, making the spectators think the blood or wine (which you may claim to have drunk in large quantities) is running out of your forehead. Then, after pretending to be in pain and grief, suddenly pull your hand away while holding the point downward; the blade will slide back out, and it will seem as though it had never been pushed into the handle. Immediately hide that bodkin in your lap or pocket and pull out another ordinary bodkin that looks exactly like it, but lacks the secret mechanism <note>original: "conceit"</note>.

---

### To thrust a bodkin through your tongue, and a knife through your arm; a pitiful sight, without injury or danger.

<margin>You will see an illustration of the design for this bodkin and knife if you turn ahead a few pages.</margin>
Make a bodkin with the blade split in the middle, so that the two parts are nearly three-quarters of an inch apart. Each part is held separate by a small curved <note>original: "bought"</note> piece of iron, fashioned in the way described later in the appropriate place. Then, place your tongue within that gap—specifically, into the curve left in the bodkin's blade—tucking the curved part behind your teeth and biting down on it. It will then appear to be stuck so firmly through your tongue that it can hardly be pulled out. * You can do the exact same thing with a knife made in this way and placed on your arm; the wound will look even more terrifying if a little blood is poured over it.

---

### To thrust a piece of lead into one eye, and to drive it about (with a stick) under the skin of the forehead, until it is brought to the other eye and pushed out.

Place a piece of lead into your lower eyelid, about the size of a metal tip on a lace <note>original: "tag of a point"</note>, but not as long (which you can do without danger). Then, using a small juggling stick with one hollow end, pretend to push a similar piece of lead under your other eyelid; however, actually hide that piece inside the hollow part of the stick. You can secretly keep the plug <note>original: "stopple"</note> or peg for the hole in your hand until the trick is done. Then, pretend to drive the lead with the hollow end of the stick away from that eye. By moving the end of the stick across your forehead to the other eye, you can push out the piece of lead you previously hid there, much to the wonder of the audience. * Some people "eat" the lead and then push it out of the eye; some put lead into both eyes, but the first method is best.

---

### To cut half your nose asunder, and to heal it again immediately without any ointment.

<margin>This is easily done; however, if performed cleanly, it will deceive the spectators.</margin>
Take a knife with a round, hollow notch <note>original: "gap"</note> in the middle and place it over your nose; this will make it look as though you have cut your nose halfway through. Always make sure that you have another identical knife without a notch to show after you pull the first one away. Use words of enchantment <note>original: "Inchantment"; magic spells or "patter"</note>, some blood to reveal <note>original: "bewray"</note> the wound, and quick sleight of hand <note>original: "nimble conveyance"</note>.

---

### To put a ring through your cheek.

There is another old trick <note>original: "knack"</note> which looks dangerous to the cheek. To perform it, you must have two rings of the same color and size. One must be cut through <note>original: "filed asunder"</note> so that you can slip it onto your cheek;

In pulling it away, spin the ring <note>original: "whirle about the Ring"</note>, and so it will be thought that you have put onto the stick the ring which was previously in your cheek.

### *To cut off one's head and lay it in a platter, etc., which the jugglers call the "beheading" <note>original: "decollation"</note> of John the Baptist.*

<margin>This was performed by a man named Kingsfield of London at St. Bartholomew’s Day <note>original: "Bartholomewtide"; a major summer fair in London</note> in the year 1582, in the sight of many people who came to see this spectacle.</margin>
To show a most remarkable execution by this art, you must have a board, a cloth, and a platter specifically made for this purpose, each with holes sized for a person's neck. The board must be made of two planks—the longer and broader, the better. Within half a yard of the end of each plank, half a hole must be cut out, so that when both planks are pushed together, two holes remain, much like the holes in a pair of stocks <note>wooden restraints used for punishment</note>. There must likewise be a hole made in the tablecloth or carpet. A platter must also be set directly over or upon one of the holes, having a hole in its middle of the same size, with a piece cut out of the side as wide as a neck, through which a head may be placed into the center of the platter. Then, sitting or kneeling under the board, let only the head remain upon the board inside the platter.

Then (to make the sight more dreadful), put a little sulfur <note>original: "Brimstone"</note> into a portable heater <note>original: "Chafing-dish"</note> of coals, setting it before the boy's head. The boy must gasp two or three times so the smoke enters his nostrils and mouth a little (which is not harmful to his health), and the head will immediately appear completely dead, provided the boy sets his facial expression <note>original: "countenance"</note> accordingly. If a little blood is sprinkled on his face, the sight will be even stranger.

<margin>Necessary observations to astonish the beholders.</margin>
This is commonly practiced with a boy trained for the purpose, who, being familiar and friendly with the company, may be recognized by his face as well as his clothing. At the other end of the table, where the second hole is made, another boy of the same size as the known boy must be placed, wearing the first boy's usual clothes. He must lean or lie upon the board and put his head under the board through the hole, so that his body appears to lie on one end of the board, while his head appears in a platter on the other end. * There are other things that could be done in this performance to further astonish the onlookers, but because they require long descriptions, I will omit them; such as putting a little dough kneaded with bullock's blood around his neck, which will look like dead flesh when cold, and will bleed when pricked with a sharp, hollow quill, appearing very strange, etc. * Many rules must be followed here, such as having the tablecloth long and wide enough that it almost touches the ground, and not allowing the audience to stay too long in the room, etc.

### *To thrust a dagger or bodkin <note>a sharp, pointed tool</note> into your guts very strangely, and to recover immediately.*

<margin>Of a juggler who, failing in the feats of his art, lost his life.</margin>
Another miracle may be shown regarding counterfeit executions; namely, that with a bodkin or dagger, you shall seem to kill yourself, or at the least make a fatal <note>original: "unrecoverable"</note> wound in your belly. Indeed, not long ago, a juggler caused himself to be killed at a tavern in Cheapside <note>a major commercial street in London</note>, from where he immediately went into St. Paul's Churchyard and died. This misfortune fell upon him through his own folly, as he was drunk at the time and had forgotten his metal plate, which he should have had for his protection.

The device is this: * You must prepare a piece of pasteboard <note>sturdy cardboard</note> made to fit the shape of your belly and chest. This must be skillfully colored by a painter, not only to look like your flesh, but including nipples, navel, hair, etc., so that when it is neatly fastened <note>original: "trussed"</note> to you, it appears to be your natural belly. Then, next to your true belly, you must put a linen cloth, and over that a double metal plate (which the juggler who killed himself forgot or willfully left out), and over the plate you place the false belly. Always ensure that between the plate and...

### *To draw a cord through your nose, mouth, or hand, so convincingly that it is wonderful to see.*

<margin>You shall see a diagram or pattern of this "bridle" on the next page.</margin>
There is another juggling trick <note>original: "knack"</note> which they call "the Bridle." it is made of two elder-wood sticks; through their hollow centers, a cord is placed. This is then put on the nose like a pair of tongs or pincers. When the cord, which goes around the sticks, is drawn back and forth, the onlookers will think the cord is passing through your nose in a very dangerous way. The knots at the ends of the cord, which keep it from being pulled out of the stick, must not be placed at the very top (for that must be plugged up) but half an inch below each end. In this way, I say, when it is pulled, it will seem to pass through the nose. Then you may take a knife and seem to cut the cord in two, and pull the "bridle" away from your nose.

## *The Conclusion, in which the reader is referred to certain diagrams of instruments used to perform various feats specified here.*

<margin>Among what kind of actions juggling should be counted.</margin>
In this matter, I could go on forever, but I hope it is enough that I have delivered to you the principles and also the main feats belonging to this art of juggling. Any man who thoroughly understands these may not only perform all these things, but may also devise other strange tricks and vary every one of these devices into other forms as he sees fit. So long as the power of Almighty God is not attributed to the juggler, and no offense is caused by rude speech or behavior, but the action is performed as a pastime for the delight of the audience—and so long as the juggler always admits in the end that these are not supernatural actions, but human devices and nimble sleight of hand <note>original: "conveyances"</note>—let all those overly critical people (who cannot offer their neighbors any comfort or benefit unless it pleases their own gloomy <note>original: "melancholick"</note> dispositions) say what they like. For this will be found to be not only a neutral <note>original: "indifferent"</note> activity, but one that greatly promotes the power and glory of God by exposing the pride and falsehood of those who claim to work miracles and pretend to be the mighty power of God, just as Jannes and Jambres <note>In the Bible, the Egyptian sorcerers who opposed Moses</note> and Simon Magus <note>A practitioner of magic mentioned in the New Testament</note> did.

<margin>A peerless fellow for sleight of hand.</margin>
If any man doubts these things—whether they are as strange to behold as I have reported—or thinks along with Bodin <note>Jean Bodin (1530–1596), a French jurist and demonologist who argued for the reality of witchcraft</note> that these matters are performed by "familiars" or demons, let him go into St. Martin's and ask for one John Cantares. He is a Frenchman by birth and an honest man in his dealings. He will show as many strange actions as these; he does not earn his living this way, but works for it with the sweat of his brow, and yet he has the best hand and sleight of hand, I think, of any man living today.

I do not speak "without book" <note>without authority or evidence</note> here. For if the time, place, and occasion were right, I could show so much in this art that I am sure Bodin, Spinaeus, and Vairus <note>Demonologists who wrote books supporting the persecution of witches</note> would swear I was a witch and had a familiar demon at my command. But truly, my study and labor in this have only been used so that I might prove them to be fools, and find out the fraud of those who make fools of them, so that they may become wiser and God may receive the honor that belongs to Him.

<summary>Scot explains a blood-spurt illusion and a "bridle" trick before concluding that juggling is a harmless art used to debunk fraudulent claims of supernatural powers. He cites a real-world juggler, John Cantares, as proof that these feats are purely physical skills.</summary>

#### CHAPTER 1.

->Concerning the Art of Alchemy, their technical terms, and devices used to deceive people and<-
->gain credit for their profession.<-

<margin>Alchemy is a craft, not a true science <note>original: "Art"</note>.</margin>
**H**ere I thought it not irrelevant <note>original: "impertinent"</note> to say something about the art, or rather the craft, of alchemy, otherwise called "multiplication" <term>multiplication: the alchemical process of increasing the amount of gold or silver</term>; which Geoffrey *Chaucer*, more than anyone else, most vividly describes. Within its depths, both witchcraft and conjuration lie hidden, by which some cheat others, and some are cheated themselves. For by this mystery (as it is said in the *Canon’s Yeoman's Prologue*):

<margin>G. Chaucer in the Canon’s Yeoman's Prologue.</margin>
> *They take it upon themselves to turn upside down,*
> *All the Earth between Southwark and Canterbury town,*
> *And to pave it all with silver and gold, etc.*
> *But they always fail to reach their conclusion <note>original: "conclusion"; here meaning the successful outcome of their experiment</note>,*
> *And they cause many people to suffer from illusions.*
> *For their materials <note>original: "stuffe"</note> slip away so fast,*
> *That it makes them beggars in the end,*
> *And by this craft they never win,*
> *But make their purses empty, and their wits thin.*

And because the practitioners of this craft want to be thought of as wise, learned, skilled, and masters of their trade, they have devised technical terms <note>original: "words of Art"</note>, obscure sentences, and epithets, and countless mixtures (which are also composed of strange and rare ingredients <note>original: "simples"</note>) that overwhelm the understanding of those who are either employed in this work or are brought to watch or expect their results. For what ordinary <note>original: "plain"</note> man would not believe that they are learned and clever fellows, <margin>The terms of the Alchemical Art, devised on purpose to gain credit for their cheating <note>original: "cosenage"</note>.</margin> having so many mystical technical terms ready at hand: such as (for a taste) their subliming, amalgamating, englutting <term>englutting: to fill or saturate</term>, imbibing, incorporating, cementing, calcining <note>original: "retrination"</note>, finishing <note>original: "terminations"</note>, softening <note>original: "mollifications"</note>, and hardening <note>original: "indurations"</note> of substances; matters burned <note>original: "combust"</note> and coagulated, ingots, tests <term>tests: vessels used in refining precious metals</term>, etc. Or who can understand (because of the sudden confusion, contradiction, and multitude of drugs, ingredients, and mixtures) the operation and mystery of their materials and workmanship! For these things and many more must necessarily be prepared and used in this endeavor; namely: orpiment <term>orpiment: a yellow arsenic mineral</term>, sublimed *Mercury*, iron scales <note>original: "squames"</note>, raw *Mercury*, groundly large <note>likely referring to a specific grade of ground charcoal or mineral</note>, Armenian bole <term>Bole Armoniack: a medicinal red clay</term>, verdigris, borax, various clays <note>original: "boles"</note>, gall, arsenic, sal ammoniac, sulfur <note>original: "brimstone"</note>, salt, paper, burnt bones, quicklime <note>original: "unslaked lime"</note>, clay, saltpeter, vitriol <term>vitriol: sulfuric acid or a sulfate mineral</term>, salt of tartar, alkali, prepared salt, clay made with horse dung, human hair, oil of tartar, alum, glass, wort, yeast, argol <term>argol: crude tartar from wine casks</term>, realgar <note>original: "Refagor"</note>, white of an egg <note>original: "Gleir of an eye"; 'glair' refers to egg white</note>, powders, ashes, dung, urine, etc. Then they have corrosive and linear waters, waters for whitening <note>original: "albification"</note>, and waters for reddening <note>original: "rubifying"</note>, etc. Also oils, washes <note>original: "ablutions"</note>, and meltable <note>original: "fusible"</note> metals. Also their lamps, their urinals <term>urinal: a glass vessel used by alchemists</term>, descensories <term>descensory: a chemical furnace for extracting oil by heat</term>, sublimatories, alembics, vials, crucibles <note>original: "crossets"</note>, cucurbits <term>cucurbit: the lower part of a distilling apparatus</term>, stills <note>original: "stillatories"</note>, and their furnace of calcination <term>calcination: the process of heating a substance to high temperatures to change its composition</term>; also their soft and subtle

The recipe is as follows:
They take the fat of young children and boil <note>original: seeth</note> it with water in a brass vessel, saving the thickest part of what remains boiled at the bottom, which they store and keep until there is an occasion to use it. To this they add wild celery <note>original: Eleoselinum</note>, monkshood <note>original: Aconitum</note>, poplar leaves <note>original: Frondes populeas</note>, mountain parsley, wolf's-bane, leaves of the poplar, and soot.
<margin>Recipes <note>original: receipts</note> for the miraculous transportation of witches.</margin>

Another recipe for the same purpose:
Water-parsnip <note>original: Sium</note>, common sweet-flag <note>original: Acarum vulgare</note>, cinquefoil <note>original: Pentaphyllon</note>, yellow watercress, common acorus, cinquefoil, the blood of a bat <note>original: flutter-mouse</note>, sleeping nightshade, and oil <note>original: Solanum Somniferum & oleum</note>. They crush all these together and then they rub all parts of their bodies extensively until they look red and are very hot, so that the pores may be opened and their flesh softened and loose. They add to this either fat or oil instead, so that the strength of the ointment may penetrate more deeply and thus be more effective.

By this means (he says), on a moonlight night, they seem to be carried through the air to feasting, singing, dancing, kissing, embracing <note>original: culling</note>, and other acts of sexual pleasure <note>original: venery</note> with such youths as they love and desire most. For (he says) the power of their imagination is so intense that almost all that part of the brain where memory resides is full of such notions. And since they are naturally inclined to believe anything, they receive such impressions and imaginings into their minds that even their spirits are altered by them, thinking of nothing else either by day or by night. And it helps their imaginations along that their usual food is commonly nothing but beets, roots, nuts, beans, peas, and so on.
<margin>Old women, whom they call "screech-owls" <note>original: striges</note> because of their resemblance to the bird, who suck the blood of little children sleeping in their cradles at night. <note>original Latin: Vetulæ, quas à frigis similitudine, striges vocant, quæ, noctu puerulorum sanguinem in cunis cubantium exsorbent.</note></margin>

Now (he says), when I considered this thoroughly, remaining skeptical of the matter, a witch fell into my hands who, of her own accord, promised to run an errand for me immediately from distant countries. She told everyone I had brought to witness the matter to leave the room. When she had undressed herself and rubbed <note>original: froted</note> her body with certain ointments (an action we watched through a crack or little hole in the door), she fell down—through the force of those sleep-inducing <note>original: soporiferous</note> or sleepy ointments—into a most sound and heavy sleep. We broke open the door and beat her severely, but the depth of her sleep was such that it took away her sense of feeling, and we left for a time. Now, when her strength and powers were weary and decayed, she awoke on her own and began to speak many vain and foolish <note>original: doting</note> words, claiming that she had passed over both seas and mountains, delivering to us many untrue and false reports. We earnestly denied them; she boldly insisted they were true. This (he says) will not happen to everyone, but only to old women who are melancholic <note>In the theory of the four humors, a melancholic temperament was considered cold and dry, making one prone to depression or hallucinations.</note>, whose nature is extremely cold and their physical evaporation small; they both perceive and remember what they see in that state of theirs.

->CHAPTER IX.<-
->*A refutation <note>original: confutation</note> of the previous foolish ideas, regarding ointments, dreams, and so on; as well as the gatherings of witches, and their consultations and banquets in various places—all of which occur in dreams.*<-

<insert>B</insert>ut if it is true, as St. Augustine and many other writers say, that witches' night-wanderings are nothing but fantasies and dreams, then all the reports of their bargains, transportations, and meetings with Diana or Minerva <note>Goddesses often associated in folklore with the "Lady of the Night" who led spirits or witches on nocturnal journeys.</note> are but fables. And therefore, those who maintain that these actions are done in actual deed and truth—when in fact they are not done at all—are lying. It would be a wonder, on the one hand (if those things happened in dreams, which the witches nevertheless claim to be otherwise), that when those witches awake, they do not...

...they neither consider nor remember that they were in a dream. It would be a wonder if their ointments—which physicians say have no power at all to produce such effects, as even the Inquisitors <note>witch-hunters and judicial investigators</note> themselves admit—should have such an operation. It is a wonder that their ointments cannot be found anywhere, except only in the Inquisitors' books. It is a wonder that when a stranger is anointed with them, the ointments sometimes (though not always) have the same effect as they do on witches; which all the Inquisitors admit.
<margin>Bartolommeo della Spina, Questions on Witches, chapter 3. 31.</margin>
<margin>New matter and worthy of being wondered at.</margin>
But regarding this last point, Friar Bartholomew <note>original: "Fryer Bartholomew"; referring to the Italian Dominican Bartolommeo della Spina</note> says that the witches themselves, before they anoint themselves, hear a great noise of musicians <note>original: "Minſtrels"</note> in the night, who fly over them with the Lady of the Fairies, and then they prepare themselves for their journey. But then I wonder again why nobody else hears or sees this troop of musicians, especially when they are riding on a moonlit night. It is a wonder that those who believe this is only a dream can be persuaded that any of the rest is anything other than dreams. It is a wonder that in dreams, witches who are old acquaintances meet so precisely together and agree upon murders, and receive ointments, roots, powders, etc. (as believers in witchcraft <note>original: "Witchmongers"</note> report they do, and as they force the witches to confess) and yet they lie at home fast asleep. It is a wonder that such preparation is made for them (as Sprenger, Bartholomew, and Bodin report) in noblemen's houses as well as in alehouses; and that they come in dreams and eat up their food; and the alewife <note>a woman who manages an alehouse</note> especially is not bothered by them for not paying their bill, or for paying with imaginary money (which they say is not solid), and that they do not talk afterward about the bill and so reveal the matter. And 
<margin>The Golden Legend: Life of Saint Germain.</margin>
it is the greatest wonder of all that the landlady <note>original: "Hoſteſs"</note> does not sit among them and take part in their good cheer. For the truth is, if any part of these meetings and their league is true, it is just as true and as certainly proved and confessed that there is constant monthly preparation made for this assembly at some alehouse or gentleman's house—as appears in the story of Saint Germain <note>Referring to a legend where St. Germain discovered "witches" were actually demons mimicking local people during a feast</note>.

->CHAPTER 10.<-

->*That most of the prophecies in the Old Testament were revealed in dreams; that we are not to look for such revelations now; regarding some who have dreamt of things that have come to pass; that dreams often prove to be the opposite of reality. Nebuchadnezzar's rule for identifying a true interpreter of dreams.*<-

<margin>1 Kings 3:5, 15.</margin>
<margin>1 Kings 9:5.</margin>
<margin>Isaiah 6.</margin>
<margin>Ezekiel 12.</margin>
<margin>Jeremiah 13.</margin>
It is held and maintained by many, and gathered from the 12th chapter of *Numbers*, that everything written or spoken by the prophets among the children of Israel (Moses <note>original: "Miſes"</note> excepted) was presented to them through dreams. And indeed, it is clear that many things which are thought to have been physically completed were only performed through dreams and visions. For instance, when Solomon asked God for the gift of wisdom, that was (I say) in a dream. And also where he received the promise that the Kingdom of Israel would continue in his lineage. So was Isaiah's vision in the 6th chapter of his prophecy, as well as that of Ezekiel in the 12th. Finally, where Jeremiah was commanded to hide his belt <note>original: "girdle"</note> in the crack of a rock by the river Euphrates in Babylon, and after certain days it rotted there, this must have been in a dream; for Jeremiah was never (or at least not at that time) in Babylon. We who are Christians must not now slumber and dream, but watch and pray, and meditate upon our salvation in Christ both day and night. And if we expect revelations in our dreams now that Christ has come, we shall deceive ourselves; for in him all dreams and prophecies are fulfilled. However, Bodin <note>Jean Bodin, a prominent French jurist and writer on demonology</note> maintains that dreams and visions continue to this day in as miraculous a manner as they ever did.

<meta>The previous page discussed the psychological nature of witches' dreams and flights, arguing they are hallucinations. This page shifts focus to the deceptive practices of alchemists, using a story of a swindled yeoman to illustrate how "magic" is often just sleight of hand and fraud.
