### Hartumim <note>Hebrew: magicians or soothsayers</note>: Of Witchcraft, Chapter 3

Through **sleight of hand** <note>original: "Legierdemain"</note>, he placed another ball of the same size into the **Yeoman's** hand. This ball contained many more **Angels** <note>a high-value gold coin featuring the archangel Michael</note> than were in the ball the man thought he had received. Now, indeed, the **alchemist** told him to store that ball of **wax** and also to perform certain ceremonies (which I thought best to omit here). After several days, hours, and minutes, they returned together as planned and found great profits from the "multiplication" of the angels. Because he was a simple man, the Yeoman was convinced by this that he would not only have a rare and remarkably good son-in-law, but also a companion who could help increase his wealth and bring great fortune and happiness to his estate. To strengthen this opinion and win further favor—but especially to carry out his clever **alchemy**, or rather his wicked purpose—the alchemist told him it was foolish to multiply a single pound of **gold** when they could just as easily multiply a million. Therefore, he advised the man to produce all the money he had, or could borrow from neighbors and friends. He assured the Yeoman that he would multiply and increase it enormously, just as he had seen happen with the small sum before his eyes. <margin>A remarkable fool.</margin> Hoping for profit and advancement, this **Yeoman** agreed to this tempting proposal. He brought out and laid at the alchemist's feet not just half of his goods, but everything he owned, could earn, or could borrow in any way. Then this juggling **alchemist**, having achieved his goal, wrapped the money in a ball much larger than the previous one. Tucking it into his shirt or pocket, he handed another ball (as before) of the same size to the **Yeoman**, to be kept safely in his chest. Because the matter was so important, they each had a key and a separate lock, so that the **ceremony** would not be interrupted, and neither could cheat the other.

<margin>A swindling trick: running away to protect the reputation of the craft.</margin> Now, once these arrangements and **ceremonies** were finished and the **alchemist's** goal was met, he told the **Yeoman** that until the appointed day and hour of his return, they should both attend to their own business. The **Yeoman** went to his **plow**, and the alchemist to the **City of London**, while in the meantime, the **gold** supposedly multiplied. But the **alchemist** (likely having more important things to do) did not come back at the appointed hour, nor on the appointed day, nor even within the year. Although the **Yeoman** felt it was somewhat against his conscience to break his promise or violate their agreement, he was overcome by a longing to see and a desire to enjoy the results of that excellent experiment. For his own security and to satisfy others, he gathered witnesses to see his honest dealings at the opening. He broke open the chest, and lo, he soon saw the ball of **wax** which he had placed there with his own hand. He thought that, at the very least, he would find his original investment—and why wouldn't it have increased just like the previous one? But alas! When the **wax** was broken and the metal revealed, the **gold** was gone, and it had turned into plain lead.

### C H A P. IV.

*A certain King deceived by an Alchemist, and a clever joke by the King's Fool.*

<margin>A King deceived by Alchemy.</margin>
The second example concerns another alchemist who came to a certain King, promising to perform many great things through his art, both in compounding and transforming metals <note>original: "transubstantiating"</note>, and in executing other feats of no less wonder. But before he began, he found a way to receive, by virtue of the King's warrant, a large sum of money as an advance <term>original: "in prest"; money paid in advance to bind a contract</term>, assuring the King and his Council that he would shortly return and fulfill his promise, and so on. Soon after, the King's Fool, among other jokes, began a discussion and "discovery" of fools. He handled that common topic so pleasantly that the King began to take delight in it and to enjoy his merry mood. Whereupon, the King insisted that the fool deliver to him a list <note>original: "schedule"</note> or scroll containing the names of all the most excellent fools in the land.

So the fool caused the King's name to be set down first, and after him the names of all his Privy Council. The King, seeing him so bold and impudent <note>original: "saucy and malapert"</note>, intended to have him punished. However, some of his Council, knowing him to be a person of pleasant wit, besought His Majesty to ask him for the reasoning behind his satire <note>original: "Libell"</note> rather than to proceed with harsh punishment against him. Then the fool, being asked why he so boldly accused the King and his Council of principal folly, answered: "Because I saw one foolish knave beguile you all, and swindle you out of such a great mass of money, and finally escape beyond your reach." "Why," said one of the Council, "he may return and perform his promise." <margin>A wise fool.</margin> "Then," said the fool, "I can fix the whole matter easily." "How," said the King, "can you do that?" "Truly, Sir," said he, "then I will blot out your name and put in his, as the greatest fool in the world." Many other practices of a similar nature might be added here to detect their knavery and the deceits upon which this art depends. Through these, readers may find more delight in reading than the practitioners find benefit in simply using the art. For it is an art consisting entirely of subtlety and deceit, whereby the ignorant and plain-minded man is outwitted through his own excessive belief, and the whims of the other sly swindler are satisfied.

<margin>Erasmus in his dialogue on the art of Alchemy <note>original: "Eras. in colloqu. de arte Alchymistica"</note>.</margin>
The third example is reported by Erasmus, whose excellent learning and wit are held in admiration to this day. In a certain dialogue titled *The Alchemist* <note>original: "Alchymistica"</note>, he finely reveals the knavery of this crafty art. Another swindling priest noticed this and dealt with him in the following manner.

He had no sooner fingered the money but he ran merrily to the dice, to the alehouse, and to the brothels <note>original: "Stewes"</note>; and who there was as lively as the swindling Sir John! <note>original: "cousening Sir John"; "Sir John" was a common disparaging nickname for a priest.</note> Who indeed this way made a kind of alchemical transformation of money. Now Balbine urged him to go about his business, but the other told him that if the matter were once begun, it were half ended, for therein consisted the greatest difficulty.

Well, at length he began to prepare the furnace; but now, forsooth, a new supply of gold must be provided as the "seed" and "spawn" of that which must be engendered and grow out of this work of alchemy. For just as a fish is not caught without a bait, no more is gold multiplied without some portions of gold. And therefore gold must be the foundation and groundwork of that art, or else "all the fat is in the fire" <note>An idiom meaning all plans have failed.</note>. But all this while Balbine was occupied in calculating and musing upon his accounts, casting by arithmetic how if one ounce yielded fifteen, then how much profit two thousand ounces might yield—for he determined to invest that much in the project.

<margin>Balbine was bewitched with the desire for gold, etc.</margin>
When the alchemist had also consumed this money, showing great labor <note>original: "travell"</note> for a month or two in placing the bellows, the coals, and such other equipment, and not a bit of profit proceeded or came from it, Balbine demanded how the world went. Our alchemist acted like a man amazed. However, he said at length: "Truly, even as such matters of importance commonly go forward, whereunto there is always very difficult access." There was, he says, a fault (which he has now found out) in the choice of the coals, which were of oak and should have been of beech. One hundred ducats <note>original: "Duckets"; gold coins.</note> were spent that way, so that the gambling house and the brothels were partakers of Balbine's expenses. But after a new supply of money, better coals were provided, and matters were more circumspectly handled. However, when the forge had labored long and brought forth nothing, there was another excuse found out; namely, that the glass vessels were not tempered as they ought to have been. But the more money was disbursed on this, the less willing Balbine was to give up, according to the gambler's habit <note>original: "Dicers vein"</note>, whom fruitless hope brings into a fool’s paradise.

<margin>Notable swindling. <note>original: "cousenage"</note></margin>
The alchemist, to put a good face upon his knavery, acted like a man "moonsick" <term>moonsick: an archaic term for being lunatic or mentally unstable, often associated with the cycles of the moon.</term> and protested with grand words full of forgery and lies that he never had such luck before. But having found the error, he would be sure enough never hereafter to fall into the same oversight, and that henceforward all should be safe and sure, and thoroughly recompensed in the end with a large increase. Hereupon the workshop is now repaired for the third time, and a new supply of money yet once again put into the alchemist's hand so that the glasses could be changed. And now at length the alchemist uttered another point of his art and cunning to Balbine; namely, that those matters would proceed much better if he sent our Lady <note>The Virgin Mary.</note> a few French Crowns <note>Gold coins.</note> as an offering. For the art being holy, the matter cannot proceed prosperously without the favor of the saints. This counsel exceedingly pleased Balbine, who was so devout and religious that no day escaped him but he said the Matins <note>Morning prayers.</note> to our Lady.

<margin>The alchemist brings Balbine into a fool’s paradise.</margin>
Now our alchemist, having received the offering of money, goes on his "holy pilgrimage" even to the next village and there consumes every penny among prostitutes and scoundrels <note>original: "Bawds and Knaves"</note>. At his return, he told Balbine that he had great hope of good luck in this business; he claimed the holy Virgin gave such a favorable countenance and such an attentive ear to his prayers and vows. But after this, when there had been great labor bestowed and not a dram of gold yielded nor gathered from the forge, Balbine began to complain and reason somewhat sharply with the swindling fellow. The alchemist still said he never had such filthy luck in all his life before and could not imagine by what means it came to pass that things went so perversely <note>original: "overthwartly"</note>. But after much debating between them upon the matter, at length it came into Balbine's head to ask him if he had not neglected <note>original: "foreslowed"</note> to hear Mass, or failed to observe his prayer hours; for if he had done so, nothing could prosper under his hand. "Without doubt," said the swindler, "you have hit the nail on the head! Wretch that I am! I remember once or twice being..."

<margin>Here the alchemist utters a notorious point of swindling knavery.</margin>
Soon after this, when all our alchemist’s money was spent and his tricks for getting more had failed, he came home with a new device. He acted like a man wonderfully frightened and amazed, piteously crying and lamenting his misfortune. Balbine, being astonished, desired to know the cause of his complaint. "Oh," said the alchemist, "the Courtiers have discovered our enterprise! For my part, I expect nothing but immediate imprisonment." Balbine was terrified, because it was a clear felony <note>original: "flat fellony"</note> to engage in alchemy without a special license. "But," said the alchemist, "I do not fear being put to death—I almost wish it would happen. Truly, I fear instead that I shall be shut up in some castle or tower, and there be forced to toil at this work and sweat in this business for the rest of my days."

<margin>Mark how this alchemist goes from one degree of swindling to another.</margin>
Now, the matter being brought to consultation, Balbine—because he was skilled in the art of rhetoric and not altogether ignorant of the law—racked his brains devising how the accusation might be answered and the danger avoided. "Alas," said the alchemist, "you trouble yourself all in vain. You see the crime cannot be denied, for it is so generally rumored <note>original: "bruited"</note> in Court. Neither can the act be defended, because of the manifest law published against it." To be short, when many ways were devised and various excuses alleged by Balbine, and no sure ground was found for their security, the alchemist finally framed his speech this way (having a present need for money): "Sir," he said to Balbine, "we use slow counsel, yet the matter requires haste. For I think they are coming for me even now to haul me away to prison, and I see no remedy but to die valiantly in the cause." "In good faith," said Balbine, "I know not what to say to the matter." "Neither do I," said the alchemist, "except that I see these Courtiers are hungry for money, and are therefore much readier to be corrupted and persuaded to silence. And though it is a hard matter to give to those scoundrels <note>original: "rakehells"</note> until they are satisfied, I see no better counsel at this time." Neither could Balbine, who gave him thirty gold ducats to stop their mouths—a man who, in an honest cause, would rather have given thirty teeth out of his head than one of those pieces out of his pouch. The alchemist took this coin, though for all his pretenses and fine excuses, he was in no danger at all. His only "danger" was the lack of money to support his mistress <note>original: "Leman or Concubine"</note>, whose acquaintance he would not give up, nor forbear her company, for all the goods he was able to get, no matter how much indirect dealing and unlawful means it required.

Well, yet now once again does Balbine furnish the forge anew. A prayer was made beforehand to our Lady to bless the enterprise, and all things were provided and made ready according to the alchemist's own asking. All necessities were generously supplied according to his liking. However, after a whole year had been consumed in this useless <note>original: "bootless"</note> business and nothing had been achieved, a strange accident occurred by the following means, as you shall hear.

<margin>The mildest and softest nature is commonly soonest abused.</margin>
Our alchemist, you see, was having an extraordinary illicit affair with a Courtier’s wife while the husband was away from home. The husband, suspecting the matter, came to the door unexpectedly and demanded entry, threatening to break down the doors. He did this, though not without great hazard and some injury. But this was soon spread abroad <note>original: "blazed abroad"</note>, so that it came to Balbine’s ear. Balbine showed by his expression that he had heard of it, though he said nothing. But the alchemist knew him to be devout and somewhat superstitious, and knew that such men are easy to be persuaded to forgive, no matter how great the fault. Thus, he devised a way to open the matter in the following manner.

At this, Balbine—who otherwise seemed to have taken a vow of silence—took the opportunity to speak, saying, "It is not hard to know the hindrance and obstacle to this; for it is sin that hinders this matter, which must not be dealt with except with pure hands." From a priest I have become an adulterer. However, the money that was sent a while ago to our Lady was not utterly lost; for if she had not been there, I would certainly have been killed. For the master of the house broke open the door, and the window was smaller than I could fit through. In that extreme danger, it came into my mind to fall prostrate to the Virgin, beseeching her (if our gift were acceptable in her sight) that she would, in consideration of it, assist me with her help. Balbine not only believed this to be true but, because of it, forgave him, religiously advising him to show himself thankful to that pitiful and blessed Lady.

<margin>Balbine is ashamed that he should be outwitted and deceived in a case of outright swindling <term>original: "flat cousenage"</term>.</margin>
Now once again a new supply of money is made, and a mutual promise is made to handle this divine matter from now on purely and holily. To be short, after a great number of such parts were played by the alchemist, one of Balbine’s acquaintances saw him—someone who had known the man since childhood to be nothing but a swindling merchant <note>original: "cousening Merchant"</note>. He told Balbine who the man really was, and that he would treat him in the end just as he had used many others; for he had always been a knave, and so he would prove to be. But what do you think Balbine did? Did he complain about this counterfeit, or cause him to be punished? No, instead he gave him money for his purse and sent him away, desiring him, out of all courtesy, not to spread the news <note>original: "blab abroad"</note> of how he had swindled him. As for the knavish alchemist, he did not care who knew it or what came of it, for he had no goods or reputation to lose. And as for his skill in alchemy, he had as much as a donkey. By this discourse, Erasmus <note>This story is adapted from "The Alchemist" in Erasmus's *Colloquies*.</note> intends for us to notice that under the golden name of alchemy there lies lurking no small calamity. Within it, there are such various tricks and sets of rare subtleties and deceits that not only are wealthy men often impoverished by the sweet allurement of this art—driven by their own greed and the flattering baits of hoped-for gain—but even wise and learned men are shamefully outwitted here. This happens partly for want of enough experience in the wiles and subtleties of the world, and partly through the softness and flexibility of their good nature, which swindling knaves commonly abuse for their own lust and profit, leading to the other's utter ruin.

### CHAPTER VI.

### *The opinion of various learned men concerning the folly of Alchemy.*

<margin>The substances of things cannot be transformed <note>original: "transmutable"</note>.</margin>
Albert <note>Albertus Magnus (c. 1200–1280), a prominent philosopher and scientist.</note> in his book of Minerals reports that Avicenna <note>Ibn Sina (c. 980–1037), a Persian polymath whose medical and philosophical works were standard texts in Europe.</note>, treating of alchemy, says: "Let the dealers in alchemy understand that the very nature and kind of things cannot be changed, but rather made by art to resemble the same in appearance and likeness. So they are not the very things themselves, but only seem to be so in appearance; just as castles and towers seem to be built in the clouds, whereas the representations shown there are nothing else but the resemblance of certain objects below, reflected in some bright and clear cloud when the air is free of density and murkiness." A sufficient proof...

<summary>This page concludes the tale of Balbine, a victim of alchemy fraud who chooses to pay off his swindler to hide his own embarrassment, and introduces scholarly arguments from Albertus Magnus and Avicenna stating that alchemy can only mimic, not change, the true nature of substances.</summary>

<meta>This page continues a critique of alchemy, transitioning from a story of a specific swindle to broader scholarly and theological arguments against the practice, citing Petrarch and Godescalcus Hollen.</meta>

<header>Hartmanm of Witchcraft. CHAPTER VI.</header>

<margin>*Francis Petrarch, Book of Remedies for Both Good and Bad Fortune, Book 1, Chapter 10* <note>original: "Franc. Petrarch. lib. de remed. utr. fort. 1. cap. 10."</note></margin>
...of this, the looking glass may be an example. And we see (he says) that yellow or orange color laid upon red seems to be gold. Francis *Petrarch*, treating the same matter in the form of a dialogue, introduces a disciple of his who was fond of the aforementioned foolish profession and practice, saying, "I hope for prosperous success in alchemy <note>original: "Alchymistry"</note>." *Petrarch* answers him: "It is a wonder where that hope should spring from, since the fruit of it never yet fell to your lot, nor has it at any time happened to any other. As the report commonly goes, many rich men have been brought to beggary by this vanity and madness, while they have exhausted themselves, weakened their bodies, and wasted their wealth trying to find the means to make gold produce gold." "I hope for gold according to the workman's promise," says the disciple. "He who has promised you gold will run away with your gold, and you will be none the wiser," says *Petrarch*. "He promises me great good," says the disciple. "He will first serve his own turn and relieve his private poverty," says *Petrarch*. "For alchemists are a beggarly kind of people, who, though they admit themselves to be bare and needy, yet claim they will make others rich and wealthy—as if the poverty of others bothered and moved them to pity more than their own." These are the words of *Petrarch*, a man of great learning and no less experience. Just as he saw the fraudulent tricks of this deceptive craft in his own time, so there has been no age since this practice was first introduced in which a few wise men have not smelled out the evil intentions of these shifty merchants and exposed <note>original: "bewrayed"</note> them to the world.

<margin>*Godescalcus Hollen, of the Order of St. Augustine, in his 10th Precept, folio 244, columns b, c, d, & 1.* <note>original: "Goschalcus Boll. ordinis S. August. in suo præcepto 10. fol. 244. col. b. c. d. & 1." Godescalcus Hollen was a 15th-century German preacher.</note></margin>
<margin>No certain ground in the alchemical art.</margin>
An ancient writer of a religious Order, who lived over a thousand years ago <note>Hollen actually lived in the 1400s; the author likely miscalculated or used a faulty source.</note>, discovering the various types of thefts, after a long list, includes alchemists—whom he calls *falsifiers of metals and minerals* <note>original: "Falsificantes metallorum & mineralium"</note>, sorcerers, and counterfeiters of metals and minerals. He places them as deep in the category of thieves as any of the rest whose injurious dealings are brought to open trial. It is asked (says he) why the art of alchemy never proves to be, in effect, what it claims in theory and promise. The answer is ready: if gold might be made by art, then it would be necessary to know the manner and process of nature in generation, since art is said to imitate and counterfeit nature. Again, it is because of the inadequacy and imperfection of philosophy, especially concerning minerals; no such manner of proceeding has been set down by the consent and agreement of philosophers in writing regarding the true and undoubted effect of the same. Whereupon one supposes that gold is made of one kind of material in this way, others of another kind of material in that way. And therefore, it is a matter of pure chance if any attain the artificial application of the active and passive elements of gold and silver. Moreover, it is certain that mercury <note>original: "quicksilver"</note> and sulfur are the materials (as they term them) of metals, and the agent is heat, which directs them; however, it is very hard to know the due proportion of the mixture of the materials which the generation of gold requires. And even admitting that by chance they attain such a proportion, yet they cannot readily repeat or do it again in another work because of the hidden diversities of materials and the uncertainty of applying the active and passive elements.

<margin>*Ibid.*</margin>
<margin>*Greed is the worship of idols.* <note>original: "Avaritia idolorum cultus."</note></margin>
The same ancient author, concluding against this vain art, says that it is forbidden by all Christian lawmakers and is in no case tolerable in any commonwealth. First, because it presumes to forge idols out of greed <note>original: "covetousness"</note>, which are gold and silver; whereupon, says the Apostle, "Greed is idolatry." Secondly, because (as *Aristotle* says) coin should be scarce and rare so that it might be valuable <note>original: "dear"</note>; but the same would become cheap and held in small regard if, by the art of alchemy, gold and silver might be multiplied. Thirdly, because (as experience proves) wise men are thereby bewitched, swindlers <note>original: "couseners"</note> increased, princes abused, the rich impoverished, the poor beggared, the multitude made fools, and yet the craft and craftsmen (oh, madness!) are still believed. Thus far he speaks. By which, in few words, he discredits that profession, not by the imaginations of his own brain, but by many circumstances of manifest proof. Regarding this practice, I think enough has been spoken, and much more than was needed.

### CHAPTER VII.

->*That vain and deceitful hope is a great cause why men are seduced by this alluring art, and why their labors in it are useless, etc.*<-

<margin>Concerning vain hope.</margin>
Up to this point, I have exposed the trickery of the alchemical art at some length, partly through logic and partly through examples. In this way, the thing itself may appear as clearly to the discerning eye of the observer as the bones and sinews of a dissected body <note>original: "anatomized"</note> appear to the physical eye of the beholder. Now it will be neither inappropriate nor irrelevant to discuss the nature of that vain and fruitless hope, which draws men forward as if with ropes—not only to admiration, but also to approval of the craft. This happens to such an extent that some are compelled mournfully to sing (as one did in ancient times, though whether as a sign of good or bad luck, I do not now well remember):
> *Hope and good fortune, farewell; hope and good luck, adieu.* <note>original: "Spes & fortuna valete"</note>

<margin>John Calvin in his commentary on Deuteronomy, sermon 127, page 781, column 1, number 40.</margin>
<margin>A maxim.</margin>
It is no wonder, then, that alchemy <note>original: "Alchymistry"</note> allures men so sweetly and entangles them in the snares of folly, since the bait it uses is the hope of gold. The hunger for gold is termed *Sacred* <note>original: "Sacra"; Scot is referencing Virgil’s "auri sacra fames," where "sacra" carries the double meaning of "holy" and "cursed"</note> by the poet. Some translate this as "Holy," not understanding that it should rather be interpreted as *Cursed* or *detestable*. This uses the figure of speech *Acyron* <note>a Greek rhetorical term for using a word improperly or with an opposite meaning</note>, where a word carrying a contrary meaning is placed in a sentence like a cloud; or by the figure *Antiphrasis*, when a word carries a meaning opposite to its common one. For what reason can there be that the hunger for gold should be counted holy, when so many millions of mischiefs and miseries depend upon it? These include treasons, thefts, adulteries, murders <note>original: "manslaughters"</note>, broken treaties, perjuries, swindlings <note>original: "cousenages"</note>, and a great troop of other outrages that would take too long to list here. And if the nature of every action is judged by its result, then this hunger cannot be holy, but rather accursed. It pulls along after it, as if with iron chains, such a band of outrages and crimes that after all their labor, expense, care, and cost, etc., they have nothing left in place of profit except a few burned bricks from a ruined furnace, a peck or two of ashes, and similar worthless stuff. They are perhaps eventually forced to sell these things when poverty has arrested them and laid his mace on their shoulders <note>Scot personifies Beggary as a bailiff or officer who arrests a debtor by tapping them on the shoulder with a ceremonial staff or mace</note>. As for all their gold, it has dissolved into its primary matter <note>original: "In primam materiam"</note>, or rather into a light puff of smoke <note>original: "In levem quendam fumulum"</note>—a mist of vapors. Nothing is lighter than this, and nothing has less substance, except for spirits, from whose nature and number these fumes are not to be excluded.

->*A continuation of the previous subject, with a conclusion of the same.*<-

<margin>Erasmus in the dialogue titled *The Fabulous Feast* <note>original: "Convivium fabulosum"</note>.</margin>
What I have explained before through logic, examples, and authoritative sources, I will now follow up and conclude with one more example. My goal is that we, like others in former ages, may judge vain hope for what it is and be no less cautious to avoid its inconveniences than Ulysses was wary to escape the enchantments of Circe, that transforming witch. This example of mine is drawn from Louis <note>original: "Lewis"</note> the French King, the eleventh of that name. While he was once in Burgundy, he became acquainted during a hunt with a man named Conon, a rustic but honest and hearty good fellow. For princes and great men take much delight in such plain, simple folk <note>original: "clubhutchens"</note>. Because of his hunting, the King often used the countryman's house for his refreshment;

## CHAPTER 13.
### Regarding the Objects Upon Which Augurers Used to Prognosticate <term>Prognosticate: To predict or formalize a prophecy about future events.</term>, with Certain Cautions and Notes.

<margin>Pliny, *Natural History*, Book 10, Chapter 6.</margin>
<margin>Aristotle, *On Auguries*.</margin>
The Pagans <note>original: "Gentiles"</note>, who write about this matter, list a countless number of objects from which they predict good or bad luck. A great deal is made of sneezing, where the number of sneezes and the time they occur are carefully noted. Tingling in the finger, the elbow, the toe, or the knee are also specific signs to be observed in this "art." However, the flight of birds <note>original: "Fowls"</note> and the meeting of wild animals <note>original: "Beasts"</note> are especially marked, with this general rule: the object or event used for divination must be sudden and unexpected. This is the same concern children and some foolish elderly people have when gathering primroses, herb-paris <note>original: "True-loves"—a plant with four leaves arranged like a lover's knot, often used in folk magic.</note>, and four-leaf clovers. Other factors include: the person who encounters such an object unexpectedly; the intention of the diviner (which determines how the object met is interpreted as an omen); and the hour in which the object is suddenly met without prior knowledge, and so forth.

Pliny reports that griffon vultures <note>original: "Gryphes." Pliny's *Natural History* 10.6 discusses vultures (*vultur*) following armies.</note> always fly to the place of a slaughter two or three days before a battle is fought; this was supposedly seen and proven at the Battle of Troy. Because of this, the vulture was considered the primary bird of augury. But among the countless types of omen-bearing animals, birds, serpents, and other creatures, the toad is the most excellent object. Its ugly deformity is said to signify sweet and pleasant fortune; because of this, some superstitious witches keep toads as their "familiars" <term>Familiars: Supernatural spirits, often in animal form, believed to assist a witch.</term>. Indeed, someone of good reputation (whom I could name) who has converted the witches themselves, has starved several of their "devils," which they kept in boxes in the form of toads.

<margin>Plutarch of Chaeronea <note>original: "Plutarch Cheronæus"</note> is mistaken here, despite all his learning.</margin>
Plutarch of Chaeronea says that the location and site of the signs we receive by augury are especially important. If we receive them on the left side, it means good luck; if on the right side, ill luck follows. He argues this is because earthly and mortal things are opposite to divine and heavenly things: that which the Gods deliver with their right hand falls to our left side, and vice versa.

## CHAPTER 14.
### The Classification of Augury; Persons Admissible into the Colleges of Augury; Regarding Their Superstition.

<margin>Agostino Nifo, *On Auguries*, Book 3 <note>original: "Aug. Niphus de Auguriis, lib.3."</note>.</margin>
Later diviners in these mysteries have divided their soothsaying into twelve "superstitions," as Agostino Nifo <note>An 15th-century Italian philosopher.</note> calls them. The first is prosperity. The second is ill luck, such as when someone leaves their house and sees an unlucky animal lying on the right side of the path. The third is destiny. The fourth is fortune. The fifth is mishap, such as when an unfortunate animal feeds on the right side of your path. The sixth is utility. The seventh is harm. The eighth is called a precaution <note>original: "cautel"</note>, such as when an animal follows someone and stops at their side without passing them, which is a sign of good luck. The ninth is unhappiness, which is the opposite of the eighth—when the animal passes in front of the person. The tenth is perfection. The eleventh is imperfection. The twelfth is confusion. So far, this is his account.

<margin>Who were not admissible into the College of Augurers among the Romans.</margin>
Among the Romans, no one could be admitted into the College of Augurers if they had a boil, or had been bitten by a dog, and so on. During their rituals, even at high noon, they lit candles. From this practice, the Catholics <note>original: "Papists"</note> carry over those points of unfaithfulness <note>original: "infidelity"</note> into their own Church. Finally, their observations were so endless and ridiculous that even a spark flying out of a fire was thought to mean something.

The author also links these ancient practices to contemporary Catholic rituals to discredit them.</summary>

### CHAP. XV.
->Of the Common People's Foolish and Superstitious Beliefs and Observations.<-

<margin>O empty folly and foolish vanity!</margin>
Among us, there are many women and weak-minded men (certainly Catholics <note>original: "Papists"</note> always, as their superstition shows) who make grand predictions based on the spilling of salt, wine, etc. In their observation of days and hours, they use as much witchcraft as in anything else. For if someone happens to fall from a horse, whether on a slippery path or by stumbling, he will record the day and hour and consider that time unlucky for travel. Otherwise, anyone who encounters misfortune will wonder if they met a cat or a hare when they first left their house in the morning; or if they stumbled at the threshold on their way out; or put their shirt on inside out; or their left shoe on their right foot—which Augustus Caesar considered the worst luck that could happen. But above all other nations (as <margin>Martin de Arles in his *Treatise on Superstition against Sorcery* <note>original: "tract. de Superst. contra maleficia"</note>.</margin> Martin de Arles testifies), the Spaniards are the most superstitious in this regard; and within Spain, the people of the province of Portugal <note>original: "Lusitania"</note> are the most foolish. For one will say, "I had a dream tonight," or "A crow croaked on my house," or "An owl flew by me and screeched" (an omen <note>original: "Augury"</note> that Lucius Sulla believed led to his death), or "A rooster crowed at the wrong time." Another says, "The moon is new <note>original: "at the prime"</note>;" another, "The sun rose in a cloud and looked pale," or "A shooting star shone in the air," or "A strange cat came into the house," or "A hen fell from the roof." Many will go back to bed if <margin>Trivial omens <note>original: "Augurifical toyes"</note>.</margin> they sneeze before their shoes are on their feet; some will grip their left thumb in their right hand when they have the hiccups <note>original: "hickot"</note>; or else they will hold their chin with their right hand while a Gospel reading is sung in church. Some think it is very bad luck if a child, or any other living creature, passes between two friends as they walk together, for they say it foretells a break in their friendship. Among the Catholics themselves, if hunters happened to meet a friar or a priest while hunting, they thought it such bad luck that they would leash their hounds and go home, despairing of any further sport that day. Indeed <note>original: "Marry"</note>, they believed that if they had had sex <note>original: "used venery"</note> with a beggar, they would win all the money they gambled for that day at dice. This same kind of folly should be attributed to those who observe (as true or likely) old verses, for which there can be no logical reason—outcomes which are brought about only by God’s power and at his pleasure. Of this sort are those that follow:

# Augury and Augurers. Of Witchcraft. CHAPTER 16.

Translated into English by *Abraham Fleming*:
*If Mary’s purification day* <note>original: "Maries purifying day." This refers to Candlemas, celebrated on February 2nd.</note>
*Be clear and bright with sunny rays,*
*Then frost and cold shall be much more*
*After the feast than was before.*

A red sky late in the day indicates tomorrow will be clear;
If it grows red in the morning, the wind or rain increases.
<note>original: "Serò rubens cœlum cras indicat esse serenum; Si manè rubescit, ventus vel pluvia crescit." This is a version of the common "Red sky at night, shepherd's delight" proverb.</note>

Translated into English by *Abraham Fleming*:
*The sky being red at evening,*
*Foreshows a fair and clear morning;*
*But if the morning rises red,*
*With wind or rain we shall be supplied.*

<margin>The word Habar.</margin>
Some stick a needle or a buckle into a certain tree near the Cathedral Church of St. Christopher, or some other Saint, hoping thereby to be delivered that year from the headache. <term>Item</term><note>Latin: "Also" or "Furthermore."</note>, maids, indeed, hang some of their hair before the image of St. Urban because they want the rest of their hair to grow long and be yellow. <term>Item</term>, pregnant women run to Church and tie their girdles or shoe-latchets about a bell, and strike it three times, thinking that the sound of it hastens their successful delivery. But since these things begin to touch upon the vanities and superstitions of incantations, I will refer you to the place where you shall see an abundance of that material, beginning at the word *Habar* <note>original: "Habar." A term often associated with charming or "binding" through incantations, derived from Hebrew.</note>.

### CHAPTER 16.
*How ancient writers vary about the matter, the manner, and the means by which things related to augury are moved.*

<margin>Averroes, 12th book of Metaphysics.</margin>
Theophrastus and Themistius affirm that whatever happens to man suddenly and by chance comes from the Providence of God. Thus, Themistius concludes that men prophesy in that respect when they speak what comes into their brain suddenly, even though they do not know or understand what they say. And since God has a care for us, it agrees with reason (as Theophrastus says) that he shows us by some means whatever shall happen. For, along with Pythagoras, he concludes that all omens and auguries are the voices and words of God, by which he foretells to man the good or evil that shall happen.

Trismegistus <note>Hermes Trismegistus, a legendary Hellenistic figure associated with hermetic philosophy.</note> affirms that all things related to augury are moved by demons; Porphyry says by Gods, or rather good Angels, according to the opinion of Plotinus and Iamblichus. Some others affirm they are moved by the Moon wandering through the twelve signs of the Zodiac, because the Moon has dominion over all sudden matters. The Egyptian astronomers hold that the Moon does not order those ominous matters, but rather a wandering star <note>original: "Stella errans." In ancient astronomy, this referred to a planet.</note>, etc.

# BOOK 15. The Discovery of Magical Circles.

Woods where anyone has killed themselves, churchyards, burial vaults, and similar places are chosen for certain spirits. So also for all types of spirits, the places where they live ought to be chosen when they are called: such as pits, caves, and hollow places for subterranean spirits; the tops of turrets for aerial spirits; ships and rocks of the sea for spirits of the water; and woods and mountains for fairies, nymphs, and satyrs—following the same order for all the rest.

<margin>The form of a circle.</margin>
And just as the places must be known, so must the manner in which the circles are to be drawn be perfectly understood. First, for infernal spirits, let a circle nine feet across be made with black, and within it another circle half a foot away, leaving half a foot of both these circles open for the magician and his assistant to enter. Between these circles, write all the holy names of God all the way around, with crosses and triangles at every name. Also, make a larger triangle on one side of the circle on the outside in this manner, with the names of the Trinity at the three corners: namely, *Jehovah* <note>original: "Pehovah." Likely a typographical error for "Jehovah," the Latinization of the Hebrew Tetragrammaton.</note>, *Holy Spirit* <note>original: "Ruah Kedesh." From the Hebrew "Ruach HaKodesh."</note>, and *Immanuel* <note>Hebrew: "God is with us."</note>, written in the little circles.

<image-desc>A line drawing of a triangle with a small circle at each of its three vertices.</image-desc>

<margin>The reason for circles.</margin>
The reason that magicians give for circles and their institution is that ground being blessed and consecrated by holy words has a secret force to expel all evil spirits from its boundaries. When sprinkled with holy water that has been blessed by the master, the ground is purified from all uncleanness. Furthermore, the holy names of God written all around have a very powerful force, so that no wicked spirit has the ability to break through into the circle after the master and student <note>original: "Scholler"</note> have entered and closed up the gap, because of the antipathy the spirits have for these mystical names. The reason for the triangle is that if the spirit is not easily brought to speak the truth, they may be commanded by the exorcist to enter the triangle, where, by virtue of the names of the Sacred Trinity, they can speak nothing but what is true and right.

But if astral spirits—such as fairies, nymphs, and the ghosts of men—are called upon, the circle must be made with chalk, without any triangles. Instead of triangles, the magical character <note>A symbolic seal or sigil associated with a specific occult force.</note> of the element to which they belong must be drawn at the end of every name.

### CHAPTER II.
#### How to raise up the Ghost of one who has hanged himself.

This experiment must be put into practice while the corpse still hangs; and therefore the Exorcist <note>In this context, an "exorcist" is one who summons or commands spirits, rather than one who casts them out.</note> must seek out the straightest hazel wand that he can find. To the top of the wand, he must bind the head of an owl, along with a bundle of St. *John’s Wort*, or *Mille-perforatum* <note>original: "Milliës Perforatum." Latin for "thousand-perforated," referring to the tiny translucent oil glands in the leaves of St. John's Wort.</note>. Once this is done, he must be informed of some miserable creature who has strangled himself in a wood or desolate place (which they rarely fail to do). While the corpse hangs, the magician must go to the aforementioned place at 12 o'clock at night and begin his conjurations in the following manner.

First, stretch forth the consecrated wand towards the four corners of the world, saying:
<margin>The ceremonies of Necromancy.</margin>
> *By the mysteries of the deep, by the flames of Banal <note>This may be a corruption of "Belial" or a specific name used in this tradition.</note>, by the power of the East, and the silence of the night, by the holy rites of Hecate <note>The Greek goddess of magic, witchcraft, and the night.</note>, I conjure and exorcize you, you distressed spirit, to present yourself here and reveal to me the cause of your calamity: why you offered violence to your own life, where you are now in being, and where you will be hereafter.*

Then, gently striking the corpse nine times with the rod, say:
> *I conjure you, spirit of this N. <note>A placeholder for the name of the deceased, from the Latin "Nomen."</note> deceased, to answer the demands that I am to propose to you, as you ever hope for the rest of the holy ones and the ease of all your misery; by the blood of Jesus which he shed for your soul, I conjure and bind you to utter to me what I shall ask you.*

Then, cutting down the corpse from the tree, lay its head toward the East. While the following conjuration is being repeated, set a chafing-dish <note>A portable heater or brazier for hot coals.</note> of fire at its right hand. Into this, pour a little wine, some mastic <note>A resin obtained from the mastic tree.</note>, and aromatic gum; and lastly, a vial full of the sweetest oil. Have also a pair of bellows and some unlit charcoal to make the fire burn brightly at the moment the corpse rises. The conjuration is this:

<margin>The Conjuration.</margin>
> *I conjure you, spirit of N., that you immediately enter into your former body again and answer my demands, by the virtue of the holy resurrection and by the posture of the body of the Savior of the world. I conjure you; I command you on pain of the torments and wandering of thrice-seven years—which I, by the power of sacred magic rites, have power to inflict upon you. By your sighs and groans, I conjure you to utter your voice; so help you God and the prayers of the holy Church. Amen.*

When this conjuration has been repeated three times while the fire is burning with mastic and aromatic gum, the body will begin to rise, and at last, will stand upright before the Exorcist, answering with a faint and hollow voice the questions proposed to it: why it strangled itself; where its dwelling is; what its food and life is; how long it will be before it enters into rest, and by what means the magician may assist it to find rest. Also, it can tell of the treasures of this world and where they are hidden. Moreover, it can answer very precisely about the places where ghosts reside and how to communicate with them, teaching the nature of astral spirits <note>In occultism, the "astral" is a plane between the physical and the spiritual; astral spirits were thought to be linked to the stars or the ethereal body.</note> and hellish beings, as far as its capacity allows.

<margin>How to lay the Spirit.</margin>
When the ghost has fully answered all these things, the magician ought—out of pity and reverence for the deceased—to use whatever means can possibly be used to procure rest for the spirit. To this effect, he must dig a grave and, filling it half-full of quicklime, a little salt, and common sulfur, put the naked corpse into it. This experiment—next to burning the body to ashes—is of great force to quiet and end the disturbance of the astral spirit.

But if the ghost with whom the Exorcist consults is of one who died a common death and received the ceremonies of burial, the body must be dug out of the ground at 12 o'clock at night; and the magician must have a companion...

### CHAPTER III.

#### How to raise up the three spirits Paymon, Bathin, and Barma: and what wonderful things may be achieved through their assistance.

<margin>Their order.</margin>
The spirit *Paymon* rules over the power of the Air; he is the sixteenth in the rank of <term>Thrones</term> <note>One of the nine orders of angels in traditional celestial hierarchy.</note> and is subordinate to *Corban* and *Marbas*.
*Bathin* has a deeper reach within the source of fire; he is the second after *Lucifer’s* familiar and has no equal for speed and friendliness in the entire <term>Infernal Hierarchy</term> <note>The organized ranking system of demons or fallen spirits.</note>.
*Barma* is a mighty ruler of the order of <term>Seraphim</term> <note>The highest rank of angels, often associated with light and fire.</note>, whom twenty legions of infernal spirits obey. His power is to transform the magician or whomever he pleases and to transport them into foreign countries.

These three spirits, though of various ranks and orders, are all of the same power, ability, and nature, and the method for raising them all is the same. Therefore, the magician who desires to consult with any of these spirits must appoint a night during the time of the waxing moon <note>The period when the moon is growing from new to full, traditionally associated with "bringing forth" or "increasing" magic.</note> when the planet Mercury is dominant, at eleven o'clock at night. He must not bring any companion with him, because this particular ritual allows for none. For the space of four days before the appointed night, he ought to shave his beard and change into clean linen every morning. He must provide in advance the two **Seals of the Earth** <note>Magical symbols or talismans representing earthly power.</note> drawn exactly upon parchment and have his consecrated girdle ready, made of a black cat's skin with the fur still on it, with these names written on the inner side of the girdle: **Lord, Lord ✠ I Am, I Am ✠ Elibza ✠ God ✠ Almighty ✠ Lord ✠ I am girded with your strength ✠** <note>original: "Ya, Ya ✠ Aie, Aaie ✠ Elibza ✠ Elohim ✠ Saday ✠ Pah Adonay ✠ tuo robore ✠ Cinctus sum ✠"</note>.

<margin>The tools to be used.</margin>
Upon his shoes must be written **The Four-Letter Name of God** <note>original: "Tetragrammaton," the Hebrew name of God, YHWH.</note>, with crosses all around, and his garment must be a black priestly robe with a friar's hood and a Bible in his hand.

<margin>The circle.</margin>
When all these things are prepared, and the exorcist has lived chastely and in seclusion until the appointed time, let him prepare a clean parlor or cellar with every crack and window closed. Then, lighting seven candles and drawing a double circle with his own blood (which he must have prepared in advance), let him divide the circle into seven parts. He must write these seven names at the seven divisions, placing a lighted candle in a brass candlestick at each name in the space between the circles. The names are: **Holy ✠ I Am ✠ Anick ✠ Sabbac ✠ Sagun ✠ ✠ Father ✠ Abalidoth** <note>original: "Cados ✠ Escherie ✠ Anick ✠ Sabbac ✠ Sagun ✠ ✠ Aba ✠ Abalidoth"</note>.

### CHAPTER IV.

### How to Consecrate all manner of Circles, Incense <note>original: "fumigations"</note>, Fire, Magical Garments, and Tools.

<margin>What things are to be consecrated.</margin>
Consecrations relate either to the person or the thing being consecrated. The person is the magician himself, whose consecration consists of abstinence, temperance, and holy garments. The things consecrated are the oil, the fire, and the water; the incense <note>original: "fumigations"</note> consisting of oriental gums and spices; the magical sword, pencils <note>original: "pensils"</note>, pens, and compasses; the measuring rule and wax candles <note>original: "tapers"</note>; the pentacles, amulets <note>original: "periapts"</note>, metal plates <note>original: "lamins"</note>, and symbols <note>original: "sigils"</note>; and the robes <note>original: "vests"</note>, caps, and priestly garments. These are the materials to be consecrated.

<margin>Pentacles.</margin>
The sacred pentacles serve as signs and charms for the binding of evil spirits <note>original: "dæmons"</note>. They consist of characters and names from the superior order of good spirits—those who are opposite to the evil ones the magician is about to summon <note>original: "invocate"</note>. They also include sacred pictures, images, and mathematical figures suited to the names and natures of spiritual beings <note>original: "separated substances"</note>, whether good or evil. Now, the method of consecrating such magical pentacles is to name the power of the holy names and figures, their ancient origins <note>original: "antiquity"</note>, and their purpose. The magician purifies the pentacle with consecrated fire, waving it over the flames.

<margin>Tools <note>original: "utensils"</note>.</margin>
When the exorcist wishes to consecrate places or tools, fire or water for magical uses, he must repeat the consecration or dedication used by King Solomon at the building of the Temple, the vision of Moses at the Burning Bush, and the "Spirit of the Lord on the tops of the mulberry trees" <note>A biblical reference to 2 Samuel 5:24, signifying divine intervention</note>. He should also mention the sacrifice that caught fire on its own, the fire that fell upon Sodom, and the Water of Eternal Life. In this, the magician must still remember to speak of the seven golden candlesticks and Ezekiel's wheels, closing the consecration with the deep and mysterious names of God and holy spirits.

<margin>Instruments.</margin>
When particular instruments are to be sanctified, the magician must sprinkle them with consecrated water, perfume them with incense, and anoint them with consecrated oil. Lastly, he must seal them with holy characters <note>Sacred symbols or letters</note>;

### CHAPTER V.

*Treating more practically of the consecration of circles, fires, garments, and fumigations.*

<margin>How circles are to be made.</margin>
In the construction of magical circles, the hour, day, or night, the season of the year, and the constellation are to be considered; as also what sort of spirits are to be called, and to what region, air, or climate they belong. Therefore, this method is to be followed for a more orderly and certain proceeding. First, a circle nine feet wide must be drawn; within which, another circle three inches from the outermost must also be made. In the center of this, you must place the name of the hour, the angel of the hour, the seal of the angel, and the angel of the day that is predominant when the work is undertaken. Note: these attributes are to be inscribed between the circles all the way around, with Alpha <note>Greek: "The Beginning"</note> at the beginning, and Omega <note>Greek: "The End"</note> at the close.

<margin>Incense <note>original: "Fumigations"</note>.</margin>
When the circle is composed, it must be sprinkled with holy water while the magician says:
> *Wash me, O Lord, and I shall be whiter than snow.* <note>original: "Asperges me," a reference to Psalm 51</note>

And as for the incense burned over them, this blessing must be said:
> *O God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, bless these your subservient creatures, so that they may multiply the force of their excellent odors to hinder evil spirits and phantoms from entering the circle. Through our Lord, Amen.*

#### ->*An exorcism for the fire.*<-

<margin>Fire.</margin>
The exorcist ought to have an earthen censer <note>a vessel for burning incense</note> in which to keep the fire for magical uses, and the purifications and incense offerings, the consecration of which is done in this manner:
> *By Him who created Heaven and Earth, and is the God and Lord of all, I exorcize and sanctify you, you creature of fire, so that you may immediately banish every phantom from you, and so that you prove not harmful in any kind. This I beseech you, O Lord, to confirm by sanctifying and making pure this creature of fire, that it may be blessed and consecrated to the honor of your holy name. Amen.*

#### ->*Upon putting on the garments,*<-

<margin>Garments.</margin>
Let the magician say:
> *By the symbolic mystery of this holy stole <note>a liturgical vestment</note> or garment, I will clothe myself with the armor of salvation in the strength of the Highest. Ancor, Amacor, Amides, Theodonias, Anitor <note>traditional magical names of power</note>. May my desired end be achieved through your strength, Lord <note>original: "Adonai," Hebrew for Lord</note>, to whom the praise and glory will forever belong.*

<margin>Practice.</margin>
When these ceremonies are finished, the exorcist shall proceed to the practical part of invocation and conjuration of all degrees of spirits, having every utensil and accessory in readiness for the performance, and proceeding according to the method in the following chapters.

### CHAPTER VI.

#### ->*How to raise and exorcise all sorts of Spirits belonging to the Airy Region.*<-

<margin>What sort of garments must be used.</margin>
The garment with which the exorcist is clothed during the performance of this ritual should, according to the opinions of the foremost magicians, be a priestly robe. If this cannot be obtained anywhere, it may be a neat and clean linen vest <note>original: "Vest," here referring to a ritual tunic or robe</note>, with the holy pentacle <note>a talisman or magical symbol, often inscribed on a disk</note> fastened to it upon parchment made of a kid’s skin. Over this, an invocation must be said, and then the pentacle must be sprinkled with holy water. Upon putting on the magical garment, this prayer must be repeated:
> *By your holy power,* **Lord of Hosts** <note>original: "Adonai Sabaoth"</note>, *and by the power and merit of your Angels and Archangels, and by the virtue of the holy Church, which you have sanctified, I clothe myself with this consecrated garment, so that what I am to practice may take effect through your Name, you who live forever and ever.*

<margin>The manner of conjuring.</margin>
Now, regarding the time of operation and the manner of it, the instructions set down previously are sufficient to direct the exorcist. However, the practitioner and his student must be mindful while on the way to the place of conjuration to repeat the sacred forms of consecrations, prayers, and invocations. One shall carry an earthen vessel with consecrated fire, and the other shall carry the magical sword, the book, and the garments. When they approach near the place where the circle is to be drawn, they must then proceed to construct it in the manner described before. Finally, they shall exorcise the spirits in the following manner:

<margin>The form.</margin>
> *Seeing that* **God** *has given us the power to crush the serpent’s head and command the Prince of Darkness, even more so do we have the power to rule over every airy spirit. Therefore, by his strong and mighty Name,* **Jehovah**, *I conjure you (naming the spirits), and by his secret commands delivered to Moses on the Mount, and by his holy Name,* **the Four-Lettered Name** <note>original: "Tetragrammaton," referring to the Hebrew name of God, YHWH</note>, *and by all his wonderful Names and Attributes:* **The Almighty, The Most High, Emilla, The Immortal, The Comforter** <note>original: "Sadai, Elion, Emilla, Athanatos, Paracletos," titles for God in Hebrew and Greek</note>, *etc. I command that you immediately appear here before this circle in human form, and not in a terrible or monstrous shape, on pain of the eternal misery that awaits you unless you quickly fulfill my commands:* **Bathar, Baltar, Archin, Anakim, Pakun.** *Amen.*

<margin>The apparitions.</margin>
When the exorcist has finished this conjuration, he and his companion shall continue constantly turning themselves to the East, West, North, and South, saying, with their caps in their hands, **Gerson, Anek, Nephaton, Basannah, Cabon**. Within a short time, they will behold various apparitions upon the ground and in the air, with various clothing, shapes, and instruments. After that, he will perceive a troop of armed men with a threatening demeanor appear before the circle; however, after they are conjured to cease their illusions, they will finally present themselves before the exorcist in human form.

Then the master must be mindful to take the consecrated sword and the cup of wine into his hands. He shall pour the wine into the fire and brandish the sword in his right hand, being girded about with a scarlet ribbon. After this, the magician shall say, **Gahire, Gephna, Anepheraton**. Then the spirits will begin to bow to the exorcist, saying, *"We are ready to fulfill your pleasure."*

Once the magician has brought the spirits to this point, he may ask whatever he desires, and they will answer him, provided the questions belong to the order of spirits they represent.

<margin>What these spirits can do.</margin>
The abilities in which they excel are these: they can grant the gift of invisibility and the foreknowledge of changes in the weather; they can teach the exorcist how to stir up storms and tempests, and how to calm them again; they can bring news within an hour of the outcome of any battle, siege, or naval engagement, no matter how far away it is; they can also teach the language of birds and how to fly through the air invisibly.

### Chapter IV
*Why God forbade the practice of witchcraft; the absurdity of the Law of the Twelve Tables, upon which the belief in their miraculous actions is based; concerning their wondrous works.*

<margin>A common and universal error.</margin>
Though it is apparent that the Holy Spirit <note>original: Holy-Ghost</note> forbade this art because of the abuse of the Name of God and the deception <note>original: "cosenage" (cozenage); fraud or trickery</note> involved in it, I admit that the customs and laws of almost all nations declare that all these miraculous works I have mentioned—and many other even more wonderful things—were attributed to the power of witches. These laws, along with the executions and judicial proceedings based on them, and the witches themselves, have deceived almost the whole world. What absurdities concerning witchcraft are written in *The Law of the Twelve Tables* <note>The earliest code of Roman law, c. 450 BCE</note>, which was the highest and most ancient law of the Romans? The strongest argument for the witches' all-powerful strength is built upon this, suggesting that the wisdom of such lawmakers could not be mistaken <note>original: "abused"; in this context, misled or deceived</note>. 

In my opinion, a stronger argument could be made on our side: namely, if the chief and principal laws of the world are ridiculous, vain, false, incredible, and even contrary to God's law in this case, then the rest of the laws and arguments for that effect are to be suspected. If that argument for the authority of ancient law were held to be true, it might prove all the Popish <note>Catholic</note> laws against Protestants, and the laws of pagan <note>original: Heathenish</note> princes against Christians, to be good and valid; for they would not have made them unless they were good. Would it not be a strange proclamation (in your opinion) that no man, under pain of death, should pull the moon out of heaven? And yet many of the most learned "witch-mongers" <note>Those who believe in or promote the idea of witches</note> base their arguments on even weaker grounds. For example, they argue: "We find in the works of poets that witches performed such-and-such miracles; therefore, they can accomplish this or that wonder." 

The words of the law are these: "Whoever shall have enchanted crops shall pay the penalty. Nor shall you lure away another's grain by enchanting it, nor shall you make a field barren" <note>original: *Qui fru-ges incantaffet poenas dato. Neve alienam segetem pelli xeris excantando, neg. Ne agrum defruganto*</note>. The meaning of this in English is: Let him be executed who bewitches corn; do not transfer other men's corn into your own ground by enchantment; take care that you do not enchant at all, nor make your neighbor's field barren; he who does these things shall die, etc.

### Chapter V
*An instance of one brought to trial based on the Law of the Twelve Tables, where the said law is proved ridiculous; concerning two witches who could do wonders.*

<margin>A notable defense <note>original: "purgation"; a legal clearing of guilt</note> of Gaius Furius Cressinus <note>original: C. F. Crassus; Pliny records the name as C. Furius Chresimus</note>, who was accused of being a witch.</margin>
Although among us, we think people are bewitched when they suddenly become poor, rather than when they grow quickly rich, you should understand that in Rome (as Pliny reports) a man named Gaius Furius Cressinus was brought to trial <note>original: "converted," likely a typo for "convented," meaning summoned to court</note> before Spurius Albinus based on these laws. Because he had been free from slavery <note>original: "bondage"</note> for only a short time and worked only in farming <note>original: "tillage"</note>, he grew rich suddenly because he had such good crops. Thus, it was suspected that he transferred his neighbors' corn into his own fields. No plea, no delay, no excuse, no denial—whether made in jest, through mockery, or through serious and honest means—would help him. He was assigned a specific day to answer for his life. # BOOK XV. The Discovery of the Conjuring of Luridan, etc.

> *Elanel.* You who ride upon the wings of the wind, and are mighty and powerful in your heavenly and celestial <note>original: "super-lunary"; literally "above the moon," meaning belonging to the higher, perfect heavens</note> motion, descend and be present, I pray you. I request of you, if I have ever deserved your company, or if my actions and intentions be pure and holy before you, bring your physical presence here and speak with your humble student. By the tears of Saints and Songs of Angels, in the name of the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost, who are one God forever and ever.

This prayer, being first repeated toward the East, must afterwards be said three times toward all four winds. Next, the 70th Psalm should be repeated from a Bible that has been consecrated in the same manner as the rest of the tools. Once these ceremonies are performed seriously, the magician must rise from his knees and sit before the crystal bare-headed, with the consecrated Bible in his hand and the wax candles newly lit, waiting patiently and inwardly for the arrival and appearance of the *Genius* <note>original: "Genius"; a guardian spirit or tutelary deity assigned to a person at birth</note>.

<margin>Signs of the appearance.</margin>
Now, about fifteen minutes before the spirit arrives, a great variety of visions and sights will appear within the glass. First, a well-worn road or path will appear, with travelers—men and women—marching silently along. Next, rivers, wells, mountains, and seas will appear. After that, a shepherd on a pleasant hill feeding a fine flock of sheep, with the sun shining brightly as it sets. Finally, there will be countless displays of birds and beasts, monsters and strange sights, noises, flashes of light <note>original: "glances"</note>, and frightening things; all of these sights will finally vanish when the *Genius* appears.

<margin>The Appearance.</margin>
And then the *Genius* will present itself in the middle of the crystal, in the exact same clothing and likeness as the person [the magician] himself, giving instructions to the exorcist on how to lead his life and correct his actions.
But especially (which is the proper work of every *Genius*), he will touch the person's heart and open his senses and understanding, so that by this means he may attain knowledge of every art and science which, before the opening of his intellect, was locked and kept secret from him.
After this, the *Genius* will be accessible <note>original: "familiar"</note> in the stone at the prayer of the magician.

### CHAPTER VIII.

->A form of conjuring *Luridan* the familiar spirit, otherwise called *Bezelah*.<--

<margin>The nature of Luridan.</margin>
Luridan is a familiar domestic spirit of the North, who has now become a servant to *Balkin*, Lord and King of the Northern Mountains. He calls himself the *Astral Genius* of *Pomonia* <note>The Roman name for the Mainland of the Orkney Islands</note>, an island among the *Orkney Islands* <note>original: "Orcades"</note> beyond Scotland. But he does not reside there exclusively; for in the days of Solomon and David, he was in Jerusalem (or Salem), then using the name *Bezelah*. After that, he came over with Julius Caesar and remained for some hundreds of years in *Cambria* (Wales), instructing their prophetic poets in British rhymes; at that time, he was surnamed *Urthin-Wadd Elgin*. From there, he moved to this island in the year 1500 and stayed for 50 years, after which he surrendered his rule to *Balkin* and has remained an attendant to this prince ever since.

<margin>His Office.</margin>
He is a spirit of the air in the order of *Glauron*, and is said to reproduce as mortals do. He is often sent by his master on errands to Lapland, Finland, and *Strik-finia* <note>original: "Strik-finia"; likely referring to Scritfinia, an archaic name for the region of the Sami people in Northern Scandinavia</note>, as well as to the northernmost parts of Russia bordering the Arctic Ocean. His job (when called by magicians) is to demolish the strongholds of enemies, destroying every night what they built the day before; to extinguish fires, and to make their gunpowder <note>original: "Gunshot"</note> so it cannot be ignited; for his nature is to be an enemy of fire. Under his master's command, he leads many legions in continuous wars against the fiery spirits that inhabit Mount *Hecla* in Iceland, where they attempt to put out those volcanic flames while the resident spirits defend the flames from his master and his legions.

# The Discovery of Witchcraft. CHAPTER VIII.

<margin>Spiritual warfare.</margin>
In these contests, the spirits often completely wipe out and destroy one another, killing and crushing each other when they meet in massive and violent armies in the air or upon the sea. During such times, many of the fiery spirits are destroyed when the enemy has lured them away from their mountain to fight upon the water. Conversely, when the battle takes place on the mountain itself, the spirits of the air are often defeated. Following these battles, great mourning and sorrowful noises are heard throughout Iceland, Russia, and Norway for many days afterward.

->*How to Conjure the Spirit Balkin, the Master of Luridan.*<-

<margin>The names of Olympic Angels.</margin>
As instructed in the previous chapter, the conjurer is told to draw the shape of Mount Hecla within the circle. He must have also been very continent and chaste for three days before carrying out his plan. When the appointed night approaches, he must take an earthen pan with fire in it, a little vial containing some of his own blood, and some of the gum or resin from a fir tree.

# BOOK 15. The Discovery of the Spirit Balkin, etc.

When he is thus bound, he will dismount from his goat and cause his attendants to move further into the valley; then he will stand peacefully before the circle to answer the magician.

After this, the magician shall begin to demand into his own possession a <term>familiar</term> <note>original: "Familiar"; a servant spirit believed to assist a magician</note> to build or pull down any castle or stronghold in a single night. He shall also demand that this familiar bring with him the **Girdle of Conquest** <note>A magical belt intended to grant the wearer victory in all conflicts</note>, so that the magician, being girded with it, may overcome all enemies whatsoever.

Likewise, if the <term>exorcist</term> <note>In this context, one who summons or controls spirits rather than one who casts them out</note> inquires concerning the dwellings of "starry spirits," he will readily answer him, describing their hierarchy, food, life, and pastimes truly and exactly.

After the magician has satisfied himself with inquiries and curious questions to the spirit, there will come from among the company a little spirit about a <note>original: "span long"; a span is approximately nine inches</note> nine inches long, looking like a small **Ethiopian** <note>original: "Ethiop"; in early modern magical texts, spirits were often described by skin color or ethnicity</note>. The great King **Balkin** will deliver this spirit to the exorcist to remain as a familiar with him for as long as his life shall last. The owner may name this familiar whatever he pleases.

The last three people who possessed this spirit were three **Northern Magicians**: the first was **Honduros**, a Norwegian, who called it **Philenar** and commanded it at his pleasure with a little bell.

After him, **Benno**, his eldest son, enjoyed the same spirit under the same name.

And **Swarkzar**, a Polish priest, was the last who possessed it under the name **Muncula**. All of these names were given to it according to the pleasure of the masters; therefore, the naming of this familiar is left to the judgment of the exorcist.

Now, when the master has taken this familiar into his custody and service, the spirit **Balkin** will desire to depart, becoming weary if the ritual continues longer than an hour. Therefore, the magician must be careful to dismiss him using this following form:

> *Because you have diligently answered my demands and been ready to come at my first call, I do here license you to depart to your proper place, without injury or danger to man or beast. I say: be ever ready at my call when duly exorcised and conjured by the sacred rites of magic. I charge you to withdraw in quiet and peace; and let peace be continued between me and you, in the Name of the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost. Amen.*

Then the spirit’s company will begin to march around their prince, and in a formal troop, they will march along the valley, while the magician repeats the **Lord's Prayer** <note>original: "Pater Noster"</note>, etc., until the spirits are quite out of sight and have vanished.

This is a complete form of conjuring the aforementioned spirit, according to the rules of **Vaganostus** the Norwegian.

# CHAPTER 10

->*The explanation of Iidoni, and where it is found, by which the whole Art of Conjuration is revealed.*<-

<margin>The broad meaning of the word Iidoni.</margin>
<margin>See Philaster, Bishop of Brescia, *Catalogue of Heresies*, regarding the Pythoness <note>original: "Vide Philast. Brix. Episc. haereseon catal. de Phitonissa"</note>.</margin>
<margin>Johann Weyer in the *False Hierarchy of Demons* <note>original: "J. Wierus in Pseudomonarchia daemonum"</note>.</margin>
This word **Iidoni** <note>original: "Iidoni"; a transliteration of the Hebrew 'Yidde’oni,' typically translated as 'wizard' or 'one who has a familiar spirit'</note> is derived from **Iada** <note>original: "Iada"; the Hebrew root 'yada,' meaning 'to know'</note>, which properly signifies "to know." It is sometimes translated as **Diviner** <note>original: "Divinus"</note>, which is a soothsayer, as in Deuteronomy 18 and Leviticus 20. Sometimes it is translated as **Soothsayer** <note>original: "Ariolus"</note>, which is one who also takes it upon himself to foretell things to come, and is found in Leviticus 19, 2 Kings 23, and Isaiah 19. To be brief, the opinion of those most skillful in the languages is that it encompasses all those who take it upon themselves to know all things past and future, and to give answers accordingly. It always follows the word **Ob** <note>original: "Ob"; a Hebrew term referring to a medium or a "spirit of divination"</note>, and in the Scriptures it is not named separately from it; it differs little from it in sense, as both concern oracles uttered by spirits, possessed people, or <term>cheats</term> <note>original: "Cozeners"</note>. 

What will cheats or witches not take upon themselves to do? In what will they admit ignorance? Ask them any question, and they will undertake to resolve it for you, even those things which none but God knows. And to bring their purposes to a better result, as well as to win further credit for the counterfeit art they profess, they recruit confederates to help them work "wonders." When they have either learning, eloquence, or nimbleness of hands to accompany their secret cooperation—or rather, their knavery—then they move beyond the rank of common witches and entitle themselves with the name of **Conjurers**. 

These people deal with no minor matters. They summon devils out of Hell and angels out of Heaven; they raise up whatever bodies they wish, even if they were dead, buried, and rotten long ago; and they fetch souls out of Heaven or Hell with much more speed than the Pope brings them out of Purgatory. These people, I say (among the simple-minded, and where they fear no law or accusation), also take upon themselves the raising of tempests and earthquakes, claiming to do as much as God himself can do. These are no small-time fools; they do not go to work with a <term>paltry toad</term> <note>original: "baggage Toad"; "baggage" was an Elizabethan term for something worthless or low-status</note> or a cat as witches do. Instead, they act with a kind of majesty and authority, calling up by name and having at their command seventy-nine principal and princely devils, who have under them as their ministers a great multitude of legions of petty devils; for example:

# CHAPTER 11

->*An Inventory of the Names, Shapes, Powers, Government, and effects of Devils and Spirits; of their several lordships and ranks; a strange discourse worth the reading.*<-

<margin>Solomon’s notes on Conjuration. Baell.</margin>
Their first and principal King (who holds power in the East) is called **Baell**. When he is conjured up, he appears with three heads: the first like a toad, the second like a man, and the third like a cat. He speaks with a hoarse voice and makes a man go invisible. He has under his obedience and rule sixty-six legions of devils.

<margin>Agares.</margin>
The first Duke under the power of the East is named **Agares**. He comes up mildly in the likeness of a handsome old man, riding upon a crocodile and carrying a hawk on his fist. He immediately teaches all manner of languages. He fetches back all those who run away and makes those who are standing still run. He overthrows all dignities, both supernatural and <term>earthly</term> <note>original: "temporal"</note>. He causes earthquakes and belongs to the **Order of Virtues** <note>A rank in the traditional hierarchy of angels; Scot is noting that these demons were believed to be fallen angels from that specific rank</note>, having thirty-one legions under his command.
