# BOOK XV. The Discovery of Conjurers Confuted.

<margin>See the title of the Book, with the Author's intent, in a marginal note on page 277.</margin>
...and John Cockars, invented and devised for the increase and maintenance of their livelihood, for the edification of the poor, and for the propagating and enlarging of God’s glory—as they protest at the beginning of their *Book of Conjurations*. I thought it good to insert their claims here for the further manifestation of their impiety, and of the witchmongers' <note>original: "Witchmongers" — Scot’s term for those who credulously believe in and promote the persecution of witches.</note> folly and credulity, so that the rest of their proceedings may be judged or rather detected. For if we seriously behold the matter of conjuration and the goal of conjurers, we shall find them, in my opinion, more faulty than those who take it upon themselves to be witches. They are manifest offenders against the Majesty of God and His holy Law, and apparent violators of the laws and peace of this Realm—although indeed they bring no such things to pass as are surmised and urged by credulous persons, cozeners <note>original: "coſeners" — swindlers or cheats</note>, liars, and witchmongers. For these conjurers are always learned, and are abusers of others rather than being abused by others themselves.

<margin>Luke 16, etc.</margin>
But let us see what appearance of truth or possibility is wrapped within these "mysteries," and let us unfold the deceit. They have made choice of certain words, by which they say they can work miracles, etc. And first of all, they claim to call devils and souls out of Hell (even though we find in the Scripture manifest proofs that all passages are stopped concerning the exit from Hell). One may go there, but they shall never get out, for *out of hell there is no redemption* <note>original: "Ab inferno nulla est redemptio"</note>. Well, when they have supposedly gotten them up, they shut them in a circle made with chalk, which is so strongly beset and environed with crosses and names that the spirits cannot get out for their lives—which is a very likely story indeed. <margin>An ironic refutation.</margin> Then they claim they can bind them and loosen them at their pleasure, and make those who have been liars from the beginning tell the truth; yes, they claim they can compel them to do anything. And the Devils are supposedly forced to be obedient to these men, and yet cannot be brought to due obedience unto God their Creator. This done, I say, they claim they can work all manner of miracles (except for "blue miracles," or those that are truly impossible) <note>original: "blew miracles" — a phrase meaning something completely nonsensical or impossible</note>, and this is believed by many to be true:

->*So light of belief is the mind of man,*<-
->*And attentive to tales his ears now and then.*<-
-><note>original Latin: "Tam credula mens hominis, & arrecta fabulis aures." Englished by Abraham Fleming.</note><-

But if Christ (only for a time) left the power of working miracles among his Apostles and Disciples for the confirmation of his Gospel and the faith of his elect, yet I deny altogether that he left that power with these knaves. They hide their cheating purposes under those wicked and foolish words, according to what Peter says: <margin>2 Peter 2; Ephesians 5; Psalms 72 & 78; Wisdom 16; Ecclesiasticus 43.</margin> *With feigned words they make merchandise of you* <note>meaning: they exploit you for profit</note>. And therefore the counsel is good that Paul gives us, when he bids us, *Take heed that no man deceive us with vain words; for it is the Lord only who works great wonders and brings mighty things to pass.* It is also written that God’s Word—and not the words of conjurers or the charms of witches—heals all things, creates tempests, and stills them.

<margin>To deny the existence or natural being of a visible, material thing is shamelessness.</margin>
But suppose the Devil could be fetched up, fettered, and loosed again at their pleasure, etc. I marvel yet that anyone can be so "bewitched" as to be made to believe that by virtue of their words, any earthly creature can be made invisible. We think it a lie to say that white is black, and black white; but it is a more shameless assertion to affirm that white "is not," or black "is not" at all. It is even more impudent to hold that a man is a horse; but it is the most apparent impudence to say that a man is no man, or to be thinned out into such a size that he may be invisible and yet remain in life and health—and that in the clear light of day, even in the presence of those who are not blind. But surely he who cannot make one hair white or black—of which, on the other hand, not one falls from the head without God’s special...

### CHAPTER XXXI.

->A Comparison between Catholic <note>original: "Popish"</note> Exorcists and other Conjurers; a Catholic Conjuration published by a great Doctor of the Roman Church; his rules and cautions.<-

<margin>Jacobus de Chusa in the book *Concerning the Apparitions of Certain Spirits* <note>original: "lib. de apparitiouib. quorundam spirituum"</note>.</margin>
**I** see no difference between these and Catholic <note>original: "Popish"</note> conjurations; for they agree in order, words, and subject matter, differing in no circumstance except that the Catholics do it openly without shame, while the others do it in secret and in the dark <note>original: "hugger mugger"</note>. The Catholics (I say) have officers for this purpose, who are called Exorcists or Conjurers, and they keep a narrow watch on other swindlers <note>original: "cofenours"</note>, as if they have gained the upper hand over them. And so that the Catholics shall be without excuse in this matter, and so the world may see their deception <note>original: "cofenage"</note>, impiety, and folly to be as great as the others, I will cite one conjuration (of which sort I could cite a hundred) published by *Jacobus de Chusa*, a great Doctor of the Roman Church. It is used to find out the cause of noise and spiritual rumbling in houses, churches, or chapels, and to conjure wandering spirits—which is always trickery and deception of the highest degree. Mark the deceptive device here, and compare its impiety with the others.

<margin>Observations for the exorcising priest.</margin>
First (forsooth) he says it is necessary to fast for three days, to celebrate a certain number of Masses, and to repeat the seven Penitential Psalms. Then four or five priests must be called to the place where the haunting or noise is; then a candle hallowed on Candlemas day must be lighted, and during the lighting, the seven Psalms and the Gospel of *St. John* must also be recited. Then there must be a cross and a censer with frankincense, and with those the place must be censed or perfumed; holy water must be sprinkled, and a holy stole must be used. After various other ceremonies, a prayer to God must be made in the following manner and form:

> *O Lord Jesus Christ, the knower of all secrets, who always reveals all wholesome and profitable things to your faithful children, and who allows a spirit to show himself in this place: we beseech you, by your bitter Passion, etc., deign to command this spirit to reveal and signify to us, your servants, without terrifying or hurting us, who he is—to your honor and to his comfort;* In the Name of the Father <note>original: "In Nomine Patris"</note>, *etc. And then proceed in these words: We beseech you, for Christ’s sake, O spirit, that if there be any of us, or among us, whom you would answer, name him, or else manifest him by some sign. Is it Friar P., or Doctor D., or Doctor Burc., or Sir Feats, or Sir John, or Sir Robert?* And so on for the others standing around <note>original: "Et sic de cæteris circumstantibus"</note>.

<margin>Note that he must be the biggest rogue or fool in all the company.</margin>
For it is well tested (says the commentary <note>original: "glofs"</note>) that he will not answer everyone. If the spirit makes any sound of voice or knocking at the naming of any person, he is the swindler <note>original: "Cofenour"</note> (the Conjurer, I should say) who must take charge of this conjuration or examination. And these, forsooth...

### CHAPTER XXXII.

#### *A recent experiment or fraudulent <note>original: "cofening"</note> Conjuration practiced at Orleans by the Franciscan Friars; how it was detected, and the Judgment against the authors of that comedy.*

<margin>A fraudulent conjuration.
Read noble stuff about this order in a book printed at Frankfurt under the title *The Franciscan Alcoran* <note>original: "Alcoran Franciscanorum" — a famous anti-Franciscan satire comparing their rules to the Quran.</note>.</margin>

In the year of our Lord 1534, at Orleans in France, the Mayor's wife died, wishing and desiring to be buried without any pomp or noise, etc. Her husband, who honored her memory, did exactly as she had asked him. And because she was buried in the Church of the Franciscans, alongside her father and grandfather, and gave them a reward of only six crowns—whereas they had hoped for a greater prey—shortly afterward it happened that as he felled certain woods and sold them, they asked him to give them some part of it for free, without payment, which he flatly denied. They took this very poorly. And whereas before they disliked him, now they conceived such displeasure that they devised this means to be revenged: namely, to claim that his wife was damned forever.

The chief workmen and framers of this tragedy were Colimannus and Stephanus of Arras <note>original: "Stephanus Aterbatensis," likely referring to Étienne d'Arras.</note>, both Doctors of Divinity. This Colimannus was a great Conjurer and had all his implements ready, which he was accustomed to use in such business. <margin>Note how the Franciscans cannot conjure without a partner in crime <note>original: "confederate"</note>.</margin> And this is how they handled the matter: they placed a young novice over the arches of the church. About midnight, when they came to mumble their prayers as they were accustomed to do, he made a great rumbling and noise. Immediately, the monks began to conjure and to charm, but he answered nothing. Then, being required to give a sign whether he were a "dumb spirit" or not, he began to rumble again; which they took as a certain sign.

Having laid this foundation, they went to certain citizens—chief men and those who favored them—declaring that a heavy misfortune had happened at home in their monastery. They did not show what the matter was, but desired the men to come to their Matins <note>Midnight prayers.</note> at midnight. <margin>O notorious impudence! To abuse such a respectable company with such shameless faces!</margin> When these citizens had come and prayers had begun, the counterfeit spirit began to make a marvelous noise in the top of the church. And being asked what he meant and who he was, he gave signs that it was not lawful for him to speak. Therefore, they commanded him to make answer by tokens and signs to certain things they would demand of him. Now, there was a hole made in the vault, through which he could hear and understand the voice of the Conjurer. And then he had in his hand a little board, which he struck at every question in such a way that he might easily

### Book 15. of Witchcraft. CHAPTER 32.

<margin>\* The accomplice playing the spirit <note>original: "confederate spirit"</note> had been coached on his part beforehand.</margin>

<margin>Otherwise the accomplice might have been discovered.</margin>

The noises could easily be heard from below. First, they asked him, \* *Whether he was one of those who had been buried in the same place?* Afterwards, reckoning many people by name who had been buried there, they finally named the Mayor’s wife; and immediately the spirit gave a sign that he was her soul. He was further asked, *Whether he was damned or not; and if he were, for what cause, for what deed or fault? Whether it was for covetousness, or wanton lust, for pride or want of charity? Or, whether it was for heresy, or the Sect of Luther newly sprung up?* Also, *What did he mean by that noise and the stir he kept there? Whether it was to have the body now buried in holy ground dug up again and laid in some other place?* To all these points he answered by signs, as he was commanded, by which he affirmed or denied anything according to whether he struck the board twice or thrice together. 

And when he had thus given them to understand that the very cause of his damnation was *Luther's Heresy*, and that the body must be dug up again, the monks requested the citizens (whose presence they had used, or rather abused) to bear witness to those things which they had seen with their eyes, and to sign a document recording what had been done. The citizens, taking good advice on the matter and fearing they might offend the Mayor or bring themselves into trouble, refused to do so. 

But the monks nonetheless took from that place the consecrated bread—which they call the Host and body of our Lord—along with all the relics of Saints, and carried them to another place to say their Mass. The Bishop’s substitute judge (whom they called the **Official**) <note>term: **Official** — the presiding judge of an ecclesiastical court</note>, hearing of the matter, came there accompanied by several honest men to investigate the circumstances more closely. Therefore, he commanded them to perform a **Conjuration** <note>term: **Conjuration** — a formal ritual to summon or command a spirit</note> in his presence. He also required certain men to be chosen to go up into the top of the vault to see whether any ghost appeared or not. **Etienne d'Arras** <note>original: *Stephanus Aterbatensis*</note> stubbornly denied that this was lawful, and argued strongly against it, affirming that the spirit should in no way be disturbed. And although the Official urged them very much to allow a conjuring of the spirit, he could not prevail.

<margin>An obstinate and willful persistence in denying or refusing to confess a fault committed.</margin>

While these things were happening, the Mayor—after he had showed the other justices of the city what he wanted them to do—traveled to the King and opened the whole matter to him. Because the monks refused to be judged by civil law, pleading their own Church laws and liberties <note>original: "privileges" — referring to "benefit of clergy," where churchmen claimed they could only be tried in ecclesiastical courts</note>, the King chose certain aldermen of **Paris** and gave them absolute and full authority to inquire into the matter. The Chancellor, Master **Antoine Duprat** <note>original: *Anthonius Pratensis*</note>, who was a Cardinal and Legate for the Pope throughout France, did the same. 

Therefore, when the monks had no further excuses to offer, they were taken to Paris and forced to give their answer. However, nothing could be wrung out of them by confession, so they were placed in separate prisons. The novice—who was being kept in the house of Master Fumanus, one of the aldermen—was examined many times and earnestly requested to tell the truth. Nevertheless, he would confess nothing because he feared that the monks would afterward put him to death for staining their order and bringing it to open shame. 

But when the judges gave him a firm promise that he would escape punishment and never again be handed over to the monks, he revealed the whole matter as it had been done; and being brought before his fellows, he confirmed the story to their faces. Although the monks were convicted and almost caught red-handed <note>original: "taken tardy with the deed doing"</note>, they still rejected the judges, bragging and boasting about their religious privileges—but all in vain. For sentence was passed upon them, and they were condemned to be carried back to **Orléans** and cast into prison. Finally, they were to be brought out into the chief church of the city and then to the place of execution, where they would make an open confession of their crimes.

Surely this was most common among monks and friars, who maintained their religion, their lust, their liberties, their pomp, their wealth, their reputation, and their knavery by such trickery <note>original: "cozening"</note> practices.

Now I will show you more specific orders of Catholic <note>original: "Popish"</note> conjurations, which are so shamelessly admitted into the Church of Rome that they are not only allowed but commanded to be used—and not secretly by night, but boldly by day. These, forsooth, concern the curing of bewitched persons and those who are possessed—namely, those who have had a Devil put into them by witches' enchantments. ### C H A P. XXXIII.

->*Who may be conjurers in the Roman Church besides priests; a ridiculous definition of superstition; what words are to be used and not used in exorcisms; rebaptism allowed; it is lawful to conjure anything; differences between holy water and conjuration.*<-

<margin>Ibid. 4. dist. 23. sent. <note>A citation to a theological commentary on the "Sentences" of Peter Lombard.</note></margin>
Thomas Aquinas <note>A hugely influential 13th-century theologian and Doctor of the Church.</note> says that anyone, even if they are of an inferior or superior rank, or even of no rank at all—and as Guillaume Durand <note>original: "Gulielmus Durandus"</note>, the commentator on Raymond <note>Likely Raymond of Penyafort, a prominent canon lawyer.</note>, affirms, even a woman, provided she does not bless the belt or the garment but the person of the bewitched—has the power to perform the role of an exorcist or conjurer, just as a priest may say Mass in an unconsecrated house. "But that power," says the *Malleus Maleficarum* <note>original: "M. Mal."; the "Hammer of Witches," a famous 15th-century manual for witch-hunters.</note>, "comes more through the goodness and license of the Pope than through the grace of the Sacrament." Indeed, examples are recorded where some who were bewitched were cured (as the *Malleus Maleficarum* tells it) without any conjuration at all. To be sure, there were certain *Pater Nosters* <note>Our Fathers</note>, *Aves* <note>Hail Marys</note>, and *Credos* <note>Creeds</note> said, and crosses made; but they say these are "charms" and not "conjurations." For they claim that such charms are lawful because there is no superstition in them, etc.

And it is worth my effort to show you how Catholics define superstition and 
<margin>And the commentary on that passage at Colossians 2.</margin>
how they explain its definition. "Superstition," they say, "is a religion observed beyond measure; a religion practiced with evil and imperfect circumstances." Also, "whatever usurps the name of religion through human tradition, without the Pope's authority, is superstitious: such as adding or joining any hymns to the Mass, interrupting any funeral dirges, shortening any part of the Creed while singing it, or singing when the organs play instead of when the choir sings, not having someone to help the priest at Mass, and such things, etc."

<margin>Liars must have good memories, and even more so must cunning exorcists. <note>original: "Mendaces debent esse memores, multo magis astuti exorcistae."</note></margin>
These Catholic exorcists often forget their own rules. For they should not directly call upon the Devil in their conjurations with entreaty (as they do), but with authority and command. Neither should they have any unknown names in their charms and conjurations. Neither should there be (as there always is) any falsehood contained in the matter of the charm or conjuration—as they say old women have in theirs, when they say the Blessed Virgin passed over the Jordan, and then Saint Stephen met her and asked her, etc. Neither should they have any other vain symbols <note>original: "Characters"</note> except the Cross (for those are the words); and they have many other such cautions which they do not observe, for they have made it lawful elsewhere.

<margin>Thomas Aquinas on the last part of Mark. Mark 16:17.</margin>
But Thomas, their chief pillar, proves their conjuring and charms are lawful by Saint Mark, who says, "These signs shall follow those who believe," <note>original: "Signa eos qui crediderunt"</note> and, "In my name they shall cast out devils," <note>original: "In nomine meo dæmonia ejicient"</note> etc. By this, he also proves that they may conjure serpents. And there he takes pains to prove that the words of God are of as great holiness as the relics of saints; whereas (in the sense they mean it) they are both alike, and indeed worth nothing. And I can tell them further, that both may be used in such a way that either of them may do a person much harm in both body and soul.

First, the person or thing in which the Devil resides must always be exorcised, and then the Devil must be conjured. They also affirm that it is as useful to consecrate and conjure *soup* <note>original: "Pottage"</note> and *meat* as it is to conjure *water* and *salt*, or other such things.

<margin>Rites, ceremonies, and relics of exorcism in the rebaptizing of the possessed or bewitched.</margin>
The correct order of exorcism in the rebaptism of a person possessed or bewitched requires that the exsufflation <note>original: "Exsufflation"; the ritual act of breathing or blowing upon a person to drive away spirits</note> and the renunciation <note>original: "Abrenunciation"</note> be performed facing the West. *Also*, there must be the raising of hands, confession, profession of faith, prayer <note>original: "Oration"</note>, blessing <note>original: "Benediction"</note>, the laying on of hands, stripping <note>original: "Denudation"</note>, and anointing <note>original: "Unction"</note> with holy oil after baptism, followed by communion and the donning <note>original: "Induition"</note> of the surplice <note>a white liturgical vestment</note>. But they say this is not necessary where the bewitched person is exorcised; instead, the bewitched person should first confess and then hold a candle in their hand. In place of a surplice, they should tie a holy candle around their bare body that is the "length of Christ" <note>Talismans measured to Christ's supposed height were common medieval charms</note> or of the Cross upon which he died—which may be purchased for money at *Rome*. *Therefore* (says the *Malleus Maleficarum*), this may be said: *I conjure you, Peter (or Barbara), being sick but reborn in the holy water of baptism, by the living God, by the true God, by the holy God, by the God who redeemed you with his precious blood, that you may be made a conjured person; that every fantasy and wickedness of Diabolical deceit avoid and depart from you, and that every unclean Spirit be conjured through him who shall come to judge the living and the dead, and the world by fire, Amen.* *Let us pray* <note>original: "Oremus"</note>, etc. And this conjuration, along with the prayer, must be repeated three times, and at the end, it must always be said: *Therefore, cursed Devil, acknowledge your sentence* <note>original: "Ergo maledicte diabole agnosce sententiam tuam"</note>, etc. 

<margin>Note that this is for one who is bewitched.</margin>
Therefore, cursed Devil, acknowledge your sentence, etc. This order must always be followed: and finally, a diligent search must be made in every corner, under every coverlet and straw mattress <note>original: "pallet"</note>, and under every threshold of the doors for instruments of witchcraft; if any are found, they must be immediately thrown into the fire. Also, they must change all their bedding, their clothing, and their home; and if nothing is found, the party that is to be exorcised or conjured must come to the church early <note>original: "rath"</note> in the morning. The holier the day is, the better, especially Lady Day <note>The Feast of the Annunciation, March 25</note>. And the priest, if he has confessed himself and is in a perfect state of grace, shall be more effective. Let the person who is exorcised hold a holy candle in their hand, etc. Always provided that the holy water be <margin>Note the proviso.</margin> thrown upon him and a stole put about his neck, while saying, *God, come to my aid* <note>original: "Deus in adjutorium"</note>, along with the Litany and the invocation of Saints. This order may continue twice a week so that (as they say) through the multiplication of intercessors—or rather, intercessions—grace may be obtained and favor procured.

There is also some question in the *Roman* <note>original: "Romish"</note> Church whether the Sacrament of the Altar is to be received before or after the exorcism. *Also*, in confession, the priest <note>original: "Confessor"</note> must learn whether the person is excommunicated and is enduring this torment because they lack absolution. *Thomas Aquinas* shows the difference between <margin>Thomas Aquinas, commentary on the Sentences, book 4, distinction 6.</margin> holy water and conjuration, saying: *Holy water drives the Devil away from the external and outward parts, but conjurations drive him from the internal and inward parts; and therefore, both are to be applied to the bewitched party.*

Sixth, for purgation; seventh, for the spiritual merit of the person bewitched. And look, the first four reasons are proven by Matthew chapter 7 and Mark chapter 4 <note>The author likely refers to the stories of healing found in Matthew 17 and Mark 9, as the chapters cited do not contain this specific story</note>, where a man presented his son, and the crowd lacked faith, and the father said, *Lord, help my unbelief*. Whereupon it was said, *O faithless and perverse generation, how long shall I be with you?* and where these words were written, *And Jesus rebuked him*, etc.—that is to say (they claim), he rebuked the possessed or bewitched person for his sins. For by the neglect of proper remedies, it appears that there were no good and perfect men with Christ; for the pillars of the faith—namely Peter, James, and John—were absent. For the fourth point—namely, the lack of faith in the exorcist—it appears that afterward the disciples asked the cause of their inability to perform the cure. For the proof of the sixth excuse, it is said that though the fault may be removed, it does not always follow that the punishment is released. Last of all, it is said that it is possible the devil was not conjured out of the person before baptism by the exorcist, or the midwife did not baptize him correctly, but omitted some part of the sacrament. If anyone objects, saying there were no exorcists in the early Church, it is answered that the Church cannot now err, and St. Gregory would never have established the office in vain. And it is a general rule that anyone or anything that is newly exorcised must be rebaptized, as must those who walk or talk in their sleep; for (they say) if you call them by their names, they immediately wake up, or fall if they are climbing, from which it is gathered that they were not truly named in baptism. Also <note>original: *Item*</note>, they say it is somewhat more difficult to conjure the devil out of someone who is bewitched than out of someone who is possessed, because in the bewitched person the devil is "double," whereas in the other he is single. They have a hundred such poor, foolish, and frivolous notes on this subject.

### CHAPTER XXXVI.

### CHAPTER XXXVII.

#### That Catholic <note>original: "Popish"</note> Priests leave nothing unconjured; a form of Exorcism for Incense.

<margin>A formal ritual for the conjuration of Frankincense.</margin>
**A**lthough the Catholics have many conjurations—so that neither water, nor fire, nor bread, nor wine, nor wax, nor tallow, nor church, nor churchyard, nor altar, nor altar-cloth, nor ashes, nor coals, nor bells, nor bell-ropes, nor copes, nor vestments, nor oil, nor salt, nor candle, nor candlestick, nor beds, nor bed-staves, etc., are without their own form of conjuration—yet for the sake of brevity, I will let the rest pass and end here with incense, which they conjure in this manner: ✠ *I conjure you, most filthy and horrible spirit, and every vision of our enemy, etc., that you go and depart from this creature of frankincense, with all your deceit and wickedness, so that this creature may be sanctified. <margin>Catholics and conjurers are deceiving partners <note>original: "cosening compeers"</note>.</margin>
**T**he Catholics, as you see, have their specific general rules and laws, such as to abstain from sin and to fast, as well as to otherwise be clean from all pollutions, etc.; and common conjurers have the exact same requirements. And if it is said that in this conjuration we speak to the spirits and they hear us—and therefore they do not need to know our thoughts and imaginations—I first ask them: Can King Bael or Amaymon, who are spirits reigning in the farthest regions of the East (so they say), hear a conjurer’s voice calling for them from the farthest parts of the West? This is especially unlikely given all the noises occurring in between, and where they might also be busy working on similar affairs. Secondly, are those spirits of the same power as God, who is everywhere, filling all places, and able to hear all men at one instant? Thirdly, where does the force come from in the words that raise the dead and command devils? If sound alone does it, then it might be done by a drum <note>original: "taber"</note> and a pipe, or any other instrument that has no life. # Regarding Witchcraft. CHAP. IX.

<margin>Read a little tract by Erasmus <note>original: "Esaf-mus"</note> titled *On Friendship* <note>original: "De amicitia"</note>, where enough is said regarding this point.</margin>The friendly association between a fox and a serpent is almost incredible; how loving the lizard is to a man, we may read about even if we cannot see it for ourselves. Yet some affirm that our newt is not only like the lizard in shape, but also in its disposition toward humans. A spaniel does not differ much in this regard, of which I could cite incredible stories. The friendship between a kestrel <note>original: "Castrel"</note> and a pigeon is much noted among writers; and especially how the kestrel defends the pigeon from her enemy the sparrow-hawk, a fact of which they say the dove is well aware. Besides these, there is the wonderful operation and virtue of herbs, which are infinite; therefore, I will only refer you to Mattioli's <note>original: "Mattheolus"</note> *Herbal*, or to others who describe such natural accord and discord. For example, some plants enjoy each other's company, while others wither away when planted near one another. The lily and the rose rejoice in each other's neighborhood. The flag <note>a type of iris</note> and the fern-bush abhor each other so much that one can hardly live beside the other. The cucumber loves water and hates oil to the death. 

And so you shall not say that herbs have no power just because I cite none here, I am content to reveal two or three small qualities and virtues that are affirmed to be in herbs; indeed, as simple as they may be, Jannes and Jambres <note>The magicians who opposed Moses in the Book of Exodus</note> might have done much with them if they had possessed them. If you poke out a young swallow's eyes, the mother swallow restores their sight—they say—with the application of a little celandine. <margin>Xanthus <note>original: "Zanthus"</note>, the author of various histories, reports that a young dragon being dead was revived by her mother with an herb called Balim. ### CHAPTER XXXIX.

->*That it is a shame for Catholics <note>original: "Papiſts"</note> to believe the deeds of other conjurors, since their own have so little power. Hippocrates' opinion on this matter.*<-

<margin>Specifically, Vincent: On the Sunday in white <note>original: "Dominica in albis," also known as Low Sunday</note>, in the octave of Easter, sermon 25. Durand regarding exorcists.</margin>
And still it seems to me that Catholics (of all people), who are indeed the most gullible and do the most to maintain the power of witches' charms and conjurors' deceptions <note>original: "coſenages"</note>, should perceive and judge conjurors' actions to be void of effect. For when they see their own materials—such as holy water, salt, candles, etc.—conjured by their holy bishop and priests, and that in the words of consecration or conjuration (for so their own doctors term them) they command <note>original: "adjure"</note> the water, etc., to heal not only the soul's infirmity but also every malady, hurt, or ache of the body; and they also command the candles, with the force of their authority and power and by the effect of all their holy words, not to consume; and yet neither soul nor body recovers anything, nor do the candles last one minute longer: with what face can they defend the miraculous works of others, as though the actions of witches and conjurors were more effective than their own? Hippocrates, being but a pagan and not having the perfect knowledge of God, could see and perceive their deception and knavery well enough; he says, *Those who boast that they can remove or help the infections of diseases with sacrifices, conjurations, or other magical instruments or means, are but needy fellows, lacking a living; and therefore they attribute their words to the Devil because they would seem to know something more than the common people.* It is a marvel that Catholics affirm that their holy water, crosses, or scare-words <note>original: "Bugswords," referring to terrifying words or threats</note> have such virtue and violence as to drive away devils, so that they dare not approach any place or person smeared with such stuff; when it appears in the Gospel that the Devil presumed to assault and tempt Christ himself. For the Devil indeed most earnestly busies himself to seduce the godly; as for the wicked, he counts them as his own already. But let us go forward in our refutation.

<header>The Discovery of Witchcraft. CHAPTER XLI.</header>

<margin>*Justin, Book 36.* <note>original: "Just. lib. 36." refers to the Roman historian Justinus.</note></margin>
These secret conjurors insist (along with Justin) on reporting and affirming that Joseph—who was a true symbol <note>original: "figure"</note> of Christ who delivered and redeemed us—was learned in these arts and thereby prophesied and interpreted dreams. They claim that those arts came to him from Moses, and finally from Moses to them. <margin>*Pliny, Book 30, Chapter 2. Strabo, Book 16.*</margin> Both Pliny and Tacitus affirm this of Moses. Also, Strabo in his *Geography* <note>original: "Cosmographie"</note> makes the very same blasphemous report; and likewise Apollonius Molon, Poseidonius, Lysimachus, and Appian call Moses both a magician and a conjuror. Eusebius refutes them with many notable arguments; for Moses differed as much from a magician as truth differs from falsehood, and piety from vanity. In truth, he confounded all magic and made the world see—and even the most skillful magicians of the earth confess—that their own deeds were merely illusions, and that his miracles were performed by the finger of God. But the claim that the knowledge of a poor old witch reaches this far (as Lambert Daneau <note>original: "Danaus," a Genevan theologian</note> affirms it does) is untrue. For the furthest tricks <note>original: "fetches"</note> that I can <margin>*Daneau in his Dialogue on Sorcerers.* <note>original: "Dan. in dialog. de fortiariis."</note></margin> comprehend are only to fetch a pot of milk, etc., from their neighbor's house half a mile away.

## C H A P T E R X L I.

### *All Magical Arts refuted by an argument concerning Nero; what Cornelius Agrippa and Charles Gallus have written about it, and proved by experience.*

<margin>Tiridates the great magician invites the Emperor Nero to a banquet, etc.</margin>
Certainly, Nero proved all these magical arts to be empty and mythical lies, and nothing but fraud <note>original: "Cosenage"</note> and trickery. He was a notable prince, having enough natural talent to have understood such matters and enough wealth to have spent on searching for them. He had no moral qualms <note>original: "made no conscience therein"</note> about it; he held special conferences on the subject; he offered and would have given half his kingdom to learn those things he heard could be performed by magicians. He brought all the cleverest magicians in the world to Rome; he also searched for books and all other things necessary for a magician; yet he could never find anything in it but fraud and sleight of hand <note>original: "Legierdemain"</note>. At length, he met with one Tiridates, the great magician, who (having with him all his companions and fellow magicians, witches, conjurors, and fraudsters) invited Nero to certain magical banquets and exercises. When Nero asked to learn these things, Tiridates (to hide his deception) answered that he would not and could not teach him, even if Nero gave him his kingdom. The reason for his refusal (I say) was for fear that Nero would discover the fraudulent tricks of it. <margin>Nero made laws against conjurors and conjurations.</margin> When Nero realized this and saw that the reputation <note>original: "fame"</note> and everything else about that art was empty, lying, and ridiculous—having only shadows of truth—and that their arts were only <term>venefical</term> <note>related to poisoning or drugs</note>, he prohibited it utterly and made good and strong laws against its use and practice, as Pliny and others report. It is a marvel that any man can be so deceived as to suppose that Satan may be commanded, compelled, or bound to the power of man—as though the Devil would yield to man beyond the laws of nature, when he will not yield to God his Creator according to the rules of nature. And since there are (as they admit) good angels as well as bad, I would like to know why they call up the angels of hell and do not call down the angels of heaven. <margin>*Cornelius Agrippa, Book on the Vanity of Sciences.* <note>original: "C. Agrip. lib. de vanitat. scient."</note></margin> But they answer this (as Agrippa says): *"Good angels (of course) rarely appear, while the others are ready at hand."* Here I must not forget to tell you how Cornelius Agrippa exposes, detects, and discredits this art of conjuration. In his youth, he traveled into the depths of all these magical sciences and was not only a great conjuror and practitioner of them but also wrote cleverly *On Occult Philosophy* <note>original: "De occulta Philosophia"</note>. However, later in his wiser years, he recanted his opinions and lamented his follies in that regard. He revealed the impiety and vanities of magicians and enchanters who boast they can perform miracles—an action that has now ceased, he says. He assigns them a place with Jannes and Jambres <note>The Egyptian magicians who opposed Moses in Exodus</note>, affirming, *"That this art teaches nothing but empty toys for show."* Charles Gallus <note>original: "Carolus Gallus"</note> also says, *"I have often tested, through the witches and conjurors themselves, that..."*

### CHAPTER XLII.

->Concerning Solomon's Conjurations, and the opinions held regarding his skill and practice in them.<-

It is affirmed by various authors that Solomon was the first inventor of those conjurations; and Josephus <note>Flavius Josephus (c. 37–100 AD), a Romano-Jewish historian.</note> is the first reporter of this, who in his first book, *Antiquities of the Jews, chapter 22* <note>original: "De Judæorum antiquitatibus, cap. 22."</note>, soberly recounts the following story; which Polydore Virgil <note>An Italian historian (c. 1470–1555) who wrote a famous history of England.</note> and many others repeat word for word <note>original: "verbatim"</note> in this way, and seem to believe the fable, of which there is scarcely a true word.

<margin>It has been proven on a patient before witnesses; therefore, it is no lie.</margin>
*Solomon was the greatest philosopher, and philosophized about all things, and had full and perfect knowledge of all their properties. But he had that gift given to him from above for the benefit and health of mankind, which is effective against devils. He also made incantations with which diseases are driven away; and he left various methods of conjuration in writing, by which the devils, giving way, are so driven away that they never return. And this kind of healing is very common among my countrymen; for I saw a neighbor of mine, one Eleazar, who in the presence of Vespasian <note>Roman Emperor from 69 to 79 AD.</note> and his sons, and the rest of the soldiers, cured many who were possessed by spirits. The method and order of his cure was this: he put a ring to the nose of the possessed person; under the seal of the ring was enclosed a kind of root, the power of which Solomon had described. The scent of it drew the devil out through his nose, so that the man fell down; then Eleazar conjured the devil to depart and return to him no more. In the meantime, he made mention of Solomon, reciting incantations of Solomon's own making. Then Eleazar, being willing to show the bystanders his skill and the wonderful efficacy of his art, set a pot or basin full of water not far from there, and commanded the devil that went out of the man that, by overturning it, he would give a sign to the beholders that he had utterly forsaken and left the man. When this was done, no one there doubted how great Solomon's knowledge and wisdom was. In this, a juggling trick was produced to confirm a deceptive act of villainy or fraud.* <note>original: "cosenage" (cozenage) means deception or cheating.</note>

Another story of Solomon's conjuration I find cited in the sixth lesson read in the Church of Rome on Saint Margaret's day, which is far more ridiculous than this. Also, 
<margin>Book 4, distinction 14. The Golden Decree, distinction 21. Rubric on Exorcists.</margin>
Peter Lombard, *Master of the Sentences* <note>A 12th-century theologian whose "Sentences" was the standard textbook of theology.</note>, and Gratian <note>A 12th-century jurist who compiled the "Decretum Gratiani," a collection of Canon law.</note> his brother, the compiler of the *Golden Decrees*, and Durandus in his *Rationale of the Divine Offices* <note>original: "Rationale Divinorum." Guillaume Durand was a 13th-century liturgical writer.</note>, all soberly affirm Solomon's skill in this matter, and especially this tale: namely, that Solomon enclosed several thousand devils in a brass <note>original: "brazen"</note> bowl and left it in a deep hole or lake; later, the Babylonians found it and, supposing there had been gold or silver inside, broke it open, and out flew all the devils, etc. And you shall see that this fable is considered credible because it is thought worthy to be read in 
<margin>Lessons 5 and 6.</margin>
the Roman Church as part of their liturgy <note>original: "Divine Service"</note>. Look in the lessons for the day of Saint Margaret the Virgin, and you shall find these words exactly <note>original: "Verbatim"</note>; which I recite specifically because it serves my purpose in several ways: namely, regarding Solomon's conjurations, the tale of the brass vessel, and the Pope's own conjurations, which extended to both faith and doctrine, and to show what kind of credibility their religion has when it is so shamefully stained with lies and fables.

### CHAPTER XLIII.

*Lessons read in all churches where the Pope has authority on Saint Margaret's day, translated into English word for word.*

<margin>Lesson for the day of the most holy Margaret, verse 5.</margin>
Holy Margaret asked of God that she might have a conflict face-to-face with her secret enemy, the Devil. Rising from prayer, she saw a terrible dragon that intended to devour her; but she made the sign of the Cross, and the dragon burst apart in the middle.

<margin>Lesson 6.</margin>
Afterward, she saw another man sitting like a black man <note>original: "Niger"; in medieval iconography, demons were often depicted as having dark skin.</note>, having his hands bound fast to his knees. Taking him by the hair of his head, she threw him to the ground and set her foot on his head. > Grant therefore, O Father, that whoever writes, reads, or hears of my suffering <note>original: "passion"</note>, or makes a memorial of me, may deserve pardon for all his sins. Whoever calls on me when they are at the point of death, deliver them out of the hands of their adversaries. And I also require, O Lord, that whoever builds a church in my honor, or offers me any candles <margin>For the priest's profit, I guarantee you.</margin> from his honest labor, let him obtain whatever he asks for his health. Deliver all women in labor who call upon me from the danger of it.

<margin>This is commonly said to happen when a witch or conjurer dies.</margin>

To him she said, "Unless you do it, you can have no part with me"; and then, look, he did it, etc. But since I have been, and must be, tedious, I thought it good to refresh my reader with a sorrowful story following from the previous matter, reported by many serious authors, word for word, in the following manner and form.

### CHAPTER XLIV.

*A curious story of a Lombard who, by Saint Margaret's example, insisted on fighting with a real Devil.*

<margin>Perverse imitation <note>original: "Kacozelidi," from the Greek for misdirected or "evil zeal."</note></margin>
There was (after a sermon where this story of Saint Margaret was recited—for such material consisted not only of their church services but also their sermons in the blind time of Popery <note>A derogatory term for Roman Catholicism used by Protestant reformers to denote the era before the Reformation.</note>)—there was, I say, a certain young man, a Lombard, whose simplicity was such that he had no regard for the convenience of worldly things but was entirely focused on the salvation of his soul. Hearing how great Saint Margaret's triumph was, he began to consider with himself how full of tricks the Devil was. And as he spoke these words, he caught her by the hair and dragged her about, beating her sometimes with his hands, sometimes with his heels, and sometimes with the hook for so long, and wounded her so severely, that he left her dying. Therefore, whatever the man of God commanded, the priest confidently accomplished and obeyed. As soon as the priest approached her to hear her confession, she—whom all Catalonia knew to have been born mute—spoke and confessed herself, pronouncing every word as distinctly as though she had never been mute. After her confession, she requested the Eucharist and Extreme Unction <note>A Catholic sacrament involving anointing with oil, administered to someone near death.</note> to be administered to her, and at last she committed herself to God. In the presence of all who came to see that miracle, she spoke as long as she had any breath in her body. The young man who killed her, being saved from the gallows by Saint Vincent's means and intercession, returned home to Italy. This story just recounted is found in the *Mirror of Examples* <note>original: "Speculo Exemplorum"; a famous 15th-century collection of stories for preachers.</note>, and is also repeated by Robert Caracciolo <note>original: "Robert Carocul"; a famous Franciscan preacher.</note>, Bishop of Aquino, and many others, and is preached publicly in the Church of Rome.

He could not speak as long as she stepped on his head, and yet he said, *"Step off, so that I may tell you—"*

### CHAPTER 46.

#### *A pleasing miracle performed by a Catholic priest.*

<margin>
In the *Mirror of Examples* <note>original: "speculo exemplorum"</note>, section 6, from the book of examples by Caesarius, example 69.
</margin>
**A**t the time when the *Waldensian* <note>A medieval Christian movement deemed heretical by the Catholic Church.</note> heresies began to grow, certain wicked men, being upheld and maintained by demonic power, showed certain signs and wonders. By these, they strengthened and confirmed their heresies and led many faithful men astray from the faith; for they walked on water and did not drown. But a certain Catholic priest, seeing this and knowing that true signs could not be joined with false doctrine, brought the body of our Lord [the Host], in the <term>pyx</term> <note>A small container used to carry the consecrated bread of the Eucharist.</note>, to the water where they were displaying their power and virtue to the people. He said, in the hearing of all who were present: *“I conjure you, O Devil, by him whom I carry in my hands, that you do not perform these great visions and illusions through these men to the drowning of these people.”* 

Despite these words, when they continued to walk on the water as they had before, the priest, in a rage, threw the body of our Lord, along with the pyx, into the river. Immediately, as soon as the Sacrament touched the element [the water], the illusion gave way to the truth. Having been proved false, they sank like lead to the bottom and drowned. The pyx with the Sacrament was immediately taken away by an angel. The priest, seeing all these things, was very glad for the miracle, but he was very sorrowful for the loss of the Sacrament, spending the whole night in tears and mourning. In the morning, he found the pyx with the Sacrament sitting upon the altar.

### CHAPTER 47.

->*The former Miracle confuted, with a strange story of Saint Lucy.*<-

<margin>Lactantius on the feast day of Saint Lucy, lessons 7 and 8. <note>original: "Lact. in die sanctæ Luc. 7. & 8."</note></margin>
How glad Sir John <note>original: "Sir John" — a common, often derogatory, nickname for a Catholic priest during the Reformation.</note> was now, it would be foolish for me to say. How he would have plagued the Devil who threw his God into the river to be drowned! But if others had no more power to destroy the Waldenses <note>original: "Waldenses" — a medieval Christian movement often persecuted as heretics by the Catholic Church.</note> with sword and fire than this priest had to drown them with his conjuring box and deceiving <term>cosening</term> sacraments, then many a life would have been saved. But I must not omit one fable of great authority, in which—though no conjuration is explicitly stated—I guarantee there was deception <term>cosenage</term> in both the doing and the telling of it. You shall read in the lesson for Saint Lucy’s Day that when she was condemned, she could not be moved from the spot even with a team of oxen, nor could any fire burn her. This went on until someone was forced to cut off her head with a sword, and yet she could still speak afterward for as long as she wished <note>original: "list"</note>. This surpasses all other miracles, except perhaps the one that Jean Bodin and the *Malleus Maleficarum* <note>original: "M. Mal." — the famous 15th-century treatise on the prosecution of witches.</note> recite from Nider, about a witch who could not be burned until a scroll was taken away from where she had hidden it between her skin and her flesh.

### CHAPTER 48.

->*Of Visions, Noises, Apparitions, and imagined Sounds, and of other Illusions of wandering Souls, with a confutation thereof.*<-

Many people, through melancholy <note>original: "Melancholy" — in the 16th century, this was considered a physical ailment caused by an imbalance of fluids in the body, often used to explain hallucinations or depression.</note>, imagine that they see or hear visions, spirits, ghosts, strange noises, etc., as I have already proven at length before. Many others, through fear stemming from a cowardly nature and temperament, or from a soft and foolish upbringing, are timid and afraid of spirits and "bugs" <term>bugs</term> <note>original: "bugs" — terrors, specters, or imaginary monsters; the origin of the modern word "bogeyman."</note>, etc. Some, due to imperfect eyesight, are also afraid of their own shadows and (as Aristotle says) sometimes see themselves as if in a mirror. And some, through physical weakness, have such imperfect imaginations. Drunk men also sometimes suppose they see trees walking, etc., according to what Solomon says to the drunkards: *Your eyes shall see strange visions, and marvelous appearances.*

<margin>Against the counterfeit visions of Catholic <note>original: "Popish"</note> priests and other deceptive devices.</margin>
In all ages, monks and priests have abused and bewitched the world with counterfeit visions. These arose from idleness and the prohibition of marriage, which made them lustful <note>original: "hot and lecherous"</note>; therefore, they devised such means to pursue and achieve their romantic desires. And the simple people of that time were so superstitious that they would never seem to suspect that such "holy" men would make them cuckolds, but instead left their beds in those instances to give room to the clergy. Likewise, little children have been so scared by their mothers' maids that they could never afterward endure being in the dark alone for fear of "bugs." Many are deceived by mirrors through the art of perspective <note>original: "Art Perspective" — the use of mirrors or optical lenses to create illusions.</note>. Many, listening to false reports, imagine and believe things that are not true at all. Many give credit to what they read in books. But a massive volume could not contain all the stories and books written about walking spirits and the souls of men that contradict the Word of God. How common an opinion was it among the Catholics <note>original: "Papists"</note> that all souls walked the earth after they departed from their bodies? So much so that in the time of the Catholic Church's dominance <note>original: "Popery"</note>, it was a common matter to ask sick people on their deathbeds to appear to them after death and reveal their state. The Church Fathers and ancient Doctors of the Church were too gullible in this regard, etc. Therefore, it is no wonder that simple common men, and least of all women, are deceived in this. In times past, God did send down visible angels and appearances to men, but now He does not do so. Through recent ignorance in religion, it was thought that every churchyard swarmed with souls and spirits.

Spirits; but now that the Word of God is more free, open, and known, those fantasies and illusions are made more manifest and apparent, etc.

<margin>This doctrine was not only preached, but also proved; note the particular instances following.</margin>
The Doctors, Councils, and Popes—who, they say, cannot err—have confirmed the walking, appearing, and raising of souls. But where do they find any such doctrine in the Scriptures? And who certified to them that those appearances were true? Truly, all of them together cannot make the lies that have been spread abroad regarding this matter suddenly become true, even if the Pope himself subscribes, seals, and swears to it ever so much. Where are the souls that swarmed in times past? Where are the spirits? Who hears their noises? Who sees their visions? Where are the souls that made such a moan for Trentals <term>Trentals: a series of thirty Requiem masses for a deceased person</term>, by which they hoped to be eased of the pains of Purgatory? Have they all gone to Italy because Masses have become expensive here in England? 

Mark this illusion well, and see how contrary it is to the Word of God. Consider how all Papists believe this illusion to be true, and how all Protestants are forced to say it is and was a Popish illusion. Where are the spirits that wandered about to seek burial for their bodies? For many of those walking souls went about that business. Do you not think that the Papists show themselves to be ungodly theologians to preach and teach the people such doctrine, and to insert into their divine service such fables as are read in the Roman Church, with all Scripture giving way to them for the time? 

You shall see in the lessons read there on Saint Stephen's Day that Gamaliel (Nicodemus's kinsman) and Abdias (his son), along with his friend Saint Stephen, appeared to a certain priest named Sir Lucian <note>original: "Sir Lucian" — "Sir" was a common title for a priest at the time</note>, requesting him to remove their bodies and bury them in some better place. (For they had lain buried in the field of Gamaliel from the time of their death until then—which was in the reign of the Emperor Honorius, a period of four hundred years.) In this regard, Gamaliel said to Sir Lucian: "I am not only concerned for myself, but rather for those friends of mine who are with me" <note>original Latin: "*Non mei solummodo causa solicitus sum, sed potius pro illis qui mecum sunt*"</note>. From this, the whole sequence can be perceived as a false practice and a counterfeit vision, or rather a wicked <term>lewd</term> invention. For in Heaven, men's souls do not remain in sorrow and care; neither do they study there how to arrange and obtain a respectful burial here on earth. If they did, they would not have neglected <term>foreflowed</term> it for so long. Now, therefore, let us no longer allow ourselves to be deceived, either by conjuring priests or melancholy-stricken <term>Melancholical</term> witches; but let us be thankful to God that he has delivered us from such blindness and error.

## CHAPTER 49.

### Cardano’s opinion of strange noises; how counterfeit visions come to be believed; concerning Popish appearances; and of Pope Boniface.

<margin>Girolamo Cardano, *On the Variety of Things*, Book 15, Chapter 93. <note>original: "H. Card lib de var. rer. lib. 15. c. 93."</note></margin>
Cardano, speaking of noises among other things, says this: "A noise is heard in your house; it may be a mouse, a cat, or a dog among the dishes; it may be a prank <term>counterfeit</term>, or an actual thief; or the fault may be in your own ears." I could recite a great number of tales about how men have even abandoned their houses because of such apparitions and noises, and it has all been due to pure and utter <term>rank</term> trickery <term>knavery</term>. 

And wherever you hear that there are such rumblings and fearful noises during the night, be well assured that it is plain trickery, performed by someone who seems to complain the most and is the least suspected. There is even a specific art for this, which for certain reasons I will not reveal. The Devil seeks daily as well as nightly whom he may devour, and he can perform his feats as well by day as by night—otherwise, he is a young devil and a complete bungler. But of all other swindlers <term>cozeners</term>, these conjurers are of the highest degree and are most worthy of death for their blasphemous impiety. However, these Popish visions and conjurations, used by both Papists and the Popes themselves, were mere deceptions; and the tales of the Popes recorded by Bruno and Platina, concerning their magi-

There are countless examples of such visions which, when they are not detected as frauds, are accepted as true stories. Therefore, when it is argued that some tales are true and some are false, until they are able to show you even one proven truth, you may answer them with this distinction: visions that are tested are proven false; those that are untested and undecided are called "true."

## CHAPTER 50.

### Regarding the noise or sound of an echo; of one who narrowly escaped drowning because of it, etc.

<margin>
Girolamo Cardano, in his book *On Subtlety*, volume 18.
</margin>
Alas! How many natural things are so strange that they seem miraculous to many? And how many fake matters are there that seem even more wonderful to the simple-minded? Cardano tells of a man named Comansis, who arrived late at a riverbank and did not know where to cross. He cried out loudly for someone to show him the ford. Hearing an echo repeat his last word, and supposing it was a man answering and informing him of the way, he tried to cross the river right where there was a deep whirlpool. He barely escaped with his life and told his friends that the Devil had almost persuaded him to drown himself. In some places, these noises of echoes are far more strange than in others, especially at Pavia <note>original: "Ticinum"</note> in Italy. In the great hall there, the echo produces many different noises or voices that seem to end so mournfully, like a dying man. Consequently, few people can be convinced that it is just an echo; they believe it is a spirit answering.

<margin>
Regarding the noise at Winchester.
</margin>
The noise at Winchester was said to be a true miracle, and there was much wondering about it around the year 1569. However, it was actually a purely natural noise produced by the wind, the hollowness of the place, and other physical factors that helped the sound seem strange to the listeners—especially to those who would add new rumors to increase the sense of wonder.

## CHAPTER 51.

### Regarding Theurgy, with a refutation of it; a letter sent to me concerning these matters.

There is yet another art practiced by these cheating conjurers, which some foolish theologians <term>Divines: priests or specialists in theology</term> claim is more honest and lawful than Necromancy <term>Necromancy: magic involving communication with the dead</term>. This is called Theurgy <term>Theurgy: a type of ritual magic intended to invoke the presence of gods or beneficial spirits</term>, in which they claim to work through good angels. However, their ceremonies are entirely papist <note>Papist: a derogatory term for Roman Catholic practices</note> and superstitious. They consist of "cleanliness," partly of the mind, partly of the body, and partly of things belonging to the body—such as the skin, clothing, the house, vessels, and household items, as well as offerings and sacrifices. They say this cleanliness prepares men to contemplate heavenly things. They cite these words of Isaiah <note>original: "Esay"</note> as their authority: "Wash yourselves and be clean, etc." I have known several superstitious people of high social standing who would often wash all their clothing based on ridiculous whims. For they say that uncleanliness corrupts the air, infects man, and chases away pure...

->The Copy of a Letter sent to me, Reginald Scot, by T. E., Master of Arts and practitioner of both Medicine and, in times past, certain vain Sciences; now condemned to die for the same, wherein he reveals the truth regarding these deceptions.<-

<margin>Note the summary and purpose of this Letter.</margin>
Master Reginald Scot, according to your request, I have outlined certain abuses worth noting regarding the work you have in hand. These are things I myself have seen within these twenty-six years among those who were considered famous and skillful in those Sciences. Because the whole story cannot be told without naming certain people—some of whom are dead and some living, whose friends still hold positions of great credit—and knowing that my enemies already outnumber my friends, I have decided it is better to withhold my hand than to commit something to the world that might increase my misery rather than relieve it. 

Nevertheless, because I am noted above many others for having had dealings in those vain Arts and wicked practices, I must inform you—and I say this in the presence of God—that among all those famous and noted practitioners I have known over these twenty-six years, I could never see any truth performed in those wicked Sciences, but only mere trickery and illusions. Even those whom I thought to be the most skillful sought to see things from me. I spent twelve or fourteen years of my own time, to my great loss and hindrance, and could never at any time see one single truth, nor even a spark of truth, in them. 

Yet at this present moment, I stand deservedly condemned for the same; for, contrary to my Sovereign's laws, the Law of God, and my own conscience, I spent my time in such vain and wicked studies and practices. I remain a spectacle for all others to take warning from. May the Lord grant that I be the last—I speak this from my heart—and I wish it not only in my native country but across the whole face of the earth, especially among Christians.

<margin>Sir John Malborne’s Book exposing the devices of conjuration, etc.</margin>
For my own part, I lament my lost time and repented five years ago. At that time, I saw a book written in the Old English <note>original: "Saxon"</note> tongue by one Sir John Malborne, a theologian from Oxford <note>original: "Oxonford"</note>, written three hundred years ago. In it, he reveals all the illusions and inventions of those Arts and Sciences—a thing most worthy of note. I left the book with the Parson of Slaugham in Sussex; if you send for it in my name, you may have it. You shall find your labor well spent, and it will greatly further the good project you have in hand. There you shall see the whole Science thoroughly discussed, and all their illusions and trickery explained in detail. Thus, I crave your pardon for what I promised you, as I am very fearful, doubtful, and loath to sign my name to anything that may be offensive to the world or harmful to myself, considering my

The conclusion, therefore, shall be this: whatever has previously been accepted as valid regarding all these fallible Arts, about which I have written extensively until now, let them now be considered counterfeit. # BOOK XVI.

## CHAPTER I.

->A conclusion, in the manner of an epilogue, repeating many of the former absurdities of the witch-mongers' <note>Scot's derogatory term for those who believe in and promote the persecution of witches</note> ideas and their refutations; and regarding the authority of James Sprenger and Henry Institor, Inquisitors and compilers of the *Malleus Maleficarum* <note>original: "M. Mal."; the *Hammer of Witches*, the most influential 15th-century treatise on the prosecution of witches</note>.<-

<image-desc>Large decorative drop cap letter 'H' featuring an ornate foliage and trellis pattern.</image-desc>

Hitherto you have been presented with what I have understood and gathered regarding *this* matter. In its substance and main parts, I can see no difference among the writers on this subject, regardless of their country, social status, rank, or religion. Instead, I find almost all of them agreeing in inconsistency, fables, and impossibilities. They scrape the substance of all their arguments out of the *Malleus Maleficarum*; therefore, since their primary authors are discredited, they must either invent new material or go to their grandmothers' maids to learn more "old wives' tales," which is what this "art" of witchcraft is actually made of. But you must know that Jacob <note>original: "James"</note> Sprenger and Heinrich Kramer (known as *Henry Institor*), whom I have had occasion to mention many times, were co-authors in
<margin>The compilers or authors of the book called *A Mallet to Brain Witches.* <note>A literal translation of the Latin title *Malleus Maleficarum*</note></margin>
the composition of that "profound and learned" book called *Malleus Maleficarum*. They were the greatest "Doctors" of this art. From them, I have gathered enough material and absurdity to debunk the opinions held about witchcraft, even though they were official Inquisitors appointed by the Pope. They were granted the authority and recommendation of all the Doctors of the University of Cologne <note>original: "Collen"</note>, etc., to summon, imprison, condemn, and execute witches, and finally to seize and confiscate their property.

These two Doctors, in order to maintain their reputations and cover up their wrongful acts, published those same monstrous lies that have deceived all of Christendom. These lies were spread with such authority that it will be difficult to suppress the credibility of their writings, no matter how ridiculous and false they are. Although they support and promote these ideas with their own self-praise, men are so "bewitched" <note>Scot uses "bewitched" ironically here to mean deluded or fooled</note> as to believe them. For proof of this, I remember they wrote in one part of their book that, because of
<margin>It is no wonder that they were so stubborn in this opinion, for God gave them over to strong delusions.</margin>
their severe proceedings against witches, they suffered unbearable assaults—especially at night. They claimed to often find needles sticking in their nightcaps <term>original: "Biggens"; close-fitting caps</term>, which were supposedly placed there by witches' charms. They claim that through their innocence and holiness, they were always miraculously protected from harm. However, they assert that they will not reveal everything that might demonstrate their holiness, for then their own praise would "stink in their own mouths." And yet God knows their entire book contains nothing but stinking lies and Catholic <note>original: "Popery"</note> superstition. Even a child may soon discern and perceive how weak, unstable, and poorly laid this groundwork and foundation is, and how unlikely it is to endure.

# BOOK XVI. 
## The Discovery of Witchcraft described.

### CHAPTER II.

*By what means the common people have been made to believe in the miraculous works of witches; a definition of witchcraft, and a description thereof.*

The common people have been so infatuated <note>original: "assotted"</note> and bewitched by whatever poets have feigned about witchcraft—whether in earnest, in jest, or in derision—and by whatever blatant liars and deceivers <note>original: "coseners"</note> have invented for their own pleasure. They have been swayed by the tales they have heard from doting old women or from their mothers' maids, and by whatever the "Grand-fool" their spiritual father, or any other morning-mass priest <note>original: "Morrow-Mass Priest," a derogatory reference to Catholic clergy</note>, has informed them. Finally, they have swallowed these ideas through the passage of time, or through their own fearful nature and ignorant imagination concerning these matters of hags and witches. They have so settled their opinion and belief upon these things that they think it heresy to doubt any part of the matter. This is especially true because they find the word "witchcraft" used in the Scriptures; using this to justify their belief is just like defending the practice of praying to saints simply because "Holy, Holy, Holy" <note>original: "Sanctus, Sanctus, Sanctus"</note> is written in the *Te Deum* <note>A traditional Christian hymn of praise</note>.

<margin>The definition or description of witchcraft.</margin>
And now to come to the definition of witchcraft, which I have purposely delayed until now so that you might perceive its true nature through the surrounding circumstances, and therefore be more likely to accept my definition after seeing the variety of other writers. Witchcraft is, in truth, a deceptive <note>original: "cosening"</note> art, wherein the name of God is abused, profaned, and blasphemed, and His power is attributed to a lowly creature. In the estimation of the common people, it is a supernatural work contrived between a physical old woman and a spiritual devil. <margin>The formal cause <note>In Aristotelian logic, the "formal cause" is the design or pattern of a thing</note>.</margin> The manner of it is so secret, mystical, and strange that to this day there has never been any credible witness to it. It is incomprehensible to the wise, the learned, or the faithful; it is a plausible matter only to children, fools, melancholic persons, and Papists <note>A derogatory term for Roman Catholics</note>. <margin>The final cause <note>The "final cause" is the ultimate purpose or end goal of a thing</note>.</margin> The trade is thought to be impious. Its effect and end are thought to be sometimes evil—such as when a person, beast, grass, trees, or corn are hurt—and sometimes good, such as when sick folks are healed, thieves are revealed <note>original: "bewrayed"</note>, and honest men recover their stolen goods. <margin>The material cause <note>The "material cause" refers to the physical elements or instruments used</note>.</margin> The matter and instruments with which it is accomplished are words, charms, signs, images, characters, and so on. Even if any other creature pronounces these words in the same manner and form as the witches do, leaving out no required or usual circumstance for the action, no one else is said to have the "grace" or "gift" to perform the task unless she is a witch, and is considered such either by her own consent or by the accusations of others.

***

### CHAPTER III.

*Reasons to prove that words and characters are but trifles <note>original: "Bables" or baubles</note>, and that witches cannot do such things as the multitude supposes they can; their greatest wonders proved to be trifles; of a young gentleman deceived.*

I trust I have sufficiently proved that words, characters, images, and such other trinkets—which are thought to be such necessary instruments for witchcraft that nothing can be accomplished without them—are nothing but baubles devised by deceivers to abuse the people. This may be further and more plainly perceived by the following short and concise reasons.

<margin>A necessary consequence.</margin>
First, consider that the Muslims <note>original: "Turks"</note> and non-believers use both different words and different characters in their witchcraft than our witches do, and even use those that are most contrary to ours. Consequently, if our methods are "bad" or "evil," then by that logic, theirs should be "good." If their witches can do anything, then ours can do nothing. For just as our witches are said to renounce Christ and despise His sacraments, so do the others forsake Muhammad <note>original: "Mahomet"</note> and his laws—which would actually be a large step toward Christianity.

<summary>Scot defines witchcraft as a "cosening art" (a scam) fueled by superstition, religious misinformation, and poetic fiction, rather than actual supernatural power. He argues that the physical tools of witchcraft—charms and symbols—are meaningless trifles, noting that different cultures use contradictory symbols to supposedly achieve the same results.</summary>

# Witchcraft is Deception <note>original: cosenage</note>. Of Witchcraft. CHAPTER III.

<margin>
It is proven <note>original: Probatum est</note> by Mother Bungie’s confession that all witches are deceivers.
</margin>
It should also be considered that all witches are deceivers <note>original: Coseners</note>. For instance, Mother Bungie—a principal witch so reputed, tried, and condemned by all men—continued in that practice and reputation for many years. She deceived and abused the whole realm, to the extent that "witch-mongers" <note>those who obsess over or hunt witches</note> came to her from the furthest parts of the land. She was even featured in various books published with authority, registered and chronicled by the name of the "Great Witch of Rochester," and reputed among all men as the chief ringleader of all other witches. Yet, by good proof, she is found to be a mere deceiver. On her deathbed, she confessed freely, without compulsion or force, that her "cunning" consisted only of deluding and deceiving the people. To maintain her credit in that deceptive trade, she possessed some knowledge of medicine <note>original: Physick</note> and surgery, and had the assistance of a friend of hers called Heron, a professor of those subjects. I know this partly from my own knowledge, and partly by the testimony of her husband and others of good reputation to whom, I say, she protested these things on her deathbed and at various other times. She also confessed that she never actually had any physical spirit or devil (as the rumor went), nor did she know how to perform any supernatural matter, despite making men believe during her lifetime that she possessed such power.

The same may be said of one "T. of Canterbury" (whose full name I will not disclose). He wonderfully deceived many in these parts, making them think he could tell where any lost item had gone, along with various other such practices, whereby his fame far exceeded others. And yet on his deathbed, he confessed that he knew nothing more than any other person, but operated by sleight of hand and tricks <note>original: devices</note>, without the assistance of any devil or spirit—except for the "spirit of deception." I say he protested this before many people of great honesty, credit, and wisdom, who can witness the same; they also gave him high praise for his godly and honest end.

<margin>
Jean Bodin, in the preface to his book *On the Demon-Mania of Sorcerers* <note>original: Dæmonomania</note>, reports this regarding a conjuring priest, formerly the curate of Islington. He also shows for what purpose; read the passage, those of you who understand Latin.
</margin>
Again, who will maintain that common witchcraft cases are not deceptions, when the great and famous instances of witchcraft—which had gained unmerited belief not only from the common people, but from men of great wisdom and authority—are discovered to be paltry tricks of deceptive scoundrels <note>original: varlots</note>? Otherwise, these cases might and would have remained a perpetual objection against my argument. Were there not * three images recently found in a dunghill, to the terror and astonishment of many thousands? <note>Scot refers to a famous 1578 discovery of wax figures of Queen Elizabeth I and two counselors, intended to kill them via sympathetic magic.</note> Great matters were thought to have been intended by witchcraft. But if the Lord preserves those persons (whose destruction was feared to have been intended) from all other wicked practices and attempts of their enemies, I do not fear but that they shall easily withstand these and similar tricks, even if they were indeed practiced against them. No doubt, if such baubles <note>original: bables</note> could have brought about such mischief by the hands of traitors, witches, or Papists, we would long ago have been deprived of the most excellent jewel and comfort that we enjoy in this world <note>meaning Queen Elizabeth I</note>. However, I confess that the fear, imagination, and doubt of such mischievous pretenses may cause trouble to those who stand in awe of them. And I wish that even for such practices, though they can never take effect, the practitioners should be punished with all extremity; because such acts manifest a treasonous heart toward the Queen and a presumption against God.

<margin>
Note this trick of the waxen images found recently near London.
</margin>

The young gentleman, being deceived by these clever tricks and too hastily yielding to the proposal, satisfied this "cunning man's" demand for money—which, because he did not have it immediately to spend, he obtained from a friend. What a fuss was made about this, and also what reports and lies were spread! But the young gentleman, who for a little while remained hopeful, feeling both joy and love, now—through the passage of time—has had his happiness seasoned <note>original: powdred</note> with doubt and despair.
