### CHAPTER IV.

->*Of one who was so bewitched that he could read no Scriptures except the Canonical ones; of a devil that could speak no Latin; a proof that witchcraft is pure deception <note>original: cofenage</note>.*<-

<margin>A strange miracle, if it were true.</margin>
<margin>There the hypocrite was outmatched despite all his faked seriousness <note>original: dissembled gravity</note>.</margin>
Here I may aptly insert another important miracle that happened within the memory of a child, which may induce any reasonable person to understand that these supernatural actions are nothing but fables and frauds. There was one man—whom for certain reasons I will not name—who was struck blind, deaf, and dumb, so that no physician could help him. This man (of course), though he was supposedly blind, dumb, and deaf, could nevertheless read any of the Canonical Scriptures; but as for the Apocrypha <note>biblical books not accepted into the Protestant canon</note>, he could read none of it. In God's name, where was the miracle in that? However, when a leaf of the Apocrypha was specially inserted among the Canonical Scriptures, he read it as if it were authentic; and thus his knavery was exposed <note>original: bewrayed</note>. Another person had a devil that answered men all their questions. Truly, her devil could understand no Latin, and so she (and by such means all the rest may be) was exposed. Indeed, our writers on witchcraft say that certain devils speak only the language of the country where they are resident <note>original: resiant</note>, such as French or English, etc.

Furthermore, in my opinion, nothing proves more clearly that witchcraft is deception, and that the instruments of witches are but ridiculous trifles <note>original: Bables</note> and altogether ineffective, than when learned and godly divines, in their serious writings, produce experiments as if they were wrought by witches and by devils at witches' commands. They explain these as miracles, although they are actually mere trifles. They misunderstand these things because they are overcome by credulity.

# Witchcraft Confuted. Of Witchcraft. CHAPTER V.

...the hollow barrel <term>pipe</term> of the key, at the reading of these words from the Psalm [*If you saw a thief, you consented with him* <note>original: "If thou sawest a Thief, thou didst consent unto him" — Psalm 50:18</note>], the book will shake and fall out of the fingers of those holding it, and the person whose name is spoken when the key moves must be the thief. On this basis, <margin>The greatest scholars <note>original: Clarks</note> are not always the wisest men.</margin> Hemmingsen <note>original: Hemingius; referring to Niels Hemmingsen (1513–1600), a Danish theologian</note> concludes that although conjuring priests and witches do not bring this to pass by the literal words of the Psalm (which have a completely different purpose), Satan quickly, with his invisible hand, gives such a twitch to the book—as he also does in the other case with the sieve and the shears—that down fall the book and key, or the sieve and shears. Up starts the thief, and off runs the Devil laughing, and so on.

But alas, Hemmingsen is deceived, as he does not perceive the trickery, or rather the deceit, involved. For where he supposes those actions to be miraculous and performed by a Devil, they are in truth mere trifles <note>original: bables</note> that do not even require much sleight of hand <term>legerdemain</term>. Any wagon driver <note>original: Carter</note> can understand the trick of it; because the <margin>A natural explanation for the previous trick.</margin> book and key, or sieve and shears, being held up in that position, must by a natural and necessary course turn and fall down within that amount of time (due to the air and the pulse beating at the fingertips). Since witches and conjurers know this from experience, they form and frame their "prophecy" accordingly; anyone who tests this themselves will clearly see it is true. By this same art, practice, or experience, you can tell what time it is if you hold a thread six or seven inches long between your finger and thumb, with a gold ring (or something similar) tied to the other end. If held in such a way that the beating of your pulse and the swinging of the ring causes it to strike against the side of a goblet or glass, it will seem to tell the time. These things are, I admit, "witchcraft"—but only because the effect or result does not come from the cause that such con artists <note>original: coseners</note> claim, and which others believe. 

It is like when they apply a medicine for a fever <note>original: Ague</note> to a child's wrists while also pronouncing certain words or charms; they say the child is healed by the power of the words, when in fact the medicine alone did the work. This is also like a simple performer's trick that lacks true sleight of hand: you might see someone thrust a pin or a small knife through the head and brain of a chicken or pullet and, with certain mystical words, seem to cure it. In reality, even if no such words were spoken, the chicken would live and be well enough, as experience teaches and proves.

Furthermore, when those who once maintained the art and profession of conjuring and wrote about it most skillfully have later published recantations and confessed its deceits—as Cornelius Agrippa did—why should we defend <margin>Cornelius Agrippa in his book *On the Vanity of the Sciences* and in the letter before his book *On Occult Philosophy*. Pliny, *Natural History*, Book 30, Chapter 1. Peter Martyr in *Common Places*.</margin> it? Also, when Great Heathen Princes of renown, authority, and learning have searched with much industry and expense for the knowledge and secrets of conjuration and witchcraft, only to find through experience that everything reported of them is false and vain—as Nero, Julian the Apostate, and Valens did—why should we seek further trials to prove that witchcraft and conjuration are mere fraud <note>original: cosenage</note>?

Also, when the miracles attributed to witches exceed in quantity, quality, and number all the miracles that Christ performed here on earth to establish his Gospel, confirm our faith, and advance his glorious Name, what good Christian will believe them to be true? And when Christ himself says, *"The works that I do, no other man can accomplish,"* why should we think that a foolish old woman can do them all, and many more?

Additionally, since Christ did not know these witches, nor spoke a single word about them during all his time here on earth—despite having such a necessary occasion to do so (if, at least, they and their "familiars" could do what he did by the Spirit of God, as is constantly claimed)—why should we suppose they can do what they say? We should instead believe they are deceivers. When they are forced <note>original: fain</note> to say that witches did not practice that art during all the thirty-three years that Christ lived, and that there were none in Job's time, and that the deceptive oracles have now ceased, who cannot see that those who maintain such beliefs are witless and mad fools? When all the mischiefs are actually accomplished by poisons and natural means, which they claim to...

He further contends that if witchcraft were real, Christ would have mentioned it, and points out that famous historical occultists eventually admitted their practices were fraudulent.</summary>

<header>### BOOK XVI. The Discovery of Witchcraft Confuted.</header>

<margin>Note that during all of Christ's time upon earth, which was 33 years, witches were silenced, etc.</margin>...be brought to pass by words, it manifests to the world their trickery <note>original: "cosenage"</note>. When all the places of Scripture, which witch-hunters <note>original: "Witchmongers"</note> use for the proof of such witches, are proved to contribute nothing to their purpose, their own fables and lies deserve little credit. When one of the chief points in controversy—namely, the execution of witches—is grounded upon a false translation, specifically *Thou shalt not suffer a witch to live*, (which in Latin is *You shall not keep a poisoner alive* <note>original: "Veneficam non retinebis in vita"</note>), where the word to every man's ear sounds like a "poisoner" rather than a "worker of miracles," and is so interpreted by the seventy translators of the Septuagint, *Josephus*, and almost all the Rabbis who were born Hebrews: why should any of their interpretations or allegations be trusted or respected? 

When the working of miracles has ceased, and the gift of prophecy also—so that the godly, through the invocation of the Holy Spirit, cannot perform such wonderful things as these witches and conjurers undertake and are said to do by the invocation of devils and wicked spirits—what man who knows and honors God will be so foolish <note>original: "infatuate"</note> as to believe these lies, and thus prefer the power of witches and devils over the godly who are endowed with God’s Holy Spirit? When many printed books are published, even with official authority, confirming such miracles performed by those deceivers <note>original: "coseners"</note> for the detection of witchcraft; and in the end, all is not only found false and accomplished by trickery, but there has been a set purpose to defame honest matrons by making them be thought of as witches; why should we believe Bodin <note>Jean Bodin (1530–1596), a French jurist and writer on demonology</note>, the *Hammer of Witches* <note>original: "M. Mal." referring to the Malleus Maleficarum</note>, etc., in their deceptive tales and fables? 

When they say that witches can fly in the air and come in through a little opening <note>original: "coan"</note> or a hole in a glass window and steal away sucking children and hurt their mothers—and yet when they are brought into prison, they cannot escape out of the bars <note>original: "grate"</note>, which are far larger—who will not condemn such accusations or confessions as frivolous, etc.? When (if their assertions were true) concerning the Devil’s usual taking of shapes, and walking, talking, conferring, hurting, and all manner of dealing with mortal creatures, Christ's argument to Thomas would have been weak and easily answered; indeed, half or all the whole world might be inhabited by devils. Every poor man's house might be rented out from under him by a devil; he might take the shape and appearance of an honest woman and play the witch, or of an honest man and play the thief, and so bring them both—or whomever he pleased—to the gallows. Who does not see the vanity of such assertions? For then the Devil might, in the likeness of an honest man, commit any criminal offense; as <margin>But Christ's argument was undoubted; Therefore <note>original: "Ergo"</note>, etc.</margin> <margin>I marvel for what purpose that magistrate went to that fellow's house.</margin> Lavater <note>Ludwig Lavater (1527–1586), a Swiss Reformed theologian</note> in his nineteenth chapter of *Of Spirits and Apparitions* <note>original: "De spectris"</note>, reports of a grave, wise magistrate in the territory of Zurich <note>original: "Tigurie"</note>, who affirmed that as he and his servant went through certain pastures, he saw in the morning the Devil in the likeness of one whom he knew very well, wickedly dealing with a mare. Upon seeing this, he immediately went to that fellow's house and certainly learned there that the same person did not leave his chamber that day. And if he had not wisely investigated <note>original: "bolted out"</note> the matter, the good honest man (he says) would surely have been cast into prison and put on the rack, etc.

<margin>Albert Krantz in book 4 of *Metropolis*, chapter 4 <note>original: "Albertus Crantzius in lib. 4. metropolis. cap. 4."</note></margin> We read a similar story of one Cunigunde <note>original: "Cangunda"</note>, wife to Henry II, the emperor of that name, in whose chamber the Devil (in the likeness of a young man with whom she was suspected to be too familiar in court) was often seen coming in and out. However, she was purged by the trial of *glowing iron* <note>original: "Candentis Ferri"</note> and proved innocent; for she walked upon glowing iron unhurt, etc. And yet Solomon says,

<margin>Proverbs 6:27, 28.</margin>> May a man carry fire in his bosom, and his clothes not be burned? Or can a man go upon coals, and his feet not be scorched?

And thus might the Devil get himself up into the pulpit and spread heresies—as I do not doubt he does in the mouths of wicked preachers, though not as crudely as is imagined and reported by the Papists and witch-hunters. And because it shall not be said that I misrepresent <note>original: "belie"</note> them, I will <margin>*Hammer of Witches*, part 2, question 1, chapter 9 <note>original: "Mal. malef. par. 2. quæst. 1. cap. 9."</note></margin> cite a story credibly reported by their chief doctors, namely, Jacob Sprenger and Heinrich Kramer <note>original: "James Sprenger, and Henry Institor"</note>, who say as follows, word for word.

# The Devil a Preacher. of Witchcraft. CHAP. VI.

### CHAP. VI.

->*How the Devil preached good doctrine in the shape of a priest, how he was discovered, and that it is a shame (after the refutation of the greater witchcrafts) for any man to give credit to the lesser points thereof.*<-

<margin>He should rather have asked who gave him orders and a license to preach.</margin>
<margin>Jean Bodin <note>Jean Bodin (1530–1596) was a French jurist and philosopher who wrote "De la démonomanie des sorciers," a famous text supporting the prosecution of witches.</note></margin>
<margin>Yet many who appear to be honest men are very credulous in this matter.</margin>

Once upon a time, the Devil went up into a pulpit and there delivered a very Catholic sermon. But a holy priest, arriving just in time, perceived through his holiness that he was the Devil. He listened closely to him but could find no fault with his doctrine. Therefore, as soon as the sermon was finished, he called the Devil to him and asked why he preached so sincerely. The Devil answered: *“Behold, I speak the truth, knowing that while men hear the Word but do not follow it, God is more offended and my kingdom is further enlarged.”* And this was the strangest trick (I think) that any Devil ever used, for the Apostles themselves could have done no more. 

Again, when—despite all their familiar spirits and ointments by which they ride invisibly—they can neither escape from the hands of those who lie in wait for them, nor get out of prison (though they claim to go in and out through mouse-holes), nor finally save themselves from the gallows (though they claim to transform their own and other bodies into flies or fleas, etc.), who does not see that they either lie or are lied about regarding their miracles? 

When they are said to transfer their neighbor's corn into their own fields, and yet remain perpetual beggars who cannot enrich themselves with money or otherwise: who is so foolish as to still doubt their lack of supernatural power? 

When no one from the beginning of the world until this day has openly shown any other trick, concept, or cunning point of witchcraft other than <term>Legierdemain</term> <note>sleight of hand</note> or <term>cosenage</term> <note>deception or fraud</note>, who will wait any longer for further proof? 

When both the common law and official injunctions condemn prophesying and false miracles, and those who believe them nowadays, who would not be afraid to trust such trickery? 

When, by this, they turn the Devil into a God who hears prayers and understands the minds of men: who would not be ashamed, as a Christian, to be so abused by them? 

When those who write most openly of these matters—except for the lying *Sprenger* and *Institor* <note>James Sprenger and Henry Institor (Heinrich Kramer), the authors of the "Malleus Maleficarum," a 15th-century treatise on the prosecution of witches.</note>—have never actually seen any of it; so much so that the most credible proof Jean Bodin provides for his wonderful tales of witchcraft is the report of his host at an alehouse where he stopped for a meal <note>original: "baited"</note>: who will listen any further to these incredible fables? 

When in the entire New Testament we are not warned about these physical appearances of devils, as we are of his other subtleties, etc.: who will be afraid of their "bogeymen" <note>original: "bugs"</note>? 

When no such bargain is mentioned in the Scriptures, why should we believe such incredible and impossible covenants? These are the foundation of all the witch-hunters' <note>original: "Witchmongers"</note> religion, without which they have no logic in the rest of their foolish assertions. 

Furthermore, if any honest conscience is consulted, they must confess they never saw a trial of such witchcraft or conjuration take effect as is now so certainly claimed. What conscience can condemn poor souls who are accused wrongfully, or believe those who impiously claim to perform those impossible things? 

When the entire course of Scripture is utterly opposed to these impossible opinions, except for a few sentences which, when rightly understood, do not support them at all: who will be seduced by their foolish arguments? 

Now that men have seen through the trickery of oracles and such trash <term>original: pelf</term>, and there is not a single oracle remaining in the world: who cannot see that all the rest of those devices have been deceptions, trickery, and lies? 

When the power of God is so shamelessly transferred to a lowly creature, what good Christian can stand to submit to such miracles performed by fools? 

When the old women accused of witchcraft are utterly senseless <note>original: "insensible"</note> and unable to speak for themselves—much less bring about such events as they are accused of...

<summary>Scot argues that if witches possessed the supernatural powers attributed to them, they would not be poor or easily imprisoned. He presents a series of rhetorical arguments to show that witchcraft is based on trickery, faulty logic, and unreliable anecdotes rather than scripture or evidence.</summary>

<margin>Witches are commonly very poor beggars.</margin>
...of it: who will not lament to see the extreme measures used against them? Since the more foolish people are always the most suspicious of being harmed by witchcraft, and the simplest and most senile <note>original: "dotingest"</note> people are suspected of doing the harm, what wise person will not see that it is all folly? If it were a simple matter for the Devil (if he can do what they claim) to give them plenty of money and make them rich—which he does not do—even though it would win him more disciples than anything else in the world, then the wise must conclude the Devil is a fool and the witches are perverse <note>original: "peevishness"</note>. Why else would they take such pains and give their souls to the Devil to be tormented in Hell, and their bodies to the executioners to be hanged on the gallows, all for small change <note>original: "nichels"</note> in a bag?

---

### C H A P. VII.

#### *A Conclusion against Witchcraft, in the form of a Logical Argument.*

<margin>A general conclusion against those whom this book addresses.</margin>
By now, all men of Kent <note>The author, Reginald Scot, lived in Kent; here he implies that the local population has been enlightened by his arguments.</note> know (except for a few fools) that *Robin Goodfellow* <note>A mischievous sprite or "puck" in English folklore.</note> is a *scoundrel*. All wise men understand that the miraculous feats of witches, being contrary to nature, probability, and reason, are devoid of truth or possibility. All Protestants realize that *Catholic <note>original: "Popish"</note> charms, conjurations, curses, and blessings* have no power, but are merely toys and tricks to keep the people ignorant and to enrich the clergy. All Christians see that to admit witches can do what they claim would be to attribute the power of the Creator to a mere creature. All well-raised children realize and see—or at least are taught—that the miracles of *magicians* <note>original: "Juglers"</note> consist of *sleight of hand* <note>original: "Legierdemain"</note> and hidden help <note>original: "Confederacy"</note>. Even pagan people are forced to admit that there can be no such meeting between a spiritual Devil and a physical witch as is imagined. For if there were, every pagan would surely have his own familiar spirit, as they would have no moral objection to befriending a Devil since they do not know God.

I have dealt and spoken with many people (though I must admit they were mostly Catholics) who maintain every point of these absurdities. Surely I think better of their judgment than of others who see through some of these deceptions but still believe the rest. This is especially true of those who understand the greater frauds of conjuring and deceit—namely, in *Catholicism*—and yet still allow themselves to be fooled by shabby *sleight of hand* <note>original: "Jugling"</note> and *witchcraft*.

---

### C H A P. VIII.

#### *Of Natural Witchcraft or Fascination.*

But because I am reluctant to set myself against all writers on this subject, or to completely discredit their stories or ruin their reports regarding the effects of *fascination* <note>The ancient belief in the "evil eye" or bewitching by sight or voice.</note> or *witchcraft*, I will now describe certain parts of it. Although I cannot accept these myself without some doubts, difficulties, and exceptions, I will allow others the liberty to believe them if they wish, as they do not directly contradict my purpose.

<margin>
*Isigonus.*
*Memphidorus.*
*Solinus, etc.*
*Leonardo Vair.*
*Jean Bodin.*
*The Hammer of Witches.* <note>original: "Mal. Malef." (Malleus Maleficarum)</note>
</margin>
Many great and serious authors write—and many foolish writers also claim—that there are certain families in *Africa* who bewitch whatever they praise with their voices. So much so that if they commend a *plant, corn, an infant, a horse*, or any other beast, it immediately withers, decays, and dies. This "mystery" of witchcraft is not unknown or ignored by our witch-believers <note>original: "Witchmongers"</note> and superstitious fools here in *Europe*. To show you examples closer to home here in *England*, as though our voices had the same effect: you will never hear a *butcher* or a *horse-dealer* <note>original: "Horse-courser"</note> bargain for <note>original: "cheapen"</note> a *bullock* or a *worn-out horse* <note>original: "Jade"</note>, but if he...

Certainly, the sentiment is godly if it comes from a faithful and godly mind. ### CHAP. IX.
### Of Enchanting or Bewitching Eyes.

<margin>The ancient Illyrian people were endowed with similar traits, if we believe the words of Sabinus, based on the report of Aulus Gellius.</margin>
Many writers agree with Virgil and Theocritus regarding the effect of bewitching eyes, claiming that in Scythia there are women called *Bithiæ* who have two pupils <note>original: "bals or rather blacks"</note> in the centers of their eyes. And as Didymus reports, some have two such pupils in one eye, and the image of a horse in the other. These women (supposedly) bewitch and hurt not only young lambs but also young children with their angry looks. There are others who keep such venom in their eyes and send it out in beams and streams so violently that they harm not only those they live with constantly, but also everyone else they spend time with—regardless of age, strength, or temperament—as Cicero, Plutarch, Phylarchus, and many others claim in their writings.

<margin>Giambattista della Porta, in his book *On Natural Magic*.</margin>
<margin>Some hold this to be the truth.</margin>
This Fascination <note>The "evil eye," or the act of bewitching by sight.</note> (says Giambattista della Porta <note>original: "John Baptista Porta Neapolitanus"</note>), although it begins by touching or breathing, is always accomplished and finished by the eye. It is an expulsion of the "spirits" through the eyes, which reach the heart of the bewitched person and infect it. Thus, it happens that a child or a young man, gifted with clear, healthy, refined <note>original: "subtil"</note>, and sweet blood, produces similar spirits, breath, and vapors springing from the purer blood of the heart. These lightest and finest spirits ascend into the highest parts of the head and fall into the eyes. They are sent forth from there because the eyes are the clearest parts of the body and are full of veins and pores. With the very spirit or vapor proceeding from them, a certain fiery force is carried out like beams or streams. Anyone who looks at sore eyes will have first-hand experience of this. For the poison and disease in the eye infect the air next to it, and this infection proceeds further, carrying the vapor and contagion of the corrupted blood; the eyes of onlookers are most likely to be infected by this contagion. By this same means, it is thought that the Cockatrice <note>A mythical serpent that could kill with a look.</note> takes life, and a wolf takes away the voice of those they suddenly meet and look at.

<margin>The object being looked at is not actually inside the mirror. <note>original: "Non est in speculo res quæ speculatur in illo"</note></margin>
Old women, in whom the ordinary course of nature no longer performs the duty of purging their natural monthly fluids <note>This refers to menopause; early modern "science" believed that retained menstrual blood became toxic and was vented through the eyes.</note>, also show proof of this. For (as the aforementioned Giambattista della Porta reports, citing Aristotle as his source) they leave a certain froth in a looking-glass because of the thick vapors coming out of their eyes. This happens because those vapors or spirits, which come so abundantly from their eyes, cannot pierce and enter the glass (which is hard and has no pores) and are therefore resisted. However, the beams that are carried in the vehicle <note>original: "chariot"</note> or conveyance of the spirits from the eyes of one body to another do pierce the inward parts and breed infection there while they search for their proper place. And as these beams and vapors proceed from the heart of one person, they are turned into blood around the heart of the other. This blood, being incompatible with the nature of the bewitched party, weakens the rest of his body and makes him sick. This contagion continues as long as the distempered blood has power in the limbs. And because the infection is in the blood, the fever or sickness will be continuous; whereas if it were caused by yellow bile <note>original: "choler"</note> or phlegm, it would be intermittent or changeable.

# BOOK XVI. The Discovery of Natural Magic.

### CHAPTER X.
### On Natural Witchcraft for Love, etc.

<margin>
"I do not know what eye bewitches my tender lambs," <note>original: "Nescio quis oculus teneros mihi fascinat agnos"</note> says Virgil; and thus translated into English by Abraham Fleming:
"I do not know
What witching eye
Is used to haunt
My tender lambs
Sucking their dams
And them enchant."
</margin>

But just as there is fascination and witchcraft caused by malicious and angry eyes that lead to displeasure, there are also bewitching gazes <note>original: "Aspects"</note> that work in the opposite way—tending toward love, or at the very least, toward gaining goodwill and liking. For if the fascination or witchcraft is brought about or provoked by desire—by wishing for and coveting any beautiful shape or appearance—the "venom" is filtered through the eyes, even from a distance. The imagination of a beautiful form then remains in the heart of the lover and kindles a fire where it is felt <note>original: "afflicted"</note>. Because the most delicate, sweet, and tender blood of the beloved person wanders there, their face is represented there, shining in its own blood, and cannot rest. It is so pulled from that place that the blood of the one who is "wounded" by love rebounds and leaps into the one who caused the wound <note>The author is describing the physical sensation of attraction as a literal transfer of spirits or blood through the gaze.</note>, according to the saying of Lucretius the poet on this subject in these verses:

> "The mind seeks that body from which it is wounded by love,
> For almost everyone falls toward the wound, and the blood 
> spurts out toward that part from which we are struck;
> And if the lover is close at hand, then a red moisture covers the face."
> <note>original: "Idque petit corpus, mens unde est saucia amore, / Namque omnes plerunque cadunt in vulnus, & illam / Emicat in partem sanguis, unde icimur ictu; / Et si cominus est, os tum ruber occupat humor."</note>

->Translated by Abraham Fleming:<-

> *And to that body it is rebounded,
> From which the mind by love is wounded,
> For in a manner, one and all,
> Into that wound of love do fall,
> And to that part the blood does flee
> From where we happen struck to be;
> If close at hand, and near in place,
> Then ruddy color fills the face.*

This much seems sufficient regarding the matter of natural magic; although much more could be added, I will end this current treatise to avoid being tedious and to move more quickly to what remains. Now, something shall be said concerning devils and spirits in the discourse that follows.

<summary>Scot explains the concept of "love at first sight" as a form of natural witchcraft or fascination, where the beauty of another person "wounds" the observer through the eyes. He concludes his section on natural magic to begin a new discussion on the nature of devils and spirits.</summary>

### A
# DISCOURSE
## CONCERNING
# Devils and Spirits.

### BOOK I.

---

#### CHAP. I.

*The Opinions of Philosophers concerning Devils and Spirits; their manner of reasoning on the subject, and the refutation of those arguments.*

<margin>Girolamo Cardano, *On the Variety of Things*, book 16, chapter 93.</margin>
<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial letter 'T' depicting a central figure amidst leafy scrolls.</image-desc>There is no question or subject (says Girolamo Cardano <note>original: "Hierome Cardane"; a famous 16th-century Italian physician and polymath</note>) so difficult to handle, nor so noble an argument to debate, as this one concerning *Devils and Spirits*. This is because, whether their existence is accepted or doubted, the eternity of the *Soul* is either affirmed or denied.
<margin>The Platonists and Stoics.</margin>
The pagan philosophers <note>original: "Heathen Philosophers"</note> reason among themselves about this in the following way.
<margin>The Epicureans and Peripatetics <note>Followers of Aristotle</note>.</margin>
First, those who maintain the immortality <note>original: "perpetuity"</note> of the soul say: *If the soul died with the body, why should men take the trouble to live well or die well? For no reward for virtue nor punishment for vice follows after this life—which otherwise they might spend in ease and security.* The other group says that *virtue and honesty are to be pursued* not for the hope of reward, but for the love of virtue <note>original Latin: "Non spe præmii, sed virtutis amore"</note>. If the soul lives forever (the others say), then the smallest portion of life is spent here. *Therefore, we who maintain the immortality of the soul may take better comfort and courage to endure with more steadiness the loss of children, and even the loss of life itself.* However, if the soul were mortal, all our hope and happiness would have to be placed in this life—which I guarantee many atheists do today. 

But both sides missed the mark <note>original: "missed the cushion"; a 16th-century idiom meaning to be completely mistaken</note>. For to do anything without Christ is to weary ourselves in vain, since only in Him are our corruptions purged. 
<margin>The highest good cannot consist in the happiness of the body or mind.</margin>
Therefore, the folly of the pagans—who place the *highest good* <note>original Latin: "Summum bonum"</note> in the physical well-being of the body or the happiness and pleasures of the mind—is not only to be ridiculed but also loathed. For both our bodies and minds are mixed with the most miserable calamities; therefore, perfect happiness cannot exist within them. Instead, the Word of God presents and offers us a hope that is most certain, absolute, sound, and sincere—one that cannot be challenged or denied by the judgment of philosophers.

<summary>This page introduces the debate over the existence of spirits and the immortality of the soul, contrasting the various schools of Greek philosophy with the Christian perspective that true happiness is found only in Christ.</summary>
<keywords>Girolamo Cardano, Devils and Spirits, Immortality of the Soul, Platonists, Stoics, Epicureans, Peripatetics, Summum Bonum, virtue, pagan philosophy</keywords>

    *   Early Modern English spelling (hee, doe, vnto, etc.).
    *   Latin phrases (*Summum bonum*).

    *   *Paragraph 1:* Refutes moral virtues (Temperance, Prudence, Justice, Fortitude) as the "Highest Good" (*Summum bonum*). Argument: These virtues only exist because we are corrupt/miserable. St. Paul (Romans 2) says justice isn't reached via nature/law alone. "Reckoning without his host" = a metaphor for a miscalculation.
    *   *Heading Chapter II:* Scot's own opinion.

Lists various weird theories (souls become spirits, spirits are mortal, spirits are wind, etc.). Mentions Papists/Catholics (specifically the Rheims New Testament) and their "worship" of angels.

    *   *meet and agree jump with* -> coincide exactly with.

    *   *Heading:* Book I. A Discourse concerning The Author's Opinion.
    *   *Margin:* Moral Temperance.
    *   *Text:* "themſelves: For they that preferr temperance before all other things as *Summum bonum*, muſt needs ſee it to be but a witneſs of their natural calamity, corruption and wickedneſs..."
    *   *Modernization:* ...themselves: For those who prefer temperance above all other things as the *highest good* <note>original Latin: "summum bonum"</note> must necessarily see it as nothing more than a witness to their natural calamity, corruption, and wickedness. They must see that it serves only to restrain the lack of self-control found in their vice-infected minds, which must be reined in with such corrections. Indeed, even the best of them fail in some point of modesty.
    *   *Margin:* Moral Prudence.
    *   *Text:* "Wherefore ſerveth our Philoſophers prudence, but to provide for their own folly and miſery..."
    *   *Modernization:* To what purpose does the prudence of our philosophers serve, except to provide for their own folly and misery, which might otherwise utterly overthrow them? If their nature were not entangled in errors, they would have no need for such caution.
    *   *Margin:* Moral Justice.
    *   *Text:* "The justice whereof they ſpeak, ſerveth but to keep them from ravine, theft, and violence..."
    *   *Modernization:* The justice they speak of serves only to keep them from plunder <note>original: "ravine"</note>, theft, and violence; and yet none of them are so just that even the best and most upright among them do not fall into great weaknesses, both doing and suffering much wrong and injury.
    *   *Margin:* Moral Fortitude.
    *   *Text:* "And what is their fortitude but to arm them to endure misery, grief, danger, and death it ſelf?..."
    *   *Modernization:* And what is their fortitude, but to arm them to endure misery, grief, danger, and death itself? But what happiness or goodness can be found in a life that must be attended by such calamities, and finally needs the help of death to end it? I say, if life is so miserable, why do they place the *highest good* <note>original: "Summum bonum"</note> within it? Saint Paul, in his letter to the Romans, shows that it is impossible for us to achieve justice through the moral and natural actions and duties of this life, because neither the Jews nor the Gentiles could ever live up to what the very law of Nature or of Moses required. Therefore, he who works without Christ is like a man who calculates his bill without the innkeeper <note>original: "reckoneth without his host"; meaning to make a plan without considering the main person or factor involved</note>.

    *   *Modernization:* For my part, I also believe this argument concerning the nature and substance of devils and spirits to be so difficult that I am convinced no single author has yet written about it in any certain or perfect way.
    *   *Text (Groups and names):* In this respect, I can neither support the ungodly and profane sects and doctrines of the Sadducees and Peripatetics (who deny that there are any devils or spirits at all), nor the foolish and superstitious treatises of Plato, Proclus, Plotinus, and Porphyry; nor yet the vain and absurd opinions of Psellus, Nider, Sprenger, Cumanus, Bodin, Michael, Andreas, Janus, Matthew <note>original: "Matcheus"</note>, Laurentius Ananias, and Iamblichus.     *   *The Theories List:*
        *   Some claim the souls of the dead become spirits—the good becoming angels and the bad becoming devils.
        *   Some say spirits or devils exist only in this life.
        *   Some say they are men; some say they are women.
        *   Some say devils take on whatever gender they please.

They also say spirits are to be worshipped.
    *   *The Papists section:* In this, they coincide exactly <note>original: "meet and agree jump"</note> with the Catholics <note>original: "Papists"</note>. Indeed, if you read the notes on the second chapter of Colossians in the *Seminary's Testament* printed at Rheims <note>The Catholic New Testament translated in 1582</note>, you will clearly see opinions as contrary to the Word of God as black is to white. This is evident in the Book of Revelation <note>original: "Apocalypse"</note>, where the angel explicitly forbade John from worshipping him.

### C H A P. III.

#### The opinion of Psellus regarding Spirits; their several Orders; and a Refutation of his Errors therein.

<margin>Such are spirits walking in white sheets, etc.</margin>
Psellus—who is considered an authority in the Roman Church and whose word is not to be challenged by any Catholic—was instructed in these supernatural, or rather diabolical, matters by a monk called Marcus. This Marcus claimed to have been intimately acquainted for a long time with a certain devil. Psellus reports, based on that devil’s own word (which supposedly understands the state of this question best), that the bodies of angels and devils are no longer made of the same single element, though perhaps they were before the fall of Lucifer. He claims that the bodies of spirits and devils can feel and be felt, and can both do harm and be harmed. He even asserts that they lament when they are struck and are burned when exposed to fire. Yet, he claims they themselves burn continually, to such an extent that they leave ashes behind in the places where they have been; as he claims (if he speaks truly) there has been clear evidence of this in the borders of Italy. 

<margin>Psellus, the same work, chapter 9.</margin>
He also says, upon similar credit and assurance, that devils and spirits excrete from their bodies a type of seed or substance from which certain vermin are spawned. He further claims that they are nourished with food just as we are, except they do not take it into their mouths; instead, they suck it up into their bodies, much like how sponges soak up water.

<margin>The same author, chapter 10.</margin>
He also says they have names, shapes, and dwelling places—which they do have, though not in a physical or worldly sense.

<margin>The same author, chapter 11.</margin>

<margin>Oh Heathenish; no, oh Papal folly!</margin>
Furthermore, he says that there are six principal kinds of devils, which are not only physical but also subject to time and the world. The **first sort** consists of fire, wandering in the region near the Moon, though they have no power to enter the Moon itself. The **second sort**, consisting of air, has its habitation lower and closer to us. These, he says, are proud and great boasters, very wise and deceitful; when they descend, they are seen with streams of fire at their tails.

<margin>The opinions of all Catholics. A cheating trickery.</margin>
He says that these are commonly conjured up to make statues appear to laugh and to make lamps turn on their own. In Assyria, he claims they often use a basin of water for prophecy. This kind of incantation is common among our own conjurers, but here it is usually performed with a pitcher or pot of water, or else in a glass vial filled with water. They say that at first, a little sound is heard without a voice, which is a sign of the devil's arrival. Soon, the water appears to be troubled, and then small voices are heard giving answers, speaking so softly that no one can hear them clearly. This is because, according to Cardan, they do not want to be challenged or rebuked for their lies.

<margin>Hieronymus Cardanus, *On the Variety of Things*, Book 10, chapter 93.</margin>
I have described and refuted this more extensively elsewhere. The **third sort** of devils are earthly; the **fourth** are watery, or of the sea. The **fifth** live under the earth. The **sixth sort** are the "Light-fleers" <note>original: "Lucifugi"</note>—that is, those who delight in darkness. These are barely endowed with senses and are so dull that they can hardly be moved by charms or conjurations.

The previous opinion refuted.

But in this, his philosophy is very improbable; for if the devil is made of earth, he must necessarily be solid <note>original: "palpable"</note>; if he is solid, he must necessarily kill those into whose bodies he enters. *Likewise*, if he were created of earth, then he must also be visible and unable to change his form in that respect, for God's creation cannot be annihilated by a creature. So, even if it were granted that they might add matter and form to their substance, etc., yet it is most certain that they cannot diminish or alter the substance of which they consist—such as choosing to be spiritual whenever they like, or abandoning the earth, water, fire, air, or whichever element they were created from. But however they imagine devils of water, air, or fire, I am sure earth must always be visible and solid; yes, and air must always be invisible, fire must be hot, and water must be moist. And of these three latter bodies, especially water and air, no form nor shape can be shown to mortal eyes naturally, or by the power of any creature.

## CHAPTER VI.

### *The Opinion of Plato concerning Spirits, Devils, and Angels; what Sacrifices they like best, and what they fear; and concerning Socrates’s familiar Devil.*

<margin>The opinion of the Platonists.</margin>
**P**lato and his followers hold that good spirits appear in their own true likeness, but that evil spirits appear and show themselves in the form of other bodies. They believe that one Devil reigns over the rest, just as a Prince reigns over men in every perfect commonwealth. Furthermore, they believe these spirits obtain their purposes and desires only by the entreaty of men and women; this is because, in nature, spirits are actually inferior to humans. They exercise authority over men only in the same way that priests do—by virtue of their office and because of religion, through which (it is said) they carry out the work of God. Sometimes, they say, the fiery spirits or supreme substances enter into the purity of the mind to achieve their goals; at other times, they act through the power of holy charms, or in the way a poor man obtains something from a Prince for God's sake through sheer persistence.

The other sort of Devils and defiled souls stay so close to the earth that they do much harm to earthly bodies, especially through lechery. The Platonists say that because Gods and Angels lack all material and physical substance, they most desire the pure sacrifice of the mind. The grosser and more physical spirits desire 

<margin>What kind of sacrifices each spirit likes best.</margin>
grosser sacrifices, such as beasts and cattle. Those in the middle region delight in having frankincense and similar modest items offered to them. Therefore, they say it is necessary to sacrifice all kinds of things to them, provided the animals are killed for the purpose and do not die of natural causes; for the spirits abhor those that die on their own. Some say that spirits are wonderfully afraid of empty threats and will leave because of them. For instance, if you tell them that you will cut the heavens into pieces, reveal their secrets, complain about them to the gods, or say you will do something impossible or beyond their understanding, they are so timid that they will leave immediately. This is thought to be the best way to get rid of them. These spirits are most commonly of the rank called "Principalities" <note>original: *Principatus*; a level in the traditional hierarchy of angels or demons</note>, which are the easiest of all to conjure.

<margin>Concerning the private devil or familiar spirit of Socrates.</margin>
They say Socrates had a "familiar devil" <note>A personal attendant spirit, known in Greek as a *daimonion*</note>, a claim which *Plato* relies on heavily. Plato uses no other argument to prove that such spirits exist except the fact that *Socrates* (who would not lie) said so. This was also supported by the fact that this devil always discouraged and forbade certain actions, not only in *Socrates’s* own affairs but sometimes on behalf of his friends; if they had followed his advice, they might have saved their lives. Socrates's disciples concluded that his devil was "Saturnal" <note>Influenced by the planet Saturn; often associated with melancholy or gravity</note> and a primary fiery devil. They believed that he, and all those who naturally know their devils, are only those called "demonic men" <note>original: *Dæmonii viri*; men supposedly in contact with spirits</note>, whom others call swindlers. They also say that fiery spirits urge men toward contemplation, airy spirits toward business, and watery spirits toward lust. Among these, some are "Martial" <note>Influenced by Mars</note>, giving courage; some are "Jovial" <note>Influenced by Jupiter</note>, giving wisdom; and some are "Saturnal," always using dissuasion and warning. Finally, they say some are born with us and remain with us all our lives, while others are mere strangers who are nothing more than the souls of departed men, and so on.

It also examines the famous "familiar spirit" of Socrates as the primary evidence used by Platonists to prove the existence of such entities.</summary>

# CHAPTER VII.

### *Plato's nine orders of spirits and angels; Dionysius’s division of them, which is not much different; all of which are disproved by learned theologians.*

Plato proposes or sets forth nine different orders of spirits, besides the spirits and souls of men. The first spirit is *God*, who commands all the rest; the second are those called *Ideas* <note>original: "Idea"; in Platonic philosophy, these are the eternal, non-physical forms or patterns of all things</note>, who gave all things to all men; the third are the souls of heavenly bodies, which are mortal; the fourth are Angels; the fifth are Archangels; the sixth are Devils, who are ministers to infernal powers, just as Angels are to heavenly ones; the seventh are half-gods <note>original: "half Gods"; likely referring to demigods or daemons in the Greek sense</note>; the eighth are Principalities; and the ninth are Princes. <margin>Dionysius, *The Celestial Hierarchy*, chapters 9, 10.</margin> From this division, Dionysius does not stray far, except that he deals (as he claims) only with good spirits, whom he likewise divides into nine parts or offices. The first he calls *Seraphim*, the second *Cherubim*, the third *Thrones*, the fourth *Dominations*, the fifth *Virtues*, the sixth *Powers*, the seventh *Principalities*, the eighth *Archangels*, and the ninth and <margin>Ephesians 6.</margin> lower sort he calls *Angels*. However, some of these (in my opinion) are evil spirits; otherwise, Paul gave us bad advice when he commanded us *to fight against Principalities, and Powers, and all spiritual wickedness.*

<margin>Dionysius, *The Celestial Hierarchy*.</margin> But Dionysius goes even further in that place, assigning a specific angel to every country and almost to every person of any importance. For example, to Judea <note>original: "Jewry"</note> he assigns *Michael*; to Adam, *Razael*; to Abraham, *Zekiel*; to Isaac, *Raphael*; to Jacob, *Peliel*; to Moses, *Metraton*, and so on. But in these discussions, he either followed his own imagination and whims, or else the corruptions of that age. Nevertheless, I would rather refute him using Mr. Calvin and my kinsman Mr. Dering than by myself or my own words. For Mr. Calvin says, <margin>John Calvin, *Institutes of the Christian Religion*, book 1, chapter 14.</margin> *That Dionysius speaks here not as if by hearsay, but as though he had slipped down from Heaven* <margin>Edward Dering, *Lectures on the Epistle to the Hebrews*, lecture 6.</margin> <margin>Malachi 3:1.</margin> *and told of things which he had seen.* And yet (Calvin says) Paul was wrapped up into the third heaven and reports no such matters. But if you read Mr. Dering’s commentary on the first chapter of *Hebrews*, you shall see this matter handled excellently. There he says *that whenever "Archangel" is mentioned in the Scriptures, it signifies our Savior Christ, and no other creature.* And it is certain that Christ himself was called an *Angel*. The names of angels, such as *Michael*, *Gabriel*, etc., are given to them (says Calvin) according to the limits of our human weakness. But because the final decision on this is neither within the reach of human capacity nor our knowledge, I will proceed no further in discussing it. Instead, I will show the absurd opinions of the *Papists* and *witchmongers* <term>those who promote or believe in the reality and power of witchcraft</term> on one side, and the most sober and probable conclusions of those who disagree on the other.

### CHAP. IX.

->Of the contention between the Greek and Latin Church touching the fall of Angels;<-
->the variance among Papists themselves herein; a conflict between Michael and<-
->Lucifer.<-

<margin>Lorenzo Anania, *On the Nature of Demons*, Book 1.</margin>
There was also another contention between the Greek Church and the Latin Church: namely, from which orders of angels those who fell with *Lucifer* belonged. Our Schoolmen say, *“They were from all nine orders of angels in Lucifer’s conspiracy.”* But because the superior order was of a more noble constitution and excellent estate, and the inferior of a less worthy nature, the greater part of the inferior orders fell as guilty offenders with *Lucifer*. Some say *the Devil himself was of the inferior order of angels*; and some say he was of the highest order, because it is written: *“Extended upon a Cherubim and protecting, I have placed you in the holy mountain of God”* <note>original Latin: "In Cherubim extentus & protegens posui te Monte sancto Dei"</note>. These people say further, *“That he was called the Dragon because of his excellent knowledge.”* Finally, these great doctors conclude *that the Devil himself was of the Order of Seraphim, which is the highest*, because it is written, *“For how did you rise in the morning, O Lucifer?”* <note>original Latin: "Quomodo enim mane oriebaris Lucifer?"</note>. Those of this sect affirm that the *Cacodemones* <note>from the Greek "kakodaimon," meaning an evil spirit or "bad demon"</note> were those who rebelled against Jove—I mean those of *Plato's* sect, as Plato himself held that opinion. Our Schoolmen differ much on the cause of Lucifer’s fall. For some say it was for speaking these words: *“I will place my seat in the North, and I will be like the Most High”* <note>original Latin: "Ponam sedem meam in aquilone, & similis ero altissimo"</note>. Others say it was because he utterly refused happiness and felt scorn for it. Others say it was because he thought all his strength proceeded from himself and not from God. Others say that it was because he attempted to do that by himself, and his own ability,

<meta>This page begins the first book of Reginald Scot's "The Discovery of Witchcraft," a landmark skeptical text first published in 1584. It establishes the author's primary argument: that attributing natural disasters and personal misfortunes to witches is a denial of God's divine providence.</meta>

<image-desc>A decorative woodcut border with a repeating pattern of squares and crosses.</image-desc>

### THE
### DISCOVERY
### OF
### Witchcraft.

### BOOK I.

#### CHAPTER I.

<margin>A challenge against the power of witches over <term>meteors</term> <note>original: "Meteors"; in the 16th century, this referred to any atmospheric phenomena like rain or lightning.</note> and the <term>physical elements</term> <note>original: "Elementary Bodies"</note>, intended to rebuke those who attribute too much power to them.</margin>

<image-desc>A large decorative initial capital 'T' with intricate floral and leaf patterns.</image-desc>The myths of witchcraft have taken such a strong hold and deep root in the human heart that few or none nowadays can patiently endure the discipline and correction of God. For if any adversity, grief, sickness, or loss of children, crops, cattle, or liberty happens to them, they immediately cry out against witches. It is as if there were no God in Israel who orders all things according to His will—punishing both the just and the unjust with grief, plagues, and afflictions in the way He sees fit. Instead, they believe that certain old women on earth, called witches, must be the authors of all men's calamities, as if they themselves were innocent and deserved no such punishment. Consequently, they do not hesitate to travel to those who are either wrongly called witches or are willing to be known as such, seeking comfort and remedies from them in times of trouble. This is contrary to God's will and commandment, which tells us to turn to Him in all our needs.

Such faithless people (I say) are also persuaded that neither hail nor snow, thunder nor lightning, rain nor stormy winds come from the heavens at God’s command. Instead, they believe these are raised by the cunning and power of witches and <term>conjurers</term> <note>Those who claim to summon spirits or magical forces.</note>. As soon as a clap of thunder or a gale of wind is heard, they either run to ring church bells or cry out to burn witches. Otherwise, they burn consecrated objects, hoping the smoke will drive the Devil out of the air, as though spirits could be scared away with such external toys. However, as *Brentius* <note>Johannes Brenz (1499–1570), a German Protestant Reformer.</note> affirms, these very actions are themselves true enchantments.

<margin>Mark 12.</margin>
<margin>In his sermon <note>original: "In conscione"</note>.</margin>

# CHAPTER XIII.

->The multiple meanings of the word "Spirit"; how diversely it is used in the Scriptures, where (in passing) it is taught that the Scripture is not always to be interpreted literally, nor yet always understood allegorically.<-

<margin>
a Exodus 31:1.
b Acts 8:19; Galatians 3.
c John 6:70; Matthew 16:23.
d 1 Corinthians 3; Galatians 3; 1 Corinthians 2; 2 Corinthians 7.
e Luke 9; 1 Corinthians 5; Philippians 1.
f 1 Thessalonians 5; 1 John 4.
g 1 Timothy 4.
h Ephesians 5.
</margin>
Those who search with the Spirit of Wisdom and Understanding shall find that "Spirits," both good and bad, are understood in various ways in the Scriptures. Indeed, they shall clearly perceive that the Devil is no horned beast. For ^a sometimes in the Scriptures, *Spirits* and *Devils* are used to refer to physical illnesses <note>original: "infirmities of the body"</note>; ^b sometimes for the vices of the mind; and sometimes also for the talents or gifts of either. ^c Sometimes a man is called a *Devil*, such as *Judas* in the sixth chapter of *John*, and *Peter* in the 16th chapter of *Matthew*. ^d Sometimes a "Spirit" represents the *Gospel*; sometimes the mind or soul of man; sometimes ^e the will, mind, and counsel of man; sometimes ^f Teachers and Prophets; sometimes ^g zeal toward God; and sometimes ^h joy in the Holy Spirit <note>original: "Holy Ghost"</note>, and so on.

<margin>
i Isaiah 11:2.
k Zechariah 12:10.
l Romans 8:15.
m 1 Corinthians 12:8, 9, 10, 11.
n Isaiah 19:14.
o Isaiah 29:10.
</margin>
To explain to us the nature and meaning of spirits, we find these words written in the Scripture: namely, ^i *The Spirit of the Lord shall rest upon him; The Spirit of counsel and strength; The Spirit of wisdom and understanding; The spirit of knowledge and the fear of the Lord*. Again, ^k *I will pour out my Spirit upon the house of David*, etc. *The Spirit of grace and compassion*. Again, ^l *You have not received the spirit of bondage, but the Spirit of adoption*. And therefore *St. Paul* says; ^m *To one is given, by the Spirit, the word of wisdom; to another, the word of knowledge by the same Spirit; to another, the gift of healing; to another, the gift of faith by the same Spirit; to another, the gift of prophecy; to another, the operation of great works; to another, the discerning of spirits; to another, the diversity of tongues; to another, the interpretation of tongues: and all these things are the work of one and the very same Spirit*. Thus far the words of *St. Paul*. And finally, *Isaiah* says, ^n *that the Lord mingled among them the spirit of error*. And in another place, ^o *The Lord has covered you with a spirit of deep sleep* <note>original: "slumber"</note>.

<margin>
p 1 Samuel 28; History 16.
q Wisdom 15:13, 29. <note>original: "Sap. 15," referring to the Book of Wisdom in the Apocrypha.</note>
r Judges 9:23.
s Numbers 5:14.
t Luke 13:11.
</margin>
As for the spirits of <term>divination</term> <note>the practice of seeking knowledge of the future or the unknown by supernatural means</note> spoken of ^p in the Scripture, they are like those found in the woman of *Endor*, the Philippian woman, the <term>girl of Westwell</term> <note>Mildred Norrington, a famous 1574 case of a girl who faked demonic possession using ventriloquism</note>, and the <term>Holy Maid of Kent</term> <note>Elizabeth Barton, a famous 16th-century "prophetess" who was eventually executed for fraud and treason</note>. These individuals were endowed with "spirits" or gifts of divination, through which they managed to gain money and deceive the people by tricks and crafty inventions. But these people are possessed by borrowed spirits, as it is written ^q in the Book of *Wisdom*, and by spirits of pure <term>cozenage</term> <note>fraud or deception</note> and deceit, as I have sufficiently proved elsewhere. Therefore, I do not deny that there are Spirits and Devils, consisting of whatever substance it has pleased God to create them with. But in whatever place it is found or read in the Scriptures, a "Spirit" or "Devil" is to be understood spiritually, and is neither a physical nor a visible thing. Where it is written, ^r *That God sent an evil spirit between Abimelech and the men of Shechem*, we are to understand that he sent the *spirit of hatred*, and not a <term>bogeyman</term> <note>original: "Bulbegger"; a terrifying specter or imaginary monster used to scare children</note>. Also where it is said, ^s *If the Spirit of jealousy come upon him*, it is the same as saying, "If he is moved by a jealous mind," and not that a physical Devil is attacking him. It is said in the Gospel; ^t *There was a woman who had a spirit of infirmity for eighteen years, who was bent over*, etc., whom Christ delivered from her disease by laying his hand upon her. By this it can be seen that although it is said that *Satan had bound her*, etc., it was actually a sickness or physical disease that troubled her; for Christ's own words explain it. Neither is there any word of witchcraft mentioned, which some claim was the cause of it.

<margin>
u Mark 16:9.
x Leviticus 26; Proverbs 24; Luke 17.
</margin>
There were ^u seven Devils cast out of *Mary Magdalene*. This is not understood so literally by the learned as meaning there were exactly seven physical Devils inside her (such as I described elsewhere), but rather that by the number "seven Devils," a great multitude and an uncertain number of vices is signified. This figure of speech is common in various places of the Scripture. And this interpretation is more agreeable with ^x God’s Word than the <term>Catholic paraphrase</term> <note>original: "Papistical paraphrase"</note>, which is—

<summary>Reginald Scot argues that biblical terms like "spirit" and "devil" are often used metaphorically to describe illnesses, mental states, or character traits rather than literal monsters. He highlights historical frauds to demonstrate how "spirits of divination" are usually human deceptions rather than supernatural entities.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Reginald Scot's skeptical inquiry into the supernatural. Having discussed the various meanings of "spirit" in the Bible, he now examines whether "demonic possession" was actually a literal inhabitation by spirits or a contemporary term for physical and mental illnesses cured by Christ's divine power.</meta>

<page-num>13</page-num>
### Miracles. Devils and Spirits. CHAPTER XIV.

<margin>Mark 8:16; Luke 4:36; Luke 7:21.</margin>
...is that Christ, under the name of the *seven Devils*, recounts only the *seven deadly sins*. Others allow neither of these explanations, because they suppose that the effectiveness of Christ's miracle would be undermined this way; as if it were not as difficult a matter, with a touch, to make a good Christian out of a vicious person as it is with a word to cure a fever <note>original: "Ague"</note> or any other disease of a sick body. I do not deny that both of these cures may be achieved by natural means over time without a miracle—one by a preacher, the other by a physician. But I say that Christ’s work in both was clearly miraculous; for *with power and authority, even with a touch of his finger and a word of his mouth, he made the blind see, the lame <note>original: "halt"</note> walk, the lepers clean, the deaf hear, the dead rise again, and the poor receive the Gospel*. Out of these (I say) he cast Devils and miraculously transformed them into good Christians, whereas before they were 
<margin>John 8:11.</margin>
living immoral lives <note>original: "dissolute livers"</note>; to whom he said, *Go your way and sin no more.*

---

->CHAPTER XIV.<-

->*That it pleased God to demonstrate the power of his Son, and not of witches, through miracles.*<-

<margin>Luke 8:24.</margin>
Jesus Christ, to demonstrate his divine power, *rebuked the winds, and they ceased; and the waves of water, and it was calm*. If neither our theologians nor our physicians can do this, much less can our conjurors, and least of all can our old witches bring any such thing to pass. But it pleased God to demonstrate the power of Christ Jesus by such miraculous and extraordinary means, providing and, as it were, preparing diseases that could be cured in no other way, so that his Son’s 
<margin>Leviticus 14:7, 8.</margin>
glory and his people’s faith might appear more clearly. These included *leprosy, 
<margin>John 9:1, etc.</margin>
lunacy*, and *blindness*; as is apparent in the Gospel, where it is said that *the man was not stricken with blindness for his own sins, nor for any offense of his ancestors, but that he was made blind so that the works of God should be shown through him by the hands of Jesus Christ.* But witches with their charms can cure (as <term>witchmongers</term> <note>original: "Witchmongers"; Scot's term for those who credulously believe in and promote the persecution of witches</note> claim) all these diseases mentioned in the Scripture, and many more—such as the gout, the toothache, etc.—which we do not find that Christ ever cured.

<margin>Matthew 4:23, etc.</margin>
Regarding those who are said in the Gospel to be possessed by spirits, it seems in many places that it is indifferent, or all the same, to say *he is possessed by a Devil* or *he is a lunatic or frantic* <note>original: "phrentick"; meaning delirious or insane</note>. In these days, such a disease is said to proceed from melancholy <note>in the medical theory of the time, an excess of "black bile" was thought to cause mental illness</note>. But if everyone who is now a lunatic is possessed by a literal Devil, then one might think that Devils could be driven out of men by medicine. But who says in these times, like the woman of *Canaan, "My daughter is tormented by a Devil,"* unless it is understood that she meant her daughter was troubled with some disease? Indeed, we say—and say truly—of a wicked person, "the Devil is in him," but we do not mean that a literal Devil has gotten into his guts. And if it were so, I wonder in what shape this literal Devil that possesses them remains. Does he enter the body in one shape and the mind in another? If they grant him to be spiritual and invisible, I agree with them.

Some are of the opinion that the woman of *Canaan* meant indeed that her daughter was troubled with some disease, because it is written—instead of saying the Devil was cast out—that *her daughter was made whole at that 
<margin>Mark 15:28.*</margin>
very hour.* According to what is said in the 12th chapter of *Matthew: There was brought 
<margin>Matthew 12:22.</margin>
unto Christ one possessed by a Devil, who was both blind and dumb, and he healed him; so that he who was blind and dumb both spoke and saw.* But it was the man, and not the Devil, who was healed and made to speak and see. From this (I say), it is gathered that those who were diseased, as well as those who were lunatics, were sometimes said to be possessed by Devils.

<sig>Bbb 2</sig> <meta>catchword: CHAP.</meta>

<summary>Scot argues that "demonic possession" in the New Testament was often a contemporary term for physical or mental illnesses cured by Christ's unique divine power. He mocks the idea that witches have more "curing" power than Christ or that literal demons inhabit human bodies as physical entities.</summary>

<header>Book I. A Discourse concerning those possessed with Devils.</header>

### CHAP. XV.
->Of the Possessed with Devils.<-

<margin>The *Malleus Maleficarum* <note>original: "Mal. malef."</note>, question 5, page 1.</margin>
Here I cannot fail to show how foolishly <note>original: "fondly"</note> various writers, namely James Sprenger and Henry Institor <note>The authors of the *Malleus Maleficarum* (1486), the most famous medieval treatise on hunting witches.</note>, record and note the reason why the Devil chooses to possess men at certain phases of the Moon. They say this happens for two reasons: first, so that they may slander such a good creature as the Moon; and second, because the brain is the moistest part of the body. <margin>* A principle in philosophy, just as the Sun acts upon dry and parched things <note>original: "in aridis & siccis"</note>.</margin> The Devil therefore considers the suitability of this (since the Moon has dominion over all moist things), so they take advantage of it to better achieve their goals. Furthermore, they say that Devils, when conjured and called up, appear and arrive sooner during certain constellations than others, in order to lead men to think there is some divinity in the stars. But when Saul was comforted by the sound of the Harp, they claim that the Devil’s departure was caused by the sign of the cross imprinted in David's veins. From this, we can see how absurd the imaginations and inventions of men are when they speak according to their own fancies without the authority of the Word of God. However, I find it very absurd that *Josephus* claims that the *Devil could be driven out of any man by the power of a root.* <margin>Josephus, *Antiquities of the Jews* <note>original: "de antiquitat. Jud."</note>; also *The Jewish War* <note>original: "de bello Ind."</note>, Book 7, chapter 25.</margin> And it is equally useless what *Aelianus* writes about the magical herb *Cynospastus*, also called *Aglaphnotis*. This is the same as *Solomon's* root named *Baaros*, which supposedly has the power to drive any Devil out of a possessed man.

### CHAP. XVI.

->*That since we are not thoroughly informed about the nature of Devils and Spirits, we must satisfy ourselves with what is provided in the Scriptures regarding them; how the word "Devil" is to be understood in both singular and plural; concerning the Spirit of God and the spirit of the Devil; concerning tame spirits; and concerning Ahab.*<-

<margin>Numbers 27:16.</margin>
Therefore, because the nature and substance of Devils and Spirits are not clearly defined in Scripture, we ought to satisfy ourselves and prepare our hearts to faithfully believe the words and meaning delivered to us there by the Great Spirit, which is the Holy Spirit <note>original: "Holy Ghost"</note>, the Lord of all spirits. We should always remember that spirits are always spoken of in Scripture as spiritual things, although for the sake of our understanding they are sometimes described in more physical and bodily terms—either in parables or by metaphors—than they actually are. <margin>2 Chronicles 18:19–21.</margin> For example (omitting the story of Job, which I discuss elsewhere), it is written: *The Lord said, "Who shall entice Ahab, so that he may fall at Ramoth Gilead?"... Then a spirit came forward and stood before the Lord, and said, "I will entice him." And the Lord said, "By what means?" And he said, "I will go and be a lying spirit in the mouth of all his prophets." Then the Lord said, "Go forth; you shall succeed..."*

This story is presented in this way to accommodate our limited understanding, especially the understanding of people in that age, who could not conceive of spiritual things except through such physical demonstrations. Yet it should be noted here that one spirit, and not many different ones, possessed all the false prophets at once. Similarly, in another place, many thousands of Devils are said to possess one man; yet it is also said in that very same place that the man was possessed by only one Devil. <margin>Mark 5:9; Luke 8:27–28; John Calvin, *Institutes of the Christian Religion* <note>original: "lib. instit."</note>, Book 1, chapter 14, section 14.</margin> For it says there that Christ met a man who had a Devil, and he commanded the foul spirit to come out of the man. But *Calvin* says: *Where Satan or the Devil is named in the singular, it refers to that power of wickedness that stands against the Kingdom of justice. And where many Devils are named in the Scriptures, we are taught that we must fight*

On the other hand, it is as plainly stated in the Scripture that some are possessed with the Spirit of God, just as others are filled and bound with the spirit of the Devil. Indeed, we sometimes read *that one good Spirit was put into a great number of people*; and again, *that various Spirits rested in and upon one man*—and yet no real or physical <note>original: "corporal"</note> spirit was intended. For example: *The Lord took of the Spirit that was upon Moses, and put it upon the seventy Elders, and when the Spirit rested upon them they prophesied.* Why should this not be considered as substantial and physical a spirit as the one that possessed the girl in the *Acts* of the Apostles? Also, Elisha requested of Elijah <note>original: "Elias"</note> that when he departed, *his spirit might be doubled upon him*. We also read *that the Spirit of the Lord came upon* $^a$ Othniel, upon $^b$ Gideon, $^c$ Jephthah, $^d$ Samson, $^e$ Balaam, $^f$ Saul, $^g$ David, $^h$ Ezekiel, $^i$ Zechariah, and $^k$ Amasai; indeed, it is written *that Caleb had another spirit than all the Israelites beside*; and in another place it is said that $^l$ Daniel *had a more excellent spirit than any other*.

Therefore, even though spirits—both good and bad—are said to be given by number and proportion, it is always the quality and not the quantity of them that is meant and assumed. However, I must confess that *Christ had the Spirit of God without measure*, as it is written in the $^m$ Gospel of John. But as for the claim that spirits can be made tame and kept at one's command, I say to those who interpret Scripture so crudely <note>original: "gross conceivers"</note> (who falsely claim that Solomon was the greatest conjurer of all) that Solomon himself says in express words: *No man is lord over a spirit, to retain a spirit at his pleasure.*

### C H A P. XVII.

->*Whether Spirits and Souls can take on bodies, and concerning their Creation and Substance, over which writers disagree and vary extremely.*<-

<margin>For every natural motion is either circular or elementary.</margin>
Some hold the opinion that Spirits and Souls can take on <note>original: "assume"</note> and inhabit bodies at their pleasure, in whatever shape or substance they desire. All Catholics <note>original: "Papists"</note> and some Protestants are of this mind, being more literal <note>original: "gross"</note> than another group, who hold that such bodies are ready-made for them. However, these writers vary regarding which elements these spiritual bodies are composed of. For (as I have said) some claim *that they consist of fire*; some think *of air*; and some *of the stars and other celestial powers*. But if they are celestial, *then* (as Peter Martyr <note>Peter Martyr Vermigli (1499–1562), an influential Reformed theologian.</note> says) *they must follow a circular motion*; and *if they are made of elements <note>original: "elementary"</note>, then they must follow the motions of those elements of which their bodies consist*. They cannot be made of air, for air is a homogeneous body <note>original: "Corpus homogeneum"</note>; thus, every part of air is just air, from which no distinct body parts can be made. For a physical body <note>original: "organical body"</note> must have bones, sinews, veins, flesh, and so on, which cannot be made of air. Neither (as Peter Martyr affirms) can an airy body receive or have either shape or figure. But some people look up into the clouds where they find (so they say) various shapes and forms even in the air. To this objection Peter Martyr answers, saying—and truly—*that clouds are not entirely air, but have a mixture of other elements mingled with them.*

### CHAPTER XVIII.

#### Certain Catholic <note>original: "Popish"</note> reasons concerning spirits made of air; of Day-Devils and Night-Devils; and why the Devil loves no salt in his food.

Many people claim (based on a fable cited in the *Malleus Maleficarum* <note>original: "M. Mal." refers to the *Hammer of Witches*, a 15th-century manual for hunting witches</note>) that spirits are made of air. They say this because spirits have reportedly been cut in two and then immediately closed up again, and also because they vanish so suddenly. However, I have already spoken about such apparitions and will soon say more: these things are seen in the imaginations of the weak and diseased rather than in actual reality and truth. These sights and apparitions were common among the unfaithful, but now, since the preaching of the Gospel, they are very rare. Just as they used to swarm among faint-hearted people—namely women, children, and the sick—they were never known to appear to those with strong bodies and healthy constitutions <note>original: "good stomacks"</note>, as I have proved elsewhere. This argues that they were merely products of fantasy and the imagination.

Now, those who imagine devils and spirits to be made of air say they must consist of that element; otherwise, when they vanish suddenly, they would leave some earthy substance behind. If they were made of water, they would dampen the place where they stand and would inevitably spill on the floor. If they consisted of fire, then <margin>Genesis 18 and 19.</margin> they would burn anything that touched them. And yet (they say), Abraham and Lot washed the feet of the angels who visited them and were neither scalded nor burnt.

<margin>Jean Bodin, *On the Demon-mania of Sorcerers*, book 3, chapter 4.</margin> I do not find it in the Bible, but rather in the writings of Jean Bodin <note>A French jurist and demonologist whom Scot frequently critiques</note>, that there are *Day-Devils* and *Night-Devils*. The same fellow says *that "Deber" is the name of the devil who hurts by night, and "Cheleb" is the one who hurts by day*. However, he confesses *that Satan can hurt both by day and night*, though he claims it is certain that the devil can do more harm by night than by day. He gives the example of how <margin>Exodus 12:29.</margin> *in a single night he slew the firstborn of Egypt*. Yet it appears plainly in the Biblical text *that the Lord himself did it*. Because of this, it seems that Bodin makes no distinction between God and the Devil.

For further confirmation of his foolish assertion <margin>Psalm 104:20, etc.</margin> that devils are more powerful by night than by day, he cites the 104th Psalm, which says: *You make darkness, and it is night, in which all the beasts of the forest creep forth; the lions roar, etc. When the sun rises, they retire, etc.* Thus, he now makes all beasts into devils, or devils into beasts. Oh, what ignorant <note>original: "barbarous"</note> blindness! This Bodin also says <margin>Jean Bodin, book 3, chapter 5.</margin> *that the Devil loves no salt in his meat, because <margin>Leviticus 2.</margin> salt is a sign of eternity and was used by God's commandment in all sacrifices*. He is abusing the Scriptures, which he is not ashamed to quote for this purpose. But now I will explain how the Scripture teaches our dull minds to understand what kind of thing the Devil is, through the very names assigned to him in the text.

---

### CHAPTER XIX.

#### That the devils mentioned in the Scriptures have their nature and qualities expressed in their names, with examples.

Those devils mentioned by name in the Scriptures have their nature and qualities expressed in their names. These names usually refer to the idols of certain nations, which were idolatrously set up instead of—or rather in spite of—God. <margin>2 Kings 1:2.</margin> For instance, *Beelzebub* means *The Lord of the Flies*, so named because he catches every simple creature in his web. He was an idol or oracle set up at Ekron, to whom King Ahaziah <margin>Matthew 9:34 and 12:24; Mark 3:22; Luke 11:15.</margin> sent messengers to ask whether he would recover from his disease, as though there were no God in Israel. This devil, Beelzebub, was reputed by the Jews to be the chief devil. The Greeks called him *Pluto*; the Romans called him *Sumanus*, meaning "the highest of the spirits of the dead" <note>original: "quasi summum deorum manium"</note>, whom they supposed...
