...experience and sense when not deceived, the rules of philosophy, or the Word of God. For alas! What an unfit instrument is a toothless, old, weak, and clumsy woman to fly in the air? Truly, the Devil has little need for such instruments to achieve his goals.

<margin>Why should not the devil be as ready to help a thief in reality as he helps a witch? <note>original Latin: L. multum. l. si quis atteri. vel sibi. These are references to specific points in Roman Civil Law.</note></margin>It is *strange* that we should suppose that such persons can perform such feats; and it is more *strange* that we imagine a thing to be possible for a witch to do which is impossible to nature and common sense. This is especially true when our neighbor's life depends on our belief in these things, and when we can see their lack of ability, which is always a barrier both to the act itself and to the suspicion of it. Because nothing is possible in law that is impossible in nature, the judge does not pay attention to or regard what the accused person says, or even what they might want to do. Instead, the judge looks at what is proved to have been committed and what naturally falls within a person's power and will to do. For the law says that to desire an impossible thing is a sign of a madman or a fool, over whom no sentence or judgment has power. Furthermore, what jury will condemn, or what judge will pass sentence against someone for killing a man at Berwick <note>Berwick-upon-Tweed: A town on the border of England and Scotland, hundreds of miles from London.</note> when they themselves and many others saw that man in *London* on the very day the murder was committed? This holds true even if the person confesses to being guilty and twenty witnesses testify to the same. In this case, I also say the judge should not weigh their testimony, which is weakened by the law's logic; the judge's authority is meant to correct the flaws of the case and maintain justice and fairness.

<margin>An objection answered.</margin>Since other natural factors might cause the calamities that witches are blamed for, let those of us who profess the Gospel and the knowledge of Christ not be "bewitched" into believing they do things that are naturally impossible and incredible to sense and reason. If people say these things are done through the help of the Devil (who can perform miracles), why then do thieves not accomplish their business miraculously? The Devil is just as involved with thieves as with the others. The kinds of mischief attributed to witches happen even where there are no witches; indeed, they continue even after witches are hanged and burned. Why then should we attribute such an effect to a cause that, even when removed, allows the effect to continue happening anyway?

### C H A P. VII.

->*By what means the name of "Witches" becomes so famous, and the various ways people hold opinions concerning them and their actions.*<-

<margin>Miracles have ceased.</margin>
<margin>People's opinions concerning witchcraft are diverse and inconsistent.</margin>Surely the natural power of a man or woman cannot be so expanded as to do anything beyond the power and virtue given and implanted by God. Rather, it is the will and mind of man that is corrupted and depraved by the Devil. God does not permit anything more than what the natural order established by Him requires. This natural order is nothing other than the ordinary power of God poured into every creature according to its state and condition. However, more will be said on this subject in the section on the confessions of witches. Nevertheless, you should understand that few or none are thoroughly persuaded, resolved, or satisfied that witches can indeed accomplish all these impossibilities. Instead, one person is deceived <note>original: cosened</note> on one point, and someone else is cheated on another, until finally, all these "possibilities"—and many more—are affirmed to be true by various people. And I have also noted this: when someone is tricked by some deceptive trifle of witchcraft and reports it accordingly—confirming a matter that is completely impossible and false as if they knew it personally, having been overcome by some kind of illusion (and these illusions are true enchantments)—that very same man will mock a similar story from someone else's mouth as a mythical tale unworthy of belief. ## CHAPTER XXII.

### *Of the Romans' chief gods called the Select Gods <note>original Latin: Dii selecti</note>, and of other Heathen gods, their Names and Offices.*

<margin>A good god and goddess for women.</margin>
There were among the *Romans* twenty idolatrous gods who were called the "Select Gods" <note>original Latin: *Dii selecti*</note>; twelve were male and eight were female, whose names follow: *Janus*, *Saturn*, *Jupiter*, *Genius*, *Mercury*, *Apollo*, *Mars*, *Vulcan*, *Neptune*, *Sol* (the Sun), *Orcus*, and *Liber*—who were all male gods. *Tellus* (the Earth), *Ceres*, *Juno*, *Minerva*, *Luna* (the Moon), *Diana*, *Venus*, and *Vesta* were all female gods. No man might claim any of these for himself alone, but they were left common and available to all men living in one realm, province, or notable city. These Heathen Gentiles also had gods who served various purposes. For example, to raise thunder, they had the "Establishers," the "Thunderers," the "Trophy-bearers," and "Jupiter the Summoned" <note>original Latin: *Statores*, *Tonantes*, *Feretrii*, and *Jupiter Elicius*</note>. They had *Cantius*, to whom they prayed for a wife and children; they thought him more fit for this purpose than *Minerva*, who issued out of *Jupiter's* own brain. *Lucina* was responsible for sending women in labor a safe delivery, and in that respect, she was called the mother of midwives <note>original: "Childwives"</note>. *Opis* was called the mother of the newborn babe. Women with child hung her image upon their belts <note>original: "girdles"</note> over their bellies and wore it there for nine months; and the midwife always touched the child with it before she or anyone else laid a hand on the infant.

<margin>The names of certain Heathenish Gods and their specific roles.</margin>
If the child were born healthy, they sacrificed to that image, even if the mother died. But if the child were in any part imperfect, or dead, etc., they used to beat the image into powder, or burn or drown it. *Vagitanus* was the god who kept their children from crying, and therefore they always hung his picture around babies' necks, for they thought much crying in youth portended ill fortune in old age. *Cuninus* (otherwise called *Cunius*) was the one who preserved their children (as they thought) from misfortune while in the cradle. *Ruminus* was to keep their breasts <note>original: "dugs"</note> from disease or infection. *Volumnus* and his wife *Volumna* were gods for young people—he for young men and she for maids who desired marriage—for those who prayed devoutly to them would soon be married. *Agrestis* was the god of the fields, and to him they prayed for fertility. *Bellus* was the god of war and warriors, as was *Victoria*, to whom the greatest temple in *Rome* was built. *Honorius* was the one in charge of innkeepers, ensuring they treated pilgrims well. *Berecinthia* was the mother of all the gods. *Aesculanus* was meant to reveal their mines of gold and silver, and they prayed to him for success in that regard. *Aesculapius* was to cure the sick (his father was *Apollo*), and he also served to keep weeds out of the corn. *Segacia* was to make seeds grow. *Flora* preserved the vines from frosts and blights <note>original: "blasts"</note>. *Sylvanus* was to protect those who walked in gardens. *Bacchus* was for drunkards; *Pavor* (Fear) for cowherds; and *Meretrix* for whores, in whose honor a temple was built in *Rome* in the middle of forty-four streets, all of which were inhabited by common harlots. ### CHAPTER XXIII.

### Of Various Gods in Various Countries.

---

<margin>Beasts, birds, vermin, fish, herbs, and other trivialities <note>original: trumpery</note> worshipped as gods.</margin>
The Egyptians were even more foolish in this regard than the Romans (I mean the heathen Romans that lived then, and not the Roman Catholics <note>original: "Popish Romans"</note> of today, for no nation comes close to these in any kind of idolatry). The Egyptians worshipped *Anubis* in the likeness of a dog, because he loved dogs and hunting. Indeed, they worshipped all living creatures: specifically, among beasts, a bullock, a dog, and a cat; among flying birds, the *Ibis* (which is a bird with a long bill that naturally devours venomous things and harmful serpents) and a sparrow-hawk. Of fish, they had two gods: namely, the *Lepidotus* fish <note>original: *Lepidotus piscis*</note> and the *Oxyrhynchus* <note>a sharp-nosed fish of the Nile</note>. The people of Sais <note>original: Saitans</note> and Thebes had a sheep as their god. In the city of Lycopolis, they worshipped a wolf; in Hermopolis <note>original: Herinopolis</note>, the *Cynocephalus* <note>a dog-headed baboon</note>; the people of Leontopolis <note>original: Leopolitans</note>, a lion; in Latopolis, a fish in the Nile called the *Latus*. In the city of Cynopolis, they worshipped *Anubis*. At Babylon, near Memphis, they made an onion their god; the Thebans, an eagle; the Mendesians, a goat; the Persians, a fire called *Orimasda* <note>Ahura Mazda</note>; the Arabians worshipped Bacchus, Venus, and *Diasaren*; the Boeotians, Amphiaraus; the Africans, Mopsus; the Scythians, Minerva; the people of Naucratis, *Serapis*, which is a serpent. *Astarte* (being, as Cicero writes, the fourth Venus, and the one whom Solomon worshipped at his concubines' request) was the goddess of the Assyrians. At Noricum, part of Bavaria, they worship *Tibilenus*; the Moors worship Juba; the Macedonians, *Cabirus*; the Peonians, *Uranius*. At Samos, Juno was their god; at Paphos, Venus; at Lemnos, Vulcan; at Naxos, *Liber* <note>original: *Liberus*; a name for Bacchus</note>; at Lampsacus, Priapus with the large genitals, who was set up at the Hellespont to be adored. In the Isle of Diomedea, they worshipped Diomedes; at Delphi, Apollo; at Ephesus, Diana was worshipped. And because they would rather play for small stakes than not play at all, they had *Acharus Cyrenaicus* to keep them from flies and fly-maggots; *Hercules Canopius* to keep them from fleas; and *Apollo Parnopeius* to keep their cheeses from being eaten by mice.

<margin>Supreme gods and their assistants.</margin>
The Greeks were the first, as far as I can learn, to have assigned the gods their principal kingdoms and offices: such as Jupiter to rule in Heaven, Pluto in Hell, Neptune in the Sea, and so on. To these they joined various commissioners as assistants: such as Saturn, Mars, Venus, Mercury, and Minerva to Jupiter; and Nereus to Neptune. *Tutilina* <note>a Roman goddess of the harvest</note> was merely a mediator to Jupiter to ensure he did not destroy the grain with thunder or tempests; people usually lit candles before her in the temple to appease her, according to the Roman Catholic <note>original: "Popish"</note> custom in these days.

<margin>The number of gods among the heathens <note>original: Gentiles</note>.</margin>
But I cannot repeat them all by name, for the gods of the heathens <note>original: Gentiles</note> were, according to reliable records such as those by Varro <note>Marcus Terentius Varro, a Roman scholar</note> and others, more than thirty thousand in number. By this, the reasonable reader may judge their superstitious blindness.

<margin>New Saints.</margin>

### CHAPTER XXV.

#### A Comparison between the Heathen and the Catholics <note>original: "Papists"</note>, regarding their excuses for Idolatry.

---

<margin>Grammarians call those "the Divine ones" who, from being mere men, were made into gods. <note>original: *Divos vocant Grammatici eos qui ex hominibus dii facti sunt.*</note></margin>
Because I know the Catholics will say that their Idols are Saints and not the kinds of Devils that the gods of the Gentiles <note>non-Christians/Pagans</note> were, you may tell them that not only their Saints, but even the very Images of them, were called *Divi* <note>the Divine ones</note>. While that word signifies gods, and consequently Idols or Fiends, if you simply add an "l" to it, it becomes "Divel" <note>Devil</note> in English. But they will also say that I do them wrong to mock them, because the Saints were holy men and holy women. I grant that some of them were indeed holy, and would be further from approving of the Catholic idolatry forced upon them than they would be grieved by the mockery used against that abuse. Indeed, just as Silver and Gold are made into Idols by those who love them too much and seek them too greedily, so are these holy men and women made into Idols by those who worship them and give them the honor that belongs only to God.

<margin>Cicero, *On the Nature of the Gods*. <note>original: *Cic. de natur. deorum.*</note></margin>
<margin>The Catholics see a speck in the eye of others, but no beam in their own. <note>A reference to Matthew 7:3-5.</note></margin>
The Heathen gods were, for the most part, good men and profitable members of the Commonwealth in which they lived, and they deserved fame, etc. In respect of this, the people made gods of them after they were dead, just as they made Devils of the Emperors and Philosophers whom they hated, or who had behaved poorly among them. And is it not exactly the same, or even worse, in the Commonwealth and Church of the Papacy? Does not the Pope excommunicate, curse, and condemn as Heretics—driving them to the bottomless pit of Hell and proclaiming them to the very Devils—all those who either write, speak, or think contrary to his idolatrous doctrine? 

When Cicero mocked the Heathen gods and attacked those who yielded such servile honor to them, he knew that the people to whom this honor was given had deserved well as citizens, and that they were owed a good reputation, but not divine status. Furthermore, the infidels who honored those gods in the hope of receiving benefits for their devotion knew and understood that the Statues and Images before which they reverently poured out their prayers were merely wood and stone <note>original: "stocks and stones"</note>, and only pictures of the people they resembled. They also knew that the parties themselves were created beings, and could not do as much as the Catholics and those who believe in witches <note>original: "Witchmongers"</note> think the Rood of Grace <note>A famous mechanical crucifix at Boxley Abbey that appeared to move, which reformers exposed as a fraud.</note> or Mother Bungie could do. And yet, the Catholics can see the errors of the Gentiles, but they will not hear of their own idolatry, which is more blatant <note>original: "gross"</note> and damnable than the others.

# Evidence of Witchcraft. CHAPTER 3.

-> CHAPTER 3 <-

-> Matters of Evidence against Witches <-

If an old woman threatens or touches someone who is in good health and who dies shortly after—or else becomes infected with leprosy, apoplexy <note>a stroke or sudden loss of consciousness</note>, or any other strange disease—it is (says Bodin) an enduring fact and such evidence for condemnation that death must follow without further proof, provided anyone has mistrusted her or said before that she was a witch.

*Also,* if anyone enters or leaves a room or house while the doors are shut, it is obvious and sufficient evidence for a witch's condemnation without further trial. Bodin never actually saw this happen; if he can show me that trick, I will agree with his foolishness. For Christ used the same power after his resurrection, not as a ridiculous toy that every witch might achieve, but as a special miracle to strengthen the faith of the Elect <note>the "Chosen," or those predestined by God for salvation</note>.

*Also,* if a woman bewitches anyone's eyes, she is to be executed without further proof.

*Also,* if anyone enchants or bewitches men's livestock or crops, or flies in the air, or makes a dog speak, or cuts off any man's genitals <note>original: "members"</note> and reattaches them to the bodies of men or children, it is sufficient proof for condemnation.

*Also,* presumptions and guesses are sufficient proof against witches.

<margin>Bartolomeo de Spina and Bodin, *On the Demon-mania of Sorcerers* <note>original: "de demon."</note>, Book 2, Chapter 2. Alexander, *Law where the number of witnesses is specified* <note>original: "L. ubi numerus de testibus"</note>. Jean Bodin, *On the Demon-mania of Sorcerers*, Book 2, Chapter 2.</margin>
*Also,* if only three witnesses say that a woman is a witch, then it is a clear case that she is to be executed. Bodin says this is certain not only by Canon and Civil Laws, but by the opinion of Pope Innocent—the wisest Pope (as he claims) who ever lived.

*Also,* the complaint of a single reputable man is enough to subject a poor woman to the rack or the pulley <note>instruments of torture used to extract confessions</note>.

*Also,* the testimony of a condemned or "infamous" <note>criminally discredited or of bad reputation</note> person is valid and allowed in matters of witchcraft.

*Also,* a witch is not to be released even if she endures all the tortures and confesses nothing, unlike defendants in all other criminal cases.

*Also,* in other cases, the testimony of many women given at once is considered legally insufficient because of the supposed "weakness and frailty of their nature or sex." However, in this matter, one woman—even if she is a party involved (as accuser or accused), is "infamous and impudent" (Bodin’s own words), or is even already condemned—may still serve to accuse and condemn a witch.

*Also,* a witness who has not been summoned but volunteers themselves is to be heard in this case, though they would not be heard in any other.

*Also,* a deadly enemy may testify against a witch if the hatred is claimed to have been caused by witchcraft, and no objection can be raised against him.

<margin>Parinus, *On the power of witnesses* <note>original: "l. poß. lestium"</note>, concerning those who are not worthy.</margin>
*Also,* although proof of perjury <note>lying under oath</note> would disqualify a witness in all other cases, in this instance, a perjurer is considered a good and lawful witness.

<margin>Alexander, Chapter 72, Law 2, etc. The execution of the Windsor Witches.</margin>
*Also,* the proctors <note>legal representatives in ecclesiastical courts</note> and advocates in these cases are forced to testify against their own clients, which they are never required to do in any other type of case.

*Also,* no one can provide evidence against witches regarding their secret assemblies except for other witches; as Bodin says, no one else is able to do so. Nevertheless, Richard Gallis <note>original: "Ri. Ga."; likely referring to the author of a 1579 pamphlet on the Windsor witches</note> writes in his foolish haste that he went to a gathering and killed the Devil with his sword and shield <note>original: "Buckler"</note> because the Devil made him stink of sulfur <note>original: "Brimstone"</note>.

<margin>Jean Bodin, Book 4, Chapter 4.</margin>
*Also,* Bodin says that because this is an extraordinary matter, there must be extraordinary handling of it, and every possible method—both direct and indirect—should be used.

<header>Book II. The Discovery: Confessions and Presumptions.</header>

### CHAPTER IV.

->Confessions of witches, by which they are condemned.<-

<margin>Is there any probability that such people would continue to be witches? <note>original: "Idem. ibid. Joan. An. ad speculat. tit. de litis confest. part. 2. non alie nem eodem. L. de ætat. 5. nihil eodem, &c. F. Bod. de dæmon. lib. 4. c. 3."</note></margin>
Some witches confess (says <note>Jean Bodin (1529–1596) was a prominent French jurist and writer on demonology.</note> Bodin) because they are desirous to die; not for the sake of glory, but out of despair, because they are tormented during their lifetime. However, these people must not be spared (he says), even though the law normally excuses those who confess out of despair.
Also, if she confesses to many things that are false, and yet one thing that may be true, she is to be seized and executed based on that one part of the confession.
Also, she is not considered as guilty if she confesses to a falsehood or a lie and denies a truth, as she is if she answers by indirect circumstances.
Also, an equivocal or doubtful answer is taken as a confession against a witch.
Also, Bodin reports that one man confessed he went out—or rather up into the air—and was transported many miles to the fairies' dance, only because he wanted to spy on where his wife went to practice <term>hagging</term> <note>original: "hagging"; refers to the activities of a witch or attending a Sabbat</note> and how she behaved herself. Because of this, there was much debate among the Inquisitors and lawyers to discuss whether he should be executed along with his wife or not. It was concluded that he must die because he did not <term>bewray</term> <note>original: "bewrayed"; betrayed or informed upon</note> his wife; which he failed to do "out of respect for the honor of his family" <note>original: "Propter reverentiam honoris & familiæ."</note>.
Also, if a woman confesses freely to this before any legal question is made, and yet afterward denies it, she is nevertheless to be burned.
Also, they affirm that this extreme severity is used in these cases because not one among a thousand witches is <term>detested</term> <note>original: "detested"; in this context, it means detected or discovered</note>. And yet it is affirmed by Sprenger in the *Malleus Maleficarum* <note>original: "M. Mal."; the 'Hammer of Witches,' a famous 15th-century witch-hunting manual</note> that there is no parish so small that many witches are not known to be there.

### CHAPTER V.

->Presumptions, by which witches are condemned.<-

<margin>Jean Bodin, *On the Demon-mania of Sorcerers*, Book 4, Chapter 4.</margin>
If any woman's child happens to die while in her care, such that nobody knows how it happened, it must not be thought or presumed that the mother killed it—unless she is suspected of being a witch. In that case, it is the opposite; she must be executed based on that presumption, unless she can prove the negative or the contrary.
Also, if the child of a woman suspected of being a witch is missing or gone from her, it is to be presumed that she has sacrificed it to the Devil, unless she can prove the negative or the contrary.
Also, though in other people's cases certain points of their confessions may be thought erroneous and blamed on a mistake, yet in the cases of witches, all oversights, imperfections, and slips must be judged as impious and malicious, and lead to her confusion and condemnation.
<margin>Jean Bodin, *On the Demon-mania of Sorcerers*, Book 4, Chapter 4. <note>Citations of various legal texts: Roman law regarding city officials and punishments (L. decurionum de pænis), and Panormitanus (Pannon).</note></margin>
Also, though a thief is not said in law to be infamous in any matter other than theft, a witch accused of witchcraft is said to be defiled with all manner of faults and infamies universally—even if she were not yet condemned, but (as I said) merely defamed with the name of "Witch." For rumors and reports are sufficient (says Bodin) to condemn a witch.
Also, if any man, woman, or child says that such a person is a witch, it is a most "vehement suspicion" (says Bodin) and sufficient to bring her to the rack <note>A torture device used to stretch the victim's joints</note>, though in all other legal cases this would be directly against the law.
Also, regarding presumptions and suspicions against a witch, the <term>common bruit</term> <note>original: "common brute"; common rumor or public outcry</note> or voice of the people cannot be wrong.
Also, if a woman, when she is arrested, cries out or says, "I am undone; save my life; I will tell you how the matter stands," etc., she is thereupon to be most vehemently suspected and condemned to die.

*   **Also**, though a conjurer is not to be condemned for curing the diseased by virtue of his art; yet a witch must die for doing the same thing.

*   **Also**, the only pity they show to a poor woman in this case is this: though she be accused of killing someone with her enchantments, if she can bring that person forth alive, she shall not be put to death. I marvel at this, since they also claim the Devil can appear in any person’s likeness or representation.

## CHAP. VI.
### Particular Interrogatories used by the Inquisitors against Witches.

I do not need to wait to refute such biased and horrible dealings, as they are so clearly impious and full of tyranny. Unless I had uncovered them using their own writings and assertions, few or none would have believed they existed. But for the sake of brevity, I will pass over them, assuming that merely citing such absurdities serves as a sufficient disproof of them. Now, therefore, I will proceed to the specific order and manner of examinations used by the Inquisitors, which are allowed for the most part throughout all nations.

<margin>*Malleus Maleficarum* on interrogations. <note>original: "Mal. Malef. super. interrog."</note></margin>

First, the witch must be asked why she touched a certain child or a certain cow, etc., after which the same child or cow fell sick or became lame.

**Also**, why her two cows give more milk than her neighbors' cows. And the note mentioned before is set down here again, to be specially observed by all men: namely, that though a witch cannot weep, she may speak with a crying voice. This claim about weeping is false and contrary to the sayings of **Seneca** and many others, who affirm that a woman weeps most when she intends the most deceit. Therefore, says the ***Malleus Maleficarum***, she must be watched closely; otherwise, she will secretly put spit upon her cheeks to seem as if she is weeping. This rule is also mentioned by **Bodin**.

### C H A P. VIII.
->Certain Cautions against Witches, and of their Tortures to procure Confession.<--

But to demonstrate their further follies, I will recite some of their cautions, which are published by the ancient Inquisitors as perpetual lessons for their successors, as follows:
The first caution is that which was last mentioned concerning weeping, which (they say) is an infallible sign.

And lest we should condemn that as superstition, they preempt us with a rhetorical device <note>original: "figure"</note> and tell us that this same practice should not seem superstitious to us. ...their flesh. This was so seriously and faithfully recorded by the Inquisitors themselves that one may believe it if they choose, though in truth it is a complete lie. <margin>2. & 6. Concerning the time and manner of terror.</margin> <margin>The blasphemous Pope Julius, the third of that name.</margin> **Jean Bodin** cites a similar story of a witch who could not be killed by the executioner, no matter what he did. But it is most true that the Inquisitor **Cumanus**, in a single year, shaved forty-one poor women and burned them all when he was finished.

Another caution is that at the time and place of torture, the hallowed objects mentioned before—along with the "seven words" spoken by Christ on the Cross—should be hung around the witch’s neck. Furthermore, a wax figure the length of Christ’s body should be tied to her bare, naked body, along with the relics of saints, and so on. All this material (they say) will work upon them so effectively that when they are racked and tortured, they can hardly stop themselves from confessing. In such a case, I have no doubt that the Pope—who showed great spite over a piece of pork <note>This refers to an anecdote about Pope Julius III, who reportedly cursed God because his cold peacock/pork dish was missing.</note>—would have renounced the Trinity and worshipped the Devil on his knees with even less compulsion.

<margin>*The Hammer of Witches*, part 3, question 16.</margin>
Another caution is that after she has been racked and subjected to every torture devised for that purpose, and after she has been forced to drink holy water, she should be brought back to the place of torture. In the midst of her torments, the accusations against her should be read to her, and the witnesses (if they wish) should be brought face-to-face with her. Finally, she should be asked whether, as a trial of her innocence, she will submit to the judgment of *burning iron* <note>original: "Candentis ferri"</note>, which involves carrying a certain weight of red-hot iron in her bare hand. But that request may not (they say) be granted under any circumstances. For both the *Hammer of Witches* and **Bodin** affirm that many things may be promised, but nothing needs to be performed; for they have the authority to make promises, but no commission to actually fulfill them.

Another caution is that the judge must take care that once she begins to confess, he does not cut off her examination, but continues it night and day. For many times, while the judges go to dinner, she "returns to her vomit" <note>An archaic idiom meaning she recants her confession or returns to her previous state of mind.</note>.

Another caution is that after the witch has confessed to harming men and beasts, she should be asked how long she has had an *incubus* <term>incubus: a demon believed to have sexual relations with sleeping women</term>, when she renounced the faith, how she made the formal pact with the Devil, and what that pact entails. This is, in fact, the chief cause of all their incredible and impossible confessions; for upon the rack, once they have begun to lie, they will say whatever the tormentor desires.

<margin>*The Hammer of Witches*</margin>
The last caution is that if she will not confess, she should be taken to some strong castle or jail. After a few days, the jailer must make her believe he is going to a distant country. Then, some of her "friends" must visit her and promise that if she confesses to them, they will help her escape from prison—which they could easily do while the keeper is away. This method (says the *Hammer of Witches*) has worked when all other means have failed.

<margin>Part 3, question 16, action 11.</margin>
In this place, it must not be overlooked that they confess on **Fridays** more than any other time. Now, say **James Sprenger** and **Henry Institor** <note>The authors of the *Malleus Maleficarum*.</note>, we must tell the whole truth: if she confesses nothing, she should be dismissed by law; and yet, by procedural order, she may under no circumstances be released on bail. Instead, she must be put into a solitary prison and there be spoken to by some "crafty person"—those are their very words. In the meantime, there must be eavesdroppers with pen and ink behind the wall to listen and note down what she confesses. Alternatively, some of her old companions and acquaintances may come in and talk with her about old matters, only to be betrayed by the eavesdroppers. Thus, there shall be no end to the torture until she has confessed whatever they want.

<header>BOOK II. The Discovery of Crimes.</header>

-># CHAPTER 9.<-
*The fifteen crimes laid to the charge of witches by witch-mongers; specifically by Bodin in "On the Demon-Mania of Sorcerers."* <note>original: "Dæmonomania"; referring to Jean Bodin's 1580 influential work "De la Démonomanie des Sorciers"</note>

1. They deny God and all religion.
   **Answer:** Then let them die for it, or at the least be treated like infidels or apostates.

2. They curse, blaspheme, and provoke God with all contempt. <note>original: "despire," likely an archaic form of "despite" meaning malice or contempt</note>
   **Answer:** Then let them face the law expressed in Leviticus 24 and Deuteronomy 13 and 17.

3. They give their faith to the Devil, and they worship and offer sacrifice to him.
   **Answer:** Let such people also be judged by the same law.

4. They solemnly vow and promise all their offspring <note>original: "progenie"</note> to the Devil.
   **Answer:** This promise comes from an unsound mind and is not to be taken seriously because they cannot perform it, nor will it be proven true. However, if it is done by anyone of sound mind, let the curse of Jeremiah 32:36 <note>original: "Jeremy, 32. 36."</note> fall upon them—namely, the sword, famine, and plague.

5. They sacrifice their own children to the Devil before baptism, holding them up in the air to him and then thrusting a needle into their brains.
   **Answer:** If this is true, I do not defend them in this; there is a law to judge them by. However, it is so contrary to sense and nature that it would be folly to believe it, whether based on Bodin’s bare word or on his assumptions—especially when so little benefit <note>original: "commodity"</note> and such great danger and trouble follows for the witches because of it.

6. They burn their children after they have sacrificed them.
   **Answer:** Then let them receive such punishment as those who offered their children to Moloch (Leviticus 20). But these are mere inventions of witch-mongers and Inquisitors who have wrung such confessions from them through extreme torture, or else believed them based on false reports, or finally won these confessions through flattery and fair promises.

7. They swear to the Devil to bring as many into that society as they can.
   **Answer:** This is false and is proven so elsewhere.

8. They swear by the name of the Devil.
   **Answer:** I never heard of such an oath, nor do we have the legal authority <note>original: "warrant"</note> to kill those who swear in that way, though it is indeed very wicked and impious.

9. They commit incestuous adultery with spirits.
   **Answer:** This is a stale, ridiculous lie, as is clearly proven later in this book.

10. They boil infants after they have murdered them before baptism until their flesh is made drinkable. <note>original: "potable"</note>
    **Answer:** This is untrue, incredible, and impossible.

11. They openly eat the flesh and drink the blood of men and children.
    **Answer:** Then they are kin to the *man-eaters* <note>original: "Anthropophagi"</note> and cannibals. But I believe no honest man in England or France will claim he has seen any of these people who are called witches do such a thing; if they did, I believe it would poison them.

12. They kill men with poison.
    **Answer:** Let them be hanged for their efforts.

13. They kill men's cattle.
    **Answer:** Then let a lawsuit <term>action of trespass</term> <note>a legal action for damages caused by direct injury to person or property</note> be brought against them for doing so.

14. They bewitch men's corn <note>grain crops</note> and bring hunger and barrenness to the country; they ride and fly in the air, bring storms, create tempests, etc.
    **Answer:** Then I will worship them as gods, for those are not the works of man, nor even of a witch, as I have proved at length elsewhere.

### CHAPTER 10.
->*A refutation of the previously suspected crimes gathered by Bodin, and the only way to escape the Inquisitors.*<-

<insert>I</insert>f more ridiculous or disgusting crimes could have been invented, these poor women (whose main fault is that they are scolds <note>A "scold" was a woman who habitually used abusive or nagging language; it was a legal offense at the time.</note>) would have been charged with them.
In this libelous writing <note>original: "libel"</note>, you can see all the charges against witches, as well as everything that any "witch-monger" <note>A "witch-monger" refers to someone who promotes or profits from the fear of witchcraft.</note> suspects or maliciously attributes to the power and practice of witches.
<margin>The question or matter in controversy; that is to say, the proposition or theme.</margin>
Some of these crimes may not only be within the power and will of a witch but can also be accomplished by natural means. Therefore, the matter in question—whether a witch can perform supernatural wonders—is not decided by these crimes. Many a dishonest person or prostitute <note>original: "knave and whore"</note> more commonly performs those wicked actions than those called witches, who are hanged for their efforts.
Some of these crimes charged against witches are denied by me and cannot be proved by them to have been committed by any single witch. Otherwise, they are so absurd, supernatural, and impossible that they are mocked by almost everyone. Such false, foolish, and legendary reports are condemned to the point where the witch-mongers themselves are ashamed to hear of them.
If part of it is untrue, why should we not think the rest is false? For all these things are charged against them at once, even by the greatest doctors and patrons of the "Sect of Witch-mongers." They produce just as many proofs for the witches' supernatural and impossible actions as they do for the others. So, if one part of their accusation is false, the other part deserves no credit. If everything alleged of their actions were true, why should we believe in Christ because of his miracles, if a witch can perform as great wonders as he ever did?
<margin>A general error.</margin>
But some will say: as for those absurd and Catholic <note>original: "Popish"</note> writers, they are not to be believed in everything they allege regarding these matters. But I assure you that almost all types of writers—from the Doctors of the Church to the Scholastic theologians <note>original: "School-men"</note>, Protestants, Catholics, the learned and unlearned, poets and historians, Jews, Christians, or Pagans <note>original: "Gentiles"</note>—agree on these matters. Indeed, these writers from whom I gather the most absurdities are considered the most credible and authoritative of all writers on this subject. The reason is that it was never thoroughly investigated; instead, every fable was accepted because the word "witch" is mentioned so often in Scripture.
<margin>The only way for witches to avoid the Inquisitors' hands.</margin>
Those who have observed the orders and customs of the Inquisitors more closely also say there is no way in the world for these poor women to escape the Inquisitors' hands—and consequently, being burned—except to "gild their hands with money" <note>This means to bribe them with gold.</note>. By this, the Inquisitors often take pity on them and release them, claiming they are sufficiently "purged." They have the authority to exchange physical punishment for a fine, applying the money to the office of their Inquisition. From this, they reap such profit that many of these simple women pay yearly pensions so they will not be punished again.

<header>BOOK II. The Discovery of Inquisitors' failures.</header>

### C H A P. XI.

*The opinion of Cornelius Agrippa concerning Witches, his pleading for a poor woman accused of witchcraft, and how he convinced the Inquisitors.*

Cornelius Agrippa <note>Heinrich Cornelius Agrippa (1486–1535) was a famous German polymath, physician, and legal scholar known for his works on the occult and his eventual skepticism toward witch-hunting.</note> says that while he was in Italy, many Inquisitors in the Duchy of Milan troubled various very honest and noble matrons, secretly wringing much money from them until their knavery was detected. Further, he says that while serving as an Advocate or Counselor in the Commonwealth of Maastricht in Brabant <note>A region now divided between the Netherlands and Belgium.</note>, he had a great contention with an Inquisitor. This Inquisitor, through unjust accusations, drew a poor woman of the countryside into his "butchery" and to an unfit place—not so much to examine her, but to torment her. 

When Agrippa undertook to defend her, declaring that in the actions alleged there was no proof, sign, or token that could justify her being tortured, the Inquisitor stoutly denied it and said, "There is one thing which is proof and matter sufficient: her mother was burned as a witch in times past." 

When Agrippa replied, affirming that this point was irrelevant <note>original: "impertinent" - in a legal sense, meaning it does not relate to the specific facts of the case.</note> and ought to be rejected by the judge as being the deed of another person, and cited reasons and laws to the Inquisitor to support this, the Inquisitor replied again that the accusation was true. He argued that witches usually conceived by spirits transformed into human shape, and that thereby witchcraft was naturally engrafted <note>original: "ingraffed"</note> into this child as a disease that comes by inheritance.

<margin>A bitter verbal attack against a cruel Inquisitor.</margin> Agrippa, replying against the Inquisitor's folly and superstitious blindness, said: "O you wicked priest! Is this your theology? Do you habitually draw poor guiltless women to the rack by these forged devices? Do you judge others to be heretics with such sentences, when you yourself are more of a heretic than either Faustus or Donatus? <note>Faustus and Donatus were famous leaders of early Christian sects (Manichaeism and Donatism) that were declared heretical.</note> Even if it were as you say, do you frustrate the grace of God's Ordinance—namely, Baptism? Are the words spoken in Baptism in vain? Or shall the Devil remain in the child, or the child remain in the power of the Devil, after being then and there consecrated to Christ Jesus in the Name of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Ghost? 

And if you defend the false opinions of those who affirm that spirits accompanying women can father children, yet you go further than any of them; for they never believed that any of those devils, along with their stolen seed, put part of their own nature into the creature. But though indeed we are born the children of the Devil and damnation, yet in baptism, through grace in Christ, Satan is cast out and we are made new creatures in the Lord, from whom no one can be separated by another person’s deed." 

The Inquisitor, being offended by this, threatened to proceed against Agrippa as a supporter of heretics or witches. Nevertheless, Agrippa did not cease to defend the poor, helpless woman <note>original: "silly woman" — at the time, "silly" meant deserving of pity or socially vulnerable.</note>. Through the power of the Law, he delivered her from the claws of the bloody monk. The monk and the woman's accusers were condemned to pay a great sum of money to the Charter of the Church of Mainz, and they remained infamous to almost all men after that time.

<margin>John Fox in the Acts and Monuments.</margin> But by the way, you must understand that this was only a petty Inquisitor and did not have as large a commission as Cumanus, Sprenger <note>Jacob Sprenger was the co-author of the *Malleus Maleficarum*, the most famous handbook for witch-hunters.</note>, and such others had; nor did he have the power that the Spanish Inquisitors have today. For these modern Inquisitors will allow no advocates for poor souls now, unless the tormentor or hangman may be called an "advocate." You may read a summary of this Inquisition set out in few words by Mr. John Fox in the *Acts and Monuments* <note>Commonly known as *Foxe's Book of Martyrs*, a highly influential Protestant account of religious persecution.</note>. For witches and heretics hold the same reputation among the Inquisitors, except that the severity is greater against witches because, through their simplicity, the Inquisitors may more boldly tyrannize and triumph over them.

<summary>This page recounts how the scholar Cornelius Agrippa successfully defended a woman against an Inquisitor who claimed witchcraft was a hereditary trait. Agrippa argued that the sacrament of Baptism cleanses any ancestral sin or demonic influence, highlighting the legal and theological abuses of the Inquisition.</summary>

# Torments of Witchcraft. CHAPTER 12.

### CHAP. XII.

*What the fear of death and the sensation of torture may force a person to do, and why it is no wonder that witches condemn themselves through confessions extorted in this way.*

Anyone who reads church histories or remembers the persecutions during the reign of Queen Mary <note>Queen Mary I of England (reigned 1553–1558), whose reign was marked by the execution of religious dissenters.</note> will find that many good men faltered for fear of persecution and later returned to the Lord. Is it any wonder, then, that a poor woman—the kind described elsewhere and tormented as described in these last few pages—should be forced to confess to such absurd and impossible falsehoods? Human nature is simply unable to endure such trials. How can she, in the midst of such horrible tortures and torments, promise herself constancy or refrain from confessing anything? Or what good does it do her to persist in denying the unjust charges against her? On one hand, there is no end to her suffering; on the other hand, if she remains silent, her accusers say she is using magic charms for silence <term>taciturnity</term>.

<margin>Peter’s apostasy—renouncing Christ.</margin>Peter the Apostle renounced, cursed, and swore he did not know his master and our Savior Jesus Christ because he was afraid of a servant girl’s threats. Or rather, he did so because of a question she asked, in which he was not nearly as trapped as these poor "witches" are. They are not examined by girls, but by shrewd Inquisitors who seek the seizure of their property <note>Inquisitors and local officials often profited from the confiscated belongings of those convicted of witchcraft.</note>. These men come to the place of judgment with minds set on maintaining their bloody purpose, sparing no kind of allurements, threats, or tortures until they have wrung out of the victims everything that either satisfies their own desires or serves to destroy the accused.

<margin>Daneau in the Dialogue <note>Lambert Daneau (c. 1530–1595), a French theologian who wrote on the power of sorcerers.</note>.</margin> <margin>The poor old [woman] 1 Cor. 10 <note>A reference to 1 Corinthians 10:13: "God... will not suffer you to be tempted above that ye are able."</note>.</margin>Peter, I say, in the presence of his Lord and Master Christ—who had instructed him in true knowledge for many years, who had forewarned him not five hours earlier, and to whom Peter had made a faithful promise—denied his Master three times against his conscience. He did this without any compulsion other than a question from a girl. Yet he was an enlightened man, placed in a high position and much closer to Christ than any "witch." A "witch’s" fall could not be as great as Peter’s because she never climbed half as many steps. A pastor’s downfall is much more offensive than the straying of one of his sheep, just as an ambassador’s conspiracy is more hateful than the falsehood of a common person, or a captain’s treason is more damaging than a private soldier’s mutiny. If you say that Peter repented, I answer that the "witch" sometimes does so as well; and I see no reason why mercy should not be shown to her in that case. It would be a mighty temptation to a simple old woman if a visible Devil (who is as ugly as Daneau and others say he is) should assault her in the manner people claim—especially when the Bible promises that no one will be tempted beyond their strength. The poor old "witch" is commonly unlearned, unwarned, and lacking counsel or friendship. She lacks the judgment and discretion to manage her life and speech, and she is much more subject to melancholy <term>melancholy</term> <note>In the early modern period, melancholy was thought to be a physical imbalance that caused depression, hallucinations, and irrational behavior.</note>. Her upbringing and social standing are so lowly that nothing extraordinary should be expected of her. Her age is also usually such that she is decrepit, which is a condition that leads people toward such follies.

Finally, Christ clearly forgave Peter, even though his offense was committed against both Christ's divine and human nature. Afterward, Christ even trusted him to lead his followers and showed him great favor and love. Therefore, I do not see why we cannot show compassion to these poor souls if they show themselves to be sorrowful for their misconceptions and wicked imaginations.

### BOOK III.

### CHAPTER 1.
*The witches' bargain with the Devil, according to the Malleus Maleficarum <note>original: "M. Mal." – a famous 15th-century treatise on the prosecution of witches</note>, Bodin, Nider, Daneau, Psellus, Erastus, Hemmingsen, Cumanus, Aquinas, Bartholomæus, de Spina, etc.*

<image-desc>Large ornate initial capital 'T' at the start of the paragraph.</image-desc>That which in this matter of witchcraft has deceived <note>original: "abused"</note> so many, and seems both so horrible and intolerable, is a plain bargain that (they say) is made between the Devil and the witch. Many men of great learning conceive it to be a matter of truth and publish it accordingly in their writings; this (by God’s grace) shall be proved as vain and false as the rest.

<margin>The double bargain of witches with the Devil.</margin>The order of their bargain or profession is twofold: the one solemn and public, the other secret and private. That which is called solemn or public is where witches come together at certain assemblies at fixed times, and not only see the Devil in visible form but confer and talk familiarly with him. In this conference, the Devil exhorts them to observe their loyalty to him, promising them long life and prosperity. Then the assembled witches commend a new disciple (whom they call a novice) to him; and if the Devil finds that young witch apt and eager in the renunciation of the Christian faith—in despising any of the seven Sacraments, in treading upon Crosses, in spitting at the time of the elevation <note>The moment in the Mass when the priest raises the consecrated bread and wine</note>, in breaking their fast on various days, and fasting on Sundays—the Devil stretches out his hand, and the novice, joining hand in hand with him, promises to observe and keep all the Devil’s commandments.

This done, the Devil begins to be more bold with her, telling her plainly that all this will not serve his purpose, and therefore requires homage at her hands. Indeed, he also tells her that she must grant him both her body and soul to be tormented in everlasting fire, which she yields to. Then he charges her to recruit as many men, women, and children as she can to enter into this society. Then he teaches them to make ointments from the bowels and limbs of children, by which they ride through the air and accomplish all their desires. Thus, if there are any children unbaptized, or not guarded with the sign of the cross or prayers <note>original: "orizons"</note>, then the witches may and do snatch them from their mothers' sides in the night, or out of their cradles, or otherwise kill them with their ceremonies. After burial, they steal them out of their graves and boil <note>original: "seeth"</note> them in a cauldron until their flesh is made into a liquid <note>original: "potable"</note>. From the thickest part of this, they make ointments by which they ride through the air; but the thinner potion they put into flagons, and whoever drinks from it while observing certain ceremonies immediately becomes a master—or rather a mistress—in that practice and profession.
<margin>*Malleus Maleficarum* <note>original: "Mal. Malef."</note> regarding the manner of profession.</margin>

# Witches' songs. Of Witchcraft. CHAP. II.

## CHAP. II.

The order of the homage done by witches (as it is written by ignorant <note>original: "lewd"; here meaning ignorant or wicked</note> Inquisitors and perverse witch-promoters) to the Devil in person; of their songs and dances, specifically the *Lavolta*, and of other ceremonies, as well as their supernatural journeys <note>original: "excourses"</note>.

<margin>Homage to the Devil.</margin> Sometimes their homage, along with their oath and bargain, is received for a certain term of years; sometimes it is for eternity. Sometimes it consists of the denial of the whole Christian faith, and sometimes only in part. The first case is when the wretched witch is absolutely surrendered to the Devil and the fires of hell. The other is when they have only bargained to observe certain ceremonies and statutes of the Church, such as concealing their faults at <term>Shrift</term> <note>The sacrament of confession and penance.</note>, or fasting on Sundays, and so on. This is done either by oath, by spoken protestation, or by a written obligation—sometimes sealed with wax, sometimes signed with blood, and sometimes by kissing <note>original: "killing"; likely an OCR error or archaic typo for "kissing," referring to the *osculum infame* or "shameful kiss" described in witch-hunt literature.</note> the Devil’s bare buttocks. This was supposedly done by a doctor named *Edlin*, who (as *Bodin* says) was burned for witchcraft.

<margin>Bartolommeo Spina, chapter 1, manual: *The Hammer of Witches* (Malleus Maleficarum).</margin> You must also understand that after they have delicately banqueted with the Devil and the Lady of the Fairies; and after they have eaten up a fat ox and emptied a butt of <term>Malmsey</term> <note>A strong, sweet wine.</note> and a bin of bread at some nobleman’s house in the dead of night: in the morning, the Lady *Sibylla*, *Minerva*, or *Diana* strikes the vessel and the bin with a golden rod, and they are fully replenished again. Indeed, she causes the bullock's bones to be brought and laid together upon the hide, and wraps <note>original: "lappeth"</note> the four ends together, laying her golden rod upon them. Then the bullock rises up again in his former state and condition. And yet, upon their return home, they are likely to starve for hunger, as *Spinaeus* says. <margin>The same author, in the same place.</margin> And this must be an infallible rule: that every fortnight, or at least every month, each witch must kill at least one child as her contribution.

<margin>Bodin, *On the Demon-mania of Witches*, book 2, chapter 4.</margin> And here some of Monsieur *Bodin's* lies may be inserted. He says that at these magical assemblies, the witches never fail to dance; and in their dance, they sing these words: "*Har har, Devil, devil, dance here, dance here, play here, Sabbath, Sabbath.*" And while they sing and dance, everyone has a broom in her hand and holds it up high. Also, he says that these night-walkings—or rather night-dancings—brought that dance called the *Lavolta* <note>A lively, leaping dance for couples.</note> out of Italy into France.

<margin>*The Hammer of Witches* (Malleus Maleficarum).</margin> A part of their league is to scrape off the oil received in "extreme folly"—I should have said "extreme unction" <note>The author is mocking the Catholic sacrament of anointing the dying with oil.</note>. But if that is so dangerous, those who wash the corpse had better take great care that they do not rub off the oil, which may also be wiped from the forehead in various other ways. If so, I perceive all its power is gone, and that’s the end of it. But I marvel how they take it upon themselves to preserve the water poured on them in baptism, which I consider to be at least as powerful as the oil; yet I think it is commonly wiped and washed off within twenty-four hours after baptism. But this matches the rest of their folly.

And it should be noted that the Inquisitors affirm that during the entire time of the witch's journey <note>original: "excourse"</note>, the Devil occupies the room and place of the witch in such a perfect likeness that her husband in his bed cannot distinguish her from his wife by touch, speech, or appearance. Indeed, the wife departs from her husband’s arms without him noticing, and leaves the Devil in her place visibly. <margin>Grillandus, in his treatise.</margin> In this, their gullibility is incredible; they insist on having a physical body in the imaginary play, and a "phantom" body in the actual bed. And yet (of course) they say that at the sign of the Cross, all these physical witches vanish away.

### CHAPTER III.

How Witches are summoned to appear before the Devil; of their riding in the air; of their accounts; of their conference with the Devil; of his supplies and their conference; of their farewell and sacrifices; according to Danaeus, Psellus, etc.

<margin>Danaeus in *Dialogues*, chapter 4.</margin>Hitherto, for the most part, these are the very words contained in the *Malleus Maleficarum* <note>original: "M. Mal."; the *Hammer of Witches*, a famous 15th-century treatise on the prosecution of witches</note> or in the works of Jean Bodin, or rather in both; or else in the newer editions of the *Malleus Maleficarum*, or at the very least from some writer or another who maintains the almighty power of witches. But Lambert Danaeus says that the Devil, often in the likeness of a court summoner, meets them at markets and fairs and warns them to appear in their assemblies at a certain hour in the night, so that he may understand whom they have slain and how they have progressed in their craft. If they are lame, he says the Devil delivers them a staff to carry them there invisibly through the air. Once there, they fall to dancing and singing bawdy songs, in which he leads the dance himself. When this dance and other conferences are ended, he supplies their need for powders and roots with which to intoxicate people. He gives to every novice a mark, made either with his teeth or with his claws, and then they kiss the Devil's bare buttocks and depart—not forgetting every day afterward to offer him dogs, cats, hens, or their own blood. And all this Danaeus reports as a truth, as if from his own knowledge. And yet elsewhere he says that in these matters they do nothing but dream, and do not actually do those things which they confess due to their "distemperature" <note>an imbalance of the bodily fluids or "humors"</note> arising from their melancholic humor. Therefore (he says), these things which they report about themselves are nothing but mere illusions.

<margin>The same author in the same place. Also in *Dialogues*, chapter 3.</margin>Michael Psellus <note>original: "Pselus"; an 11th-century Byzantine philosopher and historian</note> adds to this that certain magical heretics—namely, the Eutychians—assemble themselves every Good Friday at night. After putting out the candles, they commit incestuous adultery: the father with the daughter, the sister with the brother, and the son with the mother. In the ninth month they return and give birth; then, cutting their children into pieces, they fill their pots with their blood. They then burn the carcasses and mingle the ashes with the blood, preserving the mixture for magical purposes. Girolamo Cardano <note>original: "Cardanus"; a 16th-century Italian polymath</note> writes (though in my opinion not very probably) that these excursions, dances, etc., had their beginning from certain heretics called the Dulcinians <note>original: "Dulcini"; followers of the 14th-century radical preacher Fra Dolcino</note>, who devised those feasts of Bacchus which are called *Orgia* <note>original: "Orgia"; Bacchic rituals or orgies</note>, where these kinds of people openly assembled. Beginning with rioting, they ended with this folly. When these feasts were prohibited, they nevertheless haunted them secretly; and when they could not do so physically, they did it only in their imagination. Even to this day (he says), there remains a certain image or resemblance of this among our "melancholic" <note>depressed or mentally unstable</note> women.

---

### CHAPTER IV.

That there can be no real league made with the Devil; the first author of the league, and the weak proofs of the adversaries for the same.

If the "league" <note>the formal contract or covenant with the Devil</note> is untrue—as are the rest of their confessions—then the arguments of the witch-mongers <note>those who promote the fear and prosecution of witches</note> fall to the ground. For all the writers on this subject hold this bargain to be certain, valid, and granted as their only fundamental rule. But surely the legal documents containing those covenants are "sealed with butter" <note>a metaphor for something that will melt away or is not solid</note>, and the seals are but baubles. What firm bargain can be made between a physical body and a spiritual one? Let any wise or honest man tell me that he has been either a party to it or a witness, and I will believe him. But by what authority, proof, or testimony, and upon what ground all this business stands, if you...

# Witches' private league. On Witchcraft. CHAPTER 5.

<margin>*Malleus Maleficarum* <note>original: "Mal. Malef."; a famous 1486 treatise on the prosecution of witches</note>, part 2, question 7, chapter 2.</margin> If you read the *Malleus Maleficarum*, you shall find—to the shame of the reporters (who vary so much in their tales and are in such contradiction) and to the reproach of those who believe such absurd lies—how these stories began.

<margin>The credit of the "real league" began to grow.</margin> For the credibility of this "league" rests upon the confession of a worthless <note>original: "baggage"</note> young fellow who was condemned to be burned for witchcraft. He told the Inquisitors (likely to prolong his life, if at least the story is true, which is taken from Nider <note>Johannes Nider, author of the 1435 work *Formicarius*</note>): "If I knew <note>original: "wist"</note> that I might obtain pardon, I would discover all that I know of witchcraft." This condition being accepted and pardon promised, he confessed the following:

The novice or young disciple goes to a church together with the minister of that profession <note>the person initiating them</note> on a Sunday morning, before the consecration <note>original: "conjuration"</note> of holy water. There, the said novice renounces the faith and promises obedience in observing—or rather, omitting—ceremonies in meetings and such other follies; and finally, they do homage to their new master, the Devil, as they covenanted.

But this is notable in that story: this young witch, fearing that his wife’s examination would expose <note>original: "bewray"</note> his trickery, told the Inquisitor: "In truth, my wife is as guilty as I am, but I am sure," he said, "that even if she were burned a thousand times, she will never confess any of these circumstances."

And this must not be forgotten: despite his confession and his accusation of his own wife, and contrary to the Inquisitors' promise and oath, both he and his wife were burned at the stake. They were the first "discoverers" of this notable league upon which the fable of witchcraft is maintained, and by which similar confessions have been forced <note>original: "extorted"</note> and embellished from similar persons since that time.

***

### CHAPTER 5.
*Of the private league, a notable tale of Bodin's concerning a French Lady, with a refutation.*

<margin>The witches' private league with the Devil.</margin> The manner of their "private league" is said to occur when the Devil—invisible, and sometimes visible—talks with people privately in the midst of a crowd. He promises that if they follow his counsel, he will supply all their needs and make all their efforts prosperous. He begins with small matters to which they secretly consent, and they do not join the fairies' assembly <note>the Sabbat or communal gathering</note>.

In this case, it seems to me that if the Devil appeared in such an external or physical shape, he would eventually meet someone who would not consent to his suggestions (unless you argue he can read their private thoughts <note>original: "cogitations"</note>), and so he would be exposed <note>original: "bewrayed"</note>. Also, the witches themselves (unless they were idiots) would see him for what he is and abandon him for breaking his promises. Yet all the writers on this subject maintain these bargains and assemblies exist; Jean Bodin confirms them with more than a hundred lies, among which I will (for various reasons) recount one.

<margin>Bodin, book 2 of *On the Demon-Mania of Witches* <note>original: "de dæmonoma."</note>, chapter 4. This does not agree with those who say this is done only by the power of the league, nor those who refer it to magical words.</margin> There was (Bodin says) a noble gentlewoman at Lyon who, while in bed with a lover, suddenly arose in the night and lit a candle. When she had done this, she took a box of ointment and anointed her body with it; after speaking a few words, she was carried away. Her bedfellow, seeing this, leapt out of bed, took the candle in his hand, and searched for the lady all around the chamber and in every corner. Although he could not find her, he did find her box of ointment. Desiring to know its power <note>original: "vertue"</note>, he smeared himself with it just as he had seen her do. Although he was not so superstitious as to use any words to help him along, he was immediately transported by the power of that ointment (says Bodin) to Lorraine, into an assembly of witches.

Which notable...

He also mocks Jean Bodin's fantastical story of a man who accidentally flew to a witches' meeting using magical ointment.</summary>

When he saw this, he was confounded and said, "In the name of God, what am I doing here?" Upon those words, the entire assembly vanished, leaving him there alone stark naked; and so he was forced to return to Lyon. But he had such a good conscience—for you may perceive by the first part of the history that he was a very honest man—that he accused his true lover of being a witch and caused her to be burned. And as for his own adultery, neither the *Malleus Maleficarum* <note>original: *M. Mal.*, a 15th-century treatise on the prosecution of witches</note> nor Jean Bodin <note>A prominent 16th-century French jurist and demonologist</note> says even a single word in dispraise of it.

<margin>Cornelius Agrippa, chapter 51.</margin>

It appears throughout all of Bodin’s book that he is deeply offended by Cornelius Agrippa, and more so, I suppose, because Agrippa recanted the very things that Bodin maintains. Bodin thinks Agrippa could work wonders by magic, and especially by his black dog. It would seem Agrippa had some skill in the art of divination; for although he wrote many years before Bodin, he uttered these words in his book *On the Vanity of Sciences* <note>original: *De vanitate scientiarum*</note>: "A certain French protonotary" (he says), "a wicked man and a con artist, has written a certain fable or miracle that occurred at Lyon," etc. I do not know who Bodin is, other than by report; but I am certain this story of his is a foolish fable. Bodin says it was performed at Lyon, and this man (as I understand) is a civil lawyer by profession.

**CHAPTER 6**

*A disproof of their assemblies and of their bargain.*

**T**hat the joining of hands with the Devil, the kissing of his bare buttocks, and his scratching and biting of them are absurd lies, anyone with the gift of reason can clearly see. It is manifest to us by the word of God that a spirit has no flesh, bones, nor sinews, which are what hands, buttocks, claws, teeth, and lips consist of. For even if we admit

<margin>Tatian against the Greeks <note>original: *Tatianus contra Graecos*</note>.</margin>

that the composition of a Devil's body (as Tatian and others affirm) consists of spiritual condensations <note>original: "congelations"</note>, such as fire and air, it still cannot be perceived by mortal creatures. What credible witness has ever been brought forward at any time to testify to this physical, visible, and unbelievable bargain, except for the confession of some person diseased in both body and mind—whether made voluntarily or forced through injury? It is a marvel that no repentant witch who abandons her trade ever confesses these things without being forced. It seems to me that their covenant made with God at baptism before good witnesses—sanctified with the Word, confirmed with His promises, and established with His sacraments—should have more power than a contract they make with the Devil, which nobody sees or knows. For God deceives no one with whom He bargains; neither does He mock or disappoint them, even though He does not dance among them.

The oath to recruit as many as they can into their league and fellowship (by which every single witch, as Bodin claims, increases their number by fifty)

<margin>The author speaks from evidence and firsthand experience.</margin>

greatly reveals <note>original: "bewrayeth"</note> their deceitful dealing. I have tested this myself, as well as the rest of their deceptive <note>original: "cousening"</note> devices. I have been with the "best"—or rather the worst—of them to see what might be gathered from their councils, and I have craftily dealt with them on these matters. Furthermore, I have sent certain elderly people to negotiate <note>original: "indent"</note> with them to be admitted into their society. But through their excuses and delays, as well as other circumstances, I have tested and found their entire trade to be nothing but a con.

I ask you, what bargain have those made with the Devil who supposedly bewitch lambs and children with their angry looks? Is it not admitted that this is a natural occurrence, even if the "bewitching" part is a lie? What bargain does the soothsayer make, who has various kinds of witchcraft and divination mentioned in the Scripture? Or is it not granted that they make none? How does it happen that we do not hear of this "bargain" in the Scriptures?

<header>Witches' Confessions Refuted. Of Witchcraft. CHAPTER VII.</header>

### CHAPTER VII.
->A Refutation of the Objection concerning Witches' Confessions.<-

It is confessed (say some by way of objection) even by these women themselves, that they do these and other such horrible things that deserve death with all severity, etc. To which I answer, that whoever carefully examines their confessions shall perceive them all to be vain, pointless, inconsistent, and of no weight—except for their contempt and ignorance in religion, which is more the fault of the negligent Pastor than of the simple woman.

<margin>Confession made by compulsion, such as by the Spanish Inquisition: See *Malleus Maleficarum* and *Bodin*. Confession by persuasion, such as by flattery: See Brian Darcy against Ursula Kempe, Jean Bodin, and *Malleus Maleficarum*, Book "On the absent person confessing." <note>original: "Mal. Mal. lef." refers to the *Malleus Maleficarum* (The Hammer of Witches), a 15th-century treatise on prosecuting witches. Brian Darcy was a magistrate involved in the 1582 St. Osyth witch trials.</note></margin>
First, if their confession is made by compulsion, by force, or by authority—such as by persuasion or under the guise of friendship—it is not to be respected. This is because the extremity of threats and tortures provokes it, or the nature of fair words and allurements constrains it. If it is voluntary, many circumstances must be considered: namely, whether she does not come forward to overthrow her neighbor, which often happens through their bitter and malicious melancholic humor <note>original: "humour"; referring to the theory of the four humors where an excess of "black bile" was thought to cause madness or depression.</note>. Then, consider whether, in that same melancholic, frantic humor, she does not desire the shortening of her own days. Aristotle says this often happens to persons subject to melancholic passions; and (as Bodin and Sprenger say) to these old women called witches, who many times (as they affirm) refuse to live, threatening the judges that if they may not be burned, they will kill themselves and so make the judges guilty of their damnation.

<margin>*Malleus Maleficarum*, Book 2, with a commentary on those who died beforehand, or those who brought death upon themselves. <note>original: "cum gloss. de iis, qui ante Volenti feniunt. mortui sunt, fibi necem conficiente."</note></margin>
I myself have known a case where such a person could not succeed in being accepted as a sufficient witness against himself, and so he immediately went and threw himself into a pond of water, where he drowned. But the law says *no faith should be placed in one who is about to die* <note>original: "mori non est habenda fides"; a legal maxim suggesting that statements made by those seeking death are unreliable.</note>, meaning his word is not to be credited. Also sometimes (as I have proved elsewhere) they confess to things of which they were never guilty, imagining that they did what they did not do because of certain circumstances. And just as they sometimes confess to impossibilities—such as flying in the air, transforming themselves into other shapes <note>original: "transubstantiate themselves"</note>, raising tempests, or moving crops <note>original: "transfer or remove corn"</note>—so they also (I say) confess voluntarily to things that no man could prove, and that no man would guess or even believe unless he were as mad as they are. In this way, they willfully bring death upon themselves, which proves they have an unsound mind.

<margin>Absurdities in Witches' Confessions.</margin>
If they confess to something that has indeed been committed by them, such as poisoning or any other kind of murder which is within the power of such persons to accomplish, I do not stand to defend their cause. However, I would wish that even in that case, too much rash credit is not given, nor too hasty proceedings used against them. Instead, the causes, properties, and circumstances of everything should be duly considered and diligently examined. For you must understand that just as they sometimes confess they have murdered their neighbors with a wish or a look, they also confess that by giving an apple (or some such thing) to a pregnant woman, they have killed the child in the mother's womb, even when nothing was added to the gift that could naturally be harmful or hurtful.

In like manner, they confess that with a touch of their bare hand, they sometimes kill a man who is in perfect health and bodily strength, even when all his garments are between their hand and his flesh.

But if this confession of theirs is examined by Theology, Philosophy, Medicine <note>original: "Physick"</note>, Law, or Conscience, it will be found false and insufficient. First, because the era of working miracles has ceased. Secondly, no reason can be given for a thing so far beyond all reason. Thirdly, no medicinal formula <note>original: "receipt"</note> can be so powerful that it could harm <note>original: "annoy"</note> a person unless it is touched with a bare hand (from which the veins pass through the body to the heart), and yet still retain its power and...

<summary>The author argues that confessions of witchcraft are unreliable because they are often obtained through torture, flattery, or the speaker's own mental illness and "melancholic humor." He asserts that many confessed acts, such as killing with a look or flying, are physical impossibilities that should be dismissed by rational medicine and theology.</summary>
