## CHAPTER 9.

### How melancholy affects old women, and the effects of it, shown through various examples.

If anyone carefully observes their words, actions, thoughts, and gestures, he will perceive that the melancholy filling their heads and occupying their brains has deprived—or rather corrupted—their judgment and all their senses. I am not referring to fraudulent <note>original: "cozening"</note> witches, but to poor melancholic women who are themselves deceived. You should understand that the power and the effects that this condition works in the body of a man—or rather a woman—are almost incredible. 

For just as some of these melancholic people imagine they are witches, and believe that through witchcraft they can work wonders and do whatever they please, others troubled by this disease imagine many strange, incredible, and impossible things. Some believe they are monarchs and princes, and that all other men are their subjects. Some think they are wild beasts. Some believe they are urinals <note>A glass vessel used for medical examinations</note> or earthen pots, greatly fearing they will be broken. Some fear that everyone they meet intends to take them to the gallows—and yet, in the end, they hang themselves. 

One person thought that Atlas (whom the poets imagine holds up the heavens on his shoulders) would grow weary and let the sky fall upon him. Another would spend an entire day on a stage, imagining he both heard and saw plays <note>original: "interludes"</note>, and amused himself greatly with this fantasy. A physician named Theophilus, who was otherwise considered of sound mind, imagined that he heard and saw musicians continually playing instruments in a certain part of his house. A man named Bessus, who had killed his father, was notably exposed <note>original: "detected"</note> when he imagined that a swallow was mocking him for it; because of this, he revealed the murder himself.

<margin>Concerning a man in great distress who, due to melancholy, was led to think he had a nose as big as a house, etc.</margin>But the most notable example of this concerns a man in great distress who imagined his nose was as big as a house. No friend or physician could free him from this idea, nor ease his grief or satisfy his fantasy, until finally, a physician more expert in these "humors" <note>In ancient medicine, the four "humors" were bodily fluids thought to control health and temperament. Melancholy was linked to "black bile."</note> than the rest used the following plan. 

First, when he was about to enter through the wide-open chamber door, he suddenly stopped and withdrew, refusing to get any closer than the doorway. The melancholic man, wondering at this, asked him why he behaved that way. The physician answered, "Sir, your nose is so large that I can hardly enter your room without touching it and, consequently, hurting it." 

"Look!" the patient cried. "This is the man who can help me! The rest of my friends flatter me and try to hide my illness from me." 

"Well," said the physician, "I will cure you, but you must be willing to endure a little pain during the treatment." The patient promised to bear it patiently, feeling a certain hope of recovery. 

Then the physician entered the room, creeping close to the walls and appearing to fear touching or hurting the man's nose. He then blindfolded the patient. Once this was done, he gripped the man's nose with a pair of pincers and poured a large quantity of blood—along with many pieces of bullock livers—into a tub he had placed before him. He had secretly brought these into the room while the man's eyes were covered. Then he allowed the man to look at the mess. After doing this two or three times, the "melancholic humor" was so lessened that the man’s mind was satisfied, his grief was eased, and his disease was cured.

Thrasyllus (also called Thrasullus), being severely oppressed by this melancholic humor, imagined that all the ships arriving at the port of Piraeus <note>The main port of Athens, Greece</note> belonged to him. He would count them and command the sailors to set sail, triumphing at their safe returns and mourning their misfortunes. The Italian man whom we called "the Monarch" here in England was possessed by a similar spirit or delusion <note>original: "conceit"</note>. Danaeus <note>Lambert Daneau (c. 1530–1595), a French theologian who wrote on magic</note> himself reports that he saw someone who...

# Book 2
## The Discovery
### Witchcraft Confessions Confuted

...firmly stated that he was a rooster; and says that through melancholy <note>original: "melancholy" — In the 16th century, this referred to an imbalance of "black bile," thought to cause depression, hallucinations, and delusions.</note>, such people were alienated from themselves.

<margin>Giambattista della Porta; Pietro Pomponazzi; Girolamo Cardano, *On the Variety of Things*, book 1; Johann Weyer, *On the Deceptions of Demons*, etc.; Aristotle; Jean Bodin.</margin>
Now, if the imagination of a melancholic person may be occupied with causes which are both false and impossible, why should an old woman accused of being a witch be thought free from such fantasies? As learned philosophers and physicians say, when their monthly melancholic flow <note>original: "flux or issue of blood" — a reference to the cessation of menstruation (menopause).</note> stops in their old age, that humor must necessarily increase within them. Because of the weakness of both their bodies and brains, they become the most likely persons to encounter such melancholic imaginations, which stay with them even when their physical senses are gone. *In this matter, Bodin labors to disprove the physicians, showing himself to be as poor a physician as he is elsewhere a poor theologian.*

But if they can imagine that they can transform their own bodies (which nevertheless remain in their original shape), how much more credible is it that they may falsely suppose they can hurt and enfeeble other men's bodies? Or, what is even less significant, imagine they can hinder the churning of butter? But what is it that they will not imagine, and consequently confess they can do—especially when they are so earnestly persuaded to do so, so sorely tormented, and so craftily examined with such promises of favor? By these means, they imagine that they shall live in great credit and wealth ever after.

If you read of the executions carried out upon witches, either in times past in other countries or lately in this land, you shall see such impossibilities confessed that no one in their right mind would believe them. Among other such false confessions, we read that there was a witch who confessed at the time of her death or execution that she had raised all the tempests and caused all the frosts and hard weather that happened in the Winter of 1565, and yet many grave and wise men believed her.

The parties themselves are still alive and dwelling in the parish of Sellenge in Kent, and the matter was performed not long ago in this manner:

<margin>A Kentish story of a recent accident.</margin>
One Ade Davie, the wife of Simon Davie, a husbandman <term>a farmer who owns his own land</term>, was reputed to be a truly honest person and of good parentage. She suddenly grew (as her husband informed me, and as it is well known in these parts) to be somewhat pensive and sadder than in times past. Although this grieved him, he was loath to let it show, lest his wife be troubled or discontented by it, or his neighbors be informed of it—fearing that poor husbandry <note>original: "husbandry" — here meaning the management of his household and wife; a husband was legally and socially responsible for his wife's behavior.</note> should be laid to his charge, which in these parts is much abhorred.

Not without tears, he could not help but ask the cause of her private thoughts and extraordinary mourning. Although at that time she covered it up, acknowledging nothing to be amiss with her, soon afterward she nevertheless fell down before him on her knees, desiring him to forgive her, for she had (as she said) grievously offended both God and him. Her poor husband, being abashed by this behavior, comforted her as best he could, asking the cause of her trouble and grief. She told him that she had, contrary to God’s Law and to the offense of all good Christians, and to the injury of him and especially to...

# Confessions Confuted. Melancholy. Of Witchcraft. Chapter 10.

<margin>Notice the Christian comfort the husband offers his wife.</margin>...to the loss of her own soul, she had bargained and given her soul to the Devil, to be delivered to him within a short time. To this, her husband answered, saying, "Wife, be of good cheer; this bargain of yours is void and has no effect. For you have sold that which is not yours to sell, since <note>original: "sith"</note> it belongs to Christ, who has bought it and dearly paid for it, even with his blood which he shed upon the Cross; so the Devil has no claim <note>original: "interest"</note> on you." After this, with similar submission, tears, and penitence, she said to him, "Oh husband, I have committed yet another fault and done you more injury: for I have bewitched you and your children." "Be content," said he, "by the grace of God, Jesus Christ shall 'unwitch' us; for no evil can happen to those who fear God."

And (as truly as the Lord lives) this was the substance of his words to me, proceeding from sincere lips and from one who feared God. Now, when the time approached that the Devil was supposed to come and take possession of the woman according to his bargain, the husband watched and prayed earnestly, and had his wife read Psalms and prayers for mercy at God's hands. There was a great rumbling below, under his bedroom window, which startled them exceedingly. For they imagined that the Devil was below, though he had no power to come up because of their fervent prayer.

<margin>Refutation.</margin>Anyone who notes this woman's first and second confessions—made freely and voluntarily—and how every detail seemed to support her story and provide grounds for her condemnation, would think that if Bodin <note>Jean Bodin (1530–1596) was a famous French judge and author of an influential book on the persecution of witches.</note> were the foreman of her jury, he would cry, "Guilty!" He would hasten the execution of a woman who would have said the same before any judge in the world if she had been examined, and would have confessed no less if she had been put on trial for it. 

But God knows, she was innocent of any of these crimes. However, she was brought low and weighed down by this humor <term>Humor: In medieval medicine, "humors" were bodily fluids (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile) believed to control health and temperament. An excess of "black bile" caused melancholy, or deep depression and delusions.</term>, so that both her rest and sleep were taken away from her; her thoughts were troubled and disquieted with despair and other such ideas that grew from her condition. And yet I believe that if any mishap had happened to her husband or his children, few "witch-hunters" <note>original: "Witchmongers"</note> would have judged otherwise than that she had bewitched them. As for her, she was so constantly persuaded that she was a witch that she judged herself worthy of death. Even while being kept in her room, if she saw anyone carrying a bundle of sticks <note>original: "faggot"</note> for the fire, she would say it was to make a fire to burn her for witchcraft. But God knows she had bewitched no one, nor caused any hurt to anyone through her imagination, except to herself.

<margin>A humorous conclusion.</margin>And as for the rumbling, it was caused by a sheep that had been skinned <note>original: "flayed"</note> and hung by the walls, which a dog had come to devour; that was the source of the noise I mentioned before. Now that she has recovered, she remains a perfectly honorable woman, far from such impiety, and ashamed of her old imaginings, which she perceives grew out of her melancholy.

### Chapter 11.
*The strange and diverse effects of Melancholy, and how this same humor, when it abounds in "witches" (or rather, old women), fills them with marvelous imaginings, and why their confessions are not to be believed.*

<margin>Girolamo Cardano, *On the Variety of Things*, book 8. Johann Weyer, *On the Tricks of Demons*, book 6.</margin>But in truth, this melancholic humor (as the best physicians affirm) is the cause of all their strange, impossible, and incredible confessions. These are so foolish <note>original: "fond"</note> that I wonder how any men can be deceived by them. However, even though these feelings appear in the mind of man, they are bred in the body and proceed from this "humor," which is the very dregs of blood. It nourishes and feeds those parts of the mind from which proceed fears, obsessive thoughts, superstitions, fasts, labors, and the like.

The author uses this to argue that many witchcraft confessions are actually symptoms of "melancholy" (clinical depression or psychosis) rather than reality.</summary>

<page-num>32</page-num>
<header>Book III. The Discovery of the Witches' League Refuted.</header>

<margin>*Aristotle, On Dreams. Girolamo Cardano, Book 8, On the Variety of Things.*</margin>
This <note>Referring to the "melancholic humor" mentioned on the previous page.</note> causes the endurance of torments and (as some say) foresight of things to come. It preserves health, being cold and dry, but it makes men subject to leanness and to the Quartan Ague <note>A fever—often associated with malaria—where the paroxysm occurs every fourth day.</note>. Those who are afflicted with it are destroyers of themselves, brave in enduring injuries, but fearful of offering violence—unless the humor <note>In Early Modern medicine, "humors" were bodily fluids (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile) believed to control a person's health and temperament. Melancholy was associated with black bile.</note> is hot. They learn foreign languages with little effort (as Aristotle and others affirm).

<margin>*Jean Bodin against Johann Weyer.*</margin>
If our witches' fantasies were not corrupted, nor their wills confounded by this humor, they would not so voluntarily and readily confess things that put their lives in danger, of which they could never otherwise be convicted. Jean Bodin <note>A famous French jurist and philosopher who was a strong proponent of witch-hunting.</note>, using a lawyer’s logic, reasons to the contrary; he acts as though melancholy were furthest of all from those old women whom we call witches, mocking the most famous and noble physician Johann Weyer <note>One of the first physicians to argue that "witches" were actually suffering from mental illness (melancholy).</note> for his opinion on that matter. But because I am no physician, I will set a physician against him—namely, Erasmus, who says that these witches, through their corrupted imagination overflowing with melancholic humors due to their old age, imagine they hurt things which they neither could nor do hurt. Thus, they think they know an Art <note>meaning: a magical skill or craft</note> which they have neither learned nor yet understand.

<margin>*Augustine, On the Trinity, Book 3. The same, On the City of God. Clementine Recognitions, Book 3. Iamblichus. Cardano. Pampa, etc.*</margin>
But why should more credit be given to witches when they say they have made a real bargain with the Devil, killed a cow, bewitched butter, weakened a child, or cursed their neighbor, than when they confess that they transform themselves, make it rain or hail, fly in the air, go invisible, or transfer corn in the grass from one field to another? If you think their confessions are sound in the first cases, why should you say they are corrupt in the others, since the confession of all these things is made at the same moment and affirmed with the same constancy—or rather, audacity? 

But you see that the first things are possible, and therefore you think their confessions are true; the others you think cannot be done, and even though you hear them confess it, you conclude that they are lying. Yet you conclude from what is possible to what is actual <note>original: *A posse ad esse*</note>, being persuaded it is so simply because you think it *might* be so. But I say, along with both theologians and philosophers, that what is imagined regarding witchcraft has no truth in action or existence outside of their imagination. The witch (for the most part) is occupied with a false cause. For whoever desires to bring about an impossible thing has a vain, idle, and childish persuasion bred by an unsound mind; for the will of a sound mind is the desire for a possible thing <note>original: *Sane mentis voluntas, voluntas rei possibilis est*</note>.

### C H A P. XII.
#### *A Refutation of Witches' Confessions, especially concerning their League.*

<margin>An objection.</margin>
But it is objected that witches confess they renounce the faith; the argument is that their confession must be true, or else they would not make it, and their fault must be worthy of death, or else they would not be executed. To this I answer as before: that their confessions are either extorted <note>meaning: obtained through torture or pressure</note> or else proceed from an unsound mind. 

<margin>The resolution.</margin>
Indeed, I say further that we ourselves—who are of sound mind and yet seek any other way of salvation than Jesus Christ, or break his Commandments, or do not walk in his steps with a lively faith—do not only renounce the faith, but God himself. Therefore, in confessing that they forsake God and embrace Satan, they do only what we all do when we sin. 

As for that horrible part of their confession regarding the "league" <note>A formal pact or alliance with the Devil.</note> which involves the killing of their own and others' children, the boiling of them to make their potions or stews, and the effects thereof; their Good Friday meetings (being the day of their deliverance); their acts of incest; and their return at the end of nine months (when women are commonly neither able to make such a journey nor to return)—it is all so horrible, unnatural, unlikely, and impossible that if I <meta>catchword: should</meta>

# Witches' Storms. Of Witchcraft. CHAPTER XIII.

...should behold such things with my own eyes, I would rather think myself dreaming, drunk, or somehow deprived of my senses, than believe such horrible and filthy matters.

How has the oil or broth of a boiled <note>original: "sodden"</note> child such power that a staff anointed with it can carry people through the air? Their drinkable liquid <note>original: "potable liquor"</note>, which they say makes one a master of that faculty—is it not ridiculous? And is it not, in the opinion of all philosophers, physicians, and theologians, devoid of such power as is attributed to it?

Their not fasting on Fridays, and their fasting on Sundays, their spitting at the time of the Elevation <note>The moment in the Catholic Mass when the bread and wine are raised.</note>, their refusal of holy water, their despising of superstitious crosses, etc.—which are all good steps toward true Christianity—help me to disprove the rest of their confessions.

->### CHAPTER XIII.<-

A Refutation <note>original: "Confutation"</note> of witches' confessions concerning the making of storms and rain; of the natural cause of rain, and that witches or devils have no power to do such things.

<margin>The ways that witches use to make rain, etc.</margin>
And to speak more generally of all the impossible actions attributed to them, as well as their false confessions, I say that there is no one who acknowledges God to be the only Almighty and the only worker of all miracles—nor anyone else endowed with common sense—but will deny that the elements are obedient to witches and at their command. Nor will they believe that witches may, at their pleasure, send rain, hail, storms, thunder, or lightning. They claim this happens when an old, senile woman throws a flint stone over her left shoulder toward the west, or hurls a little sea sand up into the sky <note>original: "Element"</note>, or wets a broom-twig in water and sprinkles it in the air, or digs a pit in the earth and, putting water in it, stirs it about with her finger, or boils hog bristles, or lays sticks across a bank where there isn't a drop of water, or buries sage until it is rotten. All of these things are confessed by witches and affirmed by writers to be the means that witches use to stir up extraordinary storms and rain, etc.

<margin>*Nider. The Hammer of Witches <note>original: "Mal. Malef." i.e., Malleus Maleficarum</note>, part 7. Bodin. Friar Bartholomew. Hemming, Daneau, etc.*</margin>
We read in the *Hammer of Witches* <note>A famous 15th-century manual for witch-hunters.</note> that a little girl, walking abroad with her father on his land, heard him complain of drought and wish for rain. "Why father," said the child, "I can make it rain or hail when and where I want." He asked where she learned this; she said from her mother, who forbade her to tell anyone. He asked her how her mother taught her. She answered that her mother committed her to a "Master" <note>A demon or the Devil.</note> who would do anything for her at any time. "Why then," he said, "make it rain only in my field." And so she went to the stream, threw up water in her Master’s name, and made it rain immediately. Proceeding further with her father, she made it hail in another field at her father’s request. Because of this, he accused his wife and caused her to be burned, and then he had his child baptized again—a practice common among Catholics <note>original: "Papists"</note> and witch-believers <note>original: "Witch-mongers"</note>. And however the first part of this story was "proved," there is no doubt that the latter part (the execution) was thoroughly carried out. If they could indeed bring these things to pass at their pleasure, then they could also hinder the course of all other natural things and laws ordained by God. For instance, they could cause it to stay dry when it should rain, or make it midnight at high noon. By those means, I say, the Divine power would become a slave to the will of a witch, so that we could neither eat nor drink except by their permission.

And that showers might be procured or stopped by witches' charms and enchantments: it is so obvious that nothing can be achieved by such means, that we do not even need to go to a philosopher's school to learn the refutation of it.

<margin>Jeremiah 16:22. <note>The author likely refers to Jeremiah 14:22.</note>
The gods of the Gentiles are demons. <note>original: "Dii gentium demonia"</note>
The natural generation of hail and rain.</margin>But Jeremiah, by the Word of God, utterly confounds everything that might be devised to maintain that foolish opinion, saying: *Are there any among the gods of the Gentiles that send rain, or give showers from Heaven? I answer that princes inclined toward battle would not have a guilty conscience in this matter, especially those who undertake unjust wars. They use other helps, devices, and engines that are as lawful and devilish as that; in their camps, neither the rule of religion nor Christian order is observed. Indeed, rapes, murders, blasphemies, and thefts are most commonly and freely committed there. Consequently, the Devil is more feared and better served in their camps than Almighty God.

But even if we assume that soldiers would be scrupulous in this, the Pope has the authority to grant a dispensation <note>a formal exemption from a church law</note> for it, as he has done in similar cases, according to the testimony of his own authors and friends. ->**CHAPTER 15**<-

Examples of foreign nations who used the assistance of witches in their wars; of "eye-biting" witches in Ireland; and of two archers who shot with familiars <note>spirits or demons supposed to attend and obey a witch</note>.

<margin>Witches in wars.</margin>
In the wars between the Kings of Denmark and Sweden in 1563, the Danes wrote that the King of *Sweden* carried four old witches about with him in camp. These witches supposedly used charms to "qualify" <note>original: "qualified"; here meaning to weaken or subdue</note> the *Danes* so that they were unable to harm their enemies. If the Danes undertook any enterprise, they were so enfeebled by those witches that they could perform nothing. Although this could not be believed at first, eventually one of these witches was taken prisoner and confessed the whole matter. He says the threads, the line, and the magical characters were found in the highway and in puddles of water.

<margin>Eye-biting witches.</margin>
The *Irish* people are incredibly devoted to the belief and practice of this. They affirm that not only their children but their cattle are "eye-bitten" (as they call it) when they suddenly fall sick. They even term one sort of their witches "eye-biters" for that reason alone. Indeed, they will not hesitate to claim that they can rhyme either man or beast to death. Also, the *West Indians* and *Muscovites* <note>Russians</note> do the same, and the *Huns* (as *Gregory of Tours* writes) used the help of witches in times of war.

<margin>Pumber the archer.</margin>
I find another story written in the *Hammer of Witches* and repeated by *Bodin*: that a certain soldier called *Pumber* daily killed three of the enemy through witchcraft using his bow and arrows. He did this as they stood peeping over the walls of a besieged castle, until in the end he had killed them all except one. The "trial" of the archer's sinister dealing and the proof offered for it was that he almost never failed when he shot, that he killed exactly three people a day, and that he had shot three arrows into a rod <note>likely a narrow target or stick used to prove accuracy</note>. This was the same man who shot at a penny on his son's head and had another arrow ready to kill the Duke of *Rheingraf* <note>original: "Remgrave"</note> who had commanded him to do it. Undoubtedly, because of his singular dexterity in shooting, he was reputed to be a witch, as he did what others could not do—nor even think was in the power of man to do. In truth, however, there was no miracle, no witchcraft, no impossibility, nor any real difficulty involved.

<margin>A skillful archer punished by an unskillful Justice.</margin>
But I can match this latter story with a local example. At *Town Malling* in *Kent*, one of Queen *Mary's* Justices—acting on the complaint of many "wise" men and a few foolish boys—arrested an archer. This was because he shot and played with a "fly," otherwise known as a devil or familiar spirit. Because the Justice was told that the archer shot better than any common shooting he had ever heard of or seen, he conceived that it could not be in God's name, but must be by enchantment. He supposed that this archer, by abusing the...

->### CHAPTER XVI.<-
### Authorities condemning the imaginary confessions of witches, and how a Catholic doctor takes it upon himself to disprove them.

<margin>Council of Ancyra, <note>original: *Concil. Aqui.* likely referring to the *Canon Episcopi* often associated with the Council of Ancyra or Aquileia.</note> recorded in the Decrees, Case 26, Question 5, Chapter "Episcopi." Augustine, *On the Spirit and the Soul*, chapter 8. Francesco Ponzinibio, *Treatise on Witches*, number 49. Grillandus, *On Fortune-tellers*, number 6. In the *Life of Saint German*.</margin> Certain general Councils, through their decrees, have condemned the confessions and erroneous beliefs of witches as being vain, imaginary, and legendary. This includes even those things that are part of their "pact"—upon which our witch-hunters <term>original: "witchmongers" — those who promote or believe in the reality of witchcraft</term> so heavily rely—namely: their night-walkings and meetings with **Herodias** <note>A biblical figure who, in medieval folklore, was believed to lead a "furious host" or "wild hunt" through the night sky.</note> and the **Pagan** gods. They claim that during these times, they travel great distances in a very short time as if on a hobby-horse; they also claim to undergo transformation <note>original: "transubstantiation," here used to mean shape-shifting rather than the Eucharistic miracle.</note>, to eat children after snatching them from their mothers' sides, and to enter men's houses through cracks and little holes where even a fly could scarcely squeeze through to disturb the inhabitants, etc. All of these things are not only declared by a general Council to be purely imaginary and the results of dreams, but are also affirmed as such by ancient writers.

The words of the Council are as follows: "It must not be overlooked that certain wicked women, following Satan's provocations and seduced by the illusions of demons, believe and profess that during the night they ride abroad with **Diana**, the goddess of the **Pagans**, or else with **Herodias**, accompanied by an innumerable multitude, riding upon certain beasts. They claim to pass over many countries and nations in the silence of the night, doing whatever those fairies or ladies command, etc." The Council continues: "Therefore, let all ministers in their various parishes <term>original: "cures"</term> preach to God's people so that they may know all these things are false, etc." It follows in the same Council: "Therefore, whoever believes that any creature can either be created by them, or changed for better or worse, or be transformed in any way into any other kind or likeness by anyone but the Creator himself, is surely an infidel and worse than a Pagan."

If this is believable, then all of their bargains and assemblies are unbelievable, as they are only confirmed by certain foolish and forced confessions. This is also supported by a legend about **Saint German**, who watched the fairies or witches during a late-night banquet. Through his holiness, he made them stay still until he sent messengers to the houses of the neighbors who appeared to be there. He found them all in their beds, and so he cried out that these were actually demons in the likeness of those women. If this story were as true as it is actually false, it would serve well to disprove these meetings and night-walkings. For if demons are only present in the likeness of witches, then the claims attributed to witches in this matter are false.

<margin>The Hammer of Witches. <note>original: *Nomus Mal.* likely a typo for *Malleus Maleficarum*.</note> *Malleus* in the question concerning witches, chapters 21, 22, 23, etc.</margin> However, because the old "hammer" of **Sprenger** and **Institor** <note>Heinrich Kramer (Institoris) and Jacob Sprenger, the authors of the *Malleus Maleficarum* or *The Hammer of Witches* (1486).</note> in their book *The Hammer of Witches* <note>original: *Malleo maleficarum*</note> was insufficient to knock down this Council's decree, a young blockhead <term>original: "beetle-head" — a play on words, as a 'beetle' is a heavy wooden mallet.</term> named **Friar Bartholomew Spina** has made a new "leaden mallet" <term>original: "leaden beetle"</term> to beat down the Council and kill these old women. In this effort, he acts like Aesop’s Ass <note>A reference to a fable where an ass tries to imitate a pet dog to gain the master's favor but fails miserably.</note> and "claws" at the Pope with his heels. He claims on his own credit that the Council is false and erroneous because its doctrine deviates from the Popish Church and is not authentic but apocryphal. He says (though untruthfully) that the Council was not called by the command and pleasure of the Pope, nor ratified by his authority—which, he claims, is enough to annul any Council. "For surely," says this Friar (who at this moment is a chief Inquisitor), "if the words of this Council were to be accepted, both I and all my predecessors have published notorious lies and committed many unjust executions..."

### Book III.
## The Discovery
### Witches' Confessions Confuted.

<margin>Augustine, *The City of God*.</margin>
<margin>Isidore, Book 8, Chapter 9. *Etymologies*, 26, Question 3, Chapter on "not a wonder."</margin>
<margin>Pontizibus on Witches, Volume 10. Laws regarding error and ignorance of law and fact, and on the questioning of possible actions.</margin>
...on their behalf is insufficient to take away the life of anyone, or to gain such credit as to be believed without further proof. For, as Augustine and Isidore—along with the rest of the more reliable <note>original: "founder"</note> theologians—say, these superstitious <note>original: "perstitigious," meaning magical or deceitful</note> things performed by witches are imaginary <note>original: "fantastical"</note>. The more reliable decrees of the Councils and the Canons of the Church also agree that in such cases, there is no ground for criminal action. Furthermore, the law says <note>original: "faith," likely a transcription of "saith"</note> that the confessions of people who are deceived <note>original: "illuded"</note> must necessarily be erroneous, and therefore should not be admitted. As the legal maxim states: *A confession must hold to what is true and possible* <note>original: "Confeſſio debet tenere verum & poſſibile"</note>. But these supernatural claims are opposite to both law and nature; therefore, it does not follow that because these witches confess to them, it is therefore <note>original: "Ergo"</note> true. The confession differs from the actual act, or even the possibility of the act. Whatever is contrary to nature fails in its own principles and is therefore naturally impossible.

<margin>According to the glosses of Baldus and others on the Law of Confessions.</margin>
<margin>As stated by Baldus and Augustine.</margin>
<margin>Additional notes on the presumption of letters.</margin>
<margin>According to Baldus.</margin>
<margin>The *Hammer of Witches* <note>original: "Mal. Malef.," referring to the *Malleus Maleficarum*</note>, Part 3, Question 5, Chapter 11.</margin>
The law also says: *In criminal cases, we must not generally rely solely on the confession of the accused* <note>original: "In criminalibus regulariter non ſtatur ſoli confeſſioni rei"</note>. In cases involving the death penalty, we must not rely absolutely on the confession of the accused party; instead, in these matters, proofs must be brought that are clearer than the light of day. In this specific crime, no one should be condemned based on mere presumptions. 

When it is argued that since only God knows a person's thoughts, there is no other way to prove the crime except by confession, the law answers this way: Their confession in this case involves an outward act that is impossible in both law and nature, and is also unlikely to be true. Therefore, *that which is not likely should not be considered* <note>original: "Quod veriſimile non eſt, attendi non debet"</note>. So, while their confessions may deserve punishment—because they show a will to commit such mischief—they do not deserve to be believed as proof that they actually have such power. For, *if the deed is absent, and they suffer only from their own opinion, they are to be counted among the company of fools* <note>original: "ſi factum abſit, ſolaque opinione laborent, & ſtultorum genere ſunt"</note>. They should not be judged based on presumptions or by a single witness, nor by the accusation of a deadly enemy (who should not be allowed to give evidence in this case, even though it pleases the authors of the *Hammer of Witches* and Jean Bodin <note>A famous French jurist and demonologist</note> to claim the opposite). 

By all standard of equity, these Inquisitors have enough tricks and devices to plague and kill these poor fools. They claim the witches' fault is the greatest of all because of their sexual contact <note>original: "carnal copulation"</note> with the Devil. Therefore, they argue witches should be punished as heretics in four ways: through excommunication, loss of status <note>original: "deprivation"</note>, loss of goods, and death.

<margin>*Malleus Maleficarum*, Question 14, Part 1, Chapter on Witches, and various legal citations.</margin>
And indeed, they find laws and provide means to maintain their bloodthirsty attitude. For it is written in their Catholic <note>original: "Popish"</note> Canons that for this kind of heretic, no matter how much they repent and return to the faith, they may not be kept alive or even held in life imprisonment, but must be put to a painful death. 

Indeed, the author of the *Hammer of Witches* writes that a witch's sin is the "sin against the Holy Ghost"—which is to say, it is unforgivable <note>original: "irremissible"</note>. He even claims it is greater than the sin of the fallen angels. In this respect, I wonder why Moses did not deliver three stone tablets to the children of Israel, or at least include specific commandments for it. It is hard to believe that the greatest sin of all would be included within a lesser commandment.

<margin>*Malleus Maleficarum*, Question 17.</margin>
But when these witch-hunters <note>original: "Witchmongers"</note> are defeated in the argument concerning confessions—so that their tyrannical reasoning cannot soak the magistrates' hands in as much blood as they desire—they resort to accusing the women of other crimes. They do this so the world might think they had some justification for maintaining their malicious fury against them.

### CHAPTER XIX.

Concerning four major crimes charged against witches, all fully answered and proven to be ridiculous.

<margin>1. Idolatry.</margin>
First, therefore, they charge them with idolatry; but alas, this is without any reason. For we properly understand idolaters to be those who perform external worship to idols or foreign gods. The furthest point that idolatry can be stretched is that those who are guilty of it are people who hope for and seek salvation from idols, or from anyone other than God, or who fix their whole mind and love upon any creature so much that the power of God is neglected and despised because of it. But witches neither seek nor believe they will receive salvation from devils; they are only deceived by them. The instruments of their imagination <note>original: "fantasie"</note> are corrupted and so deluded <note>original: "infatuated"</note> that they suppose, confess, and say they can do things that are as far beyond their power and nature as it is to kill a man at **York** before noon when they have been seen at **London** that same morning, and so on. But if these latter "idolaters," whose idolatry is purely spiritual and committed only in the mind, should be punished by death, then every covetous man or anyone else who sets his affection too much on any earthly creature would have to be executed—and yet perhaps the witch might escape scot-free <note>original: "foot-free"</note>.

<margin>2. Apostasy.</margin>
Secondly, apostasy <term>Apostasy</term> <note>The total desertion or departure from one's religion or principles.</note> is charged against them, from which it is inferred that they are worthy to die. But apostasy occurs where someone of sound judgment forsakes the Gospel, which they have learned and known well, and not only embraces impiety and unbelief but attacks and resists the truth they formerly professed. But alas, these poor women do not try to defend any impiety, but after receiving good counsel <note>original: "admonition"</note>, they repent.

<margin>3. Seducing of the people, proven false.</margin>
Thirdly, they would have them executed for seducing the people. God knows, they have very little skill in rhetoric or art to seduce anyone, except perhaps to tell a tale of *Robin Good-fellow* <note>A mischievous nature spirit or "puck" from English folklore.</note> and be deceived and seduced themselves. Neither their age nor their sex should allow any such accusation to be considered just, for they themselves are poor, seduced souls. For my part (as I have said elsewhere), I have proved this point to be false in the most obvious way.

<margin>4. Sexual intercourse with an *Incubus*, proven false.</margin>
<margin>How the Devil plays the Succubus and Incubus.</margin>
Fourthly, regarding the accusation which all the writers use against them concerning their sexual intercourse with an *Incubus* <term>Incubus</term> <note>A male demon traditionally thought to have sex with sleeping women.</note>: the foolishness of men's belief is as much to be wondered at and mocked as the witches' own vain and impossible confessions. For the Devil is a spirit and has neither flesh nor bones, which are necessary to perform this action. And since he also lacks all biological organs and sperm produced from blood <note>original: "feed engendred of bloud"; early modern science believed semen was a refined form of blood.</note>, it would be foolish to spend too much time disproving something that does not exist in nature. And yet I must say something here because this opinion is so strongly and universally accepted, and the fables about it are so numerous. Because of this, the authors of the *Hammer of Witches* <note>original: "M. Mal.", referring to the *Malleus Maleficarum*, a famous 15th-century witch-hunting manual.</note>, as well as Bodin, Hemingius, Hyperius, Danaeus, Erastus, and others who take it upon themselves to write on this subject, are so deceived—or rather, they seek to deceive others. I wonder at their foolish belief in this matter. For they claim without doubt that the Devil plays the *Succubus* <term>Succubus</term> <note>A female demon traditionally thought to have sex with sleeping men.</note> to a man to take from him the seed of generation, which he then delivers as an *Incubus* to a woman, who often becomes pregnant that way. That child, they claim, will naturally become a witch; they even assert that *Merlin* was such a person.

### CHAPTER 20.

*A request to such readers as are reluctant to hear or read filthy and obscene matters—which of necessity must be inserted here—to skip over the next eight chapters.*

<margin>A preface <note>original: "præoration"</note> to the readers.</margin>
<insert>B</insert>ecause I am forced (for the more obvious revealing and exposing of this most filthy and horrible error) to stain my paper by writing certain of their beastly and obscene assertions and examples, which they use to confirm this doctrine of theirs—being myself both ashamed and reluctant to even think about such filthiness, even though it is for the purpose of condemning it—I must entreat you, the readers, whose chaste ears cannot well endure to hear of such abominable lecheries as are gathered out of the books of those witch-believers <note>original: "Witch-mongers"</note> (even though they are Doctors of Divinity and otherwise of great authority and reputation), to skip over a few pages. In these pages, I have, like a servant <note>original: "Groom"</note>, shoved their obscene material (even that which I myself loathe) into a stinking corner, so to speak. However, I hope this is done in such a way that the other parts of my writing shall remain pleasant, and this section will be kept as hidden away as possible.

## CHAPTER I.
*Regarding the opinions of witch-believers <note>original: "Witchmongers"</note> concerning evil spirits, and how they claim these spirits can create bodies for themselves that are more excellent than those God made for us.*

---

<margin>*Malleus Maleficarum*, Part 2, Chapter 4, Question 1. <note>The *Malleus Maleficarum* (The Hammer of Witches) was a famous 15th-century treatise on the prosecution of witches.</note></margin>

James Sprenger and Heinrich Kramer <note>original: "Henry Instor"</note> in the *Hammer of Witches*, agreeing with Bodin, Barth, Spineus, Daneau, Erastus, Hemmingius, and the rest, engage in a lewd discourse. They labor to prove, through a foolish kind of philosophy, that evil spirits can not only take on fake earthly forms and shapes of men, but can also counterfeit hearing, seeing, and other senses. They likewise claim that spirits can eat and devour food, as well as retain, digest, and eliminate it. Finally, they claim these spirits use various kinds of physical activities, but especially excel in the use and art of sexual intercourse <note>original: "Venery"</note>. 

For the *Hammer of Witches* says that the eyes and ears of the mind are far more subtle than bodily eyes or physical ears. Indeed, it is affirmed there that as spirits take on bodies and the likeness of limbs, they also take on minds and the likeness of human actions. 

But, by the way, I would have them answer this question: Our minds and souls are spiritual things. If our physical ears are stopped, what can they hear or understand of any external wisdom? And truly, a man with such a bodily constitution as they imagine for these spirits—who "make themselves," etc.—would be of a far more excellent substance than the bodies of those whom God made in Paradise. If this were true, the Devil's workmanship would exceed the handiwork of God the Father and Creator of all things.

<margin>If his bodily eyes were missing, he would see very poorly indeed.</margin>

They say some witches have practiced that trade of lechery with an *Incubus* for twenty or thirty days together, as was confessed by forty-eight witches burned at Ravensburg <note>original: "Ravenspurge"</note>. 

Furthermore, Thomas Aquinas, Bodin, the *Hammer of Witches*, Hyperius, and others attempt to prove what kind of "impressive" fellows the *Incubus* fathers upon these witches.

This is "proven," first, by the Devil's cunning in discerning the differences in the semen that falls from men. Secondly, by his understanding of the suitability of women for receiving such seed. Thirdly, by his knowledge of the constellations, which are favorable to such physical effects. And lastly, by the excellent physical makeup <note>term: complexion</note> of the women the Devil chooses to father such notable persons upon—which they claim is the cause of the greatness and excellence of the children born this way.

### CHAP. IV.
*That the power of reproduction is hindered both outwardly and inwardly by witches; and of various people who had their genitals taken from them by witches, and restored again by the same means.*

They also affirm that the virtue of reproduction <term>original: "Generation"</term> is hindered by witches, both inwardly and outwardly. For, intrinsically, they repress a man’s courage and stop the passage of his seed so that it may not descend to the vessels of reproduction. They also cause harm externally with images, herbs, and so on. To prove this is true, you shall hear certain stories out of the *Malleus Maleficarum* <note>original: "M. <margin>*Malleus Maleficarum*, Part 2, Question 1, Chapter 6.</margin>
A young priest at Mersburg, in the Diocese of Constance, was bewitched so that he had no power to be with any woman other than one. To be delivered out of that thraldom, he sought to flee to another country where he might practice that priestly occupation more freely. But it was all in vain; for he was always brought as far backward by night as he had gone forward during the day before—sometimes through the air, as though he flew. If this is not true, I am sure that James Sprenger <note>one of the presumed authors of the *Malleus Maleficarum*</note> is lying.

For the further confirmation of our belief in the *Incubus*, the *Malleus Maleficarum* cites a story of a notable matter that took place at Ravensburg, which is as true and as wholesome as the rest. A young man lying with a girl in that town (he says) was forced to leave his instruments of sex <term>original: "instruments of Venery"</term> behind him because of the deceptive art of witchcraft, so that in that place nothing could be seen or felt but his plain body. This young man was told by another witch to go to the woman he suspected and seek her help. Soon after, meeting her, he entreated her kindly, but that was in vain. Therefore, he caught her by the throat and said, "Restore me my tool, or you shall die for it!" Because she was swollen and black in the face and ready to die from his boisterous handling, she said, "Let me go, and I will help you." While he was loosening his grip <note>original: "losing the towel", likely referring to his hold on her neck or head-covering</note>, she put her hand into his codpiece <term>a decorative pouch at the crotch of men's breeches</term> and touched the place, saying, "Now you have your desire." At that very instant, he felt himself restored.

<margin>James Sprenger in *Malleus Maleficarum*, Part 2, Question 1.</margin>

### CHAPTER 7.
Of various Saints and holy persons who were exceedingly lewd and lustful, and by certain miraculous means became chaste.

<margin>In the *Lives of the Fathers* <note>original: "col. patrum"</note>.</margin>

"Yes," said he, "with all my heart."

And when they had made him swear a solemn oath to do so, they picked him up and castrated <note>original: "gelded"</note> him. One of them held his hands and another his feet, while the third cut out his testicles <note>original: "stones"</note>. But the story says it did not actually happen, except in a vision. Nider writes a similar story of Thomas, whom two angels cured of that lecherous disease by placing a girdle around him which they had brought down from heaven.

### CHAPTER IX.

<margin>Jason Pratensis regarding brain diseases, chapter 16.</margin>
Now, being wearied with the recital of so many lecheries—most horrible, very filthy, and fabulous actions and passions of witches, together with the spirit *Incubus*—I will end with a true story taken out of Jason Pratensis <note>Jason van der Velde (1486–1558), a Dutch physician.</note>, which, though it is crude, is not quite as unclean as the rest.

"There came," he says, "lately a Mass-priest unto me, making piteous moan and saying that if I did not help him, he would be undone and utterly overthrown, so great was his infirmity. 'For,' he said, 'I used to be fair and fat, and of an excellent complexion; and look how I appear now, being a mere ghost consisting of skin and bone, etc.' 'What is the matter?' asked Jason. 'I will show you, sir,' said the priest. 'There comes to me, almost every night, a certain woman unknown to me, and lies so heavy upon my breast that I cannot catch my breath; I have no power to cry out, nor do my hands serve me to shove her away, nor my feet to move from her.' I smiled," said Jason, "and told him that he was afflicted with a disease called *Incubus*, or 'the mare' <note>The "nightmare," historically viewed as a weight or creature sitting on the chest during sleep.</note>, and the rest was fantasy and vain imagination. 'No,' said the priest, 'it cannot be
<margin>The priest is stubborn in the error of his fantasy.</margin>
so; for by our blessed Lady, I tell you nothing but what I saw with my eyes while awake and felt with my hands. I see her when she comes upon me and I strive to repel her, but I am so weakened that I cannot. For a remedy, I have run about from place to place, but could get no help. At length, I went to an old friar who was considered an extraordinary fellow, thinking to have help at his hands; but I didn't get a bit of help from him, except that for a remedy he told me to pray to God—whom, I am sure, I had already wearied with my tedious prayers long before. Then I went to an old woman,' said the priest, 'who was said to be a cunning witch; and she told me that the next morning, about the dawning of the day, I should urinate and immediately cover the chamber pot, or stop it with my right <term>nether-stock</term><note>A stocking or hose for the lower leg.</note>, and before night the witch would come to visit me. And although,' he said, 'respect for my holy orders somewhat terrified me from following her advice, my many necessities, and especially my pains, moved me to try her words. And by the Mass,' said the priest, 'her words turned out to be exactly true. For a witch came to my house...'"

### CHAPTER 11.

*That the Incubus is a natural disease: with remedies for the same; as well as Magical cures expressed here.*

<margin>What the Incubus is, and who are most troubled by it.</margin>
But in truth, this *Incubus* <note>original: Incubus; a male demon believed to have sexual intercourse with sleeping women; here used to describe sleep paralysis</note> is a bodily disease (as has been said), although it extends to the troubling of the mind. It is called by some "the Mare," and it oppresses many in their sleep so severely that they are unable to call for help or move themselves under the burden of that heavy humor <note>In ancient medicine, "humors" were bodily fluids believed to control health and temperament.</note>. This is engendered by a thick vapor proceeding from indigestion and rawness in the stomach; as this vapor rises into the head, it oppresses the brain, so much so that many are weakened by it, being haunted by it nightly. Those most troubled with this disease are those who, being subject to it, lie flat on their backs; therefore, to turn and lie on one's side is an immediate remedy. Likewise, if anyone hears the groaning of the person and speaks to them so as to wake them, they are immediately relieved. However, there are "Magical" cures for it; for example:

*St. George, St. George, our Lady's knight,*
*He walked by day, and so he did by night:*
*Until such time as he her found,*
*He her beat, and he her bound,*
*Until her truth she to him pledged,*
*He would not come to her that night.*

In this charm, "St. George, our Lady’s knight" was named three times. Also: Hang a stone over the afflicted person’s bed—a stone that naturally has such a hole in it that a string may be passed through it—and so let it be hung over the diseased or bewitched person, whether it be man, woman, or horse.

<margin>Malleus Maleficarum, part 2, question 2, chapter 1, column 2. Leonhart Fuchs on the method of curing.</margin>
Also, you shall read in the *Malleus Maleficarum* <note>original: M. Malefic.; a famous 15th-century treatise on the prosecution of witches</note> that Excommunication is very notable, and better than any charm for this purpose. There are also other verses and charms devised for this disease, which is the common excuse for the ignorance of bad physicians. But Leonhart Fuchs <note>original: Leonard Euchsius; a renowned German physician and botanist</note>, in his first book and 13th chapter, not only describes this disease and its causes but also sets down very learnedly the cure for it, to the utter confusion of the "witch-mongers'" folly in this matter. Hyperius <note>Andreas Hyperius, a Flemish Protestant theologian.</note>, being much bewitched and blinded in this matter of witchcraft, hovers around the interpretation of Genesis chapter 6, from which the opinion of the *Incubus* and *Succubus* <note>A female demon believed to have sexual intercourse with sleeping men.</note> is forced. "The sons of God saw the daughters of men, that they were beautiful; and they took wives for themselves of all whom they chose, etc." <note>original: Viderunt filii Dei filias hominum, quod elegantes essent, acceperunt filii in uxores ex omnibus, quas elegerant, &c.</note> He seems to maintain this, even though no firm reason or proof can be brought out of Scripture regarding the evil spirits *Incubus* and *Succubus*, using these very words: "These things are spoken of as probabilities, since we are destitute of the support of the Scriptures in this matter." <note>original: Hæ ut probabilia dicta sunt, quandoquidem Scripturarum præsidio hac in causa destituimur.</note> It is as if he were to say: "Take this as being probably true according to human reason, because we lack Scriptures to maintain the validity of the cause."

<margin>Tertullian in the book 'On the Apparel of Women.' Sulpitius Severus in the 'Abridgment of Sacred History.'</margin>
Tertullian and Sulpitius Severus interpret "the sons of God" <note>original: Filios Dei</note> in that passage to be angels or evil spirits who became enamored with the beauty of those young women, and finally fathered giants by them. This is thoroughly disproved by John Chrysostom <note>An influential Early Church Father</note> in his 22nd Homily on Genesis, but especially by the context of the text itself.

### BOOK V.

### CHAP. I.

*Of Transformations: ridiculous examples brought by the adversaries to confirm their foolish doctrine.*

<margin>7. Bodin, book 2, *On the Demonomania of Sorcerers*, chapter 6 <note>original: "Bod. lib. 2. de damon. cap. 6." refers to Jean Bodin's 1580 work *De la démonomanie des sorciers*</note>.</margin>
<image-desc>Large decorative initial capital 'N' at the beginning of the paragraph.</image-desc>Now, so that I may use the very absurdities contained in their own authors—even in their principal doctors and latest writers—to confound those who maintain the transformations of witches, I will show you some of the material which Bodin <note>Jean Bodin was a famous French jurist and a prominent believer in the reality of witchcraft</note> (their chief champion of this age) has gathered out of the *Malleus Maleficarum* <note>original: "M. Mal.", a famous 15th-century manual on hunting witches</note> and others. With this, he labors to establish this impossible, incredible, and supernatural—or rather, unnatural—doctrine of transformation.

<margin>7. Bodin abuses Scripture to prove a lie. The private parts then first breaking out <note>original Latin: "Pudenda tunc primum erumpentibus"</note>.</margin>
First, concerning the Devil, Bodin says that he most properly and commonly transforms himself into a goat, confirming that opinion by citing the 33rd and 34th chapters of Isaiah <note>original: "Esay"</note>, where there is not a single word suggesting any such thing. However, he sometimes allows the Devil the shape of a "blackmoor" <note>A common historical term for people of North African or Sub-Saharan African descent; used here as a demonic trope</note>, and, as he says, the Devil used to appear to Maud Cruse, Kate Darey, and Joan Harviller. But I wonder whether the Devil creates himself when he appears in the likeness of a man, or whether God creates him when the Devil wishes it. As for witches, he says they specifically transform themselves into wolves, and transform those whom they bewitch into asses—though elsewhere he contradicts himself on this. But although he affirms that it can naturally happen for a girl to become a boy, and for any female to be turned into a male, yet he says this has no connection to "lycanthropy" <note>the mythical transformation of a person into a wolf</note>. In the case of lycanthropy, he says that men are wholly transformed, and he cites infinite examples of this. First, he tells of one Gilles Garnier <note>original: "Garner"</note> who, in the shape of a wolf, killed a girl of twelve years old, ate up her arms and legs, and carried the rest home to his wife. Also, he claims that Pierre Burgot <note>original: "Peter Burget"</note> and Michel Verdun <note>original: "Michael Worden"</note>, having turned themselves into wolves with an ointment, killed and eventually ate an infinite number of people.

<margin>7. Weyer, book 6, *On the Deceptions of Demons*, chapter 12 <note>original: "Wier. lib. 6. de mag. cap. 12." refers to Johann Weyer's *De praestigiis daemonum*</note>.</margin>
Johann Weyer <note>original: "Wiewers", a Dutch physician and early critic of the witch trials</note> sufficiently refutes these stories. But until you read that, consider whether Pierre could eat raw flesh without falling ill <note>original: "surfeiting"</note>, especially the flesh of his own kind. Also, he tells of an arrow shot into a wolf's thigh; the wolf later returned to his human shape and was found in bed with the arrow still in his thigh—which the archer who shot it recognized clearly. Also, that another man, while in the form of a wolf, had his wolf paws cut off, and in a moment he became a man without hands or feet.

<margin>7. Bodin is a glutton for lies <note>original Latin: "mendaciorum helluo"</note>.</margin>
He even accuses one of the highest princes in Christendom, in recent days, of being one of these witches. He claims the prince could turn himself into a wolf whenever he pleased, and asserts that he was spied upon and often seen performing this villainy because he wanted to be considered the King of all Witches. He says that this transformation is most common in Greece and throughout all Asia, as foreign merchants have reported to him. For in the year of our Lord 1542, when Sultan Suleiman <note>original: "Solimon"</note> reigned, there was such a powerful multitude of these kinds of wolves in Constantinople that the Emperor drove 150 of them together into one flock, which then departed from the city in the sight of all the people.

<margin>That the devils correspond to the unclean beasts.</margin>
28. But more specifically, the opinion of the ancients is that, according to the division of the clean and unclean beasts in the Law given to Moses, the shapes of devils are arranged in the Infernal Kingdom. Thus, the most perverse and powerful among the devils represent the most ugly and mischievous among the animals, according to the following division: for instance, such devils as **Astaroth**, **Lucifer**, **Bardon**, and **Pownok**, who incline men and incite them to pride and presumption, take the shapes of *horses*, *lions*, *tigers*, and *wolves*. Those who incite men to *lust* and *covetousness* take the forms of *pigs*, *serpents*, and other filthy reptiles or envious beasts, such as *dogs*, *cats*, *vultures*, *snakes*, etc. Those who incline men toward *murder* have the shapes of every *bird* and *beast* of prey. Those who answer human questions regarding *philosophy* or *religion* have more tolerable shapes, almost human, but with crooked noses, like *mermaids* or *satyrs*. And regarding all the rest, it should be noted that because no single lust or vice rules without being mixed with others in evil spirits, they do not have the distinct shape of one single beast; rather, they are compounded into monsters, with serpent-tails, four eyes, many feet and horns, etc.

<margin>The shapes of damned souls.</margin>
29. And as these are the general shapes of devils, the specific shapes of damned souls are to be considered in the same manner as the rest, with only this difference: they are more prone to transform themselves and vary their appearances. However, for the most part, damned souls retain the human shape in a magical manner, so that the greatest part of that countless number appear in their former shapes—especially when they appear in sleep to their surviving acquaintances. Their appearances are very dismal and melancholy, like the ghosts of the "astral source" <note>This refers to the "astral body," a concept in Western esotericism representing a layer of the soul between the physical and the spiritual</note>.

<margin>Their times and seasons.</margin>
30. Now, to speak of the times and seasons of their appearance. The more skilled magicians align their times with astrological hours, especially those of *Saturn*, *the Moon* <note>original: "Luna"</note>, and *Venus*, during the Moon's increase, and either at midnight or twelve o'clock at noon. In these hours, they also prepare their garments, caps, candlesticks, figures, metal plates <note>original: "Lamins"</note>, pentacles, and circles for conjuration. As for the times regarding their "infernal courses," the fittest times are when they rise up in "the Wrath" or when they sink into "the Despair," which is a mystery known only to the learned conjurers of Europe.

<margin>Their places of appearance.</margin>
31. Regarding this physical world, they can most easily appear in solitary places after the sun has set; for they are naturally enemies of the sun, because it stands as a symbol <note>original: "type"</note> of the Mediator <note>meaning Jesus Christ</note>, or the Heart and Center which they lost utterly in their fall. Now they are destitute of it, like a wheel without an axle. Indeed, the lack of this center is the chief cause of all their torment and the cause of the "gnawing worm" <note>A biblical reference to eternal remorse or the pangs of conscience</note> that rises within them when they reflect on their irrevocable sentence and irrecoverable loss.

<margin>When tempests reign.</margin>
32. Among magicians, times of hail, snow, wind, tempest, and lightning are considered easy times for conjuring. They say that such ceremonies will prove very effective if a conjurer begins his exorcisms in the hour and day of the *Moon* <note>original: "Luna"</note>, in the middle of a furious storm of lightning, rain, and thunder, in a low vault or cellar that is enclosed and secluded. Also, when the wind blows high without rain, they say the devils are nearer to the kingdom of this world and may be solicited or raised with great ease at such a season. This is because they delight in all extremities of weather, being themselves the primary cause of the disorder of elements <note>original: "properties"</note> in the Kingdom of Nature.

<margin>According to the geography of regions.</margin>
33. However, they can appear more easily in some countries than in others, depending on the constellations. They delight much in the extremities of the two poles toward *Lapland*, *Novaya Zemlya* <note>original: "Nova Zembla"</note>, *Greenland*, and *Tartary*; and in the South toward the islands scattered about the borders of the *Unknown Land* <note>original: "Terra Incognita"</note>. They are also easily summoned on the shore among high rocks and precipices, or in

62 BOOK II. A Discourse concerning Infernal Spirits.

They inhabit deserts and wildernesses far from towns or people. It is also said that they pay great attention to the movement of the tides when they appear to those who summon them in coastal <note>original: "Maritime"</note> or seafaring <note>original: "Plagiary" - likely referring to regions near the shore or areas frequented by sea-raiders</note> places.

<margin>Their Ranks and Orders.</margin>
34. Regarding their ranks or orders, it is difficult to discover the truth because we do not know for certain which orders of angels fell from heaven. Most people believe that many fell from every order. However, those who better understand the nature of the heavenly hierarchies have proved that no one can fall from a specific rank unless the entire rank follows. Therefore, it is more reasonable to judge that before the devils fell, the hierarchy of heaven consisted of three ranks or orders: namely, the Order of **Uriel**, the Order of **Michael**, and the Order of **Lucifer**. The Order of **Lucifer** is now entirely in *Hell*. The order under **Michael** is the dominion of *Heaven*. The last, which belongs to **Uriel**, exists more within the dominion of the "third principle" of the stars, governing the *planets* and their various influences.

<margin>In three distinctions.</margin>
35. Consequently, the catalog mentioned earlier—transcribed by the author of this *Discovery* <note>The author likely refers to Reginald Scot's famous 1584 skeptical work, "The Discoverie of Witchcraft," which listed various demonic hierarchies</note>—is entirely made up and fictitious. It falsely claims that these many types of devils rule over various legions within different ranks, such as *Seraphim*, *Powers*, *Thrones*, *Dominations*, *Cherubim*, and so on. In reality, the entire kingdom of Hell consists of only one hierarchy: that of **Lucifer** and his legions, who were reduced by their own defiance into the mournful <note>original: "Lacrymable"</note> state in which they now remain, and shall remain forever. When seriously considered, this doctrine proves that the attempts of conjurers and magicians are completely useless, and their forms of invocation are nothing but vanity and lies.

<margin>Their numbers.</margin>
36. We can consider their numbers more closely if we remember that they consist of only one hierarchy and no more. However, we must admit there is no set limit to their count, because their nature allows them to grow <note>original: "Germinate"</note> and multiply as they please, contracting or expanding themselves according to the power of their imaginations. Yet, even if this is granted, there is still a fixed number of original devils. While the number of damned souls is infinite and beyond measure, they do not require more physical space because of their numbers; they are capable of packing a thousand legions into the body <note>original: "carcass"</note> of a single man. Authors' opinions vary: some believe their numbers equal the *stars*, while others compare them to the *sands on the seashore*. Whatever the case, it is certain they are innumerable to the human mind.

<margin>Their natures and properties.</margin>
37. We must now consider their natures as they relate to the source or quality of Hell. They never rest, nor are they affected by the length or shortness of time, or the cycle of day and night. The wickedness they committed in this life is their constant torment, which magically gnaws and eats away at them, perpetually boiling up within. The only relief <note>original: "refrigeration"</note> they find is during those moments when the peak of their wickedness drives them to blaspheme God and imagine themselves rising above heaven and goodness; these distorted fantasies serve as a kind of sport or pastime for them, lasting for about forty minutes in our time. But this gives them no real advantage; <margin>Their torments.</margin> instead, it adds to their suffering, for pain is felt more intensely after a break. Agony would not truly be agony if there were no respite or pause. This is because opposites are more clearly seen when placed side by side <note>original: "Nam contraria juxta se posita majus eluceſcunt"</note>. Yet, their torments vary greatly; the suffering of one, compared to another, is like a mere dream or fantasy. I am referring here to the damned souls, and not the devils; for the pain and sorrow of the devils is many thousands of degrees greater than that of the lost souls, according to nature and reason. He who falls from the greatest height suffers the most, and the best things, once corrupted, become the worst <note>original: "optima corrupta sunt peſſima"</note>.

It also explores the psychology of demonic torment, explaining that spirits experience pain through their own past sins and find only brief, illusory relief through blasphemy.</summary>

# Of Infernal Spirits. Devils and Spirits. CHAPTER V.

<margin>The variety of torments.</margin>
38. But astonishing <note>original: "wonderful," meaning awe-inspiring or terrible</note> and many-sided are the torments which all members of the infernal troops suffer, according to the various lusts they lived in while they were on the earth. The cruel murderers who died in the boiling source of blood and envy suffer the greatest torment; they are continually murdering in their imaginations. Like men in a dream, they seek to do what the lack of a physical body <note>original: "Organ"</note> will not allow. For according to the wisest writers on this subject, this is the torment and misery of all the damned: *that they are continually wishing and wanting; and in these persistent desires <note>original: "wouldings"</note>, they generate ideas and representations, which are the images <note>original: "species"</note> of their continual aggravations and deceiving fantasies.*

<margin>The nature of their suffering.</margin>
39. Those who were buried in lust and gluttony, drunkenness and lewdness, are also in miserable torments, though much lesser than the first group. They are continually imagining their former pleasures in the imagination <note>original: "Magia," referring here to the creative or magical power of the soul's mind</note> as if in a dream, which torments them cruelly when they "wake." They are often hanging, stabbing, and mangling themselves for love, and perpetually sinking down into sorrow and despair—especially if they died while in love or at the height of their planetary passions <note>original: "Astral affections," referring to emotions believed to be governed by the stars</note>, leaving behind a heap of desires and lusts which are the only cause of all their torment. We may well compare their torments to the passions of depressed <note>original: "Melancholy"</note> people, or those who pine away for the love of women in deserts, woods, and mountains. Such troubles of the mind are absolutely the greatest and heaviest that the conditions of this world can produce—I mean the disturbances of the mind in general.

<margin>Their torment in the source of anger.</margin>
40. Such souls in whom the boiling source of anger and rage lived, if they die unrepentant <note>original: "unmortified"</note>, also enter into a most dreadful kind of torment. This torment continually arises like a biting worm and hungry fire to double and pile up the excess of despair upon them, especially if they dominated others through anger while they lived in this world. Also, those who lived in pride and envy are forever seeking to pull God from His throne, reaching high in their imaginations like men who dream. They still seek the Kingdom of Heaven only to insult it and boast within it; but the nature of heaven is utterly hidden <note>original: "occult"</note> and foreign to them. Consequently, they can never find, taste, hear, nor see it, even though it exists throughout their own specific environment. This adds perpetually to their misery and arises at times with horrible pangs and gnawings, like the annoying and frustrating pains and aches of a human body—the kind that cease for a while and then begin to shoot and ache at intervals <note>original: "by intercourse"</note>, such as gout, toothaches, headaches, convulsions, stomach cramps <note>original: "Gripings"</note>, and kidney stones <note>original: "the Stone"</note>.

<margin>In all the five senses.</margin>
41. Thus their torments are briefly described, but in truth, the human mind is not able to fully describe their cruel miseries and the continual pangs they brought upon themselves; for every faculty is sufficiently plagued. The sense of hearing is disturbed with harsh and rugged sounds which are naturally repugnant to that organ, just as rough and scraping sounds in the physical world offend the ears and set the teeth on edge by affecting their tender fibers. Their sight is likewise cruelly offended and frightened with monstrous appearances and ideas represented continually to their imaginations. And there is no loathsome taste in the kingdoms of this world—whether animal, vegetable, or mineral—which they are ever free from, being continually pestered and suffocated with the filthy fumes and smokes of hellish fruits, such as sulfurous stinks and abominations.

<margin>By their acquaintance on earth.</margin>
42. Neither are the other senses of touch and smell left behind in sharing these same torments, which their own sins perpetually excite and create for them. Besides this, they are forever vexing one another. If any are in the same misery with those they knew here on earth, the very magical knowledge, perception, or remembrance of that acquaintance afflicts and wastes away <note>original: "macerate"</note> their souls and all their senses beyond what can be spoken or imagined.
